Abstract
This dissertation investigates the shaping and manifestation of power notions and dynamics among the
Andoque, an Indigenous people of Northwest Amazonia, Colombia, through three types of
entanglements: within the Indigenous population, with nonhuman entities in the Andoque territory, and
with non-Indigenous agents. My analysis is informed by myths, oral histories, and biographical
trajectories collected during ethnographic fieldwork in the Andoque ancestral territory between April
2018 and June 2019 and from interviews with Andoque migrants in Leticia, as well as observations of
economic transactions, political assemblies, and other social interactions. Building on anthropological
literature on the continuity between human and nonhuman relations in animism/perspectivism and on
familiarization and mastery as asymmetrical relational frameworks in Amazonia, I explore power
beyond the realm of leadership and the public political arena, and define it within a context-transcending
framework of exchange. I demonstrate that power is manifested in the capacity of both human and
nonhuman agents to transform their relationships from symmetrical exchanges of bodies, vital
principles, material goods, and action into asymmetrical ones that benefit their efforts to produce
persons, while countering adversarial imbalances. Power stems from and facilitates the conversion of
potentially harmful affinal relatives into safer, more benevolent consanguineal kin, and manifests in the
preconditions of exchange: the capacity to refuse or suspend exchange and to participate in the
transaction as its agent, rather than the transacted object.
Spanning the fields of politics, economy, kinship, myth and ritual, my analysis can be narrowed into
exchanges within three conceptual domains with largely overlapping distinctions: ontological, kinship,
and spatial. In the ontological domain, exchanges are rooted in the animist principle of shared
interiority among beings with distinct bodily forms. This shared interiority leads to a default reciprocal
homosubstitution of persons of one kind for those of another. Meanwhile, capable individuals engage in
ontological manipulations to create asymmetry with nonhumans by enforcing heterosubstitutive
exchange, in which they compensate for game with vegetal substances, or exploiting homosubstitution
in sorcery assaults, transforming human victims into prey. Ontological manipulation is closely related to
graded agency, which becomes apparent in kinship practices and imagery. Here, despite the
Andoque’s cognatic kinship principles, their strong clan identities foster attempts at asymmetry in interclan relations. Agnatic descent is associated with higher agency over non-agnatic kin, non-kin, and
nonhumans. In humans, diminished agency resembles states of domination, while in nonhumans, it can

11

parallel—but does not equate to—the objectification seen in naturalism. Finally, power is anchored in
spatial perceptions. The Andoque consider themselves as living at the center of a world axed upon the
river’s course, resulting in the division of surrounding space into upriver, closer to the river source, and
downriver, nearer to the river mouth. Using procedures of familiarization, appropriation, and
encompassment, those living at the center draw upon forces, elements, and mythical figures associated
with the river source for their survival and prosperity amid rival human and nonhuman centers. A
similar pursuit of encompassment characterizes the center’s relationship with the river mouth—an
affinal realm representing non-Indigenous people. This spatial framework also encapsulates historical
trajectories of slavery, extractivism, and, ultimately, efforts at preservation, where asymmetrical
exchanges between the Andoque and non-Indigenous agents redefine power dynamics between the
former and nonhuman beings.
My findings reveal that the uncertainty in exchange with human and nonhuman beings renders relational
asymmetries inherently precarious. The knowledge required to establish and sustain these imbalances is
a critical and contested resource, made even scarcer by a genocide in the early twentieth century that
eradicated many sages and oral traditions. Furthermore, Andoque members often express their concerns
about their vulnerability within power dynamics involving non-Indigenous agents, nonhuman entities,
and even members of their own group. Therefore, considering the context of near demographic collapse,
increasing assimilation into Colombian society, and a continuous precarious position in the regional
economy, this research examines power within a society experiencing an enduring crisis of power.
My research contributes to the broader debate on power within the social sciences and political thought
by highlighting the continuum between social interactions among humans and those involving
nonhumans in societies where nonhumans are recognized as agents. Concurrently, I push forward the
research into the human-nonhuman relational continuum within Amazonian animism and perspectivism,
establishing power as both the outcome of and the instrument for an enchainment of symmetrical and
predominantly asymmetrical relationships, and revealing the interplay between power dynamics of
human-nonhuman relations and those between Indigenous and non-Indigenous agents. My approach
reveals the power dynamics permeating relationships in an Amazonian sub-region characterized by
agnatic ideology—namely, the Caquetá-Putumayo—thereby elucidating the social and ontological
transformations in the recent history of its Indigenous inhabitants. My analysis thus challenges the

12

perception of egalitarianism often associated with Indigenous Amazonia, allowing for a comparison of
the animist configurations in the Caquetá-Putumayo with other societies within this region and beyond.

Resumé
Cette thèse porte sur les conceptions et la dynamique du pouvoir parmi les Andoque, un peuple
autochtone du nord-ouest de l’Amazonie en Colombie, interrogeant comment celles-ci sont façonnées et
se manifestent à travers trois types d’imbrication : au sein de la population autochtone, avec les entités
non humaines du territoire, et avec les agents non-autochtones. Notre analyse s’appuie sur des mythes,
des histoires orales et des trajectoires biographiques recueillies lors d’une enquête de terrain dans le
territoire ancestral andoque et lors d’entretiens avec des migrants andoque à Leticia, ainsi que sur des
observations de transactions économiques, d’assemblées politiques et d’autres interactions sociales. En
nous fondant sur la littérature anthropologique portant sur la continuité entre les relations humaines et
non humaines dans l’animisme/perspectivisme et sur la familiarisation et la maîtrise en tant que modes
asymétriques de socialité en Amazonie, nous définissons le pouvoir dans un cadre d’échange et
l’étudions au-delà du domaine du leadership et de l’arène politique publique. Nous démontrons que le
pouvoir se manifeste dans la capacité des agents humains et non humains à transformer des relations
symétriques d’échanges de corps, de principes vitaux, de biens matériels et d’actions en relations
asymétriques qui profitent à leurs efforts pour produire des personnes, tout en contrebalançant les
déséquilibres adverses. Le pouvoir provient de et facilite la transformation de parents affins
potentiellement dangereux en parents consanguins plus bienveillants, et se manifeste dans les
préconditions de l’échange : la capacité de refuser ou de suspendre l’échange et de participer à la
transaction en tant qu’agent, plutôt qu’objet échangé.
Couvrant les domaines de la politique, de l’économie, de la parenté, du mythe et du rituel, notres analyse
peut être distillée à des échanges au sein de trois domaines conceptuels avec des distinctions largement
enchevêtrées : ontologique, de parenté et spatial. Dans le domaine ontologique, les échanges sont
enracinés dans le principe animiste d’une intériorité partagée entre des êtres aux formes corporelles
distinctes. Cette intériorité partagée conduit à une homosubstitution réciproque par défaut de personnes
d’un type pour celles d’un autre. En revanche, les individus capables se livrent à des manipulations
ontologiques pour créer une asymétrie avec les non-humains en imposant un échange hétérosubstitutif,
dans lequel ils compensent le gibier avec des substances végétales, ou en exploitant l’homosubstitution
dans les assauts de sorcellerie, transformant les victimes humaines en proie. La manipulation
ontologique est étroitement liée à l’agentivité graduée, qui devient apparente dans les pratiques et les
imageries de parenté. Dans ce contexte, malgré les principes de parenté cognatique des Andoque, leur
15

forte identification clanique favorise les tentatives d’asymétrie dans les relations entre les clans. La
descendance agnatique est associée à une plus grande agentivité en comparaison avec les parents non
agnatiques, les non-parents et les non-humains. Chez les humains, une agentivité diminuée ressemble à
des états de domination, tandis que chez les non-humains, elle peut être parallèle, mais ne pas équivaloir
à l’objectification du naturalisme. Enfin, le pouvoir est ancré dans les perceptions spatiales. Les
Andoque se considèrent comme les habitants du centre d’un monde orienté sur le cours du fleuve,
résultant dans la division de l’espace environnant en amont, plus proche de la source du fleuve, et en
aval, plus proche de l’embouchure du fleuve. En utilisant des procédures de familiarisation,
d’appropriation et d’englobement, ceux qui vivent au centre s’appuient sur des forces, des éléments et
des figures mythiques associés à la source du fleuve pour leur survie et leur prospérité parmi les centres
humains et non humains rivaux. L’englobement caractérise également la relation du centre avec
l’embouchure – un domaine affinal représentant les personnes non-autochtone. Ce cadre spatial
encapsule également les trajectoires historiques de l’esclavage, de l’extractivisme et de la préservation,
où les échanges asymétriques entre les Andoque et les agents non-autochtones redéfinissent les
dynamiques de pouvoir entre les premiers et les êtres non humains.
Nos données démontrent que l’incertitude dans l’échange avec les êtres humains et non humains rend les
asymétries relationnelles intrinsèquement précaires. La connaissance nécessaire pour établir et maintenir
ces déséquilibres est une ressource essentielle et disputée, rendue encore plus rare par un génocide au
début du vingtième siècle qui a éradiqué de nombreux sages et traditions orales. De plus, les Andoque
expriment souvent leurs inquiétudes quant à leur vulnérabilité au sein des dynamiques de pouvoir
impliquant des agents non-autochtones, des entités non humaines et même des membres de leur propre
groupe. Par conséquent, compte tenu du contexte de quasi-effondrement démographique, d’assimilation
croissante dans la société colombienne et d’une position régionale économique continuellement précaire,
cette recherche examine le pouvoir au sein d’une société connaissant une crise de pouvoir persistante.
Cette recherche contribue au débat sur le pouvoir dans les sciences sociales et la pensée politique en
soulignant la continuité entre les interactions sociales parmi les humains et celles impliquant des nonhumains dans les sociétés où ces derniers sont reconnus comme des agents. Simultanément, elle fait
progresser les études sur le continuum relationnel humain-non humain au sein de l’animisme et du
perspectivisme amazoniens, établissant le pouvoir à la fois comme le résultat et l’instrument pour un
enchaînement de relations symétriques et principalement asymétriques, et démontrant l’entrelacement

16

des dynamiques de pouvoir entre les humains et les non-humains, d’un côté, et celles entre les
autochtones et non-autochtones, de l’autre. Notre approche révèle les dynamiques de pouvoir qui
imprègnent les relations dans une sous-région amazonienne caractérisée par l'idéologie agnatique – à
savoir, le Caquetá-Putumayo – éclairant ainsi les transformations sociales et ontologiques dans l’histoire
récente de sa population autochtone. Notre analyse remet ainsi en question la perception de
l’égalitarisme souvent associée à l’Amazonie, permettant une comparaison des configurations animistes
dans le Caquetá-Putumayo avec d’autres sociétés de cette région et au-delà.

Un résumé détaillé de la thèse en français, incluant l’introduction complète et les sommaires des
chapitres, est disponible en annexe 6.

‫שמייצגים אוכלוסיות לא‪-‬ילידיות‪ .‬המסגרת המרחבית הזו אף תורמת להבנת התהליכים ההיסטוריים של עבדות‪,‬‬

‫אחרות באמזונס ובחלקים אחרים בעולם‪.‬‬

‫‪20‬‬

Resumen
Esta tesis investiga la formación y manifestación de nociones y dinámicas de poder entre los Andoque,
un pueblo indígena del noroeste de la Amazonia colombiana, centrándose en tres clases de relaciones: en
tres clases de imbricaciones: dentro de la población indígena, con entidades no humanas en el territorio
andoque y con actores no indígenas. Mi análisis está basado en mitos, historias orales y trayectorias
biográficas recopiladas durante un trabajo de campo etnográfico en el territorio ancestral andoque entre
abril de 2018 y junio de 2019. Igualmente, se basa en observaciones de transacciones económicas,
asambleas políticas y otras interacciones sociales durante este período, y entrevistas con migrantes
andoque en Leticia. Basándome en la literatura antropológica sobre la continuidad entre relaciones
humanas y no humanas en el animismo/perspectivismo y sobre la familiarización y la maestría como
marcos relacionales asimétricos en la Amazonia, exploro el poder más allá del ámbito del liderazgo y la
arena política pública, definiéndolo dentro un marco conceptual transaccional. Demuestro que el poder
se manifiesta en la capacidad de actores humanos y no humanos para transformar los intercambios
simétricos de cuerpos, principios vitales, bienes materiales y acción en en sus relaciones con otros, en
intercambios asimétricos beneficiosos para la fabricación de personas, así como contrarrestar
desequilibrios adversarios. El poder surge de y facilita la conversión de parientes afines potencialmente
dañinos en parientes consanguíneos más seguros y benevolentes, y se manifiesta en las precondiciones
del intercambio: la capacidad de rechazar o suspender el intercambio y participar en la transacción como
su agente, en lugar del objeto transaccionado.
Cubriendo los campos de la política, economía, parentesco, mito y ritual, mi análisis vuelve cada vez a
intercambios ocurriendo dentro de tres dominios conceptuales cuyas distinciones son, en gran medida,
superpuestas: ontológico, de parentesco y espacial. En el dominio ontológico, los intercambios están
arraigados en el principio animista de interioridad compartida entre seres con formas corporales
distintas. Esta interioridad compartida conduce por defecto a la práctica de homosustitución recíproca de
personas de una clase por las de otra. Mientras tanto, individuos capaces participan en manipulaciones
ontológicas para crear asimetría con no humanos por medio de intercambios heterosustitutivos, en los
que compensan las presas con sustancias vegetales, o explotando la homosustitución en ataques de
brujería, transformando a las víctimas humanas en presas. La manipulación ontológica está
estrechamente vinculada con la agentividad graduada, que se manifiesta en prácticas e nociones de
parentesco. Aquí, a pesar de los principios de parentesco cognático de los Andoque, sus fuertes

21

identidades clánicas fomentan intentos de asimetría en las relaciones inter-clánicas. La descendencia
agnática se asocia con una mayor agentividad sobre parientes no agnáticos, no parientes y no humanos.
En los humanos, la agentividad disminuida se asemeja a estados de dominación, mientras que en los no
humanos, puede paralelizarse, pero no equivaler, a la objetivación vista en el naturalismo. Finalmente, el
poder está anclado en percepciones espaciales. Los Andoque se consideran viviendo en el centro de un
mundo centrado en el curso del río, resultando en la división del espacio circundante en río arriba, hacia
la cabecera, y río abajo, hacia la desembocadura del río. Utilizando procedimientos de familiarización,
apropiación y englobamiento, aquellos que viven en el centro aprovechan las fuerzas, elementos y
figuras míticas asociadas con la cabecera del río para su supervivencia y prosperidad en medio de
centros humanos y no humanos rivales. Una búsqueda similar de englobamiento caracteriza las
relaciones del centro con la desembocadura del río, un reino afín que representa a las personas no
indígenas. Este marco espacial también engloba trayectorias históricas de esclavitud, extractivismo y, en
última instancia, proyectos de preservación, donde los intercambios asimétricos entre los Andoque y los
agentes no indígenas redefinen las dinámicas de poder entre los primeros y los seres no humanos.
Mis hallazgos revelan que la incertidumbre en el intercambio con seres humanos y no humanos hace que
las asimetrías relacionales sean inherentemente precarias. El conocimiento requerido para establecer y
sostener estos desequilibrios es un recurso crítico y disputado, hecho aún más escaso por un genocidio a
principios del siglo XX que erradicó a muchos sabios y tradiciones orales. Además, los miembros del
pueblo andoque a menudo expresan sus preocupaciones sobre su vulnerabilidad dentro de las dinámicas
de poder que involucran a agentes no indígenas, entidades no humanas e incluso miembros de su propio
grupo. Por lo tanto, considerando el contexto de una casi-exterminación demográfica, la creciente
asimilación en la sociedad colombiana y una posición precaria continua en la economía regional, esta
investigación examina el poder dentro de una sociedad que experimenta una crisis de poder duradera.
Mi investigación contribuye al debate más amplio sobre el poder dentro de las ciencias sociales y el
pensamiento político al resaltar el continuo entre interacciones sociales entre humanos y aquellas que
involucran a no humanos en sociedades donde los no humanos son reconocidos como agentes.
Concurrentemente, contribuyo al conocimiento antropológico sobre el continuo relacional humano-no
humano dentro del animismo y perspectivismo amazónicos, estableciendo el poder tanto como el
resultado de, como el instrumento para un encadenamiento de relaciones simétricas y
predominantemente asimétricas. Asimismo, demuestro la continuidad entre las dinámicas de poder de

22

las relaciones humano-no humano y aquellas entre agentes indígenas y no indígenas. Mi investigación
revela las dinámicas de poder que impregnan las relaciones en una subregión amazónica caracterizada
por la ideología agnática, a saber, el Caquetá-Putumayo, elucidando así las transformaciones sociales y
ontológicas en la historia reciente de sus poblaciones indígenas. Mi análisis desafía así la percepción de
igualitarismo a menudo asociada con la Amazonía indígena, permitiendo una comparación de las
configuraciones animistas en el Caquetá-Putumayo con otras sociedades dentro de esta región y más
allá.

A Note on Language
Throughout this dissertation, I underline Spanish words (e.g., secretario, poder), except for proper
names;
I italicize Andoque words (e.g., ɵpáha, pɵ’te), apart from proper names;
And I italicize scientific names of flora and fauna (e.g., Cecropia sciadophylla).
In addition, italics are (sparsely) used for emphasis.

In transcribing words in the Andoque language, I employ the conventions developed by Jon Landaburu
(in Andoque Andoque and Landaburu, Forthcoming), and which have undergone several changes since
his first analysis of this language (Landaburu 1979). The alphabet developed by Landaburu includes 12
consonants (b, d, f, h, k, m, n, p, r, s, t, and y, as well as ñ), and 15 vowels. These vowels include nine
simple vowels, pronounced as follows:
Front

Central

Back

Close

i

ʉ

u

Middle

e

ɨ

o

Open

a

ɵ

ɒ

Additionally, there are six nasal vowels. These include the nasalized versions of a, e, i, o, and ɒ (a̰, ḛ, ḭ,
̰o, and ̰ɒ), as well as n, representing the nasalized version of the vowels ʉ, ɨ, and ɵ.
An apostrophe (’) represents glottal stop, which can follow all vowels.
The Andoque language is tonal. Vowels can carry both tones that are proper to the specific word in
which they appear, and mechanic tones, depending on the lexical combination in which the word
appears. Proper tones are marked by one accent (e.g., á), while mechanic tones are marked by two
accents (e.g., a̋).

38

Glossary (Terms in Local Spanish)
Ambíl. A term referring both to tobacco paste (yʉbʉ) and tobacco juice (yʉbʉdíe). Both
substances are obtained by mixing cooked tobacco leaves with different amounts of vegetal salt.
Cabildo. A modern Indigenous council elected by reserve members to mediate relations with the
State and other external institutions. The Andoque have two such councils, for each Indigenous reserve,
each one including a governor, a secretary, a treasurer, and a prosecutor.
Cacique. A maloquero and traditional leader (captain) above clan level.
Caguana. A non-fermented beverage, made with starch from bitter manioc boiled with water,
often mixed with different fruits.
Casabe. Flatbread prepared from bitter manioc.
Fariña. Toasted crumbs of bitter manioc mash.
Mambe. Coca powder, prepared from toasted and pulverized coca leaves combined with ashes of
yarumo leaves (Cecropia sciadophylla).
Mambeadero. The space at a maloca, a house, or a shack, where yarumo leaves are burned and
where coca powder (mambe) is prepared and consumed, usually during the afternoon and evening hours.
It is the main male forum for socialization. A participant is called mambeador (plural: mambeadores).
Maloca. A residential and ceremonial house, with political and economic functions that were
more pronounced before the rubber genocide. Headed by a maloquero, or captain.
Manguaré. A pair of monoxil drums, stationed at some malocas and serving for communication
and rhythm in ceremonial dances.
Manicuera. A non-fermented beverage from grated tubers of a poisonous variety of manioc.
Tipití. A tubular-like press woven from fibrous materials, used to remove the toxic cyanidecontaining juice from grated bitter manioc pulp.

These words are not underlined throughout the dissertation.

Introduction
It is thanks to the dead fish leaving the Araracuara sector that living people can enter it. After the
government-owned Satena airline company ceased operating flights to and from this village on the
Middle Caquetá River, the weekly cargo flights of merchants arriving empty from San José del Guaviare
in search of frozen fish to satiate the appetite of the citizens of Bogotá have remained the only means to
travel there from this town, which connects the Colombian Amazon to the Andean cordillera by land. It
was on one of these flights that I first landed in Araracuara one April morning in 2018, a peculiar
addition to an already motley ensemble: two Colombian workers of the National Natural Parks agency, a
Spanish missionary, a German tourist, a British employee of a human rights organization, and several
Murui-Muina residents of Bogotá visiting their home communities from which they had fled due to
threats posed by armed dissident groups. As the soldiers inspected my passport, wondering aloud what
could have brought an Israeli to Araracuara, and I inspected the Indigenous crowd gathering at a
distance to welcome the new arrivals, the senior of the two National Natural Parks workers (Parques
Nacionales Naturales; hereafter, Parques), having overheard my intention to conduct ethnographic
fieldwork among the Andoque people, cynically wished me well, saying: “They are a very hostile
bunch, they have this reputation of always refusing everything and not collaborating with anyone; all
they think about is money. Do you know they even used to mine gold?”
Having been greeted and picked up by my contacts from the Andoque Atta Ant Clan, I noted to myself
that my new hosts were not as horrible as they were depicted. However, two days later, I witnessed the
hostility to which she referred directed against her junior colleague during an assembly at the maloca
(residential and ceremonial house) of Mario Andoke, of the Deer Clan. The junior representative
unsuccessfully attempted to reach joint practical decisions concerning the team, methodology, budget
for logistics, and timetable for a wo Attarkshop aimed at formulating a “cultural plan for territorial
management” that the Andoque had previously asked Parques to support. Several participants now
accused the agency of failing to provide the required support for their reserve’s territorial expansion as
agreed, while the neighboring Chiribiquete National Natural Park had doubled in size during that period.
While some tried in vain to convince Parques’ representative to try the coca powder that they had
prepared for the meeting, others vehemently criticized his organization, challenging Parques’ right to
intervene in the Andoque’s territorial management. Levy Andoke, a university-educated reserve
member, entrepreneur and regional politician residing in Bogotá, employed a complex legal jargon that

41

was largely incomprehensible to many among his kin and other Indigenous participants. He contended
that such plans assume that Indigenous people are “traditional Indians” who only want forest
preservation and oppose development out of ecological concerns, while disregarding their present-day
economic hardships. Most other Andoque participants were only willing to collaborate with Parques if
they were paid for preservation and demanded high wages to the elders, whose knowledge on the
territory and the maintenance of relationships with its nonhuman co-dwellers would contribute to
formulating the document. After declaring that Parques considered Indigenous people as allies, the
representative finally admitted that for his organization, preservation was the end, and Indigenous
people were the means. “The Whites only give rights to trees, not to people,”1 one participant
complained to me during a break. “They want us to live like the Indians of the Apaporis: naked,
barefoot, but happy, but we have needs!” said another, referring to Indigenous groups who epitomize
“pure Indians” for the Andoque and are considered the protégés of Parques and the non-governmental
organization Gaia Amazonas. The participants inflated the budget for logistics and insisted: “We have
needs; like Parques, an Andoque only works for money.” As a result, the meeting failed to achieve its
goals.
I, on the other hand, left the meeting in high spirits, having seized the opportunity to introduce myself to
the reserve members, particularly the elders and young leaders, and obtained their consent to stay with
them and carry out my research. My self-presentation was followed by those of the elders, who occupied
seats at the mambeadero—the space where coca powder is prepared and consumed in later hours of the
day—while other men were sitting on benches to their right and left, and female participants observed
from the rear of the maloca. Fisi (“Rock’s Edge”) of the Eagle Clan was the first to present himself,
referring to himself as the cacique (captain above the clan level), and was followed by the five clan
captains. After their presentations, a peculiar silence fell, as if everyone was waiting for someone else to
speak. “What about you, Milciades?” someone addressed Levy’s father sitting on a bench to the right of
the entrance. “What about me?” said Milciades, also known by his Indigenous name Tañe (“Stationary
Sun”). “I am not a captain, nor do I have a maloca anymore.” However, this did not prevent Tañe from
later telling me, when I commented on the impressiveness of Mario’s large maloca, that his own maloca
had been even bigger. Before returning to the discussion with the Parques representative, the participants
inquired about whom I planned to work with. I managed to evade the question for the moment by stating
The term “Whites” (blancos), as used by the Andoque, refers to all non-Amerindians. I often employ this term to designate
non-Indigenous people.
1

42

that I hoped to first get to know as many members as possible by staying for two weeks in the settlement
of each clan. The participants approved of this idea and decided on a timetable for my visits to each
clan. However, one elder discreetly approached me later, expressing that if I wished to work with him,
he would not agree to my working with any other elder. While slightly taken aback, I was nevertheless
glad to have survived my first community assembly.
Therefore, a mere two days into my fieldwork with the Andoque, it was impossible to overlook the
manifold tensions that pervaded this small Indigenous society. These tensions were everywhere: in the
strained interactions with representatives of the state and environmental organizations, which were
marked by the suspicious and combative position employed by the Andoque; the ongoing competition
for prestige and knowledge among elders; the noticeable disparity in access to external resources
between Levy and the other members—and by extension, Levy’s clan and other clans; the marginalized
role of women in such assemblies, in comparison to men, and, lastly, there existed an ingrained fear,
competition, or animosity towards animals and other nonhuman entities that inhabited the forest and
river—an underlying sentiment that I could not fully grasp at that moment, yet played a significant role
in shaping the backdrop for the other tensions.
This dissertation thus explores the question: How are notions of power constructed and negotiated, and
how do power dynamics play out in different entanglements 1) among the Andoque members, 2)
between them and the nonhuman co-dwellers of their territory, and 3) between them and non-Indigenous
agents? As I will demonstrate throughout this dissertation, power is manifested in the capacity of both
human and nonhuman agents to transform their relationships from symmetrical exchanges to
asymmetrical ones across various contexts—an endeavor that is grounded in Indigenous conceptions of
kinship and space. Power stems from and facilitates the conversion of potentially harmful affinal
relatives into safer, more benevolent consanguineal kin. It is deeply anchored in spatial perceptions that
interpret predatory dynamics within a cosmos axed along a river’s course, encompassing the river
source, the midstream, and the mouth. This spatial framework also encapsulates historical trajectories of
colonial trade, exploitation, and, ultimately, efforts at preservation, where asymmetrical exchanges
between the Andoque and non-Indigenous agents redefine power dynamics between the former and the
nonhuman entities of their environment.

43

The Andoque and their Territory
Official data sets the total population within the two Andoque reserves in June 2018 at 343 individuals
(Ministerio del interior 2020). This number includes, apart from Andoque reserve residents, also nonAndoque inhabitants and some Andoque emigrants living in other Indigenous reserves and Colombian
cities, primarily Bogotá and Leticia. A survey I conducted upon my arrival in April 2018 showed that
the Andoque population living in their ancestral territory numbered 176 individuals, with an estimated
83 Andoque individuals living outside the territory, and 92 non-Andoque individuals who are members
of the Andoque reserves. This non-Andoque population represents settlers and members of other
Indigenous peoples who married into the Andoque kinship network or live in their reserves as guest
residents. In general, the Andoque population is embedded in wider networks of alliance and
coexistence with members of other Indigenous and non-Indigenous people in the larger Araracuara
sector. They also maintain relations of exchange, which vary in intensity, with Andoque emigrants. This
research primarily focuses on the experience, perspectives, and memories of Andoque individuals living
on their ancestral territory. However, it occasionally touches upon the experiences of emigrants or the
non-Andoque spouses of Andoque individuals insofar as their experiences are relevant to the themes
discussed in this dissertation.
The Andoque are part of the larger cultural complex of the Indigenous peoples living in the CaquetáPutumayo interfluve and self-identifying as “People of the Center,” together with the Féénemɨna (or
Muinane), Bora, Miraña, Nonuya, Ocaina, and peoples speaking Murui-Muina dialects (Nɨpóde, Bue,
and Mɨnɨka), previously known as the Uitoto.2 Unlike these neighbors, whose languages divide into two
linguistic families, the Andoque speak an isolated language.3 The name Andoque is an exonym of
Murui-Muina origin (Adokɨ), meaning either “People of the Axe” (Thomas Griffiths, pers. comm.,
October 2021), or “People of Upriver” or “Mountain” (Landaburu 1979, 13 n.1; Echeverri 2022, 35 n.5).
The endonym Pɵɵ Síɵ́hɵ concords with the former interpretation, alluding to the stone axes that the
Andoque found in subterranean deposits in their territory and traded with neighboring peoples prior to
the arrival of non-Indigenous people with their metal tools. Throughout this dissertation, I will employ
the exonym as it is the name currently used by the members to refer to themselves while speaking
In this dissertation, I refer to individuals and groups of the Murui-Muina using the specific ethnonym provided by the cited
ethnographer or mentioned interlocutor. However, if they refer to these groups or themselves as Uitoto/Witoto/Huitoto, I
maintain this terminology in direct quotes or speech, while, in indirect speech and my own narrative, I use “Murui-Muina.”
3
Jolkesky (2016, 284–85) identifies a genetic relation between the Andoque and Urequena languages, but the latter, once
spoken along the Putumayo river, became extinct during the nineteenth century.
2

44

Spanish, which is the language most commonly used in both daily and political contexts, including the
surprising majority of mambeadero sessions and spaces for the ritual consumption of coca; “Andoque”
(or “Andoke”) is also the most common last name of Andoque members.
The Andoque ancestral territory encompasses the land south of Tapir River (Ḭtɵse, or the Caquetá),
extending from Spawning River (Ḭ ́’pá̰se, colloquially known as Monochoa River) in the west to Drawing
River (Hḭ’ḭse, also called Quinche River) in the east, and Green River (Pasḭse, also referred to as
Cahuinarí River) in the south. North to the Caquetá, it covers the area enclosed between Plantain Leaf
River (Kɒ́’kɒpuse) and Oropendola River (Kɒtise), located east to Otter River (Oédise, colloquially
known as Yarí River), and the area stretching between Salt River (Ñɒ’Kɒse) and the Caquetá. To ensure
clarity while respecting the significance of local nomenclature, I refer to minor rivers by the English
translations of their Andoque names, while for the main rivers—Caquetá, Yarí, and Cahuinarí—I use
their commonly known names.
The Andoque population currently inhabits two Indigenous reserves established on this territory: 1) the
Indigenous reserve Andoque de Aduche on the north bank of the Caquetá, which extends over an area of
188,466.17 hectares (after its expansion in December 2020; Resolution 033/1988, Accord 030/2004,
Accord 140/2020), and 2) the Andoque de Aduche “Special Management Zone” within the Predio
Putumayo pluri-ethnic Indigenous reserve, covering an area of approximately 211,180 hectares south to
the Caquetá and centered around Macaw River (Áduse)4 (Resolutions 030/1988 and 057/1989).

4

Commonly transcribed Aduche, this river gave its name to the reserve and the special management zone.

45

Figure 1. Map of the Andoque ancestral territory, Indigenous reserves, and national parks in the Middle Caquetá. Design:
Gadiel Levi

The climate and botanical indicators of the Andoque’s ancestral territory correspond to the definition of
humid tropical forest (Holdridge et al. 1971, 43). Annual precipitation ranges between 3000–4000 mm,
with a high percentage of rainfall during the rainy season between April and July, and the dry season
reaching its peak between December and February. Temperatures oscillate between 24–26°C, and the
relative humidity ranges between 85–90% (IDEAM 2010). The territory is situated approximately 150300 meters above sea level and consists of four major geomorphic units: the flood plain of the Caquetá
River, a white-water river; the flood plain of Amazonian-origin clear and black-water rivers, which
represent all the other streams and rivers in the Middle Caquetá; the tertiary sedimentary plain; and the
hard rock formations mainly consisting of plateaus of Paleozoic sandstone (Duivenvoorden and Lips
1993, 150). Each zone is home to distinctive soil types and plant communities—riparian vegetation and
palm swamp forest in the Caquetá alluvial plain; tall, high biomass terra firme forest dotted with
saltlicks and marsh and palm swamps in the tertiary sedimentary plain, and low, dense forest, caatinga,
and savanna vegetation on the sandstone plateau (Griffiths 1998, 25–26).

46

Like other People of the Center, the Andoque society consists of patrilineal clans. Currently, Andoque
members belong to eight clans—Eagle, Sun, Deer, Atta Ant, Beetle, Spix’s Guan, Mauritia, and
Anaconda—of which only the first five are considered viable, as the others include only women or
childless men. Before the enslavement, atrocities, and genocide committed by agents of the Peruvian
Amazon Rubber Company (or Casa Arana) in the early twentieth century, the Andoque population was
estimated at 10,000 individuals (Whiffen 1915, 59), and during our conversations Andoque elders
mentioned as many as 35 clans from that period.
Akin to neighboring People of the Center, kinship terminology among the Andoque presents similarities
with both the Eskimo and Hawaiian types (Karadimas 2000b; londoño Sulkin 2012, 160–67; Lucas
2019, 163–65). Like the Eskimo system, the Andoque distinguish between parents and their siblings but
not between patrilateral and matrilateral relatives. Additionally, like the Hawaiian system, they employ
different terms for real siblings and classificatory ones (cousins), although the terms for the latter
represent a variation on the terms for the former (e.g., ḭ́ ekó ’ɵɵ for a same-sex cousin, meaning “poor
sibling”). Typical of the Caquetá-Putumayo, Andoque kinship differs from the Dravidian type prevalent
throughout Lowland South America, which also entails absence of prescriptive marriage rules and
justifies their consideration as a semi-complex society that, on the surface level, contains only negative
marriage rules not to marry relatives. However, data shows a tendency to marry immediately beyond the
circle of incestuous relations and thus renew endogamous alliance after several generations (Gasché
1976; Karadimas 2000b; Lucas 2019, 158–63).
Residence is patrilocal, and a husband may pass a period of one year or more of bride service with his
wife’s family—an ideal which seldom materializes today in practice. Andoque members most
commonly live in nuclear family stilt-houses in settlements corresponding to patrilineal descent,
consisting of several brothers, their wives (who are, for the most part, non-Andoque), and children. Few
families live in malocas—longhouses that in the past sheltered entire lineages and adjunct personnel and
functioned as economic, political, and ceremonial units—and others use their malocas for cooking, coca
preparation in the mambeadero, and general activities throughout the day, while sleeping in adjacent
houses. The Andoque malocas host meetings with outsiders, as in the opening vignette, and they—or
small maloquitas sheltering men’s mambeadero spaces—serve as the social centers of the settlements in
which they are located. Andoque members reside in seven settlements (veredas) along the Caquetá and
Macaw Rivers, as well as in the large pluri-ethnic settlement of Araracuara in the Indigenous Reserve

47

Andoque de Aduche on the northern bank of the Caquetá River. Additionally, several Andoque families
live in the settler village of a corregimiento status, Puerto Santander, which faces Araracuara on the
southern bank of the Caquetá. This village is built on the Andoque ancestral territory but is not
considered part of the Predio Putumayo Indigenous Reserve.
The Andoque’s ritual and daily practices, cosmological principles, and ways of knowing and engaging
with plants and animals allow them to be largely classified as “animists” according to Philippe
Descola’s (2005) scheme of four modes of identification or ontological regimes. According to his
definition, members of animist collectives tend to perceive similarity between themselves and all or
most entities in their surroundings on the level of interiority (subjectivity, agency, mental and emotional
states, social norms, etc.), while recognizing dissimilarities on the plane of physicality (bodily forms and
principles, and external manifestations). This mode of identification is diametrically opposed to the
modern Western “naturalist” dispositions, which acknowledge similarities between all entities on the
level of physicality while denying them in the realm of interiority. There is no equivalent in the
Andoque language to the English (and Spanish) word “animal” to refer to all faunal beings except
humans. Bei is the general term for fish, which are also counted among the dú’u ño̰ḛ (“water persons”)
along with reptiles (such as arrau river turtles and caimans) and dolphins. Hiɵfo is the general term for
birds, while ḭsu classifies all terrestrial animals resembling humans in their habitat above ground. This
category includes both game animals such as the tapir and predators like the jaguar, as well as monkeys
(which are also doɨsua, “animals of above”), and the armadillo and land turtle (which are also yakafi
síɵ́hɵ, “armored ones”). It excludes terrestrial birds (ñó̰ʼifoa, “land birds”), serpents (na̰yuni síɵ́hɵ,
“biters”), and earthworms and other animals living within the earth (ñó̰ʼiño̰ḛ, “earth persons”).
Competing with humans for space and resources, the ḭsu category’s members, collectively, are the
subject of more elaborate conjectures concerning their cultural traits and social norms and institutions,
paralleling those of humans.
Similar to neighboring People of the Center, the Andoque’s livelihood is based on itinerant horticulture
and the cultivation of key crops such as bitter manioc, coca, and tobacco, hunting, and fishing. They
differ from other Indigenous Amazonians in consuming coca powder (a practice shared only with the
Tukanoan and Arawakan groups of the Vaupés-Lower Caquetá Rivers), in preparing tobacco as a paste
or liquid (unlike these and other groups in their vicinity), in their non-possession of native alcoholic
beverages and in their elaboration of the manicuera drink from a poisonous manioc variety (Echeverri

48

2022, 35–36). Another significant aspect of their livelihood is participation in the regional cash
economy. This participation involves occasional wage labor and primarily revolves around the sale of
local harvests and products to settlers and merchants. The Indigenous population of the region has
engaged in trade with non-Indigenous agents and their Indigenous middlemen from downriver (today’s
Brazil) since the seventeenth century (Pineda Camacho 1985) and participated in all the region’s
economic bonanzas, mostly led by non-Indigenous agents. The first documented economic boom in the
region was the slave trade, stretching from as early as the seventeenth century until it was superseded by
rubber tapping at the turn of the twentieth century. The Indigenous population first extracted rubber for
Colombian bosses and later under the Casa Arana, which employed genocidal practices until leaving the
region in the 1930s. This activity nonetheless continued in more humane conditions until it finally ended
in the 1990s. Its decline, beginning in the 1970s, precipitated Indigenous participation in the animal pelts
boom of the 1970s, commercial fishing from that decade onwards, cocaine production in the 1980s, and
gold mining in the 2000s. The surge of environmental projects starting in the 1990s, with the Andoque’s
involvement, represents another regional economic boom. This includes the carbon offset deals that took
off in the 2020s after the conclusion of my fieldwork.
The participation in the regional extraction economy is part of a larger process in recent decades,
whereby the Andoque have been drawing closer to national society. In 1938 and following Colombia’s
expulsion of Peruvian troops and rubber bosses, the state founded the Araracuara Penal Colony on the
north bank of the Caquetá, which served as a catalyst for the development of the settler village Puerto
Santander. During that decade, Catalan-Spanish Capuchin fathers founded boarding schools (also called
“orphanages”) in La Chorrera and La Pedrera, with a handful of Andoque youth attending the latter.
More substantial schooling began with the foundation of the missionary boarding school in Araracuara
in the 1970s (initially located in Puerto Santander), which prohibited the use of Indigenous languages.
Later, community schools with bilingual pedagogic principles were founded after the 1991 Constitution,
which recognized Colombia’s ethnic and cultural diversity. Despite the availability of bilingual
education, the combined effect of schooling, the continuous presence of settlers in Andoque territory,
and marriages with non-Andoque individuals resulted in the decline of their native language among
people under 50 years old and the rise of Spanish.

49

Previous Research on the Andoque and Their Neighbors
The People of the Center stand out within the Indigenous Amazonian landscape due to some of the
historical processes and ethnographic traits mentioned earlier. The first process is the rubber genocide.
Many Indigenous populations across Amazonia endured severe exploitation, forced labor, and brutal,
often deadly, abuses by rubber barons and tappers during the two rubber booms from the 1870s to the
1940s. However, the genocidal practices and reign of terror by Casa Arana in the Caquetá-Putumayo
sub-region were particularly destructive (Nugent 2018, 13), leading to the complete annihilation of
certain Indigenous groups, a drastic decline of all others, including the Andoque, and the displacement
of entire populations (Pineda Camacho 2000). Among the societies that reconstituted and revitalized
their cultures after the expulsion of the Peruvian agents and troops, there remains a pronounced notion
of disconnection from their pre-genocide histories (Echeverri 2010). Nevertheless, many among the
People of the Center, including the Andoque, continued to extract rubber in the aftermath of the
genocide, sometimes working with ex-employees of Casa Arana, whose descendants, such as the fish
merchants operating flights into the Araracuara sector, still have a considerable impact on the local
economies and societies of the Caquetá-Putumayo sub-region.
A second particularity concerns kinship. Contrary to the typical lack of unilineal features across
Amazonia or their non-combination with an ideological emphasis on descent principles (S. Hugh-Jones
1993, 95–96), the People of the Center’s patrilineal clan identities and patrilocal residence patterns
combine with an agnatic ideology, which is at odds with their simultaneous cognatic consideration of
both patrilateral and matrilateral relatives as kin. The agnatic emphasis is crucial for understanding the
particular form that slavery—a now recognized Indigenous Amazonian practice dating back to the preColumbian era and relevant also in extra-colonial contexts (Santos Granero 2009b)—took among the
People of the Center before it was superseded by rubber exploitation. While the main mechanism for
producing slaves in Indigenous Amazonia, for either domestic service or trade with non-Indigenous
agents, was the capture of individuals in raids (ibid),5 in the People of the Center’s history, it was the
very principle of agnatic descent that produced slaves—or, in local terms, “orphans.” These were
individuals who, during times of warfare and sweeping epidemics that exterminated entire populations,
found shelter in, or otherwise married into the malocas of their affinal or matrilateral kin. Not belonging
The Bolivian Yuqui case stands out in that, according to David Jabin’s (2016) reconstruction, the slaves of this society were
initially Siriono captives. Over time, these captives were replaced by distinct slave lineages—possibly the descendants of
Siriono captives—who were deliberately nurtured and raised in ways that perpetuated their status as Others.

5

50

to the clan of their new captain, they held a lower, servile status in relation to the latter and his clan
members and could eventually be traded as slaves for externally manufactured goods (Echeverri 2022;
Karadimas 2001; Lucas 2021).
Another characteristic of the People of the Center, closely linked with their agnatic ideology, is the
special status they accord to mythology and the esoteric dissemination of key myths within the
population. Unlike some Amazonian societies, such as the Achuar, where the knowledge of mythology
is in principle open to all yet elicits a general lack of interest or is downplayed in comparison with
ritualized expressive forms that nonetheless draw on it (Descola 1986, 239, 248), the People of the
Center hold mythical narratives in high regard and restrict their knowledge to their respective clans or to
other relatives who have proven their commitment and discretion. This is especially true for the origin
myths of clans, which serve, to a certain extent, as totemic principles for their respective members—who
draw on them for help and inspiration in moments of crisis—as well as any other story that recounts the
origin of specific practices, such as maloca construction, coca preparation, dance organization, and the
performance of cures and spells (Londoño Sulkin 2000, 329–30). These stories serve as a charter, not in
the plain Malinowskian (1926) sense of affirming or challenging territorial rights and claims to status
and ritual prerogatives, as in the origin stories of the Tukanoan groups of the Vaupés River (S. HughJones 2019b), but in Pierre-Yves Jacopin’s (2010) adaptation of the term to the broader mythology of
the region, channeling agency from one episode to another until the final episode delegates it to today’s
humanity—the narrator and listeners who are now in a position to reenact the mythical feats. Similar to
the Tuaknoan political economy of knowledge described by Stephen Hugh-Jones (2010; 2019b), among
the People of the Center’s competing patriclans, the power imbued in myths leads to their preferential
transmission within the clan.
The mythology, ritual life, and practices of the People of the Center inhabiting the Middle Caquetá have
been documented by scholars and explorers as early as the first half of the nineteenth century, with
scattered references and observations concerning the Andoque (Spix and Martius 1981 [1823]; Crévaux
1883; Robuchon 2010 [1907]; Whiffen 1915; Tessmann 1999; Preuss 1994). Research dedicated to the
Andoque began with the linguistic study carried out by Jon Landaburu (1979), who introduced the
younger anthropologists Roberto Pineda Camacho and Manuel Antonio Guzmán to the Andoque
community. Guzmán wrote his undergraduate thesis on their social organization and participation in the
rubber economy in the 1970s (Guzmán Gonzalez 1971), and Pineda collaborated with Landaburu in a

51

masterful anthology and commentary on Andoque mythology (Landaburu and Pineda 1981; Landaburu
and Pineda 1984), alongside publishing solitary works on the Andoque’s history, economy, adoption of
foreign technologies (primarily the metal axe), and the ways in which all these dimensions of their lived
world are represented in myth and ritual (Pineda Camacho 1975; 1979; 2014). Pineda and Landaburu’s
insightful and meticulous works on the Andoque, as well as Pineda’s later studies on the history of the
Casa Arana and the Caquetá sub-region (Pineda Camacho and Llanos 1982; Pineda Camacho 2000;
1985), remain significant bibliographical resources for understanding Andoque society, and I drew on
them extensively to complement my own data on cosmology and to gain a comparative perspective on
myth narration across historical contexts.
Landaburu and Pineda represent a generation of scholars who inaugurated scientific anthropological
research of the People of the Center between the 1960s and 1980s, alongside Jürg Gasché, Mireille
Guyot, Horacio Calle, and Jean Patrick Razon. They engaged in salvage documentation of their
mythologies and focused on these peoples’ impressive reconstruction process following the devastating
genocide and displacement in the early twentieth century. Later research during the 1990s among the
People of the Center emphasized a gap between the cannibalistic discourse of pre-genocide times and
contemporary sociality and politics of inter-ethnic collaboration, stressing Indigenous discourse that
portrayed humans as inherently superior, as opposed to nonhuman beings who embody immorality. This
research mainly concerned the Murui-Muina and Féénemɨna (Echeverri 1997; Griffiths 1998; Londoño
Sulkin 2000), although we may also consider Landaburu’s analysis of the Andoque’s post-genocide
mythological transformations and Monica Espinosa Arango’s (1995) insistence on an Andoque
communal striving for conviviality as part of this irenic trend in research. By contrast, the publications
of Dimitri Karadimas (2005), Oscar Iván García (2018) and María Luisa Lucas (2019) among the
Miraña, Murui-Muina, and Bora, respectively, bring to the fore the predatory cosmology and more
hierarchical tendencies still very much alive between captains and orphans, and record dynamics of
power that are essential for the present dissertation.
During the 2000s and 2010s, several anthropology students carried out short-term research among the
Andoque. Nelsa de la Hoz Melo (2005) discussed one ceremonial dance (Tu’si, or Multiplying Tree),
from the point of view of her hosts from the Sun Clan, while Levy Andoke Andoke (2011) from this
clan wrote his undergraduate thesis on the Andoque’s post-genocide recuperation process, primarily
focusing on the memory preserved by his own clan members and his mother (from the Eagle clan). Lena

52

Yanina Estrada Añokazi (2017) provided in her doctoral dissertation a panoramic outlook on the
Andoque people, including limited analysis of their perception of the territory, based, to a certain extent,
on interpretations by Murui-Muina interlocutors. Finally, Else Audren (2017) artfully captured in her
Master’s thesis the Andoque’s dilemmas, internal frictions and cosmological aspects surrounding gold
mining and the attempts to legalize it in 2016, despite the short duration of her fieldwork in that year.
These publications provided me with further ethnographic details, myth versions, and information on the
Andoque people in recent decades. However, none of them reflects a major ethnographic description of
the Andoque society in its full complexity by weaving together cosmology and history, kinship and
economy, ritual and politics—which is precisely what this dissertation attempts to achieve by studying
the evasive yet context-transcendent notion and dynamics of power.
Power in the Social Sciences and Political Thinking
Power is one of the most debated concepts in the social sciences and political thinking, with its
definitions varying across time, place, political convictions, and methodological concerns. To discuss
power in Indigenous Amazonia, it is necessary to provide a concise overview of several definitions,
distinctions, and points of contention that have shaped this ongoing debate, and which I discuss here in a
thematic order, rather than the chronological order of their emergence.
The first significant aspect is power’s observability and the sphere where it should be sought. In
conventional definitions, power must be seen and have discernible outcomes within specific contexts,
particularly decision-making in the political sphere, to be considered as such (e.g., Dahl 1957). In
contrast, critical scholars tend to view power as a hidden force which is most effective when least
observable, operating informally and transcending specific contexts, without even requiring explicit
action (Lukes 2021, 5, 79–84). “Secrecy lies at the very core of power,” wrote Elias Canetti (1981, 290),
pointing out the asymmetry of knowledge that is constitutive of power, as the powerful person sees
through others without allowing others to see through them (ibid, 292). Uncovering power structures
thus represents an act of resistance. What Foucault regarded as a historical transition from the display of
power to power over individuals who are displayed (1977), David Graeber defined as coevality of two
modalities of power (2001, 95). From an economic perspective, Graeber further discussed money as
embodying a generic agency and dangerous power precisely when it is not “tamed” by coins that grant it
visibility or displayed through valuable objects (ibid, 103).

53

The second aspect is the distinction, in Steven Lukes’ terms, between “power to” and “power over.” The
former refers to general agency, encompassing the capacity, facility, or ability to act and influence
outcomes, while the latter denotes a relation of domination that is inherently social and characterized by
asymmetry, and can be regarded as a subspecies of “power to” (Lukes 2021, 39, 74, 78). This distinction
can be traced back to the Latin language, which distinguishes between potentia and potestas, and was
developed by Baruch Spinoza, for whom “potentia signifies the power of things in nature, including
persons, to exist and act. Potestas is used when speaking of being in the power of another” (ibid, 78).
Focusing on power as domination, Spinoza further classified the means to secure compliance to
mechanisms concerning the subordinate’s body, such as physical bondage or actual or potential
violence, and symbolic means targeting their mind, such as causing fear and deception (ibid, 91–92).
This division brings us to the third aspect—the distinction between power and violence. Similar to the
mind/body duality, the differentiation between power and violence cannot be separated from the
culture/nature divide, which permeates Modern Western thought, delineating epistemology from
ontology, the symbolic from the physical, social constructs from natural facts, and the political and
historical from the given and timeless (Descola 2013; Latour 1993). As physical force, violence is
abrupt and immediate, while power unfolds over a certain extension of space and time that serves more
readily as substrate for symbolic complexities (Canetti 1981, 281–82). The contrast between a “natural”
violence and a “socialized” power is implied in Max Weber’s work, where violence is glossed as a given
and the focus is placed on the social arrangements considered legitimate for its exercise, particularly the
state (e.g., Weber 1968). This perspective is echoed by Alessandro Passerin d’Entrèves (1967), who
considered power as a form of violence that is institutionalized or qualified by law, deriving its
legitimacy from the Hobbesian social contract. On the other hand, Hannah Arendt sought to further
radicalize the distinction between these two notions in her work On Violence, where she defined power
as the property of groups, which concerns the ability of the group members to act in concert (1969, 40–
44), while portraying violence as instrumental, capable of being carried out also by individuals. Whereas
power preserves the consent that brought the social laws into existence, violence aligns with natural
strength, which the implements of violence are designed and used to multiply and can finally replace
(ibid, 46). Arendt further distinguished both violence and power from authority, which involves
unquestioning obedience based on respect for the person giving the order or the office they hold (ibid,
5). Violence is unpredictable, because “while the results of men’s actions are beyond the actors’ control,
violence harbors within itself an additional element of arbitrariness; nowhere does Fortuna, good or ill
54

luck, play a more fateful role in human affairs than on the battlefield” (ibid, 4). This recalls the potential
of violent actions to provoke equally destructive retaliation from their victims, unlike more enduring
forms of power and domination which are based on respect and consent (either genuine or based on
deception). However, as demonstrated by Caroline Ashcroft (2021), a comprehensive examination of
Arendt’s complete works reveals a more complex interplay between power and violence, where violence
can also contribute to the constitution of the political sphere. This interplay resonates with the oscillation
identified by Walter Benjamin (1996) between “lawmaking violence,” which establishes a new law, and
“law-preserving violence,” which enforces an existing law. In other words, and unlike a natural fact,
violence can only be understood through its connection to law, just as the law can only be understood in
relation to violence.
A fourth important point of contention in scholarly debates over the concept of power has revolved
around whether power is essentially repressive, dispossessing and restricting those on whom it is
exercised in various physical, procedural, or ideological measures and to different extent, thereby
inhibiting their resistance and confrontation with the powerful (Bachrach and Baratz 1962; Gramsci
1977), or also encompasses productive and disciplinary dimensions, shaping the actions of individuals
and channeling their agencies toward different ends (Foucault 1977; 1980). The latter approach is
exemplified by Michel Foucault’s influential concept of subjection or subjectivation, which refers to the
constitution of individuals as subjects in a double sense, as agents with specific dispositions and as
subordinates to power (1980, 60).
Foucault’s work has also prompted a significant shift in the social sciences and political thought, moving
away from conceiving power as possessed by groups or individuals who exert it at will upon others,
toward considering power as a constitutive dimension of social relations themselves. This dimension
infuses social relations with an asymmetrical balance of forces, generating various forms of domination
and subordination among individuals who, in turn, are constituted by power (Garland 1990, 138).
However, notwithstanding this multiplicity and pluri-directionality of forces—where all subjects are
constituted by different forces yet maintain a level of freedom to resist—games of power can solidify
into fixed states of domination, wherein particular individuals and groups acquire and preserve (i.e., they
possess) a superior capacity to control and “produce” others (Foucault 1994, 283).
The fifth aspect of power to be discussed here is its comparativeness, which is interrelated with the
objective of its exercise, and, thus, with notions of value and hierarchy. This interrelation underlies the

55

common understanding that individuals or groups differ from one another in their respective abilities to
maximize their attainment of their objectives while minimizing efforts. In such comparisons, one person
would be considered more powerful than another if the former can bring about outcomes that are more
“significant” than those produced by the latter (Lukes 2021, 79–85). “But how do we judge the
significance of outcomes?” Lukes asks, and then replies: “The most natural answer is: we look at their
effects upon the interests of the agents involved” (ibid, 85). The concept of interests directs us to what is
important in people’s lives, and thus the greater ability of one person or group to further their own
interests and affect the central or basic interests of another may indicate their superior power (ibid, ibid).
However, the question of what is basic or central to people’s lives is controversial. Is it, for example,
their economic situation, their personal security and lives, or the status and prestige of themselves or of
their group (however this is defined)?
Therefore, the comparative aspect of power is inseparable from the multiplicity and contention of
values. As Friedrich Nietzsche argued through his concept of “will to power”—that force driving
organisms to preserve their lives and enhance them through growth—value judgments can themselves
be the stakes of power struggles, leading to people’s attempts to make prevail the value judgments that
are favorable to them (Nietzsche 1968, 400). One of these value judgments, Nietzsche contended, is the
value of “truth,” highlighting the interconnection between power and knowledge. Nietzsche thus put
forward the perspectivist idea that beings strive to compel others to accept as a norm their perspective on
the world—i.e., the amount of reality they can grasp, become masters of, and utilize for their service
(ibid, 480–81).
On the other hand, from a structural point of view, Louis Dumont demonstrated how values can be
hierarchically ranked. In general, hierarchy is a principle of gradation of elements in an ensemble in
relation to that ensemble (Dumont 1980, 66). Values and other elements become superior to others when
their relation to the whole is such that they come to encompass the other values and elements that
contradict them, like the right hand encompasses the left, the category of “Man” encompasses women,
or purity encompasses political power in the Indian context that he explored (ibid, 75–79, 239– 45;
2013). Although Dumont perceived power through a Weberian lens as legitimate force (idem 1980, 153)
and, on that basis, distinguished it from hierarchy, which is essentially a feature of religion or
cosmology, one can suppose that power may also be involved in determining the hierarchy between the

56

components of a whole or manipulating the definition of that whole in such a way as to allow for a
certain hierarchical arrangement of its components.
It is noteworthy that the power to which these scholars refer is exercised by human beings, who alone
are considered social agents endowed with a will or the capacity to manipulate or be manipulated by
symbols. On the other hand, nonhuman entities, from inanimate things to animals and plants to spirits
and gods, have traditionally been considered in modern Western “naturalist” sciences (including the
social sciences) as either natural forces that may limit human action or be acted upon by humans; as raw
materials to be transformed by humans into material products; or as symbolic constructions to be
invented by them, particularly in the case of spirits and gods (Descola 2005, 114–65, 302–06). In this
way, the ultimate stake in the inter-subjective struggle between the master and slave in G.W.F. Hegel’s
parable is domination that would reduce the latter into an object, i.e., a non-agent (2019, 91–98). Marxist
thinking reflects an instrumentalization of exerting power over nature for the exercise of power among
people, or the continuity between these two forms of control. In Karl Marx’s political economy, the
exercise of power among humans is based on their unequal appropriation of nonhuman objects, such as
land, livestock, and other means of production, and control over the process whereby these are
transformed into products (1976). The thinkers of the Frankfurt School later factored in the effects of the
instrumental rationalizing tendencies that emerged during the Enlightenment to argue that the human
pursuit of control and mastery over nature in modernity eventually extends to the domination of human
beings by other human beings (Horkheimer and Adorno 2002). On the other hand, we observe a
different approach to the agency of nonhuman entities in Actor-Network Theory, where nonhuman
“actants” can, like human agents, participate in the course of action and even hijack it, interfere and
affect social relations between individuals, and consolidate or undermine social structures and power
asymmetries (Latour 2005, 63–86). However, even the recognition of nonhuman agency by ActorNetwork Theory seems to refer more to these entities’ “power to” than their “power over.” With a focus
on cosmology—once the researcher incorporates the ontological premises of the society under scrutiny
to their analytical toolbox—David Graeber and Marshall Sahlins (2017) suggested that human power
and authority in both state and stateless societies emulate the ruling cosmic powers, with figures
reflecting the “stranger-king” pattern incorporating and capitalizing on such meta-human forces.
Graeber and Sahlins’ non-separation of humanity from nonhumanity in studying political power is vital
for the study of Amazonia, where the extension of agency and “power over” beyond humans renders

57

many of the other definitions and conceptualizations of power dynamics presented above inadequate or
in need of significant revision. Incorporating nonhuman agency is crucial not only for exploring the
specific dynamics in human-nonhuman relationships but also for understanding inter-human interactions
in a socio-cosmos perceived by its inhabitants as inherently affected by the actions and potentials of
nonhumans.
Power in Indigenous Amazonia
Anthropologists of Indigenous Amazonia have addressed some of these dimensions of the concept of
power, increasingly factoring in native perceptions of nonhuman agency. However, as we will see, the
main approaches in this literature have tended to highlight socio-political and ontological egalitarianism
characterized by symmetrical relationality.
The study of power in this region was largely pioneered by Pierre Clastres’ (1989) Society against the
State. Despite assuming that power is inherent in social life (ibid, 23), Clastres primarily focused on the
formal political function of the chief in his study of power (or its absence). While he admitted that the
chief exercises power in a peaceful mode through persuasion and reconciliation (ibid, 30), Clastres’
analysis was rooted in the perception of power as essentially repressive. Based on evidence that
Amazonian chiefs cannot legitimately exercise violence on group members or expect obedience outside
the bounded context of war expeditions, Clastres concluded that “the space of chieftainship is not the
locus of power,” and that the chief of the tribe “is not a chief of State” (ibid, 205–06; see also Lowie
1948). Challenging common assumptions that the absence of a state structure in “primitive societies”
stems from an evolutionary failure to develop it, Clastres proposed that these societies intentionally
rejected power (understood as political authority or even sovereignty) just as they rejected nature,
because they “apprehend power as the resurgence of nature” (ibid, 44). Amazonian societies deliberately
place chiefs outside the social fabric to reduce their power to impotence, relegating them to a mere
formal position, and ensure separation between speech, violence, and wealth. They achieve this through
three asymmetrical flows of exchange between the chief and other society members—words, goods, and
women—that are opposed to the symmetrical exchange among “ordinary” society members. On the one
hand, the chief is obligated to provide his society members with abundant oratories, but this speech
amounts to empty formulae without reciprocation or even attention by other members. In addition, he
faces constant demands to share his goods in a way that prevents him from accumulating wealth. On the
other hand, the chief receives more women than other members, resulting in an asymmetry that leaves

58

him indebted to other men (ibid, 27–47). The external position of the Amazonian chief to his society,
combined with the embeddedness of economy in society, characteristic of other primitive societies, also
rules out the existence of a political economy (ibid, 199). Though Clastres does not explicitly state this
point, it appears that the balanced exchange of words, goods, and women among “ordinary” members
generates the power inherent in society as a collective rather than being possessed or exerted by
individuals. The sole function of this power, it seems, is to restrict the chief. We are thus left with a
somewhat Arendtian perception of power without appropriate analysis of the actual mechanisms through
which this power is constituted or made effective. Furthermore, this analysis concerns only the relations
among the male members of the group, whose power over women—who only figure here as objects of
exchange—is taken for granted.
Clastres’ provocative model was widely criticized in Amazonian ethnography but, to a large extent, it
has also laid the foundation for subsequent discussions on power in this region. Similar to Clastres,
Waud Kracke (1978) examined power among the Kagwahiv within the formal political sphere,
observing power that does not operate through repression and coercion, but relies on persuasion.
However, contrary to Clastres, rather than incompatibility between chiefs and their societies, Kracke
demonstrated how groups coalesce and form around leaders, defining leadership as a set of functions
that promote group formation and inhibit fission. These functions include the “commotive function,”
which motivates a group to work toward a common goal, and the “arbitrational function,” which
encourages conviviality and adherence to the group’s informal code of conduct. The types of leaders
who perform these functions are referred to as dux and rex, respectively (ibid, 84). Drawing on
psychological models, Kracke explored different leadership styles and motivations behind followership.
Embedding these models in the Kagwahiv kinship landscape, Kracke asserted that leaders achieve this
position primarily by giving their daughters to men and thus holding a matrimonial debt that guarantees
the following and labor of the sons-in-law for varying periods of time (ibid, 35–37, 235–36). This
finding challenges Clastres’ notion of indebtedness of the chief to this group through polygynous
chieftainship (ibid, 14).
Kracke’s observation that the scarcity of women makes a man’s father-in-law the only person with a
sound basis to exercise control over him (ibid, 37) leads us to Peter Rivière and Terence Turner’s works
on Amazonian political economies, which, contrary to Clastres’ model, do not overlook or take for
granted the power that men exert over women. Rivière (1983) criticized Clastres’ argument that

59

Amazonian economies are not political because they do not involve the accumulation and appropriation
of surplus wealth. Drawing, among other things, on Turner’s observation that in central Brazil political
economy is based on social rather than material production and reproduction (T. Turner 1979, 168),
Rivière argues that, given the short supply of human labor in Guiana, wealth depends on the successful
manipulation of human resources and their incorporation into the community. Although he focuses on
the prestige and wealth of the group leader, Rivière’s analysis provides us with generational and
gendered mechanisms that reveal wider power dynamics, taking us beyond the circumscribed sphere of
leadership. In these broader dynamics, elder men appropriate the products of their sons-in-laws, and men
in general appropriate the surplus value of female production for their own political advancement (ibid;
see also Rivière 1987).
Contrary to Rivière, Turner goes beyond the exploitative aspect of this political economy to also explore
its productive dimensions, wherein the surplus product is not objects or services but persons as
symbolically objectified forms of value that reproduce social hierarchy (T. Turner 2003). The hierarchy
to which Turner refers is the encompassment of women’s labor by men’s labor, and of the matriuxorilocal household by the segmentary units, themselves encompassed by communal organization that
elaborates ceremonies controlled by men (ibid, 15–18; see also Lorrain 2000, on whose approach he
draws). The fact that these political economies involve persons and not goods sets limits to
accumulation, as willing persons can leave a leader, and communities tend to split beyond a certain
demographic size (Rivière 1983, 352–53), which results in revolving hierarchies, rather than fixed ones
(T. Turner 2003, 20).
The emphasis on hierarchy refutes the view, held by Clastres and reflected elsewhere in the literature, of
sweeping Amazonian egalitarianism (e.g., McCallum 1990; Overing 1989, 161–62). In Michael
Heckenberger’s (2005) study of the deep temporality of Arawak political power in the Xingu, hierarchy
emerges as a crucial discursive foundation for the operation of power. Heckenberger’s research, drawing
on both archaeological evidence and contemporary ethnography, reveals that the chief does not possess
any coercive power, although he can undoubtedly influence and control the actions of others (ibid, 330).
Xinguano power, according to Heckenberger, involves the control over the construction and operation of
human bodies (ibid, 312). This power is hierarchical, as it is graded along genealogical principles and
organized as a concentric and pyramidal model (ibid, 63–65). It is also spatialized, as it is performed by
individuals in the village plaza and invested in this site, which is itself perceived as a person embodying

60

buried ancestors and taking part in a ranked regional system of village-persons. Based on archaeological
data, Heckenberger hypothesized that such networks of settlements amounted in pre-Columbian times to
galactic polities (ibid, 124–26).
The spatial embeddedness of hierarchy is central to another Amazonian sub-region, located closer to the
Andoque. I am referring to the Arawakan-Tukanoan system, extending from the Rio Negro and Vaupés
rivers to the Apaporis and Lower Caquetá. In the Tukanoan case, mythology recounts the successive
emergence of the ancestors of the sibs, which constitute the different language groups of this sub-region.
These ancestors traveled upriver in a primordial anaconda-canoe and exited it at spots along the river in
order of seniority, with senior sib ancestors disembarking more downstream than junior sib ancestors.
These myths serve as an ideal model with different levels of practical applications, for land occupation
and usufruct rights of river segments. According to the model, the elder the sib, the lower downstream it
is positioned, resulting in a greater abundance of fish yield and more significance access to regional
exchange networks (Goldman 2004, 90–91; C. Hugh-Jones 1979, 33–40; S. Hugh-Jones 1993; Vidal
1999). This hierarchy also manifests in leadership and ritual prerogatives, involving varying degrees of
power to engage in exchange with nonhuman beings and influence them to ensure the well-being and
reproduction of the human group.6 The geographical proximity between the Arawakan-Tukanoan system
and the People of the Center also translates to certain similarities in social organization, such as
patrilocality, a strong ideology of agnatic descent, and notions of hierarchy. Therefore, I return to this
sub-region several times as a privileged comparative case to elucidate my arguments.
The embeddedness of hierarchy in myth leads us to the agency of nonhuman entities and the power
