required to engage in successful exchange with them, as well as the power and prestige derived from
such exchange. Philippe Descola and Fernando Santos Granero criticized Clastres for disregarding the
sphere of ritual and communication with nonhuman entities, where shamans play a key role, and through
which they acquire prestige and political influence (Descola 1988; Santos Granero 1986). Both authors
argue that in Amazonian societies, shamans can gain greater political influence than titular chiefs to
orient group members, because they possess scarce ritual knowledge allowing them to exert control over
reproductive processes and material or symbolic resources on which the group relies. Various
ethnographers have documented how shamans contend with powerful spirits and animals whose powers
The Arawakan societies vary in their degree of conformity to the myth of the ancestral anaconda-canoe and the spatialized
hierarchy enshrined within it, although such hierarchy is manifested in the aforementioned political and ritual realms
(Andrello 2006; Bourgue 1976; Hill 1985; van der Hammen 1992).

6

61

are connected to their predatory capacities, as well as how they draw on the powers of such nonhuman
entities to cause, cure, or prevent diseases and other misfortunes (e.g., Déléage 2009; Langdon and Baer
1992; Reichel-Dolmatoff 1975). In these accounts, we observe the dual depiction of power as both the
property of specific shamans and apprentices (e.g., Langdon 1992b, 47), on the one hand, and the
property of cosmic networks, or “global energy systems” (Langdon 1992a, 13), on the other. The
shaman’s interactions with these energy systems turn him into “a living embodiment of power”
(Langdon 1992b, 59)—a description falling closer to a Foucauldian concept of power as the property of
social relations themselves. In Chapter 7 of this dissertation, I describe a similar phenomenon, where
Andoque members refer to the central concept of tne’túi, which I provisionally gloss here as “power as
spirit,” as both imparted from the cannibal god Sı̰ ́di and the property of the predatory networks that he
oversees, and the temporary possession of individuals, representing their ability to access Sı̰ ́di’s
predatory networks and tilt them (and Sı̰ ́di himself) to their benefit.
However, one seldom finds detailed accounts of continuities between such shamanic inter-specific
exercise of power and the exercise of power among human beings, Indigenous and non-Indigenous alike
(e.g., S. Hugh-Jones 1994; Santos Granero 1993), to which Graeber and Sahlins refer, and which is a
central focus of this dissertation. Furthermore, the term “shaman,” as this Siberian-borrowed concept is
commonly used in the literature, often conflates ritual specialists who operate on various scales, employ
distinct knowledge and methods, and communicate with various classes of nonhuman entities. S. HughJones (1994) differentiates these practitioners as “horizontal shamans” and “vertical shamans,” two ideal
types that respectively correspond to egalitarian or hierarchic aspects or ideologies within the societies
where they operate (sometimes in tandem). This distinction also illuminates the political economies of
knowledge of ranked Amazonian societies—e.g., in Northwest Amazonia (Andrello 2010; S. HughJones 2019b)—where the knowledge essential for “vertical shamanism”—which garners political clout
and prestige—is shrouded in secrecy and transmitted within high-ranking patrilines, as opposed to the
more experimental and accessible knowledge of “horizontal shamans.”
Descola’s call to reconsider shamans as political agents falls within the broader intellectual endeavor
seeking to align the object and method of research according to Indigenous Amazonian notions of
society and social relations. These notions concern not solely human subjects, but also extend to
nonhuman entities, such as the myriad animals, plants, and spirits with whom individuals communicate
in both ritual and everyday occasions (Descola 1986). The approach put forward by Descola and other

62

anthropologists associated with the Ontological Turn led to a call to revise modern Western definition of
politics as a sphere where only human beings count as moral subjects and social and political agents.
Instead, this approach proposes a notion of “cosmopolitics,” which acknowledges that nonhuman
entities may also occupy these positions (de la Cadena 2010). Before we proceed to “cosmopolitical”
accounts of Amazonian power, it is crucial to briefly digress and delve into the kinship dimension of
Amazonian ontology.
The Ontological Turn in Amazonian anthropology has heavily drawn on the study of kinship in the
region, and the association presented among many Indigenous peoples, with varying degrees and in
different contexts, between matrimonial exchange and predation. According to Descola (1998), the
regional predominance of cognation and Dravidian kinship turns consanguinity and affinity into
relatively abstract logical operators for considering and acting towards a wide array of entities and
situations. Affinal relations are particularly notable in this respect because, owing to their unstable and
often conflictual nature, they serve throughout the region as “an excellent metaphorical support to
qualify relations with the exterior” (ibid, 36). The consideration of affinity as analogical to predation is a
key component of Descola’s revival and redefinition of the concept of animism as a mode of
identification where the elementary categories structuring social life are used to organize the relations
between human and nonhuman beings (Descola 1996, 87–88). This definition would later be generalized
to consider animism as a mode of identification characterized by the premise that all, or most, beings of
the cosmos are endowed with continuous and commensurate interiorities (subjectivity, agency, mental
and emotional states, social norms, etc.), as opposed to discontinuous and incommensurate physicalities
(bodily forms and principles, and external manifestations) (Descola 2005).
On the other hand, Eduardo Viveiros de Castro frames the relation between affinity and predation in
terms of continuity, rather than analogy, with affinity representing a specific actualization of the generic
relational model of predation (1993, 184–86). Furthermore, nonhuman entities as well as humans with
whom one cannot marry—categorized as “potential affines”—represent affinity more than virtual
affines (people with whom one can marry), real affines (with whom one has married), and, evidently,
consanguineous kin, precisely because actual alliance or its prospects introduces consanguinizing
elements that dilute affinity (idem 2001; Viveiros de Castro and Fausto 1993). This interpretation is
rooted in Viveiros de Castro and Carlos Fausto’s critical adaptation of Dumont’s model of Dravidian
kinship to Amazonian reality through another Dumontian concept—namely, that of hierarchy, as

63

discussed earlier. In contrast with the “equistatutory” structure of Asian Dravidianate, where the
categories of affinity and consanguinity stand in balance to each other, in Amazonian Dravidianate,
affinity encompasses consanguinity at the supra-local level, with consaguine kin living far from ego
being “affinized” and treated as affines, particularly in matters of politics, ritual, and cosmology that
transcend the local community. On the other hand, affinity is encompassed by consanguinity at the local
level, where real affines are treated as consanguines (a process referred to as consanguinization, or
familiarization) (Viveiros de Castro 1993; 2001; Viveiros de Castro and Fausto 1993). In other words, in
Amazonia affinity “stands as the given dimension of the cosmic relational matrix, while consanguinity
falls within the scope of human action and intention” (Viveiros De Castro 2001, 19). Here it is crucial to
recall that, unlike most Amazonian societies (including the Tukanoan and Arawakan neighbors, who
share an agnatic ideology), the Andoque and the other People of the Center do not adhere to the
Dravidian kinship model. However, similar to the Warao—who also deviate from this model—the
Andoque share some of the concentric dimensions of Vivieros de Castro and Fausto’s model (Allard
2010, 98–99). On the local level, they show a certain tendency to consanguinize affines, even though the
strong patrilineal identities in the region lead them to differentiate between consanguineous and affinal
co-residents. More importantly, Andoque cosmology closely aligns—perhaps even more than that of
their neighboring People of the Center—with the prevalent Amazonian concept of inherent meta-affinity
and potential affinity as a “determined alterity” mediating relationships with the outside (Viveiros de
Castro and Fausto 1993, 151). As discussed in Chapters 1 and 2, their cosmology features two
interconnected spatial systems centered around a river course, with potential affines for those living at
the river’s midpoint inhabiting the two extreme points—the river source and mouth—of each system.
Notably, Andoque mythology frames commerce with Whites as a marital exchange, a perspective that is
either more pronounced or distinct compared to their neighbors (Griffiths 1998, 247; Karadimas 2005,
360–67, 171–75; Lucas 2019, 372–73; see Chapter 12).
Despite employing the concept of hierarchy between categories, Viveiros de Castro’s overall
theorization of Amerindian perspectivism, onto which his argument that affinity is a specific
materialization of a generalized predatory relationality can also be mapped, does not acknowledge the
possibility of asymmetries. According to Viveiros de Castro, Amerindian perspectivism is based on the
premise that animals, spirits, and other nonhuman entities see themselves and other members of their
kind as human, while they perceive the entities they prey on as peccaries or other animals preyed upon
by humans, and the entities that prey on them as jaguars, spirits, or other entities that represent human
64

beings’ predators (1998). Perspectivism implies multinaturalism, as the equally human cultural
representations produced by various persons of diverse species constitute as many
worlds/natures/ontologies as the number of specific bodily forms from which these representations are
projected. For example, a given liquid may be seen as blood in a human world but perceived as maize
beer in a jaguar world (ibid, 477–78). In this sense, the same relation between two entities that one of
them may perceive as predation may be perceived by the other as sexual relations, i.e., an affinal
alliance. Such may be the case when a human being mistakes a forest spirit for another human and
engages with it in a social activity befitting two humans, rather than a human and nonhuman. In such
situations, the human party behaves in such a way because it is “overpowered by the non-human
subjectivity, passes over to its side, transforming himself into a being of the same species as the
speaker” (ibid, 483). To my knowledge, this instance stands as the only occurrence where Viveiros de
Castro addresses the notion of power or asymmetry of relations in his perspectivist model, momentarily
bringing it closer to Nietzsche’s understanding of this term as the attempt of each being to impose its
perspective on reality on others, driven by each being’s will to power. By contrast, such overpowering is
central to the present dissertation.
In their critique of the symmetry bias in new studies of Amazonian animism and perspectivism, Luiz
Costa and Carlos Fausto refer to Viveiros de Castro’s general perspectivist/multinaturalist project as “a
disjunction of perspectives that are never reducible one to the other, nor to a global figure of the One”
(2010, 99). They continue, “Viveiros de Castro’s perspectivism thereby corresponds to the politics of
Pierre Clastres—it is a religion against the state” (ibid, ibid). In other words, excluding the asymmetrical
nature of the father-in-law/son-in-law relationship throughout Amazonia (Fausto 2008, 350), marital
exchange and predatory relations between two subjects are potentially symmetrical, as both parties can
equally hijack each other into their kinship network or reality. In the case of actual predation, the game
animal can counter-prey on its predator in the form of illnesses or other misfortunes (Viveiros de Castro
1998, 472), and Viveiros de Castro’s model does not allow for any in-built measures to disperse this
ambiguity.
Costa and Fausto equally criticize Descola for downplaying asymmetrical relationality and hierarchy in
animist societies, notions whose existence he acknowledges, in the case of the Indigenous Americas,
only in societies he defines as “analogical,” where all human and nonhuman entities present
discontinuities in relation to both interiority and physicality (2010, 99). For the Southeast Asian

65

contexts, other scholars have noted the compatibility of animism with hierarchical structures. There, the
universalized subjectivity among beings is not segmented horizontally across bodies, but is graded
vertically, such that each being possesses a different level of spirit or potency (K. Århem 2015b, 25).
Consequently, domesticated animals, which are considered lower in this hierarchy, may be manipulated
and sacrificed to protect human lives (Sprenger 2015, 34–35; see also Descola 2023). Returning to
Amazonia, Costa and Fausto question Descola’s argument that animism is congruent only with
symmetrical modes of relations, where the parties hold equal ontological status and the relations
between them may be reversed, such as exchange, gift, and predation (Costa and Fausto 2019, 213).
Conversely, they call for exploring the possibilities that the idiom of mastery, prevalent throughout in
Amazonia, holds for understanding both contemporary regional animism and state-like structures of
domination that were more common in Amazonia prior to European conquest (Costa and Fausto 2019,
100; e.g., the structures explored by Heckenberger 2005).
Fausto and Costa’s works on mastery and its closely related notion of familiarization are crucial for the
present discussion of Amazonian notions of power. Firstly, these works reflect the common regional
ontological principle concerning the social agency of nonhuman beings and their commensurate
interiority with that of humans. Secondly, they introduce significant elements of asymmetry into the
symmetrical model of predation/alliance. In the case of the notion of familiarization, or, more precisely,
familiarizing predation, Fausto does this by recasting the regional idiom of affinal relationality into
political-economic terms, considering familiarizing predation as the “main schema of appropriation in
Amazonian symbolic economies” (Fausto 1999, 937). In this process, the appropriated other, who is
typically considered an affine—whether an in-marrying spouse, a newborn child, the dead enemy’s
spirit, or animals hunted or captured as pets—is endowed with the affects and dispositions of the
captor’s consanguineal group (ibid, 939; 2007, 502). This process implies reducing any danger of
predation or other form of hostility by the transformed patient toward the transforming agent and their
kin and converting the patient’s behavior into one that would be beneficial toward them. Fausto and
Costa point to the asymmetry of familiarization, which converts the symmetrical meta-affinal processes
of marital and predatory exchange into meta-filial relations modeled after vertical consanguinity ties and
complements them in the Amazonian production of kinship (Fausto 2008; Costa and Fausto 2019;
Fausto and Costa 2021; 2022).

66

The conversion of symmetry into asymmetry takes place through the idiom of mastery, which points to
the master’s ability, by determining the direction of familiarization, to align the pet’s agency to their
own, thereby becoming a magnified person, a “plural singularity.” Mastery is scalable, as human and
nonhuman masters can own other persons, material and non-material items (myths, dances, or spells), or
places and species (Fausto 2008; Costa 2017). The Amazonian pet-master dynamics represents the
subjectivating form that Hegel’s master-slave dialectics assumes in this region, where none of the parties
is reduced to an object (Fausto and Costa 2021, 5). The pet keeps its agency and subjectivity, and it is
precisely this alterity that serves to magnify the master. However, and although familiarization and
mastery reflect greater asymmetry than marital alliance and the act of inter-species predation, the nonextinguishment of the pet’s agency means that these relations are also potentially inversible, as the pet
can familiarize its master and incorporate their agency and vitality to its own, rather than the other way
around (Costa and Fausto 2019). Nonetheless, this inversibility should not be viewed as a simple
relational reversal between two stable parties, as the measures and effects of familiarization and mastery
leave traces on the parties, participating in the very constitution of the “animist subject” (ibid, 214–15).
This echoes Foucault’s conceptualization of power as subjectivation, which appears in regional
ethnography in Santos Granero’s treatment of power as the agent’s capacity to form and transform the
subjectivity of the patient, or to extend their own subjectivity to that of the patient (Santos Granero
2009a), and in Harry Walker’s description of the Urarina’s processes of subject formation through
chains of asymmetrical companionships between different agents, human and nonhuman alike (baby and
placenta, a person and manioc beer, a shaman and a plant, etc.) (2013). Walker’s study also leads us
back to the relations between Amazonian power and leadership, as he concludes that since Indigenous
notions of autonomy preclude any possibility of coercion by the leader, leadership relies on the ability to
inspire and mobilize others. Therefore, real power in Amazonia involves the capacity to form selves and
social groups to begin with, i.e., to form subjects that could be inspired and mobilized (ibid, 214).
However, Fausto and Costa’s model represents the specific regional modality of the general notion of
subjectivation and the way it is articulated with both concrete and abstract structures of kinship and
dynamics of predation in the region. Furthermore, the proliferation of asymmetries in relations among
humans and between them and nonhumans in Andoque discourse and practices, coupled with their
pronounced focus on masters and notions of ownership, renders this model particularly pertinent for this
dissertation’s interest in power dynamics. In Andoque, the notion of mastery is encapsulated in the noun

67

ño̰, which literally means “person,” and which I render throughout the dissertation as “owner-person” to
distinguish it from other kinds of persons. This term is particularly revealing when the “pets” in question
are nonhuman entities and abstract things, like a myth, dance, or spell, as it implies that the
master/owner of that entity or thing is its personification: their agentive, human-like aspect. Within this
relationship, the inferior party is identified by one of two terms that imply varying degrees of predatory
agency, submissiveness, and alienability: ḭéna̰, or “pet,” and ’ihɵ́ɵ, which means “orphan.” The former
term typically refers to a being of another species or bodily form accompanying and assisting its master,
while the latter designates a subordinate and alienable affinal relative adopted by the master. The multiscalarity and context-transcending ability of Fausto and Costa’s model make it an advantageous
framework for uncovering continuities across various instances of power exertion, as well as the
contradictory forces that sometimes operate within Andoque reality.
Another useful aspect of this model is the emphasis on commensality as a central practice
complementing predation in the creation of persons and groups. This should be understood within the
context of an Amazonian cosmos where differences among beings are based on physical rather than
inner attributes, hence kinship is actively produced through the fabrication of bodies (Vilaça 2002).
Here, the direction of feeding introduces asymmetry, supplanting the fed person’s previous kin
attachments with a new consubstantiality with the feeder (Fausto 2007a; Fausto and Costa 2013). This
aspect underscores the usefulness of the gift perspective for the study of Amazonian societies, based on
the gift-like qualities of the substances consumed. The relatively limited exploration of the gift paradigm
in Amazonia has been attributed to the “homosubstitutive” logic prevailing there, where things cannot
stand for persons as they do in transactions objectified as “gift exchange” in Melanesia, where gift
theory has evolved (Descola 2001; McCallum 1989). However, S. Hugh-Jones has demonstrated the
relevance of the gift paradigm for understanding the secret flute cults and the ceremonial, as well as
ongoing exchanges in the Tukanoan-Arawakan complex of Northwest Amazonia, where we observe
homologies between body parts and substances, on one hand, and artefacts and natural species, on the
other (2001; 2013). By adopting Marylin Strathern’s conceptualization of “gift exchange” as mediated
exchange—where a detached part of person A passes from them to person B—or unmediated
exchange—where A directly works on B—to displace a prior relation registered in B (1988, 178–79,
292), Hugh-Jones contends that in exchanges in Northwest Amazonia, different aspects of the donors’
identities are objectified in the items they transact. This feature reemerges in barter trade throughout
Amazonia (S. Hugh‐Jones 2013, 371), and underpins the familiarizing dimensions of feeding, as
68

discussed above. The gift paradigm is pertinent to the current study for two reasons. First, because trade
is essential to the Andoque ethos and objects often serve as metonyms for persons. Second, because gift
exchange establishes hierarchies and relations of domination among individuals through the exchange of
non-equivalent gifts (Gregory 2015, 13–14; Mauss 2002)—a dynamic most evident in the Andoque’s
sharing of ritual substances.
This literature review furnishes the components necessary to propose an analogy between
alliance/predation and familiarization and mastery, on the one hand, and violence and power and
domination, on the other. Like alliance/predation, violence reflects symmetry in that its exercise is likely
to result in less sustainable control and domination over its object over time. Unless complemented with
symbolic manipulations or other repressive means, violence exercised by one party can escalate into a
brawl or duel, which reflects a wider symmetry between two parties. While modern Western thinking
tends to view violence as closer to nature than domination, and, therefore, akin to physical force, as part
of the given plane of reality, alliance/predation is perceived in Indigenous Amazonian as the inherent
fabric of cosmo-sociality between members of different groups and species, before the elements
participating in them are appropriated into personal or collective bodies (social groups and species). In
other words, while both violence and alliance/predation pertain to the given plane of reality in each
ontology, what this plane constitutes varies across ontologies.
Conversely, familiarization and mastery involve the manipulation of bodies and symbols to form more
lingering forms of asymmetry and control whereby one party’s agency is aligned to that of another. In
this regard, they resemble various forms of domination, such as the legitimation of violence by law,
hegemonic discourse, or decision-making procedures. Like these latter forms of domination,
familiarization and mastery are also actively produced or constructed, as opposed to the given plane of
reality. However, here again it should be noted that the constructed plane of reality varies across
ontologies. While the three examples of domination that I mentioned may be glossed as “social” or
“cultural,” familiarization and mastery target primarily the patient’s body (the plane that in modern
Western thinking would be regarded as “nature”), as they aim to disconnect the patient from the
generalized affinal fabric and connect it with the bodily form and dispositions of the master as its metaconsanguine.
The final approach to the notion of power in Amazonia that I will examine here is that of Steven
Rubenstein, which represents a combination of human-nonhuman communication, political economy,

69

and psychoanalysis. In his works on power among the Shuar, Rubenstein demonstrated, first, how the
relations that individuals establish with warrior souls in visions magnify their agency to fight and
exchange with other human and nonhuman beings, and, second, how the circulation and/or accumulation
of this and other forms and signs of power by Shuar individuals, representative organization, and nonIndigenous institutes in different periods reflect and create asymmetrical relations among them (2007).
Furthermore, Rubenstein (2012) introduced a complex model based on the works of both Clastres and
Jacques Lacan to explain how Shuar visions involving nonhuman entities both constitute a subjectivity
which is fundamentally different from a bourgeois one and produce personal power that is not translated
into political domination. While drawing on Clastres’ argument on the Amazonian disjunction between
violence and speech to explain the inexistence of power as coercive authority among the Shuar,
Rubenstein explained the formation of Shuar subjectivity by recourse to Jacques Lacan’s distinction
between the Real, Imaginary, and Symbolic, and his theory concerning the mirror stage. Lacan argued
that in this stage a child growing in a Western or bourgeois society internalizes his own self-image and
is initiated into the Imaginary register of reality—which consists of images people form of themselves
and of others. This internalization is a critical stage in the process whereby the symbolic register—the
part of reality that enters into language—colonizes the real, which is the part of reality that has hitherto
resisted language. Conversely, Shuar individuals do not enter the Imaginary through a mirror stage but
through the visions of encounters with nonhuman beings who represent subjects other to themselves,
experiences they encounter from early childhood. This inauguration of the imaginary leaves vast
territories of the Real that are not colonized by the symbolic but rather entail the colonization of the
latter by the former (ibid, 51, 54). While these unmediated visions serve to magnify their power and
agency, people come to identify language as the realm of misrecognition, resulting in a stark divide
between power and speech (ibid, 52). The loss of the warrior spirit gained in visions through sharing the
vision with other people in conversations signals a dissonance between sociality with nonhumans and
sociality with humans, as well as a disjuncture between the acquisition of power and its performance
(ibid, 56–57). Emphasizing the link between power, opacity, and secrecy, Rubenstein argues: “Power
was derived not from a coordination of the Imaginary and the Symbolic (whether it be ‘God’ or ‘the
People’) but rather from a coordination of the Imaginary and the Real” (ibid, 66; see also idem 2007,
369).
While thought-provoking, the model laid out by Rubenstein is only marginally relevant for
understanding Andoque power dynamics, because of the Andoque’s bigger emphasis on an ideology of
70

descent, downplaying of uxorilocal bride service, and, most significantly, lack of employment of
hallucinogenic substances (at least at the present). However, I borrow from Rubenstein the cue to
engage Lacan’s framework concerning the three registers of reality in an analysis of power. This will
serve me to propose the hypothesis, in Chapters 9 and 12, that various nonhuman entities referred to as
fi’du in Andoque or diablo in Spanish, as well as money and cash as opposed to specific externally
manufactured goods, are considered particularly potent and threatening because they belong to
territories of the Real register of reality that have not yet been symbolized through names and myths,
and, in this way, tamed. Juxtaposed with Rubenstein’s works, this hypothesis can serve, in due course,
as a basis for comparing forms of power across Amazonia, which falls outside the scope of the present
dissertation.
Additionally, Rubenstein’s work is an inspiring effort to engage in symmetrical analyses of Indigenous
people’s interactions with both the “traditional” nonhuman world and modern non-Indigenous
institutions, such as the Market and State, as well as Indigenous ones, particularly representational
organizations. His writing thus represents one strategy for bridging the gap between political-economic
approaches and ontological ones in Latin American anthropology (Lazar 2022), amid increasing
critiques against the latter approach for flattening ethnographic complexities, neglecting historical
changes, and privileging authoritative voices to reproduce ontological discourses opposed to nonIndigenous ones, which portray future utopias yet are often irrelevant for “real-world” problems (Bessire
and Bond 2014; Graeber 2015; Nadasdy 2021). In exploring the power dynamics occurring in the
Andoque’s interactions with both nonhuman and non-Indigenous agents, my research also aims to
overcome this divide.
Conceptual Framework and Argument
This dissertation examines the notions of power of a specific Amazonian society—namely, the Andoque
people—and explores the intricate dynamics of power within this society, as well as between Andoque
members and other human and nonhuman agents. I do not define power in terms of coercion, nor do I
privilege searching it in the realm of leadership or the public political domain (e.g., community
assemblies or representative organizations). Instead, I conceptualize power within the framework of
exchange, as one’s ability to transition from symmetrical movement of bodies, vital principles, material
goods, and action in exchanges between beings, to asymmetrical movement of these elements that
benefits one, while counteracting adversarial asymmetries. This definition implies that power also

71

manifests in the preconditions of exchange: the capacity to refuse or suspend exchange and to participate
in the transaction as its agent, rather than the transacted object. Inevitably, we must define “benefit,” or
the objective of these exchanges. In broad strokes, this objective would be one’s affirmation and
enhancement of life, as captured by Nietzsche’s “will to power,” or, in more Amazonianist terms, the
production of persons (Fausto 1999, 936–37; T. Turner 2003, 11).
Conceptualizing power within an exchange framework does not imply that it is necessarily harmonious;
indeed, predation represents a hostile form of exchange. More broadly, in analyzing various instances of
trade and gift giving, I interpret these activities through the lens of predatory logics. Furthermore, the
dimension of symmetry and asymmetry must be evaluated against the overall goal of producing persons.
Therefore, predation is potentially symmetrical in that, without familiarizing his game, the hunter risks
being assimilated into the animal’s society instead of using the prey to sustain his own life and produce
kin. Conversely, trade can be asymmetrical if the items exchanged only helps one party in achieving
these goals, while harming the other.
My focus in this dissertation rests on the capacity of agents—leaders and ordinary members alike, along
with nonhuman entities as perceived by the Andoque, and collectives such as clans or the entire
Andoque people—to reshape horizontal relations of predation and alliance into vertical relations of
familiarization and mastery, where they control exchange and align the agency of others to their own.
While spanning the fields of politics, economy, kinship, myth and ritual, my analysis of Andoque power
dynamics can be narrowed to exchanges within three conceptual domains and sets of distinctions, which
sometimes overlap but are distinguished here for explanatory purposes: ontological (humanity vs.
nonhumanity), kinship (agnatic and cognatic consanguinity, and affinity), and spatial (river source,
middle of the river, and river mouth).
In the ontological domain, exchanges are rooted in the animist principle of shared interiority among
beings with distinct bodily forms. This shared interiority leads to a default reciprocal substitution of
persons of one kind for those of another. Meanwhile, capable individuals engage in ontological
manipulations to create asymmetry with nonhumans by enforcing heterosubstitutive exchange, in which
they compensate for game with vegetal substances, or exploiting homosubstitution in sorcery assaults,
transforming human victims into prey.
Ontological manipulation is closely related to graded agency, which becomes apparent in kinship
practices and imagery. Here, despite cognatic principles, the strong clan identity fosters attempts at
72

asymmetry in inter-clan relations. Agnatic descent is associated with higher agency over non-agnatic
kin, non-kin, and nonhumans. In humans, diminished agency (e.g., in orphans) resembles states of
domination, while in nonhumans, it can parallel—but does not equate to—the objectification seen in
naturalism.
Finally, my analysis demonstrates how the Andoque’s notions and dynamics of power intricately
intertwine with their perception of space. The Andoque, both as an ethnic group and as distinct clans,
consider themselves as living at the center of a world axed upon the river’s course, resulting in the
division of the space surrounding this people (and each individual clan) into upriver, closer to the river
source, and downriver, nearer to the river mouth. The key “power as spirit” previously mentioned,
tne’túi, originates from the river source and the predatory capabilities attributed to the mythical affinal
relatives inhabiting this cosmic region. The center and the people living at the center draw upon this
power for survival, protection against competing human and nonhuman centers, and overall well-being
and prosperity, through diverse procedures of familiarization and appropriation that seek to encompass
the river source, together with its mythical heroes and ritual elements. A similar pursuit of
encompassment characterizes the center’s relationship with the river mouth—an affinal realm
representing non-Indigenous people, who historically approached the Andoque territory from that
direction. I explore the numerous strategies the Andoque have employed over time to harness the forces
originating from the river source in order to familiarize the river mouth, dispose of the objects and
capacities associated with it, and ensure that exchanges with agents downstream do not lead to perilous
imbalances in the dynamics among various centers in their own territory.
The aspects of ontological manipulation, graded agency, and encompassment are hierarchical features of
the Andoque’s animism whose achievement relies on knowledge of myth and ritual procedures.
Individuals and groups draw on this knowledge to establish and maintain asymmetries with nonhuman
beings in a bid to extend and maintain similar imbalances in their interactions with other human beings
(Andoque, non-Andoque, or non-Indigenous), and vice versa. However, the uncertainty in exchange
with both kinds of beings renders these asymmetries, as well as the additional asymmetries that people
aim to establish through them, inherently precarious.
My research contributes to the broader debate on power within the social sciences and political thought
by highlighting the continuum between social interactions among humans and those involving
nonhumans in societies where nonhumans are recognized as agents, thereby furthering the works of

73

Actor-Network theorists, as well as Graeber and Sahlins. Concurrently, it advances the exploration of
the human-nonhuman relational continuum within Amazonian animism and perspectivism, pioneered by
Descola and Viveiros de Castro. My approach reveals the power dynamics permeating relationships in
an Amazonian sub-region characterized by agnatic ideology and associated kinship conceptions and
practices—namely, the Caquetá-Putumayo. Building on Fausto and Costa’s theories of familiarization
and mastery in Amazonia, my research establishes power as both the outcome of and the instrument for
an enchainment of symmetrical and predominantly asymmetrical relationships. I demonstrate how these
processes are integrated into space and embodied in myth and narrative, underscoring their significance
across various contexts, including extractive and preservationist economies. My study thus challenges
the perception of egalitarianism often associated with the region, allowing for a comparison of the
animist configurations in the Caquetá-Putumayo with those in other areas, as studied by Århem and
Sprenger.
Dissertation Structure
The structure of this dissertation reflects the constitutive role of space in defining Andoque notions and
dynamics of power. It is organized into four parts, each dedicated to specific components of space as
perceived by Andoque members. The first part starts with the concept of “center,” demonstrating how it
is interwoven with notions of power. It links the multivalence of the concept of “center” with two
registers of exchange, where proficiency navigates and reinforces power: the cannibalistic system, in
which persons can be exchanged with each other, and the captaincy system, where persons are
interchangeable with nonhumans objects. The tension and partial overlap between these two registers
mirror the interplay and convergences between two mythological strata, pointing to conflicting ideas
about agency as either disseminated among group members or predominantly possessed by their
captains. This part also explores the power-infused practices of familiarization through which centers are
formed and individuals are shaped as members of specific clans and are attributed clan origins.
The second part explores how power is appropriated from the river source through processes of
familiarization of and mastery over key cultural elements—the maloca, manioc, tobacco, and coca—and
the prime notion of tne’túi to which the people at the center receive access through these elements. By
aligning the agency of these elements and the beings associated with them to their own, they draw on
these forces to prey on different beings and determine the direction of familiarization in exchanges with
them.

74

The third part, titled “Power in a Cosmos of Multiple Centers,” investigates the continuities between
power asymmetries: how those among human centers influence and are influenced by those involving
human and nonhuman centers, and how each set of asymmetries may instrumentalize the other. This is
exemplified by the Andoque’s notions of territoriality and “territorial management,” in their political
economy of knowledge, and in people’s efforts to utilize achievements in predation or familiarization of
nonhumans for aggressions or familiarization vis-à-vis other human beings, and vice versa. It
particularly emerges in ceremonial exchanges where both inter-human and human-nonhuman tensions
are dramatized and assuaged, with a contemporary inclination among Andoque captains and members
for dances that create and maintain asymmetrical affinal exchange with humans and nonhumans alike.
In the fourth part I turn to the river mouth, exploring the idioms of predation and affinity that the
Andoque employ for conceptualizing power relations with non-Indigenous agents, as well as their
efforts to act on these relations and how these relations impact the Andoque’s exchanges with nonhuman
entities. Here, previously explored elements of ontology, kinship, and space—namely, agnatic identity,
forces from the river source, and ontological manipulation, respectively—are key to the Andoque’s
successful navigation of the complex web of relationships that underpin both extractive and
preservationist economies.
The organization of the dissertation according to the Andoque’s power-laden spatial categories reflects a
prioritization of space over time, or, in other words, an encompassment of time by space. Therefore, I do
not necessarily examine different historical periods strictly in chronological order, but rather, I do so
whenever it is relevant to understanding the spatial category or spatialized dynamics under discussion.
For instance, in Part I, which focuses on the center and its associated fluvial systems, I explore the
Andoque’s demographic and cultural reconstruction following the early twentieth-century rubber
genocide up until the 1960s. This period is addressed here because it exemplifies a significant endeavor
to establish a consanguineous center primarily operating within the captaincy system. In part III,
dedicated the relationship between centers, I return to the history of kinship dynamics mainly from the
1960s onward—after the center constituted during post-genocide years disintegrated into its clan
components, or centers. Furthermore, I reserve the examination of the Andoque’s economic history to
Part IV, where I discuss their interactions with non-Indigenous agents connected to the river mouth,
agents who have pushed for and/or organized these economic activities. However, it is important to note
that the discussion of the river mouth in the final part of this dissertation does not imply that the contents

75

of the previous parts reflect some pre-contact or ahistorical reality. The Andoque’s cosmological
conceptions and cultural practices cannot be examined in isolation from the interactions with nonIndigenous agents and their Indigenous intermediaries in which the People of the Center have engaged
over the past two centuries. Therefore, I have endeavored to provide as complete a historicized picture
as possible of the various conceptions and practices that I discuss throughout the dissertation, whenever
I possessed sufficient information or a sound basis to form hypotheses.
Methodology
This dissertation is based on ethnographic fieldwork carried out between April 2018 and June 2019
within the Andoque ancestral territory, as well as interviews with Andoque migrants in Leticia in July
2019, and a field visit in the territory in July-August 2021. Additionally, between May and August 2023
I have conducted several video and in-person interviews with interlocutors in Bogotá and Leticia to
complement information. During my extended period of fieldwork, I rotated among seven Andoque
settlements, including the pluri-ethnic Araracuara, spending varying amounts of time in each settlement.
Over time, research interests, interpersonal dynamics with my hosts in each settlement, and different
circumstances in their lives, such as their travels and engagements, led me to primarily divide my time
between two settlements: Puerto Alegría, where the maloca of Fisi from the Eagle Clan is located, and
San José, the main settlement of the Sun Clan, where I stayed at the house of Tañe and Irene. This
strategic rotation enabled me to foster relationships and engage in conversations with members of all
clans. It exposed me to diverse versions of myths, ritual traditions, accounts of recent historical events,
interpretations of contemporary community politics, and even gossip, all of which are essential for
comprehending abstract notions of power and concrete power dynamics.
The emphasis on both “notions” and “dynamics” of power corresponds to this dissertation’s endeavor to
explore both Andoque discourse and practice. My overall discussion walks the fine line between
interlocutors’ discourse and insights drawn from myth narratives concerning Indigenous forms of power
and its possession, including ideal leadership and authority, on the one hand, and fieldwork observations
reflecting a historical moment marked by a near-total breakdown of Indigenous leadership and authority,
on the other. This breakdown occurs within the context of persistent asymmetries in exchange with nonIndigenous agents, including market actors and the State. Both traditional and modern Andoque
leadership (i.e., clan captains and elders and cabildo governors and members) are nowadays weak,
fragmented, and appears to fall short of the standards set by both the leaders and ordinary society

76

members. Furthermore, the knowledge required to establish and sustain power asymmetries became a
scarce symbolic resource following a genocide that eradicated many sages and oral traditions. As a
result, it is highly contested by individuals and clans today, and subject to intricate dynamics of
concealment and disclosure within the Andoque society that are symptomatic of their competitions over
power. My understanding of the intricate politics of knowledge among Andoque members, including
people’s choices regarding which kind of information they are willing to share with each other and those
they prefer to keep concealed, guided my ad hoc decisions during the drafting of this dissertation. I
considered whether, when discussing varying versions of myths, ritual traditions, or accounts of recent
events, I should disclose or anonymize the names of my source, in some cases employing pseudonyms
signaled as such with an asterisk (*). This approach aimed to strike a balance between acknowledging
my interlocutors for the invaluable knowledge they provided and avoiding any potential exacerbation of
internal disputes or competitions over knowledge.
My fieldwork consisted of participant observation, during which I joined household members in their
daily activities. These included gardening, preparing coca powder, gathering forest resources, fishing,
and, on rare occasions, hunting—an activity where my hosts shyly admitted that I was more of a
hindrance than an assistance. Additionally, I attended various events that were irregularly held,
including internal assemblies, meetings with external agencies, conventions of the regional
representative association, and activities financed by environmental organizations. At some of these
events, I served as a secretario, documenting the proceedings at the appointment of the Andoque.
Information was gathered both during these daily and irregular activities and in conversations at the
house on other occasions, particularly during the mambeadero sessions. My interlocutors frequently
expressed nostalgia for the past state of this nocturnal male social space, which they claimed was once
subject to a stricter etiquette. In the past, a hierarchy granted speech rights based on age and ritual status,
the gatherings were larger, sometimes with dozens of participants, and the frequency of elder visits were
higher. During these visits, dialogues between elders took place in specialized codes, effectively
excluding younger participants. While I would have been eager to attend and document a heavily
ritualized session, the less formal nature of today’s mambeaderos has offered some benefits for my
research. The smaller gatherings, typically no more than seven individuals, allowed for a more
comfortable atmosphere for engaging in conversation. This informality turned many mambeadero
sessions into opportunities for deliberate information sharing, either through the initiative of my
interlocutors, who introduced various myths and topics, or through my own, as I probed in-depth about
77

themes observed during daytime activities. These rather spontaneous mambeadero conversations
substituted for interviews, which were infrequent and mostly reserved for Andoque members in cities
where time was limited. Even these interviews were unstructured, resembling free-flowing
conversations where I steered the discussion towards specific questions I had prepared or themes I
intended to explore.
During my conversations with Andoque members, I collected myths from any willing narrator,
sometimes gathering various versions of the same myth. In my dissertation, I selected the most complete
version for clarity and endeavored to remain faithful to the original storyteller’s account. I incorporated
details from other interlocutors only when essential for understanding and provided they did not
contradict the chosen narrative. Additionally, I aimed to convey the Andoque’s polyphony by
acknowledging the existence of multiple versions and interpretations of each myth. On some occasions,
I included hypotheses about certain myths suggested by individuals who were not regarded—or did not
regard themselves—as authoritative, to illustrate the personal significance and varied interpretations of
these myths in people’s lives.
The centrality of mythology and its analysis in this dissertation mirrors the significance of mythical
narratives in the lives of the Andoque, particularly for their “charter” aspect, in Jacopin’s (2010)
abovementioned reformulation, as a conduit for transmitting agency and providing narrators and
listeners with “a social but non-normative vade mecum” (ibid, my translation). Drawing inspiration from
Percy Cohen’s (1969) view that different approaches to mythology complement and enhance each other,
I examine mythical narratives through structural, historical, sociological, psychological, and ritualrelated lenses. In the context of this research, I consider mythology as a medium through which the
Andoque justify, explore, and enact power relations with human and nonhuman beings.
My fieldwork was primarily conducted in the Spanish language, which is nowadays the predominant
spoken language among Andoque members. The Andoque rarely use their native language in
conversations with each other, and mastery of this language is, with a few exceptions, limited to people
over fifty years old, who often opt for using Spanish even in their interactions with each other. I mostly
encountered Andoque conversations on rare occasions when Andoque elders visited each other’s
mambeadero. Younger members have a passive understanding of the Andoque language and are familiar
with various concepts and terms in the language, ritual formulae, and names of different species, ownerpersons, and places. However, this knowledge is rarely accompanied by the ability to engage in

78

conversations in Andoque, whether on daily matters or within a mambeadero setting. Due to these
factors, I abandoned my attempts to learn Andoque as a spoken language after the initial few weeks of
fieldwork. Instead, I focused on specific inquiries into words, concepts, and ritual formulas pertinent to
my research, which remain recognized and meaningful even to those who are not fluent in Andoque.
Furthermore, I recorded, transcribed, and translated various ceremonial songs and several central myths
in the native language with the assistance of Andoque members. These practices contributed to my
understanding of this language and facilitated passive comprehension of certain conversations that I
encountered.
In my conversations with both elders and younger interlocutors in Spanish, I aimed to “control
equivocations.” This approach, as defined by Viveiros de Castro, refers to the awareness of speakers
embedded in different ontological registers that the same shared sign may actually refer to different
objects in each of these registers (2004). To achieve this, I carefully paid attention to the semantic,
pragmatic, and contextual aspects of their use of different Spanish terms. I also inquired about the
Andoque terms they would use if the conversation were conducted in that language, along with the
nuanced messages these native terms might convey.
However, it is important to acknowledge the limitations resulting from my lack of proficiency in the
Andoque language. This limitation prevented in-depth research into etymologies, morphology, and
semantics, which could have further illuminated the main concepts, notions, and mythical narratives that
I analyzed. Additionally, I could not factor in members’ use of pragmatic elements crucial to
establishing authority, such as the modalities of knowledge through which speakers indicate their
relation to the narrated information (Landaburu 2007). Nonetheless, it is worth noting that these forms
of establishing authority are scarcely used in contemporary times due to decline in native language use
and might not even be recognized as such by many Andoque members who possess limited knowledge
of the language, potentially diminishing their effectiveness.
Another limitation arises from restricting fieldwork to just one Indigenous group, which is part of a
regional network of exchanges with other Indigenous and non-Indigenous participants, while only
marginally engaging with non-Andoque individuals. This ethnic bias led to incomplete and
asymmetrical information regarding the Andoque’s matrimonial and ceremonial exchanges with their
neighbors. Complementing this information with similar accounts by these neighbors could have
provided deeper insights into the Andoque’s role in the regional power dynamics.

79

This dissertation exhibits a noticeable gender bias since the majority of my interlocutors, particularly
those who dedicated long hours to explaining cosmology, myth, and ritual, were men. I was promptly
welcomed into men’s mambeaderos, where my daily work of preparing coca powder earned me the
knowledge they generously shared. By contrast, I quickly discovered that interacting with young or
married women might lead to inconveniences with their family members, such that my substantial and
detailed conversations with female members were limited to two elders, in contrast to the broader age
range of my male interlocutors. Despite my inquiries into garden work and other female actitivies and
knowledge, the absence of full integration into these pursuits—akin to my involvement in men’s
activities—resulted in a relative dearth of information on these topics and on female concepts of power
that are undeniably associated with them. Furthermore, I learned that the practical aspects of mythical
narratives yield slightly different versions tailored for individuals of distinct genders. Consequently, I
was not exposed to the same myth versions shared with girls before marriage, pregnant women, or
young mothers. It is evident that a woman anthropologist would likely have gained access to different
information, which could complement or challenge some of my interpretations.
While I was fortunate to be surrounded by both elder and younger members who were generally willing
to share their experiences and insights, their cosmo-politics of knowledge often imposed certain
limitations on the information that they were willing to divulge. I refer here to the logic discussed in
Chapters 8 and 9, according to which the voicing of names of powerful entities, or the recitation of
mythical narratives and ceremonial songs invoking such entities, require specific ritual procedures or
even ceremonial dances; otherwise, these entities might retaliate against the speaker or their family.
References made by members to the risks involved in revealing their origin myths (as explored in
Chapter 10) or to fellow members who lost spiritual and ritual capabilities after disclosing knowledge of
different myths or ritual procedures to external researchers in the past (as discussed in Chapter 13),
suggested that certain information was withheld from me to prevent similar vulnerabilities or a loss of
power. Consequently, I refrained from pressing for certain kinds of information, such as specific healing
formulae or procedures to establish contact with owner-persons. During my fieldwork, I respected these
boundaries, guided by a similar perspective to that articulated by Rubenstein, who noted that “my task as
an anthropologist was not to uncover the truths behind a secret but to understand the power of the secret”
(2004, 1058). Certainly, the process of analyzing the collected data and subsequent writing compels the
ethnographer to explore and extend the information provided by the interlocutors by formulating
hypotheses and unveiling concealed patterns of thought, action, and narrative—efforts driven by our
80

academic “will to power” along with its interconnected desire to make the world comprehensible and
thereby governable, hopefully for legitimate purposes. I hope that my resulting interpretation remained
within the boundaries set by my Andoque friends and interlocutors, and that they do not perceive this
research as undermining the very power that I sought to study.

81

82

Part I
Power at the Center

83

84

Introduction
This dissertation employs the cosmo-spatial framework of the Andoque—a people self-identifying, like
other groups of Caquetá-Putumayo sub-region, as “People of the Center”—to explore their notions and
dynamics of power. Consequently, in order to analyze the Andoque conception of power within this
framework, it is essential to unpack the concept of the “center”: dʉi. The chapters in Part I address the
question: How does the concept of “center” permeate and inform other key notions, elements, practices,
and institutions in Andoque society that are relevant to understanding Andoque notions of power?
Scholars exploring analogous concepts related to the notion of “center” among neighboring peoples
have highlighted its spatial, corporal, moral, and ontological connotations (Echeverri 2022; García 2018;
Karadimas 2005; Londoño Sulkin 2012; Lucas 2018). Similarly, the word dʉi in the Andoque language
goes beyond its spatial meaning and also signifies “true,” “real,” and “proper” (verdadero, propio).
Thus, the root dʉ appears in constructions that convey the veracity of a particular assertion (dʉiǵ,
“indeed”) or the correct timing of fruits’ maturation on a specific tree, which then qualifies it as a
“proper” tree. Like other People of the Center, the Andoque consider themselves “real humans,” because
they reside at the very “center,” a place inhabited by morally upright humans who exemplify proper
human behavior. These real humans are contrasted with animals as well as with the “People of
Animals”—the Indigenous groups living along the Mirití, Apaporis, and Vaupes Rivers (Karadimas
2005a, 71; Londoño Sulkin 2000), who engage in balanced reciprocal exchange with affinal relatives
and with animals perceived as such (Descola 1998; 2013, 345–52). As we will explore further below,
the concept of dʉi is closely associated with that of origin: the place and process through which persons
come into being and acquire their physical bodies. Things, people, animals, and plants are considered
“proper” when they inhabit their original site or territory and act in accordance with their origins, as
recorded in mythology. This relativistic and somewhat universal notion suggests that everything
possesses its own center. However, as Echeverri astutely notes regarding common perceptions
throughout the Caquetá-Putumayo sub-region, this universal characteristic of “center” is often
contradicted by another attribute, as the concept provides “an irreducible principle of ethnic identity
(‘We are the People of the Center, and only us’)” (Echeverri 1997, 201; cf. Londoño Sulkin 2012, 6).7

Contrary to other Amazonian societies such as the Araweté and the Yanomami (Kelly 2011, 169–70; Viveiros de Castro
1992, 4; idem 2001, 27), the center among the People of the Center indicates identity and essence, such that they are not
societies “without an interior” (Viveiros de Castro 1992, 4). Inasmuch as the identity of the “center” heavily draws on the
alterity of the “river source,” as we will shortly see, this alterity is domesticated and encompassed by a notion of essence.

7

85

For the Andoque, the concept of dʉi carries a deictic value. While each one has their own center, there is
only one “true” center for any given person—the place where they are located, from which they speak,
and ideally, the place from which they originated. Dʉi thus functions as a perspectival deixis (Viveiros
de Castro 1998) that indicates the spatially-conditioned human nature of the speaker and inevitably
measures the proximity or distance of other beings from this human nature.
As is evident from the emphasis placed on the god Egret of the Center (Dʉiyo’fí), the archetype of
chiefly authority, within Andoque mythical narratives (Landaburu 1993; Landaburu and Pineda 1984;
Pineda Camacho 1975), it is clear that Andoque members themselves highlight the political connotations
associated with the concept of the center more explicitly than their neighboring peoples. This finding
aligns with research conducted on other Amazonian societies, which also identify the center as the seat
of power and authority (Goldman 2004, 348–55; Heckenberger 2005). Within various contexts, the
Andoque convey the idea that what is considered “proper” (dʉi) to one holds the potential to both
empower and jeopardize them. For instance, tutelary ceremonial dances provide protection to those who
receive a name within them and those who organize them in an appropriate manner. These dances
bestow individuals with the power to interact with both the human and nonhuman realms, making these
dances inherently “proper” to these individuals. However, inadequate performance of a “proper” dance
places the organizer at significant risk precisely because the dance is intimately connected to their
personal development and power. Furthermore, certain dances are regarded as more “proper” to specific
individuals because their origin sites are closer to the origin sites of these individuals’ clans.
This leads us to delve into the spatial dimensions of dʉi and to an interconnected question: What
characterizes the nature of the space of which dʉi is the center? At its core, dʉi can be translated as
“middle.” For instance, dʉipoo refers to midnight, while dʉinńkńn denotes midday. The term, along with
its equivalents in other languages spoken by the People of the Center, carries a dual spatial meaning. On
one hand, it signifies the inland or terra firme region situated away from the main rivers and floodplains,
and, on the other, it denotes any middle point along the river, not at the extremes (Echeverri 1997, 22;
Lucas 2018, 193). While the first meaning of dʉi is defined by environmental criteria that are relatively
rigid, the second meaning functions as a spatial deixis through which the speaker refers to their position
along the river axis, locating other people and places either upstream or downstream from their own
position (Landaburu 1985, 35–36). The entire Andoque linguistic system revolves around the fluvial
axis, which also corresponds to altitude and to the sun’s movement from east to west. The verbal prefix

86

yi- indicates actions directed towards the river source, which is higher than the speaker and towards the
west. Conversely, the prefix si- signals actions directed towards the river mouth, which is lower than the
speaker and towards the east (ibid). The two other cardinal points along this fluvial axis are obai (river
source) and oká (river mouth). These points also serve as spatial deixes. Rather than indicating specific
locations places where the river starts or ends, obai can refer to anything or anyone situated upstream
and higher from the speaker, towards the west, while okɒ́ can point to anything or anyone located
downstream and lower from the speaker, towards the east (ibid, 35–36). For the Andoque people, who
reside in the Middle Caquetá, Egret of the River Source (Obaiyo’fí) symbolizes leadership from upriver,
the Indigenous peoples living there and as far as the Andes, and Colombians in general. Egret of the
River Mouth (Okɒ́yo’fí), on the other hand, represents leadership from downriver, the Indigenous
peoples living there, Brazil and the Brazilians, the Amazon, the ocean towards which it flows, and
Whites in general, who arrived from that direction. Presently, the Andoque primarily refer to the second
spatial meaning of “center.” As a result, this dissertation’s analysis of the Andoque notion of center is
firmly grounded in the fluvial axis on which this center is positioned.
However, in this second meaning as a middle point along a river, dʉi is also a multivalent concept. In his
exploration of historical dynamics among the People of the Center, Echeverri pointed out “the
permutations in the center.” These are the diverse values, including mythical figures and ritual and work
instruments, that these peoples have associated with the concept of “center” over the course of their
recent history, spanning at least 150 years (Echeverri 2022, 112–13). Echeverri argues that these
permutations revolve around the distinction between an exogamic process and open system on the one
hand, and an endogamic process and closed system on the other (ibid). However, I find the distinction
between exogamy and endogamy to be an inadequate framework for comprehending the “permutations
of the center” among the Andoque, and I will limit my explanation to three points. Firstly, exogamic
dimensions, such as inter-clan (and, to a lesser extent, inter-ethnic) matrimonial alliances, are integral to
the pre-genocide system that Echeverri characterizes as endogamic. Conversely, the period following
recuperation has witnessed a pronounced tendency toward ethnic endogamy (see Chapter 4). Secondly,
Echeverri categorizes the two Andoque terms for Whites, “Burners” (duiɵ́hɵ) and “Traders” (dohaɵ́hɵ),
into the respective processes. He associates “Burners” with the endogamic process and “Traders” with
the exogamic one. However, it is noteworthy that both terms appear in the same Andoque myth (see
below, M5), challenging this strict categorization. Thirdly, the stone axe, positioned by Echeverri within

87

the endogamic process, is, to my knowledge, entirely absent from the ancient Andoque mythological
stratum.
However, the notion of “permutations of the center” is useful for exploring the multivalence of the
concept of “center.” As Echeverri notes based on Landaburu (1993), Egret of the Center is associated
with one meaning of “center,” while the eagle god Nénéfi (or Ñé’ñéfi) is linked to an arguably more
ancient one. Indeed, the Andoque recognize two layers in their mythology. The first comprises “Human
Beings’ Stories” (historias de gente), also referred to by maloqueros as “Captaincy Stories” (historias de
capitanía). These stories primarily focus on the mutual visits and occasional conflicts involving three
egret characters. Contemporary Andoque elders often credit these stories for their wisdom. The second
layer consists of “Animal Stories” (historias/cuentos de animales), typically associated with sorcerers
and tricksters. In these tales, various animal heroes engage with each other, often deceitfully,
lasciviously, or aggressively. Landaburu (1993) suggests that the egret mythology represents a more
recent, horizontalized adaptation of the older animal mythology. He interprets the parallelism between
the three egret heroes—whom he believes symbolize entire collectives—and their relatively peaceful
interactions as a departure from the vertical predatory dynamics that define that ancient mythic layer.
As presented by Landaburu, the distinction between the two kinds of myths roughly corresponds to the
opposition among other People of the Center, between the “Basket of Life,” which contains peaceful
discourse and myths and wisdom words propelling human sociality and regional conviviality suited for
the post-genocide “Time of Abundance,” and the “Basket of Darkness” which contains cannibal and
bellicose discourse that was common before the rubber genocide, during the “Time of Animals”
(Echeverri 2010; Lucas 2019, 115–40). As Echeverri and Lucas observe for the Murui-Muina,
Féénemɨna and Bora, people are reluctant to delve into the Basket of Darkness and relegate the
knowledge it contains to private mambeadero sessions. In contrast to their neighbors, the Andoque do
not utilize “basket” as a metaphor for knowledge, and the two kinds of stories do not imply mutual
exclusivity as the basket metaphor would suggest. During my fieldwork I observed how individuals
vacillate between these two mythical registers, as Animal Stories or elements found in them kept
appearing in mambeadero sessions, casual conversations, dream interpretations, and evaluations of
social, political, and economic actions in which people engage.
Therefore, I argue that the two mythical strata encode two distinct cosmological and political economic
fluvial systems of exchange, in each of which the concept of “center,” in its meaning as the midpoint

88

along a river, carries a different value. To characterize these systems, I borrow the terms
“heterosubstitution” and “homosubstitution,” originally employed to denote the possibility, in a given
society, of substituting nonhuman entities for humans, or the impossibility thereof, with the
corresponding limitation that one human can only be substituted by another human (Descola 2001;
Godelier 1982). According to Descola, homosubstitution is typical of native Amazonia, while
heterosubstitution characterizes Melanesian societies, where humans can be exchanged for non-human
entities. This distinction is evident in practices such as bride wealth and homicide compensation, which
involve the exchange of pigs and other objects and are prevalent in Melanesia but are mostly absent
from Lowland South America, except among the Wayuu and Mapuche. In these latter societies, cattle,
acquired through contact with the Spanish, replace humans in similar contexts (Descola 2001, 110–13).
My use of these two terms aligns with that of Stephen Hugh-Jones (2013, 368), who refers to
heterosubstitution as the exchange of elements of different kinds and homosubstitution as the exchange
of elements of the same kind. This underscores heterosubstitutive practices in Amazonia as well, such as
the exchange of items and substances that embody aspects of their givers and producers, acting as their
extensions and substitutes, and the occasional exchange of valuables for women (ibid, 370–71).
Accordingly, I view the exchange system encoded in Animal Stories as the homosubstitutive system,
and the system encoded in the egret mythology as the heterosubstitutive system. Based on the
Andoque’s perceived contrast between cannibalism and captaincy, which will be explored below, I refer
to these systems as the cannibalistic and captaincy systems, respectively.
In the homosubstitutive-cannibalistic system, persons—of both the human and nonhuman kinds—are
exchanged and consumed in order to generate other persons. The fluvial axis of this system heavily
relies on vertical metaphors. The headwaters, seen as closer to the sky and the stars, is considered to be
populated by predatory beings like jaguars and eagles. In contrast, the river mouth is associated with the
ground and underground levels, and inhabited by forest game animals, aquatic beings, and the deceased
in the underworld. On the other hand, the heterosubstitutive-captaincy system is defined through the
interchangeability of persons for other items. This system reproduces the well-attested regional
association between the river mouth and Whites and Indigenous people serving as brokers in trade with
them (Echeverri and Pereira 2005; Lucas 2018, 27–30), and involves the notion of exchangeability
between individuals and metal axes (Echeverri 2022, 100–101). It is noteworthy that, as with the Wayuu
and Mapuche cases, this convertibility strongly applies to objects obtained through contact or exchange
with non-Indigenous agents, suggesting that the drive to generalize the heterosubstitutive principle into a
89

spatial system originated from interactions with them. However, the substitution of vegetal offerings for
game animals is equally rooted in the captaincy system and relates to the broader association between
the river source, the patriline, ancestral knowledge, and horticulture, which is sparsely documented or
not documented at all among neighboring groups. Contrary to Descola’s assertion that Amazonians do
not explicitly draw homologies between body parts or physiological substances, on the one hand, and
artifacts and natural kinds, on the other (2001, 112), the exchangeability within this system is expressed
through the equation made by neighboring peoples and the Andoque, as we will explore, between a
human being and an axe, and in myths in which humans originated from cultivars.
In this first part of the dissertation, I aim to highlight both the tension and partial overlap between these
two systems while exploring the different meanings that the concept of dʉi acquires within each system.
Additionally, I will demonstrate that, similar to other Amazonian notions of meta-affinity, the Others
within each system, particularly those associated with the extreme points of the fluvial axis (i.e., river
source and river mouth), are considered potential affines. By contrast, the center is formed through
power-laden practices of familiarization, which ideally establish a sense of conviviality and
harmlessness among members of a particular group. These practices encompass name giving, nurturing,
the shaping of bodies, and work efforts aimed at producing abundant food. By examining the various
notions, elements, practices, and institutions associated with the concept of “center” in each system—
ranging from body, clan, and name to language and axes—this first part provides an initial topology of
the notion of power within the Andoque cosmos and society. The insights gained here will serve as a
foundation for further discussions in subsequent chapters.
In the first two chapters, I examine the two fluvial systems and the meaning that dʉi acquires from the
relations it maintains with the river source and river mouth within each system. I show that in each, the
center is associated with two distinct aspects: the ability to halt exchange and to participate in it as a
subject rather than object. I suggest viewing these aspects as the preconditions for the employment of
power as defined in this dissertation, i.e., engaging in beneficial asymmetric exchange. In Chapter 3, I
explore the interrelated notions of formation, origin, and clan. I discuss how persons are shaped and
integrated into these centers and how these centers sustain themselves, primarily through the practice of
name giving, which assigns newborns to a specific clan origin. Lastly, Chapter 4 investigates a crucial
process of center formation in Andoque recent history: their recovery from the rubber genocide that
occurred during the first three decades of the twentieth century.

90

Chapter 1. The Egret Universe and Its Center
Egret of the Center
Egret of the Center plays a significant role in the egret mythology and is highly esteemed in
contemporary Andoque discourse. It is believed that Egret of the Center resides in Mnfɵsíkn (Site of
Tears/Site of Rage), a rock formation located at the headwaters of several rivers within the Andoque
territory. This figure is seen as the embodiment of the center and the people living there and is often
likened to Jesus or a manifestation of Jesus specific to that region, serving as a mediator between human
beings and the Creator. While yo’fí, in its plain sense, refers to the great white egret (Ardea alba), Fisi
Andoque, the cacique and highest traditional authority, interprets Duiyo’fí as “Mature Mouth of the
Center.” This is a mouth that produces words that are as mature as a fully developed organism or an
accomplished person. While this etymology is grammatically possible, it remains uncertain (Jon
Landaburu, pers. comm., November 2022). Nonetheless, it provides insights into Fisi’s understanding of
the attributes associated with this deity, which he considers as a role model for the captaincy position.
The word dʉi not only associates this mature mouth with the center but also describes it as a “true”
mature mouth. Fisi further explains that the extended version of the name, which is Duiyo’hafisé,
translates as “the Center’s/True Mature Advice.” In the mythical register, yo’fí signifies captain. In the
contemporary local interpretation, this word conveys the notion that a captain’s words hold immense
weight, to the extent that physical force is unnecessary, resonating with common Amazonian
manifestations of political power as persuasive, rather than coercive (e.g., Clastres 1989), and, more
specifically, with the “arbitrational function” of leadership, which fosters conviviality among group
members (Kracke 1978, 84). The plans and desires of a captain manifest through his people’s actions,
influencing human and nonhuman interlocutors without resorting to violence.8 This expressive virtue is
connected to the term used in everyday contexts to refer to flesh-and-blood captains, or maloqueros:
po’soo. This term translates to “the famous” or “the resounding,” alluding to the sounds of grinding coca
in the maloca’s mortar, of playing the manguaré (ku’dɨ; a pair of monoxyl drums) for ritual and general
communication purposes and playing the multiplying beam (tu’sí) in the eponymous dance.
