No doubt, the egret’s long beak (fí, like mouth) is one of the reasons for which it assumes this role of a
“mature worded leader.” It also assumes this role for its ambulatory nature, as it is often spotted along
the banks of the main rivers on its way up or downriver, an ethological trait that leads the Andoque, like
the Bora, to evoke the egret in myths about war and exchange with other agents along these rivers
(Guyot 1972, 164).
The story “the Coca of the Animals” (M1, see Appendix 1), teaches us about the qualities that egret
figures should ideally possess, such as intelligence, diligence, decorum, self-restraint, and agility. In this
story, Egret (Yo’fí) embodies these virtues during his mission for proper coca powder preparation and
consumption, unlike the other animal figures who fail to perform the different tasks of the process and

92

receive undesirable bodily forms upon consuming this substance. Egret perceives things as they truly are
and is not deceived by the illusions that abound in the forest, where the daughter of Shadow Egg
(Ká’hoihádi) sends her men to gather yarumo leaves for ashes to mix with coca powder. If mischievous
animal figures had not intervened, Egret’s success in coca preparation would have resulted in the
voluntary surrender of coca to humanity by its original mistress, so that men today would be able to
benefit from the plant without the many restrictions accompanying it.
Egret of the Center is the “true” egret-leader (dʉi) among other such figures. Captains attribute their
power to this figure, with whom they communicate in order to gather and lead people and manage the
territory in a manner that enables prosperity, reproduction, and protection from diseases and other
harms. The power of Egret of the Center, in turn, hinges on the proper utilization of coca. In certain
instances, as depicted in the myth “Coca of the Orphans” as relayed to Landaburu and Pineda by Yiñékɒ
(“Feverish Fluff”)(M2, see Appendix 1)—the Andoque captain after the genocide and during their
research, from the Eagle Clan—the coca plant is depicted as the posthumously-transformed Egret of the
Center. In this myth, the two orphaned sons of Egret of the Center identify the coca plant as their father
transformed and reconnect with his wisdom and instructions upon preparing and consuming the coca
powder. They then interpret a thunder as a warning given by their father, to whom they refer as
Carnivorous Thunder (Sḭ́ di Dú’di), of an imminent flood from the east.
I have been told this story several times in different versions. In one version, Egret of the Center is not
portrayed as the father but as the younger brother who acknowledges that the coca is the transformed
father. In another version, which was told by members of the Sun Clan, the father is Egret of the River
Source, and his son is Egret of the Center, who was born on the Andoque territory. Seated at this upriver
maloca, Egret of the River Source saw in his vision how his son was sitting by himself at his maloca
without coca, “like a woman.” He then ordered his wife, Egret of the Center’s mother, to give their son
coca, a plant that would endow the latter with appropriate thinking and help him create human beings—
namely, the Andoque themselves. The mother gave him the plant, which was, in fact, the father, with
instructions on how to use it. After consuming the coca, Egret of the Center learned through dreams how
to create the Andoque people. When he woke up, he gave names to fruits and cultivars that exist today,
the ones for human consumption, because hitherto there were only wild fruits, which belonged to the
animals. He asked his mother to prepare manicuera drink, and the mother herself turned into the manioc

93

species for manicuera. Then, he created the Andoque people. He is the one who controls their territory,
and he still lives there.
Egret of the River Source
In another myth (M3, see Appendix 1), the origin of coca and all other garden cultivars is credited to
Egret of the River Source. Wishing to live with the Shadow Egg’s daughter, he overcomes the father-inlaw’s ruses through self-restraint, constructs a maloca, and clears a forest plot for a garden. He then
returns to the river source, and the thunder he emits signals to Shadow Egg to burn the cleared plot. In
response, his mother, the Lady Beetle of Life (Pḭɵfikn), scatters all the garden cultivars from the sky,
and serves caguana and manicuera beverages to her daughter-in-law, enabling her to give birth to a boy
and then a girl. When the wife peels the manioc, the tuber sounds “po!”, foretelling that her son will
become a captain. Egret of the River Source shares tobacco and coca with Shadow Egg and his men and
initiates a dance. After the first song, while sitting on his seat (kupa) at the mambeadero, his name
changes from Egret of the Source to Egret of the Center. He then says:9 “I am Egret of the Center. We
are going to consume coca, we are going to lick tobacco. Yes. This is my name. I am from the Center of
the Earth […].”
Similar to this first maloquero and garden owner, upon whose design the first man and woman were
created through the mediation of manioc, a captain ideally transforms his men into real human beings,
hɵ́ihɵ́, by planting and raising them (yi…pií) like cultivars (koisé) in the garden (e.g., Landaburu and
Pineda 1984, 234). As I show in Part II, the maloca that Egret of the River Source created and the
cultivars associated with him are fundamental to the processes of thinking, relating to others, acting on
various entities in one’s environment, and managing the territory, thereby playing a crucial role in
acquiring and exercising power at the Center.
In a heterosubstitutive logic, the cultural elements that Egret of the River Source brings replace him.
After erecting the maloca, he returns upriver instead of consummating his matrimony to Shadow Egg’s
daughter. Rather than fertilizing his wife through his own bodily fluids, he accomplishes it through the
rain resulting from the deliberate burning of the garden, which he instructed his father-in-law to
perform. This rain then showers down his mother’s cultivars upon the land at the center (analogous to
his wife’s body). Instead of a direct sexual activity, which is associated with predation, Egret of the

River Source opts for the practice of the gift—the rain and cultivars, which serve as metonyms for him.
On the other hand, the caguana and manicuera beverages, prepared by his mother, operate in the
opposite direction as nonhuman elements that catalyze the creation of human children. We may thus see
this story as setting the exchange rate between persons and cultivars and the power to exchange one for
the other.
Another elder who recounted me this story told me that it was Egret of the Center, not Egret of the River
Source, who created the pui roof, while others confuse on different occasions these two egret-figures.
The relationship between them, whether it is either affiliation or transformation, points to a certain
consubstantiality. Although the notion of transformation might imply a diachronic shift between them,
where Egret of the River Source ceases to exist upon assuming the name Egret of the Center, people
emphasize that Egret of the River Source remains in his original dwelling place on Hummingbird Hill
(Pá̰di Tuɒ́i), a hill of the canyon of Angusturas on the Caquetá River, upriver from Araracuara.
Nonetheless, Egret of the River Source maintains a certain alterity in relation to Egret of the Center, an
alterity which is considered constitutive of the Center and its powers.
We may interpret Egret of the River Source as an embodiment of the “stranger-king” figure: an outsider
to his subjects who possesses superior power and ultimately civilizes them (Graeber and Sahlins 2017,
5–7). However, in the Andoque case, the Amazonian tendency to appropriate alterity is evident,
resulting in a more dialectical process of assimilation. From the perspective of the center, Egret of the
River Source, who is an affine from upriver, becomes familiarized through the mythical narrative, in the
end of which he is called Egret of the Center. Within the narrative, it can be seen as an act of selfaffinization, as he assumes this name, containing the location of his wife’s family, once he relocates
there. Egret of the River Source thus becomes an ancestor for the people living at the center, and that
fluvial deixis is associated with ancestry and origin. According to Pineda (1979, 45 n.4), the association
with the long-beaked hummingbird (pá̰di) and Hummingbird Hill also carries ancestral connotations, as
the word is composed of “semen” (pá̰) and “penis” (di).10 Egret of the River Source represents the proto10

We find echoes of a Murui-Muina association of patrilineal ancestry and the upstream direction, contrasting with the
feminine affinal world and its association with downstream, in García’s discussion of the division among this people. The
Murui, who live upstream in masculine malocas of five pillars, claim a direct link to the Creator Father Juziñamui. On the
other hand, the Muina, who live downstream in feminine malocas of four pillars, claim communication with Juziñamui’s son,
Buinaima (García 2018, 159). This Andoque and Murui-Muina association of ancestry with the river source contrasts with
the ancestral anaconda’s ascent upstream from the river mouth in Tukanoan and Arawakan origin myths. In those myths, the
anaconda drops sib ancestors along the rivers, and the settlement pattern follows with elder sibs living downriver from

95

Egret of the Center—proto-leadership, proto-self-restraint, proto-intelligence, and proto-diligence—but
he only becomes real, dʉi, once he is seated on his seat, in his mambeadero, at his maloca: at the very
deictic center from an Andoque narrator’s point of view. His familiarization represents the full
incorporation by the Andoque of the elements he brought, and their control over the reproduction of
these elements. In Dumont’s (2013) terms, it is an action of hierarchical encompassment, where the term
“center” contains the key components of “river source.”
However, the version of the myth recorded by Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 165–76) presents an
additional perspective on the direction of familiarization. In this version, the narrator Yiñékɒ emphasizes
the moments when Egret of the River Source provided Shadow Egg with coca and tobacco, especially
before the celebration of the dance where he would assume his new name (ibid, 172–73). Anticipating
our later discussions in Part II regarding how the provision of these substances to others instills in them
benevolent dispositions toward the donor, we can assert that Egret of the River Source familiarizes
Shadow Egg and his household members by providing them coca and tobacco. In this way he manages
to become their leader and teacher and engage them as his workers in his designs. This is evident, for
example, in his provision of food for the house posts, identified as his wife’s relatives (ibid, 175). Thus,
we witness here dialectics of familiarization: the river source is familiarized by the center as part of the
same process through which the center is familiarized by the river source. Nevertheless, Egret of the
River Source’s assumption of the name “Egret of the Center” is critical, indicating that difference is put
to the service of identity, and not vice versa, contrary to Viveiros de Castro’s observations for the
Araweté and other Amazonian societies (1992, 4; 2001, 27).
Egret of the River Mouth
Such familiarization does not occur in relation to Egret of the River Mouth. In various myths, the river
mouth is portrayed as extremely hostile, and the corresponding egret represents perverse leadership and
worthless advice. In a key myth called “The War of the Speaking Tree,” whose contours I summarize
here (M4; Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 56–57), this war begins after Egret of the River Mouth visits
younger sibs (S. Hugh-Jones 1993, 238–39; C. Hugh-Jones 1979, 239; Goldman 2004, 90). Interestingly, according to
Elizabeth Reichel, the settlement pattern of the Arawak-speaking Yucuna, who are the people of the Vaupés-Apaporis area
living the closest to the People of the Center, aligns more closely with the latter’s association between ancestry and river
source, as elder sibs live upriver from younger sibs (Reichel 1989, 78–79; but see van de Hammen 1992, 30, 128). The
Tukanoan association of ancestry with downriver nevertheless does not preclude its association with the thunder and its
abode in the sky (S. Hugh-Jones 1993, 105)—which, for the Andoque, are continuous with the river mouth.

96

Egret of the Center. While returning home after being well received by his host, Egret of the River
Mouth crosses a log bridge over a stream where his host’s wife is bathing. Filled with desire, he cannot
help but gaze at her, leading him to fall off the bridge and nearly die. Egret of the Center saves him, but
Egret of the River Mouth cannot forgive the humiliation and sends the ruthless Speaking Tree
(Hɵɵ́idɨtákń) to disrupt life at the center. As Fisi told me, Egret of the River Mouth allowed himself to
be disturbed by the wife of his host at an earlier stage during his visit, as he sat facing his host and stared
at the female area of the maloca’s rear. Fisi concluded that visitors to a maloca should sit next to their
host, aligning their perspectives to look outward.
However, Egret of the River Mouth is not entirely negative, and the goods he possesses are desperately
needed. This is illustrated in M5, which narrates the origin of trade with Whites (see Appendix 1). The
myth recounts how the daughter of Egret of the Center engenders the dog, metal axe and other tools,
which are then appropriated by Trader Egret of the River Mouth (Okɒ́yo’fí Dohaɵ́hɵ), who also abducts
the woman, leaving the violent Burner Egret of the River Source (Obaiyo’fí Duiɵ́hɵ) both spouseless
and toolless. In response, her brother travels to the river mouth to negotiate for the return of some of
these essential goods, referred to in Andoque as kahɵ́ɵi, which literally means “our missing [things].”
This leads to a series of visits and exchanges, during which foodstuffs and beverages unique to each
party are traded as offerings (ɵtasé) and payments (ɵpáha), with Egret of the Center’s word “moving
forward” (yahuha hɵɵ́i) as he provides more foodstuffs than he receives. Finally, the two parties trade
work-essential goods for the rubber latex demanded by Egret of the River Mouth.
This story represents the Andoque’s understanding of their interactions with non-Indigenous people in
general and the dynamics of the rubber period in particular. It associates the river mouth with
manufactured goods, especially metal tools, acquired through direct or indirect exchange with nonIndigenous people. The myth follows a clear heterosubstitutive logic, evident from the beginning with
the engendering of nonhuman objects by a woman. This woman is eventually taken by a husbandcaptor. As will be discussed in Chapter 9, bride taking often establishes de facto matrimonial exchange,
as the asymmetrical transference of women requires a counter-transfer in the opposite direction, based
on the homosubstitutive principle that human life is compensated by another human life. However, when
the woman’s brother visits his brother-in-law, he does not seek marriageable women among his affinal
relatives. Instead, he requests some of the objects engendered by his sister, which can be seen as his
nephews, and, more precisely, marriageable nieces. These objects would contribute to the social

97

reproduction of his group in a similar way to how his sister contributed to the reproduction of her
husband’s group. In other words, humans (represented by the sister) are portrayed here as
interchangeable with merchandise, which itself it interchangeable with ritual substances, rubber, and
manioc sap, all of which can replace each other.11
In contrast with Egret of the River Source in M3, the affinal Egret of the River Mouth is never fully
familiarized and encompassed by the center. Instead, it is the metal axe and other merchandise, begotten
by a woman from the center, that become affinized. As a result, the people at the center lose control over
the reproduction of these objects and remain reliant on the river mouth to acquire them.
As we learn from M6, which recounts the origin of swidden work (see Appendix 1) and relayed to
Landaburu and Pineda by Yinñéfɵkn (“Striped Feather”), an Andoque man from the Eagle Clan who
had survived the genocide and was the eldest member of the community during their research, work
itself is associated with the river mouth. In this story, Egret of the River Mouth, also known as Axe
Egret (Pɵɵyo’fí) and Work Egret (Báőiyo’fí), wields his metal axe to fell trees in Sun’s (Ḭɒ̰) garden in
order to unite with the latter’s daughter. He evades predation by his father-in-law and manages to safely
cut down the most dangerous tree through the combination of a ruse and collaboration with various
figures. Upon narrating this myth, my interlocutors referred to the tree that Sun asked his daughter’s
suitors to fell as “Stone Tree” (fisidɨtákń), explaining that its fruits killed the suitors because they
transformed into stones when hitting them.
Through the metal axe, Axe Egret/Egret of the River Mouth embodies a significant aspect of leadership:
the capacity to coordinate work projects (particularly in clearing gardens), organize workers, as
demonstrated by Axe Egret’s management of animals in the story, and protect them during work, as
exemplified by his ability to safeguard himself from Sun’s harm.12 Thus, while the “mature mouth”
translation of yo’fí refers to the arbitrational function of leadership, or the rex leader type, in Kracke’s
(1978, 84) terminology, Axe Egret exemplifies the commotive function, or the dux leader type. Prior to
organizing collective work (fokaa), a captain shares the tale of Axe Egret to safeguard his workers from
potential mishaps, such as tree collapses, snake bites, and conflicts among workers. The captain’s
reputation and leadership heavily rely on motivating people for work (horticultural or otherwise) to

ensure abundance. This abundance, in turn, enables demographic growth and hospitality, which
enhances the captain and his people’s influence. It also facilitates the distribution of foodstuffs and other
substances to human and nonhuman beings, aiming to prevent conflicts and foster conviviality in diverse
contexts.
The goods and substances from the river source and the river mouth serve to both complement and
counter each other. While the work instruments obtained from the river mouth are essential for clearing
gardens and planting the cultivars appropriated from the river source, the substances derived from these
cultivars serve to counter negative elements originating from the river mouth, providing the center with
an advantageous position in exchanges with people from that direction.13 We will revisit this theme in
Part IV. For now, we turn to the significance of “center” within the context of this captaincy river
system.
On Axes, Captains, and Orphans
In a perspectival manner, we may say that, seen from the river source, the people at the center are
cultivars; seen from the river mouth, they are goods. However, the center in the heterosubstitutivecaptaincy system also embodies two qualities that reflect the preconditions for exercising power, as
defined in this dissertation: first, the capacity to refuse or suspend exchange, and second, the status of
being the exchanging agent, rather than the exchanged object. These are essential for affecting beneficial
asymmetrical exchange of different elements.
The suspension of exchange is symbolized by the autochthonous stone axe. According to M5 on the
origin of trade, the axes that were not taken by Egret of the River Mouth remained under Axe Hill. The
Andoque discovered deposits of stone axes in this and other sites of their territory, likely left behind by a
previous civilization. These axes were utilized for horticultural purposes prior to the introduction of the
metal axe. In mythology, those who discovered the stone axes are known as the “Piercers” (Yɒ’nnkń),14
proto-human heroes who navigated the Caquetá River and its tributaries, providing names to these
waterways, creating human language (albeit with mispronunciation from the perspective of
contemporary Andoque speakers, see Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 224–25, n.19), and healing the

Figure 5. A Murui-Muina Stone Axe. Source: Musée du quai Branly, Inventory no. 71.1975.26.60.

In a region where lithic materials are scarce, the significance of this resource cannot be overstated. The
axe plays a crucial role in horticultural work, which is central to maintaining a human identity. As
Griffiths (2001) argued in relation to the Nɨpóde, engaging in diligent labor and adhering to gardening
practices, as well as proper consumption of cultivars, serves as an ongoing affirmation of human identity
within a dualistic cosmology. According to this cosmology, human beings were bestowed with the
knowledge and tools necessary for swidden agriculture and the cultivation of “true” crops, while
malevolent beings were relegated to the bodily forms of game animals (ibid, 251–55).
As a potent instrument, the axe gave rise to the use of more abstract expressions of power in the
Andoque language, embodying the ability to act and to form and transform things and people. “I am
afraid of your axe” (hapɵɵ oyíta̋i), says the man who clears a new garden plot in the forest and
acknowledges the owner-person of that location, before demanding that that spirit show him the same
fear-respect in return, due to his own “axe,” or power (opɵɵ hayíta̋i, “you are afraid of my axe”). The
stone axes are also connected to humans as social beings participating in communal projects. As Pineda
cogently suggested, the limited effectiveness of stone axes necessitated large-scale communal efforts to
clear garden plots, whereas with the introduction of metal axes, clearing could be done by members of

fact, looked upon as veritable gifts from the gods” (1915, 94). For the story concerning the discovery of the stone axes, see
Pineda Camacho 1975, 474–75. For other achievements by the Piercers, see Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 204–10.

only one clan or even nuclear family (Pineda Camacho 1975, 457). However, at the group level, the
stone axe symbolizes economic autonomy, representing the autochthonous power to produce and sustain
social groups materially. This power translated into the ability to acquire various goods from other
Indigenous groups. Neighboring peoples attest that their ancestors obtained stone axes from the
Andoque before trade with the Whites became widespread (Guyot 1979, 103; Pineda Camacho 1975,
459). Moreover, the exonym Andoque, by which this people is known today, means “People of the Axe”
in the Murui-Muina language (Adokɨ; Thomas Griffiths, pers. comm., 2021).16 However, Landaburu
(1993, 151) seems to be correct in arguing that as a self-designation, “People of the Axe” (Pɵɵ Síɵ́hɵ),
which occupies a marginal place in mythology, became common after the rubber genocide, as part of
Yiñékɒ’s project to create a unified ethnic identity for the remaining speakers of the Andoque language
to transcend the history of conflicts among distinct clans. Tellingly, the construction of collective
identity centered around an object embodying self-sufficiency occurred during a period when the
Andoque were already integrated into global economy through rubber extraction and the consumption of
externally manufactured goods through the mediation of the rubber boss. However, in embodying selfsufficiency, the stone axe symbolizes the power to withdraw from potentially adverse exchange.
The axe is metonymic for people who engage in work using axes. “Lending someone an axe” signifies
joining him as collaborator in clearing a garden plot. In dreams, axes stand for people as workforce.17
However, this also includes metal axes. During the period of trade with Europeans and Brazilians from
downstream until the late nineteenth century, the metal axe, along with other items grouped under the
“axe” category, was not simply a metonymy for an Indigenous individual; it was the accepted exchange
value for them throughout the Caquetá-Putumayo region (Echeverri 2022, 100–101; Pineda Camacho
1985, 77–80). As is evident in the ancient songs from the region cited by Echeverri and Pineda and
expressing sorrow, fear, and critique of captains trading their people, a person would not want to be
traded for an axe (and the other merchandise for which it stands). This brings us to the second aspect of
the center in the heterosubstitutive-captaincy system: the vertical distinction between orphans and
captains.

“Orphans” (i’hɵ́ɵá síɵ́hɵ) is one of the terms used to designate the people living and working in a
maloca who are not consanguineous kin to the captain, in addition to the more general terms “workers”
(báɵ̋i síɵ́hɵ) and “youth” (yɨḛn síɵ́hɵ). These terms express different aspects of their position in relation
to the captain: juniority, availability as a workforce, and lack of agency. The concept of “orphans” is
common among the People of the Center. Since the captain is regarded as a father to his people, an
orphan is someone who has lost their captain for various reasons and has sought protection by joining
another maloca. In Lucas’ analysis of Bora kinship system, orphans are also classificatory nephews who
marry into a maloca, thereby becoming de facto “bereft” of their original captain-fathers and headed by
captains from another clan (Lucas 2019, 203–10; 2021). Therefore, the captain-orphan relationship
reflects the transformation of asymmetrical affinity into asymmetrical consanguinity through a metaaffiliative adoption relationship, forming a type of master-pet dynamic (Costa and Fausto 2019; Fausto
2008, 333). Lucas convincingly demonstrates that orphanhood exists along a gradient, where a person’s
degree of orphanhood in relation to the captain varies, ranging from being a direct descendant of the
captain to being his son-in-law to being held as a war captive in his maloca. The level of control exerted
by the captain and the services expected from the individual increase as they become “more orphan,”
while the nurturing and protection they receive from the captain diminish (Lucas 2021, 16). According
to Lucas, orphans occupy a liminal space between humanity and animality, and joining a maloca is their
way of securing their existence as social, human beings (ibid, 14–15). As marginalized members of their
host clans, they were the ones who were traded for manufactured goods in the past, but their
incorporation into malocas after the genocide facilitated processes of recovery (Echeverri 2022, 96,
112–13; see also Chapter 4).
In Andoque, ’ihɵ́ɵ means “one for whom there is absence,” thus i’hɵ́ɵá síɵ́hɵ can be understood as
“people of absence” or “people in need.” They assume a role marked by lack and submissiveness
relative to the captain, who personifies the collective agency of his people and the nonhuman entities he
engages for their benefit (see Chapter 5). Orphanhood is an acquired condition. As Oiara Bonilla (2005)
observes for the Paumari, submissiveness towards non-Indigenous bosses can reflect agency,
particularly in neutralizing predatory dangers by eliciting the superior’s pity and care. Similarly,
Andoque orphans sought the protection of captains from various human and nonhuman dangers,
including from the captain’s own predatory potential. However, Bonilla’s claim that the Paumari’s
capacity for submission acts as a predatory weapon (ibid, 59) may be overstretched for the Andoque
orphans, whose status in the past could lead to their exchange as slaves (ḭnhḛ́sói). Orphans thus lack
102

predatory agency, and reversing this status requires reclaiming such agency. For example, in the myth of
the orphan pipe blower (M7, see Appendix 1), this character, residing in the maloca of his maternal
relatives who have killed his father, regains his agency by obtaining a phallic weapon associated with
his paternal lineage—namely, the blowpipe of his father, which his mother has hidden from him.
The captain-orphan relationship can be further understood by comparison with the relationship between
a pet, ḭéna̰, and its owner, ḭ́ ’ɵsiɵ́ɵhɵ. The pet is typically of a different species or bodily form from the
owner. While it is fed (ɵsé) by and accompanies (ɵʼɵhɵ/ḭ́ ’ɵ́ɵhɵ) the owner, the pet maintains its
alienness and agency, which the master utilizes. Yet, the relationship is asymmetrical; “companionship”
implies assistance (ḭ́ ) and the “essence” of companionship is the master (ḭ́ ’ɵsiɵ́ɵhɵ literally translates to
“help-essence-companion”), making the pet the master’s helper, not the other way around. By contrast,
an orphan has less agency and resembles a cultivar, planted and grown by the captain (yi…pǵi), who
maintains with his orphans a relationship marked by greater control, ownership, and alienability. Besides
being “accompanied” by his orphans, as their captain, a maloquero is also pa̰kói, meaning “the one who
commands,” based on the verb pa̰ that denotes both “to command” and “to send,” similar to its Spanish
translation mandar (Andoque Andoque and Landaburu, forthcoming). This may be linked to the fact
that, as discussed in Chapter 9, both orphans and cultivars may serve as rather tame objects of exchange
“sent” between transacting agents. Game animals, in their non-dangerous state for human consumption,
are depicted both as the orphans of their owner-persons—or nonhuman captains, also considered
yo’fís—and as fruits in the eyes of these masters. Orphans can be detached from their maloca and given
to others, similar to how an owner-person can allow a hunter pick some of the “fruits” in its “garden”
(i.e., the forest). This can be formulated in the following manner:
captain : orphan :: gardener : cultivar :: owner-person : game animal
A captain, as the owner of orphan-cultivars, has the ability to exploit them or delegate their exploitation
to others, as epitomized by the historical slave trade, a phenomenon that authors, both past and present,
have recognized as bolstering captains’ prestige and authority (Echeverri 1997, 97; Spix and Martius
1981, 230). This is similar to how, as we will see in Chapter 9, nonhuman owner-persons can also accept
vegetal offerings in exchange of their personnel, whose predation is delegated to the human hunter.
Although Fisi associates the word fí (“mouth”) in the concept yo’fí with a captain’s faculty of speech,
this word also reveals the captain’s capacity to devour his men or concede this predation to others.
Mythology includes cautionary tales about what people refer to as “false yo’fís,” individuals who
103

attempted to assume the role of captains but failed due to their inability to control their aggressiveness.
In one tale (M8, see Appendix1), Egret’s son dies after the father receives a jaguar as game for a dance
and cannot control the power of the feline. Enraged, Egret hangs his wife upside-down, transforming her
breast into two manguaré drums.18 In another tale (M16, see chapter 6), Egret desires the skins of the
jaguars of the stars that have descended to earth. When he wears them, he sees his people as game and
devours them.19 While they are referred to as false yo’fís, their portrayal by Fisi as predecessors to Egret
of the Center further elucidates the Egret ideal, reflecting the implicit reliance of a captain’s authority on
violence. Moreover, the contemporary ideal of peaceful leadership associated with the concept of yo’fí,
exemplified by Egret of the Center, stands in stark contrast to the historical reality among the Andoque
and other People of the Center. Before the rubber genocide, the captain’s authority was based on his
predatory potential and the display of war trophies in the form of ritually consumed enemies at his
maloca (Lucas 2021; de Wavrin 1948; Whiffen 1915). As any other Amazonian owner, the captain is a
protector of his group members who appears as a predator to outsiders (Costa 2010; Fausto 2008). In
what appears to be a Clastrian safeguard to prevent the captain’s exploitation of power coercively, the
stories of the “false yo’fis” serve as a warning to captains, urging them to resist the temptation to prey on
their own people and encouraging them to control their anger when interacting with them. Contrary to
this unjust aggression, the captain’s historical role in the slave trade reflects the delegation of predation
to outsiders for the “common good”—allowing non-traded group members to use acquired metal tools
and other merchandise for projects of prosperity and social reproduction headed by the captain.
The distinction between captain and orphan and their distinct degrees of agency reflects a tendency
towards what Kaj Århem (2015) describes as hierarchical animism, a form of animism found in
Southeast Asia. According to Århem, this type of animism posits a universalized subjectivity among
beings, similar to “standard” animism, but instead of segmenting this subjectivity horizontally across
bodies, it grades it vertically, assigning each being a different level of spirit or potency (ibid, 25). This
hierarchizing dimension is not unfamiliar in Amazonia either (Fausto 2007a, 503), and we can view the
captain-orphan relation among the Andoque as an historically-specific manifestation that tends toward
greater hierarchization.

To fully comprehend and contextualize the relationship between the egret universe and the captainorphan hierarchy, it is necessary to delve into Landaburu’s (1993) exploration of the emergence and
consolidation of egret mythology. Drawing on recordings from the 1960s and 1970s of myth versions
narrated by Yiñékɒ and his son Fisi, on the one hand, and Yiñékɒ’s adversaries, particularly Yinñéfɵkn,
on the other, Landaburu highlights the contrasting perspectives presented in these narratives. Yiñékɒ’s
versions assign a crucial role to the three egret-gods who traverse the river horizontally, while
Yinñéfɵkn’s align more closely with Animal Stories, featuring heroes belonging to diverse faunal
species who navigate both the vertical and horizontal realms, even encountering celestial beings. While
Ñé’ñéfi (pronounced Nénéfi by other narrators), a cannibal god associated with the origin of the Eagle
Clan and engaged in war with heroes associated with other Andoque clans, takes center stage in
Yinñéfɵkn’s narratives, Egret of the Center assumes the main protagonist role in Yiñékɒ’s versions.
Egret of the Center partakes in war and exchange along the river with two other egret gods who, despite
occupying positions along the watercourse, belong to the same species as Egret of the Center.
Landaburu posits that Yiñékɒ homogenized the Andoque mythology by attributing different egret
identities to older heroes and restructuring the narratives along the horizontal axis of the river, which
facilitates exchange among human peers, both Indigenous and non-Indigenous. The egret figure was
chosen to convey a social character and human likeness, based on the double status of this bird as both
prey and predator, which, nonetheless, does not eat humans. This shift contrasts with the vertical axis
extending from the sky to the netherworld and involving figures positioned in predatory relationships.
According to Landaburu, this reconfiguration served as a powerful ideological tool wielded by Yiñékɒ,
aspiring to embody Egret of the Center, in his quest to forge a comprehensive Andoque identity and
foster peaceful exchanges among clans and with external agents.
However, despite Yiñékɒ’s significant role in systematizing the egret mythology and attributing new
traits and narrative functions to the egret figures, it is important to note that egret figures predated him.
As can be observed in M6, egret heroes were not unfamiliar to Yinñéfɵkn, and we also find them in
myths related to fluvial expeditions and exchange among other People of the Center (Echeverri and
Pereira 2005; Guyot 1972; Lucas 2019). It is possible that these ambulatory, fluvial birds gradually
became integrated into Andoque mythology during the nineteenth century, as mobility along the
Caquetá and Cahuinarí Rivers—where they are frequently spotted—became a growing concern due to
increased commerce with Whites. However, it is important to note that an egret figure represents a
collective of humans in a manner akin to that of their captain, who embodies them, similar to any owner
105

representing their personnel (Fausto 2008). My interlocutors emphasized that the primary designation of
this figure is captaincy; it only secondarily refers to human groups. This implies that the equivalence and
commensurateness attributed to the different egret figures in mythology conceals the hierarchical nature
of the system, as each egret-captain has orphans, cultivars, or objects at their disposal, which they can
potentially exchange with other egret-captains. The expressive capacity of a yo’fí, characterized by a
“mature mouth,” may thus point not only to the captain’s arbitrational function or predatory potential,
but also to his negotiating orphans for objects with other captains—i.e., to heterosubstitution, the
principle permeating the egret mythology. Based on this argument, I suggest that the egret universe
represents the ideology of the pre-genocide slave trade and the dimension of ongoing heterosubstitutive
trade among human and nonhuman entities, and should not be viewed as specific to the post-genocide
reconstruction.
In conclusion, the first aspect of the center in the captaincy system relates to self-sufficiency and the
suspension of exchange, symbolized by the stone axe. The second aspect concerns the distinction
between captains and orphans/cultivars, or the subjects and objects of exchange. This vertical dimension
of domination is crucial for engaging in horizontal exchanges with others, where issues of supremacy
and potential domination come into play. It is within this vertical dimension that the political and
economic act of valuation takes place, allowing the human or nonhuman captain to exert power by
assessing the relative value of his people and determining who should be exchanged for goods/vegetal
offerings.20 Thus, I posit that involvement in the slave trade, irrespective of the material benefits it
provided, enhanced the status of captains.
Shifting our focus to the cannibalistic system and the mythological underpinnings of the egret stories,
we will now examine the significance of the center in this specific context.

As Rubenstein argues for Xikrin chiefs, based on Fisher’s ethnography, chiefs controlling exchange with non-Indigenous
agents “are producers of ‘exchange-value’” (Rubenstein 2004, 157; see also Fisher 2000, 121).

106

Chapter 2. The Predatory Cosmos and Its Center
Elevation and Predation
Predatory capacities are central to determining the direction and asymmetrical nature of diverse
exchanges within the Andoque reality, and they are perceived as differentially distributed across space.
The cannibalistic fluvial system relies heavily on the difference in altitude between the river source and
mouth, transforming the horizontal fluvial axis into a vertical one. The river source is associated with the
forest canopy, the sky, and the stars, while the river mouth is connected to the underground. Within this
system, those located upstream and at higher elevations prey upon those located downstream and at
lower elevations. Jaguars (ḭño̰)—a category that includes the jaguar itself (Panthera onca; ḭño̰) and other
large terrestrial predators—are associated with the river source. Their captain, Sı̰ ́di, embodies the
cannibalistic and predatory principle of the cosmos and resides upstream. He is linked to masculinity
and the imposition of paternity through its association with the phallic-stinged bumblebee (Jara 1995,
156), and the thunder that echoes from upriver carries his messages (cf. M2). Eagles (kádánni), a
category that includes the harpy eagle (Harpia harpyja: ñḛmḭ kádánni) and other birds of prey, dwell in
the sky. Their captain, Nénéfi, resides in the sky above the Site of Tears at the center. Sitakara, another
aggressive god whose name combines two names of herbs used for assault sorcery (Pineda Camacho
1982, 27), resides in Spawning River (Ḭ ́’pá̰se, known also as Monochoa River), located on the border
between the Andoque and the Murui-Muina ancestral territories (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 216).
Landaburu and Pineda (ibid, 113) document a myth in which Sitakara is described as one of the stars,
which are depicted as predatory ocelots (Leopardus pardalis). I was told by Fisi that Sitakara is the
captain of certain aggressive monkeys, and, consequently, he is also associated with the forest canopy.
By contrast, those living downstream and at lower elevations are perceived as game, including animals
on the forest ground and aquatic creatures like fish. The guardians of these game creatures, such as
animals’ person-owners residing in underground malocas beneath lakes and hills, as well as caimans,
stingrays, and anacondas in the rivers, are powerful beings that prey on those who wish to harm their
“people.” The center of the river, located between the ground and the sky, is inhabited by human beings
who are both predators and prey (see also Landaburu 1985, 37).
In analyzing similar perceptions among the Miraña, Karadimas emphasizes a perspectival logic that also
exists in Andoque thinking. According to him, the cosmos is divided into two sets of dualities: looking
up from the center, a subject sees entities as predators and becomes their prey, while looking down, they

107

see entities as prey and assume a predatory position (Karadimas 2005b, 299). As in Miraña mythology
(ibid, 352), this division is reflected in Andoque myths, where a hero’s position along the river and on
the vertical axis determines how they perceive their affines: Sun, who is associated with high elevations,
is a predatory figure, while Shadow Egg, who lives under a pile of leaves on the ground, represents prey;
upriver affines are seen as jaguars, while downriver affines are seen as aquatic beings protected by
predatory owners. Shadow Egg, for instance, perceives his daughters’ suitors—the deer, tapir, and
earthworm sons of Tatoañei from the headwaters of the Macaw River (Áduse)—as jaguars. By contrast,
Sun/Capybara (Sɒ̰’ḛ ́ ),21 who lives along a tributary of Drawing River (Hḭ’ḭse), sees his affines from the
river mouth as fish headed by their caiman uncle, stingray grandmother, and anaconda grandfather
(Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 190–201).
Based on this information and Landaburu’s genealogical inquiry into Andoque mythology, we can now
reassess the character of Egret of the River Source. Similar to Egret of the Center, previously known as
Nénéfi, Egret of the River Source appears to embody a less violent version of Sı̰ ́di, Sitakara, and
Tatoañei. Like Sı̰ ́di, Egret of the River Source communicates with the people living at the center through
thunders echoing from upriver (see M3). Like Sitakara, he is associated with the origin of garden fruits
and cultivars (Pineda Camacho 1982, 27).22 Similar to Tatoañei, a predatory figure whose sons seduce
and inflict diseases on the daughters of Shadow Egg (see M20 and Chapter 9), Egret of the River source
seeks marriage with a daughter of Shadow Egg living at the center. Some narrators describe Sḭ́ di as the
father of Egret of the River Source, just as Nénéfi is depicted by members of the Eagle Clan as the father
Egret of the Center.23 These gods are considered the egrets’ fathers because they represent analogous
characters in an older mythological layer, preserving the aggressiveness and supernatural powers that
their “sons” may require under certain circumstances. As a result, these older gods are still invoked for
purposes such as healing or divination that are beyond the realm of captaincy.
The vertical character of the cannibalistic system is manifested in its purest form in the classification of
animate entities from the point of view of any given being into “People of Above” (kadaiño̰e) and

“People of Below” (kakńño̰e). From a human standpoint, the People of Above include celestial bodies,
predatory birds, jaguars, which encompass terrestrial animals that prey upon humans, and stars, which
are also classified as jaguars. On the other hand, the People of Below include game animals, their
owner-persons, the dead, and aquatic creatures. Some of the People of Below are invisible chthonic
entities, such as the owner-persons representing animals’ agency, knowledge, and reproductive forces,
as well as the souls of human beings who have fallen prey to animals and their owner-persons, joining
the animals’ houses of reproduction in lakes and beneath the hills.
Personhood, Agency, and Humanity
Personhood and agency, critical for evaluating power dynamics, are inextricably linked to predatory
capacities within the cannibalistic system. In the Andoque language, the term denoting “person,” ño̰,
refers to any being endowed with agency and intentionality. The jaguar epitomizes personhood and
agency, as the word ḭño̰ translates to “one who is endowed with the quality of personhood” (Jon
Landaburu, pers. comm., October 2022).24 Similarly, the eagle (kádánni: “song-dance of our above”), as
a predator singing and dancing in the sky, represents maximal agency, since singing-dancing at a
ceremonial dance is the apex of territorial management. These perspectives align with those of the
Miraña, who believe that “achieved humanity is found among the heavenly bodies: all those found
‘below’ are indistinctively ‘animals’” (Karadimas 2005b, 313). Since human beings can also be
perceived as game animals by their predators, they are not the ultimate humanity. According to the
Andoque, other beings along the predation axis would view themselves and their species as occupying
the central position of humanity. This differs from the restricted version of perspectivism that Londoño
(2005; 2017) attributes to the Féénemɨna. According to this approach, animals may perceive their cospecifics as human but their behavior towards each other can never be as moral as the behavior of real
human beings. In this Féénemɨna thinking, animals acknowledge human moral superiority and recognize
that human set the standards for morality, thus making it impossible for animals to compare to humans
in this respect (ibid). My Andoque interlocutors, on the other hand, while considering themselves real
human beings and striving for asymmetrical power relations with animals (see Part III), do not claim
that animals acknowledge human moral superiority. During a discussion on the definition of “animal”
(ḭsu) at a workshop aimed at formulating a cultural plan for territorial management in December 2018,
Elias, a maloquero of fifty-years-old, expressed the prevailing view by stating: “What seems to us like
24

Pineda interprets the jaguar as representing “the abstract Ego; the abstract masculine Desire” (1979, 46; my translation).

109

disorder is their [the animals’] order. They are criminals for us, but we also appear as criminals to
them.”
The Andoque’s inclusive view of agency and personhood, extended to nonhuman entities as well, aligns
with Descola’s (2013) definition of animism as a mode of identification perceiving similarities in
interiority among beings. Accordingly, the center along the Andoque’s cannibalistic river system is
defined not by interiority but by physicality—the criterion by which animists discern dissimilarities
among beings. This center is the speaking human body capable of suspending predation of its own kind.
Since the concept of human physicality cannot be comprehended in isolation from the process by which
animals acquired their current bodily forms, we need to briefly explore this process.
In everyday Andoque discourse, it is often mentioned that the People of Below are those who attempted
to live like human beings but, due to their immoral behavior, were punished by the Creator with animal
bodily forms and were forced into the ground. This transformation can also be seen as affecting their
houses, which became covered with mud and turned into the hills we see today. However, as I will
demonstrate shortly, this cosmogonic principle should not be taken literally in the Andoque context,
despite the perspectives of other ethnographers in the region (e.g., Londoño Sulkin 2005, 13; Griffiths
1998, 57–58). Londoño is notable for his insistence that, for the People of the Center in general, animals
are defined by their immorality, which thus gives this version of perspectivism an essentialist character
rather than a relational one (Londoño Sulkin 2005; 2012; 2017). While Londoño interprets human
predation on animals literally as hunting, he considers Féénemɨna accounts of animal predation on
humans through illnesses and madness as metaphors for asocial sentiments and behavior taking over
individuals who are depicted as ill or mad. Therefore, he places moral evaluation above relations of
predation, subjugating, in Viveiros de Castro’s (1996) terms, “the symbolic economy of alterity” to “the
moral economy of intimacy.”
My findings support the need to distinguish the Andoque from this generalization. This exception may
be attributed to the relatively limited influence of Christian morality on Andoque discourse during the
formative years following the genocide, unlike the Féénemɨna and Murui-Muina populations, where
missionization appears to have had a broader impact. Moreover, these two groups have a formalized
discursive genre, known as rafue among the Murui-Muina, which diverges from standard mythology.
Rafue encompasses abstract ideas, concentrating on the Creator and the lessons he imparted to
humanity—elements not found among the Andoque, Bora, and Miraña (Echeverri 2022, 43–45; Gasché

110

2009). This does not imply that the Andoque lack any moral discourse regarding animals or that they do
not view animals as morally flawed. However, there exists a dialectical tension between this moral
discourse and a discourse aligned with the logic of reciprocal predation, a tension that we must highlight
and explore, rather than flatten or deny. Nonetheless, as I will show in Chapter 9, my research aligns
with Els Lagrou’s (2017) suggestion, critiquing Londoño, that moral discourse largely adheres to the
logic of the relational predatory matrix, rather than the other way around. Contrary to Londoño’s
interpretation of Féénemɨna discourse, the Andoque trace the immoral sentiments and behavior
experienced by people, along with people’s cases of illness and madness, to real predatory actions on the
part of animals, rather than considering them as metaphorical in nature. They perceive these sentiments,
behavior, and illnesses as transformative forces that shape human thinking and, ultimately, transform
their bodies into those of animals. As for the Cashinahua’s perception of the Inka cannibal beings cited
by Lagrou, in Andoque thinking, animals “are not other because they are bad, but they are bad because
they are other” (ibid, 491). Among the Andoque, the sense of otherness to be cautious of extends not
only to animals but also to members of other clans.
The trope suggesting the Creator punished past human generations for transgressions of his laws and
their aggression toward each other is only superficially present in Andoque mythology. It is more
commonly the result of people’s rationalization and simplification of intricate and diverse mythical
narratives, particularly in certain contexts such as when introducing an outsider to their mythology. A
closer examination of mythology would assist in unraveling this cosmogonic principle and exploring the
intertwined processes of human and animal bodily formation.
Unlike neighboring People of the Center (e.g., García 2018; Karadimas 2005), the Andoque do not tend
to explicitly mention the Creator in their mythical narratives. However, during mambeadero sessions
and other conversations with men and women of various ages, they attributed to him the important role
of creating the world, referring to him as tiɵi, “[he] who made everything.” Andoque Andoque and
Landaburu (forthcoming), note that doékositoɵ is one of the Andoque terms for “the Creator.” In M20, a
predatory figure bearing the name Doékositoɵ, which Raquel convincingly translates as “Yellow
Achiote Deer” (dóő—yellow; a’kosi—achiote; pe’toɵ—deer; see Chapter 9), is considered the son of
Tatoañei. Tatoañei is closely associated with the carnivorous god Sḭ́ di, who holds a pivotal position in
Andoque cosmology in overseeing all activity and collecting the spirits of the dead (see Chapter 7).
However, in this myth, Doékositoɵ represents dangers to humanity, and this reference for the Creator is

111

not commonly used. The term most often used to refer to such a figure is kahaǵtı̋ ɵ. In my discussions
with various interlocutors, they associated the Creator with different figures, such as Nénéfi, Egret of the
River Source, or the three gods whose names are only revealed during preparations for ceremonial
dances. In his article on the names of Andoque divinities, Landaburu interprets kahaǵtı̋ o not as a name of
a specific god, but as a concept representing an archetypical model for later designs, mentioning the
maloca of the god Tomirepa as the kahaǵtı̋ o of his informant Yinñéfɵkn (Landaburu 1993, 153). In
personal communication, Landaburu agreed that a closer translation would be “that which was formed
for us.” Interestingly, the term kahaǵtı̋ o shares the same structure as yahaǵtı̋ o, “that which was formed
for him [the animals],” which refers to the owner-persons of animals (Chapter 8), and signifies also
“my/our origin” (ohaǵtı̋ o/kahaǵtı̋ o), which people use to designate their clans. This suggests that while
these owner-persons protect nonhuman beings, the Creator safeguards humans. While there is no
consensus on the Creator’s specific identity and role in mythology, and he cannot be associated with a
specific site within the territory like many other gods, it appears that the Creator is mythology, he is the
territory. More precisely, the Creator is the specific arrangement of mythology and territory which a
speaker views as favorable and beneficial for him or her, and which they seek mobilizing in a given
context. The term “the Creator” should thus be understood as the personification of the archetypical
model through which the speaker and elements from their surrounding environment were formed. This
model encompasses the gods and mythical heroes that the speaker relies upon, depending on their clan
origin, ritual specialization, and other factors.25
Therefore, the acquisition of animal bodily forms was not authored at once by one god called the
Creator, but rather represents the cumulative result of the deeds of various heroes and events that
occurred in multiple myths. These bodily transformations are sometimes associated with immoral
behavior, such as an old man becoming a tapir after repeatedly stealing pineapple from his daughter-inlaw’s garden (which hints at sexual indecency) and falling into a trap set by his son (M21, Chapter 9).
Similarly, the brothers of his daughter-in-law who consume the man’s raw flesh without sharing it with
his son also undergo the same transformation (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 108–13). However, more
often, and in line with other Amazonian mythologies, we find numerous stories where the physical
forms and characteristics of animal species result from their sedimented actions as depicted in these
narratives. These actions are not necessarily negative, and the bodily transformation can also result from
Cf. how the Miraña break the term “the Creator” to different names, each one linked to different components of the reality
that he created, in Karadimas 2005b, 270–71.
25

112

acts of revenge, mischievousness, or even healing by other heroes. Such are the transformations
undergone by animals after consuming coca for the first time in M1, the black dots on the back of the
Bujo ceratophrys frog resulting from the pot of tar spilled on her by her husband in another story,26 or
the veinous appearance of a bat’s wing due to the tobacco leaf attached to its body by the orphan
blowgun hunter to replace and heal its wounded wing in M7 (see Appendix 1).
Mythology also depicts instances of collective bodily transformation. In a version of the story M3 told to
me by Tañe, Egret of the River Source, after constructing the maloca and establishing the garden,
organized a dance where he transformed his wife’s previous suitors into white-lipped peccaries (Tayassu
pecari). This transformation was a consequence of their wickedness, constant fighting among
themselves, and attempts to sabotage his project. This episode from the egret mythology, which appears
somewhat detached from the broader narrative, seems to represent a moralistic layer overlaid on another
story that serves as one of the foundational elements of Andoque hunting culture and as the origin myth
of the Head (Ḭtai) ceremonial dance. In that story (M18, Appendix 1), the brothers-in-law of a dance
organizer—who are sometimes identified as a group of the proto-human Piercers—are transformed into
white-lipped peccaries by the owner-person of these animals as a response to their excessive hunting of
his “children.” Rather than being a punishment for an abstract moral transgression, the motive in this
story is driven by revenge based on the principle of reciprocal predation.
Two Andoque myths that recount a primordial flood highlight the tension between the predatory and
moral logic at work in bodily transformation processes.27 In both myths, people seek refuge from the
flood by taking shelter underground and emerge as animals once the waters recede, while a new
humanity begins to inhabit the surface of the earth. In one myth (M10, Chapter 4), the flood is triggered
by the consumption by the protagonists of the marrow liquid of Nocturnal Curassow (Nothocrax
urumutum), with the other members of its body already being consumed by other characters. This event
lends itself more easily to moral interpretation, as their chewing on the marrow can symbolize, as Urbina
noted in a parallel Murui-Muina myth, an extreme act of revenge that prevents the species from
regenerating (Urbina Rangel 2010, 125).

By contrast, the transformation in the other flood myth clearly follows a predatory logic. This story, “the
Eagle’s Flood” (M9, Fisi 4/10/18; 12/7/21), recounts that Nénéfi’s wife created two harpy eagles, male
and female, using manioc starch. At that time there were no animals, and so she also created lizards for
PLATE XV.

the eagles to feed on. However, once they had a son, the male harpy eagle started devouring Nénéfi’s
people. The latter were terrified: they could not safely walk around or bathe in the river. In response,
Nénéfi set a trap for the eagle, using a saki monkey (Pithecia monachus) entangled in a hammock as
bait. As the eagle descended to catch the monkey, it got entangled in the hammock as well. Nénéfi
captured the eagle’s son and brought him to his maloca. The people then consumed the eagle’s son,
covered the maloca with earth, which transformed it into the hill now known as the Site of Tears, and
used the eagle’s bones to make the síiru flute. While searching for his son, the eagle recognized the
voice of his son in the sound of the flute coming from beneath the earth. Enraged, it attacked the
maloca-turned-hill from the rooftop, prompting the sheltered people to cut off one of his talons from
inside the house. In pain and bleeding, the eagle flew away, dropping his blood on the earth, forming
DUKAIYA (OKAIXA) BEAD DANCING-GIRDLE

stones and giving rise to the Harpy Eagle Clan (on other occasions, Fisi also said that it was the origin of
all Andoque clans). As the eagle flew downriver, it dammed the river with its outspread wings, resulting
in a flood. After the water receded, the people who emerged from beneath the earth were no longer
humans but animals.

The myth elucidates the vertical structure of the cannibalistic cosmos:

eagles in the sky above, game animals under the earth below, and between them, as both predators and

114

prey, is the new humanity formed on the surface of the earth. The distinguishing feature of human
beings is their intermediate position and the corresponding bodily attributes that accompany it.
This myth underscores the potential for transformation among persons of different kinds across the
vertical space, leading us to the notion of homosubstitution that prevails within the cannibalistic cosmos:
the body and life of one person, human or otherwise, can be compensated through the body and life of
another person. I propose that this homosubstitutive logic prevailed while the life of Andoque-speaking
clans centered around the smaller rivers inland, away from the main rivers. During that period, the
human groups they interacted with, including other Andoque-speaking clans and non-Andoque groups,
shared relatively similar practices and attributes, allowing for interchangeability of members and
resources. Heterosubstitutive elements undoubtedly coexisted with the predominance of
homosubstitution. These elements include the impregnation of ritual substances with intentions during
preparation and sharing, and the replacement of hunted game with vegetal offerings to owner-persons,
both will be explored further below. However, the opening of the Andoque economy to trade along the
main rivers with non-Indigenous people, who had different practices and attributes and could provide
objects not found in their ancestral territory, entailed a greater emphasis on the principle of
heterosubstitution, expanding it into an organizing spatial logic. In this logic, the river source, center,
and river mouth participate in the exchange of things that are, in principle, incommensurate. The
authority of negotiating captains became necessary to facilitate this exchange, determine the value of
things and thus make them exchangeable.
The more intuitive exchangeability along the smaller rivers, where the value of a person’s life and body
is equivalent to those of other persons, reduces the hierarchical and captaincy-dependent nature of the
homosubstitutive-cannibalistic system compared to the heterosubstitutive system. It is in this sense that
the egret mythology is considered more suitable for captaincy than the earlier Animal Stories.
Body and Speech
Akin to the heterosubstitutive-captaincy system, the center of the cannibalistic, homosubstitutive system
embodies the two necessary qualities for exercising power: the suspension of exchange and the
involvement in it as its agent rather than patient. Here, these two qualities are expressed through the
idiom of the body, oɵsí, “that which is really mine.” Referred to also as odi, the body holds significant
symbolic value in the Andoque language, indexing authority and power when it reaches a mature form.
The body’s central role in the Andoque concept of power echoes the argument of Seeger et al. (1979),
115

who extend the anthropological focus on the body as a potent signifier of social ideas and phenomena
(e.g., Douglas 1982; V. Turner 1967), contending that the Amerindian socio-logic is, in fact, a physiologic.
Reflecting widespread Amazonian perceptions that babies and children are more vulnerable to predatory
and familiarizing actions by nonhumans (Fausto 2007a, 505), the ability to participate in the
cannibalistic system’s exchange as a powerful predator, rather than as vulnerable prey, is represented by
the mature body of an adult, in contrast to the undeveloped body of a child. The term yosuɵ, which
literally translates to “adult, fully developed land animal,” refers to both larger individual animals
leading their respective groups and human captains leading their people. As in the word yo’fí for egret
leaders, the term yo suggests the idea of physical maturity, which is associated with the potential to both
harm and benefit others. By contrast, the term yɨḛn, referring to babies, children, and youth, is used
interchangeably with “orphans” when describing a maloquero’s workers, emphasizing the vulnerability
of the younger individuals. However, it is important to note that a young being surrounded by nurturing
and cooperative kin is more likely to develop into a body incorporating greater agency compared to an
orphan, who is characterized by a lack of kin and agency.
Certain kinship terms also incorporate the notion of physical maturity. For example, yodi, meaning
“uncle,” is used to refer to any G+1 adult male who is recognized as having a more mature body than the
speaker. The terms yodisu and yodikn take this notion one generation up and are used to refer to men and
women of G+2, respectively. The physical maturity of those older than ego is associated with their
superior knowledge, as seen in the plural form yodɨsua, which designates the cohort of elders whose
guidance and wisdom are sought by the younger generation in personal and collective matters. This agebased hierarchy exhibits greater dynamism than the hierarchy based on lineages that is prevalent in the
discourse of captaincy today, and which seems to be linked with the trade system.
These terms draw on certain physical attributes associated with masculinity. The classifier -dɨ, found in
these terms, is used to describe trees with firm trunks. The word for body, odi, is derived from the
concept of something long, straight, and rigid, contrasting with -tá, a classifier used for trees with
sinuous, serpentine trunks and for worm-like shapes in general (Jon Landaburu, Pers. Comm., October
2022). Based on this distinction, the rigidity and linearity of -dɨ convey abstract ideas of confidence and
fortitude, highlighting the stability of things that “hold firm.” For example, ḭdɨhako means “right side”
(firm side, side of the body-trunk), while í’tahako means “left side” (sinuous, unfirm side). This

116

classifier also conveys masculinity, as -dɨ means “man” or “Mister,” in contrast with to -sn, which
means “woman” or “Lady” (or with -kamikn, which conveys the same meaning in the mythical register).
These gendered physical attributes are reflected in important terms related to ownership and authority in
ritual matters. The term ḭdɨño̰ can refer to the organizer of a ceremonial dance or the owner of a maloca,
representing the “person-body trunk” of that dance or maloca. Similarly, the term ḭdɨá, refers to the
cacique, the leader above clan level, emphasizing the idea that the leader is the body-trunk of his group.
Here it is noteworthy that my concept of the “captaincy system” does not imply that captains are
nonexistent or incompatible with the logic of the cannibalistic system. Rather, they are crucial agentive
actors protecting their “young” or “orphans,” or i’hɵ́ɵá—which literally means absence, referring to
either agency itself or a figure embodying it, such as a parent or captain—from predation through the
ceremonial dances they conduct and other ritual procedures undertaken at their malocas. However, in
this system, captaincy is not an organizing spatial principle.
The body is also contrasted with the images that it generates—its shadow, reflection in the water, and,
with the introduction of photography, its printed reproductions, all referred to as ká’hɵi. The shadow,
formed when sunlight hits the body from above and casts onto the ground, is associated with game
animals, whose existence is shaped by the predatory gaze upon them. In mythology, Shadow Egg’s
people are game animals, residing in his proto-maloca at the center constructed from a heap of leaves,
and consuming cultivars that are in fact wild fruits (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 143). Employing
camouflage and deceit tactics used by game animals, Shadow Egg deceives his sons-in-law, concealing
his people and preventing them from perceiving them as game animals and vegetal matter. In contrast,
Sun, who can be viewed as a mythical transformation on the figure of Shadow Egg, preys on his sons-inlaw. Representing the opposite principle, the sun resides high in the sky, and while enabling clear
perception of objects and people—an essential requirement for hunting—it cannot be stared at. The
body is located between these two optical-predatory poles; it is through bodies that sunlight produces
shadows.
The second quality of the center within the vertical-fluvial cannibalistic cosmos, which embodies the
suspension of predatory exchange, is speech. In cosmogonic narratives, the emergence of animal bodies,
which excludes the primordial humanity from attaining full human status, coincides with the
development of human language. According to the chronological framework that Andoque members
often apply to these narratives, the Piercers appeared after the flood, during which the primordial

117

humanity lost its bodily form. These proto-human heroes, who deprived dangerous faunal beings of their
powers and created various fish and game animals, were the ones who “discovered” the Andoque
language and experimented with it, thereby “producing” the territory by naming its rivers and other
sites. Tellingly, the same beings who bequeathed the items that allow the suspension of exchange within
the captaincy system—the stone axes—also passed on language to the Andoque, which permits the
suspension of exchange within the cannibalistic system. However, the Piercers mispronounced the
human language, and were themselves transformed into game animals (specifically, white-lipped
peccaries) or lost their body forms, becoming owner-persons of game animals in different sites of the
territory.
In contrast to the agency conveyed by ño̰ (person), hɵ́ihɵ́, “human being” coveys the idea of likeness,
which enables sociality. In our conversations, Fisi deconstructed this term into “speaking” (hɵɵ́i) and
“disappearing” (hɵ́ɵi). While this etymology appears uncertain (Jon Landaburu, Pers. Comm.,
November 2022), the interpretation is thought-provoking: a human being is human in the eyes of others
of their kind insofar as they can engage in speech and their bodies are subject to the same forces of
demise and decay. One of the roles of a captain is to create human beings, understood as a community of
agentive equals who exchange words instead of resorting to aggressive actions. However, to achieve this
end, the input from the river source, the direction of jaguars and other predators, in indispensable. The
Andoque clans whose ancestral territories are located deeper inland, away from the Caquetá River, claim
descent not only of the proto-human Piercers, but also of a mythical collective of maladroit figures
called Shadows (Ká’hɵi Síɵ́hɵ) (see Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 217–24). Through this claim, they
acknowledge their reliance on forces from the river source, who, like Egret of the River Source,
bestowed upon them paternity, elevating their proto-culture to a fully developed culture befitting human
beings, complete with a real maloca, cultivated gardens, and ceremonial dances, which enable to
exercise greater predatory agency. Certain sites towards the river source, associated with gods and
heroes residing there, such as Hummingbird Hill and Spawning River (Pá̰di Tuɒ́i and I’pá̰se,
respectively), allude to semen (pá̰), similar to the patriline (hḛpa̰). The rainbow from that direction is
associated with vegetal fertility, which itself serves as a metaphor for human fertility.28 The strong
association between the river source, ancestry, and the notion that agency extends from that direction
The verb bɨ signifies “to bear fruits,” and is thus associated with wild fruits (bɨi), which reproduce independently of

towards the center merits referring to the Andoque as not simply “People of the Center” but as “People
