Two Mythological Layers, Two River Systems
Landaburu’s observation that egret mythology overlays an earlier mythological layer provides essential
tools for understanding how older notions of predation underlie subsequent notions regarding the agents
and objects of exchange. In the egret mythology, the river source retains its violent character from the
old predatory layer, represented by Burner Egret of the River Source, who leaves the center in anger
upon discovering that the mother of merchandise has already departed with Egret of the River Mouth
(M5). The Andoque make a distinction between the beneficial Trader Whites from the river mouth and
the aggressive Burner Whites from the river source, whose embodiment today can be seen in armed
dissident groups originating from the cordillera. They also differentiate between the rifle from the river
source, known as duidi, and the one from the river mouth, referred to as ḭkn. While duidi, which literally
means “burner tube,” is dangerous and is linked in mythology to Sı̰ ́di, ḭkn also refers to a spear and even
dancing rod, and, like the latter, is viewed as an instrument that can contribute to people’s livelihood and
well-being. M5 also explains the common association in ceremonial songs between the violence
exercised by Whites from downriver and jaguars (see Chapter 12), a category of predators that,
according to the logic of the predatory system, should inhabit the river source rather than its mouth.
According to this myth, the ocelot conceived by the mother of merchandise escaped from the center,
which is located upstream from the river mouth, and whose population is thus perceived as jaguars by
those inhabiting the river mouth. The dolphin (Inia geoffrensis), which appears in other myths related to
exchange with the river mouth and symbolizes dangerous seduction by Whites, is classified as an
anaconda, which is a predator from downriver.
Landaburu’s observations on Andoque mythological layers should also be considered within the broader
context of the establishment of the captaincy system as superimposed upon the cannibalistic one. In the
context of the slave trade, a captain’s ability to designate individuals as orphans relied on his predatory
capabilities. These were demonstrated in wars where he could obtain captives and protect his own men,
while other captains fell, leaving their dependents orphaned. Similarly, the practice of making vegetal
offerings to the owner-persons of animals presupposes the logical antecedence of cannibalistic
retaliation by these entities. This threat prompted the development of such offerings as a compensatory
measure for protection.

119

Each system articulates processes of predation, familiarization, and exchange differently. As will be
explored in Chapter 9, homosubstitution and hunting cosmology require the familiarization of prey after
capture or consumption, transforming the horizontal predatory relation into a vertical relation of
domination where humans consume game animals rather than vice versa. By contrast, the egret
mythology and heterosubstitutive-captaincy system place familiarization at the forefront. Unlike
Tatoañei’s ravenous sons, Egret of the River Source’s predation on Shadow Egg and his people takes the
form of familiarization as he incorporates them into his maloca and political endeavors. Simultaneously,
Egret of the River Source utilizes them as elements to fulfill his designs and constitutes his people as
cultivars that he has planted and grown. These cultivars do not pose dangers to him and can be
eventually detached from himself. While the river source is associated with the patriline, those traded
with agents from the opposite direction exist outside the patriline or are rejected from it. This trade
should be viewed as the delegation of their predation to a third party. In other words, while the
homosubstitutive system involves predation followed by familiarization, the heterosubstitutive system
involves familiarization followed by exchange, which may have predatory implications but should not
be reduced to mere predation. As the alignment of agency is a critical element of power, it is noteworthy
that the Andoque cosmos contains two systems with differing sequences of agency alignment within
their respective action schemes. In line with the analogy outlined in the introduction between
familiarization and predation, on the one hand, and violence and power, on the other, the cannibalistic
system embodies a horizontal model of violence that is more easily reversible, while the captaincy
system adheres to a vertical, domination-oriented model of power.
These two models coexist within Andoque society, and I will examine their manifestations in various
contexts in the following chapters. In the next stage of our exploration, we shall proceed to discuss the
process whereby the center and the persons embodying it are actively produced.

120

Chapter 3. The Production of Centers
As explored in the previous chapters, both the captaincy and cannibalistic cosmo-economic systems,
which utilize the river as a central axis, are conceptualized around the idea of an affinal space
encompassing a consanguineal center. Whether this center is represented by a social, speaking humanbodied person or an axe-person, with all the productive and hierarchical implications it carries, this
center also must be produced. Just as the captaincy system builds upon the foundations of the
cannibalistic system, so the existence of the productive axe-person assumes the prior socialization of the
individual into becoming a speaking human-bodied person. This socialization involves attributing
origins to the newborn child, incorporating them into a clan, and introducing them to the broader
community and territory through ceremonial name giving. In this chapter, I delve into the interconnected
concepts of formation, origin, and clan, and examine the power-laden practices through which a
newborn child is shaped into a human-bodied person and becomes a member of a specific center.
Clan and Origin
In Andoque cosmology, everything and everyone—people, animals, plants, diseases, artifacts, cures,
spells, dances, and so on—have their origin, which can be traced back to an entity who created them, a
specific site where they were formed, and a myth that narrates their creation. The origin myth of a
person, animal, or object allows others to understand their behavior or characteristics in the present and
enables manipulation for various purposes. Ohaǵtiɵ̋, which translates to “my origin,” literally means “my
principle,” “my Creator,” or “that which was formed for me” (see the earlier discussion on kahaǵtiɵ̋). It
signifies formation and transformation—as there is no notion of ex-nihilo creation, the former is always
a specific instance of the latter—as well as making and fabricating. The notion of origin is closely linked
to the connotation of “true” or “real” associated with the concept of the center (dʉ), because people
consider themselves truly human when they reside on their territory of origin and rely on the animals,
plants, and substances created alongside them on that specific territory.
The origins and formation of any person can be traced to two processes: physical formation and the
assignment to a clan through the act of name giving. Physical formation involves feeding the child (ɵsé)
and adhering to specific dietary practices, primarily by the mother, although certain rules also apply to
the father. These practices are reminiscent of other Amazonian peoples where children are actively
shaped as kin to distinguish them from the potential kinship ties in the forest, preventing them from
becoming closely associated with animals or, in other words, falling ill (Vilaça 2002; see Chapter 9).
121

After the weaning stage and until they can walk independently, children should predominantly consume
plant-based foods (nowadays, the preparation of oatmeal shakes has become increasingly common), and
the introduction of fish and meat occurs gradually (Gómez López et al. 1998, 122–40). During this
process, the child’s father or grandfather “prays on” various fish and game, making them safe for the
child to consume, often by referring to these animals as fruits and other cultivated plants (Fausto 2007a,
503–4; S. Hugh-Jones 2019a, 106). This practice signifies a greater male involvement in the child’s
physical formation. However, male authority assumes a more significant role in the name-giving
process, which necessitates prior discussions on the clan.
Haǵtiɵ̋, meaning “origin,” is also used to refer to clans, as they are the relevant social units for tracing
origins within the Andoque collective. Unlike Tukanoan and Arawakan groups in the Rio NegroVaupes-Apaporis region (e.g. Andrello 2006, 379–400; C. Hugh-Jones 1979, 33–40; S. Hugh-Jones
1993), the Andoque do not have a unifying origin myth for all the clans. According to Fisi, the cacique,
all the Andoque clans originated from the hill known as the Site of Tears. In the center of the site lived
the leader Egret of the Center, along with his father Nénéfi, and from different corners of the hill, all the
Andoque clans emerged. However, in private mambeadero sessions, members of all clans often
contradict this version, stating that each clan has its own origin site and story, and that only the Eagle
Clan, which is Fisi’s clan, originated there. Fisi’s description lacks support from any mythological
narrative, while myths about the origin processes and sites of specific clans abound. For example, the
Sun Clan traces its origin to Araracuara, the site of the fight between the Sun and the Moon. The Deer
Clan traces its origin to an area near the Site of Tears, which they occupied before the rubber genocide,
and other clans likewise claim to have originated in the territories they occupied prior to that upheaval
(see Figure 6). Without a clear and rigid hierarchy between the clans, as described in the Rio NegroVaupes-Apaporis region, the argument that the Site of Tears is the origin site or cosmological center of
the entire Andoque people should be understood as another way for the Eagle Clan to assert its
hegemony over the other clans (Landaburu 1993).29

Neither can we clearly identify at present a rigid hierarchy between lineages pertaining to the same clan, such as the case
for the Bora (Lucas 2019, 174). Although the sons of elder brothers in some clans play a more central role in community
affairs, the small number of remaining clans and the small general population preclude any clear conclusion.

Similar to the Féénemɨna, the Andoque believe that each clan has had since Creation its own territory,
names, speech, temperament, and specific teachings, which include cures, capacities, and specializations
such as leadership or warfare (Londoño Sulkin 2000, 329–30). Prior to the genocide, clans were
organized around malocas, each led by a captain (po’soɵ), who held certain ritual prerogatives and
axes—both actual working tools and workers to operate them. During that time, inter-clan exogamy
prevailed. Despite Fisi’s insistence that there has always been an ḭdɨa, or supra-clan cacique, from the
Eagle Clan who unified all the Andoque, his and other peoples’ oral historical accounts of inter-clan
warfare suggest that, like in the Miraña case (Karadimas 2013, 188), some clan captains merely acted as
peacemakers between warring clans, serving as counselors to temporarily align the perspectives and
interests of multiple clans in forming alliances. Today, marriage between individuals of the same clan
origin is still considered incestuous, and suspicion among clans persists (Chapter 10).
The animal, plant or natural element referred to by the clan’s name is interconnected, through the clan’s
origin myth, with other animals, plants, or elements. For instance, the Atta Ant Clan is also known as the
Jaguar Clan because the myth tells of how this ant was formed from the jaguar’s blood drops. It is also
connected with the ba’kósı̋ okń spider and the edakń tree (neither identified). The Eagle Clan, on the
other hand, is associated with water, rocks and cascades, as well as the manioc species from which the
heroine of M9 created the first eagles. These elements operate in a totem-like manner, where their origin
myth and other characteristics, whether physiological, ethological, or related to their use, serve as a
source of names for clan members. Clan members also turn to these myths for protection, healing, or
support. For example, members of the Eagle Clan are named after different episodes of the myth of the
cannibal eagle (M9) as well as after various rock formations, eagles’ feathers, and other bodily postures
of these birds. On the other hand, members of the Sun Clan are named after different episodes of the war
story between the two brothers, Sun and Moon, over a woman. They are also named after the various
124

manifestations and effects of these two celestial bodies throughout the day or year.30 The construction of
proper names from clan appellations (Lévi-Strauss 1962, 173) is also found among other People of the
Center (Gasché 2009, 15; cf. S. Hugh-Jones 2002, 50 for the Tukanoan case). However, it is distinct
from other Amazonian cases, such as the Mebengokre, as explored by Lea, where names primarily serve
to evoke the ancestors of the household in which they are transmitted (Lea 1992, 136).
People often declare “our God is our origin,” a statement that embodies two significant ideas. Firstly, it
personifies the very process of the collective’s formation, attributing agency to the forces that brought
them into existence as members of that collective. Secondly, it reflects people’s reliance on these forces
for their own protection. In this manner, the strength, bravery, and cunning displayed by both the
primordial humanity and the cannibal eagle during their mythical struggle are regarded as sources of
power and inspiration for the Eagle Clan. In the case of the Sun Clan, a woman whose children belong
to that clan shared with me that when her son was in prison, she would pray, drawing upon an episode
from the Sun and Moon myth where Moon successfully evaded a trap set by Sun. “I knew that he [her
son] could not die in prison, because neither did his origin die there,” she said. However, clan origin
stories also expose their members’ vulnerabilities and can be exploited by outsiders for curses or
negative intentions. For instance, outsiders may intentionally incite conflict among brothers from the
Sun Clan over a woman by drawing upon the strife between Sun and Moon in mythology. Due to this
risk, as we will explore further in Chapter 10, people are cautious about sharing their origin myths with
outsiders.
Names and Their Powerful Bestowal
Name giving, ɵti, is a powerful moment of familiarization in which a child is bestowed with a (clan)
origin, thus becoming integrated into the clan’s origin narrative and endowed with the recognition and
dispositions that will serve them in engaging in future beneficial exchanges. The verb itself combines
“making” (ɵ) and “name” (ti), a noun which is itself identical to the verbal root “to make, form,
transform,” emphasizing the transformative nature of assigning a name to someone. By receiving a name
associated with a specific clan, the child is fully embraced as a member of that clan, as clan affiliation is
not solely determined by biological lineage. In principle, names can be drawn from both parents’ clans,
and it was once common for mothers to name some of their daughters after their own clans. Among the
For the myth on Sun and Moon, see Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 43–55. For the myths and lists of names of members of
the two clans, see Estrada 2017, 197–204, 215–21.
30

125

fourteen women who returned to the ancestral territory as part of Yiñékɒ’s group in the 1930s, three
were named after their mothers’ clans. However, this practice has practically ceased. In regional
ethnography, matrilineal name giving is interpreted as a means to repay a debt to the wife-giving clan in
the first generation after marriage, rather than waiting for four generations for a female descendent to
marry into that clan (Karadimas 2000, 609–10; Lucas 2019, 239–40). While acknowledging that this
practice predates the rubber genocide, members of the Andoque community associate it with the
aftermath of that catastrophic event and claim that it serves as a noble cause for one to restore his
spouse’s clan. However, in practice, Andoque men prefer connecting their children to their own origins,
thus preserving the vitality, memory, and names of their own clans, which indeed serves as one of the
functions of name giving (cf. S. Hugh-Jones 2002, 51). Except for children born to non-Indigenous or
absent fathers, who are automatically affiliated with their mothers’ clans, there were only two girls born
after the genocide who received names after their matriclans upon birth. Both were born in the 1940s,
and in one of these cases, the father changed the girl’s name to his own clan during her childhood. In
another notable case, Raquel, a maloquera married to a Murui man of a lesser lineage, gave her only
male son from that man a name after her own clan. Two other children of hers—one son from a previous
husband and a daughter from the Murui man—voluntarily chose names from the repository of their
mother’s clan rather than names associated with their fathers’ clans. Nonetheless, these cases are
exceptional.
Due to their content, clan names are distinct from two other classes of names that are nonetheless used
more frequently to address or refer to people: “White names,” which encompass Christian names,
Spanish names, and names with an Anglo-Saxon flavor, often given to children owing to their sound or
the exotic character of the non-Indigenous person recommending them; and nicknames, which are given
to people based on some odd or funny physical or behavioral trait, or due to their resemblance to another
person or an animal.
Clan names are bestowed by elder members, typically males, who reportedly spend two nights at the
mambeadero, recounting the clan’s myth and examining its name repository. While there is a strong
appreciation for revitalizing the clan’s name repository, some individuals prefer not to give children
names of exceptionally powerful ancestors. Such a name could potentially endanger the young bearer, as
the formidable owner-persons with whom the ancestor used to communicate may seek out the new
bearer, expecting to continue the exchange they had with the previous owner. Without a suitable

126

offering, these ancestors and owner-persons could cause harm to the new name bearer. This perspective
reflects the belief that assuming a particular name establishes a mimetic situation, where the name owner
is placed in the same relational position with respect to both human and nonhuman entities as the
previous name owner. There is no strict rule or preference for name attribution, as seen among other
regional peoples who often pass down the name of a real or classificatory G+2 relative (cf. S. HughJones 2002, 50–51; Lucas 2019, 169). However, there appears to be a minimal genealogical distance
observed. Only Raquel bestowed her father’s name on her son (who is the child’s G+2). Her brother’s
opposition to this practice seems to reflect a widely held belief that giving a child the name of a
deceased parent, whom one has seen alive, diminishes the significance of that parent’s death and
amounts to a resurrection. Out of respect for death and its nonhuman agents, it is customary to give
names that do not evoke personal memories—specifically, names of individuals from G+3 and beyond.
As among the Féénemɨna, name giving represents a powerful act of subjectivation, through which one
person forms another by bestowing specific behaviors, characteristics, capacities, and defenses upon
them (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 40–41, 62; see also Walker 2013, 140–41). This practice is not limited to
children but extends to adults as well, as names can be changed throughout one’s life to accommodate
changing personal circumstances. The logic of naming is also utilized for purposes of sorcery and
healing. In these contexts, by giving a patient object X the name of a referent object Y, one manipulates
X, endowing it with the behavior or characteristics of Y.31
The power and impact of clan names, which involve acting on the named person (see also Whiffen
1915, 154), partly explain why clan names are rarely used. Instead, people are usually addressed by their
nicknames, White names, or formal titles such as Gobernador ([Reserve] “Governor”) even by their own
mothers. Using clan names to address elders is considered utterly disrespectful (further discussed
below). While all Andoque members possess Indigenous clan names, most of these names are often
disregarded by others, treated as mere nicknames. They are frequently forgotten by individuals outside
the clan or beyond the nuclear family, and even their bearers may hesitate to utter them when requested.
Following Lucas’s terminology, we can refer to these names as “ordinary names,” contrasting them with
“tutelary names” (2019, 169–70) that are widely considered “real.”32

31
32

See also Chapter 9. For this practice among neighboring peoples, see Londoño Sulkin 2012, 72–75; Lucas 2019, 292–93.
On the hierarchizing aspect of unequal name giving, see Turner 2003, 19.

127

A tutelary name is bestowed on a child by a maloquero during one of several ceremonial dances. These
dances serve as an introduction of the child, or sometimes two children of different sexes, to the entire
community and particularly to the personified territory and origin. The purpose of the ceremonial name
giving is for the territory and origin spirits to recognize, protect, support, and safeguard the named
individuals. Some elders take pride in their knowledge of which names are more favorable, as they
believe such names ensure greater support and stronger defense from the owner-persons of the territory
and origin. Tutelary names are given during the dances River Turtle-Carrier Band (Bisokń Paadi),
Fausíya, Head (Ĩtai), and Armadillo (Féíko). While there is some variation in the age at which children
can be named, with some setting the maximum age at one year, Fisi argues that children can be given a
name even up to the age of four. However, based on an analysis of familial stories and ritual practices, it
appears that children can only receive a name during a dance if they do not have a younger sibling. Once
a younger sibling is born, the focus of ceremonial name giving shifts to the younger brother, and
children who have surpassed the age limit or have a younger sibling are considered “adult” and can be
named alongside other adults in the Multiplying Tree (Tu’sí) or Fausíya Dances. However, such name
giving does not carry the same level of leadership and prestige as the River Turtle-Carrier Band and
Head Dances or an individual naming at the Fausíya, nor is it specifically associated with child
protection like the Armadillo Dance (see Chapter 11).
The significance of tutelary names lies in the belief that the child becomes identified with the specific
dance in which they are named, for better or worse. On one hand, those named in a particular dance are
granted a privileged status as organizers of that dance, and the spiritual owner of the dance is more
likely to accept their offerings, thereby enhancing the effectiveness of their own dances. On the other
hand, if they neglect their designated dance or fail to name their child or nephew in it, the owner-person
may cause them harm, as the act of naming serves as a lifelong invocation of that entity that should be
accompanied by proper offerings and ceremonial continuity.
Since name-giving dances belongs to either the peɒɵsí (red) or pó’fiɵ (white) ritual specialization, those
who receive a name in these dances are considered to belong to one of the two specializations and
possess the prerogative to organize or actively participate in other dances associated with that
specialization. As will be discussed in Chapter 11, each specialization is associated with specific
personal characteristics, so the elder who bestows a name in a dance and assigns a particular
specialization is shaping the individual as a specific type of person.

128

The defense provided by tutelary names has a more collective nature, extending not only to the named
child but also to their siblings. Not all siblings of maloca families are given names in these dances, and
there is a belief, particularly upheld by Fisi and his family members, that only one child from each
family should receive a tutelary name. Typical of his “centralist” tendency, Fisi justifies this by
explaining that if everyone were to be named in the dance, the significance of the names would
diminish, as the territory and its owner-persons cannot attend to the calls of all individuals. “There was
only one Nénéfi, only one Egret of the Center,” he says, associating the uniqueness of these deities with
the appropriate uniqueness of individuals engaging in communication with them. However, other
members believe that ideally, the first-born and second-born siblings should be named, with each one
receiving a name in a different dance. This viewpoint aligns with the broader framework of the two
ritual specializations discussed in Chapter 11, as well as with the Bora and Miraña practices, where the
first-born siblings of both sexes receive “beautiful” names and the second-born siblings receive “ugly”
names (Karadimas 2005, 38–39; Lucas 2019, 170–72).
The aforementioned observations primarily concern male children. When a boy is given a name, it is
common for his real or classificatory sister to be given a name alongside him. Girls without brothers
may receive a name by themselves, typically in the Head, Fausíya, Armadillo, or Multiplying Tree
Dances, but not in River Turtle-Carrier Band. During the name-giving ceremony, the name-giving elder,
ideally the host, stands inside the maloca with the mother and child. They declare the name to another
elder, preferably the guest, using the phrase “you shall call me” (onáháé’ni), a formula inherited from
the Piercers (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 225 n.20bis). The guest repeats the name, and the host calls
him to consume X’s coca—X being the child’s new name. “Come consume X’s coca,” the guest then
summons his men, and each one approaches the coca, stating “I am going to consume X’s coca.” The
same sequence repeats with the tobacco paste and vegetal salt. The following morning the same is done
with meat and the rest of the food. The name thus becomes widely known to group members and to the
owner-persons of the territory through repetition and the consumption of substances imbued with the
intention to instill the name and the child’s identity in the participants (for similar observations among
the Féénemɨna, see Londoño Sulkin 2000, 393). This performative speech act solidifies the child’s
affiliation with a human center. Names that are not declared in such a way are rarely recognized or are
quickly forgotten.

129

The accurate pronunciation and proper response during the name declaration are crucial, as any errors
can place the child in grave danger, potentially leading to their death. An incident from the 1970s
provides an illustrative example in which a Nonuya man gave a name to his Andoque nephew. My
interlocutors attributed the child’s death a few years later to the mispronunciation by the uncle of certain
utterances in Féénemɨna, the language used for the ceremony. In another instance, a maloquero shared a
story where his longstanding rival had asked him to teach the formula for giving his grandson a name in
a specific dance. However, during the actual name-giving ceremony, the grandfather forgot the correct
formula. In response, the rival-teacher intervened, tearing the vegetal salt from his hands and performing
the ritual himself to spare the child from potential accidents or diseases. These stories, reflecting
conflicting positions in power struggles, should not be taken at face value. Nevertheless, they highlight
the influence and control that name givers possess over the named children, capable of ensuring their
well-being by correctly linking them to a strong origin and a consanguineous center, or potentially
causing harm if performed incorrectly and allowing them to drift into the affinal faunal world.
It should be emphasized that the power of name giving is predominantly held by men. Both the
ceremony itself and the selection of names, including cases where girls received a name based on their
mother’s clan, are caried out by men. This can be viewed as a variation on the common Amazonian
pattern of “subordinating women’s biological reproductive powers within more prestigious processes
and relations of social reproduction controlled by men” (T. Turner 2003, 22). While women play an
important role in the physical formation of their children, which ties them to the human group, name
giving represents an additional practice of familiarization that carries notions of prestige and is solely
conducted by men. However, it is important to note that in the Andoque perspective, this familiarization
is performed precisely to protect the child and the group from the affinal world, from which women who
marry into the group, including the child’s mother, originate.
While physical formation and name giving are means of creating a center through “familiarizing
downwards,” extending kinship from parents and elders to children, the center is also continuously
reaffirmed and produced through “upwards familiarization.” I use this term to describe the naming
avoidance and use of consanguineous kinship terms when addressing elders of G+1 and beyond, i.e.,
yodɨ (uncle), píta (aunt), yo’tapɵ (grandfather), yota (grandmother). This practice not only refrains from
exercising power over the addressed person by using their clan name, but also places the speaker in a
position of inferiority and humility in relation to the elder. It is an acknowledgement of the elder’s

130

superior knowledge and power, with the implicit intention of eliciting protection and care from them.
Similar to the formulae used when addressing the owner-persons of the territory’s sites, where people
identify themselves as their grandchildren to avoid harm, children are instructed to show respect to both
known and unknown elders by calling them “grandfather” or “grandmother.” Elders recall being scolded
by their parents when they were children for staring at old people and their physical signs of aging, as it
was believed that these elders could cast a spell to make the child age rapidly or acquire similar
blemishes. Therefore, the “respect” shown by using kinship terms should be understood as a feigned
humility rooted in fear, particularly fear of sorcery. These instructions also extend to youth in general.
One of my interlocutors explained that a man should avoid using the term “father-in-law” when
referring to a man who has the ability to bewitch him, and even when the man in question is unknown
and classified as an affine, it is safer to address him as “uncle” or “grandfather,” alongside the offering
of coca and tobacco as tokens of respect for men in general, and fish and game, for all elders of G+2.
Thus, the use of affinal terminology frames the situation as one of predation between rival centers, while
the use of consanguineous terminology frames it in terms of protection and nurturing within the same
center, where the younger member provides foodstuffs to the elder in exchange for teachings and
defense. Through such practices, a person can expand their center in certain situations, encompassing
individuals who are both potentially dangerous and beneficial.
Having discussed, in this chapter, the power-laden processes by which people are assigned specific
centers, in the following chapter, we move from conceptual analysis to the examination of one historical
process of center formation which is crucial for understanding the Andoque’s present reality—namely,
their post-genocide recuperation.

131

132

Chapter 4. The Center Reemerges After the Flood
How do the notions of center and its formation, as discussed in the previous chapters, elucidate the
Andoque’s recent history, and what significance did the captaincy and cannibalistic systems, along with
the concepts of exchange and power of each, hold for them in formative historical moments? In this
chapter, I propose some answers to these questions by exploring the Andoque’s recovery from the
devastation inflicted upon them by the agents of the Peruvian Amazon Rubber Company, known as the
Casa Arana. This process encompasses early attempts to reassemble under the leadership of Dóñékɒi
(“Yellow Fluff”) in the 1910s–1920s; the deportation of the majority of Dóñékɒi’s group in 1928, and
the subsequent regrouping of surviving Andoque survivors in the latter half of the 1930s. Led by
Yiñékɒ, Dóñékɒi’s son, they reconstructed the Andoque as a linguistic and ethnic group firmly
established in their ancestral territory.
The main elements of the demographic and cultural recovery process have been masterfully explored by
Landaburu (1993), focusing on Yiñékɒ as the primary catalyst for the Andoque’s post-genocide
transformation. Landaburu asserted that Yiñékɒ had played a vital role in shifting the Andoque’s focus
away from internecine clan politics and towards peaceful engagement with others, especially with nonIndigenous agents. According to Landaburu, evidence of this shift can be seen in Yiñékɒ’s decision to
resettle closer to Araracuara and the Caquetá River, rather than in the ancestral territory of his clan, the
Eagle Clan. Furthermore, Landaburu argued that Yiñékɒ had reworked the Andoque mythology by
replacing the cannibal god Ñé’ñéfi, strongly associated with the Eagle Clan, and other heroes
symbolizing different Andoque clans and occupying hierarchical positions signifying their predatory
nature, with egret figures associated with their residence along the horizontal fluvial axis. He suggested
that Yiñékɒ had not entirely discarded these ancient gods but confined them to the celestial realm, where
they provide assistance and guidance to people through the mediation of the shaman or captain.
Additionally, Landaburu attributed to Yiñékɒ the inclusion of orphan figures in some myths,
symbolizing current vulnerability yet a potential for reclaiming agency and empowering others, and
representing Yiñékɒ’s humble origin. Finally, he described endogamy as a strategic value for this
process of rehabilitation (Landaburu 1993).
In general, my analysis in this chapter agrees with Landaburu’s conclusions. However, I draw on oral
accounts gathered from Andoque members, additional data from mythology, and post-genocide kinship
and economic dynamics, to further substantiate some of Landaburu’s findings and provide a nuanced

133

perspective on others, and to integrate these historical data into the conceptual framework of this
dissertation. I argue that Dóñékɒi emphasized the significance of collaboration and exchange with nonIndigenous agents crucial for the revival of the Andoque people. Future endeavors to constitute the
center would thus recognize that the primary spatial system for this center is the captaincy system, rather
than a cannibalistic one. Yiñékɒ assumed the mission of creating this center. Through an analysis of
competing versions of another flood myth, “The Orphans’ Flood,” I will contend that while Yiñékɒ
acknowledged the orphan status of himself and other survivors, his utilization of preexisting mythical
narratives reveals an attempt not to merely replace earlier gods, but to gain access to their predatory
agency and abilities. This attempt reflects the Andoque’s drawing on the cannibalistic system as well. I
will examine the predatory dimensions of the Multiplying Tree Dance, which were considered essential
for achieving demographic growth after the genocide. Additionally, I will examine the kinship, ritual,
and economic factors that allowed Yiñékɒ to establish himself as the core (ḭdɨá, or cacique) of the
survivor group, and analyze the actions he undertook between the 1930s-1950s to shape a unified center,
exert control over others, and familiarize them by aligning their agencies to his own. Lastly, I will
highlight specific historical moments that either marked or influenced the dissolution of this center
starting from the 1960s. This chapter demonstrates how the cosmo-economic systems and the production
of centers, as previously discussed, manifested in recent Andoque history. It serves as a historical
narrative of a pivotal period for the Andoque, emphasizing power dynamics relevant in later chapters.
Dóñékɒi: Preferring Exchange over Predation
Instead of providing a comprehensive account of the atrocities inflicted upon the Andoque and other
indigenous peoples of the Center by the agents of this company during the early twentieth century, I will
offer a summary of the key events. For an in-depth understanding of these events, I recommend
consulting the testimonies of primary witnesses such as Walter Hardenburg (1913), who conducted a
visit to the area in 1907, and Roger Casement (1912; 1997), who investigated these crimes on behalf of
the British parliament in 1910; scholarly analyses by Pineda Camacho (2000) and Michael Taussig
(1986); Carlos Páramo Bonilla’s (2008) portrayal of Armando Normand, a notably sadistic agent of the
Casa Arana who oversaw the section known as “Andoques” or “Matanzas” (literally meaning
“Massacres”), where the Andoque community was located, and Zoila Erazo’s first hand testimony
concerning this man (Chirif 2017, 229–44). These sources offer a more detailed exploration of the
subject matter.

134

After more than a decade of relatively small-scale rubber extraction headed by Colombian bosses who
engaged the Indigenous work force through a combination of enticing them with manufactured goods
and employing violence, Julio César Arana entered the Caquetá-Putumayo region in 1899. By 1905,
Arana had successfully established a monopoly over rubber extraction and gained complete control over
the Indigenous workforce in the region (Pineda Camacho 2000, 55–75). During this period, the
production of rubber reached unprecedented levels, while the Indigenous population experienced a sharp
decline. They were subjected to enslavement, torture, rape, and other forms of brutal mistreatment, as
well as severe hunger due to the excessive demands of rubber work, which left them with insufficient
time to cultivate crops or gather food. The magnitude of terror and extermination inflicted upon the
People of the Center becomes evident when examining Hardenburg’s summary of the atrocities in
thirteen points:
1. The pacific Indians of the Putumayo are forced to work day and night at the extraction of rubber, without the
slightest remuneration except the food necessary to keep them alive.
2.

They are kept in most complete nakedness, many of them not even possessing the biblical fig leaf.

3.

They are robbed of their crops, their women, and their children to satisfy the voracity, lasciviousness, and avarice of
this company and its employees, who live on their food and violate their women.

4.

They are sold wholesale and retail in Iquitos, at prices that range from £20 to £40 each.

5.

They are flogged inhumanly until their bones are laid bare, and great raw sores cover them.

6.

They are given no medical treatment, but are left to die, eaten by maggots, when they serve as food for the chiefs’
dogs.

7.

They are castrated and mutilated, and their ears, fingers, arms, and legs are cut off.

8.

They are tortured by means of fire and water, and by tying them up, crucified head down.

9.

Their houses and crops are burned and destroyed wantonly and for amusement.

10. They are cut to pieces and dismembered with knives, axes, and machetes.
11. Their children are grasped by the feet and their heads are dashed against trees and walls until their brains fly out.
12. Their old folk are killed when they are no longer able to work for the company.
13. Men, women, and children are shot to provide amusement for the employees or to celebrate the sábado de gloria, or,
in preference to this, they are burned with kerosene so that the employees may enjoy their desperate agony
(Hardenburg 1913, 184–85; see also Casement’s endorsement of these statements [1997, 255]).

In the wake of the international scandal caused by Hardenburg’s denouncement and Casement’s
investigation, Peru opened a judicial inquiry into the Casa Arana’s operations in 1911 and issued orders
for the capture of several company leaders. However, the Peruvian authorities soon withdrew the
charges (Pineda Camacho 2000, 178). As World War I diverted international attention away from the

135

region, the company continued its operations, albeit with a gradual decline in rubber extraction due to
falling prices (ibid, 183–89). While mistreatment of Indigenous people persisted during this period, it
appeared to be less severe than in first decade of the century, with greater concessions to Indigenous
people to engage in horticultural practices for sustenance. This relative “unworsening” (desempeorar) of
enslavement conditions, as described by Pineda, may explain the little support for the cause of the
Murui-Muina captain Yarocamena in 1917, who initiated a rebellion against the company (ibid, 2000,
160), along with the longstanding distrust between clans and language groups that Casa Arana agents
exploited to incite conflict. Instances of resistance occurred sporadically, including some uprisings by
the Andoque (e.g., Cornejo Chaparro and Yllia Miranda 2009, 187, 189). Many other Indigenous people
sought refuge on the north bank of the Caquetá River and downstream near Campoamor on the MiritíParaná River, beyond the Peruvians’ reach, where Colombian rubber bosses offered a relatively less
violent environment for rubber gathering (Pineda Camacho 2000, 145–47). In 1924, after the SalomónLozano treaty recognized Colombian sovereignty north to the Putumayo River, Casa Arana agents
initiated the deportation of thousands of individuals from the People of the Center to Peru, including a
reported 361 Andoque people headed by Dóñékɒi, Yiñékɒ’s father (ibid, 194; Razón 1984 in Lucas
2019, 73). The operations of Casa Arana in the Caquetá-Putumayo region came to an end when they
were pursued by Colombia, whose government had previously refrained from taking action regarding
these territories, during the armed conflict of 1932. By the conclusion of this conflict, the Andoque
population had been devastated. From an estimate of 10,000 people reported by Whiffen during his visit
in 1908 (1915, 59), only some thirty survivors remained in the Caquetá region and returned, in the mid1930s, to their ancestral land, under the leadership of Yiñékɒ.
Presently, the Andoque people exhibit a collective reluctance to discuss the period known as “the Time
of Peru” (el tiempo de Perú). Andoque elders, in particular, refrain from delving into this topic. Some
explain that they have never asked their parents and grandparents about that period because the
survivors would start crying. They also express their aversion to discussing those dark times when
Indigenous people, including the Andoque, fought against and oppressed each other while serving the
interests of the Peruvians. Similar to the inclination observed by Echeverri (2010) among the People of
the Center to heal from that upheaval rather than remembering it, Andoque elders generally consider
dwelling on such memories as “useless” (no sirve). The elder Germán, for instance, said, “I used to tell
my father, ‘Don’t tell me about the Casa Arana; tell me [other] stories, teach me spells, teach me things
that I could use!’” Instead of recounting the few oral accounts collected, this discussion will center on
136

the roles attributed to Dóñékɒi, Yinñéfɵkn and Miguel Zumaeta in these narratives, which shed light on
the subsequent establishment of the center under Yiñékɒ’s leadership. The account derived from the
transcript of the mambeadero conversation with Fisi and Nestor (see C1, in Appendix 2) represents the
roles assigned to these three individuals during the genocide and recovery by other interlocutors.
However, while some interlocutors shared narratives describing a gradual encroachment of Peruvians
into Andoque territory and the initial enticing of Indigenous populations into rubber gathering through
the provision of manufactured goods, Fisi and Nestor’s account depicts the Casa Arana’s agents arriving
abruptly in Andoque land and forcibly compelling people to work for them. Despite Fisi’s assertion that
Dóñékɒi’s father taught him about the Speaking Tree and other important traditions that a captain should
master, it seems that Dóñékɒi belonged to a lesser lineage withing the Eagle Clan than Yinñéfɵkn,
whose father’s maloca received the goods. Fisi’s saying that “Dóñékɒi’s father gave Yobidi Kadanni,
Yinñéfɵkn’s father, the power to fight when they [Dóñékɒi and Yinñéfɵkn] were still children” may be
an acknowledgement of hierarchical difference between them. Dóñékɒi’s inferiority is also suggested by
Landaburu (1993, 150). According to the information provided to Estrada Añokazi by Andoque
members, Yinñéfɵkn ceded control to Dóñékɒi, and not vice versa, because he had been trained for a
medicinal specialization and did not like captaincy (2017, 199). In the testimony that Landaburu and
Pineda collected from Yinñéfɵkn, the eldest survivor of the genocide at that time, his father’s authority
is extensively described, but Padamnta, Dóñékɒi’s father, was not mentioned among the clan captains of
the period preceding the genocide. Yinñéfɵkn only mentioned that Dóñékɒi had become one of the two
captains when rubber extraction was already underway (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 237). As Fisi
recounts, Dóñékɒi only had a maloca after the end of Normand’s supervision, which appears to mark the
conclusion of the most devastating period for the Andoque people.
Dóñékɒi’s ascent to captaincy appears to be influenced by both his resourcefulness and flexibility
represented in bridging clan divisions and gathering surviving individuals from various clans, estimated
to be around 300 people (ibid, 239; Landaburu 1993, 150), and by his pragmatic approach to
collaboration with the Casa Arana’s overseers. Similar to other captains in the region, Dóñékɒi was
provided with weapons by the company agents to secure rubber extraction by his people. It is important
to consider these actions undertaken by Dóñékɒi (and other regional captains) as strategic measures
aimed at minimizing torture, suffering, and extermination inflicted by the company agents. This

137

involved providing the required amounts of rubber to settle inflated debts that were impossible for
Indigenous people to measure and to acquire much-needed manufactured goods and metal tools.
Although Fisi describes how Dóñékɒi received weapons from Normand, he particularly highlights the
former’s collaboration with Miguel Zumaeta. This collaboration eventually led to Zumaeta’s initiative to
relocate Dóñékɒi’s group to the safer Metá River, north of the Caquetá, where he would continue rubber
extraction with them independently of the Casa Arana, thus protecting them from the company’s
intended deportation to Peru. In Fisi and Nestor’s narrative, Zumaeta emerges as the savior of the
Andoque people, rescuing them from Normand’s sadistic treatment. Miguel Zumaeta belonged to a
family that was closely allied with Julio Arana: his sister Eleonora was Arana’s wife, his brother Pablo
was the company’s general manager, and his other brother Bartolomé was killed by a Bora man while
overseeing rubber extraction in the Putumayo (Casement 1997, 250). Nevertheless, and although Miguel
Zumaeta seems to have worked with Arana from an age as early seventeen (Guzmán Gonzalez 1971,
53), Fisi and Nestor describe him as a military commander who arrived to the region to capture
Normand following the order of his superiors. Contrary to their account, Normand was not arrested in
the Caquetá-Putumayo region by a military commander who brought him back to Peru and later returned
to produce rubber. After facing prosecution by Peruvian courts following Casement’s investigation,
Normand fled to various countries before being caught and extradited to Peru. He was then imprisoned
in 1913 and escaped prison in 1915 (Páramo Bonilla 2008, 80). My elder interlocutors acknowledged
that Miguel was also violent and would punish their parents if they brought insufficient rubber
quantities. The fact that he had taken multiple Indigenous spouses or concubines, including two
Andoque women, without necessarily seeking the consent of those women or their families, further
demonstrates how he preserved the sexually predatory patterns exhibited by previous rubber bosses.
However, his rule was perceived as less arbitrary and disproportionately violent compared to previous
overseers. Other interlocutors concur that under his command, Dóñékɒi and his people were allowed to
engage in horticultural practices for their own sustenance and hold ceremonial dances that promoted
crop abundance and social reproduction, whose felicitous organization increases a captain’s prestige.
The testimony of Duñékɒ (“Water Fluff”), a survivor from Yiñékɒ’s generation, as presented by Pineda

138

(2000, 198–201), illustrates the interconnected trajectories of Andoque individuals with Zumaeta’s
occasional travels to sell rubber and acquire goods on their behalf.33
It is difficult to determine the duration of Dóñékɒi leadership before the deportation of his group to Peru
in 1928, after Zumaeta’s superiors discovered his plan to secretly relocate the Andoque population to a
safe area on the Metá River, north to the Caquetá, for which he ordered the Andoque to prepare several
years earlier by clearing garden plots. It is also unclear whether Miguel Zumaeta assumed control
immediately after Normand’s flight, as Fisi recounts, or later. Guzmán, for instance, stated that he was
only sent by the Casa Arana to reorganize the Andoque’s work in 1925 (Guzmán Gonzalez 1971, 53). It
appears that Dóñékɒi was already captain by 1917, because, according to members’ accounts, he refused
the tobacco that Yarocamena shared with captains to invite them to join his revolt, which is dated to that
year (Pineda Camacho 2000, 163). In another conversation with Fisi and Nestor, they mentioned that the
only Andoque clans to join the revolt were the Ara, Opossum, and Toad Clans—the same clans
suspected of the unjust violence against the priests and nuns (see C1), which allegedly unleashed the
Peruvians’ extreme abuse and violence against the Andoque. While one reason for the refusal of most
Andoque people to support Yarocamena may be the earlier hostility between this Murui-Muina captain
and Andoque clans, it is also possible that another factor was the relatively lenient working conditions
under the agent overseeing the Andoque’s rubber work at that period. As Pineda argues for the region as
a whole, the limited Indigenous support for Yarocamena may be attributed, in part, to the relative
“unworsening” of work conditions in the years following Casement’s report and especially the global
decline in rubber prices during WWI (Pineda Camacho 2000, 160). Whether the Andoque’s overseer at
that time was Miguel Zumaeta who had already reached some understandings with Dóñékɒi or another
agent, Dóñékɒi’s lack of support for Yarocamena’s cause may have also contributed to his portrayal as a
pragmatic Indigenous leader in the eyes of the Casa Arana’s agents, including Zumaeta.
Dóñékɒi’s preference to work with Zumaeta (and possibly previous Casa Arana agents) was
accompanied by a more restrained approach to combat, as described by Fisi when he mentions that
Dóñékɒi “set aside his weapon to become a cacique and organize dances.” However, Dóñékɒi’s
disengagement from combat is also connected to his position as the leader of a group comprising

In his thesis, Levy Andoke adopts a more critical tone towards Zumaeta, stating that upon his return from captivity by the
Casa Arana to the Andoque territory, “he never provided any explanations to the rest of the people [the Andoque survivors]
about the [Andoque] people who had been captured alongside him. His response did not extend beyond stating that he did not
know what had happened to them. Nevertheless, the Andoque accepted him once again” (L. Andoke 2011, 61–62).

33

139

survivors from multiple previously internecine clans. This dual withdrawal from fighting, both with
other Indigenous clans and non-Indigenous agents, alongside a focus on work and exchange with the
latter, forms the political backdrop for the strengthening of the Egret mythology—or the political project
that this mythology aims to achieve. Therefore, this process, which Landaburu (1993) attributed to
Yiñékɒ, may predate this captain and have its roots at least in his father’s captaincy.
As Landaburu noted, the transition from the vertical animal mythology to the horizontal egret
mythology aligns with the political centrality of Yiñékɒ and the marginality of Yinñéfɵkn, who, in the
eyes of Landaburu’s interlocutors, embodied old clan identities and aggressive, cannibalistic tendencies.
This memory persists among Andoque members today, who widely agree that Yinñéfɵkn, as a young
person in the early twentieth century, participated in the cannibal dances held during that period.
Interestingly, Andoque members tend to exaggerate Yinñéfɵkn’s collaboration with the Casa Arana
agents. While he admitted in his testimony to catering for Indigenous prisoners (Landaburu and Pineda
1984, 238)—presumably following the Peruvians’ orders—several interlocutors described him as a
permanent guard at the company’s service, who later also held a similar position at the Araracuara Penal
Colony. However, this is doubtful since the colony was founded in 1938 when he would have been
almost 50 years old, according to my estimation. Some even claim that in both positions he consumed
the flesh of dead prisoners. In contrast to this unrestrained voracity, Dóñékɒi’s pragmatic, work-oriented
approach is evident in his preference, reported by his grandchildren Fisi and Irene, to utilize the captives
he received as laborers rather than consuming them. The memory of the two men thus exemplifies the
distinction between the cannibalistic and captaincy systems.
The deportation to Peru decimated Dóñékɒi’s group, with a reported 361 individuals being deported.
However, today there are very few Indigenous people in Peru who identify as Andoque, and the
Andoque language does not appear in the Peruvian register of spoken Indigenous languages (Chirif
2017, 228). Dóñékɒi himself never set foot on his homeland again, but Miguel Zumaeta did come back
in the 1930s to resume rubber work with the surviving Andoque, now under the leadership of Dóñékɒi’s
son, Yiñékɒ. As Guzmán pointed out, rubber, the resource that nearly annihilated them, became a
coveted source of income and economic stability that they did not want to abandon (Guzmán Gonzalez
1971, 76–77). The main river, along which persons are exchangeable with objects and hierarchy
between orphans and captains prevails, remained the primary spatial axis for the Andoque, rather than
the smaller rivers along which persons are exchanged for other persons. The history of Yiñékɒ’s group,

140

which we will now examine, also reveals a gradual movement toward the Caquetá River, where the
majority of Andoque population resides today.
The Orphans, Latent Eagle, and Multiplying Tree
Yiñékɒ’s evasion of capture when Dóñékɒi and most of his people were deported to Peru and his
subsequent initiation into Andoque traditions were pivotal in this people’s recuperation process. As I
will show in this section, Yiñékɒ’s eventual reworking of these traditions and emphasis on specific
dances were geared toward empowering the Andoque survivors and rehabilitating their agency by
reconnecting this center with the aggressive and fertilizing powers of the river source.
Reportedly a boy of ten to twelve years old when he lost his family, Yiñékɒ managed to escape with a
small group of individuals. Over the following years Yiñékɒ and other survivors found refuge in La
Palma, a location downstream on the Caquetá River near La Pedrera, where Miraña and Yucuna
communities also resided. During this time, the Andoque population experienced additional losses due
to epidemics that struck the region in the late 1920s and early 1930s, including diseases such as measles,
smallpox, and flu (Pineda Camacho 2000, 196–98), and which were attributed to the sorcery of
neighboring groups.
As Casement had already observed in 1910, elders had become a rare sight in the Caquetá-Putumayo,
especially among the Andoque, as Normand had killed all the elders who could not collect rubber and
who had been suspected of advising the younger generations against collecting rubber (Casement 1997,
250). As a result, the majority of survivors who gathered in La Palma or sought refuge in the forest
elsewhere were relatively young. Andoque members today tend to downplay the role of the surviving
elders, attributing to them a disparaging attitude towards Yiñékɒ and a discouraging stance toward the
recovery efforts in general.
In the years after the deportation of his father’s group, Yiñékɒ reportedly wandered among the Yucuna
and Tanimuca along the Mirití River, recovering his ancestral traditions through experimentation with
hallucinogenic plants and particularly by learning from an elder of the Oropendola clan, called Mnkoena
(meaning uncertain) (L. Andoke 2011, 48). Andoque members today express differing versions
concerning the extent of Mnkoena’s role in Yiñékɒ’s apprenticeship process, and the contrasting
versions held by Tañe and Fisi also reflect their own claims for knowledge and power. Tañe represents
an expansive version in which the wise old man, through his shamanic skills, realized that the Andoque

141

in La Palma were targeted by Bora and Miraña sorcerers, and came to their rescue, protecting these
young refugees who were unable to defend themselves. Mnkoena, who, according to Tañe, belonged to
the Miraña Oropendola clan, cured for the Andoque their ancestral territory after decades during which
it had been neglected and abused, and transmitted to Yiñékɒ knowledge that is rooted in the Miraña
traditions, bestowing upon him his spiritual power, or tne’túi. “This is what the late father-in-law told
me,” said Tañe, quoting Yiñékɒ in Andoque, “‘My uncle Mnkoena gave me his power, this is how I
have this knowledge (o yodɨ yatne’túi bɵñe nima ao dotañé). We are no longer orphans, the late
[Yiñékɒ] said, because we have this power with us.” When I inquired about the source of Yiñékɒ’s
power, Tañe clarified that it derived from the Miraña elder, not from Dóñékɒi. This version of
transmission, bypassing the direct father-to-son lineage, aligns with Tañe’s position as a man of Miraña
paternal descent, who bases his aspiration for leadership on the power and knowledge entrusted to him
by Yiñékɒ to prepare his son (and Yiñékɒ’s grandson) for captaincy (see Chapter 10).

Figure 8. Tañe Andoke Andoke toasting coca leaves (Photo taken by the author)

On the other hand, Fisi, whose claim to power is based on the transmission of knowledge and power
from father to son, portrays Mnkoena as a mere laborer at the maloca where he lived before the
genocide, responsible for coca pounding (un pilador). Fisi limits Mnkoena’s role to assisting Yiñékɒ in
reconnecting with his late father’s heritage. “Mnkoena offered my father coca, but he refused, saying
that coca is dirty (feo), that it’s an earthworm, because that was the story that he knew [M1], and told
him: if my father was still alive, I would ask him to give me a story with which I could mambeate
(mambear, consume coca powder),” said Fisi. “Then Mnkoena told him the story of the coca of the

142

orphans [M2], and my father started mambeating. If he hadn’t told him that, I wouldn’t have any
knowledge (no tendría idea), and my father wouldn’t have any knowledge, so that’s how he saved me.”
According to Fisi, Mnkoena recognized Yiñékɒ’s father as a great captain, guided the young orphan in
his leadership path, and directed his efforts towards recovering his clan traditions and the knowledge
possessed by Dóñékɒi.
Fisi’s reference to M2 is significant because in this myth the coca plant aids the orphans in overcoming
their separation from their father, Egret of the Center, referred to as Sḭ́ di at the end of the narrative, and
learn the teachings of this potent cannibal god from the river source despite his physical absence. More
particularly, Sḭ́ di’s thunder serves as a warning to his orphaned children, alerting them to an imminent
deluge of fiery water advancing from the east, i.e., the river mouth. This aligns with the arrival of Casa
Arana agents who penetrated Andoque territory by traversing the Cahuinarí and Igará-Paraná Rivers
upstream. The image of orphanhood holds a significant position in contemporary mambeadero discourse
and mythical narratives, whether portrayed as two orphan brothers in some myths or two brothers and
one sister in others. In what follows, I demonstrate how this image, as it appears in the flood myth
alluded to in M2, empowered the recovering Andoque group and facilitated its repositioning within the
cannibalistic cosmos.
This flood myth, M10, as narrated in Appendix 1, is referred to as “the Orphans’ Flood.” It is considered
a benign myth, contrary to the dangerous M9 recounting “the Eagle’s Flood.” In its present form, M10
incorporates the former myth as one of its episodes. In this story, two orphans trigger the flood by
chewing on the marrow of Nocturnal Curassow (Sábúdui; Nothocrax urumutum). The hot liquid pouring
out of the bone submerges the earth, right when the spread wings of the eagles dam the river (M9).
Alongside several animals, the orphans find refuge from the flood water on a growing tree, from the top
of which they see Hummingbird Egg (Pá̰di hádɨ) going downriver to steal from there an ember to lit new
fire for the surviving humanity instead of the one extinguished by the flood. This is the only Andoque
myth I have heard that involves episode sequences resembling those found in movies or TV series, with
cross-cutting. One moment, the orphans climb a tree and witness Hummingbird Egg going downriver to
steal fire. Then, we shift to another maloca to witness the stealing episode, followed by Hummingbird’s
return to the Center. Finally, we return to the orphans who perceive the imminent break of dawn and are
fed by their mother from above. The closest example I have for such cross-cutting in Andoque
mythology is M20 (see Appendix 1), where the scenes shift only once, between the adventures

143

undergone by the girl who goes under the earth and the ones undergone by her sister who reaches the
sky, and not twice, as in the flood myth.
The exceptional sequence of episodes in M10 provides evidence of the recent and somewhat disjointed
introduction of the theme of the orphans, which can plausibly be attributed to Yiñékɒ, who taught Fisi
the myth recorded in Appendix 1. In the version recounted to me by Raquel and transmitted to her by
Yinñéfɵkn, the two brothers are identified as Nénéfi, the elder, and Hummingbird Egg, the younger,
who encourages his elder to consume the boiling marrow of Nocturnal Curassow. In this version there is
only one cross-cutting instead of two, which follows a vertical logic, like in M20. As the water level
rises, Nénéfi is compelled to climb up to the sky on a seed that transforms into a tree, while
Hummingbird goes downriver to acquire a new fire, which Crestless Curassow then swallows and
defecates. This latter episode symmetrically mirrors Hummingbird Egg’s prior consumption in this
version of another hot element, namely, the marrow of Nocturnal Curassow, a bird resembling Crestless
Curassow physically but seen as its opposite because of its nocturnal singing habits, in contrast to the
crestless curassow’s morning singing (in Fisi’s version, the orphans are the ones who consume the
marrow). I assume that Yinñéfɵkn and Raquel’s version predates Fisi’s due to its more traditional
sequence of episodes and neater symmetrical structure. This version also bears greater resemblance to
Murui-Muina and Miraña narratives, where two brothers—Sun and Hummingbird in the Murui-Muina
variant, or two hummingbirds, according to the Miraña—cause a flood of boiling water by sucking the
hot marrow of a nocturnal curassow (Karadimas 2005, 315; Urbina Rangel 2010, 123–34; see also
García 2018, 222, n.60).34 The ascent described in Yinñéfɵkn and Raquel’s version, undertaken by
Nénéfi, the captain of eagles residing in the sky, also aligns with the other flood myth (M9), where the
flood separates the beings that inhabit the different vertical layers: Nénéfi’s creatures and extensions—
namely, the eagles—in the sky, Nénéfi’s people (the animals) beneath the earth, and human beings in
between on the earth’s surface.
It appears that Yiñékɒ (or possibly his father) replaced Nénéfi with the orphans and attributed to them
the action that originally belonged to Hummingbird Egg, and which triggers the flood (the
encouragement to suck the marrow). In line with Landaburu’s (1993) overall argument concerning
Yiñékɒ’s mythological reworking, I suggest that this substitution was aimed to remove specific clanIn another Miraña myth, which resembles M9 in that those living below the hero and hunted by him capture his son, the
hero is called Sun (Karadimas 2005b, 310–11). There are evident parallels between Sun and Nénéfi within Andoque
mythology as two predators living in the sky.
34

144

related elements from the narrative in order to make this much-needed myth about resilience more
relatable to members of other clans who have experienced significant losses in their own oral knowledge
and myth traditions. However, Landaburu’s interpretation of the centrality of the orphanhood theme in
the aftermath of the rubber genocide may be too restrictive. Based on another myth where they create
manguaré drums and a multiplying beam that outperform Pineapple’s (Tomirepa) ritual instruments,
Landaburu suggested that the orphans represent Dóñékɒi and Yiñékɒ, who were themselves bereft of
parents and belonged to a lesser lineage whose members had not held captaincy positions in the past,
and who managed to lead the group, instead of Yinñéfɵkn, who was born into a higher lineage (ibid,
153). However, myth heroes do not necessarily represent individuals with deliberate objectives, and as
ideologically powerful as they may be, we cannot assume that they were devised as mere tools for
promoting the leadership of specific historical figures. From a wider perspective, myth heroes can also
embody cosmic, social, or psychic forces that become subjects of reflection, fear, admiration, or hope
for the listeners, and the symbolic universe of mythology serves as a repository of elements for the
construction of both personal and collective identities.
In considering the theme of the orphans from this perspective, and in light of the previous discussion on
orphanhood as a lack of agency and predatory capacity, it becomes apparent that the orphans symbolize
the state in which the survivors found themselves in the 1930s. The orphanhood theme was central in the
discourse of other People of the Center (Pineda Camacho 2014, 108). These people were orphans not
only because they lacked parents, particularly fathers, or captains, but also because they had fallen prey
to the Casa Arana and now lacked the agency and predatory capacity typically embodied in such
knowledgeable elders and leaders, who would protect them from attacks by other groups or vengeful
nonhuman entities. The condition of deprivation, poverty, and hardship experienced by orphans also
provides an explanation for the disobedience of the orphans in M10 to the given orders and their
satisfaction of hunger through the consumption of the marrow. This action, which leads to the
catastrophic event, is performed or initiated in Raquel’s version and in the Murui-Muina narrative
(Urbina Rangel 2010, 124) by Hummingbird Egg, whose motives are voraciousness and mischief.
However, rather than being a permanent genealogical position or a marker of humble origin versus
captaincy, this orphanhood is a reversible status from which the orphan can emerge as a fully
empowered individual with greater agency. Therefore, the theme of the orphans should be viewed not
only as a strategic tool to advance a political project, but also in a broader transformative manner, as a

145

means to reconstitute the surviving Andoque as empowered agents endowed with a predatory capacity.
The act of placing the orphans on the growing tree instead of Nénéfi should not be interpreted solely as
an attempt to erase an element associated with the Eagle Clan from the myth. In fact, and although
Yiñékɒ’s version of the orphans’ flood myth became the widespread one, Nénéfi was not removed from
Andoque mythology, and his myths are still told in mambeaderos, even by Yiñékɒ’s sons. Instead, this
substitution can be understood as endowing the orphaned survivors with Nénéfi’s capacities and
elevating them to the position of this powerful eagle god, or at least to that of the members of the Eagle
Clan. It is a way to restore their center, reconstruct the space in which they exist by perceiving the river
source and the river mouth, and to receive the chili from the sky that would empower them, granting
them protection and the predatory abilities necessary to escape the position of prey and become fully
human again.35
The rehabilitation of predatory agency was also a key objective of the Multiplying Tree Dance (Tu’sí) in
post-genocide period. This dance was geared toward demographic growth by reestablishing links with
the aggressive and fertilizing river source. Fisi and other interlocutors told me that Dóñékɒi revived this
ceremonial dance, although Landaburu inferred from his data that it was not celebrated until Yiñékɒ’s
time (1993, 155). Both Fisi and Mario, his close ritual collaborator from the Deer Clan, recounted to me
that Sifa, a powerful sorcerer from Mario’s clan, played a crucial role in preserving the cherished
traditions associated with this dance and passing them down to Dóñékɒi. This recollection may serve as
a way for them to recall the historical relationship between their clans as one characterized by alliance
and mutual dependence, rather than warfare (ibid, 148, 158 n.9).
The Multiplying Tree Dance is also associated with the orphans and the flood myth. M11, in Appendix
1, as narrated to me by Fisi, recounts how the orphans, seeking to multiply humanity and crops again,
led the flood survivors to prepare a dance beam referred to as “Multiplying Anaconda” (Tu’sí Hɵpɵ) and
representing Red Anaconda (Pe’pai), one of the Creator’s sons, who had entrenched underneath the Site
of Tears, in the headwaters of several rivers in the Andoque territory (and hence, in the “river source”),
during the flood. To safeguard the beam and protect it from malevolent figures such as Green Tapir
(Pa’si Ḭtɵ), the people danced and sang:

On another occasion, Fisi and Nestor told me that the orphans first created a dancing beam from the açai
palm, which was formed from the anaconda’s entrails, calling it “multiplying açai” (pnta tu’sí) and
celebrating a dance so that human beings would become as numerous as the açai fruits. It was only later
that they decided to search for a harder beam that would embody Multiplying Anaconda itself, choosing
the ma̰kapa tree (see also Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 91–95).
This dance, to which we will return upon exploring the Andoque ritual system in Chapter 11, is
considered the seat (kupa) of all other dances. Since the illnesses and misfortunes in general, and the
genocide in particular, are perceived as forms of nonhuman predation over humans, the dance was
celebrated, as Irene explained to me, “to multiply people, so that nothing will become an animal.” It is
associated with patrilineal continuity and the dominance of agnation over exchanges with real and
potential affines. Consequently, it serves as the firm seat of the identity of those who partake in its
celebration. One of the songs sung during the dance expresses:
This is our seat that he tells us about.
The cooled-down seat (u’ɵikupa) that he tells us about.
To which we came happy (hóño).
And from it: Rise up (tánőyikakn)! Rise up! Rise up!
Rise up, you, to whom we have come.

The phallic multiplying beam symbolizes Red Anaconda. The descent of this powerful yet discrete
predator under the Site of Tears during the flood and its reemergence above ground can be interpreted as
representing fortitude and resilience, which gained heightened significance for the group of surviving
Andoque after the rubber holocaust. By dancing upon this beam, the ceremony reestablishes the
connection with the fertilizing forces of the river source. The multiplying beam is also associated with
the morning rainbow that appears in that direction, heralding an abundance of healthy crops to those
diligent enough to witness its early morning appearance, hail to it, shake the fruit trees and play the
manguaré. This rainbow also bestowed colors upon birds in mythic times. Consequently, the multiplying
beam is contrasted to the destructive afternoon rainbow that appears in the direction of the river mouth,
bringing illness and discomfort to those who do not seek shelter from the light rain that accompanies it.
In mythology, this rainbow, that bestowed color upon fish, is associated with different malevolent

147

figures, depending on the person discussing it, one of these figures being the transformed Green Tapir,
mentioned in M11 and discussed in Chapter 9.36 The demographic growth sought in this dance is thus
accompanied by defense from the dangerous forces of the river mouth. In addition, it is also
accompanied by an assertive stance toward other Indigenous adversaries, who are remembered for their
past infringements upon the Andoque. For instance, the following song mocks Pei, the Féénemɨna
captain and Dóñékɒi’s enemy (see C1, in Appendix 2):
He cares for her, he cares for her (yatúknḭ́ mḭ’i, literally: she entered his heart),
She’s here, I see that it’s her.
She’s here,
The daughter of late fellow (saámḭ) Pei.
The People of Eagle came with her.
They still haven’t eaten her (hɨo̰beɵ).

Or this song belittling Yarocamena’s revolt, referred to here through the translation of his name into

Who can it be who is causing a movement?
