The Making and Unmaking of Yiñékɒ’s Center
“Your father was the one who united us, here,” Yinñéfɵkn was recorded by Landaburu and Pineda as
saying to Fisi concerning Yiñékɒ, the latter’s father. “He gathered us in one place… We stayed in his
[maloca]. There was no one else to unite us… For sure, we seemed dead; when your father arrived here,
we immediately [went] with him, to one and only site, and then we became human again. We grew once
more, but [before that] we were nothing” (1984, 242). Further ahead, Yinñéfɵkn is quoted explaining
this: “One, by himself, is like a dead man. It is when several [people] reunite with a captain that they
start to become human once again” (ibid, 243 n.27). This section examines how Yiñékɒ established an
Andoque center between the 1930s and 1950s, positioned himself at its core, and enlisted other
survivors as workers to his vision. It also outlines dynamics that led to the dissolution of this united
center in the following decades. While the historical narratives in this section may initially appear overly
detailed, it is important to bear in mind their significance. In a small group like the Andoque survivors,
specific marriages, tensions, and seemingly minor events can have considerable consequences. Some of
the occurrences discussed here play a pivotal role in understanding the current power dynamics explored
in the subsequent chapters.
During their stay in La Palma, Yiñékɒ lived with different Bora and Miraña women and had children
with one of them. After separating from his last non-Andoque wife and uniting with Pa̰’fó of the
Tanager Clan, he became the captain of the group of Andoque survivors, which included 12 men
(including himself) and 14 women, leading them to resettle their territory. Since Pa̰’fó herself did not
later occupy any ritual positions in the future malocas and ceremonial life as expected of a maloquero’s
wife—Teresa would prepare the feminine ritual offerings and train Yiñékɒ’s daughter Irene to assume
this position during the latter’s teen years—it is tempting to consider that the relatively large number of
kin that she and her mother possessed played an important role in Yiñékɒ’s decision to marry her, or
placed him in an advantageous position to lead the group once they united. Table 14 in Appendix 3
provides a detailed list of the members of the small survivor group, followed by explanations on how the

149

matrimonial union with Pa̰’fó gave Yiñékɒ access to eleven individuals whom he could recruit for work
out of a group of twenty-five people. Pa̰’fó was also a classificatory cousin of Yiñékɒ from the side of
her mother Mɵɒ, and although my interlocutors were unable to trace with precision the genealogical
links between them or determine their degree of relatedness, they agreed that their union would
otherwise be considered incestuous. Similar to other People of the Center, the Andoque maintain a semicomplex alliance structure, wherein marriage with real or classificatory bilateral cousins is considered
incestuous and spouses are ideally sought among third or even four-degree cousins (Gasché 1976;
Karadimas 2000; Londoño Sulkin 2012, 160–67; Lucas 2019, 148–66). Despite the small size of the
survivor group, this matrimony was the only one between cousins to which my interlocutors could
identify. It thus seems that Yiñékɒ married Pa̰’fó as part of a deliberate plan (in which his mother-in-law
may have also been involved) to position himself at the center of the Andoque survivor group and thus
gain six young men as brothers-in-law, whom he could attract to collaborate with him in building the
maloca on the ancestral territory.38 In the conceptual framework employed throughout this thesis, we
may say that by marrying Pa̰’fó, Yiñékɒ effectively preyed upon her network of kin and familiarized
them by aligning their agency to his own.
The small Andoque group’s return to their ancestral territory in the mid-1930s coincided with their
resumption of rubber gathering under Miguel Zumaeta. Zumaeta took two Andoque wives (among
multiple other wives), including Ines (7 in Table 14) as well as non-community member from the Tree
Clan and a classificatory granddaughter of (14). While Zumaeta lived on the Caquetá River in the
settlement built in front of the Araracuara Penal Colony, which would later be called Puerto Santander,
Yiñékɒ’s group settled near Armadillo River (Feikɵsé), relatively remote from the Caquetá. Yiñékɒ
built five malocas in total, one near Armadillo River, and the others on different points along Macaw
River. The location of these later malocas, closer to the Caquetá River, indicates the Andoque’s
increasing reliance on trade with settlers and the growing significance of selling the large fish from the
Caquetá to merchants starting from the 1970s.
Yiñékɒ organized his people for work with Zumaeta and it was to his malocas that the fruits of their
labor arrived—the goods that Zumaeta bought for them and distributed between the men based on the
amounts of rubber that they had gathered (although rubber tapping often involved the joint work of
This preference for a consequential marriage despite the genealogical proximity reflects the “endogamic ideology”
identified by Landaburu (1993, 155–56) and Pineda (1979, 52–53) in M23 (see Chapter 9), where the hero’s union with the
sister promises greater stability and protection against external hostilities than his previous union with a foreign woman.
38

150

husbands and wives, the latter were not compensated directly like the men). While Yiñékɒ himself did
not handle the distribution of goods, and although the value of the goods they received was significantly
lower than that of the rubber they turned over to Zumaeta, accommodating the fruits of their work was
crucial for portraying him as a capable leader who could negotiate with the Whites and secure benefits
for his people after decades of more deadly exchange. Today’s elders still remember the festive
occasions when the group members would gather at the maloca to receive goods. Rubber tapping
increasingly focused on the northern bank of the Caquetá River, particularly in the areas surrounding the
Yarí, Mesai, and Amú Rivers, an area that did not fall within the ancestral territory of any Andoque clan,
but whose trees had not suffered excessive tapping during the Casa Arana period. Mnkoena, although
not physically joining the group in resettling the territory, is believed to have spiritually “healed” that
area, providing Andoque names to its locations and owner-persons to ensure the safety of the group’s
work there, and teaching Yiñékɒ these names and the methods of negotiation with these owner-persons.
Zumaeta and Yiñékɒ reached understandings concerning the division of time between periods for rubber
gathering, called fábricos, and periods dedicated to subsistence economic activities such as felling forest
plots and tending to gardens in the dry season, and to the celebration of the main ceremonial dances
during the rainy season (By the 1960s and 1970s the two fábricos took place between late February and
May and between August and December [Guzmán Gonzalez 1971, 103; Pineda Camacho 1979, 34]).
Since the earlier genocide was attributed to the wrath of the territorial owner-persons due to the
Andoque’s excessive rubber extraction, Yiñékɒ, during this later period of rubber tapping, implemented
specific ritual measures to protect his group from such catastrophes, as will be discussed in Chapter 13.
Not long after their settlement in Armadillo River, Pedro encountered Yinñéfɵkn and his daughter
Teresa (Sédieikn, “Clarified Water”), who had not fled to La Palma, during a rubber excursion in the
forest.39 He brought them back with him, and took Teresa as a wife, before she would later become
Umberto’s (18 in Table 14) wife. As mentioned earlier, Yinñéfɵkn’s family seemed to hold a higher
status than Yiñékɒ’s, but Yinñéfɵkn himself did not build his own maloca, possibly due to his age and
perhaps because he could not gather enough people, given that Yiñékɒ had already established himself
as the core and center of the group. Yiñékɒ, who was Yinñéfɵkn’s classificatory nephew, utilized the
training provided by Yinñéfɵkn to his daughter Teresa. He enlisted Teresa, his classificatory cousin, as
his assistant in the preparation of feminine ritual offerings for dances, while his classificatory brother-inYinñéfɵkn had two other daughters who died without marrying and having children, but my interlocutors are undecided as
to whether they died before or after they joined the group.
39

151

law Umberto became responsible for the preparation of masculine ritual offerings (the “secrets,”
secretos; the person in charge of preparing them is referred to as secretario/secretaria). Yinñéfɵkn is
remembered by the elders today as a supporter as well as rival of Yiñékɒ, and their relationship
exemplifies the tension between captaincy and healing specializations and the distinction between red
and white ritual specializations, which will be discussed in Chapter 11. Yinñéfɵkn healed women and
children from illnesses associated with malevolent animals, assisted Yiñékɒ in selecting Indigenous
names for children, organized ambivalent dances such as River Turtle-Bamboo at Yiñékɒ’s maloca, and
taught some of my interlocutors certain myths and healing spells that Yiñékɒ considered inappropriate
for him as a captain. Some people attribute Yiñékɒ’s death to a creeping sorcery attack authored by
Yinñéfɵkn decades earlier, and say that by taking Teresa as his worker, Yiñékɒ saved her from the
deadly fate reserved to the children of sorcerers.
During another rubber excursion that I assume to have taken place in the early 1940s, the members of
Yiñékɒ’s encountered and added to their group a family from the Hɵí Kádánni (“Owl Eagle”) lineage of
the Eagle Clan. This family had previously lived with them in La Palma and included Pakn’dadiei
(“Sinking in Water”), his wife Mo̰da (“Plucking [a Cacique Bird]”), and three sons, the eldest of which,
Joselito (Sn’diei, “Hard Water”), having taken his stepmother from his father while in the forest and
assumed the role of family head. Joselito used to refer to Yiñékɒ as “my elder brother” (ohaɩ́ɵsí,
literally, “the essence for me”) both on account of his younger age and his acknowledgement of
Yiñékɒ’s claim that his own lineage, Ñedánńéi/ Ñḛmḭ Kádánni (“Starch Eagle,” or Harpy Eagle),
represents the true essence of the Eagle Clan, because it is the direct descendant of the harpy eagle
formed in mythology from the starch balls made by Nénéfi’s wife (M9), while Joselito’s lineage is of
secondary Eagle order. Like Yinñéfɵkn, Joselito also assumed the role of healer without challenging
Yiñékɒ’s captaincy.
Another person incorporated into the group in an asymmetrical fashion was Pedro, who was the only
non-Andoque man in the group’s early period. As will be discussed in Chapter 10, the Andoque have
welcomed other Indigenous people into their group on the condition that they were women or families
with marriageable daughters. However, Pedro’s case was distinct as he had Miraña origins, though
differing accounts exist regarding whether his Miraña identity stemmed from his mother or father’s side,
a distinction that holds implications for one’s identity in a predominantly patrilineal society. According
to Pedro’s children and grandchildren, who belong to the Sun Clan, Pedro’s father was an Andoque man

152

from the Sun Clan who had a Miraña wife, similar to his ancestors who had intermarried with the
Miraña for several generations. However, the members of the Eagle and Deer clans, including Irene,
Yiñékɒ’s daughter who married Tañe, Pedro’s son, offer an alternative version. They explain that
Pedro’s father was Miraña of the Paca Clan who disguised himself as a member of the Miraña Sun Clan
during the Casa Arana period to evade retaliation from the Peruvian rubber bosses for hostilities
committed by his original clan. Pedro’s father was a Miraña man married to Paikn (“Tanager Kept in the
Hand”), an Andoque woman of the Tanager Clan and Mɵɒ’s sister (according to Irene, she was Mɵɒ’s
cousin). Mɵɒ adopted Pedro and cared for him after his father had died. His children from the union
with Teresa, as well as his first son from his union with Ines, were named after their mothers’ clans
(Eagle and Anaconda Clans, respectively). This naming convention is typically followed when the father
is non-Indigenous or does not actively participate in raising the child with the mother. However, when
Yiñékɒ decided to give a name to Pedro’s second son, Tañe (“Stationary Sun”), at an Armadillo Dance,
he invented a new clan that had never previously existed within the Andoque system—the Sun Clan.
Yiñékɒ took charge of selecting names for Pedro’s children and grandchildren, and even Tañe
acknowledges that it was his father-in-law, rather than his biological father, who provided significant
teachings about his clan, including its origin story about the Sun and Moon. Supporting the accounts of
the Eagle and Deer clans, Pedro’s great-granddaughter is named Paikn, like his presumed Tanager
mother. However, this name now bears a new meaning befitting the Sun Clan—“Nascent Moon.” It is
worth noting that although Pedro’s grandson Levy initially provided me with his clan’s version
involving Miraña descent through the maternal line and Andoque descent through the paternal line, his
undergraduate thesis stated the opposite (L. Andoke 2011, 73).
According to Fisi, Pedro expressed a desire to maintain a Paca identity, but Yiñékɒ advised him that the
affiliation to the sun would provide better protection to his family, emphasizing that “The sun is the only
one that never dies.” By selecting names for Pedro’s children, as well as teaching them their clan origin
myth and training the eldest two for ritual roles (Delio and Tañe), Yiñékɒ exerted a significant influence
on their clan’s formation, surpassing his involvement in the affairs of other families. The rationale
behind bestowing a Sun identity upon Pedro’s family appears to be the creation of a manageable alterity,
which should be understood within the interplay of predation and familiarization, where each party
involved seeks to ensure the direction of domination by the agency of the other. By establishing Pedro’s
children as a distinct Andoque clan, they would become eligible for marriage and contribute to the
group’s demographic growth project. Simultaneously, their association with a central Andoque myth
153

through their names would align them with the thinking of members of other clans, inhibiting the
imposition of foreign Miraña perspectives on their future spouses and children. However, as will be
discussed in Chapter 10, Pedro’s non-Andoque origin and fewer kinship ties to other group members
paradoxically positioned his sons at the core of the Andoque kinship system, granting them more access
to political power.
The Andoque person with whom Yiñékɒ maintained the most balanced relationship appears to be To̰fi
of the Deer Clan, who was regarded as Yiñékɒ’s classificatory uncle. Their relationship was
characterized by a ceremonial exchange, highlighted by the reciprocal invitation to participate in ritual
dances. Over the years, To̰fi constructed three malocas at a distance from Yiñékɒ’s malocas to ensure
autonomy for each one of them, with the group members divided between the two malocas. To̰fi was
supported by Alejandro (numbered 9 in Table 14, Appendix 3) and Duñékɒ (13) as his secretarios and
workers. Alejandro was To̰fi’s distant cousin and Duñékɒ was his wife’s distant cousin, and thus his
brother-in-law, although my interlocutors could not specify the geneological links between the two and
To̰fi and his wife (and which may not have been too close, as Duñékɒ’s daughter would later marry
To̰fi’s son). To̰fi was later also greatly assisted by his two sons-in-law, who fulfilled substantial bride
service periods alongside him. While To̰fi’s children, Mario and Raquel, emphasize that their father was
Yiñékɒ’s equal, Yiñékɒ’s children tend to describe To̰fi as his subordinate, learning ritual skills and
knowledge from their father. Interestingly, although To̰fi named his daughter and grandchildren, Yiñékɒ
bestowed a name on To̰fi’s eldest son, Mario. Paradoxically, that name giving in the River TurtleCarrier Band Dance associated with primogeniture and leadership (Chapter 11) at To̰fi’s first small
maloca, also marked the moment when Yiñékɒ recognized To̰fi as his peer and the leader of a distinct
clan center. This recognition came after a period in which To̰fi had organized dances with Yinñéfɵkn,
who initiated him into captaincy. Despite To̰fi’s independence of Yiñékɒ, it was Yiñékɒ and not To̰fi
who later trained Mario for captaincy and ritual organization. Nevertheless, this may owe in part to
To̰fi’s premature death around 1970, when Mario was still very young.
Yiñékɒ “created” many of the children of the group by bestowing names upon them at ceremonial
dances. With the exception of Fisi, Yiñékɒ’s son, and Juan, the son of Rosa “China” and César (20 and 4
in Table 14), who did not receive ceremonial names due to the absence of a maloca during the early
years in Armadillo River, Yiñékɒ gave names to seven children, who were the firstborns of his men’s
unions, in the Armadillo Dance, also referred to as “Baptism Dance,” which serve to protect children by

154

granting them a name. In subsequent years, Yiñékɒ started giving names in more central dances. In
addition to Mario, To̰fi’s son, he named his two children Irene and Rodolfo at the Fausiya Dance.
Among the members of the following generation, born from 1965 onwards, and alongside several lesser
ceremonial name givings, Yiñékɒ aimed to cultivate future leadership within the Andoque group by
giving names in the River Turtle-Carrier Band Dance to the firstborn sons of four new fathers, including
his own grandson Hernando, To̰fi’s grandson, and two of Pedro’s grandchildren. People today explain
that through these ceremonies, Yiñékɒ instilled in them the disposition to acquire knowledge and power
similar to his own in adulthood. By contrast, Yinñéfɵkn bestowed a name upon only three persons, who
were his own son and two of the female descendants of To̰fi, who was regarded as his apprentice during
the latter’s youth, while To̰fi himself gave names to only three persons as well—his younger daughter
and the two grandchildren born to his elder daughter with a Féénemɨna man. Out of a total of 36 naming
rituals since the Andoque’s regrouping (see Table 15, Appendix 4), an impressive 18 were conducted by
Yiñékɒ. This number is even greater if we count the 19 individuals who were given as adults a name or
had their old name changed by Yiñékɒ in one Fausíya dance in the 1960s (see Table 16, Appendix 4)—a
collective name giving that has not since been paralleled by any other maloquero. While such name
giving to adults (a term also encompassing children past the first few years of their life) does not carry
prestige and is not considered to involve a transmission of powers equaling name giving to children, we
may view it as a diluted form of a name giver’s participation in the formation or transformation of the
name recipient’s subjectivity.
Yiñékɒ went beyond name giving and provided training to several sons and daughters within his group,
who are the group’s elders at present, in leadership and ceremonial roles: his sons Fisi, Rodolfo, and
Ignacio; Mario, To̰fi’s son; Juan, the eldest son of his brother-in-law César; and Delio and Tañe, Pedro’s
sons. Among the women, he trained his daughter Irene and Raquel, To̰fi’s daughter. While Rodolfo and
Ignacio were trained for the White ritual specialization, which focuses on exchange with human and
nonhuman real and potential affines, the other men were initiated into the Red specialization, which
centers on agnatic identity. Presently, as explored in Chapter 10, these individuals and other observers
offer varying perspectives of these trainings. Some people say that Yiñékɒ granted each person a unique
yet equally valid body of knowledge to prevent power struggles among them, while others assert that
Yiñékɒ entrusted some of them with the true versions of myth and procedures while excluding others, or
that he withdrew his spiritual support from specific individuals after they disappointed him.

155

People explain that Yiñékɒ wished to prepare these individuals to assume the leadership of their
respective clans in the future, recognizing that as the group expanded, relying on a single captain would
no longer be feasible, and clan affiliations would regain significance; in other words, there would no
longer be one Andoque center, but several clan centers. While this dissolution was influenced by the
gradual demographic growth of the Andoque, I identify three specific historical moments during the late
1950s and early 1960s that accelerated this process. These moments undermined the foundations of
Yiñékɒ’s authority, which relied on the control over work and exchange with Whites, his claim for
superiority within the Eagle Clan, and his ability to compel others to align with his vision. I discuss
these moments here in relative detail because they elucidate the power and authority previously exerted
by Yiñékɒ, and because they shaped the current divisions and dynamics between centers that will be
explored in the following chapters.
The first moment, as identified by Guzmán (1971, 110–11), involves the increased control by the rubber
boss over the Andoque’s labor. After Miguel Zumaeta’s death in 1952, his son Ernesto took over the
management of the rubber business until his own demise in 1956, when his brother Lisardo assumed
responsibility. In 1958, Lisardo was joined by his brother Alberto, and they divided the rubber business
between themselves—Lisardo working with the Féénemɨna, and Alberto with the Andoque (ibid 1971,
55–56). In 1959 Alberto and his Andoque workers found a group of Murui refugees near the Amú River,
consisting mostly of members of a single extended family who had been hiding in the forest since the
Casa Arana persecutions. Alberto recruited them for rubber work, and together with Yiñékɒ, arranged
the redistribution of the group’s women, who had previously married their relatives due to a lack of
available men, among single Andoque men. According to Guzmán, when the Murui captain died a year
or two later, Yiñékɒ was accused of sorcery, and Alberto significantly reduced his collaboration with
him in order to gain the trust of his new Murui workers (ibid, 110–11). Additionally, my interlocutors
recall that in that period Alberto ceased to distribute goods at Yiñékɒ’s maloca, thereby eliminating this
important symbolic element that had signified the captain’s role as the provider of abundance. Unlike his
father, who had resided on the Caquetá River at a distance from his workers, Alberto chose to live closer
to the Andoque, near Weed River (Pá̰ñe̋mnḭsé, often called “Rice River”). Instead of distributing goods
at Yiñékɒ’s maloca, Alberto started distributing them at his house, further deepening the Andoque’s
perceived disconnect between their captain and rubber work. Additionally, after only a few fábricos
under Alberto’s management, and no doubt also due to their advanced age, Yiñékɒ and most of his
contemporaries retired from rubber tapping, leaving the work to be carried out by their children. This
156

retirement created or exacerbated a generational division within the group, where, for the first time since
regrouping, those responsible for ceremonial dances and other ritual traditions were not the same
individuals who were involved in work and exchange with Whites. From oral accounts, it appears that
youth viewed knowledge and teachings of the elders as irrelevant to their own daily concerns, while the
elders felt neglected by their children. In a personal communication (October 2022), Jon Landaburu,
who began working with the Andoque in 1969 when that working arrangement was still in place, shared
that during fábricos, while the young men and their wives were in rubber camps on the north bank of the
Caquetá River, the elders at the main settlements and the linguist working with them experienced
hunger.
The second historical moment marking the dissolution of the center formed by Yiñékɒ was Joselito’s
rupture with Yiñékɒ in 1960, following the death of his son, Agustín, from a snake bite during one of
the first fábricos with Alberto. According to Agustín’s brother Germán, Joselito simply did not want to
live anymore around Yiñékɒ’s maloca because revisiting the place where his late son had lived was too
painful for him, and he decided to settle by the Caquetá River. While this sentiment is often cited as the
reason for the relocation of families after the death of their loved ones, other interlocutors attributed it to
Joselito’s resentment toward Yiñékɒ for not actively attempting to heal his son from an incident that is
not considered fatal if an apt and willing healer is within reach. Interlocutors from the Sun, Eagle, and
Deer clans relayed to me the explanation provided by Yiñékɒ and the elders supporting him after the
incident. According to that explanation, Agustín was not Joselito’s biological son but the son of a
member of the Carijona people, according to some, or of the Yucuna, according to others, who had
given him a perfume (chondu) several years earlier during Agustín’s visit. The perfume was allegedly
meant to conquer women but was actually devised by the Carijona/Yucuna father to kill his son in
revenge for his preference to live with Joselito. The perfume drove Agustín to madness to such an extent
that during rubber work in the forest he would incessantly fantasize about women, boast about his sexual
exploits, and let himself be seduced by dolphins who appeared to him in the form of women (see
Chapter 9). This made him susceptible to incidents such as snake bites, from which he could not be
cured. Yiñékɒ tried to heal him, but upon sucking the bite, he immediately sensed the traces of harmful
perfume, which could have utterly destroyed such a powerful person, and distanced himself from the
patient, as even the sight of a person affected by such a perfume could endanger him. According to one
interlocutor, Joselito was angry at “his older brother” for giving up on his son and for developing a
version of the events where Agustín was partly responsible for being bitten and, as such, incurable.
157

From Yiñékɒ’s friend, Joselito became his foe. Given the explanations provided to me on other
occasions about the importance of ceremonial dances and ritual procedures carried out by the captain for
safety during rubber tapping and other economic activities, I also assume that Joselito may have become
critical of Yiñékɒ’s capacity to negotiate with nonhuman entities to ensure the safety of his men. Instead
of gathering rubber with the rest of the youth, Joselito’s brothers and sons started working as guards at
the Araracuara Penal Colony and pioneered in harvesting fish from the Caquetá in large quantities for
sale. This deviation from the collective economic activity and the involvement in the extraction of faunal
resources instead of vegetal ones was severely censured by Yiñékɒ and the elders supporting him, who
assumed that Joselito was engaging in dangerous negotiations with owner-persons for success in fishing
and warned their sons not to follow his example. The premature deaths of Joselito, his brothers and most
of his sons are today regarded as the outcome of revenge by these owner-persons for their excessive
fishing. The break with Yiñékɒ’s captaincy reached a climax in Joselito’s creation of a competing
maloca in 1974, which he inaugurated with the River Turtle-Carrier Band Dance associated with
leadership and primogeniture (See Chapter 11), thereby signaling that he is no longer Yiñékɒ’s “younger
brother.” The tension between Joselito’s and Fisi’s descendants persists. Germán is today the declared
captain of the Eagle Clan because he would not accept Fisi’s double authority as both clan captain and
general cacique, but Yiñékɒ’s descendants rarely consult him or respect his authority. They and the
descendants of Yiñékɒ’s supporters still belittle both Joselito’s old maloca, and his nephew Heriberto’s
current maloca.
The third historical moment marking the dissolution of the center formed by Yiñékɒ was Umberto’s
decision to stop collaborating with him as his secretario in the end of 1960s and early 1970s. According
to several interlocutors, Umberto, who was a dedicated worker, became upset when Yiñékɒ’s new sonin-law, Tañe, did not comply with the custom of bride-service and did not participate in the maloca’s
ceremonial work. When Yiñékɒ relocated from Armadillo River to Macaw River, Pedro’s family,
oriented toward exchange and intermarriage with Whites, moved to the Macaw River mouth. Unlike
Irene’s first husband, a Murui-Muina man who lived at the maloca and is often mentioned as an example
of a hardworking, respectful son-in-law, Tañe did not relocate to his father-in-law’s maloca after uniting
with Irene—a union affected despite her parents’ objections—and it was rather Irene who immediately
moved to his father’s settlement. During that period, Tañe focused on rubber work and nurturing
alliances with his brother-in-law Alberto Zumaeta, and did not collaborate with Yiñékɒ in ceremonial
activities until the birth of his second son in 1973. Although my interlocutors did not explicitly share this
158

interpretation with me, I surmise that Yiñékɒ’s failure to impose temporary uxorilocality and bride
service on his son-in-law was taken by Umberto and other elders as a sign of his diminishing power and
a factor in diminishing his authority. If he could not align the agency of his son-in-law to his own, how
could he lead and coordinate work with the wider group? If he could not incorporate his son-in-law into
his maloca for a period generally respected by custom and instead lost his daughter immediately to her
husband, how could he protect group members from other modes of incorporation by affines, such as
illnesses? Umberto was replaced by Mario, but some interlocutors attribute Yiñékɒ’s diseases to the
Mario’s lesser skills, compared with Umberto, in preparing ceremonial offerings. Umberto’s
descendants have remained somewhat aloof from the group’s dances, preferring to learn ceremonial
songs from Joselito rather than resuming their father’s collaboration with Yiñékɒ and his successors.
Along with his sons, Umberto left Yiñékɒ’s settlement after his wife’s death around 1975, as he could
no longer bear seeing the places where she had lived and worked. The relocation of other families away
from Yiñékɒ’s malocas in the 1970s and 1980s is often attributed to similar grief over relatives.
Part I began with a discussion of the concept of “center” and an exploration of the two cosmo-economic
systems present among the Andoque to understand the meaning of the concept within each system. The
discussion revealed distinct notions of power associated with the center in each system. On one hand,
the heterosubstitutive-captaincy system emphasizes the economic power symbolized by the axe and its
metaphors, representing the ability to exert influence over others and the hierarchical process of
exchanging persons for an axe. On the other hand, the homosubstitutive-cannibalistic system emphasizes
the attainment of full development by the body which conveys notions of danger, wisdom, and authority,
and speech as the suspension of exchange within this system. The historical account of the Andoque’s
recuperation process demonstrated how a center was formed in a specific historical context and how its
members positioned themselves within these two cosmo-economic systems: as a captain and his
subordinates trading with Whites in the captaincy system, and as orphans striving for reproduction by
regaining their predatory agency in the cannibalistic one. It also discussed three historical moments
marking the dissolution of this center, which can be mapped onto the two systems: the captain’s
diminishing role as a trader and work coordinator, and growing doubts over his predatory position vis-àvis human sons-in-law and nonhuman agents seeking to harm his men (such as Agustín’s snake). In Part
III, we will delve into the conception and functioning of power within a cosmos characterized by
multiple centers, both nonhuman and human ones, including such clan centers as those that reappeared
during this dissolution. However, before delving into that discussion, Part II will examine the
159

importance of the river source and the appropriation of its powers in center formation, powers we have
touched upon throughout this chapter, especially through the references to the Multiplying Tree Dance
and the invocation of the deity Sḭ́ di.

Part II
Appropriating Power from the River Source

162

Introduction
As I mentioned in the previous part, the cultivars and knowledge that Egret of the River Source brings to
the center are treated as constitutive elements of the identity, power, and authority of those living at the
center. I this part, I explore the four main items brought by this egret figure: the maloca and its
instruments, manioc, tobacco, and coca. I focus on the capabilities with which they endow the people
living at the center for participating in beneficial asymmetrical exchanges with human and nonhuman
beings, and the spiritual power, tne’túi, to which they, and particularly coca and tobacco, give access,
and which my male interlocutors often cited as the translation, in the Andoque language, of the Spanish
word poder (power).
The maloca and three cultivars have been widely discussed by ethnographers of the People of the Center
and the Tukanoan speaking groups of Northwest Amazonia. These scholars have compared the different
ways in which these peoples construct their malocas and process substances from these cultivars, and
how they consume them and perceive their origins and effects, suggesting models for how the cultivars
and the substances elaborated from them form a whole in each cultural complex (e.g., Echeverri and
Pereira 2005; Echeverri 2015; Gutierrez 2020; C. Hugh-Jones 1979, 169–234; S. Hugh-Jones 2014).
The association made by the Andoque between the maloca and the three cultivars, on the one hand, and
the river source, on the other, directs me, in this part, to examine these elements as part of this
dissertation’s spatial theory of power. Here, the center acquires access to the forces held by the river
source and contained in these elements through the familiarization of these elements and the spiritual
entities mastering them. The forces of the river source are associated with its position within the two
cosmo-economic systems explored in the previous part: the captaincy and cannibalistic ones. Likewise,
the elements explored in this part both endow their users with predatory agency and serve them in
exchanges with affinal others, including those associated with the river mouth.
The capabilities granted by the three substances (as well as the ceremonial dances held at the maloca, as
we will see in Chapter 11) enable their producers and consumers the capacity to subjectivate human and
nonhuman others: to shape and transform their subjectivities, or to extend their own subjectivities to that
of the patient (Santos Granero 2009a). Within the Amazonian landscape, this Foucauldian concept of
power takes the form of familiarization: the transition from real or potential affinity to consanguinity
(Fausto 1999, 939). Familiarization is also the means through which these elements and the capabilities
that they possess become part of people’s arsenal, representing an important moment in the formation of

163

a relationship of mastery with these elements and their owner-persons. The owner-persons of the items
discussed in this part are the deities and mythical figures who were the first ones to create them, or the
animals or persons that these items were in mythical times before they transformed into what they are
today, and who continue to represent these items’ agentive aspect. It is the familiarization of these items’
owner-persons that gives Andoque members access to the capabilities and potentialities that they hold.
Two common means to familiarize others, as explored in the literature, are feeding them, thereby
fabricating the pet’s body as consubstantial with the master’s (Fausto and Costa 2013), and addressing
affinal relatives through kinship terms reserved for consanguineal ones (e.g., Taylor 1983). In this part, I
describe another form of familiarization through the narration of myth. This form is especially visible in
myths on the origin of tobacco and coca. Through comparison with myths of neighboring peoples, we
can detect in these myths a transition from control over these plants by a feminine figure associated with
the affinal world, into control over these plants by a masculine figure or consubstantiality with an
agnatic relative’s body. A similar pattern is seen with manioc: in one myth, it is appropriated from
women, while in another, it is shaped to align with male expectations. As we have seen in previous
chapters, this literary technique also appears in relation to Egret of the River Source, whom the narrative
familiarizes in M3, at the end of which he calls himself Egret of the Center. Therefore, it is not
surprising that tobacco and coca, brought to the center by Egret of the River Source in that myth, go
through a similar transformation in other myths as well. In other words, both the river source as a totality
and the different elements imported from there are familiarized to align their agency with those of the
people living at the center. Given the Andoque’s emphasis on patrilineal clan identities, I also refer to
this process as “agnatization” to highlight the attempts to subsume affinal exchanges within the project
of agnatic continuity and reproduction.
However, as Costa and Fausto have shown, the direction of Amazonian mastery relations is invertible,
as the familiarized pet can become a familiarizing master who dominates its previous master (Costa and
Fausto 2019, 206). This explains the dangers arising from maloca elements which are not “fed” properly
or from the substances whose consumption is accompanied with the narration of the “wrong” stories. It
also accounts for the delicate interplay between river source and center in Andoque cosmology: in M3,
Egret of the River Source achieves power by mastering the beings living at the center: the anacondas,
whom he turns into beams, and his father-in-law, whom he provides with coca and tobacco. However, at
the end of the myth, as noted above, he is familiarized by the same center that he has previously

164

familiarized. The invertibility of mastery relations is thus also the very mechanism that allows the center
to incorporate powers from the river source.
Finally, these authors emphasize that although familiarization can manifest through propitious actions
like feeding, these actions ultimately conform to the predatory framework of the self’s appropriation of
alterity. Similarly, the subsequent chapters demonstrate that while familiarization through the substances
may operate within a gift logic, these substances ultimately refer to the predatory principle of the
cosmos—the carnivorous deity Sḭ́ di located upriver.

165

166

Chapter 5. The Maloca
The maloca (ḭpɨko, “house,” and particularly bopɨkókn̋, “big house”) is a key institution that combines
residential, social, ceremonial, and political functions. Until the massacres and displacements of the
early twentieth century, the Andoque malocas were pluri-familial houses centered around one clan or
lineage. Today most people live in nuclear-family stilt houses, and there were four Andoque malocas
upon my arrival in April 2018—Fisi, Mario, Heriberto, and Raquel’s—and three when I left in July
2019, as the latter was abandoned a year earlier. The number of Andoque malocas returned to four in
2020, when Tañe built his fourth maloca, but dropped to three again after Fisi dismantled his maloca in
June 2021 in the hope of building a new one (which has not been finished until the conclusion of this
dissertation).40

Figures 9–12. Andoque malocas, from top-left to bottom-right: the malocas of Fisi (May 2018), Raquel (April 2018), Tañe
(July 2021) and Mario (July 2021) (Photos by the author)

People can decide to abandon their malocas for any number of reasons, from the banal crumbling of the thatched roof to a
need of temporary rest from dance organization or a series of catastrophes befalling its inhabitants. They can build new ones
as long as they can secure the necessary workforce, either through persuasion or, as is increasingly the case nowadays, by
hiring laborers.
40

167

Currently, only two Andoque captains and their nuclear families live in their malocas, while the other
malocas serve for the preparation and consumption of food and coca, ceremonial dances, and political
assemblies. Through the rituals held in the maloca, people transform potentially harmful foodstuffs into
life-bringing substances and negotiate with powerful owner-persons to evade diseases, accidents, and
other forms of predation by these entities, thereby promoting the group’s well-being and social
reproduction. The maloca holds an economic function that was more marked before the rubber upheaval
when it roofed tens or over a hundred people (Whiffen 1915, 48, 63): the processing and exchange of
foodstuffs and other substances, the coordination of collective agricultural work and work with nonIndigenous agents, and the distribution of the produce or gains from each such effort. In that period, the
maloca occasionally served as a garrison from which its residents launched aggressive operations, and
where they celebrated victory and exhibited war trophies (Pineda Camacho 2005). Today, meetings with
non-Andoque and non-Indigenous agents held at the maloca communicate to outsiders the social
cohesion necessary for such negotiations, as well as the image of “authentic,” “traditional Indians,” a
strong symbolic instrument that Indigenous people deploy on such occasions (Conklin 1997).
The Andoque maloca is an octagonal structure of four main poles and secondary stakes, roofed with pui
palm leaves, reaching about 8 meters high, with approximately 12 meters in both length and width.
Despite some architectural particularities and the different construction techniques among each ethnic
group, the Andoque maloca shares many similarities with those of other peoples in the Northwest
Amazonia (Gutierrez 2020). They all served similar functions in the past and many of them underwent a
transition to becoming political and ritual centers, acting as a centripetal force in settlements of nuclear
family houses (Franky and Mahecha 2018, 82–83). They all have a sexual division of the internal space,
with the front public area considered masculine, where male visitors are received and where coca is
prepared and consumed, and the rear residential area considered feminine, where food is produced and
consumed (Correa Rubio 1996, 252; García 2018, 424–25). Additional spatial division exists between
the residential compartments of the captain and his family members, and those of residents pertaining to
other categories, such as affines and orphans (Correa Rubio 1996, 249; Lucas 2019, 185–88).
Throughout the region, the maloca is conceived as a larger symbolic representation of the human body
(Gasché 1972, 207; Guyot 1972; Karadimas 2005, 369–99; Londoño Sulkin 2012, 87; Lucas 2019, 182–
83) and models the entire ethnic territory or cosmos (Cayón 2017, 225–50; Goldman 2004, 124–31; S.
Hugh-Jones 1993; García 2018, 176–77; Echeverri 2005, 234). As a ceremonial unit, each maloca is part
of a larger network of ritual exchange with specific allied malocas and holds certain ritual prerogatives,
168

whose enactment reproduces local hierarchies and amounts to claims to political status. In the VaupesApaporis region, we see this reflected in the ceremonial artefacts, musical instruments and immaterial
possessions such as myths and chants held by each Tukanoan descent group (S. Hugh-Jones 1993, 109–
10), while in the Caquetá-Putumayo, this is notably seen in the legitimacy, which depends on birth
order, to hold manguaré drums and a dance beam (Andoque: Tu’sí; Murui-Muina: Yadiko) or to perform
certain dances (Gasché 2009; García 2018, 133–34; Guyot 1972; Karadimas 2005b, 38–41).
To avoid duplicating these ethnographic similarities, I refer the reader to the rich literature cited above.
To explore the power embodied in the maloca, my discussion focuses on the maloca as a heterogenous
assemblage of human and nonhuman beings, whose alignment of agency empowers the captain to
manage the territory and navigate external dangers and opportunities.
The Andoque maloca serves as a concrete manifestation of the prototypical maloca created in mythology
at the center of the world, and each maloca symbolizes the center of the world for its residents.41
However, it is also associated with the river source in different ways. Entering a maloca is expressed
through the prefix yi- which implies ascent, “as if the maloca were a higher zone in comparison with its
surroundings, closer to the west, closer to the sky” (Landaburu 1985, 37). Sḭ́ di, the carnivorous god who
is depicted by some as the father Egret of the River Source and the captain of jaguars from upriver, is
said to protect the malocas modeled after the one built by his son, devouring those wishing to harm them
and their residents. However, although the agents arriving from the river source and the things that they
bring with them are usually perceived as legitimate, life-giving Others, they remain Others, and as such,
are open to criticism through the idiom of the “center.” For instance, the brother of one of the captains,
himself trained in his youth to be one, claimed that “maloca-less” people, like himself, can possess more
knowledge and ability to manage the territory than captains because the maloca did not originate at the
center. Although the original maloca was built there, its founder and the knowledge for its foundation
came from the river source. Therefore, according to him, having a maloca is not a necessary condition to
access knowledge and power.
The two possible maloca positions in relation to the river are explained through the maloca’s important
role in defending the people from dangers coming from the river mouth. The ideal maloca is depicted as
opening onto the east, allowing the maloca owner, seated at his mambeadero, to look toward the river

41

For similar conception among the Miraña and Bora see Karadimas 2013, 196 and Lucas 2019, 182, respectively.

169

mouth, from which most epidemics, enemies, and dangers arrive. However, the four successive malocas
of Tañe, as well as one of Yiñékɒ’s malocas, were built in the other direction, looking onto the West,
and more specifically, to Parrot Savannah (Kɒ́’i Popái), also called Pet Savannah (Ḭéna̰ Popái), a
powerful site controlled by Tofidei, a mythical warlord who is considered as a guardian of the Andoque,
defending himself in mythology from anaconda enemies coming from the river mouth (see Chapter 9),
and whom Tañe indeed cites more often than others as a major spiritual support.
Similar to the perception documented among the Miraña (Karadimas 2013, 196), the mambeadero is the
center of the maloca—indeed, the center of the center—from which the wider territory is organized.
Called taafi taɨ, “site of [yarumo] ashes”, it is a circle of dry, solid earth where yarumo leaves are
burned, and around which the male residents of the maloca or nearby clan members gather every
evening to prepare and consume coca powder. It is located in the masculine part of the maloca, next to
main entrance. This location, which contrasts with the mambeadero’s location among the Miraña and
Murui-Muina—closer to the feminine space, or at the limit between the masculine and feminine ones
(García 2018, 425; Karadimas 2005b, 373)—may owe to the fact that, while these two peoples perceive
coca as a woman, the Andoque consider it a male agent (cf. M2).

170

Figure 13. Ground plan of Fisi’s maloca. Design: Gadiel Levi

The mambeadero serves as the main forum for male socialization, where men chat about the day’s
events, politics, and gossip. As night falls, the conversations become deeper, touching on mythology,
cures, and analysis of disease and other risks and harms that approach the community and should be
diverted. The mambeadores sit in a semicircle, facing the main entrance. When visiting another’s
maloca, they should sit next to the host, rather than facing him. This way, the visitor avoids repeating
Egret of the River Mouth’s fate of distraction by his host’s wife (see Chapter 1) and instead aligns his
perspective with the host’s, both of them looking at the same dangers and opportunities.
Women who are present at the maloca during mambeadero sessions often listen to these talks from the
rear part and can intervene indirectly by commenting aloud to other women present. However, in
settlements without a maloca, coca is prepared and consumed at shacks to which women rarely go. This
decreases women’s participation in daily supra-familial decision-making (as opposed to externally
sponsored community assemblies) and seems to increase their alienation from all that is objectified as la

171

cultura—namely, mythology, dances, and other traditional elements, which become increasingly marked
as men’s business.
In the past, each adult male resident, and especially the maloca owner, used his own self-crafted
backless seat, called kupa, for these sessions, on which other people could not sit. The seat is a powerful
symbol of authority and rootedness in one’s territory. One’s native, Indigenous language is also referred
to as kupa—it is one’s seat, the basis from which one deploys powerful words to act on reality—whereas
sofa is whatever language one may speak, like Spanish nowadays. It is thus telling that today Andoque
malocas do not have the traditional seats, but rather one or two modern seats with a reclined back, and
most mambeadores sit on whatever they can find at the house, like cut-down tree logs or even empty
gasoline cans.
Seated at his mambeadero, the captain’s influence goes beyond the visible conversations he holds with
human visitors. The yarumo burning circle is referred to as katí, “our mother,” because it represents the
territory, which nourishes the people living on it like a mother. A captain is said to be able to spiritually
discern in the circle in front of him the entire ancestral territory, including the territories of the different
beings inhabiting it, and in this way engage in invisible dialog and negotiations with nonhuman entities
to promote the well-being and reproduction of his human community. An apt captain who converses
with nonhuman beings at his mambeadero can manage and intervene in the sites of the ancestral
territory.
The mambeadero is thus one of the things in which the power of the maloca residents, and especially the
captain, is invested. Two other such important things are the manguaré drums and the multiplying beam,
which are not found in all malocas, as their elaboration depends on knowledge not possessed by all
captains. While the manguaré is found in the masculine area, to the right of the main entrance, the
multiplying beam lies to the left of the entrance, crossing through the male and female spaces, as can be
expected from a phallic object that fertilizes the territory and the community.
As Londoño rightfully observes for the Féénemɨna, malocas are “perhaps the most heavily symbolically
charged objects in their [People of the Center’s] world besides human bodies” (2012, 153). As shown in
the works cited above, the People of the Center’s ethnography is replete with accounts of the maloca’s
corporal symbolism. Admittedly, the word designating the rafters descending from the maloca’s ridge in
the Andoque language, to which the pui palm leaves are attached, is ḭ’tanńḛ, which also means “bones,”
and the word for “door” is fí, which also means “mouth.” However, these words can apply not only to
172

malocas but also to all kinds of constructions. Conversely, the symbolism that Andoque captains stress,
and which is also attested in regional ethnography, is one in which the different parts of the maloca and
its main instruments embody powerful spirits of nonhuman entities who defend the house and the group
and back the captain’s actions, as well as mythical figures with whom the captain communicates for
support (Guyot 1972, 162–65; Londoño Sulkin 2012, 85–86; Karadimas 2005b, 386–93). I propose to
view these instruments as nonhuman entities familiarized by the maloca residents—and above all, by the
captain—to make their capabilities available for their human masters, who can align these entities’
agency to their own for their defense and benefit.
The four main poles (paisé) are anacondas (cf. M3) that are “fed” in ceremonial dances, as people leave
game for them, brought by the guests to appease the potentially dangerous anaconda spirits of the
territory.42 The multiplying beam is a powerful anaconda as well, representing the mythical red
anaconda Pe’pai, and the rafters are snakes. The manguaré drum is an old woman, as it once was in
mythology (see M8); the mortar for coca pulverization is an old man, who bestows teachings upon the
one using it, and the earth floor is an extension of Lady Beetle of Life (Pḭofikn), who created the entire
earth—a feminine, life-giving figure, in contrast with the masculine, predatory elements erected on it.43
People can also carve different animals on these parts and instruments, such as anacondas or caimans on
the poles or multiplying beam, or eagles or bats on the lower beams of the rooftop, thereby bestowing on
it the strength, agility, or other characteristics of these animals (see also Whiffen 1915, 91). By
“naming” these parts and instruments after different nonhuman and mythical beings or carving their
figures on them, people invoke these powerful beings and ask them to defend the maloca and support
their actions. After paying a visit to another’s maloca, an ill-willed person can dream of a caiman, an
anaconda or an eagle grabbing him, and, as a result, turn ill: these are the spirits who defend the maloca
warning him (and recall the maloquero’s anecdote about the multiplying beam’s predation on his rival
after a ceremonial dance in Chapter 4). The defense that Sḭ́ di grants the maloca is of a similar nature.
Furthermore, maloca dwellers say that when nobody is home, the instruments they use daily and that are
identified with them, such as the coca mortar, chase away sorcery and different malevolent animal
spirits.

Cf. Guyot 1972, 165.

(2005, 373–81).

173

As among the Féénemɨna (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 71), the Andoque captains refer to these elements as
consanguine kin, in a way that reflects the familiarization of such external, potentially dangerous agents.
However, they enact “upwards familiarization” by employing kinship terms of relative seniority to
invoke these elements for the protection and assistance that these elements would provide their “true”
descendants. In such a way, the coca mortar and multiplying beam are referred to as grandfathers, the
manguaré as a grandmother, the mambeadero, as already noted, as a mother, and the poles as maternal
uncles.44 These kinship terms exemplify people’s dependence on these nonhuman beings for protection
from and ability to act upon other agents—both nonhuman and human.
The maloca thus emerges as a magnified entity (Fausto 2008; Strathern 1991), comprising various
persons and heterogenous relations that cannot be reduced to its human inhabitants. The maloca, in turn,
magnifies its human constituents, who should themselves be viewed as heterogenous sets of entities that
constitute each person as a plural singularity, as they rely on the forces and characteristics of diverse
things and beings. This magnification reaches its peak with the maloca owner—the ḭdɨño̰, or “personbody trunk”—for whom the forces and capabilities of the different constituents of the maloca are the
most accessible, enabling him to align their agency to his own to achieve well-being in daily and
ceremonial contexts. However, given the risk that the relations of dominion would be inverted, the
employment of kinship terms toward maloca components is not devoid of risk for the human side:
powerful anaconda poles, if not properly fed, or a manguaré or multiplying-beam grandfathers neglected
by their “grandchildren,” will exact their revenge on the captain and his people for having invoked them
in vain. In such cases, it would be these components who eventually familiarize humans, and not vice
versa.
The captain is not only the master of such nonhuman elements, but also of his people—the maloca
residents and workers. A visual indicator of a captain’s power is the size of his maloca, which is
measured by the size of the floor between the four main poles used for dancing during ceremonies. The
larger the floor, the more people can dance and make the captain’s dances resound (as a po’soɵ, “the
famous”), and the social networks that the dances maintain are wider. Tañe of the Sun Clan boasts about

having had the biggest floor in his previous malocas (9m2), bigger than Fisi’s (8m2) and Mario and
Raquel’s malocas (7m2). The size of the maloca depends on the number of people at the captain’s
disposal for this and other interrelated works, such as clearing garden plots and organizing dances.
Male elders’ control over the workforce was theorized by Rivière and Turner as a political economy of
persons, where older men control the productive and reproductive activities of younger men and women,
using the material or nonmaterial surplus they produce for the organization of dances to build and retain
a following (in the Guianese case; Rivière 1983) or for the social reproduction of persons as carriers of
symbolic value through naming and household affiliation (in the Kayapo case; Turner 2003). As
mentioned in Chapter 1, while the terms “orphans” and “youth” evoke the vulnerable status of the
captain’s personnel and the expectation of his protective and instructive role—including his capacity in
the past to trade them—the term “workers” (báɵ̋isíɵ́hɵ) reflects the contribution that these individuals
make to the work efforts and projects headed by the maloquero. Therefore, I propose to view the
captain’s ability to align workers’ agency to his own as the inter-human counterpart of the relations of
dominion through familiarization that he maintains with the maloca’s nonhuman components.
The malocas that I visited during fieldwork did not count with these categories of people, most
particularly “orphans,” as the last captain to have possessed them was Yiñékɒ, who attracted survivors
of different clans and ethnic groups to his maloca after the genocide. Additionally, people describe a role
referred to in Spanish as secretario, a worker responsible for preparing tobacco paste and coca powder
for the maloquero in everyday and especially ceremonial dances, when such offerings (ḭtaséa) are
prepared in very small amounts to establish a dialog with guardian spirits. If the maloquero’s wife lacks
the necessary ritual knowledge, he would also have a secretaria to prepare offerings of manicuera
beverage for dances. However, Yiñékɒ and To̰fi are depicted as the last captains to have had relatively
permanent secretarios and secretarias. By contrast, “youth” and “workers” were not described as
categories of the past, and my interlocutors reported that people considered as such passed significant
periods of time in recent decades at different malocas. Their affiliation to each maloca seems to have
owed to different reasons: bride service, economic prosperity, and charisma. Fisi, who has six biological
and adopted daughters, disposed of his sons-in-law and his daughters’ suitors from different ethnic
groups as workers. These men, of Nipóde and Yucuna origin, lived in his maloca in the 1980s, 1990s2000s, as well as for a short period in 2021, helping to build or remodel the maloca and organize dances.
Economic prosperity is often mentioned as having attracted people and families from different clans, as

175

well as a Murui-Muina family, to Tañe’s first maloca during the 1980s–1990s when he coordinated
work with non-Indigenous entrepreneurs. Finally, Raquel and Elias’s maloca housed many unmarried
young men during its heyday in the 1990s. In this case, people cite Raquel’s hospitality and provision of
food, and her son Elias’ contagious enthusiasm in learning how to organize dances, as the reasons
behind that maloca’s popularity.
Whatever the reason that attracts people to a maloca, the captain’s good temper, sexual integrity, and
ability to organize people for work make workers stay, as the captain does not hold any repressive power
over them; the desertion of workers of any of these three malocas is attributed by outsiders or by the
captain’s rivals to his loss of one or more of these virtues.
Throughout the region, a common way to discredit a maloca is by claiming that it was built through a
project or financed by the State, implying that workers were obtained through paid wages rather than by
nurturing proper social relations and exchange with them (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 154). People often
doubt the legitimacy of some of these captains, arguing that they were not born to captaincy lineages and
do not possess the proper knowledge to manage malocas and conduct ceremonial dances. Nevertheless,
all the existing Andoque malocas were either built or renovated using external funds. However, the
captain’s capability, as well as that of his sons, to manage such funds for the benefit of their workers
should also be considered on par with more “traditional” virtues of taking care of the workers’ wellbeing and controlling predatory anger and sexual desire. Moreover, it does not negate the need for the
captain to motivate people for work and set a personal example. In 2020–2021 Andoque captains
received funds to build or renovate malocas through a regional project funded by the program Visión
Amazonía for strengthening traditional governance. One captain, who constructed a new maloca,
managed his funds efficiently and contracted members of his and other clans for the work. On the other
hand, another captain and his sons frivolously spent a significant portion of the funds during a couple of
days in Puerto Santander. Consequently, people were reluctant to help them afterwards, especially since
the nuclear family members were working only sporadically. Although this captain enjoyed the
occasional contributions by another member of his clan, two sons-in-law, and external visitors such as
two French filmmakers who were eager to film the inauguration dance and myself as I was on a visit
there, the maloca remains incomplete at the time these lines are written. This illustrates the importance
of motivating workers even in externally sponsored projects, as well as for captains who, like this

176

particular one, are recognized by most Andoque members as the highest authority in ritual and other
traditional matters.
At first glance, the construction of a maloca simply signals the captain’s authority and power—the fact
that he can obtain many people to work with him. However, we should also understand it as contributing
to the construction of this authority and power, as well as to the shaping of the captain’s persona and
even his body (as well as those of his family members), with which the maloca is, in fact, continuous.
This notion finds support in a host of conceptions and practices, chief among them being the idea that a
burned-down maloca predicts its leader’s death, and any break-in or damage to its main ritual
instruments, such as the manguaré or multiplying beam, is considered a bad omen for him or his family.
Moreover, as noted earlier, these two latter instruments, along with the coca mortar, also serve as vocal
extensions for the captain, allowing his voice to resound far away, like a po’soo. The captain is supposed
to be firmly based at his maloca, seated in his mambeadero, ready to receive visitors, and not to wander
around; he must not leave the circle of ashes for too many nights, lest it “cool down” and the spiritual
power dwelling in it dissipates, leaving the maloca vulnerable to the influence of evil spirits and
animals. Upon death, the captain and his family members are buried under their maloca, and after a
captain’s death the maloca is often abandoned or even intentionally burned down.
The idiom of mastery and familiarization serves as a unifying prism for understanding the participation
of both human and nonhuman beings in the constitution of the owner—in this case, the captain—as a
magnified person, thus enhancing his ability to protect his people. Egret of the River Source, who was
the first to create the maloca, and Sı̰ ́di, his carnivore antecedent from upriver, are two powerful masters
whom a person must familiarize and gain mastery over in order to become a captain at the center. In the
following chapter, we discuss the plants associated with Egret of the River Source, examining they ways
in which the center appropriates them in order to exchange with, prey on, and familiarize various human
and nonhuman beings.

177

178

Chapter 6. The Main Cultivars
While the maloca is a magnified entity that enhances the power of its human constituents and their
captain and locks in essential forces from the river mouth, Andoque members also say, “The power of
the Indigenous lies in the garden” (el poder del indígena está en la chagra)—a statement that I
sometimes heard specifically in relation to women. The garden’s power encompasses at least three
aspects: economic, as gardening allows household subsistence and relative independence from the cash
economy; social, because through sharing and exchanging products elaborated from garden crops,
people create and maintain social relations, as well as participate in the formation of the bodies and
subjectivities of those consuming them; and spiritual, as some of these substances are used to
communicate with nonhuman entities for various purposes. In essence, gardening enables both to
suspend exchange (at least to some extent), and to engage in a beneficially asymmetrical exchange. Like
elsewhere in Amazonia, swiddens are cleared by men and are planted and maintained mainly by
women.45 Since, like other Peoples of the Center, the Andoque accord special importance to manioc,
tobacco, and coca, these are the cultivars I will explore in this chapter, in this order.46 Although, in
mythology, all domesticated plants were brought from the river source to nourish human beings instead
of the wild plants that remained for the animals, these three crops are the most identified as truly
befitting human beings. As with neighboring peoples, these plants are intimately connected with the
origins of human beings. They are associated with human bodily substances and are considered to
embody their qualities; their proper preparation and consumption are believed to enable the formation of
true human beings. This distinguishes humans from faunal beings and protects them from the hostile
forest environment (Echeverri 2015; Griffiths 1998, 146; 2001; Londoño Sulkin 2012, 94–96). This
chapter discusses the capabilities that each plant bestows upon its producers and consumers, and the
two-staged familiarization process surrounding these plants, where the ability to shape the subjectivities
of others for better or worse, align their actions to one’s own, and engage in beneficial exchanges
depends on mastery over the plant and associated nonhuman entities.
Manioc
In this section, I briefly survey Andoque manioc (Manihot esculenta) production and discuss the
capability that its derivatives grant women who master this plant, the nonhuman entities associated with
45
46

For a detailed study of the Andoque’s horticultural practices, see Pineda Camacho 1982.
For a list of the cultivars grown in Andoque gardens, see Pineda Camacho 1982.

179

it and its preparation techniques, to act on others—a capability which is today in decline due to recent
shifts in social and economic reality.
The Andoque associate the garden with female fertility, viewing it as continuous with women’s bodies,
such that their provision of garden produce to their families is seen as continuous with their provision of
food to their children during gestation. As Echeverri (2015) notes, among the People of the Center,
women are considered to be constituted through the cultivation and processing of manioc, chili, and
other tubers and fruits, just as men are constituted through the cultivation and processing of coca and
tobacco. Manioc holds a prominent position in Andoque gardens, and nourishing family members and
other people with its derivatives is conceived as an important female manifestation of power and of
women’s capability to form people.47
According to mythology, the origin of humankind can be traced back to manioc. In one version of the
myth about the origin of cultivated plants (M3), the day after the garden plot was burnt, Egret of the
River Source’s mother-in-law discovered two manioc tubers in the garden, from which men and women
evolved.48 In another myth, Yellow Manioc Leaf (Dopuikn), Nénéfi’s wife, used dough of the manioc
for manicuera (pa̰ḛ́pa) to create the cannibal eagles, from which the Eagle Clan emerged.49 Therefore,
women’s work in maintaining their gardens, harvesting manioc, and processing it is seen as crucial for
the regeneration of humankind.50
Furthermore, this regenerative aspect is associated with women’s own physical regeneration. As we
have seen in M3, Egret of the River Source’s wife received the cultivars and the knowledge on how to
grow them from Lady Beetle of Life, her mother-in-law. This primordial goddess is referred to as katí,
“our mother,” as she seems to have preexisted all other named gods and heroes in Andoque mythology,
the main gods among which are her sons (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 71). Lady Beetle of Life lived in
the Site of Tears, where she built a house reaching the sky. When the flood began, she salvaged all
cultivated plants by taking their seeds and propagules to the sky, from where she showered them back on

earth with the rain that resulted from the burning of Egret of the River Source’s garden. After the flood,
she descended to earth, to live within it, pushing up to the surface fresh soil instead of the one devastated
by the flood. Today, she is identified with a nymph called Biroriokn (Fidicina chlorogena), which builds
tall mounds (Figure 14). This nymph is classified as a beetle, although once it matures it is classified as
a cicada, which is considered immortal, because, instead of dying, the cicada is thought to transform to a
beetle again—a beetle that will, in turn, become a cicada (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 71–72, 255).
Like in a Baré myth where the vertical pipe built by these larvae allows passage from the underground
to the earth’s surface (S. Hugh-Jones 2016), this “beetle” epitomizes regeneration. Similar to the
Yucuna’s Ñamatú, this master of the earth and subsoil responsible for the soil’s regeneration is a
woman, and more precisely—a primordial mother (Reichel 1989, 83). We can assume that it is assigned
a female sex, and delegates to women the control over the horticultural domain, the cultivars, and the
capabilities these hold to regenerate society, because of women’s own ability to regenerate their very
bodies, i.e., through menstruation.51
