Wrongfully assuming a strict linear chronological order of Andoque mythical narratives, Fabiola Jara claims that “the
Andoque’s mother [Lady Beetle of Life] cannot be unequivocally classified as a woman” (1996, 227). Jara bases her claim on
the fact that the abovementioned episode occurs before the establishment of sexual distinction in a myth which follows it
chronologically, and on the Andoque’s present-day consideration of beetles in general as male insects who exist without
females, fathering the larvae on their own by inseminating palm trees. However, my interlocutors unequivocally referred to
Lady Beetle of Life as a female character through the feminine suffix -kn and especially the title kamikn which is strictly
feminine and translates into “Lady” or Doña.
51

181

The Andoque cultivate numerous manioc variants, which they categorize into three types: bitter manioc
(máa̋doi) with variants that give either white or yellow tubers; sweet manioc (hɵ́kődoi), and manioc for
manicuera (pa̰ḛ́pa̋dɵi). Among these, the most widely cultivated type is bitter manioc. During my
conversations with women, they mentioned twenty-one variants of bitter manioc cultivated in their
gardens, out of which seventeen are considered proper Andoque ones, which were created with the
Andoque and have a name in their language.52 Most of these variants have white tubers. The remaining
ones are associated with specific ethnic groups from whom Andoque individuals obtained their
propagules, usually in exchange for Andoque manioc. This exchange of propagules establishes bonds of
mutual nurturing that sometimes stretch across long distances, as each propagule is intimately linked
with the woman who cultivates it and is identified with her ethnic group.53
Manioc serves as a key ingredient in the preparation of various products: different types of casabe
manioc bread (poɵte); fariña toasted crumbs (dʉ’hakópi); caguana beverage (bui), for which the starch is
mixed with boiling water, and manicuera drink (ko’ko), made of a special manioc species (both drinks
are non-fermented). Additionally, the leaves are cooked and used as a spice called pi’na. Both
manicuera and caguana hold special ritual significance. The former is associated with milk and the latter
with semen, and each beverage is concocted for ceremonial dances, either by women or men,
respectively. During the dances, a small amount of each beverage, along with small amounts of tobacco,
vegetal salt, and coca, is offered to the owner-persons. This extremely potent and delicate procedure is
known as ḭtaséa and is referred to in Spanish as secretos.
The preparation process of casabe, which is carried out exclusively by women, is the most complex and
laborious among the different manioc derivatives. This process is similar to the second preparation
method that Londoño describes among the Féénemɨna (2012, 109–10), with increasing use of motorpowered grating machines to replace manual graters. In recent years, due to intermarriage and
conviviality with the Murui-Muina, another type of casabe—“dry casabe,” or “Uitoto casabe”—has
become more frequent, and its preparation process is also detailed by Londoño (ibid). During this
process, poisonous liquids are obtained and mixed with chili to prepare the chili broth (kokoeta).
The relationship between the status of women and manioc work has been widely discussed in
Amazonian ethnography. Peter Rivière (1987) sees the variation in the amount of time women dedicate
52
53

For a partial list, see Andoque and Castro 2013, 80.
For a similar practice and conception among the Guianese Piaroa, see Heckler 2004.

182

to manioc work in a given society as a function of the degree of control exercised by men over them,
considering manioc work to have lower prestige compared to men’s hunting. The case of the Tukanoan
groups in Northwest Amazonia exemplifies for him the tedious, taxing, and repetitive character that this
work can receive in virilocal, exogamous, and patrilineal societies. However, other authors have argued
differently, highlighting men’s recognition of the significance of women’s manioc work in different
Amazonian societies (e.g., Descola 1986; Guss 1989; Heckler 2004).
In the case of the Andoque, the complexity of the situation becomes evident. On the one hand, similar to
other practices of feeding in Amazonia (Fausto and Costa 2013), the provision of manioc derivatives by
women creates a vital dependency. Through manioc production, women can influence others,
fabricating them as kin and as specific kinds of persons—as consanguineous persons, who would behave
favorably to these women and their kin. This grants women a certain power and challenges the notion of
manioc work solely as a means of women’s subordination entrenched in an unchanging social structure.
On the other hand, historical shifts in patterns of manioc preparation and consumption, as well as
changes in community demographics, have reduced the centrality of women in manioc production and
their access to the power that comes from providing manioc derivatives.
In Andoque discourse, hɵɵ́i (“word”) stands for thoughts that are externalized through speech and
action,54 and people usually refer to gardening, cooking, and manioc preparation as “a woman’s word”
(tí’i nihɵɵ́i). Admittedly, “a woman’s word” includes various things that men may perceive as
unfavorable, such as women’s potential to distract men and sabotage their plans for conviviality and
social organization, of which Andoque mythology provides numerous instances—for example, the
casabe prepared by the mother in M2 that caused her husband’s death because it contained her anger.
However, men also acknowledge other, more beneficial “women words,” through which the latter can
act on others and influence their actions to contribute to the household and lineage into which they
marry—primarily by providing manioc products.
Manicuera epitomizes woman’s capability to act on others through the manipulation of manioc. It is
considered women’s signature substance, just as coca and tobacco are men’s signature substances, as the
quantity and quality of manicuera a woman serves attests to her worth. However, in contrast to these two
masculine substances, which hold predatory potentialities, manicuera acts on others through its

54

For a similar concept among the Murui-Muina, see Echeverri 2022, 43.

183

regenerative, life-giving aspects. Women often declare that manicuera is their force (tí’i kasn’bei), using
the word sn’be which carries physical connotations and is used to describe torrential waters, a fastrunning animal, or whatever person who can work hard and carry heavy weight. While coca and tobacco
can also be referred to as “men’s force” (yó’hɵ yasn’bei), men usually refer to the power that these
substances give them through the evocation of the more abstract auxiliary spirit tne’túi, as we will see in
the following sections.
As among the Féénemɨna, an Andoque maloquera is expected to always have a manicuera ready to
welcome visitors and appease them, transforming whatever negative feeling they may have, such as
anger and jealousy, into a more favorable approach toward the maloca residents (Londoño Sulkin 2012,
109–11). Upon starting to prepare a ceremonial dance, and together with tobacco paste and coca powder
shared by the host captain, the maloquera serves manicuera to the dance workers to guarantee their
unanimity. By giving them that drink, she infuses in them her intention to carry out an effective, lifegiving ceremony (de la Hoz 2005, 60–61). The serving of manicuera in the dance itself is important
because, by appeasing the guests, the host also appeases the spirit masters (Chapter 11). Like the other
substances discussed in this chapter, manicuera provision reflects a gift logic, where a detached part of
its producer passes to its consumer, potentially affecting the latter’s dispositions. However, nowadays,
this female power is rarely exercised, as manicuera is very seldom prepared and consumed by Andoque
members, including at the Andoque malocas: during my fieldwork, I only drank it twice, at two
households out of the seven among which I rotated. Interestingly, Raquel served me manicuera during
my first days in her maloca—perhaps as a way to make my stay and research favorable to her and her
family.
Gardening and manioc processing involve vast knowledge passed from mother to daughter, from which
men, for the most part, are excluded, increasing their dependence on women. Girls are trained from an
early age for gardening, harvesting manioc, and identifying variants by name, which encapsulates
information about the proper ways to use that variant and cater for it. In addition to the technical skills, a
manioc producer should also master symbolic ones. Both manioc plants and the tools used for
processing them are humanized, and maintaining a good relationship with them is important for
achieving a big yield and producing large amounts of starch. The plants are said to grow faster if their
“mother”—the woman who has planted them—visits them often, showing them love (Andoque and
Castro 2013, 75). On one occasion, when I cut myself grating tubers with Irene, she told me that it

184

happened because we were talking: “The person who grates manioc must keep silent because grating is
like cleaning the grater’s face, like you do for a person you love; if you’re distracted while doing it, the
grater thinks you don’t love it, it gets jealous, and hurts you.” Women increase the efficiency of manioc
processing through certain symbolical techniques rooted in mythology. When separating the starch from
the pulp, women may exhale on their hands while invoking Lady Kḛkḛ (a frog, dendrobates sp.), who
used to sleep until the afternoon, going to the garden to collect the small tubers discarded by her co-wife,
Lady kɒ’kɒ (Bujo ceratophrys; also means vulva), but who managed to gather a larger amount of starch
than her co-wife did.55
Girls are trained in manioc processing and casabe preparation so they can later provide healthy food for
their children and engage in a relatively symmetrical exchange of foodstuffs with their future
husbands—an arrangement referred to as “mutual demand” by Gow (1991). However, people often
express their concern that nowadays girls spend less time with their mothers because they attend school,
resulting in diminished learning opportunities about gardening and manioc processing. Living with boys
and away from their parents in the boarding school of Araracuara, a rising number of girls become
pregnant in their teen years or hastily move in with their boyfriends without acquiring the necessary
knowledge a woman should have. “The young girls who get married today don’t know even how to flip
a casabe!”, exclaimed one woman. People fear that these girls run the risk of raising unhealthy children
and becoming trapped in asymmetrical, unstable matrimonial relationships.
Men’s acknowledgement of the power that women exercise through manioc preparation is also
demonstrated by the only exception to the performance of manioc work by women: caguana for
ceremonial purposes. This beverage, which on everyday occasions is prepared by women, is elaborated
by men for ceremonial dances and for the preliminary ritual of caguana serving (obiikoi), which is held a
night before the major tutelary dances. Caguana, symbolizing semen, is drunk in large amounts in
dances to ensure the drinkers’ health and fertility.56 However, everyday caguana is not considered as
potent as manicuera, but it becomes especially important when prepared for the caguana serving ritual,
where it is also mixed with mauritia (Mauritia flexuosa) dough identified with the belligerent guardian
hero Tofidei (“Mashed Mauritia Fruit”). It is consumed in this ritual for the defense of the patrilineal
group organizing the dance before the affinal exchange during the dance itself, which may put the

55
56

For a similar practice among the Féénemɨna, see Londoño Sulkin 2012, 112.

185

organizers at risk (see Chapter 12). Based on the presumption that foodstuffs are infused with the
subjectivities of their producers, I propose that men prepare this ceremonial caguana themselves to
ensure that no affinal element, such as women, intervenes in its elaboration.
In this regard, it is noteworthy that while in practice, girls are typically trained for manioc work by their
mothers, M3, shared by both men and women, presents a different perspective. According to the myth,
the knowledge of manioc species and processing techniques comes from the mother-in-law, Lady Beetle
of Life. This might reflect an agnatic ideal according to which, upon marriage, a woman’s manioc work
should be tailored to suit her husband’s and future children’s needs, as they belong to a different clan.
Another mythical narrative, M12 (see Appendix 1), also alludes to such an ideal. In this story, manioc
first grew as fruits on trees tended by female animals, who poisoned the orphan pipe blower U’ḭknñemn
with the casabe they provided, as the manioc starch of which it was made did not rest for three days,
failing to neutralize the poisonous liquid it contains. It is revealing that the mythical figure who fells the
manioc tree and foresees the descent of manioc from the sky— associated with the river source and with
Lady Beetle of Life’s bestowal of the tubers and instructions how to prepare manioc to the benefit of
humanity—is this trickster hero who struggles in different ways against his mother and maternal
relatives to regain the agency possessed by his late father. This myth seems to reflect the idea that, left to
their own device, women (and by extension their origin clans) have the power to harm men (and people
in the clans to which they marry) through the provision of manioc derivatives. Consequently, there is an
underlying idea that manioc production by women should be regulated or contained by the family into
which a woman marries, reflecting the agnatic encompassment of affinal agency. However, my male
and female interlocutors did not mention any actual practices of such calibration.
Other historical processes have eroded the exercise of female power through the provision of manioc
derivatives. While traditionally casabe, along with chili paste, was considered the typical manioc-based
companion for meat or fish, nowadays most families replace it with fariña due to its easier preparation in
large quantities and its ability to be stored for extended periods. The fariña preparation process is similar
to the one reported by Estorniolo among the Baniwa (2020, 476–86), with the exception that the
Andoque use a heavy object, such as unused beams, to squeeze out the liquids instead of a tipití. Fariña
is a relatively recent addition to the Andoque diet. Unlike other manioc products, it holds no ritual
significance. People explain that it entered the region through Brazilian merchants and Peruvian rubber
bosses but gained widespread popularity during the post-genocide rubber boom, when men and some of

186

their wives lived for several months a year in rubber tapping camps.57 Fariña, which can withstand
equatorial humidity and be stored for long periods, was the rubber bosses’ cost-effective means to feed
their workers in the absence of manioc gardens or sometimes women to process manioc. As a
consequence, people became increasingly accustomed to consuming fariña during work seasons, and in
today’s unbalanced gendered demographics, where relatively many Andoque men live without a spouse,
men also partake in fariña production, which is not as gendered as casabe preparation. Additionally,
since people prefer using the starchier yellow variants for fariña production, these variants, mainly of
non-Andoque origin, dominate many people’s gardens, at the expense of Andoque variants on which
women hold superior knowledge. This increase in fariña production signifies a certain decrease in men’s
dependence on women and weakens women’s ability to exert influence on men through the provision of
manioc products more closely identified with them and their regenerative forces.
Therefore, the potentialities that manioc holds for women to act on others, familiarize them, and imbue
them with a subjectivity favorable to themselves and to their kin should rule out claims that manioc
work is an unequivocal way to subordinates them to masculine control. However, the present-day
decline of the centrality of women’s knowledge and skills in manioc preparation corresponds to their
general disempowered position in society, which is reflected, inter alia, in the general belittling of their
ritual, political, and economic role by men.
Tobacco
While manioc production is predominantly a female activity and area of mastery, the two other principal
substances that the center received from the river source—coca and tobacco—are associated with men.
Nowadays, tobacco paste stands in stark contrast to casabe, as the latter is prepared exclusively by
women and is consumed by everyone, while the former is prepared by men and is also consumed by
women, as well as children. Coca, on the other hand, is both prepared and consumed solely by men—not
even by post-menopausal women, as people say was the case for tobacco before the rubber upheaval. 58
The only exception is Fisi’s wife and their daughters, which people attribute to the wife’s Macuna
origin—as Macuna women consume coca. However, even they do not consume it in public.

For a similar rise of fariña consumption in similar conditions among the Xikrin of Central Brazil, see Fisher 2000, 83.
Whiffen (1915, 68, 144), by contrast, reported both substances to be a taboo for women and children, without mentioning
age-related exceptions.
57
58

187

Despite Echeverri and Pereira’s (2005) convincing case for coca’s advent in the Colombian Amazon as
late as the nineteenth century, these two substances are usually treated in the literature on the People of
the Center in an a-historical manner, as if they have always co-existed and complemented each other in
fabricating true human bodies and subjectivities (e.g., García 2018; Karadimas 2000; 2005).
Ethnographers of neighboring peoples have shown tobacco’s association with agnatic transmission, in
contrast to coca’s association with affinal exchange (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 79; García 2018, 410, 449–
50). Authors have demonstrated how these substances are used for the seemingly opposing ends of
predation and the construction of sociability. On the one hand, these substances have been described as
participating in the formation of real, moral human beings, who are compassionate for kin, in control of
their anger and desires, and capable of defending themselves from the immoral nonhuman beings
seeking to sabotage human society (García 2018, 457–58; Griffiths 1998; Londoño Sulkin 2012). On the
other, Indigenous interlocutors attribute predatory capabilities to these substances, and especially to
tobacco (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 79; García 2018, 454). Predation and sociability may in fact be seen as
complementing each other. Among the Féénemɨna, clan members conceive of themselves as
consubstantial because they stem from the same tobacco plant; hence, this tobacco promotes sociable
sentiments and actions within the group while imposing aggressive measures toward the outside
(Londoño Sulkin 2012, 99–101). With respect to the Murui-Muina, Echeverri described tobacco as a
predatory agent which does away with anti-social elements: through “tobacco hunting,” people make
negative sentiments and behavior materialize as animals that they subsequently hunt (Echeverri 1997,
153–54). The ambiguity of these substances—and especially tobacco—as they oscillate between
predation to sociability, is also contextualized within the regional transition from “the Basket of
Darkness” to “the Basket of Life.” In a Bora myth, published by Lucas (2019, 373–74), Egret-of-CoolTobacco creates a tobacco plant that transforms into a person called Tobacco-of-Knowledge (also called
Tobacco-of-Leadership). After this person re-transforms into a tobacco plant, Egret asks his
grandmother to remove the plant Tobacco-of-Animals from the maloca’s patio, whose leaves then
transform into different jaguar species. Tobacco, which is associated with jaguars in various Amazonian
societies (Fausto 2004; Lévi-Strauss 1964, 107–8; Métraux 1946, 60–62), assumes among neighboring
peoples moralistic, peaceful names, such as “cool tobacco,” “tobacco of enlightenment,” or “tobacco to
cause to feel shame” (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 99–100).
In this section I examine Andoque tobacco culture and demonstrate the various attributes and
capabilities it bestows upon people for sociability, leadership, and healing. I argue that these attributes
188

stem from tobacco’s association with predation and with its ability to familiarize others in order to
appropriate their bodies, vital elements, and agencies. Similar to coca, which will be discussed in the
next section, Andoque members link tobacco to the carnivorous Sḭ́ di to relations of predation/alliance
along the river. In other words, the affinal dimensions of tobacco and coca are a crucial factor
determining their potency in the familiarization of other human and nonhuman affines. Therefore, these
substances must themselves undergo familiarization, a process reflected in their preparation etiquette
and evident in mythology, where the affinal element is encompassed by agnation. Tobacco, for example,
which is linked with the affinal outside, is rendered useful to the center through the consanguinizing
effect of vegetal salt; it transitions from embodying affinal relatives to representing the hero’s father. In
the case of coca myths, as compared with those of neighboring peoples, affinal figures—the wife and the
father-in-law—are marginalized, leading to a largely agnatic origin myth for coca, where it sprouts from
the deceased father’s body (M2). Such measures ensure that these substances are more closely identified
with their producers, enabling the latter to employ them more effectively to engage in asymmetrical
exchanges that are beneficial to themselves and their kin.
The tobacco (tá’u) cultivated by the Andoque is Nicotiana tabacum, although they often refer to a
stronger “wild tobacco,” found in the forest and said to have been consumed by sages, healers and
sorcerers in the past, and that probably belongs to the species Nicotiana rustica. The cultivation and
preparation of tobacco require specific knowledge and self-restraint that is not equally shared by
everyone, resulting in unequal amounts of tobacco that each person can deploy for different purposes.
Unlike manioc and coca, but like peanuts, tobacco seeding and growing necessitates a special diet that
avoids certain substances considered “too strong”—too acidic or high in fat, such as peach palm beer,
cashew apples, larvae, and certain types of fish to prevent infestation of the tobacco plant with worms.
Alcohol consumption is also prohibited as it may lead to the leaves drying out and hindering the plant’s
growth. The Andoque recognize that these dietary guidelines may apply to them, but not to Whites, as
they believe that Whites’ tobacco plants can grow tall and healthy regardless of their diet, “because this
is how the Creator left it for us.”59 Due to their inability to strictly adhere to this dietary regime, the
Andoque claim that they now have less tobacco (and peanuts) than their ancestors, who supposedly
possessed greater self-control.

See also Pineda Camacho 1982, 30. For a similar diet among the Murui-Muina, see García 2018, 437, and Griffiths 1998,
131.
59

189

The traditional way of consuming tobacco is as tobacco paste (yʉbʉ) or tobacco juice (yʉbʉdíe), both
referred to in regional Spanish as ambíl. To prepare ambíl, tobacco leaves are harvested, washed, boiled,
and the filtered juice is cooked and stirred for many hours with added manioc starch, charcoal, specific
seeds (e.g., maraca seeds [Theobroma bicolor]), or tree barks for smell, taste, and viscosity. In times of
tobacco shortage—and even for ritual purposes—ambíl can also be prepared from unrolled cigarettes,
that are cooked in the same process. Once prepared, ambíl can be stored for long periods of time. To use
it, people mix it with vegetal salt that reduces the tobacco’s acidity and activates amylase secretion,
allowing for the absorption of the plant’s alkaloids (Echeverri et al. 2001). A larger proportion of salt to
tobacco yields a milder paste preferred by women, while tobacco paste and juice with smaller quantities
of salt are considered more masculine, being stronger and more effective in attracting “the knowledge of
the jaguar.”60
Salt preparation is the most complex and ritualized part of the process. While salt can be extracted from
the roots, leaves, stems, or other parts of many plants, only several dozen have a name in Andoque and
are considered suitable for the preparation of tobacco paste.61 For the Andoque, vegetal salt is associated
with a feminine entity, and mythology (M13, Nestor and Fisi, 20/10/18) tells of Lady Salt (Ñɒkɒkn), the
original master of salt plants. According to this myth, she sent her sons to find salt, but each plant either
deceived the searcher, appearing to him as a person and sending him somewhere else, or simply ran
away and transformed into a tree. Many salt plants received their names from the ways they reacted
when meeting the searcher: dedekn “running on tiptoes”; foíñɒkɒ, “tinamou salt,” because it whistled
like a tinamou bird, etc. The youngest son managed to find the salt plants in much the same way that
Egret did it in M1, simply by embracing it and not being misled by its speech. The salt plants that did
not pose any problems, are considered the most adequate for salt preparation for ritual dances. Since the
last son managed to find salt, Lady Salt ceded the salt to men but attached a curse to it: if men were to
think of women or have sex while engaging in this work, they would obtain very little salt or of a bad
quality that would distract people from the right track.
On the way back home, the package of harvested salt plants must not be laid on the ground, because “the
salt will remain wherever it was laid”—and not at the bottom of the pot, as it should—resulting in a

In the Murui-Muina distinction between the feminine Muina and masculine Murui, the former’s ambíl is milder, saltier,
and in native definitions, “sweeter” than the latter’s (García 2018, 159).

small yield. Back in the house, the plants are burned on specific woods that are known to burn out fast.
The ashes are placed on a filter of the ko’tiñepo fern leaves (Pteridaceae sp.) at the bottom of a conic
funnel made of wild plantain leaves (Phenakospermum guyanense), and the water poured over the
funnel and gathered in a vessel under it absorb the salt found in the ashes. This water is then boiled
while carefully stirring it to achieve the ideal state where all liquids evaporate yet the salt, obtained at
the bottom of the pot, does not burn. During this process, those who have gathered the salt plants cannot
urinate or talk excessively so as not to let the salt evaporate with the water.
When preparing vegetal salt for a ceremonial dance, the restrictions are more numerous and severe: the
producers cannot eat during the boiling of the salty water; they cannot leave the maloca or speak to
anyone outside their team until salt from the first batch of burned plants is obtained; nobody present at
the maloca can be angry, have sexual intercourse or think of sexual affairs, and other visitors cannot
enter the maloca, especially not pregnant women or their husbands. Infraction of these rules will damage
the salt quantitatively and qualitatively, resulting in a little amount of “ugly” salt, unsuitable for spiritual
dialog. Obtaining poor salt for a dance is considered a bad omen, that can augur different misfortunes,
even the death of its producers. Often figuring in people’s speech as a metonymy for other ritual
substances, vegetal salt is described as analogous to money for non-Indigenous people: by offering salt,
a person can converse with human and especially with nonhuman beings, convincing them not to attack
him and to support his actions.
What capabilities and powers does tobacco grant those who use it? Tobacco paste plays a crucial role in
engaging in dialog with nonhuman entities for a wide array of purposes: to protect one’s family and
community from the territory’s many dangers, to safely visit certain sites of the territory in which
powerful spirits are said to live, for a successful hunt, to heal people or bewitch them, and to learn and
memorize myths, spells, and other ritual procedures, all of which require exchange with certain guardian
spirits. Alongside coca, when tobacco is used for healing, sorcery, or teaching, it familiarizes people for
better or worse, making these patients consanguineous with the person employing it or with the spirits
whom he invokes. When used in communication with nonhuman entities, tobacco is likewise used to
familiarize these entities, transforming their actions into ones that are favorable to the human
interlocutors (see Chapter 9). Smoked tobacco, in the form of manufactured cigarettes, is used for
certain spells and cures, as well as to keep away malignant spirits when walking in the forest.

191

Tobacco plays a pivotal role in ceremonial dances, as the host captain shares it alongside coca—and
manicuera, served by the maloquera—with his workers to instill in them his intention of carrying out an
effective, life-giving ceremony. This act serves as a form of familiarization, whereby the captain and his
wife imbue their people with the feelings and inclinations that they themselves possess, aligning their
people’s actions with their own. Tobacco paste and salt are also given to the guest upon inviting him to
the dance for the same purpose. During the event, tobacco paste and juice are served to the singerdancers who challenge the host group by voicing complaints through their songs about insufficient
amounts of food, ritual substances, or the general poor organization of the dance (see Chapter 11).
Again, these substances are offered to align their subjectivity with that of the dance organizers and to
offset their affinal, predatory tendencies. Tobacco defines the ritualized relations between host and
guest, as the guest is referred to as ḭtáufa: “the one who receives tobacco.”62
The predatory nature of tobacco permeates Andoque discourse and practices. Narrators associate
tobacco’s origin to that of “the coca of the orphans” (M2), recounting that after the dead father budded
as a coca plant, he then budded as tobacco. Fisi commented to me that the first tobacco was named tosé
because when the plant budded the orphans heard it clacking, “to!” like a jaguar’s fang. Subsequently,
they heard the sound “ta!”, and the elder asked the younger: “what is it?”, to which the latter replied:
“tá’u; tá’u ḭño̰” (“tobacco; jaguar tobacco”). The orphans realized that through the consumption of
tobacco, they could transform into jaguars, learn how to sing jaguar songs, and invoke the jaguar’s
aggressive spirit and its powers to assist them in waking life and dreams. At first glance, this origin story
seems like a variant of a myth on the origin of tobacco found also among the Murui-Muina and Bora,
where the plant is the son of the Creator or of a deity, and is associated with the wisdom transmitted
within the patriline (García 2018, 443–47; Lucas 2019, 372–74). However, by revisiting the jaguar fangs
after exploring other origin myths below, I will demonstrate that the vertical, agnatic bond presupposes a
horizontal, affinal relationship, from which tobacco draws its predatory attributes.
Pineda reports ceremonial sowings taking place as late as the 1970s, during which tobacco seeds are
scattered in all directions, naming them “jaguar tobacco,” “harpy eagle tobacco,” and “anaconda
tobacco” (Pineda Camacho 1982, 30). Unlike coca sub-varieties named after these predatory animals
and consumed exclusively by sorcerers, this practice was common for all kinds of tobacco. Tobacco

62

For a similar definition of ritual partners among the Bora, see Guyot 1972, 173; Lucas 2019, 203.

192

endows its consumers with a predatory perception, which, within the perspectival cosmos they inhabit,
places them in a superior position in relation to their human and nonhuman adversaries.
Like coca, tobacco grants people access to tne’túi, the auxiliary spirit imparted by Sı̰ ́di (see Chapter 7),
and, as we will see below, to its related ocelot spirit masisi. In addition to seeing themselves as created
from manioc tubers, as in M3, the Andoque also tell a story where a man and a woman were created
from the tobacco smoke blown by this carnivorous god who resides upriver.63 Reflecting recognition of
the predatory, aggressive tendencies inherent in human beings and essential for survival and
reproduction, this myth leads us to the importance of tobacco sharing among people, as tobacco paste is
also shared, alongside coca powder, in the nocturnal mambeadero sessions, to produce weighty words
and cogent discourse. In an encounter between two tobacco-consuming men (or parties), the
commensality implied in the sharing of tobacco creates a convergence of predatory perspectives.
Through this convergence, the two sides assume together the same predatory stance towards a third
party, relegating the latter to the position of prey. As predation is projected towards the outside,
conversation can flow inside, between the two sides.
The predatory principle also appears in the origin story of tobacco for captaincy, as published by
Landaburu and pineda (1984, 163–65). In this myth (M14), summarized in Appendix 1, Paternity Canoe
(O̰poipúkn; today it is the Heliornis fulica sungrebe, Andoque: koé) is sent fishing with his wife by her
father, Shadow Egg. He suddenly hears sighs coming from where his later father used to smoke fish. He
finds a small plant and rejoices: “So this is my father’s heritage! I’m going to live like my father. I am
going to have personnel like him!” The People of the Stars (fɵɵ’ko síɵ́hɵ), the to̰’ḛdi nocturnal
butterflies and Hummingbird bless the plant, from which Paternity Canoe prepares tobacco paste to
share with his people. The latter say: “The captain of the center of the earth is living off his father’s
words.” Egret of the Center also visits Paternity Canoe, exchanging pineapple for tobacco seeds.
The beings who bless the plant live in the air or sky and are thus connected with a superior predatory
position; the Stars, as we have seen in Chapter 2, are especially carnivorous. Paternity Canoe is said to
live in Spawning River (Ḭpá̰se, commonly known as Monochoa), which lies upriver from Araracuara, at
the westernmost limit of the Andoque ancestral territory (cf. Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 76). As a
sungrebe, Paternity Canoe (as well as his father) is a predator of fish, and we can infer that the tobacco
For a similar story among the Féénemɨna, see Londoño 2012, 97–98. Akin to the Bora (Lucas 2019, 138), the Féénemɨna
consider themselves as descended from tobacco.

63

193

plant grows from the fish that his father used to smoke, i.e., from the affinal relatives coming from
downriver from Spawning River. Tobacco’s association with agnation thus presupposes an earlier
association with affinity, to which we will return below. More precisely, tobacco is associated here with
affines from downriver (and not from the river source), who are thus perceived as aquatic beings by a
hero who resides upriver from them and is an animal living on the river surface, i.e., higher than them.
From myths related to Shadow Egg examined above, we can infer the reason why Paternity Canoe
needed his father’s help: to perceive the fish that Shadow Egg probably hid from him, as is his custom.
It is by sharing the blessed tobacco with the fish he has caught, that he creates a predation-based
commensality with them, familiarizing them and turning them into his personnel. The center acquires
the tobacco through marital exchange. Even though in usual discourse Andoque members describe
tobacco as a masculine agent, dream interpretation betrays its feminine origin, as a dark or pregnant
woman in dreams signifies abundant tobacco paste. This feminine tobacco is exchanged for pineapple,
which possibly stands for the sister of a man from the center for the Andoque, as it does for the Miraña
(Karadimas 2005b, 351–52).
Tobacco is not only used for predation, but also for countering predation, namely for healing, which is
itself a predatory a procedure where the healer and his auxiliary spirit prey on the pathogenic agent.
M15, detailed in Appendix 1, narrates the origin of tobacco for healing, and sheds further light on
tobacco’s association with agnation and affinal relations. In this myth, Paternity Canoe goes night
fishing with his wife, Sun’s daughter. With every fish he catches, her body is consumed piece by piece
without his notice, until she vanishes by dawn. Sun threatens to devour Paternity Canoe unless his
daughter is restored. While the latter ponders this challenge, he hears a sound from where his late father
used to smoke fish. The tobacco plant he discovers there leads him to Cashew Apple-Anaconda
(Kɒ̰́n̋nkn hɵpɵ), which has swallowed his wife. After cutting open the anaconda’s belly and retrieving
his wife’s bones, Paternity Canoe blows tobacco smoke over them, reconstructing her functioning body
and bringing her back to life.
In another version of the story that I was told, the protagonist’s name was Egret of the River Source, and
it is possible that Paternity Canoe is the latter’s precedent in the pre-egret mythology. “My father told
me that if you live with a woman from another tribe, you must learn this story, in case she falls ill and
you need to save her, or else you will be in trouble with her family,” told me Fisi, who indeed married a
Macuna woman, upon telling me this myth. Therefore, tobacco, which embodies the father and draws its

194

powers from agnation, is essential for exogamous exchange. Albeit a predator of fish, as a sungrebe
Paternity Canoe is also a potential game for Sun, who represents a higher elevation stratum. When
threatened with such predation, Paternity Canoe turns to his father, who assumes here the role of a
shadow, or specter (both are ká’hɵi)—the very opposite of the light-giving sun—to counter the actual
predation by the anaconda and the potential predation by Sun.
In the specific alliance-predatory constellation of this myth, which includes Sun instead of Shadow Egg
as father-in-law, the fish and anaconda represent Paternity Canoe’s relatives or the people that he (or his
father) has turned into relatives. They are depicted as fish because they retain affinal traces that account
for their recalcitrance towards Paternity Canoe, leading them not to respect him and prey on his wife.
This is also why Sun threatens to take revenge on Paternity Canoe by devouring him—to compensate for
his daughter’s being devoured by her affinal relatives.
Nonetheless, the two myths involve a certain ambiguity as to tobacco’s origin: Does it embody the
father or the fish that the father smoked? This ambiguity points to ambíl’s function not solely as a
predatory substance, but, more precisely, as a substance that allows to move from predation to
familiarization, transforming horizontal relations of alliance into vertical mastery and leadership
relations. Therefore, I suggest that tobacco does not inherently embody the father or fish but rather the
verticalizing potentiality granted by the father of turning fish/affines into complacent consanguines.
This ambiguity also leads us from the familiarizing potentiality of tobacco in Andoque eyes to its
familiarized aspect. These myths, especially M15, represent an interesting variation on tobacco myths
from the Apaporis River, which are clearer in terms of the plant’s affinal origin. In the Barasana myth
documented by S. Hugh Jones (1979, 298), Fish Anaconda is angry with the hero Yeba for having
married his daughter without his consent and threatens to devour him unless he provides him with meat
and fruits. Through his daughter, he gives Yeba a fish-shaped tobacco cigar. Despite being told not to do
so, Yeba eats it, causing his belly to swell, experiencing violent diarrhea, and eventually defecating
outside the house, from which tobacco plants grow. Similar myths exist among the Cabiyari, Taiwano,
and Yucuna, where the father-in-law gives the hero specific instructions on where to defecate around the
house (Correa Rubio 1996, 352; Kabiyari et al. 1989, 86–87; von Hildebrand 1979, 428). In these myths,
the tobacco is received from the father-in-law and represents his children or relatives (the fish, for whom
the anaconda is the master). In the Tanimuka myth, the nocturnal butterfly blessing the tobacco plant—
like it does in M14, without any mention of kinship status—is explicitly referred to as the hero’s father-

195

in-law (von Hildebrand 1979, 429). In contrast, for the Andoque, the tobacco is associated with the
affinal fish that have already been caught, processed, and maybe even consumed by the hero’s father.
The Andoque myths reflect a transition from considering tobacco as a plant deriving from the affinal
realm and received from real affines (hosts in dances) or potential ones (animals in mythology), to
considering it, as is common among the People of the Center, as agnatic, passing within the clan from
father to son. This affinal import must be familiarized and mastered by the Andoque living at the center
in order to be fully beneficial for them.
We can now revisit the origin of the tose tobacco and its association with jaguar fangs. This detail
emerges in a myth distinct from M2, to which Fisi linked it, yet due to the underlying theme of
knowledge being indirectly transmitted from father to orphans, it is clear why he associated the two
stories. My interlocutors referred to this myth as “the Story of False Egret and the Jaguars from the
Stars,” as it recounts a captain’s failure to control his aggressiveness. Because of its perceived danger,
this story was told to me only in fragments. In this myth (M16), as it is summarized in Appendix 1 from
the version recorded by Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 123–27), Nénéfi, who resides in the sky,
dispatches his men, the ocelots of the stars, to hunt on earth. While they are catching fish from a stream,
Egret of Center steals the clothes they have placed on the riverbank. Upon discovering the theft, the
ocelots negotiate with him, leaving him one suit. When the Egret dons the suit at a dance, he devours his
guests, except for two who manage to escape and burn the maloca, trapping Egret inside. Thanks to the
moisture in his nostrils, Egret’s nasal bone does not burn; it transforms into bees instead, and these are
detected by Sı̰ ́di, another bumblebee, who reports it to Nénéfi. Masisi, the jaguar spirit associated with
Nénéfi, descends to earth and circles the jaguar fangs, seeking vengeance for the deeds committed
against his father.
Hence, jaguar fangs draw the jaguar spirit associated with predators—Nénéfi and his messenger, Sı̰ ́di.
The name of one of the bees created from the ocelot’s nostrils, as Fisi explained to Jara, sheds further
light on the relevance of this myth to our tobacco discussion: ñɒ’kɒkn, meaning “Lady Salt” (1996, 242).
Jara notes that the Andoque regard all insects of the Hymenoptera order as masculine, viewing their
sting as the penis through which they transform the stung animal into their offspring (ibid, 247). The
nostrils’ retained moisture, which spared them from burning, thus emerge as the moisture of semen.
Indeed, as Echeverri and Oscar Román-Jidutjaaño observe for the Murui-Muina, the significance of
vegetal salt goes beyond its chemical role in facilitating alkaloid absorption; it is symbolically linked

196

with semen. By contrast, tobacco is associated with menstrual blood, such that mixing the two
substances parallels fecundation (Echeverri and Román-Jitdutjaaño 2013, 10). This explains the strict
etiquette concerning the preparation of vegetal salt among the People of the Center, which the authors
view as a model for sexual education, as it instructs young men how to control and channel their desires.
This is why a pregnant dark woman in Andoque dreams represents abundant tobacco paste: it
symbolizes feminine tobacco impregnated by the man’s salt. If tobacco is associated with women and a
man’s affinal relatives, adding salt is necessary for familiarizing them, instilling that man’s dispositions
in them to ensure the alignment of their agency to his and his clan’s, and not vice versa. Similar to M13,
young men must overcome their mothers and, by extension, their maternal relatives, to find salt plants
and create their own semen to pass on their patrilineal clan identity. Without producing salt (or
containing semen to give to his wife) a man is easily overpowered by his wife’s family, as is
demonstrated in the M17 (see Appendix 1), where Pretty cannot produce salt as effectively as his
powerful father-in-law Sun, resulting in his body diminishing, leaving only his head, instead of
reproducing and expanding.
Returning to M16, we note that, as Egret of the Center, overtaken by the fire symbolizing the alien
predatory aggressiveness he had imprudently appropriated, was consumed, the only element to remain
vital and capable of reproduction and regeneration at the center was the part associated with semen.
Similar to how consanguineal semen withstands the influence of affinal others, vegetal salt allows users
to resist the all-destructive predatory capacity of tobacco. In other words, vegetal salt facilitates the
familiarization, or perhaps more precisely, the “agnatization” of tobacco.
To be sure, Echeverri and Román-Jitdutjaaño’s assertion of an analogy between vegetal salt and semen
is situated within a larger argument, where the preparation of vegetal salt epitomizes the Murui-Muina’s
perspectives on the preparation procedures of their main substances—manioc, tobacco, coca, and salt—
as a means of purifying elements from their immoral and anti-social valences. Such decontamination is
deemed necessary to convert these elements into beneficial substances contributing to human
reproduction. Salt plants and other nonhuman elements encapsulate diseases and negative thoughts and
emotions that the Creator once rejected from his body, and burning and filtering them enable people to
rid them of these impurities, converting them, in the case of salt plants, into vegetal salt, which fosters
human well-being and produces truly human bodies (Echeverri 2001; idem 2002; Echeverri and RománJitdutjaaño 2013). Based on my observations concerning Andoque salt (and yarumo preparation, as

197

elaborated in the next section) and relevant myth narratives, it becomes evident that these moral
teachings warrant consideration within the context of a predatory cosmos. Here, copulation is a way of
preying on others, constituting part of more englobing schemes of mastery and familiarization.
Therefore, the addition of vegetal salt to the Andoque’s (and the People of the Center’s) tobacco paste is
a further element reflecting the greater agnatic control and asymmetry that they strive to achieve in
marital exchange compared to the peoples of the Vaupés-Apaporis, who consume tobacco in the
unadulterated forms or cigars or snuff, and where efforts are made to balance this exchange (Descola
1998; 2013, 345–52; S. Hugh-Jones 1993). This may also explain why the Andoque tolerate the
consumption of tobacco paste by women, which contains more salt than the one ideally consumed by
men, while disapproving of their coca consumption. Some elders even cheerfully told me about their
granddaughters’—and not grandsons’—taste for this substance, reflecting a more active encouragement.
This tolerance or encouragement may be a means to imbue dispositions favorable to men’s patriline
among their wives and female descendants. In this regard, tobacco paste is indeed diametrically opposed
to manioc derivatives, especially manicuera, as it is a substance produced by men and consumed by
everyone, allowing the male producers to influence the subjectivities of female consumers as well.
It is noteworthy that while M14 and M15 associate tobacco with affines from downriver—namely fish
and anacondas—M16 more readily links its potency to the ocelot stars above, and M3 recounts its
arrival from upriver, alongside the maloca and all the other cultivars brought by Egret of the River
Source. In the latter myth, tobacco is depicted as yet another element from upriver appropriated by the
center in a dialectical process of familiarization where Egret of the River Source takes hold of the center
and ultimately identifies himself with it. This double spatial origin is symptomatic of the multivalence of
tobacco for the Andoque. The familiarization of tobacco in Andoque mythology operates differently
than the mutual exclusivity presented in the Bora myth summarized above, where the old, jaguar
tobacco is eradicated with the emergence of the new tobacco, which is the hero’s son. In contrast, the
Andoque tobacco myths reflect the coexistence of multiple layers, allowing the plant’s users to draw,
according to context, both on the power of the consanguineous father or captain and the power of affinal
relatives. In the next section, after examining the capabilities with which coca endows its consumers, we
will observe the specific version of appropriation by agnatization undergone by this plant.

198

Coca
On everyday occasions during my fieldwork, the Andoque talked considerably more about coca than
about tobacco, depicting coca as more central to their existence as true human beings, and as a substance
which endows them with knowledge and access to power on a more daily basis. However, tobacco
maintains its privileged position in ritual dances. Whereas coca is prepared and consumed in large
amounts in dances and is offered to the spirits along with the other substances, it does not have a specific
role like tobacco paste in the protocols of ritual exchange between host and guest, and between humans
and nonhumans. In this section, I show that the core capability that coca provides its producers and
consumers is the maintenance of true human thinking. This theme recurs among the People of the Center
(e.g. Griffiths 2001; Londoño Sulkin 2005; Echeverri 2015). The proper preparation and consumption of
coca are among the defining traits that distinguish true humans from animals, who lack true coca,
tobacco, manioc, cultivated fruits, malocas or language. By analyzing the Andoque coca myths, I link
this theme to sexual self-restraint, a prevalent motif in regional coca mythology. This examination
demonstrates how the notion of “true humanity” is connected to resisting the familiarizing and diverting
influences of both human and nonhuman affines—including Whites—thereby safeguarding one’s center.
In M2, Erythroxylum coca var. ipadu is termed hí’píe, which people translate as “moaning and alive”
(hií: “to moan”; pḭ́ : alive), alluding to the father who continued to live through the plant and whose sighs
became the sound that the plant made when budding. However, this name, like other names for the plant
in Northwest Amazonia, is a derivative of the Tupi name for the plant, ipadu. This serves as one of the
evidence which Echeverri and Pereira mobilize to argue for the relatively recent arrival of coca to the
Colombian Amazon and the commencement of its cultivation in that region, no sooner than the 1820s
(2005, 132). During that period, the People of the Center’s growing exchange with non-Indigenous
people along the main rivers introduced them to chickens and dolphins, which inhabit these large
rivers—two animals that also bear similar names with common Tupi or Quichua roots in all the region’s
languages (ibid, 132–33). The terminus post quem of 1820 is justified based on the absence of this plant
and of its rich, easily perceptible culture in the writings of von Spix and von Martius, who visited the
region between 1817 and 1820, with the earliest reference to coca culture by Thomas Whiffen, who
visited the area in 1908–1909 (ibid, 135–36). The authors propose that the Bolivian species descended
from the Andes to the Upper Amazon in the eighteenth century and became established in the Caquetá
River and Northwest Amazonia during the nineteenth century, where it received a mode of preparation

199

and consumption that distinguishes it from Andean coca culture (ibid, 137–38). However, von Martius
did report seeing coca plants for the first time and their preparation in the Northwest Amazonian style
close to Tefe, where the Caquetá/Japurá River converges with the Amazon/Solimões (von Spix and von
Martius 1981, 182). Furthermore, he explicitly mentions the use of coca powder by the people living
along the Caquetá (whom he collectively termed “Miranhas”; Echeverri and Pereira 2005, 135), stating:
“I had the opportunity to see on the Japurá how a chief of a group of Miranhas, who was about to
embark on a prolonged expedition, provides each of his companions with a regular dose of this powder,
using a spoon made of manatee bone, to ensure them against fatigue” (von Spix and von Martius 1981,
183; my translation).64
Nevertheless, von Martius’ hypothesis that coca arrived in the Amazon from Peru suggests a certain
degree of foreignness that this substance presented during that period as well, and thus, based on
Echeverri and Pereira’s linguistic evidence I assume that the plant entered the region, and that the
contemporary mode of coca preparation and consumption became common there relatively shortly
before von Martius and von Spix’s visit. In any case, and unlike the other elements examined in this
chapter and the preceding one and attributed to Egret of the River Source, coca’s arrival from an area
associated with the river source is a historical fact.
Much like among other peoples in Northwest Amazonia, coca is ingested in the form of a powder called
mambe in local Spanish. Among the Andoque, this coca is known as ma̰ ̰ó sé, a term that alludes to eating
a powdered substance. Coca consumption and preparation are activities exclusively undertaken by men.
They insert ample quantities of coca powder into the inner sides of their cheeks, where it remains for
hours, gradually absorbing into their saliva as the powder dissolves slowly. Men consume significant
amounts of coca daily: during various daytime tasks, while preparing mambe in the afternoon and
evening, or when joining others in mambeadero sessions. Moreover, they use it to stay awake during
nighttime fishing or hunting activities.
Many men prepare mambe daily, in the afternoon and evening, while others prepare it once in two or
three days. Mambe cannot be prepared offhandedly; its preparation process adheres to a series of

64
It is also worth noting that Echeverri and Pereira cite a list of daily tasks performed in that region and published by von
Martius and von Spix, which does not include coca preparation, as evidence for the absence of coca culture in the region
during that period (Echeverri and Pereira 2005, 135). However, it is important to consider that this list only concerns
women’s tasks (von Spix and von Martius 1981, 234). If anything, the absence of coca preparation from this list shows that it
was performed exclusively by men back then, as it is today.

200

meticulous rules. Adherence to these rules signifies the preparer’s reverence for the coca spirit, which, in
turn, bestows greater access to knowledge and power. The coca leaves are attentively handpicked to
prevent damaging the buds, and during this process the garden owner also removes unwanted weeds,
otherwise the plant stops growing, thinking that its owner no longer loves it. Upon returning from the
garden, people search for yarumo leaves in secondary forests. These leaves’ ashes are mixed with the
coca powder to shield it from moisture and temper the potency of the plant’s alkaloids, enabling their
absorption. Upon arriving home, the coca leaves are toasted and then ground into a fine powder using a
mortar. Subsequently, this powder is combined with the yarumo ashes and sieved through a delicate
cloth until an ultra-fine consistency is achieved. Typically, the entire process takes place on the same
day, and some people claim that the spirits of the coca or yarumo leaves disperse if these elements are
left overnight without undergoing full processing. The instruments used today for the process represent a
mix of local craft and industrial manufacture. On the one hand, coca leaves are gathered in traditionally
woven baskets, and the mortar and pestle are made from the granadillo tree (Brosimum rubescens Taub.)
in a process that is subject to many rules. On the other hand, the leaves are toasted upon big tin plates
crafted from repurposed gasoline barrels, and the powder is sieved into emptied, used gasoline tanks.
The preparation of coca by one or more men signals the commencement of the nocturnal mambeadero
session. As the hours pass, the conversation transitions from basic updates on the day’s events to
ritualized discussions about cures, defenses, and even myth narrations. At intervals, those engaged in
coca preparation invite each mambeador to take a spoonful of the powder, while others, including
participants, may offer tobacco paste or even cigarettes.
People say that before the rubber upheaval, every captain had his team of coqueros responsible for coca
preparation. These individuals were tasked with different phases of the process. In return for the coca
they provided to their captain, he would reciprocate by sharing words in the form of myth narrations and
other teachings. This reciprocal exchange continues during initiation processes, where young initiates
offer their instructors mambe and tobacco paste in exchange for knowledge. The hierarchical dimension
of coca preparation persists to this day in the expectation that young people, especially visitors from
another maloca, would grind the coca leaves of senior men, as well as in the custom of serving the first
spoon of coca to the eldest person present, justified through the notion of “removing the coca’s grey
hair,” i.e., to prevent younger mambeadores from aging too quickly. Mambeadero participants cannot

201

depart as they please. Instead, the maloquero or the eldest man present disperses participants, holding
the privilege to conclude the verbal exchange.
What abilities and powers does coca confer upon its consumers? Much like tobacco, coca serves as a
tool for communication among human beings and with nonhuman entities for diverse purposes, from
visiting sites with powerful guardian spirits and obtaining game, through healing and learning myths and
ritual procedures, to sorcery. The coca plant is believed to possess a spirit, and establishing a connection
with this spirit is crucial for accessing its knowledge and powers. The owner-person of the coca, referred
to as “the coca spirit” (hí’píe tne’túi), is believed to embody the plant. It is regarded as the spirit of the
father who passed away and was reborn in the form of the plant, indirectly caring for his children (see
M2). Taking care of the plant, preparing the powder diligently, and consuming it with respect enables
individuals to establish a personal connection with its owner-person. This connection results in insights
into forthcoming events, as well as instructions and additional assistance.
Similar to the warnings and instructions that the orphans received in M2, tne’túi is a spirit originating
from Sı̰ ́di, the leader of jaguars embodying the carnivorous principle in the world, who possess
foreknowledge of impending death and other future events, as most occurrences can be mapped onto the
relational dynamics of predation (see next chapter). The advice of coca, alongside that of tobacco, can
be imparted to certain individuals during their waking hours, but is more commonly received during
sleep. Dreams, which will be explored further in the upcoming chapter, are experienced by everyone,
but many of them are deemed imprecise and even deceptive, while dreams incited by the coca spirit in
adult men—since they are the exclusive consumers of this substance—are portrayed as brief and precise.
A mambeador can also invoke dreams on specific subjects by deliberately contemplating those subjects
during his waking moments. Yet, the induction of dreams by the coca spirit is tied to a less favorable
inclination it possesses: incessantly posing queries to those who partake in its consumption, particularly
concerning myths and other topics discussed while using coca, thereby preventing them from sleeping
peacefully. Mambeadores risk remaining tired the following day, thereby impairing their ability to
provide sustenance for themselves and their families, and thus growing weak, sick, and eventually
becoming feeble, ailing, and prematurely aged in both appearance and vigor while still young. The
coca’s owner-person is demanding, and within an animistic account of addiction, it is said that it wants
to be consumed in greater quantities and frequency to better engage with the myths it has grown
accustomed to. Additionally, this owner-person has an irritable and indolent aspect that can cause its

202

consumer to wake up late and express discontent in the morning, and so it is recommended to vomit
after consuming large amounts of coca, to get rid of those negative aspects and remain only with its
teachings. However, when people criticize others, they would limit the influence of the coca spirit.
Reflecting on the origin of violent actions and erratic utterances by another individual, an elder once
conveyed to me, “Who taught him these things? The coca spirit itself doesn’t teach you anything, you
always learn it from someone.”
The relationship with the coca’s owner-person, along with coca consumption in general, plays a pivotal
role in sociability and the expression of cogent speech. I have never observed people shouting or
expressing anger at the mambeadero. Even in households where family members used to engage in daily
conflicts, the mambeadero remained a “demilitarized zone.” Furthermore, commitments made at the
mambeadero hold greater significance than those made elsewhere, and statements uttered while
consuming coca carry more weight and are treated as having a heightened truth value, reflecting
individuals’ authentic positions and beliefs. “An Indian without mambe says only lies (puras mentiras),”
commented an interlocutor in reference to a person who only rarely consumed coca and thus could not
be relied upon. This belief rests on the notion that the coca spirit is invoked and is present during
conversations held with mouthfuls of coca. To lie in such a circumstance is seen as a betrayal of the
spirit, and any thought or utterance influenced by coca has the potential to alter an individual’s
relationship with it.
Each person establishes a distinct connection with the coca spirit, and a person’s thoughts and actions
are believed to shape his relationship with this owner-person, which is reflected in the quality and
quantity of coca they possess. The quality of coca (and tobacco paste) produced by an individual who
narrates “ugly” (feo) myths about animals and employs his coca for malevolent practices will change to
“ugly mambe,” suitable only for such purposes. Animals are said to consume coca at the mambeadero of
such a person, bringing along their undesirable traits such as idleness, envy, and anger that can attach
themselves to those consuming coca in that space. As will be explored in Chapter 13, the practice of
coca powder sale is thought to endanger people’s rapport with the coca’s owner-person because the
grower cannot control the thoughts and deeds of the powder’s consumers in the city—whether they are
Indigenous or not—and so the owner-person may become displeased with the outcome, resulting in the
drying up of the plant and its eventual death.

203

People infer on the strength of the connection of others to that spirit by observing how they grow the
plant, how they prepare the powder, and the quantity and quality of coca that they possess. Upon
meeting others, men usually exchange their coca jars in an act of conviviality that also allows them to
know if the coca spirit backs the actions of their interlocutor, and if, as a result, they should fear and
respect them.
Since the coca powder contains the thoughts and intentions of the person who has grown and prepared it,
sharing mambe with others serves to form and transform their bodies and subjectivities. On the one
hand, as we will see in Chapter 9, people can bewitch others by giving them coca that they name after
some animal or a poor mythical figure, thereby rendering them consanguineous with that animal or with
the owner-person of the myth and transforming their behavior or certain physical aspects for the worse
into those of the animal or figure in question. By contrast, initiation to healing, sorcery and other ritual
functions, or the teaching of mythology, involves the daily preparation of coca powder and tobacco
paste by the initiate for consumption by himself and the tutor. The tutor blesses these substances by
invoking the owner-persons of the cures, spells, songs, ceremonies, or myths he wishes to teach the
initiate, and by consuming these substances with him, he transforms his subjectivity, inculcating this
knowledge in his body.
Initiation into coca consumption is ideally conducted in a similar manner, where the young
mambeador’s father or another elder invokes one of coca’s origin stories while presenting the first coca
spoon to the initiate. The intention behind this procedure is to bestow upon the young mambeador the
capabilities enshrined in that specific narrative. Nevertheless, as Londoño (2012, 104–6) notes for the
Féénemɨna, it was common to hear many men comment that they had started consuming coca without
such proper initiation, “just like that” (así no más), or after clandestinely taking it from their fathers. One
man told me that this was the reason he could not fall asleep after consuming coca, thereby alluding to
the belief documented in M1, which asserts that an individual’s behavior and thoughts during the initial
phase of coca consumption solidify into enduring habits and personality traits. It is also said that those
who commence coca consumption “just like that” can become yellow and thin, harboring earthworms in
their stomachs, as the first coca was an earthworm, according to that myth.
The two coca origin myths that we have encountered offer different capabilities to coca consumers. M1
is referred to as the origin story of coca for healers and sorcerers, as it bestows upon people the ability to
understand animal behavioral particularities and to consume coca with persons of different species, two

204

capabilities which are vital for the communication with animals and their spirits that these practices
require. M2, on the other hand, is the origin story of coca for wisemen in general, as it narrates the
transmission of ancestral knowledge in the absence of flesh-and-blood instructors and the direct
reception of information from Sı̰ ́di (see next chapter). A third origin story exists, related more
specifically to the concepts of center, real humanity, and real captaincy. It recounts that the coca was
initially a towering tree with five branches. Four branches extended to the east, west, north, and south,
imparting knowledge of sorcery, healing, the utilization of aromatic herbs in witchcraft, and the art of
transforming into jaguars to the populations in those regions. Meanwhile, the fifth branch, situated at the
center, remained reserved for the Andoque people, along with an aromatic herb designated for the
rightful leader’s use. This coca story is shared to impart defensive strategies for personal and collective
well-being, as well as the accurate approach to preparing ceremonial dances and conducting activities
for the betterment of humanity.
This brings us to the importance of coca consumption and being truly human. Ongoing and proper coca
consumption and preparation are considered to endow men with proper human thinking. Once, an elder
told me that the previous night he had gone fishing and had lost his way in the river, a clear indication
that a diablo—a forest or riverine spirit—had been after him, trying to confuse him to harm and devour
him. “So I asked myself: How is it possible that someone will change my thinking, when I am ‘wellmambeated’ (cuando estoy bien mambeado)? I am human (soy gente), I consume coca, I speak. I am not
an animal, I am human.” As we will see in the Chapter 9, a person who does not think and behave like a
human being, operates in such a way because he has already been familiarized by animals and their
spirits: this person has been spiritually devoured by the animals and their spirits, and it is only a matter
of time before their body will follow suit and they will fall ill, die, and be physically taken by these
malevolent beings. By fostering human thinking, sociability and moral behavior, coca consumption
protects people from falling prey to animals and their owner-persons.
Although, as we have seen above, coca is important for speech, I received from my interlocutors the
impression that its primary role for people nowadays is fostering true human thinking, rather than
engendering words and facilitating their exchange, as among neighboring peoples. Among the Miraña,
this production of words by coca, which is likened to semen, from men’s mouth, which is likened to a
vagina, is related to exchange with nonhumans. These words are then transacted with the masters of
animals, facilitating access to the game these beings engender (Karadimas 2000a, 453). Among the

205

Murui-Muina (where Karadimas’ model for the Miraña is largely endorsed, see García 2018, 428–30),
the production of words is related to exchange between consanguines and affines, explaining why their
mambeaderos are located between the maloca’s female and male areas (ibid, 425, 430–31). However,
for the Andoque, coca’s capability for maintaining true human thinking is inextricably linked to a crucial
emphasis they introduce to the notion of exchange: ensuring a beneficial asymmetry in it, or, in other
words, dominating it by encompassing it within agnatic identity.
In Miraña and Murui-Muina mythologies, the coca plant is a woman, and the hero obtains her from her
father-in-law, who initiates him into coca preparation. In those myths, the hero’s ability to control his
sexual desire determines the quality of coca he prepares (Echeverri and Pereira 2005, 141–49; García,
412–21; Karadimas 2005, 129–42; for the Bora variant, see Lucas 2019, 93–95). However, in Andoque
mythology, coca is associated with male figures: in M1, it is the transformed earthworm suitor of Lady
Sun, and in M2, it is the transformed father, Egret of the Center. Furthermore, the Andoque myths
highlight the complete incompatibility between women and coca. In M1, the coca is deliberately
dissociated from any connection with women, and the heroine relinquishes the plant to men after they
disgrace her using a distinctively feminine trait—namely, menstrual blood. To be even more explicit,
M1 asserts that the heroine places a curse on men, warning that if they allow themselves to be distracted
by women, coca will lead to their downfall. In M2, the creation of beneficial, knowledge-providing coca
arises from the husband’s refusal to comply with his wife’s demands and the latter’s predatory attitudes
toward him, reflected in her anger and refusal to feed him.
The dissociation between coca and women in these myths is also expressed through the themes of sexual
transgression and self-constraint. The phallic earthworm’s vampiric feeding on the girl’s leg in M1 is a
clear allusion to sexual relations, and in other contexts, it is counted among Tatoañei’s sons who
descend to the center from upriver to court Shadow Egg’s daughters. In depicting coca as masculine and
as the product of sexual transgression, M1 resembles myths from the Apaporis River, where coca
embodies the transformed hero’s brother following his sexual involvement with his sister-in-law, either
consensual or not (von Hildebrand 1979, 436–39; S. Hugh-Jones 1979, 297; Kabiyari et al. 1989, 92–93;
among the Yucuna the brother dies without having sex with his sister-in-law, see van der Hammen 1992,
154–57). Closer to home, among the Miraña and Murui-Muina, the transgressing brother or suitor exists,
but does not transform into the coca plant (García 2018, 413; Karadimas 2005, 136–37). It seems that

206

for the Andoque, the transformation of the transgressor is crucial for underscoring a theme common to
the coca myths of the People of the Center—namely, sexual self-restraint.
This theme is emphasized in M1 through the unfavorable consequence of the transgression: female
control over the coca plant. The male figure’s lack of restraint reflects the control that women exert on
him through his desires, inevitably leading to a woman’s command over the plant into which she
transforms him. Her identification as Lady Sun, Shadow Egg’s daughter, clarifies why men labor for
her—they are her suitors, tested by Shadow Egg in various myths. Yet, Shadow Egg himself is absent
from this narrative. Before the men reclaim the coca through deception, one man nearly acquires it
legitimately through his proficiency in preparing coca powder, particularly his capacity to perceive and
collect yarumo leaves. The parallel between this episode and the myth narrating the origin of salt (M13,
which likely predates it, considering tobacco’s more ancient tradition) is significant, warranting a short
digression to discuss yarumo.
As a bright substance added to temper and absorb the alkaloids of a darker substance, yarumo ashes
mixed with coca have a clear parallel with vegetal salt added to tobacco. Yarumo, like salt plants, is wild
and not cultivated by humans. The discipline required for preparing its ashes is similarly bound to sexual
conduct, focusing on prohibitions such as not urinating or avoiding contact with the penis. Similar to the
stricter sexual protocols surrounding vegetal salt, adhering to these restrictions demonstrates one’s
mastery over sexual impulses, or, in other words, over one’s semen. Echeverri and Karadimas noted the
association between yarumo ashes and semen among the People of the Center (Echeverri 2015, 94;
Karadimas 2000a, 448), a connection exemplified in the Andoque’s yarumo gathering episode in M1,
which follows the precedent of M13. This interrelation of semen, salt, and yarumo explains the
otherwise peculiar reference to Shadow Egg’s daughter as “Lady Sun,” suggesting she is related to the
mythical predator and father-in-law, who is Shadow Egg’s antithesis. This nomenclature arises from the
perception of salt as the equivalent of semen that enables the suitors of Sun’s daughter to withstand her
father’s destructive fire (see M17, in Appendix 1). Thus, the heroine is named Lady Sun to signify the
link between semen and the substance she aims to hide. Egret (almost) retrieves the coca by exhibiting
mastery over his sexual urges. In parallel to tobacco’s “agnatization” through vegetal salt, skillfully
prepared yarumo ashes facilitate the “agnatization” of coca, channeling its power for the benefit of one’s
patriclan.

207

The woman in M1 has the cautionary role of warning men against succumbing to temptation and
distraction by women. In a patrilineal and patrilocal clan society like the Andoque’s, being distracted by
women—whether they are one’s real or potential wife, one’s mother pertaining to a different clan from
one’s own, or one’s sister who will marry into another clan—is metonymic for being diverted by one’s
real or potential affines.65 Thus, the Andoque do not view coca as a link to the affinal world or a
facilitator of communication with it; rather, they see it as a defense against predation by real or potential
affines. Its purpose is to safeguard them from the risk of ceasing to exist as real humans— understood
both as human beings and as members of their respective clans. This illuminates why Egret, who
symbolizes captaincy, is the suitor nearest to legitimately retrieving coca from Lady Sun: the captain
ideally represents agnatic continuity and the resistance of the center against perilous temptations by
human and nonhuman affines. The trickery by which the animals undermine Egret’s success also
explains why, despite containing an egret figure, this story is currently known as “Coca of the Animals,”
instead of “Coca for Captaincy” like M2.
This might also clarify why, even though both tobacco and coca were off-limits for women and children
in the early twentieth century, only coca remains prohibited today. While tobacco paste is shared with
women as a familiarizing agent, coca is consumed exclusively by men, serving as a means for them to
distinguish themselves from women and the cosmo-social reality that they represent.66 This rationale
could also illuminate why, unlike the Miraña (Karadimas 2000a, 444), even post-menopausal Andoque
women do not partake in coca consumption. It is as if the female trait that conflicts with coca
consumption is not fertility, which a woman loses at that stage, but her inherent affinal nature, which she
can never disavow.
The view of coca as a consanguineous, largely anti-affinal substance is enshrined in M2. Drawing a
comparison with a similar Miraña myth, “the Myth of Second Creation,” as documented by Karadimas
(2005, 236–48) is enlightening. In the latter myth, after the Creator fashions garden cultivars and
humans, people continuously communicate with him and provide him with offerings. However, as they
become more critical of him, he refuses these offerings, saying that he is not hungry, until one day he

the uxorilocal Achuar, for whom women are associated with consanguinity, and men with affinity (Descola 2001, 98).
