vanishes. His two sons are then left alone at the maloca until one day they recall their father (the
Creator) and renew the offerings. Subsequently, the father guides them in recreating a new garden. Two
distinctions between this Miraña myth and M2 are especially pertinent here. First, the former does not
attribute the father’s disappearance to his wife’s refusal to feed him; instead, it faults people of both
sexes for this vanishing.67 Second, the Miraña variant does not claim that the coca plant (or tobacco) was
created from the vanished father’s body. The Andoque stand out by portraying coca as an agnatic agent
that largely contradicts an affinal principle. In other words, they perceive coca as a defensive tool for
men against the affinal world, where women, relatives by marriage, and, ultimately, spirits and animals,
strive to ensnare men through familiarization, diverting them from their respective centers.
Interestingly, M2 acknowledges the significance of affinal relatives. It is the younger brother, often
linked with affinal Others in Andoque thinking and ritual life, who recognizes the coca plant as the
father, not the elder brother, whose stationary position symbolizes firstborns’ connection with agnatic
continuity (see Chapter 11). This realization comes after he consumes the manicuera leftovers made by
the mother, who belongs to a different clan in a patrilineal society. In the version narrated by members
of the Sun Clan, the mother, who does not die, facilitates the coca plant’s transfer from the father to the
(one) son at the former’s demand. Thus, while women and affines are generally marginalized in these
myths, their mediation appears essential for connecting with Sḭ́ di, linked to ancestry and depicted as the
deceased father, and for accessing his teachings. Hence, the father represents the goal while the mother
serves as the means to achieve it. Andoque coca myths thus seem to reinforce a theme common to the
People of the Center’s views on coca and sexual restraint: affinal exchanges are encompassed by agnatic
identity, not vice versa.
Adhering to the patriclan’s traditions is crucial for maintaining true human thinking, vital for engaging
in advantageous exchanges with others. While the previously mentioned anthropologists of neighboring
peoples (notably Karadimas and García) primarily focus on exchanges with nonhuman entities and
Indigenous affines, the timing of the People of the Center’s adoption of coca—during their increased
trade with Whites—also prompts a consideration of coca’s significance in the context of these
exchanges. We may recall that in M5 (see Appendix 1), Egret of the Center gains an advantage over
67
Furthermore, it could be argued that the Miraña myth attributes greater responsibility for this disappearance to men rather
than women. Unlike men, women do not criticize the Creator. This is why he persists in accepting women’s offerings of
casabe and manicuera while declining men’s offerings of coca and tobacco. Only when men begin to suspect that the Creator
favors women’s offerings over men’s due to his romantic involvement with them, does the Creator cease accepting casabe
and manicuera offerings as well (Karadimas 2005b, 239).

Egret of the River Mouth because while the latter offers the former two substances—cigarettes and
liquor—the former provides three—tobacco paste, manicuera, and coca powder. As narrated to me by
Fisi, the myth draws parallels between manicuera and Egret of the River Mouth’s liquor, referred to as
“axe-manicuera” (pɵɵkó’koa), and between cigarettes and tobacco paste, with Egret of the Center’s
words being “it is tobacco, just like yours.” Given these parallels, we are left with the impression that
the “surplus” substance allowing the “word” of Egret of the Center to “proceed” (huha) beyond that of
his opponent was coca, for which the latter had no equivalent counterpart. As stated in Part I, the
Andoque view the river source, with which coca is associated, as a protective force against dangers from
the river mouth, which is connected with Whites. While my interlocutors did not explicitly draw this
association considering the perceived predation by Whites and territory owner-persons due to extractive
operations within the colonial economy—themes to be explored in Part IV—I suggest that coca is also
crucial in managing these exchanges. The critical issue is not the participation in exchange per se but
benefitting from it and mitigating its risks by adhering to one’s human center.
Coca and tobacco thus share many similarities, particularly the power they confer to familiarize others,
in a range of contexts spanning healing, initiation, and sorcery. This familiarization has both predatory
and defensive aspects. However, the two substances differ in the nuances they emphasize in this process:
tobacco is imbued with stronger predatory connotations, while coca is seen as more defensive. The
familiarization associated with these substances is, in fact, double-staged, as the influence on the human
or nonhuman recipient hinges on the subjugation of both the plant and its owner-person to the will of the
giver, a dynamic which is both encoded in mythology and reenacted during the preparation process.
These measures can be seen as additional ways in which these potent plants, originating from the affinal
outside, are agnatized, so that their derivatives reinforce the words and deeds of their producer, rather
than external intentions, such as those of the plants’ original owner-persons, conveying results beneficial
for the producer and his clan and aligned with his origin. A similar ideal appears in relation to manioc
and its derivatives, where, as previously discussed, there is an expectation within the clan receiving the
wife that she produces derivatives that benefit her new clan, rather than her clan of origin. With all three
cultivars, the act of sharing that activates their efficacy involves a gift logic, where a part of the
producer-donor passes to and affects the consumer-recipient. This metonymic dimension is underpinned
by the heterosubstitutive idea that humans can be replaced by the substances they produce and offer to
others. In certain contexts, which will be detailed in Part III, these offerings can be used to successfully
prey upon others in a homosubstitutive fashion. Therefore, the interplay between these two logics of
210

substitution underscores the dialectics of gift-giving and predation in Andoque cosmo-social
interactions.
However, before we delve into the discussion on predation, to fully understand how the river source and
its associated elements are familiarized and mastered by the people living in the center to magnify the
latter, the next chapter will explore the auxiliary spirit, tne’túi, to which tobacco and coca give access.
We will examine how gaining this access represents the relationship of mastery with Sı̰ ́di, who imparts
this spirit.

211

212

Chapter 7. Tne’túi: Power as Spirit
The discussion in previous chapters regarding the maloca and the substances obtained from the river
source, which grant the center access to spiritual power for thinking and acting, would remain
incomplete without an exploration of this spiritual power: tne’túi. Tellingly, it is this term, which I
translate as “auxiliary spirit,” that my male interlocutors have chosen to render the Spanish word poder,
“power.” In this chapter, I present the association between tne’túi and the river source, as this spirit is
imparted by Sḭ́ di, the carnivorous god from upriver. By examining the relationship between tne’túi and
yono̰píi, the tutelary spirit, I show how people gain access to the auxiliary spirit by familiarizing Sḭ́ di,
thereby harnessing his capabilities and knowledge to their own use. The interplay between the auxiliary
spirit and the tutelary spirit represents another manifestation of the center’ establishment of mastery
relations with the potent agents from the river source. Finally, through the analysis of Andoque dream
and omen theories, I discuss the nature of this spiritual power and its operation.
The Soul, Auxiliary and Tutelary Spirits
Tne’túi and yono̰pii are two of the three invisible components of the person, according to the Andoque
conception. To better understand them, I will discuss them after presenting the third invisible
component—namely, mo̰no̰i, or “soul.” Mo̰no̰i encompasses the superficial traits of the person, their
habits and character that can be discerned from the outside—just like the face, mono. Albeit possessed
by all human and nonhuman beings, the mo̰no̰i works differently among each class of beings, depending
on its physicality. Under normal conditions, the mo̰no̰i’s mental, perceptual, and emotional states and
faculties, and those expressed through the root mo̰no̰ (e.g., listening [ɵaɵmo̰no̰toáa̋ñe], understanding
[domó̰no̰ḛ], being attentive [ḭmo̰no̰ḛñe], feeling drunk [yimo̰no̰] and becoming disheartened [yómo̰no̰]),
are experienced in accordance with one’s physical body, the substances one consumes and the people
with whom one consumes them, thereby allowing the smooth functioning of the kinship network. The
mo̰no̰i therefore mediates the passage between the person’s subjectivity and physicality. Although it
normally stays within the body, some three days before a person dies, the mo̰no̰i can produce a specter
or double called ḭtámo̰no̰i (literally, “soul without someone”) that, being a bodiless lookalike in the form
of the person, wanders around, making the imminent death known. Mo̰no̰i can also be translated as
“consciousness,” because it grants the ability to discern people and things for whom and what they are,
thereby enabling the judgement which is crucial for functioning in everyday life. The mo̰no̰i is the
passive, most vulnerable component of the person, and as such can be harmed or devoured by others.

213

The function of the mo̰no̰i can also be compromised or altered by external agents, leading to behaviors
spanning from foolish and incomprehensible actions to violent actions against kin —like the false yo’fi
whom jaguars endowed with “enemy consciousness” (yó’őmo̰no̰i), making him perceive his people as
prey (M16). When such transformations occur in the forest, the victim identifies themselves as an
animal (ḭsu otimo̰no̰i, “animal-transformed soul”) and remains there, leading a bodiless, invisible
existence, a situation referred to in Spanish as encantarse (“to be enchanted”).
Upon death, the mo̰no̰i goes either to the origin site of the deceased’s clan or to the owner-person of the
animals. Some people further explain that this depends on the form of death: the mo̰no̰i of people
suffering violent death—like most deaths are in local thinking (Karadimas 1999)—from diseases or
accidents sent by the animals and their owner-persons, or by sorcerers who manipulate these spirits—
goes to live at the origin site of the animals and spirits responsible for their death. By contrast, the souls
of the few people who manage to defend themselves from such assaults reach the origin site of their
clan, where they remain alive. After a person dies, their mo̰no̰i can appear to their living relatives as a
specter, ká’hoi (which also means “image” or “shadow”) around the burial site or the places that the
deceased used to frequent while alive, attempting to perpetuate and deepen the living’s grief over the
loss, confuse their senses, and, ultimately, seduce them into joining them.
Besides mo̰no̰i, human and nonhuman beings also possess yono̰píi (possible meaning: “sprout of
remedy”). Similar to a propagule that grows from the place where it has been planted, the yono̰píi is
rooted in the heart, serving as the source that activates and commands various organs. It generates
thoughts, articulates speech, enables the planning of actions, and facilitates the experience of dreams.
This mental faculty possesses a somewhat substantive existence, as it is said to travel when its possessor
thinks or dreams on people or places located far away. This carries the risk that, when projected over a
great distance, the yono̰píi could be detected and targeted by malevolent spirits. A person’s yono̰píi
cannot be in more than one place at the same time. Consequently, people avoid hunting during
community assemblies or ceremonial dances, times when the elders’ yono̰píi is not focused on the forest
and the pacification of its potentially harmful nonhuman dwellers, and those venturing there are exposed
to the latter’s aggressions.
Given that all the objects in the world are either persons and/or are cared for by persons (“ownerpersons”), thinking about any person or thing always summons their spirits or the spirits of the persons
guarding them. This amounts to a dialogue with these beings. Therefore, thinking necessitates

214

knowledge of the origin stories of these diverse objects of thought, as well as the names of their ownerpersons. This body of knowledge is sometimes referred to in Spanish as ley de origen (“the Law of
Origin”), and in Andoque as katakádɨñḛ́ nḭe ɵ́ḛ́kńḭ́ sofa—“that which the word of the beginning says.”
What this word communicates, in this context, is the codes of proper conduct between the territory’s
human and nonhuman co-dwellers. Since the names of owner-persons are expressed in the native
language, the content of this law varies from one Indigenous territory to another, contributing to the
perceived distinctiveness of these territories from each other. Hence, people explain that true thinking,
which enables healing, sorcery, and the negotiations with the owner-persons of the territory that are
essential for hunting, farming, and overall well-being, is only possible within one’s own territory. Only
within this domain is one familiar with the origin myths of the different sites and species, along with the
names of the owner-persons in the local language. For the Andoque, such active, engaged thinking is
claimed to be possible within the borders of their ancestral territory and to their segment of the Caquetá
River from the mouth of Spawning River (Ipá̰sé, known as Monochoa) upstream to that of Green River
(Pasḭsé, known as Cahuinarí) downstream. Nevertheless, Andoque members’ thinking can extend further
along the Caquetá, from Córdoba cascade downstream to Angusturas canyon upstream, but in a more
passive manner. In this mode, they can detect dangers approaching their territory and communicate with
the spirits of knowledgeable elders residing in those territories to expand their perception range. While
Andoque members acknowledge that certain Indigenous outsiders living on their territory can heal or
bewitch effectively, they emphasize that due to their foreign origin, they are excluded from engaging in
the deeper communication with spirits necessary for the more fundamental territorial management that
occurs at the mambeadero and during dances.
While possessed by all creatures, the strength of yono̰píi varies among persons. When it is strong, the
yono̰píi serves as a tutelary spirit, safeguarding its owner by alerting them to dangers and enemies, and
providing more vivid, precise dreams. It plays a role in influencing a young man to express willingness
to learn different myth and ritual practices—as elders would not otherwise impose training—and it
dictates their capacity to endure the physical trials of an initiation process, a process that would confer
upon them the possession of this knowledge and the power it entails (see Chapters 9 and 10). The
yono̰píi’s strength is determined by its degree of access to the auxiliary spirit tne’túi, which is endowed
with greater mobility.

215

Tne’túi translates literally to “learning of the heart,” or “learning of the internal organ.” It is linked to the
heart and liver, both referred to as tú (although the heart is colloquially referred to as pḭḭ́ túkn,
“liver/internal organ of life”), as well as to the chest, tútann (“internal organ-bones”). Beyond
encompassing a range of emotional states (such as happiness [hɵ́tutú], sadness [na̰í’hotú], fear [yítuíkő],
and anger [mntú]), the liver and particularly the heart are attributed with more profound mental
processes like having faith, thinking, remembering, and attentiveness—all expressed through the verb
ĩtu. The tne’túi is a faculty characterized by the proficiency, maturity, and collaboration of these four
mental processes. It embodies active thinking that is deeply grounded in understanding one’s own
origins as well as those of myriad entities and beings in one’s environment. Tne’túi is usually translated
in Spanish as conocimiento (knowledge), espíritu (spirit), poder (power), and even brujería (sorcery), as
it empowers the tne’túo—the knowledgeable human and nonhuman agent endowed with it—not only to
protect themselves from other agents, but also to prey on them invisibly, in ways that will be explored in
Chapter 9. Unlike the mo̰no̰i (the soul), a person’s tne’túi remains imperceptible to others unless
intentionally disclosed through assaults, cures, narrations, or ceremonial performances. Unlike the
yono̰píi (the tutelary spirit), it does not truly pertain to the person, which is why I translate it as
“auxiliary spirit.”
The tne’túi stems from Sḭ́ di, the cannibal god, who is associated with the thunder from upriver and is the
head of the jaguars and of the jaguar principle that various entities use for both visible and invisible
predation. This name might be of a foreign origin (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm. 2022), and is part of the
verbal construction sı̰ ́ di onótii: “to do Sı̰ ́di [with someone],” i.e., to devour them. Sı̰ ́di is the youngest
sibling among Lady Beetle of Life’s offspring who inhabit the maloca beneath the Site of Tears. Sı̰ ́di is
also the name of an unidentified bumblebee, a category of insects associated with ocelots (which are
included in the jaguar category) and are considered masculine and carnivorous (Jara 1995, 156;
Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 125). Prior to hunting, one can appeal to Sı̰ ́di by offering coca and tobacco,
requesting his assistance in obtaining his orphans—the animals that this god considers marginal
members of his group and that he can thus discard. Through sorcery, in an act called ḭsiéso—
“(transformation into) a thing of their own (i.e., another person’s game)”—people communicate with
Sı̰ ́di, asking him to devour the victim’s soul (mo̰no̰i), resulting in physical demise shortly afterward.
Therefore, contact with Sı̰ ́di is considered diabólico, reserved for elderly individuals without offspring
linked to any maloca, whereas captains are bound to the life-affirming Egret of the Center. However, as

216

I witnessed on several occasions, even captains invoke Sı̰ ́di for healing purposes, summoning this deity
to devour the pathogenic agents and eradicate illness.
So far, I have mentioned several nonhuman entities whose interaction facilitates the achievement of
different ends. For instance, interaction with Egret of the Center is essential for leadership, while
engagement with Lady Beetle of Life promotes regeneration. Within this cosmology, engaging with Sı̰ ́di
occupies a privileged position. Considering that nearly all deaths result from overt or covert predation,
and non-fatal illnesses, accidents, and conflicts represent incomplete predatory actions, Sı̰ ́di is regarded
as the ultimate agent behind death and afflictions. Furthermore, as the good fortune of one often
corresponds to the misfortune of another, Sı̰ ́di possesses a heightened awareness of events unfolding
throughout the territory well before they materialize. It is revealing that, in Andoque language, the same
verb do expresses both “to know” and “to see.” Sı̰ ́di knows everything because he observes everything
from his elevated vantage point at the river source. Various Andoque myths and other tales recount of
groups that were annihilated, devoured, or transformed into another class of beings, except for one
individual who managed to save themselves by climbing up a tree or onto the top beams of a maloca.
From this vantage point, they witnessed the entire event and could later recount it to others, passing
down the knowledge of such events to today’s people (for example, M19 and M18).
The tne’túi, “learning of the heart,” can be understood as a frequency through which Sı̰ ́di imparts
knowledge to both human and nonhuman beings, transmitting insights about the predatory cosmos to
those attuned to this frequency and enhancing their sensitivity and awareness of the logic governing this
cosmos. People can establish a connection with it in two primary ways: first, by deeply assimilating
mythological wisdom, and second, by consuming coca, tobacco, and the wild varieties of these plants
and other vision-inducing herbs (sita, mḭʼno̰éi, tɒ’di) that are said to not be commonly consumed in the
present. While all beings in the world possess a yono̰píi that communicates, to some extent, with tne’túi,
the potential to intensify this communication through the consumption of specific substances associated
with men or controlled by them elucidates why women are less likely to be considered tne’túɵ—
powerful sages.
As Karadimas (2005, 65–66) observed for the Miraña, this also explains why the tne’túi is registered not
only at the heart, but predominantly at the liver. The liver filters the forces and knowledge of the beings

217

that Sı̰ ́di has transformed into game, before disseminating these elements throughout the body.68 The
strong link between Sı̰ ́di, thoughts and knowledge, and the digestive system is also echoed in the
commonly held idea that consuming various non-Indigenous foodstuffs and substances, particularly
spices, onions, and garlic, renders the body impervious to Sı̰ ́di’s teachings.69
Based on my findings, I propose to view access to the tne’túi as the result of dominating Sı̰ ́di. As
discussed earlier, this domination, which aligns the pet’s capabilities and actions with the master’s
intentions, is achieved through the process of familiarizing predation: the transformation of the
prospective pet into kin, achieved, among other methods, through feeding. The more a man engages in
hunting or bewitching others, the more he provides sustenance to Sı̰ ́di through his prey, thereby further
solidifying his control over him. An illustrative example of this is the cannibal dances prior to the rubber
upheaval, where the consumption of human beings fed Sı̰ ́di, securing control over him and enhancing
access to the tne’túi he imparts (see Chapter 10).70 The outcome of Sı̰ ́di’s familiarization is the
possession of a strong tutelary spirit, yono̰píi, whose horticultural and domesticated connotations are
further buttressed by its synonymous terms ɨpǵánn, containing the word “sprout” (pǵ), and oéna̰, meaning
“my pet.”71 While the tne’túi is primarily associated with the jaguar managed by Sı̰ ́di, and dreaming of a
jaguar companion indicates attunement to this frequency, yono̰píi, appears in dreams as a dog
companion. The tne’túi exists largely outside the body, while yono̰píi is internal to it, akin to a
domesticated version of the wild jaguar that roams the forest, embodying its power and knowledge.72
Equipped with this explanation, we can now revisit the instruction to narrate primarily captaincy and
clan origin stories at the mambeadero, while refraining from the narration of animal stories, which affect
the very essence of the coca and tobacco produced and consumed at that mambeadero, rendering these
substances only suitable for asocial thinking and behavior, as encoded in these stories. Narrating
captaincy and clan origin stories ensures the preferred direction of familiarization and mastery, as it
feeds Sı̰ ́di with messages considered beneficial to the clan and human society, harnessing Sı̰ ́di’s
capabilities to the service of the yono̰pǵi of the narrator and of his fellow mambeadores. On the contrary,

recounting predatory animal stories, drawn from Sı̰ ́di’s sylvan affinal realm and representing the basis of
power for his nonhuman entities, can result in the mambeadores being assimilated by Sı̰ ́di.
Consequently, their thoughts, actions, as well as their coca and tobacco, become aligned with this deity’s
potent will.
Upon death, the person ceases to receive the tne’túi, and the yono̰píi departs to the origin site of sorcery,
which varies for each class of beings. For the Andoque, this location is Tatoañei, a hill situated at the
headwaters of the Macaw River, near Site of Tears, which is also the name of a predatory mythical
figure (see Chapter 9). It is at Tatoañei that the yono̰píi reunites with Sı̰ ́di, who, being the author of
death, also oversees the covert violence of witchcraft. In contrast with the physical, more concrete
aspects of the deceased encompassed by the mo̰no̰i, which are considered perilous and should be kept at
a distance, the more abstract yono̰píi held by a wise person can be coveted by their living relatives. The
latter can ensure that the deceased’s yono̰píi remains with them, allowing an adult or a child to inherit
the knowledge accumulated by the deceased throughout their lifetime. This is achieved through further
acts of familiarization, by recounting in the mambeadero the origin myth of the deceased along with
other significant captaincy myths associated with them and their family members. This approach
prevents Sı̰ ́di from reclaiming the domesticated yono̰píi, thereby preventing its return to his affinal
realm. On the one hand, the impersonality of the tne’túi, which permeates the cosmos without
permanently belonging to any flesh-and-blood individual in particular, resonates with other Amazonian
notions of power as resulting from shamans or warriors’ temporary access to or harnessing of such
forces for their benefit (Langdon 1992a; Rubenstein 2007). On the other hand, the possibility for
members of a family or clan to continue benefitting from the teachings that tne’túi has registered in the
yono̰píi of their deceased relative even after the latter’s death, contradicts, to some extent, Amazonian
perceptions of such power as being non-accumulable (Rubenstein 2007, 362). This avenue of
accumulating spiritual power and enticing its persistence within the patriline is related to the Andoque’s
greater emphasis on agnation, the idiom of mastery, and agnatic identity as a firmer basis for engaging
in asymmetrical exchanges with others.
Omen and Dream Interpretation
The interplay between the personal yono̰píi and the general tne’túi gives rise to the person’s spiritual
power. To understand the nature of this power, we now turn to two faculties that serve as its main
building blocks as well as its manifestations in people’s lives: omen interpretation and dreaming. Prior

219

to delving into this discussion, it is imperative to acknowledge the local premise that the visible, lived
plane of reality is determined by the invisible, virtual plane, whose tenets are established in the mythical
tales surrounding the origins of the myriad classes of human and nonhuman beings inhabiting the world.
Sı̰ ́di prowls this invisible domain, wherein human and nonhuman entities coexist in a state of ontological
equality predating any physical distinctions, searching out vulnerable souls. This leads us back to the
notion of origin discussed in Chapter 3, shedding light on why knowing one’s origin holds such
importance in acquiring access to tne’túi’s power. It allows individuals to identify themselves and their
kin within the virtual realm, and thereby grasp the underlying forces animating them there. This
understanding enhances their chances of survival and successful exchanges within the physical realm.
The logic of omens and dream interpretation arises from this determination of the visible by the
invisible. The interplay between the tutelary and auxiliary spirit enables the person to effectively attune
to the invisible realm of myth and spirits, such that the spirit of a powerful person can actively
participate in the events of that realm, rather than being caught off guard or influenced as a passive
victim when events unfold in the visible, physical world.73 I will begin by exploring the Andoque’s
divination theory and then proceed to their dream theory.
General signs are usually referred to through the verb hɵɵ́, meaning “to tell,” as countless nonhuman
entities tell things, providing insight into forthcoming events. For example, many birds and animals
foretell rainfall or its absence, while fish behavior anticipates rising river water levels, and differentcolored lightning and thunders from various parts of the territory serve as indications of war, disease, or
sorcery. Numerous natural phenomena are also interpreted as omens for human destinies. Some omens,
termed as ḭtanńéso—“[transformation into] something of bones”—concern the fate of future victims,
such as the laughing falcon’s (Herpetotheres cachinnans) song, heralding an impending death.
Conversely, other omens unveil the emotions or intentions of future aggressors. For instance, the
extraordinary roar of the Araracuara rapids forecasts that a human being is about to drown somewhere
along the Caquetá River, even outside Andoque territory. In such cases, the recommended behavior
reveals the rationale behind Indigenous divinatory theory and its specific form of determinism. In the
subsequent days, a knowledgeable person who has discerned this sign would exercise increased caution
Walker (2010) finds among the Urarina a similar alignment between birds whose songs are portentous and a person’s
“heart-soul” (suujue), which gives its owner moral and practical advice and is a precondition of reflexive self-awareness. The
authority of both lies in their “privileged access to reality as well as its derivation from a source that lies beyond experience,
giving voice to the unspeakable” (ibid, 17)—in the concepts used here, this reality is the virtual, invisible one.
73

220

while fishing or might even abstain from it entirely. This individual would also advise their kin to do the
same, so that the calamity “will go somewhere else” and befall other, less perceptive or vigilant
individuals. The underlying idea is that the calamity must happen to someone because the omen refers to
a present or past event or situation and not to a future possibility. While we, as humans, hear the roar of
rapids, this sound represents, in fact, the joyful cheer of the fish and other entities inhabiting the falls:
“We made it! We got him!” These nonhuman entities celebrate because they have already ensnared a
human soul (mo̰no̰i) within the virtual realm and surrendered it to Sı̰ ́di, heralding the imminent
occurrence of physical death. The event is thus predetermined for the predator, but remains
undetermined for any specific prey. Therefore, people should exercise caution to ensure they do not
become the prey in question.
Another example illustrating this conception concerns the flight of the boat-billed heron (po’nn;
Cochlearius cochlearius), which foretells an arrest by the police or military forces. When this heron
passes above them, people should not turn their heads to look at it, lest they be the ones taken away. The
idea is that the armed forces of the Whites, which this heron represents, have already captured
somebody’s soul (mo̰no̰i) in the virtual realm, and by turning their head, a person discloses the weakness
of their spirit (yono̰píi), which will make them, rather than other people, fall prey to Whites in the
physical world.
In John Austin’s (1962) terminology, these examples reveal a conception of omens as constative acts
that simply depict a given state of affairs—whether in the past or present—in the invisible realm, and
that correspond to future events in the visible one. The powerful-spirited individual is the one who
perceives these omens, knows how to interpret them, and protects themselves and their relatives
accordingly. However, in other cases, also referred to as ḭtanńéso, the translation as “omen,” which
reflects a representative logic, can be misleading. These signs possess a performative nature, as the
production of ominous actions by those with weak spirits triggers the calamity. This holds true for
stumbles, falters, and other missteps by the main singer-dancers, who belong to the group of formal
guests in ceremonial dances. There are numerous accounts of individuals who have passed away, or
whose spouses or children have, shortly after forgetting the lyrics of a key song in a dance, stumbling
during the performance, or even experiencing their rattle anklets falling off while dancing. To counteract
this, people rehearse songs and dances and even collaborate with their fellow singer-dancers to establish
a sign to cover for each other in case one forgets the lyrics, preventing any expression of forgetfulness.

221

The underlying notion is that during ceremonial dances, the predatory spirits of the territory remain
watchful over the dance and the individuals summoning them through songs and dances. Even though
no act of predation has taken place in the virtual realm, as in the rapids or boat-billed heron examples,
the spirits would seize any vulnerability or lack of respect displayed by the participants and consume
them. This notion suggests that rather than merely representing an object in reality that has preexisted it,
the misstep is, in Austin’s words, a performative act that generates that object. On such occasions,
people silently remark “páa hɵ́má,” “[he could] not anymore” (ya no [pudo]), alluding to the idea that
the participant’s tutelary spirit was too feeble, leading to a lack of respect for the ceremonial dance and
its hosts, as he had not rehearsed the songs and dances sufficiently or secured his anklets properly.
Consequently, a misstep occurred that rendered him vulnerable to the spirits.
Dreaming (knéi, literally: “somebody said”) serves as another conduit through which individuals acquire
insights into the virtual, invisible realm. Dreams offer entry into that realm even to those with less
powerful thinking during their waking life, but they are deemed less reliable than other divinatory signs.
Consequently, upon learning about another’s insightful dream, a person can validate their interlocutor’s
oneiric experience: “nobody said it to you; you saw it!” (hɵ́má hakné’i; ɵhaḛpó’kni!).
The Andoque dream theory is not exceptional in the Amazonian landscape, in that they consider the
spirit to leave the body during sleep to wander (yo̰nfɵi) “in a plane of reality where the everyday
corporeal and linguistic constraints are suspended” (Descola 1989, 440), and receive, first and foremost,
presages encoded in a structure of symbolic inversions or permutations according to specific principles,
as well as more explicit messages from persons who appear as themselves (Basso 1987; Descola 1989;
Kohn 2007). The presages and messages that men and women receive in dreams arrive from their
ancestors, and men also receive messages from the mythical father who turned into coca and tobacco
and is identified with Sı̰ ́di, as we have seen in M2. Like other omens discussed above, dreams are
usually considered as foretelling future events in the visible realm by disclosing events that have already
happened and states prevailing at present in the invisible one (Galli 2012, 253). The events foretold in
one’s dreams concern not only one’s own life, but also those of one’s relatives and of others who are on
one’s mind. Therefore, people share their dreams with others, especially when warnings are required.
The main keys to Andoque dream interpretation, which sometimes overlap, are: perspectivism, mythical
origin, metonymy, formal resemblance, homology of effects, and direct representation. These keys are
surveyed in Appendix 5, where I also demonstrate that some of these dream categories reflect the

222

spiritual powers of the dreamer as well as others. However, to understand how dream interpretation
plays a role in power dynamics, it is crucial to recognize that dreams not only mirror the extent of an
individual’s spiritual power but can also be manipulated by those who wield significant spiritual
authority. This stems from the fact that the actions that people take in relation to dreams, regardless of
their interpretive key—their framing, rejection, or very elicitation—depend on their spiritual strength
and can, at the same time, increase or decrease it.
People can invoke empowering guidance and additional information in dreams concerning the matters
that occupy their thoughts by purposefully meditating on a particular subject (e.g., organizing a
ceremonial dance or the fate of a specific relative), while simultaneously consuming coca and tobacco.
Additionally, they can engage in consultations with specific ancestors or auxiliary spirits before retiring
for the night, ensuring that the figure appearing in their dream will be the chosen ancestor or spirit rather
than a malevolent animal spirit in disguise (e.g., people can invoke an auxiliary jaguar spirit by
methodically naming all the jaguar’s body parts from head to tail).
An important indicator of a person’s spiritual prowess lies in their ability to reject ominous dreams or to
avert the misfortunes they foretell. Following an unfavorable dream experienced by oneself or a family
member, it is advisable to avoid engaging in activities that align with the same category of misfortune
indicated by the dream. For instance, if one dreams of burning yarumo leaves, it is prudent to abstain
from entering the forest to prevent the risk of a snake bite. Similarly, after dreaming of rubber latex
pouring from a tree, one should beware when handling machetes and other tools to avoid accidental
injury and bleeding. Upon awakening from a dream portending illness, accidents, or death, or upon
hearing such a dream recounted by a relative, people have at least two options. First, they may dismiss
the dream as inconsequential, for example, by discarding a dream on eating food as the banal result of
coca consumption before going to sleep, rather than as an impending disease, or by interpreting grapes
in a dream (which portend tears and grief) as simply referring to seeing jaguar footprints, whose shape
resemble that of grapes, the previous day. The ability to do this both depends on one’s spiritual strength
and increases it, because a feeble-spirited person would immediately lend themselves to bemoaning their
fate, which, in turn, would weaken their spiritual resilience against these and other adversities.
Another option is to “transfer” the calamity to people living elsewhere. This is done through formulas
such as kahakoño̰e nboka nahuhai bo so̰doi oknéi: “may the thing that I know from my dream proceed to

223

people [living] on our side [i.e., elsewhere].”74 To do that, a person must be able to identify the
misfortune foretold by the dream and know its origin, as explained by Mario:
“Dreams have meanings, this is why they were created, this is why one must know ‘This dream, what does it
mean?’—so that one can say ‘No, you don’t have a reason to come here, you must go somewhere people don’t know
you.’ So the one who wanders like a person on whom one dreams, goes somewhere else, where nobody knows who
he is. Because if one knows about it [if one knows what the dream means] one says, ‘I dreamed of that, but this is
not [for] here, it is not for me, go away wherever you wanna go!’ Then the spirit says, ‘This badass (verraco) knows
me! I’d better go somewhere else!’”

A person’s mastery of dream theory also informs the framing and interpretation of dreams. Some people
discard long, serpentine dreams as nonsensical because “dreams should be short and accurate, like
thinking,” and they only accord significance to short and precise ones. However, the interpretive keys
discussed above imply a reduction of many dream narratives—even the shortest ones—to shortened
sequences and even to a single image that can be submitted to inversion, homological comparison,
mythological exploration, and other interpretive actions (Descola 1989, 443). The ability to frame
dreams and decide which sequence or image merits interpretation, affects a person’s capability to
beware of dangerous situations or to take advantage of future opportunities.

A person’s spiritual strength also determines how long they would remember the dream and, as a result,
how long they would be attentive and refrain from risky behavior. People disagree on how long a person
should be cautious after an ominous dream—from merely three days to the indeterminate moment when
one hears that the calamity has befallen elsewhere. Mario claims that cautiousness is needed for one
orbital period of the moon (one month):
“If nothing happened within a month, then nothing is going to happen. Because nobody can be attentive for so long.
Boredom is boredom. As a human being, one gets bored of such things [being cautious]. Within one month
everything passes, within one month everything changes, this may be that ‘climate change’ you Whites talk about
[laughing]… well this is how I see it. Each month everything changes, goes to other parts where people are not
careful and can be screwed (se pueden joder).”

It is precisely when a person forgets the dream and that they must refrain from certain things or places,
that the calamity befalls them. This absentmindedness is interpreted as the defeat of their soul by the
animal spirits, that exposes them to the actual misfortune.
As in the Kalapalo case analyzed by Ellen Basso (1987, 98), dreams are not merely constative acts
pointing to an event that would have occurred even in their absence, but rather performative acts that
elicit such events. An elder woman who claims that most personal misfortunes at the Araracuara sector
are pre-communicated to her in dreams said that, since cucuy fruits (Macoubea guianensis) portend
tears, one should not think of them in the afternoon: if one does not carry on this image into one’s
dreams, the misfortune causing the grief on which the cucuy announces will simply go elsewhere.75 Like
ominous missteps in ceremonial dances, a person dreams in such a way due to the weakness of their
spirit that made them look for the image of cucuy fruits or of other ill portents, whose appearance in the
dream will signal vulnerability to predatory spirits, and will thus generate the calamity.
In conclusion, this chapter explored how power registers in and manifests through the components of the
person and their attunement to, and participation in, the invisible predatory dynamics informing people’s
relationships in the visible reality, enabling them to better navigate and control the exchanges these
relationships involve. Similar to the other elements explored in this part of the dissertation—the maloca,
manioc, tobacco, and coca—the spiritual power that emerges from the interplay between the auxiliary
spirit and the tutelary one is associated with the river source and draws upon the mythical heroes from
We find an inverse phenomenon, that nevertheless points to a similar logic, among the Achuar, who actively summon
certain dream presages by reciting in their waking hours specific anent songs that allude to the imagery of those presages
(Descola 1989, 447).

familiarization, and competition among the various human and nonhuman centers that inhabit the
Andoque territory. In these exchanges between centers, the spiritual power and empowering elements
derived from the river source serve as crucial resources.

Part III
Power in a Cosmos of Multiple Centers

227

228

Introduction
As we have seen in Part I, the Andoque’s concept of “center” acknowledges the existence of multiple
centers, each one acting as such for the people inhabiting it. Furthermore, the animist tenet that
nonhuman entities are also endowed with an interiority continuous with that of humans, leads to the
conception of the cosmos as composed of multiple human as well as nonhuman centers. In this part of
the dissertation, I ask: What are the power dynamics among human centers and between them and the
nonhuman ones? How are asymmetries in exchange among human centers articulated with asymmetries
in exchange with nonhuman centers? To contextualize the approach through which I will explore the
power relations among centers in the subsequent chapters, I provide a brief review here of the literature
concerning the Amazonian analogy between inter-human relations and human-nonhuman relations, as
well as the asymmetrical ontologies held by the People of the Center.
Anthropologists have long argued that the relations between people and nonhuman beings in Amazonian
societies are analogous to relations among human beings in these societies. Descola’s comparative study
involving three Amazonian collectives—the Jivaro, Campas, and Tukano—illustrates how different
modes of relations, such as predation, gift-giving, and reciprocity, structure both inter-human and
human-nonhuman relationships within each collective (Descola 1998; 2013, 336–59). According to
Descola, the Jivaro seek to appropriate the bodies and identities of affinal others in various contexts of
their lives, including hunting, capturing wives and children, warfare, or head-hunting, in order to
reproduce themselves without any intention of reciprocating the bodies or identities obtained. By
contrast, the Campas employ predation logic in relations with other specific categories of human and
nonhuman beings while viewing their relations with other peoples, species, and spirits as guided by
generosity and benevolence (idem 2013, 352–58). Finally, the Tukanoans engage in reciprocal exchange
with both human affines—members of other linguistic groups comprising the Vaupés system—and
nonhuman entities (idem 1998; 2013, 345–52). For instance, the masters of animals return the souls of
the humans they kill to the birth house of their clan, and hunters return the spirit of the slain animals to
their place of origin (K. Århem 1996).76

76
Here it is also important to note that earlier analyses of human-nonhuman affinal reciprocity among the Tukanoans and
other peoples pertaining to the Vaupés social complex emphasized the human-nonhuman symmetry, based on the
thermodynamic model where human groups strive to maintain a balance between their input and output of the vital
substances they share with nonhumans (“energy”) (Reichel 1989; Reichel-Dolmatoff 1971; 1976; van der Hammen 1992;
von Hildebrand 1983). By contrast, later accounts focused on the Tukanoan Macuna pinpointed both the human-nonhuman
asymmetry reflected in the privileged role of human beings, and shamans in particular (Cayón 2011; 2017), in fertilizing

229

As demonstrated in previous chapters, the Andoque appear to align more closely with the generalized
predatory relational model than with the other two models. As we will see in Chapter 9, illnesses and
other misfortunes are considered as the animals’ way to take revenge of the humans who hunt them and
whom they generally resent for their speech capacity. Additionally, while the Andoque occasionally
engage in exchange with nonhuman entities to prevent such misfortunes, they reject any idea of alliance
with them. Their dances, as we will see in Chapter 11, reflect a primary concern with protecting the
human group, with the regeneration of some nonhumans being a by-product. Despite the belief that the
souls of the dead Andoque may go to specific ancestral origin sites such as the Site of Tears, the
guardian spirits of animals are not believed to send them there after consuming their body. On the
contrary, and similar to the Miraña’s “impossible quest for the kalos thanatos” (Karadimas 1999),
human souls are more likely to be incorporated into the sites of origin of the nonhuman entities and
pathogens inflicting that death. As to inter-human relations (Chapter 10), while Andoque members often
cite “sister exchange” as the ideal, they have also taken different means in recent history to establish a
non-reciprocal marital exchange, including the creation of a gender gap.
On the other hand, the Andoque’s emphasis on patrilineal descent, the hierarchy between captains and
orphans (which was greater before the genocide) and between ceremonial specializations, as well as the
ceremonial relationships between maloca owners (e.g., García 2016; Gasché 2009; Lucas 2021), brings
them closer to their Tukano neighbors (and the Yucuna, on the south border of the Vaupés system). This
similarity owes not so much to a logic of reciprocal exchange between human groups and between
humans and nonhumans, but to the “superordinate” dimensions of the Andoque society. I draw here on
S. Hugh-Jones’s (2019 [1996]) borrowing of Mary Helms’s (1993) terms “acquisitional polities” and
“superordinate societies” that seeks rendering Descola’s model of structural homology more politically
and ideologically informed. According to Hugh-Jones, the Jivaro groups, along with the Yanomamö and
Araweté, exemplify acquisitional polities in their constant search “to dominate the outside and the
‘other’ in order to strengthen and legitimate their own political center,” with “other” to be understood as
both human and nonhuman entities. By contrast, the Tukanoans are similar to the Xinguanos and Bororo
in being a superordinate society “who seek[s] to expand the scope of influence of an ordered center by
the defensive control of the external powers that threaten their integrity” (S. Hugh-Jones 2019a, 112).

nonhuman species and maintaining the order of the cosmos, and the separate circuits within which human and animal vital
energies circulate (K. Århem 2001). Additionally, among the Arawakan groups bordering with the Tukanoan complex, an
ideology of mutual predation nearing the Andoque’s complements reciprocal exchange (Estorniolo 2020).

230

Such a defensive attitude toward external cosmic powers exists among the People of the Center,
including the Andoque, and is evident in the processes through which they filter and decontaminate
different substances of nonhuman origin, deemed, in Echeverri’s interlocutors’ words, “the husk that the
Creator was left with after having created humanity” (Echeverri 2001). Echeverri takes the metaphor of
decontamination from the People of the Center’s domestic culinary practices to reject the analogy
between inter-human and human-nonhuman relations among these peoples, an analogy which is rooted,
in turn, in what he perceives as anthropologists’ over-emphasis on hunting practices, which has given
rise to the ethnographic topos of a link between affinity and predation. Contrary to the widespread
association between affines and nonhuman beings, Echeverri stresses the barrier that the People of the
Center perceive between humanity and nonhumanity, and these peoples’ justification of predation
through moral discourse, with animals’ representing dangers to human sociality.
This ontological asymmetry has been enshrined in the substantive perspectivism that Londoño identifies
among the Féénemɨna, who posit the existence of “a substantive humanity and a true human perspective
[which is] exclusively that of the human species” (2017, 485). The exceptionalism of homo sapiens is
linked to Londoño’s argument that the Féénemɨna do not possess a native model of predatory affinity or
affinity-like predation, despite evidence that in mythology, in-law relations are presented as predatory
relations (idem 2012, 139) and that both game and marriageable women are named as fruits (idem 2005,
18). Although Londoño describes both affines and game as “others” who endanger the domestic group
and, as such, must be transformed in order to be incorporated into that group without harming it, he
stresses the critical difference between the two categories: “Affines are Real People, and hence easily
transformed… animals, on the contrary, are irredeemably evil” (idem 2005, 18). However, both
Londoño and Echeverri acknowledge that mere membership in the human species does not
automatically guarantee one’s true human status. For example, Londoño mentions the Féénemɨna’s
belief that the People of the Center are more human than other human groups. Similarly, statements
expressed in clan mambeadero sessions suggest that certain clans consider themselves more virtuous
than others and claim to have been created at the true center of the world, implying a higher degree of
humanity (Londoño Sulkin 2010, 280; 2012, 6). Therefore, it becomes evident that further information
on clan dynamics and inter-clan relations is necessary to assess the degree of dis/continuity between
humanity and animality. Additionally, such information is vital for determining whether inter-human
relations and human-nonhuman relations are analogous or connected in a different manner.

231

In the Andoque case, the link between affinity and predation seems to be stronger than among the
Féénemɨna. Beyond the mythological representations of in-law relationships as predatory, as
demonstrated in previous chapters, Andoque members interpret dreams about sexual intercourse or
avoidance thereof as foretelling disease (i.e., predation by nonhumans) or successful hunt, respectively.
Additionally, as we will see in Chapter 9, the Andoque view different cases of illness and death as
consequences of sexual relations with nonhuman beings. They explain that a person who is attacked by
any animal, from snakes to bullet ants, should kill it, because animals would bewitch the game escaping
them, just like a person is said to be prone to bewitch the lover who has left him or her for another. Not
only are affines associated with animals, but predation by one category is continuous with predation by
the other. Animals are “deviators,” yoíkőɵ, in that associating with them can make people deviate from
their bodily core (odɨ) and from the course set for them by the embodied principles of their clan
origins—just as yoíkő and ḭdɨ are opposed to each other and are translated as “false” and “true/proper,”
respectively. This deviation can render the person vulnerable to other human clans and groups (i.e., to be
absorbed in them), or to disease and death incurred by animals. The traditions transmitted within each
clan protect people from such predatory deviation. Therefore, while members of other clans are
marriageable because they are human, associating with them exposes an individual to other origin
principles, myth versions, and patrilineal traditions that may deviate that individual from their own
patrilineally-transmitted traditions, and, as such, would leave them defenseless in case they are
aggressed by animals. As we will see in Chapters 9 and 10, undesired relations with animals can lead to
undesired relations with people, and vice versa.
The continuity between inter-human relations and human-nonhuman ones is evident in Andoque
members’ frequently mentioned strategy of transferring catastrophes elsewhere, that we have seen in the
previous chapter. This approach contrasts with Echeverri’s model of decontamination, which seeks to
neutralize all harms and pathogens. While his model assumes the subjection of predation to morality, the
Andoque’s strategy is predatory, as it directs malignant nonhuman entities toward other people. In other
words, for the Andoque, predation remains a central logical operator, which does not only mark analogy,
but also underlies the continuity, between inter-human and human-nonhuman relations.
However, predation is not the sole logical operator within this continuum of relations: the closely related
notion of familiarization, which eludes both Londoño and Echeverri, plays a significant role. In their
analyses, both anthropologists group affinal relations and reciprocal exchange together, as evidenced in

232

Echeverri’s reluctance to refer to nonhumans as “potential affines,” in contrast to the real or virtual ones
(Viveiros de Castro and Fausto 1993). Consequently, he does not explore the decontamination of
substances of nonhuman origin, which transforms them into life-giving for humans, as a particular form
of familiarization.77 As we have seen in previous chapters, Andoque cosmology aligns more readily with
the widespread Amazonian notion of inherent meta-affinity. Unlike Echeverri’s approach, and in line
with the Andoque’s more explicit connection between affinity and predation, the following chapters
explore the relationships among multiple centers not only through the lens of the continuum between
inter-human relations and human-nonhuman ones but also considering the continuity between predation
and familiarization. In this continuity, familiarization emerges as an asymmetric moment that constitutes
the human and nonhuman centers taking part in the predatory exchange. The mastery dimension of
familiarizing predation is especially relevant for examining the continuity between inter-human and
human-nonhuman relations since it highlights the significance of familiarizing various foodstuffs and
nonhuman elements as a fundamental step to familiarize humans. In Amazonian ethnography, an
example of this continuity is the Wari’ parents’ practice to neutralize meat to promote the transformation
of a child into their human kin (Vilaça 2002). In the Andoque case, as we observed in previous chapters,
the captain shares ritual substances that have been previously familiarized with his men before a dance
to ensure their good-spirited collaboration.
The notion of continuity is also key here because familiarization itself represents a continuum of
asymmetrical relations, ranging from neutralizing the dangers inherent in affinal others to manipulating
them for different ends. Exploring the different positions along this continuum that one enacts towards
both human and nonhuman real and potential affines, we can gain a deeper understanding of the
previously mentioned concept of ontological asymmetry prevalent among the People of the Center
(García 2018; Griffiths 1998; Londoño Sulkin 2005; Lucas 2021).
This part is divided into four chapters. In Chapter 8, I discuss the Andoque’s general perception of their
ancestral territory, characterized by the presence of various nonhuman centers, where notions of
asymmetrical exchange and domination prevail. The exclusion of competing human groups from this
territory is expressed through the idiom of managing relations with these nonhumans. In Chapter 9, I
explore the spectrum of relations between human and nonhuman centers, encompassing predation of one

Cf. the paradigmatic case in Echeverri’s cited article (2001) of vegetal salt, which, once decontaminated, is conceived as
milk and sperm—i.e., as consanguineous substances.
