class of center by another, counter-predation, familiarization and, ultimately, mastery for different
purposes. Chapter 10 delves into relations among human centers, with a primary focus on the patrilineal
clan. It examines aspects such as warfare, rivalry, distrust, and secrecy among clans, as well as the ways
in which these antagonistic attitudes intersect with previously explored relations with nonhumans.
Evidently, this chapter also discusses the terms for establishing exchange and alliances between rival
human centers. Finally, Chapter 11 presents the Andoque ceremonial dances as sites of convergence
between the antagonisms and efforts of familiarization and mastery, which characterize relations among
human centers and between them and nonhuman ones.

234

Chapter 8. The Territory and Its Persons
In this chapter I address the question: What is the ancestral territory, how is it defined, and who are the
social and political agents operating within it? The main concept for territory or land in Andoque is
ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí. In Spanish, Andoque members most commonly employ the word territorio, while sometimes,
particularly when comparing their land with those of other peoples and nonhuman beings, they use
mundo (“world”). During the workshop in December 2018, which the meeting with a representative of
the Colombian National Natural Parks agency (Parques Nacionales Naturales, hereafter, Parques)
described in the introduction sought to plan, and which aimed at formulating the initial components of
the Andoque’s “cultural plan for territorial management,” the Andoque embarked on defining the
fundamental concepts of their land, inevitably starting with territorio. In my designated role as secretary,
and following lively debates by the Andoque participants, encompassing both youth and elders, I typed
and edited the ensuing definition:
“The territory is called ‘Land of Life’ (pḭiñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí) because it is composed of various classes of living beings, each
endowed with their customs, thought, history, and powers; these living beings keep the territory alive through their
own lives and the interrelations between them. Before its creation, the world was a big fire, emitting heat, and full of
illnesses, diseases, war, anger, and disorder. The first action taken by the Creator was to cool (ú’ɵi) this fire,
resulting in order and well-being. The stories of the living beings are inscribed in the territory, in their sites of origin
and where they have lived, practiced their powers, elaborated their own customs, and fought with others. Upon
creation, the Creator left some rules for each living being and assigned certain persons to be in charge of the sites
where these beings were created and where important events in the history of the territory had taken place. Bits and
pieces of the thinking and speech of the Creator through which the world was formed and that are inscribed in it,
have been transmitted to the living beings through the origin sites of each animal species and especially through the
origin sites of each clan of the People of the Axe. Therefore, once we take into account the history, the sites of the
territory, and the other components of the world, the thinking and speech of the People of the Axe participate in the
management of the territory and are crucial for its order.”

The participants arrived at this definition by contrasting it with the definition of territory held by Whites,
which I provided in response to their request, and according to which, in this standard definition,
territory is an area where a group of people holds jurisdiction and enjoys exclusive usufruct rights. Upon
hearing my definition, Nestor, Fisi’s son of the Eagle Clan, commented: “So they don’t take into
account the life of trees and animals, as we do! Because, for us, the territory has many owners!” As a
result, the definition reflects the shared origin and destiny of human and nonhuman co-dwellers of the
land, along with the animist recognition of the latter’s subjectivity and agency. This definition also
acknowledges that nonhuman entities control and protect the different sites and species of the land,
235

aligning with the conceptions of other Amazonians where the cosmos consists of overlapping domains
and traversed by human and nonhuman ownership relationships, challenging Western cartographies of
discrete property zones (Fausto 2008). However, when I read the final document aloud for approval on
the final day of the workshop, Nestor requested to qualify his statement regarding multiple ownership,
stating: “But the territory was given to us so we could use it.” Elias, a maloquero of fifty years old,
emphasized, reflecting the assumption that non-Indigenous people also adhere to the preservationist
standards they demand of Indigenous communities: “The plan must make it clear that we, as humans,
are superior to Nature and dominate it. This is how things have been since Creation. So that the White
won’t say that we’re like him, who is dominated by Nature.”

Figure 16. Nestor Andoke Macuna burning plants for the preparation of vegetal salt (Photo taken by the author)

Although no Parques personnel attended the workshop, Andoque participants expected them and other
non-Indigenous officials to read the resulting document, and so inserting these statements was intended
to prevent future foreign intervention based on claims of biodiversity preservation, as the participants
thought that acknowledging the existence of nonhuman owner-persons might make Whites infer that the
Andoque had no right to it. However, the conception of human superiority vis-à-vis nonhumans in the
Andoque territory cannot be reduced to this context. At first glance, this can be attributed to an
oscillation among Andoque members between animist perceptions of the land and naturalist
perspectives, where nonhuman entities are seen as objects accessible for human use, lacking autonomy,
subjectivity, and agency. Although, as will be explored below, contemporary territorial politics may
contribute to the development of such ontological ambiguity and adherence to naturalist perspectives,
236

this chapter demonstrates how the apparent contradiction in the statements expressed during the
workshop can also be explained within the framework of the Andoque’s animist conception of territory.
As I will show, the Andoque’s version of animism is hierarchical, enabling the ontological asymmetry
which is on par with the asymmetrical exchanges sought between humans and nonhumans, and,
ultimately, among human centers, to be explored throughout this part of the dissertation. While drawing
on data from the entire fieldwork period including my later visit in 2021, I return in this chapter to the
statements made during the territorial management workshop and the mambeadero sessions at Fisi’s
maloca during and following that week, where he elaborated on the workshop themes.
Creator-Persons and Site-Persons
As elsewhere in Amazonia, the Andoque consider the human or nonhuman person who created a given
material or immaterial thing, human or nonhuman persons and groups, who protects it from predation by
others—although not necessarily by that creator—and/or allows for its reproduction as the owner or
master of that thing, person, or group (Brightman 2010; Brightman et al. 2016; Fausto 2008). In
Spanish, Andoque members often refer to owners as dueños, while in the native language the term
denoting mastery or ownership is ño̰, “person.” This term conveys the idea that the owner/master of a
given entity or group of entities is its personified aspect.78 Thus, similar to other Amazonian notions of
ownership and mastery (Costa 2017; Fausto 2008; Viveiros de Castro 1998, 471), the owner-person is
endowed with subjectivity, intentionality, and agency, enabling it to act on behalf of those it personifies,
akin to a captain and maloca owner who serves as the “person-body trunk” of his personnel. Countless
deities and spirits are considered “the persons” (nño̰e) of the species, substances, instruments, myths,
dances, sorcery spells, illnesses, cures, and other cultural practices that they created or were the first to
employ in mythology. To stress this aspect of owner-persons, I refer to them here as “creator-persons.”
To benefit from the things or practices they personify (or to protect oneself from them, if that thing is an
illness), one must converse with “those who created that work” (báɒ̋i oa tiɵ) to align their agency with
one’s own; in other words, to master these masters. Conversely, mentioning the names of these creatorpersons or contemplating on the origins of the things they own without offering them coca powder,
tobacco paste, and manicuera (sometimes a ceremonial dance is also required) amounts to summoning
them empty-handed. In turn, they would seek out those invoking them, causing harm through disease
and other predatory acts if the invoker does not provide them with any offering. During a mambeadero

78

Despite their similarity, ño̰ and ñó̰i (“earth”) do not share a common root.

237

session at his maloca after one of the workshop days, Fisi formulated the following phrase to his
interlocutors Nestor and Elias, who inquired about the traditional rules for managing the territory: “One
does not invoke them [the owner-persons] without [offering] anything [i.e., ritual substances]” (hɵ́má
niḛ nbokani). This is also why, at different moments during fieldwork, people refrained from telling me
certain myths in detail or at all, or refrained from explaining about powerful disease.
In the Andoque’s accounts on the owner-persons of animals and of other nonhuman beings, two types of
dominions can be discerned: mythical ascendence and micro-ecosystem habitat. In this regard, the
Andoque resemble their Murui-Muina neighbors, as observed by García, who distinguish between the
masters of single-species groups (to which I prefer to call more precisely “groups of a single mythic
origin”) and the masters of multi-species groups (or “groups of multiple mythic origins”) (2018, 225–27,
245–50). According to García, the former maintain filial and protective relations with the animal
personnel, while the latter maintain relations of affinity and predation with their personnel, dominating
this multi-species group similar to how a human captain dominates his people. The different
relationships that each type of master maintains with its personnel roughly corresponds to the Achuar’s
distinction between the “game mothers,” who both protect and prey on their “children,” and the “game
ama̰na̰”—the leaders of game animals, with whom hunters dialog to ensure success (Descola 1994b,
257–60).
The Andoque refer to various nonhuman entities as ḭsu yahaǵtı̋ ɵ: “those who were created for the
animal(s).” Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 82 n.100) also translate this as “principles/princes of the
animals” (principios/príncipes) to convey both the power of these animate beings, and the idea that they
serve as molds for the animals they created, imprinting them with key characteristics such as ecological
stratum, predatory status, and behavior. The primary creator-persons include Nénéfi, the captain of
eagles and creator of most birds; Sı̰ ́di, the captain of jaguars and of the predatory principle in land
animals; Red Anaconda (Pe’pai), the captain of anacondas, fish, and the predatory principle in the latter;
Pineapple (Tomirepa), the captain of game animals, and Sun, who created the monkeys (doɨsua,
“animals of above”). The predatory aspect of these creator-masters—except for Pineapple, who is a fruit
and is associated with the “fruit” dimension of various species where they serve as prey to others—
signals the agency of these species and their ability to prey on others in various ways. Other lesser
creator-persons include Moon, who created many edible fish; Usiñémn, who created some white-lipped
peccaries (íń; Tayassu pecari) by attaching peccary eyes to a group of blind hunters (see Chapter 9);
Shadow Egg, and many others. These owner-persons, sometimes referred to as the grandfathers
238

(nyo’tapɵ) of the species they created, protect them, and can be invoked in shamanic incantations to
promote their reproduction.
After the initial creation of these species, as stated in the workshop document, the Creator appointed
guardian spirits to oversee the sites where they were created and where they live and reproduce.
Collectively known as ’i’bo ño̰e (“persons of there”), these owner-persons possess specific sites referred
to as ḭño̰e fɵsí, meaning “a persons’ place.” To stress this aspect, I refer to them as “site-persons.”
Similar to the Yucuna, the specific names given to each such person and their corresponding sites
indicate the existence of distinct micro-habitats within the Andoque territory (Reichel 1989, 80). They
personify the sites they safeguard and the plants and animals that inhabit them. Such conception is
attested in such statements as “The owner of that site is already tired,” explaining why people refrain
from clearing forest plots for gardens in areas that have been overexploited. Through site-persons, the
land is personified in general, allowing, for example, “to talk with the land” (ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí ɵma hɵɵ́ñe). The
site-persons are also sometimes referred to as ḭsu yahaǵtı̋ ɵ. This is because, while the mythical heroes
who originally created the different species maintain a loose oversight of their creations, the site-persons
take on the role of actively protecting their personnel—the animals and plants of these species living
within their domains—and ensuring their continuous reproduction. There are instances where the two
categories “creator-persons” and “site-persons” converge, either because the mythical heroes who
created certain species, cultural practices, or illnesses are associated with specific sites, or because they
created them while passing through such sites.
The site-persons have the responsibility to regulate predation among their personnel, as the beings
within their domains feed on each other, and to protect them from external predators such as animals
from other sites and human beings. As in Fausto’s (2008) depiction of the typical Amazonian owner,
the’i’bo ño̰e appear as predatory affinal figures to outsiders, and as protective, father-like figures to their
own personnel. When entering a site with a powerful site-person, visitors must take precautions to avoid
rain, thunderstorms, and attacks by the site-person’s “pets” (éna̰), which include snakes and other
dangerous animals. In a silent manner, the visitor should address the owner while offering coca powder,
tobacco paste, and vegetal salt specifically prepared for that occasion, acknowledging the entity as the
site-person and expressing that they are only passing through without any intention to cause harm.
Importantly, the visitor should also identify himself by name and as the site-person’s grandson (haɵ́tɵ
knɵ́tɵ) and the inhabitant of the territory. He can add to it an assertive statement, such as the one shared
with me by an elder interlocutor: Koi mn oa ḛ́’dɨ kḛ́’e. Oɨ bo’ɨ.—“Don’t tell me ‘Who are you?’ I am [a
239

person you know].” It is advised to avoid hunting in sites with more powerful site-person and instead
hunt in those with less powerful ones. A hunter should provide similar offerings (ḭtaséa) to a site-person
in whose domain where he wishes to hunt, assuring them that his intention is solely to provide food for
his family and not to cause unnecessary harm. Before clearing trees to create a garden plot and during
the period of its use, men should make coca and tobacco offerings to the site-person of the area and
engage in dialog with them to ensure the safety and well-being of themselves and their families. While
the Andoque (as well as their neighbors [García 2018, 237]) commonly refer to these dialogs as seeking
permission from the site-persons, the approaches reflected in some reported formulas vary from kind yet
decisive notice to confrontation and intimidation. Examples range from “I am now going to work here
for a few years and then leave some fruits for your children [the animals],” to “I will work here to
provide for my wife and children; you [the owner], go away from here and look elsewhere, don’t pay
attention to me!” to “I will not harass you, and do not harass me, let’s fear each other” (kaha yinayíhai).
Some site-persons are depicted as a big, usually predatory species, such as a jaguar, an anaconda, a
snake, or a large fish (e.g., Pseudoplatystoma sp.), who serve as the foundation on which other
organisms of the site—sometimes even the water in the case of a backwater site—depend. Other sitepersons are completely invisible, while some are persons who happened to pass in the site and are still
living there (ñe nɵi), within its ground. This is why site-persons are often referred to as kakńño̰e
(“People of Below”), signifying earlier human generations (see Chapter 2).
The way people currently describe such disappearances suggests a view of the site-person as
personifying the entirety of beings living within their domains. It is believed that the mo̰no̰i (soul) of the
victim of a specific disease, sorcery attack, or physical aggression by animals, goes to the origin site of
that specific disease, sorcery spell, or animal. In other words, the soul becomes trapped by the owner of
the species, illness, or cultural practice (referred to as dómo̰no̰i, meaning “soul taking”). For instance, if
a person dies from a snake bite, their soul is believed to go to the place from which snakes originated.
Predation by site-persons, and the subsequent entrapment within their invisible malocas in their
domains, is inferred only when a person’s body completely disappears there. One such case occurred
during my fieldwork when a non-Indigenous Colombian man drowned in the Araracuara rapids. The
People explained that if he had died, his body would have resurfaced somewhere along the river.
However, since this did not happen, people inferred that he was “enchanted” (encantado) and his soul
was taken (dómo̰no̰i) by Fisio̰ ́ hḛkn (“Rock Harbor”) the owner of the rapids, in whose maloca (which
seems to humans like underwater rocks) he now lives. Such utter disappearance implies that his body
240

was consumed by more than one species, possibly even by many or all of them; in short, it was
consumed by the site itself, which is personified by its site-person. As a result, rather than going to the
origin site of the aggressor species, the victim’s soul stays in that specific site. People who have
disappeared in either the recent or distant past, and whose souls can be thus traced to specific sites such
as rapids, saltlicks, and lakes, become mediators between their living kin and the site-person. I was told
that, as a White person, I could turn to the drowned Colombian man, who, despite having a black
complexion, was blanco like me in that he was non-Indigenous, whenever I want to visit the rapids or
fish there. I could ask him to represent me before the rapids’ site-person, ensuring that I would not be
harmed, similar to how Andoque fishermen turn to Sitepa, an Andoque man who drowned there in the
distant past. The memory of Sitepa (or the drowned Colombian person) enhances the personification of
the site, as reflected in the name of the site-person, thereby further facilitating communication with it.
The site-persons are sometimes also referred to as diablos (“devils”). This term alludes to their
nonhuman and extraordinary existence, which is largely invisible but can manifest itself in the form of a
shadow or some other exceptional vision or sound. It also refers to the potential harm they can cause to
those visiting their site or abusing it or their animals, even long time after the abuse has taken place.
Despite being grouped with other diablos collectively called fi’du in Andoque, the site-persons have
distinct characteristics. The other fi’du are mobile, proactively aggressive, and of a purely malign
character, actively seeking out people in the forest and even in their gardens to assault them. By contrast,
the site-persons primarily adopt a defensive stance and are immobile. The difference between these
fi’du, which will be examined in the next chapter, and the site-persons can be compared to the difference
that exists between individual hunters who enter the forest to communicate with and prey on animals on
their own behalf, and captains, who communicate with enemies and prey on them for the entire group,
operating from their malocas.
Ño̰ ́ ifɵsi: Territory as Connectivity
Beyond multiple ownership, the definition of the Andoque territory above reveals a perception that
combines both space and connectivity, which serves as the platform for asymmetrical exchanges among
the territory’s human and nonhuman co-dwellers. The term ño̰ ́ i means “earth, soil,” while fɵsí refers to
place, where the defining aspect is not boundaries but interrelatedness. As Nestor explained during
workshop discussions, “The word ño̰ ́ i has no sense on its own, it’s just the earth when you take it from
the ground and hold it in your hand—it’s dead. Only when the earthworm eats it does it become

241

ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí.” Later in the mambeadero session at his maloca, Fisi further explained to me that ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí is the
upper layer of the earth which tree roots reach, providing nourishment for the tree and for the beings
living above ground. Similar to Echeverri’s interpretation of the People of the Center’s conception of
territory as appetite or desire, which drives different human and nonhuman beings to connect with others
(and their respective territories) for growth and reproduction (2005), what constitutes a territory is the
connectivity between the classes of beings deriving nourishment from it and from each other. As we will
see in the following chapters, this connectivity is perpetuated in ritualized negotiations, providing
insights into why Andoque members sometimes translate ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí as “world,” implying a particular logic
and order reminiscent of the Greek concept “cosmos” and the fundamental essence of the Spanish word
mundo, which conveys notions of elegance and propriety.
Ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí means “this world,” referring to where Andoque people live. However, like the shorter form fɵsí,
it is a generic term, and Andoque interlocutors acknowledge the existence of many such worlds. Some
of these worlds are inhabited solely by nonhuman entities, while others include also human peoples of
other groups. Andoque interlocutors mention various ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí that overlap with their own, as well as
others that are encompassed by it, bordering with it, or located far away from it. Furthermore, while
these diverse worlds have a spatial dimension, not all of them necessarily manifest in our geographical
space, but rather exist as realms of spiritual management. Among the worlds mentioned by Andoque
interlocutors are the worlds of neighboring Indigenous peoples, the World of the (Ocelot) Stars (fɵɵko
fɵsí), the Netherworld (kakn ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí), the (Game) Animals World (ḭsu yañó̰ḭ́ fɵsí), the Birds World (hiɵfo
yaño̰ ́ ifɵsi), the World of the Center (dʉi ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí), the World by Our Side (of the Caquetá, on its northern
bank) (kahako ño̰ ́ ifɵsi), the Worlds of the River Source and River Mouth (ɵbai ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí and ɵkɒ́ ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí,
respectively), the Whites World or the City (duiɵhɵ yañó̰ḭ́ fɵsí; literally, the Burners World), the Worlds
of Heat (pa̰i ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí) and Darkness (tipɵnnɵ́ɵ̋i fɵsí) from which different kinds of disease and sorcery
originate and where the spirits of the dead reside, as well as the general kusi ño̰ ́ ifɵsi, or “another world,”
denoting the worlds the Andoque do not know.
In each world or territory, there are different site-owners whose names, approaches to them, and the
composition and extension of their domains—the sites and animals they protect—are inscribed in the
distinct origin myths of each world or territory. These aspects are typically unknown to inhabitants of

242

other worlds/territories.79 Consequently, visiting another territory—be it the World of Darkness or the
Land of the Bora people—without a local companion (human or nonhuman) who can appease the
owner-persons is considered dangerous. Engaging in activities like hunting or creating a garden in such
worlds/territories, particularly those geographically materialized worlds inhabited by other ethnic
groups, is even more perilous. Similar to the beliefs held by the Féénemɨna (Londoño Sulkin 2000, 330),
living outside one’s ancestral land exposes individuals to illnesses and harms caused by owner-persons
who perceive them as intruders. Additionally, the knowledge possessed by foreigners does not offer
protection against local harms because effective healing and protection procedures rely on
communication with specific owner-persons whose authority is limited to their own territory. This
renders cultural practices, including cures, sorcery, and ceremonial dances, ineffective when performed
in other territories. Even the act of thinking itself is affected, since it requires invoking the spirits who
guard the myths, substances, practices, species, and sites that serve as objects of thought. Spatial
disorientation is thus linked to mental disorientation and submission to the authority of locals who
dictate what one can and cannot do in a particular ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí.
By highlighting another person’s foreignness to a specific ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí, a native of that world/territory asserts
their greater capacity to survive and thrive there, claiming authority over the outsider. This way, as
Christopher Gregory points out, cosmological discourse regarding stewarding the land through
communication with nonhuman beings intertwines with and validates political practices that restrict the
access of others to that land (1997, 115–16). This discourse is also on par with the widespread use of
localized rituals and place sacredness in advancing land claims, both vis-à-vis the State and with other
ethnic and religious groups (e.g., Stadler 2020). Thus, the fact that Andoque members asked me to
define territorio on the first day of the workshop and expressed surprise at the lack of recognition by
Whites regarding nonhuman ownership does not imply that their frequent use of this term is not
underpinned by another of its key dimensions: the privileged use and enjoyment of a space by a
particular human group.
Owners vis-à-vis the State
Ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí’s connectivity is also critical for the Andoque’s negotiations over power in relation to the State.

243

2018, the Andoque were asked to contribute to the introduction section of a “Life Plan” for CRIMA’s
peoples that the two organizations were drafting, and to which members of the other three ethnicities
had already contributed. Those members had provided “words of wisdom” from their respective
ethnicities, such as “abundance,” “life,” or “make dawn,” which served as superordinate categories
under which they described their values. When asked if they agreed with these concepts, the Andoque
participants were perplexed. Levy of the Sun Clan dismissed them altogether: “We don’t have all that.
The first word for the Andoque is territorio.” Many of my male interlocutors made similar assertions in
different contexts throughout fieldwork.
However, the meaning of the notion of territory has changed over time, and with it, so has the notion of
territorial property. Since the creation or transformation of persons and things establishes a relation of
property between them and the creator/transformer, the Andoque attribute varying degrees of ownership
over different spaces based on the nurturing of relationships with their nonhuman inhabitants that affects
their behavior or by transforming the land through the establishment of gardens, which is the clearest
example of a person’s property.80 As stated in Chapter 3 and similar to other People of the Center
(Echeverri 2009; Karadimas 2013, 188), the clans, not the Andoque as a unified political group, were
considered the human owners of their territories prior to the rubber genocide. The notion of clan
ownership persists today through the implicit yet widely recognized boundaries that separate the areas
for hunting and fishing—particularly for commercial ends—of the different Andoque settlements, which
in most cases correspond to clans. Members of different clans assert their exclusive right to hunt or fish
in these areas by evoking their spiritual management there, achieved by ongoing interactions with the
site-persons. I observed various instances where individuals criticized or reprimanded members of other
settlements or clans for encroaching on their management areas, and it is said that before the genocide,
such trespassing could lead to violent conflicts or inter-clan wars. However, as explained by different
interlocutors, the ownership of a territory by one clan did not completely prevent members of other clans
from accessing it. Through marriage, a man would gain access to the lands of his wife’s clan, where he
could clear forest plots for gardens, like a Nɨpóde man who continues to tend to and expand the gardens
that he established near his Andoque father-in-law’s maloca during the period of uxorilocality. While
Andoque-speaking clans populated the land south of the Caquetá River, stretching from the mouth of
Spawning River in the west to the mouth of Green River in the east, these arrangements made it

80

For a similar Miraña perception, see Karadimas 2013, 184–85.

244

challenging to clearly demarcate clan and ethnic territories. Instead of fixed boundaries, territories were
differentiated through the relationship of their residents to topographical and hydrological sites, such as
rivers, rock formations, and waterfalls, where important mythical episodes occurred, and which are
inhabited by powerful nonhuman site-persons with whom those residents communicated. Many of these
sites were not possessed by Andoque-speaking clans in the conventional sense of exercising sovereignty
over them. Some sites lie outside the area inhabited by these clans, like Angusturas canyon upriver from
Spawning River or Córdoba cascade downriver from Green River. Other significant sites, such as the
Site of Tears, have never been settled by humans because they are believed to be occupied by nonhuman
mythical heroes.
While ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí conveys the notion of connectivity between human inhabitants and nonhuman co-dwellers
of the land, and the eventual restriction of foreign usufruct based on such connectivity, the concept of
territorio implies connectivity with another agent—namely, the State—through recognition. The
Andoque’s contemporary use of the term territorio cannot be divorced from the processes of Indigenous
political mobilization and State’s recognition of their lands and rights in recent decades, such that to
understand this use of the term we must also examine these processes. Roberto Pineda, who conducted
fieldwork with the Andoque in the early 1970s, shared with me in personal communications (January
2022) that during his time there, the concept territorio had not played a prominent role in their discourse,
even among the then Spanish-speaking youth who are now the group’s elders. He attributed the
emergence of this concept to Fisi’s two-year stay in Bogotá in the late 1970s when the future cacique
began mentioning “territory” to him, emphasizing more systematically the connections between its sites
and mythology. Pineda attributes this change to the influence of Andean political discourse to which Fisi
was exposed during that period. However, this does not imply that Andoque members did not previously
discuss their ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí (or the ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí of other beings) or link mythical tales with specific sites within the
land. Jon Landaburu, whom I also asked about the temporal depth of the concept’s use in Andoque
discourse, reminded me that the first words Yiñékɒ had addressed to him, followed by the myth of Sun
and Moon, had been: “I who knows, I will tell you about this place/land (ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí)” (See also Landaburu
1979, 279). Yet, the choice to translate this term most frequently into territorio when speaking Spanish,
instead of mundo or tierra (“land”), especially when interacting with State agents, aligns with the
centrality of the notion of “territory” in Indigenous, Afro-Colombian, and peasant struggles in Colombia
and Latin America since the 1980s. This demand for territory is more politicized than the previous one
for land (tierra), adding a decolonial flavor to these struggles (Beuf 2019; Escobar 1999, 225–26).
245

The new emphasis on territory in the discourse of Fisi and other members during the 1970s, as
mentioned by Pineda, may have also been motivated by the information imparted to them by Pineda and
Landaburu regarding the advocacy efforts by activists in Colombia—including missionary-linguist Paul
Witte—for state recognition of Indigenous land occupation and titling areas for exclusive Indigenous
land use (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm., October 2022). Pineda and Landaburu also actively campaigned
for this cause among Andoque members, collecting signatures and facilitating communication with State
authorities. Their efforts coincided with a fortunate turn of events when the Ministry of Agriculture
showed disinterest in the lands of the dissolved Araracuara Penal Colony, considering them too remote
from the site of Araracuara. This led to the declaration of the “Reserva Indígena Andoque de Aduche” in
1975 on the northern bank of the Caquetá River, alongside the Indigenous reserves Monochoa and
Puerto Zábalo-Los Monos (Useche Losada 1994, 174). While they were not yet recognized as legal
owners, this achievement provided the Andoque with a designated area under their disposal, which,
according to Landaburu (pers. comm., October 2022), brought them a sense of pride and increased their
sense of self-worth in relation to non-Indigenous people.
Paradoxically, the land north of the Caquetá River has never been part of the ancestral territory of any
Andoque clan, as they traditionally resided south of the Caquetá. As described in Chapter 4, the northern
bank served as a refuge zone for Andoque survivors of the genocide and became the center of rubber
extraction in following decades. Only a minority of the sites in that area carry Andoque toponyms,
which are attributed to Mnkoena’s territorial healing in the 1930s and are only loosely connected to
mythical narratives. However, today that land is also perceived as the Andoque’s ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí, and the elders
engage in dialogs and negotiations to maintain connectivity and ensure conviviality between its
nonhuman dwellers and the people living or operating there.
In 1988, this reserva was upgraded to resguardo—property that is inalienable, imprescriptible and
unmortgageable. During the same year, the land south of the Caquetá was also declared resguardo: the
pluri-ethnic Indigenous Reserve Predio Putumayo, inhabited by various People of the Center. This
reserve was established on the lands previously held by the Casa Arana and purchased by the Colombian
bank Caja Agraria in 1939 after the company’s de facto expulsion during the Colombo-Peruvian
conflict. This accomplishment was the result of a struggle by Indigenous leaders, priests, and other
activists between 1986 and 1988 to persuade the President of Colombia Virgilio Barco to acquire these
lands from the bank and give them back to the Indigenous peoples whose ancestral territories they were
(Echeverri 2022, 89–90; Pineda Camacho 2015, 37–44). As a result, each Indigenous people was
246

allocated a “Special Management Zone,” although these zones have never been formally demarcated,
with some Andoque members claiming that some of the lands falling within the Special Management
Zones of their Murui-Muina, Féénemɨna, and Nonuya neighbors are part of their own ancestral territory.
One of the actors leading this struggle was the Regional Indigenous Council of Middle Amazonas
(CRIMA), a collective representative organization established in 1985. CRIMA brings together the
Andoque, Murui-Muina, Nonuyna, and Féénemɨna groups of the Araracuara sector, with the primary
aim of protecting their constitutional and international rights and advocating for the establishment and
consolidation of Indigenous territorial entities. Additionally, CRIMA also plays a role in accessing
public and private funds and implementing projects for the benefit of these peoples. Interestingly,
CRIMA’s four founders were Murui-Muina inhabitants of Araracuara whose previous work in the Penal
Colony gave them greater familiarity with state agencies and their discourse (Audren 2017, 31).
Through this organization, Andoque people have been integrated into the Colombian Indigenous
movement and its political discourse, most notably Levy, who served as CRIMA president multiple
times during the organization’s rotational leadership between ethnic groups, actively participated in the
National Organization of the Indigenous Peoples of the Colombian Amazon (OPIAC) and ran for the
position of governor of the Department of Amazonas. The Andoque also undertook campaigns to secure
land rights independently of CRIMA. In 2012, when Parques sought to obtain the free, prior, and
informed consent of neighboring Indigenous peoples for the planned expansion of the Chiribiquete
National Natural Park, the Andoque conditionally consented in exchange for the active support of the
agency in the bureaucratic process of expanding the Andoque de Aduche Reserve to lands adjacent to
the expanded park (PNN 2018, 16). The reserve’s expansion was officially declared in December 2020.
The Andoque’s involvement in campaigns to secure land rights has been influenced by previous
territorial discourse and validation of land occupation through relationships with nonhuman entities but
it has also affected the ways in which people conceive of their land and perceive their position in
relation to these entities. On the one hand, similar to other Indigenous peoples in Amazonia and beyond
(e.g., S. Hugh-Jones 2010; Kennedy 2002; Urbina Rangel 1997), mythical narratives and their
connection to the landscape are utilized to pursue land claims and are perceived as useful to achieve this
end. In a private conversation, a young man shared that their Murui-Muina, Féénemɨna, and Nonuya
neighbors had received large portions of Andoque ancestral territory because his father, a leader who
was allegedly too shy to directly address state agents, entrusted the representatives of these peoples with
Andoque myths and teachings (to which he referred as “the Andoque word” [la palabra andoque]),
247

asking them to convey it to the non-Indigenous on his behalf. However, these non-Andoque participants
later presumably appropriated Andoque sites of origin to their respective Special Management Zones
within the Predio Putumayo Reserve by presenting these stories and teachings as their own. Whether the
events unfolded as described by the young man, it is evident that members view mythical narratives as a
legitimate basis for territorial claims. For this reason, some members explained to me that during the
territorial management workshop, which included also the participation of the Nɨpóde teacher of the
community school, they had not specified the name and location of different sites, because, according to
one elder, “the Uitoto, Nonuya, and Muinane, they all publish things that they have heard among the
Andoque, and then they say that these words are theirs; they can screw us through these very stories (nos
pueden joder con estas mismas historias).”
Furthermore, many interlocutors expressed their belief that their entitlement to land is reversible and
contingent upon maintaining proper relationships with the nonhuman co-dwellers of the territory
through ceremonial dances and other rituals. Fisi told me in one mambeadero session in October 2018:
“I remember when we went to La Chorrera and President Barco [Virgilio Barco Vargas] declared the [establishment
of the] Predio Putumayo Reserve, he told us: ‘This land is yours, respect it. Live like your ancestors, take care of the
land, heal (saneen) it.81 But today we can no longer fool anyone, we no longer live like our ancestors did, we don’t
have the same thinking. The only Indian (índio) here is X, he is the only here who thinks like an Indian, and he’s not
here [X was temporarily in Bogotá for a long period for medical treatment].”

Several months later, when I accompanied Levy to visit the members of the Atta Ant Clan to update
them on the outcome of their appeal for state tutelage regarding the REDD+ project Visión Amazonía
and to persuade them to support the REDD+ project he was leading with a private company (see Chapter
14), Levy talked with the participants about the financial opportunities associated with his carbon offset
deal. He explained that by entering such a deal, they could fund a project to revitalize the Andoque
language and provide language instruction to the youth. He emphasized that the ability to speak their
native language is crucial for effectively managing the territory through spiritual dialogues with its
masters. He further warned that if they were unable to communicate with the nonhuman entities through
their native language, it could potentially lead to the revocation of the reserve declaration by the state.
While it is possible that this statement does not reflect Levy’s personal understanding of Colombian
laws concerning Indigenous reserves and was used as a persuasive argument, it was nevertheless

81

See this quote from the president’s speech in Pineda Camacho 2014, 38.

248

grounded in the assumption that his interlocutors, who ranged in age from 30 to 80 years old, held
similar convictions. The assumption that non-Indigenous powerholders and state agents share animist
views regarding the impact of ceremonial dances and rituals on the physical state of the territory was
expressed in various contexts. During the territorial management workshop, for instance, when Andoque
members were discussing their ecological calendar, Fisi expressed his objection to specifying which
ceremonial dance should be held in each season. He explained: “I don’t want the Whites coming to me
[in this or that period], saying ‘you’re a maloquero, so here, hold a dance!’” However, while the reversal
of Indigenous land titling is an unfortunate yet plausible scenario in a volatile region during a period of
ecological, economic, and political uncertainties, it can be assumed that if such reversal were to occur,
state agencies would likely rely on more naturalist criteria as grounds. Such criteria may be
unsustainable land use by Indigenous landholders or viewing language and ceremonies primarily as
reflections of ethnic identity rather than tools for spiritual territorial management. Nevertheless, in the
eyes of many members, the connectivity between the human and nonhuman components of the territory
serves as the basis for the connectivity with the state, expressed in the form of the latter’s recognition of
Indigenous territorial occupation and property rights over the land and its resources.
On the other hand, this recognition by the state, as well as the Andoque’s attempt to acquire or maintain
it, modifies their discourse regarding territory and reflects a new relationship to the land. This new
relationship demonstrates the internalization of Euro-American definitions of territory as an area of
exclusive ownership and usufruct rights by a group of people, in this case, the Indigenous people or
language group rather than clans. This group maintains a one-to-one relationship to the territory, which
shares contiguous borders with other similar (Indigenous) territories, as has been observed among North
American natives subsequent to land titling (Nadasdy 2012; Thom 2014). The notion of usufruct rights,
where the human proprietors can utilize the nonhuman elements within their property, kept resurfacing
during the territorial management workshop, as Andoque participants expressed concerns about
potential future restrictions on land use by state agencies or their dictations to adhere to a low ecological
footprint lifestyle in the name of an assumed primordial ancestral tradition. In order to assert traditional
human utilization of the land and superiority over its nonhuman co-dwellers, participants evoked the
historical ecological impact exerted by the Andoque prior to the genocide, when the Indigenous
population was significantly larger. They pointed to the remnants of past gardens evident in the vast
expanses of secondary forest (rasrtojo; tanntaǵ, literally “abandoned place”) that now cover their
ancestral territory. Nestor, for example, said:
249

“Let’s look at the land use. How they [our ancestors] used it and where? Land was used throughout the entire territory,
wherever it could be used, and people only respected the hills, in respect of the spirituality of the beings that created
them. So they respected the cananguchal[es] (inundated site[s] with mauritia palms), the area around the lake[s], but
everywhere else, they worked [there]. They never took care of the forest. Because we walk around the entire territory
and see that it is all pure rastrojo[s], you don’t see primary forest [monte firme] there, just pure cashew [trees], guacuri
[umari trees]. Only at the headwaters, next to the stream sources do you find primary forest, and along the stream
banks. They cared of the water, [we know that] because we see they didn’t fell trees there.”

The logic of a one-to-one relation between the language group and the territory is reflected in the
automatic subsumption of the territories of extinct Andoque clans under a broader pan-Andoque
territory. Grounding land claims in Western style cartography promotes a perception of territorial
boundaries from an aerial perspective, resulting in maps that contain borders based on straight aerial
lines, detached from the engaged experience with the forest environment or the intricacies of inter-clan
and inter-ethnic matrimonial land access (cf. Thom 2009; Tselouiko 2015). During an internal assembly
to discuss activities for the demarcation of borders with the Féénemina and Murui-Muina inhabitants of
the Monochoa Reserve north of the Caquetá, one elder broached the problem of land encroachment in
the territory south of the Caquetá. He warned that a family of descendants from the Andoque Toad clan,
residing in La Chorrera since the displacements of the genocide period, had settled around the
headwaters of Drawing River with the objective of reclaiming their clan’s ancestral lands. The other
participants agreed that this must be prevented, based on an implicit identification between the Andoque
territory and their reserves as the only legitimate representative political bodies for the Andoque people,
wherein individuals descended from Andoque clans can only access the reserve territory solely as
reserve members.
The idea that Indigenous territories should be contiguous and mutually exclusive became more salient in
light of carbon projects, where forest carbon in each territory must be quantified to enable the issuance
of carbon credits and prevent double counting. During my fieldwork, as news spread about Levy and his
non-Indigenous business associates in the company Yauto developing a carbon offset project on the
territories owned by the peoples represented by CRIMA that would encompass reserves on both sides of
the Caquetá, some interlocutors raised concerns over the need to officially clarify the internal ethnic
borders between the “Special Management Zones” of the Predio-Putumayo Reserve. These interlocutors
argued that large portions of land currently occupied by neighboring Murui-Muina, Nonuya and
Féénemɨna communities were actually part of the Andoque ancestral territory, which means that they
would benefit financially from forest carbon stocks belonging to the Andoque. When Yauto’s project
250

finally commenced in October 2022, following consultations with Andoque members but not those of
the Murui-Muina and Féénemɨna communities upstream from Araracuara, the company recognized the
area settled by the latter as part of the Andoque’s “Special Management Zone,” allocating the Andoque
the carbon credits corresponding to that area. Due to objections and legal actions taken by the MuruiMuina and Féénemɨna, the company and the Andoque acknowledged a territorial overlap and committed
to engaging in dialogue between the community representatives to establish a mutually agreed upon
method of benefit distribution (Bermudez Lievano 2023).
This new economic arrangement has also influenced the Andoque’s relations with sites controlled by
powerful and dangerous spirits. During my visit in July-August 2021, when private carbon offset
projects were already taking shape in the Caquetá-Putumayo region, the inhabitants of the PredioPutumayo Reserve who reside closer to the Putumayo River and were negotiating their own carbon deal,
convened an assembly of all the communities of this multi-ethnic reserve in La Chorrera to clarify their
internal borders. Upon their return to the Aduche reserve, the Andoque delegates reported a land dispute
with the Bora, who claimed ownership to Site of Tears. Although many mythical narratives are set in
this site and they have been continuously engaging in spiritual dialogue from their mambeaderos with
the spirits living there for safety and prosperity, no Andoque clan has ever settled on the site itself.
However, as part of the new economic arrangement where forest elements are perceived as resources
and generate profit without being physically extracted and risking relations with the spirits, Andoque
members began to view Site of Tears in terms of actual possession granting them exclusive usufruct.
The consideration of the territory as the exclusive possession of human beings in certain contexts and its
elements as object to be utilized by them, can be classified as “naturalist,” in contrast with the animist
perspective expressed in other contexts, where the land is perceived as possessed by various owners,
both human and nonhuman. As will be explored in Chapter 13, the Andoque exhibit a fluctuation
between treating the nonhuman co-dwellers of their land as inanimate resources in some contexts and
recognizing them as social and political agents in others. This fluctuation may reflect what Paul Nadasdy
(2021) terms “ontological indeterminacy,” borrowing the concept of indeterminacy from physics to
critique the multiple-world thesis, which assumes that different ontologies represent different realities
(see below). Indeterminacy denotes the incompatibility of experimental apparatuses that produce
different phenomena of the same but indeterminate reality, just as light can be both a wave and a
particle, depending on how it is measured. In Nadasdy’s shift from ontology to phenomenology,
nonhuman entities, such as animals, plants, and land, can be either animate or inanimate beings, either
251

social partners or natural resources, depending on the way we engage with them. This indeterminacy can
occur both at the inter-social level—when two societies differ regarding the way they perceive a given
thing—or at the individual level, as the same person can perceive a given thing as a subject or an object,
depending on context. In Nadasdy’s terms, territory is an indeterminate object for the Andoque, and can
be both the property of some humans who dispose of its nonhuman components as resources and the
connectivity between multiple classes of beings and owners. Although I do not exclude the presence of
such ontological indeterminacy in the Andoque case, I propose to interpret it as inherent to the
asymmetrical version of animism to which the Andoque subscribe, and which also becomes manifest in
their conception of territory.
Animist Asymmetries
To discuss Andoque asymmetrical animism in the context of their territorial conception and thoroughly
grapple with its dimensions of power, domination, and human superiority, it is necessary to revisit the
multiplicity of ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí territories/worlds in Andoque cosmology and draw comparisons with Viveiros de
Castro’s (1998) interlinked and predominantly symmetrical concepts of multinaturalism and
perspectivism.
As discussed in this dissertation’s introduction, Viveiros de Castro’s concepts of perspectivism and
multinaturalism are based on the common Amerindian premise that nonhuman beings possess
subjectivity commensurate with that of other species and essentially human, although species differ from
each other in their bodily forms. Every species’ body, in turn, is understood as a sign of its affects,
dispositions or capacities, “which render the body of every species unique: what it eats, how it
communicates, where it lives, whether it is gregarious or solitary, and so forth” (ibid, 478). In other
words, the body of every being is a manifestation of its relations with the various persons (and bodies) in
its environment, particularly predatory relations, as “the central dimensions, possibly even the
fundamental dimension, of perspectival inversions refers to the relative and relational statuses of
predator and prey” (ibid, 471). Although the core of ethnographic data that Viveiros de Castro’s
mobilizes for his argument concerned Indigenous conceptions of ontological translations across species
boundaries, his conceptualization expanded to the intra-human domain with the advocacy for
anthropologists to prioritize the method of translation, which accentuates the differences between the
presumably incommensurate worlds occupied by themselves and their informants (2004). This
perspectival methodology served as a theoretical starting point for proponents of the multiple-world

252

thesis. Arguing for a one-to-one relationship between people and worlds or reality, these authors assert
that different peoples inhabit distinct worlds, which may be incommensurable, particularly in the case of
Indigenous versus non-Indigenous collectives (Blaser 2009; de la Cadena 2010).
While Viveiros de Castro equates the concept of world with species-specific ontologies, the Andoque do
not consider that each species inhabits its own ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí. Similar to the Miraña (Karadimas 2005b, 293),
they classify animal worlds based on their predatory positions, such as the worlds of game animals,
ocelot stars, and birds, indicating the significance of predatory relational positions in perspectival
inversions. However, predation is not the sole principle distinguishing one world from another. As we
have observed, the distinguishing factor between worlds is their mythic origins, which determine the
prevailing relationships among their inhabitants and the domains of their owners. The division of human
beings, who typically do not prey on each other, into different worlds is based on the relational
perspective projected by each human group onto the beings in their environment, or, in other words,
how they connect with them. These humans, like the nonhumans in their worlds, are believed to have
different “origins” that shape their forms and patterns of connectivity with the other beings in their
respective worlds.
However, the aspect in relation to which the Andoque’s conception of ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí diverges most
significantly from Viveiros de Castro’s perspectivism-multinaturalism nexus is the territorial aspect,
where life in a specific land emerges as a condition to achieving a full human status. According to my
interlocutors’ statements, it is only on one’s land, where one knows the names of the owner-persons,
their domains and how to communicate with them, that one can ensure one’s own human status by
protecting oneself from predation by others who try to undermine one’s humanity. The myth of the pipeblower Uiknñemn exemplifies the close connection between a person’s human status and the land. In
this myth (M7, see Appendix 1), the hero’s mother takes him as a newborn baby to sip water from
different streams within the ancestral land—Speaking River, Sitting River, Crawling River, Standing
River, Walking River, Running River, and finally, Dancing Rod River (Ḭknsé)—to help the baby grow
quickly and be healthy.82 When I asked for further clarification about the different rivers, José*, the
narrator of the myth, said that the specific names and order of most of the streams are not crucial, and a
narrator can create any river name granted that it describes a stage of a child’s development. However,
he emphasized that the last stream on the list must be Dancing Rod River because it is through

82

This episode precedes the events narrated in a shorter version of this myth found in Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 133–41.

253

participating in ceremonial dances with a rod that a person truly becomes human. Therefore, while a
person may perceive themselves as human in general, they are fully human only within a space where
they can engage in the distinctively human cultural practice of ceremonial dance. This practice, as we
will explore in Chapter 11, epitomizes the acting upon and even controlling the interconnectedness of a
specific world. In other words, in the Andoque’s perspectivism, world and ontology are not
synonymous. Worlds should be understood as places or dimensions where ontologies are stabilized,
although these worlds may not necessarily materialize in the physical or geographical sense.83 While
game animals may see themselves as human in all environments, it is specifically within the Animals
World, encompassing various sites such as saltlicks, forest clearings, and particularly lakes and their
surroundings (which are strictly avoided for hunting or visiting), where they express their humanity to
its fullest extent. Animals are fully human in those spaces because they hold there their own ceremonial
dances to exert greater control over their destiny and ensure their reproduction.
Contrary to the assumption made by proponents of the multiple-world thesis that each individual
belongs exclusively to a particular world or reality, the Andoque’s description of overlaps between
certain worlds indicate the multiple origins of certain beings, and their corresponding ability to adhere to
multiple connectivity logics. For instance, the overlaps between the Whites World and the Worlds of the
River Source and River Mouth imply that Whites can behave based on either the predatory and
destructive nature associated with the river source, or the exchange and trading orientation linked to the
river mouth. Conversely, when one territory/world encompasses another, it conveys a more
asymmetrical logic.
As Karadimas (2013) argues for the Miraña people, the extent of the Andoque’s ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí is not
determined by that which lays outside it, as would be the case in a Western concept of territory as a
delimited space. Instead, it is defined by the center’s capacity to maintain relationships with both human
and nonhuman beings residing within it—essentially, its ability to foster connections with other centers.
Therefore, when one world encompasses another, it signifies the encompassment of one world’s origin
by another. Subsequently, the inhabitants of the former possess the ability to exert dominance over their
relationships with the inhabitants of the latter, drawing upon their familiarity with these origin myths.
This dynamic is observed in the Andoque World and the Animals World, where through ceremonial

Cf. Descola’s concept of “worlding” as “stabilization of certain things of what happens to us” (2014, 272), to which I
would add: “a stabilization of ourselves,” i.e., of the stabilizing person.
83

254

dances, the human inhabitants of the Andoque world can influence and control their interactions with the
inhabitants of the Animal World. In contrast, while the inhabitants of the Animal World perceive
themselves as humans, they lack this capability.
To reflect this asymmetry, the workshop participants dictated the following phrase to me in the last day,
to include it immediately after the description of the ancestral territory’s boundaries:
“The first word of ordering given by the Creator was: this Land of Life is for you, the People of the Axe, to be born
and live on it, use it and reproduce, under the condition that you take care of the forest and the beings living in it,
otherwise the owners of nature, whom he left in charge of the sites of origin, will punish you.”

During a mambeadero session at his maloca a few evenings later, Fisi returned to the definition of
“territory” and the position the Creator assigned to human beings within it:
Fisi: The word pḭiñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí, the Whites don’t understand. They think that there, there is the life of the forest [that this
word alludes to the life of the forest]. Yes, life is there, the crops (cosecha) are there, from this we live. This does not
mean that we are not going to work there, that we cannot excavate [for clay] to prepare pots, that we cannot excavate
to get fire [gold? See Chapter 13], or the axe.
Eliran: So pḭiñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí has many meanings?
Fisi: Many! Look, when we say kahaJ́ bɵñe yatii, it means “he did it for us,” so we could live, so we could work, so
we could fish to eat, the animals he made for us to eat, fish he made for us to eat… But not to finish them all, not to
finish with the forest.”

Based on the infrequent and inconsistent use of “the Creator” (kahaǵtı̋ o) in Andoque mythology and
overall discourse, in contrast to other figures and deities, I suggest that we should not take these
statements at face value as reflecting an existing territorial asymmetry. Instead, considering our previous
discussion in Chapter 2 on the usage of the term “the Creator” by a given speaker to establish or justify
situations that are favorable to them, I suggest that we consider the evocation of “the Creator” as a
cosmopolitical tool to deliberately produce the desired territorial asymmetry. When I asked Fisi during
another conversation to clarify the statements that I had collected from him and other interlocutors
between the owner-persons of the land and those of animals, he asserted: “The owner of the land is only
one, the Creator, and it is to him that a person makes ḭtaséa [offerings] in a dance. Egret of the Center
represents him for us.” Being kahaǵtı̋ o—“that which was created for us”—the Creator is of the same
kind as ḭsu yahaǵtı̋ o, “those who were created for the animal(s),” or the owner-persons overseeing the
animals originated and living in their domains. The Creator is thus a being with an open-ended identity,
who protects the person invoking them, similar to how the animals’ owner-persons protect their own

255

personnel. At the same time, the Creator is far superior to any master of a site and of animals because he
is tiɵi, “[he] who made everything,” and is associated with the omniscient Sḭ́ di through the figure of
Doékositoɵ (see Chapter 2). The use of the term kahaǵtı̋ ɵ represents the attempt of a given individual to
tap into this potent defense and assistance through that individual’s specific origin stories. In relation to
the concept of territory, it seems that the Creator does not embody a specific entity with a fixed identity
or even a loosely defined set of attributes, whose first word of cosmic ordering was to allow the
Andoque to live, use, and reproduce on the ancestral land. Instead, the Creator should be seen as a figure
invoked whenever the Andoque wish to exert their power over the land, exploiting or harvesting animals
and plants without incurring repercussions from them and their owner-persons. This is done alongside
other techniques of mastery over nonhuman beings and to establish asymmetry in interactions with
them, which will be explored in the following chapters.
Anthropologists have observed the interconnectedness between the notions of a Creator god and those
considering concessions made to humans to utilize his creation or prey on the nonhuman beings
inhabiting the creation among Amazonian peoples as near as the Murui-Muina (García 2018, 370–74)
and as far as the Warí (Vilaça 2009; 2016). As discussed in earlier chapters, ethnographers studying the
People of the Center often interpret this interconnectedness through a moral lens, thereby attributing the
enmity of animals toward human beings to the preference given to the latter by the Creator, which, in
turn, stems from the animals’ failure to comply with the Creator’s rules (García 2018, 372–73; Griffiths
1998, 57–58; Londoño Sulkin 2005, 13). The Andoque data allow us to both distance this Indigenous
people from such generalizations and to question the exclusivity of the moral perspective in analyzing
neighboring groups. The limited presence of this figure in Andoque mythology and its meaning once it
is juxtaposed with the owner-persons of animals indicate that for this people, the Creator is not simply a
mythological figure who established human superiority over nonhumans. Instead, it functions as a figure
of speech to articulate and cultivate this superiority, seeking to prevent symmetry in the generalized
predation within the land and ensuring the encompassment of the Animals World and other worlds of
nonhumans or potentially hostile beings by the Andoque’s pḭiñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí. The invocation of the Creator
emphasizes that every form of connectivity, including that of ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí, is perceived from the perspective
of a specific being who seeks to assert their dominance and encompass competing perspectives within it.
Finally, it is important to note that the territory is not homogenous in relation of its susceptibility to
being dominated by human beings or recognizing their superior position. This can be inferred from
people’s explanations of the two kinds of proto-human beings who named the streams and other sites in
256

different parts of the territory: the Shadows (Ká’hɵi síɵ́hɵ) and the Piercers (Yɒ’nnkn). The Shadows
inhabited the inland areas around Site of Tears, away from the main rivers, and gave names to the
smaller streams and sites in those regions. By contrast, the Piercers lived in the part of the territory
bordering the Caquetá River and named the streams flowing into the Caquetá and the sites along them.
People tend to speak more about the Piercers, likely because they currently inhabit the same area as
these quasi-mythical beings, where the latter left visible traces in the form of petroglyphs, showcasing
their extraordinary ability to pierce hard materials like stone or wood with their bare hands. Another
possible explanation may be the association between the Piercers and significant feats that benefit
people today, such as “healing” the territory by stripping various nonhuman beings—beings which they
would subsequently depict in their petroglyphs—of the primordial forces they possessed in the past, and
discovering the stone axes linked to productivity and economic autonomy. The Piercers were more
similar to nowadays humans than the Shadow People, and the animals into which they transformed—
predominantly white lipped-peccaries—resemble human groups in both organization and ferocity. The
Shadows, on the other hand, transformed into small and mostly harmless animals like opossums or
crickets, making it tempting to associate them with Shadow Egg, who headed such small animals when
he was the maloquero of these “people” in the center. The Shadows did not leave visible marks on the
landscape, and in the stories about them, referred to as “jokes” (chiste), and which are neither serious
like the “Captaincy Stories” nor dangerous like the “Animal Stories,” they engage in nonsensical
actions. In a joke-story recounted to me by several interlocutors and recorded by Landaburu and Pineda
(1984, 217–24), the Shadows attempt to capture the moon, mistaking its reflection (ká’hɵi) in the water
for the celestial body itself. The Shadows do not directly impact reality but rather act upon its images,
much like how a shadow projected from a person or object depends on them without altering their state.
Similarly, the Shadows did not modify or intervene in the state of persons and things as the Piercers did,
who could pass through them, creating or destroying them.
Based on the fact that the Piercers are said to have operated in an area that the Andoque approached only
in relatively recent times, while the Shadows lived where Andoque clans resided in the more distant
past, I suggest that the narratives about the Piercers were developed during the expansion or movement
of Andoque clans towards the Caquetá. These narratives reflect the Andoque’s increasing engagement in
trade with non-Indigenous merchants, allowing them to exert greater control over their territory and
assert superiority over its nonhuman co-dwellers. At the same period, the sites inland, away from the

257

Caquetá River, continued to bear names given by weaker beings who could not shape the territory in the
same manner.
This hypothesis provides another example of how the Andoque’s notions of human domination over the
land and its nonhuman co-dwellers not only coexists with their animist ontology but also stem from it,
drawing upon its inherent tendency for asymmetry while further deepening this inclination. The
discussion in this chapter regarding the agents operating within the ancestral territory, encompassing
both human and nonhuman entities, both Andoque clans and non-Indigenous people, as well as the
persistent pursuit of asymmetry that permeates their interactions, will guide us in our exploration of the
relationships between human and nonhuman centers in the subsequent chapters, as well as the dynamics
between the Andoque center and the non-Indigenous “river mouth” in Part IV.

258

Chapter 9. Power in Human-Nonhuman Relations
Having explored, in the preceding chapter, the concept of ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí, and analyzed, in Parts I and II, the
notion of center and its reliance on appropriated power from the river source, this chapter addresses the
following question: How is power exercised in relationships between the human and nonhuman centers
that constitute ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí? The chapter offers a panoramic view of these relationships, demonstrating how
symmetric schemes of predation turn into asymmetric relations of familiarization and mastery. After
examining predation by humans in the form of hunting and fishing, we will discuss how nonhumans
prey on humans and transform them into their kin through illnesses, accidents, and other ailments. We
will then explore how people counter such attempts of familiarizing predation by nonhumans, and how
they form mastery relations that enable them to align the powers of nonhuman pets to their own for
various shamanic purposes, particularly sorcery and healing. An important dimension of domination
explored here is one’s ability to incorporate others into one’s reality, a key version of which in the
Amazonian context is familiarization. Throughout the chapter, I examine how various faculties and
actions such as odors, sexual self-restraint, symbolization, and consciousness, contribute to this
incorporation or assist in resisting it, thus elucidating some nuances of the native notion of power.
Additionally, I demonstrate how the hierarchical version of their animism aids the Andoque in managing
perilous interactions with nonhumans. They achieve this by manipulating the agency of game animals
and transforming homosubstitutive-cannibalistic exchanges into heterosubstitutive ones involving
vegetal substances.
Predation by Humans
As in other parts of Amazonia, the Andoque’s protein intake depends on seasonally varying ratios
between hunting and fishing. Most Andoque members, except for the Sun Clan, state that their pregenocide ancestors, who lived in the hinterland away from the main rivers, mainly consumed tinamou,
curassow and guan (Cracidae family), paca (Cuniculus paca), acouchi (Myoprocta pratti), and agouti
(Dasyprocta sp.), along with small stream fish. Conversely, larger game, like white-lipped peccary
(Tayassu pecari), collared peccary (Dicotyles tajacu), tapir (Tapirus terrestris), deer (Mazama sp.),
armadillo (Dasypus kappleri), and monkeys (especially the woolly monkey [Lagothrix lagothrica]),
were hunted less frequently, primarily for ceremonial dances. While in pre-genocide times the Andoque
used various techniques to hunt land animals, from blowpipes with curare-dipped darts and (scarce)
rifles, to dogs, different traps, burrow smoking, and collective clubbing (battue), rifles are currently the

259

most widely employed technique, alongside occasional hunting with dogs, and trapping rodents in the
garden. Since rifle ammunition costs COP$8,000-10,000 (roughly €1.5-2) per bullet in Puerto Santander,
it is more cost-effective to hunt larger game (paca and larger), than small rodents and birds, especially
since larger game is often sold to settlers in the village.84
Another set of techniques essential for hunting birds and mammals relate to what Rane Willerslev terms
“mimetic empathy,” which refers to the hunter’s ability to imagine himself in the game animal’s
position, reproducing the animal’s perspective (2007, 106–10). These techniques vary from tracing
game through footprints, bitten fruits, and other physical signs, to erotic and emotional strategies,
whereby hunters relate to animals as persons, imitating the voices of females in heat or young in distress
to draw male or parent animals within shooting range or to make them freeze for the moment required to
hit them.85 This seduction works both ways and terrestrial animals and their owner-persons employ the
same stratagems to prey on humans, as we will see below. The appropriative dimension of hunting and
fishing, whereby external beings of an affinal nature are familiarized (Fausto 1999; 2007a), and their
material essence becomes part of the hunter’s essence, and, by extension, the essence of the human
group, is expressed through the reference to game as ósía: “that which is mine,” similar to how one’s
body (osí) is what one owns, their real essence (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm., October 2022; cf. Stolze
Lima 1996, 38). The verb ḭsía is normally used only to refer to faunal victims, including fish, while
killing both people and animals is also denoted through the root bu’, which literally means “destroy, tear
down, uproot,” and can also be employed in relation to plants and inanimate things. The possibility of
communication with terrestrial and aviary game also manifests in people’s avoidance of using such
explicit terms before the animal is actually killed, due to these animals and their owner-persons’ ability
to hear people’s intentions from a distance. Therefore, Andoque hunters hide such intentions, telling
others that they are simply “going wandering” (andar; yo̰nfɵi), a practice evidenced in other Amazonian
societies (e.g., Walker 2013, 171–72).

For more information on the Andoque and their Murui-Muina neighbors’ hunting techniques, see García 2018, 254–56,
and Pineda Camacho 1982, 40–43. See the latter source (pp. 35–38) also for information on the gathering of smaller fauna,
such as frogs and larvae, which I do not discuss here.

hunter aims to contribute to forest animals’ reproduction by sexually arousing them during hunting expedition (ibid, 222).
This attitude seems to be related to the Tukanoan inclination toward reciprocal affinal exchange with animals, as opposed to
the People of the Center’s tendencies toward generalized predation.
