Since fish do not normally share the space with humans, oblique references to killing are less strictly
observed before fishing. This activity provides the larger part of Andoque members’ protein intake,
which consists of fish such as the pintadillo catfish (Pseudoplatystoma sp.) and smaller species, such as
the ray finned Anostomidae (homima), the sábalo and sabaleta (both are Brycon sp.), etc. These fish are
caught in Macaw River and its affluents, and sometimes the Caquetá, using canes and hooks, nets,
harpoons, static lures in flooded areas in the wet season, and occasionally stream poisoning with
barbasco plants in the dry season. Larger fish from the Caquetá, such as the catfish Brachyplatystoma
filamentosum, Brachyplatystoma flavicans, and Phractocephalus hemiliopterus, are caught with nets,
longlines, and harpoons, but while they are sometimes consumed by the Andoque, they are more often
sold to fish merchants who sell them in Bogotá.86 Non-shamanic communication with fish and other
aquatic animals such as river turtles for predatory purposes is restricted to luring them through baits of
fruits or other fish due to their aquatic habitat. Andoque members’ preference for small fish over big
ones, and especially game animals (birds and mammals), owes in part to the relative abundance of fish,
which makes fishing a more reliable source of food than hunting. It is rare for a man to return from
fishing completely empty-handed, which is not the case for hunting, where it is more common (resulting
in the hunter’s resort to fishing on his way back home). However, this preference is also related to the
Andoque’s perception of hierarchy among nonhuman beings and the graded agency that allows each
species to prey on humans, as I will explain below.
The Ambivalence of Predation
Animals are regarded as dangerous, inimical beings. Tañe explained to me once as we were getting
ready for a forest excursion: “Walking in the forest is no game. You must be fierce as you go [andar con
rabia], and when you see an animal, you must kill it; kill it and eat it, so that other animals will be
afraid.”87 Animals are “deviators,” yoíkóɵ, in that they cause people to lose their minds and engage in
socially unacceptable behavior—a “false” behavior, as opposed to a “proper” (ḭdɨ) human one—and
become something (or somebody) they should not be, thereby preventing them from realizing their
human potential culminating in the social reproduction of the human group. The deviation of humans
from their core (dɨ) by nonhumans can take different forms, from confusion and disorientation while
hunting to undesired effects of consuming game to more proactively predatory actions. These actions by

86
87

For more information on fishing in the Caquetá, see Rodríguez Fernández 1991.
Cf. people’s avoidance to consume animals that approach a settlement mentioned below.

261

animals are seen as expressions of the brujería (“sorcery”) of animals and their guardian spirits—or, in
Andoque, their tne’túi—their auxiliary spirit depending on connection with Sı̰ ́di. While these actions are
sometimes attributed to animals’ anger and jealousy of humans whose creation as speaking beings
stripped the former of the ability to speak, in other times they are explained as analogous to human’s
engagement in hunting. They are seen as animals’ ways to defend themselves from predation, take
revenge for such predation, and guarantee the reproduction of their own species by appropriating others
(namely, humans) and integrating them into their society, even in cases where animals’ bodies are
consumed by humans. Like affinal alliance, predation is symmetrical, and the hunter or eater who
wishes to incorporate the game into their body and society runs the risk of being controlled by the game
and incorporated into its society (Fausto 2007a, 505–6)—hence the importance of introducing
asymmetries by “familiarizing predation.” In what follows we explore animals’ strategies to oppose and
invert predation, starting with sabotaging hunting expeditions.
Confusion while hunting can cause hunters to mistake their human companions for the game they are
looking for, leading them to shoot them instead of the desired target. Disorientation can occur when a
hunter becomes too focused on a specific animal, such as a monkey fleeing in the canopy, and forgets to
monitor the location of the sun, which is usually used as a reference point in the forest. Here mythology
proposes edifying precedents, in the form of the two Andoque variations along the vertical axis of
predation on the figure of a powerful father-in-law unwilling to give his daughter away: Shadow Egg
and Sun. As we have seen in several myths (M1; M3; M14), and based on game animals’ strategy to use
camouflage to avoid predation, Shadow Egg conceals his people from predation by the son-in-law, who
wishes to use them as game or raw materials, by tricking him into thinking they are human. Shadow Egg
overcomes his sons-in-law by transforming them into “useless” beings (yoóka ibañe nyatii) who are “out
of order” (yoó) in the double sense of the phrase, as they both act outside the norm, and do not achieve
the desired results. The competition over knowledge and perception between Shadow Egg and his sonsin-law is expressed through the verb dú’ha, which can mean both dominating and mocking someone
(Andoque Andoque and Landaburu, forthcoming), and which my interlocutors interpret in this context
also as avoiding falling into their trap. In contrast, Sun preys on his sons-in-laws overtly (e.g., M15;
M6). When walking in the forest, hunters should follow the example of this ultimate predator rather than
Shadow Egg’s ruses. In M3 and M1, the egret figures dominate Shadow Egg and his daughter by not
regarding the various entities they encounter in the woods as real humans, but as raw materials. This

262

domination involves one’s capacity to assume a predatory stance vis-à-vis the other and incorporate
them into one’s reality, as opposed to being deceived by the other and incorporated into their reality.
However, a person who overhunts is more likely to become confused or lost while hunting, and may
even encounter extraordinary phenomena, such as animals that do not die after being shot, speaking
animals (a man who had hunted too many white-lipped peccaries reported hearing a peccary telling him
“Do not bother me anymore”), or an animal ceremonial dance—an incident Tañe related to me in the
first person. According to him, one night some thirty years ago, during a period when he was hunting
tapirs in large numbers in the saltlick near Tar Waterfall to send money to his son studying in Leticia, he
shot an extremely large, white-eyed tapir (“like a horse”) that was not disturbed by the gunshot.
Immediately after, he started hearing people talk around him—all those who have been “enchanted” (se
encantaron) in previous generations, transforming into nonhuman spirits and remaining there. He
refrained from looking at them, but rather ran away, terrified by the tapir diablo. Three years later, he
returned there at night, climbed a high hunting post, and waited for a tapir when he suddenly heard
people heavily stomping beneath him, but did not see anything. Upon descending from his post, a
terrible smell hit him. “The devil is going to change my body (cambiar el cuerpo) with this smell,” he
told himself. Breathing with his flashlight attached to his nostrils to avoid that smell, he escaped the
saltlick without looking at the place from which the voices were coming, because “The tapirs wanted to
change my sight (cambiar la vista).” The next morning, he saw tapir footprints at the saltlick and
realized that he had indeed witnessed a tapir ceremonial dance. From then on, he cut down on his
hunting activity. Such apparitions are usually taken as warnings to the hunter before the animals and
their owner-persons take more destructive measures to prey on him and on his family members,
familiarizing them by aligning their bodies and perspectives with those of nonhumans. However, they
are also ḭtannéso (“[transformation into] something of bones”), which, as discussed in Chapter 7,
represents an existing state of affairs, in this case—the already altered state of the hunter. The hunter’s
ability to understand animal speech and perceive their dances is an indication that he is drifting away
from the human society and is on his way to assimilate to the animal’s society, that he is being
transformed (ti) into an animal.
The other actions undertaken by animals to deviate people from their human core, such as illnesses,
madness, death, accidents, conflicts, and other afflictions, represent further extents of familiarization by
nonhumans, which I will examine below. However, before delving into these actions, it is crucial to
consider M18, which vividly portrays the continuity between people’s predation on animals and
263

animals’ familiarization of humans. This myth, as detailed in Appendix 1, serves as a cautionary tale on
the dangers of excessive hunting in everyday situations and is one of the stories on which the Head
ceremonial dance draws. The myth recounts how the affinal relatives of a dance organizer undertook a
hunting expedition for white-lipped peccaries prior to the dance. They captured an entire herd with a big
net, killed them, ate some, and smoked the rest, except for one severed head. A hunter, preferring to eat
a tinamou, observed from a distance an old man named Ka’ákɵpidɨ who was using his own eyes as a
substitute for fibers to weave a basket, and decided to spend the night on a tall tree branch. At night, he
watched the old man remove his fellow hunters’ eyes and throw them into the basket. When the men
woke up, the blind hunters followed the survivor to the celebratory maloca, where they received tobacco
paste, mambe, and manicuera, and then continued back into the forest. They gradually transformed into
peccaries through vegetal materials that their captain attached to their bodies or that became stuck to
them during their journey in the forest and upriver. Their transformation was completed when, upon
reaching Faukuyadeefɵ (Forest of “Faukuya,” a bird of the Tyrannidae family; also planet Jupiter
[Andoque Andoque and Landaburu, forthcoming]), the hero Usiñémn attached grape-like (unidentified)
piyɒdɨkni fruits to their eye sockets, endowing them with new eyes.
Fisi, who told me the version summarized here, did not clarify whether the herd captain is the survivor
who preferred tinamou over peccary and climbed a tree or the raw peccary head. It may, in fact, be a
case of dual captaincy, as the two seem to be transformations of each other, as hinted by another version,
narrated to me by Raquel (8/7/19)—who learned it, in turn, from Hóñoéna̰i (“A beautiful Spix’s Guan
pet”; Alejandro, a genocide survivor). In this version, one of the hunters was scolded by his fellows at
the beginning of the story for scaring away the peccaries by shooting at them with a blowpipe, a useful
weapon for hunting monkeys and birds (such as the tinamou) but useless for large game, including
peccaries. “They’re angry with me because they don’t know that the peccaries will never be finished,”
he thought and left the hunters’ group, joined the fleeing herd (supposedly under a peccary guise), and
led it back to where he had been scolded by his fellows. At night, he weaved a net (dʉʉ́kn) from
chambira leaves (tɵkóñe; Astrocaryum chambira) by tying the chambira fibers to the sleeping peccaries’
legs, and then called the other people to kill them, which they happily did. Another man who went to
take a bath at dusk saw the elder Ka’ákɵpidɨ weaving a basket, and at night he saw him collecting the
other hunters’ eyes in it. Since the scolded hunter led the peccaries to their place of slaughter and then
disappeared from Raquel’s narrative, it is tempting to see him as the peccary whose cut off head was left
raw, away from the fireplace, in her version as well. The idea that the raw peccary head led the blind
264

people to the dance would thus reflect a perfect reversal, where the person scolded by his group for
shooting one animal leads his group to become a group of animals. In both versions, then, massive
hunting or consumption by humans of agentive animals (peccaries) leads to humans’ transformation into
those game animals, whereas hunting or consuming a single, less agentive animal (the tinamou) allows
the hunter to either remain human or to maintain his agency, a faculty whose unequal distribution among
beings distinguishes humans from game animals, as we shall see below.
This myth bears resemblance to Mundurucu and Kayapó-Kubenkranken myths of the origin of meat that
Lévi-Strauss analyzed, where the tinamou hunter is the one who transforms people into collared or
white-lipped peccaries (1964, 93–94). Although in these and other myths of meat origin the tinamou
hunter and other heroes transform their brothers-in-law into peccaries to dispose of their meat (ibid, 92–
105), in the two Andoque versions the hunters (who are wife-givers) are not transformed into peccaries
by their brother-in-law, although their brothers-in-law in the wider sense—namely, present-day maloca
owners—end up disposing of their meat at the Head dances they organize. Not only did the maloquero
brother-in-law not transform the hunters into game in the Andoque version, in Raquel’s narrative, upon
her brothers’ arrival at the dance, the maloquera—an extension of her husband—served them manicuera
to reverse their transformation, but there was not enough beverage for all of them. Those who drank
manicuera regained their sight and became fully human again, while those who did not drink it ran away
into the forest as peccaries. Rather than a reflection on the dynamics between two human brothers-inlaw, the Andoque myth—that today serves as a cautionary tale to warn against excessive killing of any
species by either an individual or a group—states the symmetry of meta-affinal relations between people
and their potential nonhuman affines. The expression of this symmetry through white-lipped peccaries is
of course not accidental. As elsewhere in Amazonia, white-lipped peccaries “offer a model for the
generic human condition itself: they are not purely predators but mortals who are preyed upon and
defend themselves bravely, live in groups, eat manioc, and possess a chief” (Fausto 2007, 507; see also
Gow 2001, 68). To this we can add, in the Andoque case, the idea that the head of a peccary herd, who
parallels human captains in leading its herd in the woods and warns them of predator attacks, is usually
red faced or, in the minority of cases, white faced (cf. Stolze Lima 1996, 23)—just like the uneven
Andoque division of captaincy into “red” and “white” specializations (see Chapter 11).
Stolze Lima (1996) based her analysis of Amerindian perspectivism on the Juruna’s perception of whitelipped peccaries and their collective peccary hunting, arguing that this confrontation is in fact a struggle
between two points of view. While humans perceive this confrontation as asymmetrical hunting,
265

peccaries perceive it as symmetrical war in which they aim to capture their human potential affines,
who, once dead, would join the peccary society (ibid; see also S. Hugh-Jones 2019, 109–10; Karadimas
2005, 344–45). A person’s death in such a confrontation represents the slipping of hunting into war, as
he assumes the peccaries’ perspective on reality (Stolze Lima 1996, 38). Here it is important to recall
that the hunters’ transformation into peccaries begins when they are stripped of their eyes and completes
once they are given new eyes. The equivalence between the human and peccary societies thus results in
the complete incongruence of their perspectives and the outward manifestations of their actions. Unlike
human beings who form groups to enforce discipline and maintain social and territorial order, whitelipped peccary herds are notorious for their lack of respect toward other persons and the disorder they
leave behind, reflected in the poor state in which they leave saltlicks, and which makes other animals
refrain from going there, to the great detriment of Andoque hunters. The Andoque’s perception of
human-peccary incongruence culminates in the Head Dance, which requires guests to bring peccaries
hunted collectively with nets. As in the Juruna tale where the shaman “invites” peccaries to a human
dance as game, rather than dancers (ibid, 23), the Head Dance represents a moment in which one society
(the human one) practices and intensifies its collective agency while another (the peccary society)
experiences collective grief, signaling and actualizing its loss of agency.
The preparation of the net to capture the peccaries from chambira leaves in Raquel’s version emphasizes
the equivalence and incongruence between humans and peccaries. Chambira is also used for weaving
baskets, like the one used by the peccary master to capture humans through their eyes. A basket consists
solely of chambira and eyes, as its interstices are called tuákɵ, which literally means “round eye.” The
capacity of these two woven instruments to contain things but also to let them pass through their holes
relates to the container-contained dialectics of familiarizing predation and mastery, which represents the
asymmetric dimension of the latter. As with the ambivalence of Amazonian mastery, which “contains
the seeds of directional inversion” because the master contains, feeds, and protects a pet that retains an
agency and can thus, in turn, overcome him or her (Costa and Fausto 2019, 214, the emphasis is mine;
see also Costa 2010), the predator contains its prey within its body, but can itself fall prey to that which
it contains. The predator runs the risk of being consumed by their prey and, ultimately, to be contained
by the latter’s society as long as the former does not achieve the impossible task of completely
familiarizing their prey by entirely extinguishing the latter’s affinal otherness (Fausto 1999, 949; Costa
2010, 16 n.14). The versatility of chambira allows for the containment of peccaries and their human

266

predators, emphasizing these dialectics. As we shall presently see, these dialectics are also at play in the
predation of humans by nonhumans through the game the former consume.
Predation by Nonhumans
The consumption of game can have a range of undesired effects, from temporary symptoms like fatigue,
stomach aches, and diarrhea, to permanent physical conditions such as skin disease and negative
behavioral dispositions. In the past, youth were reportedly advised to avoid certain foodstuffs, such as
the pacarana, the skin of furry animals, the water used to cook armadillo meat, or the kɵrɵfe catfish
(Pimelodus sp.). The beliefs regarding eating these foodstuffs betray the idea that a person may
physically resemble the animal he or she eats: eating a pacarana, a rodent with a dark body dotted in
white stains, would make the eater become grey-haired; eating the skin of a furry animal would make
the eater feel incessantly cold and in constant need to cover themselves, like that animal; drinking stock
consisting of the vitality of an animal living in burrows in the ground would make the drinker fear to
advance in the opposite direction, i.e., climbing up trees, and eating the “narrow-waist” kɵrɵfe catfish
would make birth difficult and dangerous for pregnant women.
In addition to the risk of physical assimilation, the substances of animal bodies are also considered toxic.
Animals’ owner-persons are believed to have infused the bodies of different species they created with
worms and other pathogens to infest (ɨkóá) the bodies of their eaters, who would maintain their appetite
but instead of gaining weight, they would become thin, weak, and their bodies and minds devitalize.
These pathogens may also contaminate the eater’s body, causing physical and mental diseases, amoral
and asocial dispositions, and a propensity toward conflicts and accidents.
Animal bodies are also considered toxic because of their daily habits, as they take on the smell of
whatever and whoever they eat. “What you Whites call ‘contamination,’ we call ‘smell’ (olor)” said
Mario, explaining that the smell of the fruits, plants, insects, and fish each animal eats suffuses its flesh
and blood, and, in turn, suffuses the bodies of those consuming that animal. The smell (ɵpo̰ ̰ó ) registers
the predatory history and, thus, the predatory potential of each being, serving as a sensory expression of
its agency—consisting, in turn, of the agencies (smells) of the beings it has consumed—and ability to
make others consubstantial with itself. As among the Miraña (Karadimas 2005b, 220), the musk scent
(séa, the same as the odor emitted from a human being’s sweat glands) of certain land animals flags
them as more prejudicial to human health. Such are white-lipped peccaries, which, contrary to most
terrestrial game animals consumed by the Andoque, are omnivorous not herbivorous, and whose dorsal

267

musk glands hunters usually cut off before bringing this game home to prevent this smell from spreading
to human abodes. In contrast with the majority of hunted land animals, most fish consumed by the
Andoque eat other fish and non-vegetal matter, and sick people express disgust of eating them,
attributing this disgust to their smell, which can aggravate their vulnerable condition. People are more
attentive to the smell of fish they catch in the Caquetá after human drownings to avoid eating fish
containing human smell and dangerous agency if they have directly or indirectly fed on the corpse. As a
marker of a given being’s identity that emanates from that being to other beings and across species, it is
not surprising that po̰ ̰ó serves as one of the terms for comparing and pointing to similarity between
different entities (Landaburu 1979, 174).88 As Karadimas (2013, 197–99) notes considering Miraña
notions of odor, smell marks each being’s temporary territory as well as the porosity of physical borders
like the skin or palisades, as odor from one being assimilates to other beings’ odors or emanates to them
and imposes itself on them. Therefore, apart from nutrition, a given being’s odor and related ability to
act on others through it also depends on its cohabitation and contact with other beings. As among the
Miraña (Karadimas 2005b, 354–58), human and nonhuman beings can borrow from trees their
ñe’pɵ́kn—different aromatic herbs and other perfumes of vegetal origin—to prey on others by seducing
them or defend themselves from such seductive predation by others. It is this contagious—or
predatory—quality of odors that explains Tañe’s fear in the saltlick that night: “The devil is going to
change my body with this smell.” His attempt to smell only his flashlight, which, after prolonged use,
must have taken the smell of his hands, resonates with Karadimas’ interpretation of Miraña men’s turn
of the twentieth century custom to carry aromatic herbs in their apron for protection from external
aggressions propagated by odors (Karadimas 2013, 198): in the absence of such herbs, concentrating on
absorbing one’s own smell can counter one’s absorption by foreign smells. It also resonates with the
practice reported to me by Fisi one morning at his maloca, which involves forcefully rubbing one’s
wrists against each other and smelling them after waking up from an ominous dream so that the negative
event would go somewhere else. One’s body odor seems to “ground” one to one’s own body, of which
the agents appearing in dreams may try to take possession, thereby safeguarding one from
disadvantageous exchanges with such agents. Beyond the many connotations of the concept “center”
explored in Part I, we can add this one—it is also olfactory.

the other term, móna̰, may be related to mo̰no̰—aspect, form, and consciousness—but this relation is not as clear as in
po̰ ̰ó ’s case (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm., July 2022).

268

The Andoque perceive an agentive hierarchy among nonhuman beings, which is also influenced by the
scent emitted by different species but is generally based on a correlation between each species’ relative
position in the food chain and body size and that species’ ability to prey on and familiarize its eaters
through disease, other misfortunes, and, ultimately, death. Cultivated plants are understandably the least
dangerous to humans as they are grown by them, followed by forest trees, whose ñe’pɵ́kn cause people
respiratory problems and headaches. Trees, however, preserve the more potent yet invisible anaconda
agency that they had before the mythical hero Tofidei turned his anaconda enemies into trees (see M23
below), hence tree crushing accidents while clearing forest plots or during windstorms are seen as their
willful aggressions against humans.89 Small fish are the least dangerous among fauna, while bigger fish
from the Caquetá can cause different skin disease or oral candidiasis (sapito; yo’fí) to the eater’s child.
Game animals are more dangerous, with large mammals considered proactively aggressive. As human
smell is said to repel such animals, a deer, tapir, peccary, or cabybara (Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris)—
and, understandably, a jaguar—that draws near a settlement or its gardens should be killed but not eaten,
as it is considered to be sent by a sorcerer to harm that settlement’s dwellers, or to contain toxins in its
body, with the aim of being consumed by the dwellers to make them fall ill (the meat can nonetheless be
sold to others). This can also happen to a person who has hunted too much, to whom game animals start
approaching on their own volition, to transmit to him and his family members the diseases residing in
their bodies and assimilate these humans to their nonhuman society.90 Such graded agency, evidenced
among other Amazonian societies (e.g., Fausto 2007, 503; S. Hugh-Jones 2019, 104; Lucas 2019, 407),
points to an often-neglected hierarchical dimension of Amazonian animism, which also sets the stage for
different actors, including human ritual specialists, to practice ontological maneuvers for manipulating
the agency of others.
Like the Tukanoans (S. Hugh-Jones 2019a, 104), Andoque members consume fish and animals higher
on the hierarchy according to their stage in life: small children should ideally only eat small fish, fruits
and tubers, larvae, and ants, while birds, turtles, larger fish, and mammals are added to their diet as they
grow older.91 The age at which a child can be given the meat of large mammals such as peccary, deer, or

tapir, which are the most dangerous game, varies among interlocutors, from five to eight years old.
Introducing any new kind of fish or meat to a child must be accompanied by that foodstuff’s spiritual
decontamination by the father, grandfather, or another elder, who transubstantiates the meat into a
harmless fruit by curing chili which he hands the mother to eat with the fish, thereby reducing the fish’s
agency by naming it after that fruit (cf. Fausto 2007, 504, especially the citation of Overing 1975, 89).
This ontological manipulation allows the eater to familiarize the animal and use its vitality to magnify
his or her own personality, rather than being familiarized by it.
The specific fruit to which each animal can be transformed is the fruit associated with that animal in
mythology and considered one of that animal’s multiple origins, as every species and human clan have
more than one origin. In the case of animals, their vegetal origin is one of the possible forms in which
they can be represented in dreams (see Appendix 5). For Andoque interlocutors, for example, peach
palm fruits stand for peccaries, sugar cane stands for homima fish, avocado represents the silky anteater
(Cyclopes didactylus), and mocambo (Theobroma bicolor) represents one paca species (and possibly the
pacarana, Dinomys branickii whose speckled fur reminds that fruit [Karadimas 2005, 347]).92 The fruit
form is the docile, safer form in which an animal can appear, the way it is perceived by its site-person. A
man crossing Tar Waterfall (Pɨdadíe) on Macaw River for hunting can offer coca powder and tobacco
paste to Lady Tar Flower (Pɨdataikn, also called Boɵtadíeikn, “Lady Splashing Water”), the site-person,
alluding to his poverty, to which the master may reply: “I have pineapple (armadillo), plantain (collared
peccary), mocambo (paca/pacarana), caimito (tapir), peach palm fruit (white-lipped peccary), and inga
beans (?), have some!” (Pineda Camacho 1982, 39; my translation; the site-person’s name in Andoque is
my addition).
As observed in Appendix 5, the other form in which animals can appear in dreams is as human beings,
most commonly a violent man or a seductive woman. Dreaming of fruits is considered an indication of
healthful game, whereas dreaming of people is an indication of dangerous meat, whose consumption
may result in disease or different aches. The Murui-Muina interpret this duality of game representations

through a combination of moral and strategic principles. They ask their auxiliary spirit before sleep to
dream of fruits so they can distinguish “legitimate victims”—which are the “delinquent” members of
their groups whose killing would not be avenged by their masters—from “illegitimate” ones whose
killing can be severely avenged (García 2018, 273–74; Griffiths 1998, 204). For the Andoque, however,
it is the strategic principle that dominates. Much like the Miraña (Karadimas 2005b, 347–48), they do
not see the dream symbols of fruit and humans as a moral dichotomy between rightful and wrongful
targets, but rather as a distinction between the unprotected, like orphans, and those belonging to a
maloca’s lineage. As previously mentioned, a hunter may petition Sı̰ ́di, “Give me your orphans.”
Animals depicted as cultivated fruits are likened to the orphans of their owner-person (ño̰), as they are
the alienable possessions of that entity, who would not seek vengeance for their loss. They are Sı̰ ́di’s
orphans in the sense of being Sı̰ ́di-less: they lack a personhood (ño̰) element and are dissociated from a
predatory agency. Conversely, the appearance of game animals as humans in dreams indicates their
agency and potential to cause harm. Unlike the docile orphans that can be freely given away as fruits,
these animals are akin to a maloquero’s consanguine kin, whose harm he would vengefully redress.
Hence, these animals are perceived as persons imbued with the personhood and agency of their ownerperson (this does not imply that all individuals avoid the risks associated with hunting and consuming
such creatures).
The relatively safe status of fish manifests also in the fact that most fish are represented in dreams as
fruits and other vegetal elements (such as the balsa tree, from whose chips Moon created some fish
[Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 49–50]), and only other, mostly dangerous aquatic animals (river turtle,
caiman, anaconda, dolphin, etc.) and a few big fish, like the catfish Brachyplatystoma filamentosum,
appear as humans. In contrast with dreams on land animals, which are commensurate with humans, the
actions taken by fish in dreams do not predict analogous actions by humans, and for some people fishing
in dreams represents a monetary gain. Neither does killing humans in dreams predict catching fish;
rather, it is a dream about stealing inanimate things from others that augurs a bountiful fish yield. The
fact that fish do not share a terrestrial existence with humans also renders them less likely to proactively
attack humans, except for dolphins, for reasons that will be discussed in Chapter 12.
Terrestrial animals as well as insects are said to leave behind them different aches for people to contract
in the places they pass through and the things they touch. For example, holding a working tool left
outside overnight and sniffed by an ocelot or on which a butterfly has rested may result in arm pains;
urinating on a bullet ant (Paraponera clavata) nest or on the footprints of peccaries, tapirs, capybaras,
271

and other large mammals may cause bladder problems, and stepping on a path previously stomped by
them or on their excrements may cause different types of knee and leg pains called fɨsé.
The epidemiological, physical, mental, and social harms that may follow the consumption of animals or
experiencing other aggressions by nonhumans and their owner-persons are collectively referred to as
enfermedades (“illnesses” or “diseases”) in Spanish, and in Andoque are expressed through the verbs yií
and ti. Illnesses and misfortunes have owner-persons, who are the entities who created them and who
would direct them at those who iterate the name of the mishap or of its owner person without providing
adequate offerings. Both verbs yií and ti convey the notion of losing human status. Yií, “to kill
consciousness,” describes one’s state of mind during the process of infirmity, drawing on the lack of
consciousness in death as well as in the temporary death of fainting, and the deranged consciousness
during illness, dizziness, and drunkenness—all are states conveyed by yi. In contrast with hɵ́ɵ, which
denotes the perceptible death or physical disappearance of a given being, yi can refer to states where the
person is still outwardly human, and their body still exists, but their consciousness has been hijacked
(Jon Landaburu, Pers. comm. November 2022). The teleological dimension is more present in the verb
ti—“to make/form/transform”—which denotes the affected person’s ultimate transformation into a
nonhuman being upon death, but also the deranged mental, physical, or social state during the negative
event that signals that the transformation to nonhumanity has already taken place. Several interlocutors
alluded to this deranged state during fieldwork after they recuperated from different afflictions, from
headaches to malaria, in remarkably similar statements, commenting to me: “yesterday I felt bad, I
wasn’t like a human being, I was—how can I say it?” (ayer me sentí mal, no estaba como gente,
estaba—¿cómo será?). In contrast with bu’, which expresses overt violence, both yií and ti are also used
to refer to sorcery attacks that seal the victim’s fate by transforming them into the prey of Sı̰ ́di and of
other powerful spirits even before their body is affected.
These verbs, yií and ti, and their combinations, i.e., tiyií, “to transform by killing consciousness”, reflect
the common Amazonian perception of illnesses and other misfortunes as the familiarization of human
victims by nonhuman agents, who turn the former into their kinspersons (Costa and Fausto 2019, 206).
This is also reflected in the interpretation of dreams where the dreamer receives food from others or has
sex with them, which is seen as foretelling a state of illness, because the people appearing in dreams are
actually nonhumans, and such actions create consubstantiality with them (see Appendix 5). The strength
of the person’s tutelary spirit, yono̰pǵi, determines whether they avoid such creation of

272

consubstantiality.93 In certain times and places, it is more likely to be affinized by the animals, their
owner-persons, or the sorcerers on whose initiative they attack. As in other Amazonian societies, where
a person is considered extremely likely to be familiarized by the animals during the period when their
body has still not achieved a full human form (i.e., during gestation and early childhood), Andoque
parents and newborn children are subject to many pre- and post-partum dietary and other restrictions
(Fausto 2007a, 505; Vilaça 2002). For example, parents are advised to avoid eating slimy or fat fish to
prevent their child from suffering from diarrhea or oral candidiasis—which is reported to have been fatal
before the arrival of Western medicine—and to avoid exerting physical force to prevent their child from
developing an umbilical hernia. In the case of male babies, these restrictions should be observed for
longer periods than when female babies are concerned because the animals are said to be angrier and
more violent after the birth of a male human child, who is expected to hunt them when growing up, than
a female one, whose garden cultivars may even nourish animals.
Beyond restrictions during apprenticeship, that will be examined below, other sensitive periods are not
related to the person’s life cycle. Elders can detect “times of word of transformation” (tisonńkn) or
“times that make the heart fear” (yítuíkőnńkn) by interpreting different natural phenomena and
especially by reflecting on them in their mambeaderos. During these periods people should beware of
what they eat and where they go to avoid illnesses and misfortunes. Most of these mishaps can be traced
to specific sites within the ancestral land where they originated and where people are more prone to
contract them, except for certain illnesses and epidemics recognized as originating from outside the land,
like malaria.
Like other People of the Center (García 2018, 102–4; Karadimas 2005, 219–21), the Andoque associate
disease and heat (pá̰ʉkói yíi), on the one hand, and healing and cooling down, on the other hand. Similar
to the Miraña (Karadimas 2005b, 226–29), their mythology also links heat and odor in an episode from
the myth of the pipe-blower Uiknñemn. In this episode, Uiknñemn escapes the flaming flatulences of
children, which cause various trees diseases (see M12 in Appendix 1, as well as Landaburu and Pineda
1984, 137–38). However, unlike these other peoples, the Andoque equally recognize the existence of
“cold diseases” (no̰sikói yíi). While hot diseases are transmitted by forest animals and are contracted in

alongside hot ones derives from the greater importance that the Andoque accord in their mythology and
epidemiology to the fluvial exchange with non-Indigenous people, who they fear may take their women
(cf. M4, M5, M23, and M22).
Lakes, hills, and waterfalls are notorious places where diseases are contracted and transformations to
nonhumanity occur, because what normally appears to people as such natural landmarks are actually
malocas owned by powerful site-persons. These entities preside over groups of nonhuman beings living
there and administer the exercise of different illnesses and misfortunes that originate in these sites and
affect human beings. Human souls devoured by these nonhuman beings through such mishaps join these
invisible malocas. For this reason, revenge by owner-persons undertaken in different predatory forms is
referred to as ḭpáha, based on páha, which conveys the notion of value, and the verbal prefix ı̰ ́ ’, which
points to the altered state of the subject (Landaburu 1979, 186).94 By devouring the soul of a human
being, the owner-person fills the void left in its house after this human or their relatives killed one of its
nonhuman beings, to whom that human is equivalent, thereby regaining that which it has lost. These
devoured people are called “disappeared” (hɵ́ɵ) due to the disintegration of their bodies, but they
continue to live in these houses in a healthy, youthful state, engaging in all the cultural practices that
living humans do, including horticulture and ceremonial dances. As we will see in the excursus section
below, these disappeared persons miss their living relatives, and should one show up in their house, they
would insistently offer them food, drinks, coca, tobacco, and sexual partners to capture them forever by
creating consubstantiality.95 As for the Krahó (Carneiro da Cunha 1978, 11), death becomes irreversible
for the Andoque once a person accepts food and sexual invitations from the dead and takes part in their
social life, and, as a result, is familiarized by them.

94
95

For the widespread association or overlap between revenge and payment in Amazonia, see Fausto 1999, 936.

274

Therefore, to avoid disease and ensuing death, a person must always reject commensality and kinship
with nonhumans. If a person is bitten by a snake, stung by an insect, or attacked by any other animal,
they should kill it; otherwise, people may scold them, asking: “Is he [the animal] your brother, that you
care for him?”. The attacking animal may interpret the failure to kill it as affection by the victim, which
can lead to future attempts to incorporate the human victim into that animal’s society through other
means. Conversely, the consumption of “consanguineous substances” associated with the patriline, and
primarily tobacco and coca, which are either mainly or exclusively consumed by men, can protect
people who find themselves in such dangerous places or situations, shielding them from being tempted
into consuming the foodstuffs of the dead and animals. More generally, the strength of one’s tutelary
spirit, yono̰pǵi, determines one’s vulnerability to such hazards.
A clear indication that a transformation to animality is fully underway is a deranged mental state whose
expressions range from spatial disorientation to uncontrollable anger and other severely asocial
behavior, to senseless speech and actions, and plain madness. In such states, a person is yipá’imo̰no̰ɵ,
“of a new/unknown soul” or yiyoíkómo̰no̰ɵ, “of a soul that makes deviate,” with the interesting stress in
the latter term not only on the problematic state of the deranged person but also on its potential to
transmit this state to others (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm., November 2022). People in such states are
acting according to “new, unknown” principles that are alien to their own human origin, and, more
specifically, like animals. Rubio*, a young man in his thirties, started showing signs of mental illness
some eight years before my arrival, after a long period of drug and alcohol abuse while working in gold
mining. His mother told me that the first sign of illness had been his getting lost on his way back home
from the village while drunk and spending the night in the forest. That event was followed by entire
days that he would pass in the forest, supposedly to socialize with animals. His habit of uprooting his
father’s coca plants during violent outbursts was interpreted by several people as actions taken by the
diablo (invisible nonhuman entity) manipulating him to destroy the plants that can counter his
deterioration into animality. Yiñékɒ is also said to have entered a temporary state of madness for several
days, during which he dressed indiscreetly, thought he was a jaguar, and asked himself, while looking at
the people around him, “Whom around here should I eat?” Upon receiving blessed coca, tobacco, and
manicuera and resuscitating, he reportedly told the person who provided him with these substances (and
whom the narrator claimed to have been his father), “Brother-in-Law, you really love me; I was an
animal, and you made me human again.”

275

Several nonhuman beings are particularly capable of familiarizing people: the fi’du beings and the
“beautiful and dangerous beings,” a category including the tapir, deer, earthworm, and dolphin. The
term fi’du, which is often translated as diablo in Spanish, refers to the entire category of extraordinary
nonhuman beings inhabiting the forest, as well as a specific such being of a female sex seducing hunters
into sexual intercourse, known as madremonte in Spanish and rendered here in the form of a capitalized
proper name, as Fi’du. Similar to the Tatuyo’s wati (Bidou 1999, 74), these fi’du beings are absent from
the main mythic narratives but feature heavily in people’s accounts of their own forest excursions and
daily activities or those of others, as well as cautionary tales for children. Beyond the Fi’du being, on
which I will elaborate below, the category includes various beings whose definitions vary among
Andoque members and is open-ended, capable of admitting any unfamiliar, potentially dangerous being
that Andoque members encounter in their own land and on the other lands they visit or work, like La
Chorrera or Chiribiquete Park, or learn of from other Indigenous people or from Colombian settlers and
folklore. These include: “One Leg” (Kapa̰, a violent tapir leg detached from its body, in Spanish:
Patasola); Ká’hɵi (a shadow or reflection in the water); Hɒ̰’ɒ̰ and Ḭtamo̰no̰ (the latter translates as “soul
without owner;” both appear as a known person); other beings lacking names in Andoque and known in
Spanish as Duende (a spirit whose seduction of women, according to some, mirrors Fi’du’s seduction of
men) or Bambero (who scares people by tapping on trees’ buttress roots, or bambas),96 and other
ɵdefɵño̰e, “forest persons,” including hybrid animals and monsters.97 Although some of these beings
appear when people do not ask the site-persons’ permission to enter their sites and when they try to
protect animals by causing hunters to lose their way in the forest, and even though the site-persons can
also take the form of a shadow or an extraordinary or non-native animal (like a horse), they should not
be confused with this largely immobile category. Fi’du entities can move and interact with humans
beyond their specific sites of origin.
The “proper Fi’du” is exclusively female. Her name derives from the long “fiiiiii…ruuuuu” whistles she
emits in the forest, and her typical mode of action is to appear in front of lone hunters at dusk or night as
a beautiful, long-haired, often naked young woman and seduce them into having sex. This renders the
hunter ill, feverish, and eventually mad, leading to his death. The sexual activity does not have to be
physical, and a dream with a sexual content while camping in the woods counts as an encounter with

Fi’du. She targets men who obsessively think and talk about sex and women, as well as men who appear
in the sexual fantasies of women far away. Therefore, young men are cautioned against engaging in
lewd speech and sexual imagination in the forest and having too many lovers waiting for them at home.
For instance, several people told me about a young Yucuna men who, while working with the Andoque
near the Mesai River during the post-genocide rubber-tapping period, ignored warnings by his elders
and incessantly boasted about his amorous exploits and sexual fantasies. One day at dusk, a beautiful
woman appeared in front of him and helped him fill his buckets with rubber. After several days of
receiving such help and flirting with her, he slept with her. His penis then swelled, he became feeble and
feverish. When he sought help from the Yucuna elders, they said they could not save him because Fi’du
had already taken his soul. Eventually, he died after a night during which Fi’du whistles echoed from all
around the rubber camp. The young man could not be saved because sexual relations with another being
is a strong way of both admitting and creating consubstantiality with that being. This consubstantiality
can also be created by receiving food and drink from Fi’du, who can lure hunters or any person lost in
the forest to her home, to join those who were previously devoured by her.
Fi’du also approaches young men during initiation into different cultural practices, such as healing,
sorcery, or ritual organization, and until the elder tutor informs them that the initiation is over. It is
important to highlight that apprenticeship to such practices is ideally undertaken before a man reaches
puberty or begins engaging in sexual activity, and people explain that when a man reaches old age, he
can reflect on the entirety of the teachings he acquired in his youth. However, during his married or
sexually active years, a man merely grazes the surface of knowledge, seeking ad hoc training for specific
needs like curing food for his wife or children and handling other simple matters. Apprenticeship to
ritual specializations comes with strict prohibitions against engaging in or even fantasizing about sexual
activity, as well restrictions on eating, the culinary equivalent of copulation: an apprentice is only
permitted to receive food from his mother or female blood relative and consume coca powder prepared
by his father or himself.
Certainly, just as the abovementioned idea that Fi’du attacks womanizers functions (or should function)
to deter men from such a behavior, the link between unfinished initiation and Fi’du attacks can be
viewed as a way for elders to impose discipline and authority on youth and make those interested in
apprenticeship commit to the arduous study process it implies. Initiation involves the narration of long,
intertwined stories of origin on the harms that sorcery causes or those that healing and dances help
overcome. Broaching these harms without sufficient elaboration that would prescribe the “antidotes” for
277

them can endanger the apprentice by unsettling his mind, or the apprentice can put them to use in a way
that endangers others. In the ontological register where these harms are associated with animals and
other nonhuman beings, this amounts to invoking them and arousing them in a way that fecundates
them, helps them reproduce and get a hold of the apprentice, instead of the other way around.
Despite the plausibility of this moralistic interpretation, it must be remembered that Fi’du stories—as
well as those of other malevolent animals, as we will see below—are ways to interpret actual death cases
rather than simple deviations from proper modes of behavior. Therefore, instead of encoding immorality
in the language of predation by nonhumans, as Londoño (2005; 2017) would have it, these stories reflect
the perception of immoral thoughts and behavior as one path through which such predation takes place.
The sexual seduction to be evaded is key in foregrounding the primacy of the Andoque’s attempt to
prevent symmetrical predation (in contrast with moral concerns). This parallels the hunting technique
where male hunters imitate the calls of females in heat to attract and shoot male animals or use mating
calls of males to lure females and rival males. As in the latter case, the predator (here, Fi’du) needs to
hold the prey in confusion and misrecognition of its true identity for a brief moment to kill it. Being
obsessed with women and purposeless sex means letting oneself be carried away by foreign affinal
principles instead of adhering to one’s true core, and can lead to such fateful distractions.
Apart from hunters, Fi’du also lures children. One story (M19, Raquel 6/7/19) recounts of an unlucky
hunter who, unable to find game for his family, shares a tuber of the elongated fi’du nḭtɒ́’dɒ, “Fi’du’s
yam” (Dioscoreas sp.) that he has found with his wife and four children. When the parents leave the
children at home by themselves the next day, an ugly woman whose hair is full of mud visits them and,
promising to cook the yam they love so much, orders the children to fetch water and wood to make fire.
When the water boils, she asks them to remove lice from her hair. While one child is cautious and
climbs the roof beams, the three others do as she asks, and as they get near her, she throws them into the
pot, cooks them, and eats them. The surviving child witnesses the entire scene from above and tracks
Fi’du as she flees into her burrow. The child then leads his parents to the burrow when they return,
where they manage to kill her by burning the red pɨdoɵtu chili (“bush dog [Speothos venaticus] chili”) in
the entrance to the burrow, forcing her out of there and away to the river source.98 While this story seems
to have the obvious function of warning children against trusting strangers and warning parents against
leaving their children without surveillance, it reflects the common Amazonian conception that children

A similar Nɨpóde version was recorded by Griffiths (1998, 319–21).

are especially vulnerable to predation by nonhumans (Vilaça 2002). Several people told me about an
adult woman who, when she was still a girl of about three or four years old, was left by herself for a few
hours at a remote garden cabin by her parents while they were working. As they did not find her there
upon their return, they searched her for hours until finally finding her by a bridge over a brook
(according to one interlocutor, diablos cannot cross bridges). The girl claimed that her father had taken
her there and then disappeared, so people inferred that a diablo appeared in front of her in the form of
her father to take her away and transform her into its kind. The elder Yinñéfɵkn healed her. The four
people telling me about this case disagreed whether this diablo was Fi’du or Hɒ̰’ɒ̰, one of them
reasoning that only Hɒ̰’ɒ̰ appears as a familiar person, while another claimed that they are in fact the
same entity and that people would say Hɒ̰’ɒ̰ to avoid iterating the name Fi’du, which is more dangerous.
The woman herself (with whom I admittedly refrained from speaking about this matter) is said to have
only learned about it when she was an adult. The same diablo returned to take a hold of her after she
gave birth to her firstborn son, driving her to kill him. She is said to have been permanently healed after
a ceremonial dance, but two people told me that all of this would not have happened had she been
baptized by a priest because this rite is said to protect children from diablos.
As in cases of sexual seduction, we also witness here the crucial role of confusion and misrecognition in
nonhumans’ imposition of their perspectives on humans (Viveiros de Castro 1998, 483) to familiarize
the latter. The diablos Hɒ̰’ɒ̰ or Ḭtamo̰no̰i (“soul without owner”) can assume the form of any familiar
person, and if the person in front of whom they appear responds to their call and follows them, or if they
betray accepting the veracity of this apparition by telling others that the familiar person appeared to
them in that place and time, their souls will be taken by these beings forever (ntamo̰no̰i yḛnni, “he [the
nonhuman being] goes with their soul”), and their physical death will soon follow. Since confusion and
misrecognition are the means through which these beings capture people, telling others that such
attempts were made and overcome, or even screaming when this happens for others to hear, ensures that
these diablos would not return to chase them. By contrast, a person who hides such encounters from
others communicates to the diablo that he or she likes it, and the latter will return once again. In AnneChristine Taylor’s analysis of similar encounters with extraordinary nonhuman beings among the
Achuar, these encounters are characterized by mutual gaze and by the lack of proper communication in
the form of linguistic exchange because these apparitions stupefy their human participants. They then
shift sensory registers when being communicated in verbal narratives told to other people who did not
see these nonhuman beings themselves (Taylor 1993a). The Andoque’s statements on such encounters
279

emphasize the causation link between the human-nonhuman and the inter-human communications:
communicating the human-nonhuman interaction with other humans is required to prevent future
communication with these nonhumans. The strength of a person’s spirit, yono̰pii, determines if that
person tells of the encounter and overcomes it or keeps it secret and is doomed forever.
Furthermore, we may view the diablos as powerful and dangerous precisely insofar as they have not
been symbolized and communicated to others and to oneself, as parts of the Real register of reality—in
Lacanian terms—that have not been symbolized and remain as a surplus of alterity, deriving their
potency from their existence within the realm of the unconscious. In Lacan’s words, “The real supports
the phantasy, the phantasy protects the real” (1981, 41). This absence of or even resistance to
symbolization is evident in the frequent disagreement among Andoque interlocutors, as well as
inconsistency in statements by the same interlocutors, with respect to the names of each fi’du entity or
the sensory impressions through which it manifests itself in front of people. In Patrice Bidou’s
understanding of the Tatuyo’s attitude toward the wati, the latter’s frightening existence and
indeterminate nature goad people to fix names upon them, symbolize reality and organize it through
myth in order to gain greater control over them and over reality at large (1998). In this regard, the fi’du
entities are the ultimate others and the ultimate affines who have not yet been familiarized—in the
double sense of the word, both in its use in Amazonian ethnography, and in common use, referring to
making something known and acquainted—by the traditions of the consanguine group; it is thus no
wonder that their preferred mode of operation is through sexual seduction.
The “beautiful and dangerous beings”—tapir, deer, earthworm, and dolphin99—follow similar principles,
and are collectively known as pa’sisíɵ́hɵ (“green/blue100 people”), sɵ’oi síɵ́hɵ (“pretty people”), and
bɨ’ɵ́kn síɵ́hɵ (“people of pleasure”). However, the first term specifically applies to the tapir, and the last
two terms apply in mythology to the dolphin.101 This generalization from the names of specific being to
the entire category is related to these beings’ ability to transform into each other, as each can shed its
own form and take that the others as well as other diablos. Nevertheless, each of these beings has a
distinct origin story, and the principles embedded within them can be also identified in people’s

People explain that these beings are dangerous because they are beautiful and seductive, leading people
to irresponsibly desire them for superficial reasons—hɵ́ño, “to seem pretty”—rather than for the
responsible love that implies care and protection and denoted by the verb tuma. Except for the dolphin,
they mainly seduce women. The earthworm, ḭtá, often also described as one of Tatoañei’s sons seeking
to seduce and harm Shadow Egg’s daughters, is said to sexually attack woman by sucking blood from
their feet and climbing into their hammocks at night. Although I was not told any specific myth about its
origin, the earthworm seems to represent a dimension of the other masculine beings attacking women:
the overabundant sexual force of the earth (cf. Karadimas 2005, 108–09, 282–83). As in the Miraña’s
link between sperm, placenta, and the earthworm’s slime (ibid, 108–09), impregnation is a key step in
the earthworm’s attack. In a story told to me by two different elders about two distinct women from the
previous generation, a victim died during pregnancy after mistaking an earthworm climbing into her
hammock at night for her husband. After death, her swollen belly immediately flattened because it did
not contain a fetus but was full of the earthworm’s slime.
In this context, the Amazonian brown brocket deer (Mazama nemorivaga; pe’toɵ) is only depicted as
male. He is considered one of Tatoañei’s jaguar sons, which signals his sexually predatory nature. He
captures the attention of women in their gardens by crunching dry branches as he walks, and if a woman
mistakes it for the sound of human footsteps, she may look up and find a beautiful young man standing
before her. Sexual relations with him are said to make her fall ill and die. Alternatively, if a woman sees
a deer in her garden, she may dream of an attractive man and become ill in real life if she surrenders to
him in the dream. In a story told by Raquel (M20) and detailed in Appendix 1, Shadow Egg’s daughter,
Hummingbird (Pá̰di), who repeatedly ignores her father’s instructions for tidy manioc work, is seduced
while working in the garden by Yellow Achiote Deer (Doékositoɵ),102 who invites her and her younger
sister to collect larvae from a mauritia palm. After they join him, he cuts down one tree to serve them
larvae and urges the younger sister to climb another tree for mauritia fruits. When she does, he seizes her
older sister and takes her to his underground home, while the palm on which the other sister sits rises to
the sky. At his home, he leaves the girl sealed in a “pot of fire,” also called “pot of transformation,”
while he goes to gather firewood. His mother finds the girl and advises her to escape from her son, who

is Fidu’s son. When Yellow Achiote Deer discovers that his prey has escaped, he pursues her. However,
she finds refuge in Acouchi’s hole in a tree trunk, under Anaconda’s “protected chest,” and under
Kingfisher’s “protected wing” while he dives in the water. Ultimately, the older sister makes it back to
her father, and her sick younger sister, atop the tree, is healed and brought down by the smoke of the
Bush Dog Chili blown on her by Red-Rumped Cacique, who is assisted by Weasel.
A slightly different version of this myth, with a reference to the seductive being as a jaguar, serves as the
basis for the Armadillo Dance to name and protect firstborn children of non-maloquero families. The
illnesses contracted by the two sisters are classified as doékositoɵ yatiyií—Yellow Achiote Deer’s
Transformation by Killing Consciousness—and, unless sexual contact has taken place, they can be cured
with incense and smoked chili that are blessed by evoking the episodes of the acouchi, kingfisher,
anaconda, cacique, and weasel. Healing with these odorous substances reflects the idea that the deer, as
well as the other malevolent animals and diablos, make people ill and transform them into animals
through their smell.103
While aggressions by deer in gardens are associated with women’s untidy horticultural practices, which
can be taken to represent sexual promiscuity, aggressions by tapirs (ḭtɵ) take place at home without any
apparent immoral behavior on the female victim’s part, who simply accepts the sexual proposition of a
person she believes to be her husband. Several people told me stories from long ago about women
whose husbands returned home in the evening after going hunting and slept with their wives, before
leaving again to try their luck in the hunt another time. When the husband came back immediately
afterwards and denied having been there earlier, the woman’s belly started to ache and she bled from the
vagina because the “husband” was, in fact, a tapir in disguise, who damaged her womb with his
monstruous penis, causing the woman to die by dawn. Andoque interlocutors trace such aggressions by
tapirs to the story M21, narrated by Fisi and detailed in Appendix 1. It tells of Dance Rod Painting
(Kɒ́dɨhḭ) who lived in Sɵ’dɨnsí (Lake of the unidentified Sɵ’dɨ bird, called Pavo Marino in local
Spanish), when it was not yet a saltlick. This man used to damage the pineapples and other plants
growing in his daughter-in-law’s garden, and even advised his son on how to catch the mysterious
intruder. However, he avoided the until his son added honey to the caguana beverage he prepared for
him. The next morning, checking the trap, the son found his father, who, upon donning his accessories,

transformed into a tapir. The son then killed him, leaving the game for his brothers-in-law from the river
source.104
The cultivars stomped by the father-in-law, particularly the pineapple emphasized by Fisi and another
narrator of a variant of this myth, are metonymic for the woman because she has planted and tends to
them.105 These vegetal elements represent the passive “fruit” aspect of the woman, as opposed to the
active “person” aspect, in which the father-in-law must perceive her to affect his harms. As we saw in
relation to curing game and will see in relation to sorcery attacks, predators need to relegate their victims
to an inferior ontological position to ensure the desired direction of predation. This means constituting
them as deer when the sorcerer is a jaguar, or as pineapples when the maligner is a tapir. While the
father-in-law’s transformation to nonhumanity in this myth emphasizes the moral injunction against men
sleeping with their daughters-in-law,106 the cautionary tales of tapir seduction express the predatory logic
that equates misrecognition with familiarization by animals. However, people view this myth as the
origin of harms that tapirs cause women, particularly those affecting their womb and their ability to
survive childbirth, and that are associated with women’s seduction by tapirs.
The last of the “beautiful and dangerous beings” is the dolphin (Inia geoffrensis), which, like other
Indigenous peoples and riverine communities in Amazonia, the Andoque associate with the Whites and
the dangerous seduction by the goods they trade and the lifestyle that can be obtained by assimilating
into their societies (e.g., Arregui 2019; Echeverri and Pereira 2005, 133; Karadimas 2005, 360–68;
Reichel 1989; Slater 1994). Dolphins, referred to as ama̰na in everyday discourse and bɨ’ɵ́kn síɵ́hɵ
(“people of pleasure”) in the mythical register, can attack both men and women by appearing as
attractive humans, having intercourse with them, and then leaving them hallucinating, feverish, and ill,
until they ultimately die. People also report seeing them at dusk or when drunk as a group of people
dressed in white and wearing accessories such as a hat, a belt, and a watch, attempting to take them to
the river with them. When they return to the site in daylight or after recuperating their senses they find
the dolphins’ accessories, but the hat is now a ray fish (to cover the dolphin’s blowhole), the belt is an
electric eel, and the watch is a crab.107 People should be cautious not to behave in any way reflecting
similarity to the dolphin’s behavior, such as splashing while bathing in the river (which the dolphin

might take at a game), or sniffling when having a runny nose (which sounds like the dolphin’s
