The Andoque associate the dolphin with the river mouth and consider it to have an anaconda origin (it is
also called ama̰na hɵpɵ, “dolphin-anaconda”), which means that it is an aquatic predator, whose
predation is expressed through seduction.108 Interestingly, the origin myth of the dolphin links it with
another seductive animal—the tapir. The story M22, summarized in Appendix 1 from the anthology by
Landaburu and Pineda, tells of Green Tapir (Pa’si Ḭtɵ), brother of the hero Tofidei (see M23, also in
Appendix 1), who discovered his wife, Lady Peccary (Ḭńkn), engaging in sexual relations with her
brother Pretty (Sɵ’oi)109 during the preparations for a dance. Green Tapir pierced both of them with his
spear and cast them into the river, where they transformed into illness and madness-inducing dolphins.
The figure of Green Tapir ties the origin of one beautiful and dangerous animal with that of another. In a
version of M21 told to Landaburu and Pineda, Green Tapir is a descendant of Dance Rod Tapir (1984,
128 n.21). According to Fisi, after transforming his wife and brother-in-law into dolphins, Green Tapir
went from house to house, knocking on doors with his bamboo cane to hurt the women living in them.
M22, whose longer version is the origin story of the River Turtle-Bamboo Dance (see Chapter 11),
represents the widespread Amazonian association between dolphins and dances. Throughout Amazonia,
dolphins are reputed to seduce people, especially women, at dances (Arregui 2019, 10; Maués 2006, 15–
16; Reichel 1989, 115). However, contrary to other dolphin beliefs, here the dolphin is not a stranger
who is unknown to the seduced woman, but rather her brother whom she knows too well. The dolphin’s
incestuous origin seems to represent the lack of reciprocity in affinal exchange by Whites, who tend to
take more women than they give—recall, for example, the asymmetrical exchange in M5—and the
violent attitude that such lack of reciprocity enables them.

Cf. the alliance between the dolphin and anaconda in the Achuar’s eyes (Descola 1986, 124–25).
Pretty is the protagonist of another myth (M17, see Appendix 1), where he marries Sun’s daughter and his way of resisting
his father-in-law’s attempts to prey on him is by refusing reproduction (only reluctantly does he give his father-in-law salt
[semen] for mixing with tobacco paste [the woman]) and becoming a parasite threatening to cause his wife’s death, instead of
preying on her and her family by creating his own powerful maloca. Amounting to a rejection of affinal alliance, this refusal
of predation should be thus considered incestuous.
108
109

284

The fact that “the beautiful and dangerous beings” are associated with undesirable behavior seems to
validate Londoño’s moral interpretation of the Féenemɨna’s perception of nonhuman beings as
embodying different vices, whose discourse people should evade if they are to adhere to the values
highly regarded in society (2005). We can, of course, see this logic at play in the notion that by
recounting their origin stories, people who do not necessarily mean harm invoke them, innocently
making them attack people and frequent the mambeadero where these stories have been told. This
translates to the prevalence of immoral thoughts and discourse in that mambeadero. It is said that people
should only think or speak about these beings and the vices with which they are associated if they know
how to reject them, for example, by evoking the figures who defeated them in mythology and how they
did it. However, we must keep in mind that, rather than general moral teachings, Andoque members are
primarily concerned with the reproduction and well-being of their clans and, secondarily, with those of
the entire Andoque community. Animal thoughts and discourse in the mambeadero are first and
foremost described as useless (no sirven) because they do not translate to actions enhancing the wellbeing and reproduction of the human group. In addition, while broaching the mythical figure and means
involved in defeating these dangerous beings evidently reflects and communicates to others knowledge
about the ways to deal with and counter the vices associated with them, people also say that upon talking
about such animals, one can immediately joke about the frivolity of some other person living far away,
thereby making the malevolent beings go after that person. In other words, not only does moral
discourse operate in these cases through a predatory logic, but moral discourse is also put at the service
of a predatory cosmology. We must remember that the stories about associating with such beings serve
to interpret and give meaning to cases of actual death and physical and mental ailments. The beauty of
these beings, as well as the beauty that can characterize Fi’du in her female manifestations, and the
sexual receptivity of their victims, are crucial for these aggressions to work, in a way that parallels the
animal’s receptivity to mate as a factor allowing the hunter to tempt it to draw near to him and thus
facilitating the hunt’s success. This requires a more dialectical formulation, where just like nonhuman
beings embody different vices, so does engaging in these vices may lead people to share a similar body
and consciousness with these beings, which is referred to as ntii, “[he/she] transformed into them,” or
ntimo̰no̰i, “[his/her] soul transformed into them [i.e., resembling their souls].”
As we have seen, similar to the Fi’du cases, the moral dimension of these cases concerns sexual
incontinence and the need to be careful where and with whom one expresses sexuality. Therefore, we
can analyze these cases through Elizabeth Reichel’s sociological interpretation of the Yucuna’s reports
285

on sexual encounters with tapirs and dolphins as reflecting reservations and ambivalence toward
matrimonial alliance and association with specific human groups, namely, the Tanimuca and Whites
(1989). However, while the Andoque clearly associate the dolphins with Whites, I could not find clues
linking the other beings discussed above with specific human groups convincingly, as Reichel does, as
she links the seduction of male humans by female tapirs to past matrimonial exchange with the
Tanimuca involving a period of uxorilocal bride service (ibid, 104–7). Instead, these beings seem to
represent in the Andoque case different negative forms of channeling sexual energy, as desiring
someone too much can render the desiring person vulnerable to different kinds of distraction from their
principles of origin by outside elements. Failure to recognize the nonhuman nature of these beings and
the consequent sexual seduction by them seem to represent and aggravate the seduced person’s
weakness of the soul (mo̰no̰i), which should remain strong if it is to recognize the things and beings in
its environment and to keep predation by other human and nonhuman beings and groups unidirectional.
Consciousness and self-restraint, particularly sexual one, thus emerge as critical for avoiding
disadvantageous exchanges with other centers and for gaining a more advantageous position to control
these exchanges. We can learn about the relation between these seduction cases and spiritual power (and
lack thereof) from their description as accumulative factors, alongside others, in determining people’s
fate. In people’s accounts of the young Agustín’s snake bite in the rubber tapping camp in the Mesai
River in 1960, they attributed the difficulty of elders to save his life to his previous seduction by
dolphins disguised as a woman that he desired, itself the result of applying a perfume previously sent to
him by his malicious absent father (see Chapter 4). The snake bite was thus incurable because the
victim’s soul had already been taken by the dolphins, who reportedly swam in the river by the camp
after he was bitten, waiting for him to join them.
Familiarizing and Mastering Nonhumans
Whereas nonhumans prey on humans and familiarize them through illnesses, accidents, conflicts, and
other misfortunes, healing procedures are viewed as counter-predatory acts. The prevention of such
aggressions by nonhumans and the enlistment of nonhumans for healing purposes, as well as for sorcery,
depend on the degree to which humans familiarize nonhumans. These practices thus represent critical
manifestations of power, understood as asymmetrical exchanges of agencies, vital principles, and
bodies, as well as avenues for magnifying and employing it. After discussing such familiarization by
humans, I will discuss the counter-predation involved in healing.

286

Offerings play a crucial role in the processes of familiarization, both to prevent aggression by
nonhumans and enlisting them for various purposes, and are important for this dissertation’s discussion
of ontological manipulation and hetero/homosubstitution. The Andoque terms ḭtasé/ɵtasé, or ɵpáha are
used for referring to offerings, a notion expressed in Spanish conversations through the term
pagamento.110 This term is widely used throughout Colombia and captures the idea of repayment and
equivalence conveyed by ɵpáha, which is also used in other contexts to designate exchange between
different people. However, Andoque interlocutors find the words ḭtasé and ɵtasé, which are the more
common terms to refer to offerings in the native language, and especially those made at ceremonial
dances, opaque. These terms point to wider notions of familiarization that go beyond mere repayment.
As shown in Part II, when prepared with specific origin myths and intentions in mind, coca, tobacco,
and manioc products serve to familiarize others, endowing them with subjectivities that are more
benevolent and less predatory toward the producer and their kin. This function of offerings is referred to
as “calming down” (sḭ́ ) the recipient. When used as offerings for powerful nonhuman entities, the
impregnation of these substances with such meanings and intentions is doubly important, alongside
stricter observance of preparation etiquette and production of smaller quantities than for daily
consumption. We have seen above several examples of such offerings that can be made before hunting
to ensure game and avoid harms by the site-persons or before clearing a forest plot for building a house
and gardening to ensure the family’s safety. As we will see in Chapter 11, they are also made at
ceremonial dances to prevent disease, accidents, and conflicts on the group level. Offerings can also be
made at different moments after hunting, and not necessarily after every single killing. Some people do
it periodically upon finishing the preparation of vegetal salt as a blanket defense against harms incurred
during the preceding weeks of hunting routine. These offerings reflect the substitutive sense conveyed
by ɵpáha, which is shared by neighboring peoples in Northwest Amazonia. The offerings to the ownerpersons are an alimentary counterpart to the game that the hunter hopes to obtain or has obtained (K.
Århem 1996, 192), and replace the owner-persons’ “personnel,” namely, the game animals as well as
trees and other resources killed or destroyed and put to human use in different ways (ETSA 1996, 229;
von Hildebrand 1983, 57).

The forms ɵtasé and ḭtasé differ in that the verbal prefix ɵ in ɵtasé means “to make,” thereby referring to the presentation
of the offering, while the verbal prefix ı̰ ́ ’ in ḭtasé denotes a change in the state of the recipient. I hereafter use ɵtasé to refer to
the action of presenting the offering, and ḭtasé to refer to the offered item.
110

287

As Clara van der Hammen shows for the Yucuna, where coca is symbolically construed as people, the
offerings do not substitute merely animals but also humans (1992, 317). Indeed, among the Desana, it
seems that the alternative for substituting animal souls for vegetal offerings is to replace them with
human souls (Reichel-Dolmatoff 1971, 82). In the Andoque context, individuals oppose the practice
(that they attribute to others) of making recurrent offerings to the owner-persons of animals and fish
before hunting or fishing to secure large amounts of game, more than a family needs for subsistence.
Based on the equivalence between human and animal life, it is held that the owner-person would thus
become accustomed to the exchange, deny the hunter game if the latter fails to provide an offering, and
prey on the hunter or his family members. This demonstrates the inversibility of familiarization, where
the fed pet can master its owner if the latter fails to act as such. It also shows that the offerings replace
not only the animals that the hunter wishes to kill, but also his own health and life, and those of his kins,
that he wishes the owner-person to spare. Interlocutors also hinted to this logic in their frequent
assertions that to name powerful owner-persons, mention their feats or narrate their myths, one must
make them proper offerings. Otherwise, the owner-person may seek out the person mentioning them
and, enraged at being provided nothing, inflict harms on this person and their kins. In these cases, no
animal life is involved, and it is as if the offerings substitute for humans, and vice versa. Offerings thus
operate in a heterosubstitutive logic where animal and human life are interchangeable with vegetal
substances.
In his analysis of the Miraña’s coca mythology and culture, Karadimas specified that the exchange for
game is not the coca powder itself, but the words that coca, together with tobacco, produces in the
mambeador’s stomach and communicates through his mouth, in the opposite direction of meat produced
in the forest and attended to by the master of animals, which enters the person’s mouth and then stomach
(2005, 197–98). This verbal dimension of offerings allows for greater symbolic flexibility, such as the
one we have just seen, where offerings now replace an animal, now replace a human, but also for a
greater manipulation of the owner-persons. García, who analyzed a Murui-Muina formula for asking the
masters for game, similar to the Andoque formula to approach the site-person of Tar Waterfall, argues
that by referring to game animals as fruits, the human speaker identifies himself with the nonhuman
master for whom animals are fruits, seeking to downplay the hunt’s transgressive dimension, and to
define the relationship with the master in terms of commensality instead of predation (2018, 262–68).
Thus, beyond mere substitutes, offerings allow the giver to manipulate the recipient and the relationship
between the two in ways that would suit the former. While Northwest Amazonia seems to stand out
288

within the Amazonian landscape in the substitutive mode that offerings can take there, the manipulative
mode of offering—where it serves as a vehicle for persuasion or commensality with nonhumans—is
attested outside it as well (e.g., Chaumeil 2010; Gutierrez Choquevilca 2010).
M21 presented an example of such a manipulative offering, with the father-in-law falling into the trap
after consuming the honey caguana, casabe, mambe and tobacco paste. In a version of that myth told to
me by the elder José*, which explains the origin of One Leg (a diablo in the form of a violent tapir leg
detached from its body), the father-in-law manages to avoid falling in the trap the first night his son sets
it, because his tutelary spirit (ɨpǵánn) realizes the danger, makes him trip on a tree stump next to the trap
and look at the ground to see that the leaves covering it were hiding a hole. The next night, the son
leaves the ritual offerings for the mysterious person, and after consuming them, the father-in-law is not
warned by his tutelary spirit, does not trip on the stump, and falls into the trap. Offerings can thus help
the giver impose on the recipient a perception of reality that serves the former’s interests.
In the version of the same myth documented by Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 108–13), we find further
details shedding light on offerings. The morning after preparing the trap, the son finds the hole empty
and the yarumo leaves covering the hole broken. His father asks his son with what leaves he has covered
the hole, telling him to try others, because “the yarumo is his friend” (i.e., a friend of the nocturnal
visitor). The son uses other leaves, placing a ripe pineapple on top of them, on which his father
comments after the desired result has not been obtained: “Son, you do not know. All of that are his
friends. The caguana made of mauritia fruits, umarí, patawa, peach palm, all of that he makes by
himself” (ibid 110–11, my translation). The father then instructs his son how to prepare the honey
caguana, a substance whose efficacy should be understood as deriving from its independence from the
nocturnal visitor, who does not make it as he does the other beverages. More precisely, the honey
caguana allows to familiarize the father-in-law because it is the combined product of the son’s wife, who
prepares manioc starch beverage embodying an affinal element alien to her father-in-law, and of the
cannibalistic bees, who, created from the burned skull of an ocelot-star person, follow a predatory jaguar
principle, and transform the starch beverage into honey (Jara 1996; Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 125).
As we have seen in Chapter 6, and like honey, the cultivars whose products are used as offerings—
tobacco, coca, and manioc—are also associated with “above”—in this case, with the river source. This
provenance grants these substances the ability to serve as predatory agents. Still, to guarantee the
direction of predation—that these agents help the offeror familiarize the recipient, and not vice versa—

289

the offeror must prepare these substances himself (or in collaboration with his wife and immediate
family members), ideally from his or his family’s gardens. This guarantees that the offeror suffuses
these substances with his own thinking and odor to counter or modify the recipient’s thinking and odor,
aligning them with his own.
My interlocutors explained that owner-persons would only consume the offerings made by individuals
whose odor they have come to know. In the case of coca and tobacco, they say that offerings prepared
for important occasions—to secure an owner-person’s help for a complicated and dangerous mission, or
for a dance—should be made from young plants, that have not been overly harvested before. Based on
people’s statements concerning the risks of coca sale (see Chapter 13), I take this recommendation to
imply that the plants from which offerings are made may become marked by the recipient’s subjectivity
and the thoughts and actions in which he or she engages after consumption, making it a better bet to use
young plants whose familiarization is easier than those of older plants that may have been affinized
through past offerings. Another measure to ensure offerings’ familiarizing capacity is to iterate the
verbal formulas accompanying them in the native language, the Andoque members’ seat (kupa).
However, this is a thorny issue because people under 50 years old do not speak and pronounce it
correctly, while for youth, even more passive mastery is restricted. There is no consensus whether
offerings made in Spanish are as effective as those made in Andoque, and at different times I received
contradicting answers to this question by the same people. The most frequent response, however, was
that although the Creator, who acts as an intermediary between people and nonhumans, understands all
languages and can be approached in Spanish, he prefers each person to approach him through the
language that he gave their people upon creation.
Offerings thus display multiple dimensions beyond the substitution of one thing for another, the aspect
that the term ɵpáha (literally, “make value”) specifically denotes. These dimensions include
manipulation, persuasion, and deception, which convey notions of familiarization more strongly. It
appears that the terms ḭtasé/ɵtasé, which are more commonly used to refer to offerings, especially those
made on ceremonial occasions, have a more encompassing meaning that covers these more thoughtshaping aspects. The notion of odor may be central to understanding these enigmatic concepts. While
Jon Landaburu does not necessarily associate the suffix -sé with odor or body, preferring to see it as a
marker of reification (pers. comm., November 2021), the olfactory references made by my interlocutors
regarding the ḭtasé offerings, along with the role of smell in bodily transformations, suggest a more

290

specific hypothesis. The term sé is found in the previously mentioned noun séa, meaning “musk”—
associated with the aggressive aspect of odor that influences surrounding beings—and also refers to
elements such as fabrics, clothes, masks, or outward appearances. These are bodily attributes that can
affect the predatory behavior of the one wearing them (see M16). As noted in Chapter 3, The verb ɵsé,
indicating the act of feeding—primarily children and pet animals—is about forming the recipient’s body
to promote consanguineous, non-predatory dispositions towards the feeder. Therefore, I propose that the
ḭtasé offering modality aims to mold the recipient’s scent, thereby transforming their body into one that
is less predatory toward the offeror and altering their agency to be more advantageous for them. The
ḭtasé offering operates in a gift logic, serving as an extension of its producer, from whom it is thus
inalienable. Through this gift, the offeror intervenes in the recipient’s subjectivity, hijacking the latter to
their own state of mind, group, or reality.
As Karadimas (2007, 106) argued in his advocacy for a greater inclusion of the gift perspective in
Amazonian ethnography, predation represents an ideology more than a practice, such that, in some
cases, gifts are proffered to justify predation, or are otherwise informed by its logic. For the Andoque,
offerings should be viewed as gifts that function within a framework of predatory relationships.
Specifically, in venatic contexts, these gifts are intended to forestall retaliatory predation (ḭpáha,
literally, “obtain value”) by owner-persons following a human’s initial predatory act and to recast the
interaction as a trade. Based on the different levels of agency, subjugation, and alienation that we have
discerned between pets, orphans, and cultivars, we may say that the ḭtasé modality establishes and
sustains a master-pet relationship between the feeder and the recipient, who becomes, to some extent, an
agentive ḭéna̰ and an extension of the offeror, while the ɵpáha modality represents an exchange of far
less agentive and more alienable orphans/cultivars between two human and nonhuman captains.
Nevertheless, the gift, thought-shaping dimension of the offering (ḭtasé) is essential for the substitutive
aspect (ɵpáha) and logically precedes it, as it can lead owner-persons to accept vegetal offerings as
equivalents of animals or human lives. This is similarly observed in Fisi’s narration of M5, where the
offering in its ɵtasé form precedes its ɵpáha form: “Egret of the Center has made the offering
(ɵyaɵtaséai) and paid him (ɵyapáhai).” The gift characteristics of the offered vegetal substance also
underscore the power asymmetries sought, as gifting allows the offeror to gain advantage and dominate
the recipient through the given item (Gregory 2015, 13–14; Mauss 2002). Fisi’s narration of M5 also
hints at this dimension. When in their ɵpáha form, offerings may be demanded from the eventual

291

recipient, similar to how Egret of the River Mouth demands them over and over from Egret of the
Center. By contrast, the recipient appears to ignore the offerings in their ɵtasé form, which are described
only from Egret of the Center’s point of view. While one might want to be a trade partner exchanging
alienable or benign items, they would not want to be on the receiving end of an item that acts as a
potentially harmful extension of its giver.
Offerings are particular cases of feeding. Similar to other cases where familiarization is achieved by
feeding (Fausto and Costa 2013, 158–59), the offering displaces the recipient’s previous relations to the
substituted element, so that the recipient would no longer perceive it as kin. This is illustrated by Lady
Tar Flower, who, after accepting the hunter’s offerings, presents him with her “fruits,” which are the
animals of her site. Lady Tar Flower’s characterization of the animals as fruits rather than people
suggests she no longer regards them through the prism of consanguinity and commensality, but rather as
non-agentive things she can consume and offer without compunction. By inducing owner-persons to
alienate the animal they own, the hunter aims to avoid retaliation that follows the homosubstitutive
logic, in which his life, or that of his kin, would be forfeited in recompense for the animal life taken.
Therefore, calming the owner-person down (sḭ́ ) signifies a shift from homosubstitution to
heterosubstitution, or from a relationship of predation, in which the owner-person may seek revenge, to
one of trade, in which it would not. The trade performed may be seen as homosubstitutive from the
nonhuman’s point of view, who receives a cultivar (offering) in exchange for a cultivar (animal). The
non-reciprocation of life that Andoque members seek to impose on nonhuman beings after their own
initial predatory act reflects a clear attempt to prevent symmetrical exchange of bodies, persons, and
vital principles by an ontological manipulation of value. This may be summarized by the following
table:

In Chapter 1, I discussed the hierarchical distinction between captains and orphans underlying the
heterosubstitutive exchange of the captaincy system. Similarly, the ɵpáha (hetero)substitutive offering
mode implies hierarchy. The primary intention of saving human lives which lies behind the performance
of this kind of offering, draws it closer to the logic of sacrifice, a practice which is largely deemed
absent from Amazonian animism but characteristic of Southeast Asian animism (K. Århem 2015b;
Sprenger 2015). The sacrificial logic involves providing nonhuman elements to spirits or deities to spare
human lives, thus assuming a hierarchy between human beings and the nonhuman elements used and
manipulated to save the former. This hierarchy is discussed by Sprenger (2015), whose focus on
Southeast Asian sacrifices of domestic animals leads him to emphasize the human-animal hierarchy it
implies and compare the centrality of animal husbandry in that region with the centrality of hunting for
Amazonian animists. According to Sprenger, in Southeast Asia, agriculture and animal husbandry
encompass hunting, while in Amazonia, hunting encompasses agriculture, as he demonstrates by citing
Descola’s discussion of the Achuar’s perception of the predatory dispositions of manioc plants (2005,
584). This Amazonian reference also compares well with the Andoque data. Among the Andoque, as
previously seen, cultivars epitomize docility and submission, comparable to orphans. As inferior to the
person cultivating them, vegetal materials can be used as substitutes for that person in negotiations with
nonhuman entities seeking their harm, much like domestic animals can be sacrificed to save the life of
the human beings rearing them in the Southeast Asian context. In a fractal manner, anyone can act as a
captain, possessing orphans in the form of cultivars, which they can then trade with nonhuman captains
for their orphans or cultivars, namely animals. This is another context emphasizing the hierarchical
nature of the Andoque’s version of animism.111 However, this tendency to create hierarchies is not
exclusive to the Andoque—as observed, heterosubstitutive offerings are also common among other
Northwest Amazonian groups, which exhibit hierarchical structures in inter-human interactions. The key
distinction lies in whether hierarchy is paired with reciprocity. In Tukanoan practice, vegetal substitutes
for human or nonhuman souls aid nonhuman reproduction (K. Århem 1996, 192–93; Cayón 2011, 144–
45). In contrast, the Andoque do not acknowledge such reproductive aid; their offerings are more aptly
characterized as non-reciprocal.

111

Interestingly, the lower hierarchical position of plants, which makes them an appropriate “payment” (ɵpáha), derives from
their status as prey. In other words, the substitutive offering is underpinned by the relational scheme of predation, similar to
how the hierarchic notions of the heterosubstitutive-captaincy fluvial system are underpinned by notions of predation
manifested in the homosubstitutive river system.

293

While the appropriative dimension of familiarization in the Amazonian context generally implies a
predatory aspect, a specific type of offering that can be made during the River Turtle-Carrier Dance is
particularly predatory. During this dance, the organizer seeks protection from nonhuman beings and
their aggressive opposition to being used and consumed by humans by invoking Tofidei. This figure is
this dance’s owner-person who defeated malevolent animals and created the forest by transforming
anacondas into trees, and the game brought to the dance by the guests is offered to four of his pets,
namely, the main posts of the maloca, which are voracious anacondas in a tree form. Tofidei (“Pounding
Mauritia Juice”), who is said to live in (and is the site-person of) Parrot Savanna (Kɒ́’i Popái), which is
also called Pet Savanna (Ḭéna̰ Popái), is considered by the Andoque to be their god of war but can be
more precisely defined as the owner-person of mastery. His myth (M23), as narrated to me by Nestor
and Fisi and detailed in Appendix 1, is a crucial tenet of the River Turtle-Carrier Dance and is essential
for examining Andoque notions of familiarization not only as preventing harms by nonhumans but also
as a way of achieving mastery over them to attain different goals. The myth recounts how Tofidei
discovers his wife’s sexual affair with two dolphin-anacondas from the river mouth by feeding and
gaining the assistance of his wife’s pet (éna̰) parrot (kɒ́’i), which she has neglected. After killing the
lovers, he transforms his wife into the cacambra bird (kaó; Daptridus ater), instructing her to watch over
the merchandise (dohai) route from the river mouth for any enemies (yó’o). News of the dolphinanacondas’ death reaches those living downriver, who prepare for war. Anacondas, stingrays, caimans,
and other aggressive fish advance in big boats by water, while the trees, still anaconda people, come by
land, and cranes by air. Tofidei’s outnumbered people are afraid, prompting Tofidei to mock them,
comparing them to women “with manioc between [their] legs.” He then prepares a spear (fɨ’ɵfá), coats it
with black poison for hunting and kodi red paint, and raises it in the maloca’s patio in the face of his
enemies. They immediately transform into trees and stones—as do some of his men who witness his
feat—while the boats become islands along the Caquetá River.
This myth explains the origin of the “cold diseases” associated with anacondas and dolphins, to which
women are more susceptible than men. In Chapters 11 and 12, this myth will help us understand the
Andoque’s perception of Whites and related ritual transformations. Other narrators, including Fisi on
other occasions, made it explicit that the spear is, in fact, Tofidei’s penis (see also Landaburu and Pineda
1984, 102). In Raquel’s version, when Tofidei erected his painted penis, his sister helped by painting her
vagina in red with achiote and opening her legs in the direction of river mouth. On another occasion
when Fisi recounted this myth, he explained that this sister, called Lady Achiote (A’kosikn), defused the
294

enemies’ anger by laughing in their direction with achiote in the inner part of her cheeks. In José’s*
version, this woman is Tofidei’s other wife, and in Yiñékɒ’s version recorded by Landaburu and Pineda
(1984, 103), Tofidei marries his sister after vanquishing the enemy.
While people generally refer to this myth as the origin story of all forest trees, at other times Fisi would
say that it is only the origin of disfigured trees (those with bent trunks, cavities, or burls), while
Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 101) record several tree species mentioned by Fisi. By turning his enemies
into trees and stones, Tofidei curtailed their dangerous agency and rendered them beneficial for humans,
in the form of wood for construction, canoe making, plant remedies, etc.112 Because of this
transformation, the River Turtle-Carrier Band, one of the two dances of the red ritual specialization, is
called Transformation Dance (Ti Nni), in which the participants re-enact the war and Tofidei’s feat. The
phallic dimension of the transformation signals an interconnection between patrilineal identity and the
reduction of other beings’ agency. Here the identity of the individuals who were traded in the past,
besides war captives, also comes to mind, as these were matrilateral or otherwise non-patrilateral kin
defined as orphans, perceived to possess less agency, and effectively treated as objects. Additionally,
Tofidei’s incestuous marriage at the end of several versions portrays endogamy as a fantasized solution
to the dangers that affinal relatives pose to the maloquero’s rule. We have already observed in several
myths (e.g., M1, M3, M13) that the agency targeted for degradation belongs to affinal relatives: persons
safeguarded by the wife or her father. The husband seeks to diminish their personhood to utilize them as
resources for creating items such as the maloca, coca powder, or tobacco paste, which contribute to the
perpetuation of his patriline. A similar conception exists among neighboring peoples (García 2018, 418;
Karadimas 2005b, 130). This theme will be further explored in Chapter 11.
According to Tañe, Tofidei’s personnel turned themselves into mauritia fruits, so that he could crush and
mix them with manioc starch to create the bɨdɨ beverage, whose orange color is classified as red, peɒi,
the color of war, thereby gaining further strength from his men to fight his enemies. The offerings to
Tofidei in this dance include this beverage so that people can likewise overcome the beings surrounding
them, and turn them from enemies to pets (ɵéna̰, “to tame, create a pet”), whose actions can be aligned
with their own.

Compare to a similar yet more restricted transformation of the dance guests in M22, which is not considered the origin of
trees in general.
112

295

This shifts our discussion from defense against the aggressions by nonhumans and their pacification to
the greater degree of familiarization manifested in harnessing their agencies for human benefit. The pet
that helps Tofidei trick his wife’s lovers and kill them is the parrot, who gives its name to the site where
the hero lives (Parrot Savanna or Pet Savanna), and who is won over to Tofidei’s side when the latter
feeds him, which is what his original owner (namely, the wife) has failed to do. The same parrot still
informs maloqueros of different things before the dance they are organizing, such as bad weather,
problems among the workers, or what animals the guests would bring.
Unlike the situation reported for other Amazonian societies, Andoque members do not possess many pet
animals, and these are for the most part dogs—literally, “pet jaguars” (ḭéna̰ ḭño̰)—not wildlife, as their
Bora neighbors do (Lucas 2019, 283). During my stays and visits in Andoque settlements I saw only
single specimens of such wildlife: a monkey, a turtle, a parrot, and other birds; one man told me that he
had a pet paca when he was younger. Unlike the chickens grown by many families, these pets are not
eaten, and while some dogs are used for hunting, most of them are not trained for this task and are kept
as mere companions. Women and children are usually the ones who take animals as pets, feed and take
care of them, but this adoption is rather loose and lacks the commitment and intimacy reported in other
Amazonian cases (Descola 1992; Erikson 1987), as these pets can be neglected or forgotten after a few
days or weeks. For example, the members of one family adopted a suckling collared peccary when
chasing its herd, and initially fed him the oat shake prepared for their son, but then, when the family left
for a few days for the village, the piglet starved to death.
On the other hand, the mythical register makes many allusions to pets, and the shamanic discourse of
sorcery and healing is based on the help that pet spirits provide to practitioners. Andoque mythology
presents various examples of animals, such as Tofidei’s parrot, who assist a hero who initially bullies
them for no reason and then heals them. These animals, especially flying fauna like birds, bats, and
butterflies, then accompany (ɵ’ɵhɵ) the hero, providing him help and particularly privileged information
on past events or on things happening elsewhere, that helps him prevail.113 Like the hunt of the collared
peccary herd that ended with the (short-term) adoption of the piglet, and as in Erikson’s model where
taming is a compensatory mechanism for destroying the other through hunting (Erikson 1987), in these
myths the hero’s initial aggression is followed by his attempt to compensate the victim. However, and as

See, for example, Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 180, and the episode in the story of the orphan blow-piper, where a bat
tells the hero that his maternal uncles killed his father and where they hide, in M7 (Appendix 1).

113

296

Descola notes in his critique of Erikson’s model (1994a, 339), this is not compensation for
compensation sake, since its objective is to absorb into the aggressor’s self the alterity and agency of the
victims. The sounds emitted by these and other animals today provide people with essential information
about risks and opportunities and serve as important omens for things to come, whose deciphering
depends on the service of another pet—the person’s tutelary spirit, yono̰pǵi/ɨpǵánn, alluding to a sprout
(pǵ), or oéna̰, “my pet.” As we have seen in Chapter 7, the tutelary spirit is considered a domesticated
version of the auxiliary spirit tne’túi, imparted by Sı̰ ́di. While the latter appears in dreams as a jaguar,
the former appears in the form of a dog. The strength of this pet spirit helps the people it “accompanies”
in overcoming challenges and predation by human and nonhuman beings and accessing the mightier
power of Sı̰ ́di for sorcery, as we will see below. The pet differs from the orphan in that it represents a
higher degree of alterity from its master and, consequently, possesses greater agency. Based on the
examples I have collected, it appears that pets differ in species or bodily form from their owners. This
contrasts with orphans, who are also human, and cultivars, which are actively grown by people.
Therefore, while orphans can be seen as a specific pet category within the meta-affiliative master-pet
dynamic, transferring them to a third party presents fewer problems than revealing one’s connection
with the pets of the ḭéna̰ category, as will be discussed in Chapter 10.
Before the rubber genocide, the Andoque used to possess other entities that contained the agency of a
powerful Others, which was accessed by taming them and making them their possessor’s i’kɒi:
“valuables,” but could also mean “a toy.” Such entities included the yóʼőnn fulgurites (literally, “enemysegments”) and trophies from cannibal dances, such as skulls, bones used as flutes, and other body parts,
especially teeth. Jaguar fang necklaces, while scarce, are still possessed by some members, allowing
their owners to harness the jaguar’s predatory capacities for healing or sorcery. The idea behind this
practice is similar to the Miraña case, where the fangs contain the jaguar’s powerful spirit, and safe
access to it is possible by removing the fangs from the jaguar’s mouth, thus eliminating its physical
predatory potential and transiting the jaguar from the status of potential affine to that of real affine, i.e.,
consanguine (Karadimas 2005b, 86–88, 160–63). According to Karadimas, and as Lucas (2019, 345–53)
showed in her reconstruction of the Bora’s anthropophagous dances, this appropriation of the enemy’s
knowledge and power seems to have also been one of the ends for keeping, exhibiting, wearing or
otherwise using the body parts of consumed people, beside increasing the prestige of their possessors.
Such use followed the symbolic familiarization of the enemy in songs depicting him as a newborn baby
(ibid, 348).
297

The yó’őnn fulgurites are considered as especially potent and dangerous by Andoque elders and are
referred to as thunder-lightening stones because they contain the predatory power of this heavenly force,
metonymic of the river source and the might of the egret affine from upriver who imposes ancestry on
the center. However, this deity is converted into consanguinity by changing his name into Egret of the
Center. As Pineda convincingly argued, the yó’őnn embodies the thunder-lightning’s female daughter,
as the lightening participates in the formation (or “birth”) of fulgurites, and because, as Andoque elders
still say today, these stones allowed the manipulation of thunder-lightnings (Pineda Camacho 1979, 47).
Therefore, like an in-marrying woman, the yó’őnn must be familiarized to tame the destructive
capacities it has inherited from its progenitors and to allow its possessor to influence them. The
possession of such stones is depicted as incongruent with captaincy today because their owners would
no longer know how to control the rage they contain and would risk ending up devouring their kin. For
example, Fisi says that his grandfather Dóñékɒi, Yiñékɒ’s father, ceded his yó’őnn to another man when
he sought steering away from fighting, for which this stone served him well, to dance celebration,
because the stone was likely to provoke uncontrollable anger that would result destructive for his own
people in this new context. This echoes an anecdote told by Lucas, where a Bora captain and his wife
expressed fear of a jaguar fang necklace that they were entrusted with, worrying that they could not
control the unknown, predatory powers of the fangs (2019, 127–28).
These ideas concerning the dangers of yó’őnn fulgurites lead us to the asymmetrical and volatile
relationship with more abstract pets: the spirits on whom the shaman relies for different ends (Fausto
1999). As Fausto and Costa have shown, these pets are unique in being significantly mightier than the
shaman, who seeks aligning the agencies of these affinal entities to his own by familiarization. As such,
they must be properly fed and satisfied, lest their power overwhelm the shaman, who would
consequently lose control of their aggressiveness and become the spirits’ pet rather than their master
(ibid; Costa 2017, 41–48, 51). I use the term “shaman” to cover all ritual and esoteric specialization,
including the organization of ceremonial dances, sorcery, and healing. The Andoque categorize all these
specializations as tne’túo—the person who has gained access to the auxiliary spirit tne’túi, a process
taking place, as we have seen in Chapter 7, through the domestication of the tutelary spirit yono̰pǵi. In
other words, the taming and familiarization of spirits and nonhuman entities for shamanic ends depends
on a previous taming and familiarization—those of Sı̰ ́di, which are achieved by yoking the latter’s
predatory capacities to one’s patriclan origin (see Chapter 7).

298

The ambivalence as to the direction of domination in this master-pet relation should also be understood
as dialectical. The shaman does not familiarize the spirits “downward” by referring to them as his sons
or grandsons but “upward” by referring to them as his grandfathers (yo’tapɵ) and to himself as their son
(ɵ́tɵ). These appellations amount to strategically evoking meta-filiation, placing the shaman in the
position of the pet to elicit protection and aid from the spirits, which are a master’s typical actions
toward pets. While Bonilla (2016) used the term “parasitism” to describe a similar disposition employed
by the Paumari toward White bosses, the term “dialectics” is better suited to the Andoque shamanic
context. This is because, by portraying himself as the spirit’s pet at certain moments, the shaman seeks
to master it at others. This dialectical nature of familiarization can also be seen in the idea that the
consumption of non-Indigenous foodstuffs—those associated with Whites and traditionally grown or
produced outside the region, such as alcohol, onion, garlic, tomatoes, and canned fish—hinders one
from performing either cures or sorcery; some say that it even renders one’s body unamenable to both
kinds of procedure. While the consumption of certain psychotropic herbs, such as sita, mḭʼno̰éi, tɒ’di, or
taino̰ (yajé; Banisteriopsis caapi)—all of which Andoque elders claim to no longer possess or grow—
can facilitate communication with spirits for these ends, the adherence to a local diet is portrayed as the
very condition for such communication. It seems that spirits would not approve of the odor emitted from
a body containing the traces of such strongly flavored foreign foodstuffs (in contrast with milder ones,
such as bread) and would not recognize it as the body of a potential consanguine kin, from whom they
would normally accept offerings (or, in the case of a sorcery victim or healing patient, whom they would
accept as offering). In other words, to be able to familiarize spirits for shamanic ends, the shaman must
be viewed (or smelled) by them as “familiar,” that is, as kin.
The familiarization operating in assault sorcery emerges as particularly dialectical. Sorcery is expressed
through the verbs é’ekńi (“to bewitch”) or ti: “to do” something to someone, or “to transform” them as
something else. In Spanish, Andoque members make a distinction between brujería (“witchcraft”) and
maldades (“maleficia”) that does not exist in the native language. They say that while people can still
perform certain maleficia, nobody today practices “real” witchcraft. This is a distinction between “high
magic” and “low magic,” each implying different kind and level of familiarization of auxiliary spirits
and nonhuman beings.
The term maldades refers to the harm that can be inflicted on others by evoking mythic events where
such harm has occurred, or a similar state to which the sorcerer wishes to subject the victim. For

299

example, the sorcerer can “name” a pregnant woman’s body after unperforated objects, causing her to
encounter difficulties during childbirth. A classic example of maldad that people often mention is the
aging of a younger person, particularly someone of the opposite sex who has rejected the advances of
the maleficarum on the grounds that the latter is too old and unattractive. This is achieved by invoking a
story where Toucan does a similar harm to Lady Sloth (see M24, in Appendix 1), who has rejected him
for the same reason, and transforms her from a beautiful woman to the ugly animal she is today.
Although interlocutors do not explain it in this way, I suggest viewing the performance of such a
maleficium as the result of a process of familiarization consisting of two feeding actions. Firstly, the
sorcerer familiarizes the powerful entity, in this case Toucan, by feeding it with ritual offerings.
Secondly, the sorcerer hands the victim over to this entity, using such formula as “You who were
formed through this [story], go now and fight them for me” (haʉ bɵñe odi oinatiiɵ ɵñe oa ɵkntakn oma
nma nayóéfíi). Although the entity in question does not prey on the victim in the sense of consuming or
devouring them, once the harm possessed by this entity is inflicted on the victim, the latter becomes
incorporated into its personnel or the kin group of which the entity is captain. In Chapters 1 and 2, I
mentioned acting as the agent of exchange, rather than its patient, or object, as a precondition for
accessing and practicing power. It should be noted that the agents of exchange here do not include the
victim, who is passively transacted between the sorcerer and the spell’s owner-person. This exchange
relies on, and deepens, the asymmetrical exchanges between these two parties, as providing persons to
the owner-person is an additional step in acquiring mastery over the spell and its owner-person. This
logic also underlies the common idea that a person should not teach sorcery or healing spells to others,
let alone to non-kin, until after he or she has successfully applied them several times. Only then, as Tañe
explained to me, “you become the spell’s owner [dueño], and its power can no longer vanish.” It appears
that a person only achieves mastery over a spell once they have sufficiently fed the spell’s ownerperson, in the form of persons, whether victims or patients, that they have surrendered to it.
Nevertheless, the practitioner cannot abuse the spell or act whimsically towards its owner-person. A man
once told me that, as a child, he laughed when Yiñékɒ experienced an embarrassing incident, and as a
result, the latter cursed him that he would forever remain short by invoking a hero who inflicted a
similar harm on another in mythology. Several years later, when Yiñékɒ saw that boy singing in a
dance, he cordially told him: “One day you will be a man.” When I asked if he had also lifted the curse,
the man, who is indeed of short stature, replied negatively, saying that the spell’s owner-person would
have become angry with Yiñékɒ for practicing it and invoking him in vain.
300

The infliction of maldades can sometimes be facilitated by providing the victim with substances, such as
mambe, tobacco paste, water, etc., “charged” by the sorcerer with the specific curse or harmful mythic
episode. Conversely, sorcery categorized as brujería is considered more sophisticated also because it
does not depend on material substances and may not have any outward expression. This term refers to
the kinds of sorcery involving the ad hoc enlisting of spirits and nonhuman beings to perform different
hostilities toward others. For example, a sorcerer can enlist dolphins or deer to seduce the victim and
make them fall ill by providing ritual offerings to the owner-persons of these malevolent animals and
their myths of origin, or enlist other large animals to approach the victim’s settlement and leave aches
and diseases on the paths where people typically walk. One elder told me that in the 1970s he had
developed heel aches after walking along a path stamped with the footprints of collared peccaries that
had been sent by a Murui sorcerer. The harms caused by such sorcerers can also be perceived as their pet
ocelots; for example, another woman is said to have suffered knee problems caused by the same
sorcerer, and which that elder perceived in his dream as two ocelots that were hostile toward him as
well. However, a more powerful shaman can go beyond these pets and dream of a person, who would
then be the sorcerer who controls them; Yiñékɒ reportedly dreamt of a person wandering around his
people’s settlements at the same time as the ocelots and peccaries haunting them.
The ultimate expression of the enlistment of animals and spirits is the self-transformation of the sorcerer
into a powerful predator—a jaguar, harpy eagle, or anaconda—to devour the victim. Yiñékɒ is said to be
the last person to have affected such transformations, drinking to that end the liquid of bitter manioc
obtained during its filtering process and containing cyanide, to allow him to go under the radar of rival
shamans who reportedly relied on yajé and other more “conventional” psychotropic herbs. People say
that in this way he transformed into a jaguar after growing weary of the assaults of another Murui
sorcerer against his personnel. After drinking the manioc liquid, he remained seated in his mambeadero,
growling and roaring like a jaguar, mimicking a jaguar attack with his hands and body. According to one
interlocutor, at the climactic moment he left his maloca running to the forest, spotted a giant anteater,
chased it to its burrow, smoked it out, killed it when it attempted to flee, and ate its heart raw; according
to another interlocutor, he ordered his brother-in-law to go and shoot a nearby deer, cut out its heart and
tongue, and throw them away. In these stories, the rival died either on the spot or shortly after that
evening. While the interlocutors stress Yiñékɒ’s jaguar transformation, this action presumes the

301

simultaneous transformation of the rival into an animal that a jaguar can prey on, and that embodies the
rival’s reduction to passiveness and victimhood.114
The victims on whom these animals are set, or on whom the sorcerer preys when self-transforming into
a predator, should be seen as the food that the sorcerer provides to his pets as part of a familiarization
process. One such extremely powerful assault sorcery is ḭsiéso, which literally means “[transformation
into] a thing of their own [i.e., another person’s game],” and which involves the use of potent herbs to
establish communication with Sı̰ ́di, whom the sorcerer asks to devour the victim’s soul (mo̰no̰i), a few
days after which the latter perishes physically. These high ranks of sorcery are dangerous for the
practitioner, as his own life and that of his family members are at risk. Firstly, they are exposed to
counterattacks by sorcerers avenging the practitioner’s victims, and secondly, like any mastery
relationship, familiarizing Sı̰ ́di is a dialectical issue. Instead of the sorcerer mastering Sı̰ ́di, this powerful
deity can familiarize the latter and his family members if the sorcerer fails to provide him with his usual
“meals,” which tend to increase in quantity and frequency. “Like a dog that you no longer feed, it will
eventually eat you,” one elder explained to me. The outward expressions of Sı̰ ́di’s predation are
diseases, accidents, and other calamities befalling the sorcerer and his family members.
Further evidence of the dialectics of familiarization in sorcery is the fate of the practitioner’s soul, which
is said to go to Tatoañei after death. Tatoañei is a rock formation located at the headwaters of Macaw
River, and it is considered the origin site of sorcery and the herbs that facilitate it. Interlocutors say that
the sorcerer Fisidú’dɨ (“Stone Thunder”) acquired the capacity to self-transform into predators and
brought sorcery herbs to the Andoque from this site in the distant, pre-genocide past. The posthumous
departure of sorcerers’ souls to Tatoañei can be seen as their incorporation into the personnel of
Pópádɨkń, a rattlesnake god who is considered the site-person of Tatoañei and who is also called
Tatoañei in mythology. As phallic in body shape as any snake is, this bushmaster (Lachesis muta) is
extremely long (over two meters) and venomous, being the most lethal viper in their territory. Tatoañei,
the other personification of this rock formation, is a powerful symbol of male sexual aggressiveness.
According to Andoque mythology (e.g., M10; M20), and as befitting a being inhabiting a high place
upriver, Tatoañei’s sons prey on the daughters of Shadow Egg who live downriver from them by
These stories are reminiscent of Echeverri’s (2022, 148–61) description of Murui-Muina shamanic practice, in which the
shaman materializes diseases and moral dangers in game animals, and hunting them signifies victory over those ailments and
dangers. However, unlike the Murui-Muina materials, the Andoque stories do not carry the same moral connotations, as the
animals in their stories represent specific human enemies, rather than only disease or more abstract dangers to the social
order.

seducing and/or impregnating them. These sexual encounters result in illnesses (as in M20) or the birth
of mischievous beings, themselves unrestrainedly phallic (like Hummingbird Egg in M10; and see
Pineda 1979, 45–46 on the hummingbird’s phallic connotation). Sorcery, including the diseases and
fatalities to which it gives rise, is intimately linked with sexual conquest, similarly to other illnesses
caused when a person becomes consubstantial with animals through sexual contact. Andoque members
say that the Creator left Tatoañei and Shadow Egg in charge of illnesses and remedies, respectively.
Therefore, to bewitch and cause disease and death by sorcery, a shaman must communicate with
Tatoañei, just as he should communicate with Shadow Egg if he is to affect healing.
Another nonhuman being whom the sorcerer can enlist to attack others is the anaconda. Given its abode
in holes, it is believed that this powerful predator maintains an underground tunnel network called
“anaconda paths” (hɵpɵ ̰obɨ), through which a shaman can travel unnoticed in an anaconda form and
attack his rival by surprise. The enlistment of this and other animals for assaults is said to be possible
only within ancestral land, whereas certain maldades that draw on mythology can be performed even
outside of it. Another key characteristic of the anaconda, its mainly aquatic habitat, is evoked for healing
purposes. We shall now turn to examine this and additional forms in which nonhuman beings are
enlisted to aid humans and defend from both sorcery and such nonhuman aggressions, as discussed in
the preceding sections.
Healing: Countering Predation by Nonhumans
The final context of exercising power in relations with nonhumans to be considered in this chapter is
healing, which is aimed at countering predatory attempts by these entities to appropriate human bodies
and lives. However, this practice depends on the support of other nonhuman agents—the cures and their
owner-persons—implying that the healer engages in an asymmetrical exchange with these agents.
Some healing procedures, expressed through the verb ɵ’nó (“to cure”), are considered simpler and
involve only herbs or other remedies (ɵ’nó̰sé) but do not require spells. Others, which are often more
complex and are used to treat more severe diseases, may also include plants and other substances, but it
is the use of spells derived from mythology to achieve efficacy that distinguishes the practice as ǵ’a
(“cure by spells”).115 As with sorcery, there is no specific word for “healer” in the Andoque language,
and this specialization is also subsumed under tne’túɵ. However, in Spanish conversations, the
This distinction resonates with the Miraña’s perception of plants without masters, which can cure “by themselves,” and
plants with masters, with whom the healer must communicate in order to make the plant effective (Karadimas 2005b, 225).

115

303

Andoque, who seldom use the word chamán (“shaman”), refer to healers as curanderos, sometimes
designating those using herbal medicines to treat simpler cases as yerbaderos (“herbal healer”). People
generally refrain from referring to themselves as healers for several reasons, including the potential
dangers involved in healing, their general reluctance to declare ritual specializations, and the lower
esteem in which the healing specialization is held (topics that will be discussed in this and the following
chapters). However, they acknowledge that most fathers know the necessary spells to treat basic
pediatric conditions and cure food for their children, and many individuals may say that they know how
to treat the symptoms of several diseases or stabilize patients’ conditions. Nonetheless, they assert that
no Andoque member today possesses the knowledge and capacity that are only attributed to past healers,
who are compared to surgeons and could completely eradicate the disease by expelling the pathogenic
agent from the body. “There are no surgeons today,” Mario told me, “We’re all nurses.” The decline of
such “horizontal shamanism” where the healer interacts with animals to address a patient’s condition
after the disease has taken hold, as opposed to “vertical shamanism” that prevents diseases and
misfortunes on the collective level, is reported for other societies in Northwest Amazonia (S. HughJones 1994; Lucas 2019, 136–38). However, Andoque members attest that in past severe cases they
turned to healers from other ethnicities, such as Murui-Muina, Miraña, and especially Yucuna, Macuna,
and other groups of the Apaporis-Vaupés system, where such “surgeons” are said to still exist.
Healing among other People of the Center is described as a process of “cooling down” the disease’s heat
and “sweetening” the pathogenic agent and the patient’s body (Echeverri 2022; García 2018; Griffiths
1998; Karadimas 2005; Londoño Sulkin 2012; Lucas 2019). Karadimas and García describe similar
Miraña and Murui-Muina perceptions of medicinal plants as curing patients by cooling them down
through the water they contain or are soaked in, and also mention that these are owned by female spirit
masters (García 2018, 116–23; Karadimas 2005b, 229–31). In his analysis of Murui-Muina healing
procedures, García identifies a complementarity between cooling down and sweetening, where cooling
down involves a change in the condition in which a given entity is found, while sweetening involves a
change in the properties inherent to it (García 2018). In contrast with their neighbors, the concept of
cooling down does not figure as greatly in Andoque healing and general discourse as it does among
these other peoples, and they do not conceive of healing as sweetening. However, cooling down is
important for healing “hot diseases,” just as heating up is important for treating the “cold diseases” that
they stress more than their neighbors, and healing also requires a change in the patient’s properties, like
the one referred to by the Murui-Muina through the notion of sweetening.
304

Healing is associated with the river mouth and “below” as a counter-predation measure, given that
predation is linked to the river source and “above.” As previously mentioned, communicating with
Shadow Egg, the owner-person of remedies, is necessary for healing. Since Shadow Egg and his
daughters often defend against attacks by Tatoañei, it is important to understand sorcery strategies for
effective healing, and vice versa. In the myths featuring Shadow Egg and/or his daughters, different
elements of their environment, that, as such, should be regarded as their kin, are disguised and appear as
human beings to their upriver “predators”—those trying to extract them and use them for various
purposes. Accordingly, to protect the victim from illness predation, a healer must recover the active
“person” aspect of the victim, in contrast to the passive “fruit” aspect on which the predatory agent, or
the sorcerer manipulating it, tries to expand and exploit. In Goffman’s (1958) terms, we may say that
both parties try to define the situation in their best interest: the pathogenic agent tries to impose a
definition where it is a human being and the victim is a fruit, whereas the healer tries to impose on this
agent, and, equally important, on the victim him or herself, a definition where the former is an animal
and the latter is a person, who, as such, possesses an agentive principle to reject the pathogen and fight
back. In essence, sorcery and healing involve ontological manipulation, which depend on the graded
agency in the Andoque’s animism.
Because their affinization by the pathogenic agent is already underway, the patient is both part of the
problem and part of the solution. To diagnose the patient the healer must go beyond the information
provided by the former, who is asked about the places visited and dreams about sexual encounters. The
healer also smells the patient to determine what nonhuman scent has settled in their body. Since the
patient is part of the problem, the healer may blow chili smoke to make them cough and expel the
pathogenic agent from their body or use other techniques to startle and frighten the patient into expelling
the pathogen, for example by sprinkling cold water on their naked body. The healer also prescribes
certain dietary rules to the patient and their family based on the patient’s specific disease or condition. It
is relatively common for the healer to recommend avoiding the consumption of large mammals such as
tapirs and deer, which have an increased capacity to affinize people. The patient’s steering away from
nonhumanity may take different forms, and the dietary rules are adjusted accordingly. The healer may
prohibit foodstuffs that resemble the disturbed condition in shape or texture, such as advising someone
with a deep cut to avoid juicy fruits or the fat domesticated pig, since the wound may worsen to
resemble these substances, producing more pus instead of drying up. During the healing and recovery
process, the patient must also maintain a distance from people emitting strong, alluring body scents,
305

such as the odors of sweat, sexual activity, menstruation, or pregnancy, as well bitches in heat and male
dogs aroused by them. These odors have the potential to stimulate the nonhuman pathogenic agent,
thereby increasing its desire to couple with the patient, contrary to the desired outcome of the treatment,
which is diminishing it. Full compliance with the healer’s instructions is necessary for the treatment to
work, as it signals the patient’s “faith” in the healer. The Spanish expression tener fe, which translates
the elusive Andoque term hnnḛ́’ḭ́ (“say yes”), refers here to one’s allegiance to the person who seeks
preventing their slide into nonhumanity. On the other hand, a failure to comply points to the weakness of
the patient’s spirit (yono̰pɨi) and their intensified nonhuman state. Because the patient is considered part
of the problem, a healer is unable to cure himself except for mild conditions whose overcoming involves
only herbal plants and does not require invoking the owner-persons of the cures, and certainly not if the
ill-condition is caused by an extremely powerful entity, like a human sorcerer or a site-person.
Healing is perceived as a power struggle between the healer and the pathogen, and the latter can also
turn against the former. One elder, for example, said that after treating many patients, his arm started to
hurt, which he took as a sign that he should be more selective in the patients he admits, lest he be
exposed to too many malevolent nonhumans. The predatory capacities of the auxiliary spirit tne’túi is
crucial for defeating the pathogen. Another elder explained to me that the necessary approach for
healing is to “arrive [to the treatment] with anger (mntúi), not fear, because if you are afraid the disease
has already won over you. If I see an ill person, I tell myself, ‘Thanks to my spirit (tne’túi), nothing is
going to happen to me,’ and I start healing.” The strength and clarity of thought provided by a person’s
access to the auxiliary spirit are crucial elements for a healing procedure to work. In Andoque members’
accounts of pre-genocide cannibal dances, and as Pineda Camacho also reports for the Murui-Muina
(2005, 226), one of the functions of these dances was to strengthen the connection between the
participants consuming the victim, and especially the shamans officiating the dance, and Sı̰ ́di to gain
better access to tne’túi to heal severe illnesses, as well as improve sorcery abilities, which also depend
on one’s tne’túi.
Whereas for any person dreaming about a flashlight’s malfunction predicts a general weakness of
thought, for a healer it may predict a patient’s death caused by the healer’s insufficient access to tne’túi.
In cases where the pathogen is sent by a sorcerer, curing is also a struggle between the sorcerer and the
healer, with the sorcerer trying to bewitch those attempting to prevent him from consuming his victims.
This is said to have occurred in the 1960s, when a non-Andoque sorcerer bewitched Andoque members

306

and the elders who treated them, and, as previously noted, reportedly deterred Yiñékɒ from treating
Agustín, whose snake bite was indirectly caused by a Yucuna/Carijona man.
While Shadow Egg is generally considered the owner-person of the counter-predatory principle, the
anaconda is specifically associated with many healing procedures, particularly those used to treat “hot
diseases.” In M20, Shadow Egg’s daughter seeks refuge from Tatoañei’s son by moving closer and
closer to water. She first finds refuge in Acouchi’s hole in the base of a tree trunk, then she is hidden by
the anaconda, and finally, under the wing of the kingfisher, who dives into the water with her. In a
variant of the myth that serves as the origin for the Armadillo Dance for the protection of children and
parturient women and narrated by Fisi, Tatoañei’s son is identified as a jaguar, and the anaconda
impregnates the girl and gives fern (ti’ñḛdɨ, Pteridaceae sp.) to this fugitive, who, after being taken
underwater with the kingfisher, gives birth there. Associated with the river and the river source, the
anaconda instills in the girl a cool principle necessary to overcoming the heat implied in her previous
state, when she was sealed in the “transformation pot,” and to counterbalance the cooking process to
which she was about to be subjected. The anaconda’s association with the curative fern is typical for its
association with trees and plants in general, and medicinal plants in particular. A healer who relies
mostly on herbal medicines told me that all the trees and plants were once anacondas, before Tofidei
transformed them into vegetal beings, and that to use them to cure, a person must turn to them as “my
grandfather anaconda” (noyo’tapɵ hɵpɵ), asking them to cool down (ú’ɵ) the patient’s body.116 Owing to
its aquatic habitat and association with the river mouth, the anaconda can counter the hot diseases
associated with the sun and the hinterland (and, by extension, with the river source), by cooling them
down, just as the water inside trees protects them from drying up under the scorching equatorial sun.117
Unlike Shadow Egg and his personnel who are plants and game animals, the anaconda is predatory in its
own right, and is positioned opposite to the sun—like in M15, where it eats Sun’s daughter. In another
myth recorded by Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 182–83), various psychoactive and medicinal plants
were created from the head of a presumptuous young anaconda who did not listen to his father’s
warnings and died while trying to devour a tapir that was too powerful for him to overcome.

The curative attributes of trees are also attested in M12 (in Appendix) where U’ḭknñemn defends from the beetle’s
flatulence by hiding in the trunk of a peach palm. For a similar myth and notion among the Miraña, see Karadimas 2005,
226–29.
117
In M17 (see in Appendix 1), the hero cannot resist Sun’s flames and ends us being burned, because he cannot produce salt,
which represents semen. In other words, his body does not contain vital liquids.
