307

While the anaconda helps cure hot diseases, the red paints of kodi118 and achiote helps cure cold diseases
associated with the river and with Whites in men and women, respectively. To use these substances,
people rely on M23, where these plants help Tofidei and his sister—the owner-persons of this
treatment—to defend from their downriver enemies. Chili is used for various conditions, and its origin
from the sky above (see M10) explains why it can counter attacks by chthonic forces, such as Fi’du who
inhabits a burrow and treats human children like vegetal beings “from below” by cooking them as if
they were yam tubers (M19).
Healers turn to various other plants and animals to effect cures, with the general idea of making the
patient resemble them in certain respects. One elder told me about a certain owl that is evoked to protect
the fetus during pregnancy and avoid miscarriage, because its nest is remarkable in remaining firm
wherever it is built and never falls. Rubbing the bark of a forest tree pɨdadɨtakń on scars, which renews
its bark annually, helps skin regeneration and scar disappearance. Another elder reportedly cured his
son’s severe stuttering during infancy by putting a cicada known to sing continuously in his mouth.
However, this same treatment is now considered responsible for this son’s excessive chattering. This is
why healing involves not only making the patient resemble the plant or animal in question but also
controlling the extent of this resemblance, which can be seen as another instance of mastering the
direction of familiarization.
In addition to these nonhuman auxiliars, people stress that to succeed, the healer and patient must
confide in the Creator, whose intervention determines the treatment’s outcome. Similar statements are
also reported among the Miraña, who contrast themselves with the “People of Animals” of the VaupésApaporis who dedicate tobacco and coca to animals for healing. In contrast, they self-identify as “People
of God” who dedicate these substances to the Creator in such situations (Karadimas 2005b, 30). These
statements also resonate with Bora and Féénemɨna discourse, where healers no longer rely on animals to
aid them as in the past, but instead use tobacco, which is considered the ancestral principle of human
beings, and as such helps them prey on nonhumans (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 71; Lucas 2019, 135–40).
However, it is important to remember that in the Andoque case, evoking the Creator is a technique of
domination. Therefore, while healing is enabled by resorting to different nonhuman entities, from
Shadow Egg and the anaconda to various animals and the owner-persons of specific medicinal herbs,
evoking the Creator and providing this entity, as well as to the other nonhuman beings involved, with
118

My interlocutors referred to this plant as carayuru, hence it may be Fridericia chica.

308

the familiarizing substances of coca and tobacco, aim to control both the direction of familiarization for
preventing the patient’s affinization, and the extent of resemblance between the patient and nonhuman
auxiliars.
To conclude the topic of taming nonhumans and their enlistment for sorcery, healing, and other ends, it
is important to note their voluntary dimension and distinguish them from involuntary ones: the arrival of
animals to people’s mambeaderos to consume coca and other ritual substances. Contrary to the
intentional familiarization of nonhuman beings to render them as pets and align their agencies to those
of their human masters, the arrival of nonhumans to people’s mambeaderos and commensality of ritual
substances with them is the result of the mambeadores’ neglect. In a song from the Fruit Dance, the
singer-dancer scolds the host for allegedly taking care of and feeding a certain scorpion:
Why do you, over here,
Care for him?
Coca Scorpion (hí’píe tɒdɵ),
Tobacco Scorpion (tá’u tɒdɵ).
You care for him (tú).
You, me, it will sting [us both].

Animals arrive in the mambeadero when they are summoned there by the mambeadores who tell stories
related to them or express discourses over social behavior and institutions related to them, without
complementing them with the parts from the origin stories of these beings depicting their demise or
limits to their power. Nonhumans then interpret such discourse as an invitation to stay, and with time,
claim an increasingly central position there. In the case of the scorpion, this is manifested in bites, and in
the case of other nonhumans, in various physical, mental, and social disorders they inflict on the maloca
residents to affinized them. Animals arrive in the mambeadero not only when they are offered words,
but also when they are provided with the coca prepared and consumed there by humans. This is why
mambeadores tend to burn in the fire the husk of coca leaves that resists filtering or carefully rub the
accidentally spilled coca powder within the mambeadero area, so it does not spread outside it and attract
unwanted beings. Such purposeful ways of discarding of coca are the material counterpart of the
discursive ways of rejecting nonhuman beings by telling their complete origin stories, and their intention
is the same: to control the extent of human-nonhuman relations and the direction of familiarization
taking place between them.

309

As demonstrated in this chapter, the relationships between human and nonhuman centers are
characterized by a continuum of familiarization, wherein each party seeks to tilt the potentially
symmetrical predatory exchange in their favor. This tilt aims to create a beneficial asymmetry, allowing
one party to appropriate more bodies, vital principles, and agency from the other party than what it
surrenders. In the next chapter, we will explore how power dynamics among human centers are
influenced by and instrumentalize these asymmetries with nonhumans. However, interested readers are
first invited to embark on a short excursus into (and out of) the “House of the Missing,” a theme from
Andoque cosmology that offers a neat topographical model for the human-nonhuman dynamics
discussed in this chapter.

310

Excursus: In and Out of the House of the Missing
During my fieldwork, I was captivated by the stories that people told me about the “House of the
Missing” (nihɵ́ɵ síɵ́hɵ ḭpɨko) in a hushed voice, as if it were a very dangerous issue. These stories serve
here to reflect on the discussion of the previous chapter, as the place they depict and the dispositions that
people enact in relation to it offer a neat model for the familiarization dynamics discussed throughout
that chapter. I first heard about this house after the drowning of the non-Indigenous worker at the
Araracuara waterfall in August 2018, because people interpreted his disappearance as an incorporation
into the House of the Missing located underneath the waterfall. Several weeks later, Irene told me
another story on such a house located near “Transformation Lake” (Tinsí) (T1, Irene, 6/2/19):
One late afternoon, Genipa Flower’s (Fɵ́ta Taihá) wife asked him to hunt undulated tinamous (foí) for their
daughter. He took his rifle and went toward Transformation Lake, where there were many such birds. After he shot
one tinamou, several men appeared and invited him to their maloca. He refused: “My daughter is hungry, and I am
only going to fetch some tinamou for her and go my way.” Suddenly, two of these men grabbed him, took away his
rifle, and beat him with it until he collapsed and lost consciousness. When he woke up, he was lying in the front yard
of a big maloca, with his rifle beside him. Upon entering the maloca, he saw many pretty young women inside and
his father—who had died old and wrinkled many years before—sitting down and sieving coca, now young-looking.
“Son, have you arrived?” asked the father, and Genipa Flower did not reply. His father then offered him some
mambe. “I haven’t come here for mambe,” replied the son, who still had some mambe in his cheek. “Then eat,”
offered the father but Genipa Flower refused, stating that he had not come there to eat. The father then offered him
one of the women, but Genipa Flower said that he had not come in search of a woman either. Genipa Flower stayed
at that maloca for seven days, without accepting any food or drink and without sleeping, standing next to one of the
main poles. After a week, the maloca residents invited him to go pick coca leaves. He joined them with his rifle.
When in the garden, he excused himself to urinate, walked slowly away and picked a ripe red chili that he saw there,
and, at a sufficiently large distance, ran away to Transformation Lake, where he had been captured, and from there
found his way back home. “I was taken,” he told his relatives upon his return, “I don’t know what kind of people
they were, because my deceased father was among them.” He took the chili that he had picked there out of his
pocket, but that chili was now dry, as if it had been smoked. A few weeks later Genipa Flower’s wife refused giving
her mother-in-law chili sauce, so the latter went in the late afternoon to look for chili in the garden, which lay far
away from their maloca and close to Transformation Lake. As his mother did not return that evening, Genipa Flower
understood that she was taken away by those same people, because a woman does not have coca to help her think
and defend herself like that man did.

Irene learned this story from her grandmother, who had allegedly known Genipa Flower in her youth
and had seen the smoked chili. Later, I discovered that Transformation Lake is not an actual place with a
permanent physical location, and that any lake where humans are transformed into nonhumans is called

311

“Transformation Lake.” This story incorporates various key elements of the generalized predatory
dynamics between humans and nonhumans discussed throughout Chapter 9 in spatial terms of entering
and exiting a certain house. Particularly, it shows how nonhumans attempt to create consubstantiality
with humans in the form of commensality or sexual relations to familiarize them and incorporate them
into their society. The story also includes the perception of conjunction between the animals, their sitepersons, and the dead, as the latter lead a perpetual existence in the invisible malocas of the animals in a
state of consubstantiality with those who have brought about their physical disappearance through
illnesses, accidents, sorcery, and sexual encounters with diablos and malevolent animals. The double
sense of the English term “missing” translates the duality of the Andoque term hɵ́ɵ, as those living in
this house both lack the important feature that would render them living humans with human kin—
namely, a body—and long to reunite with their living relatives. For this reason, they try to seduce them
into joining them there, and people without relatives in such houses are said to be more easily released
by the residents. Women are an easier prey to such attempts of affinization because they do not consume
regularly or at all the “familiarizing substances” of coca or tobacco like Genipa Flower and other men.

Figures 17–18. Irene Andoke Andoke (left) and Raquel Andoke Andoke (Photos taken by the author).

When told by most people, such stories serve as a warning for others not to wander away from home in
the afternoon, let along actively seek out these houses, lest they fail to resist the temptation to reunite
with their dead relatives and become trapped there as well. Raquel told me a similar story when
312

explaining to me about the dangers of excessively mourning a beloved person, which hampers the
mourner’s ability to move on with their life. Raquel also attributed her story to Irene and Fisi’s
grandmother, who was allegedly the niece of the hero, here called Yitai. Her story (T2, Raquel, 8/7/19)
coincides with Irene’s story in that the hero’s mother is refused rotten manioc leaves for the preparation
of pí’na̰ sauce by her daughter-in-law and is captured by the missing while going to her garden in the
afternoon, in the same way that Genipa Flower’s mother is refused chili by her daughter-in-law, leading
to her capture in Irene’s story. While in Irene’s tale, the arrival at the House of the Missing is entirely
accidental, in Raquel’s story it is the result of curiosity. Yitai arrives there before his mother and
following his daughter’s sudden death, an event which leaves him consumed by grief in such a way that
he abstains from eating for three months and only consumes coca and tobacco to learn what has
happened to her. After three such months he leaves his house, thin and weak. A broad path takes him
“below” (kaknka) to a big maloca, where he sees his daughter and many other people whom he knows to
be long dead. Happy to reunite with him, his daughter offers him caguana beverage which he refuses,
and the maloquero offers him coca powder and tobacco paste which he likewise rejects. During the days
he stays there he only consumes the coca and tobacco that he has brought with him and sees another
newcomer arriving every couple of minutes. The maloca residents are happy to receive those who were
good people, whose loss is lamented by the “People of Above” (kadaiño̰e), directing them to the right
side of the house. Conversely, they transform into harmless stones, devoid of agency, those newcomers
known to be wrongdoers in their previous life, laying them at the left side of the maloca, lest they try
transgressing against their new kin as well. After several days there, the man in charge of pounding the
coca leaves, who recognizes Yitai from his previous life “above,” offers to take him back home, leads
him to the path through which he arrived, and warns him against looking behind or telling people what
he has seen there. Yitai takes chili, achiote fruits, and mḭʼno̰éi herbs for sorcery that he sees around the
maloca, and after the coca pounder leaves him, he cannot resist looking back and seeing that man
running away in the form of a tapir. Yitai continues walking until finding himself in a pond surrounded
by mauritia palms (a cananguchal), which he realizes to be the entrance to that maloca. From there, he
easily finds the way home, where he accepts food and drinks from his wife, a sign that he has finally
overcome his daughter’s death, but does not tell her or anyone else what he saw. When his mother
disappears a few months later and he sees her footprints leading to the mauritia palm pond and her
basket lying on the ground, he understands what has happened to her, and is not absorbed by grief,

313

because he knows that he will meet her there again someday in the future. This finally happens after he
breaks his promise, telling people what he has seen in that house, and then dies.
Similarly to Irene’s story, Raquel’s story about the House of the Missing is also a cautionary tale,
conveying the widespread Amazonian belief that excessive grief and remembrance of the deceased pose
a threat to their living relatives (Karadimas 1999; Taylor 1993b). However, while Irene’s story depicts
the arrival at the House of the Missing as an accident to be avoided at all costs, Raquel’s story contains
three elements that suggest an alternative interpretation where people may intentionally venture into that
house to acquire knowledge and skills. These elements are the hero’s intentional fast to detach himself
from living kin to learn about his daughter; the mention of remedy fruits and particularly the shamanic
mḭʼno̰éi herb he takes when leaving the house, and his name, Yitai, whose meaning Raquel claimed to
ignore, but that Fisi often translates as “training” or “initiation,” as the verb yita means “to learn/study.”
Despite this, Raquel’s narrative suggest that Yitai’s apprenticeship was driven by potentially dangerous
curiosity and uncontrolled feelings. Conversely, Fisi clearly expressed to me the intentional, trainingrelated approach to the House of the Missing.
I learned about this interpretation when I returned to the Andoque reserve after a short stay in Bogotá in
March 2019. During my stay in Bogotá, I had my own mystic experience involving the use of
psychotropic substances and a strong sensation of visiting during the trip the House of the Missing,
which had captured my imagination throughout my fieldwork. The following month, during a
mambeadero session at Fisi’s maloca, I shared my experience with him and his sons, seeking validation
of my own interpretation of the event or any other insights they may have had. Although my narration
was followed by cumbersome silence, the following afternoon, while he was lying in his hammock, Fisi
called me to teach me about that enigmatic house (T3, Fisi, 13/4/19):
“One can arrive there when one gets drunk with yagé (ayahuasca) or wild tobacco. What one sees in these trips is
real. In the beginning, all animals were crickets, sɒ’sɒ: beetle-cricket, ant-cricket, deer-cricket, acouchi-cricket,
armadillo-cricket. After them came the clans: beetle, deer, ant… These were already the Piercers, those who spoke,
who knew fire, who knew the pot [for toasting], trees [for construction], names [who started naming things], they
started building houses. Because the houses [that existed] before them [those of the animal-crickets] were piles of
leaves and thorns, like the leaves of that coconut plant that grows over there, in the forest. Whenever they tried to do
something good, it turned out malign; this is why the Piercers transformed them into animals when they cursed them
with the Creator’s word. They transformed them into white-lipped peccaries, collared peccaries, deer, tapirs, to be
able to do good things [once they were consumed]. We, the descendants of the Piercers, speak better than they did,
we only eat food cooked by fire and no longer eat raw meat, while the forest fruits are left for animals—mauritia and

314

all other fruits. But if we kill too many game animals, I need to go there [to the forest] and give them [the animals]
something in return for what we’ve killed; and then I become a captain. And if I don’t repay them, their god, what
we call the diablo, nhaJ́tiɵ̋ (“that which was made for them”) will take me in exchange for the animals I’ve killed.
Then someone else, one of my sons, or even you, if you drink yajé, can arrive to that house and see me. [Inside the
house people ask you:] ‘Do you want to eat?’ [You say:] ‘No.’ [They ask:] ‘Do you want coca?’ [You say:] ‘No.’ If
you don’t eat, you don’t mambeate (mambear: consume coca), you win. [They say:] ‘Ah, you came for that… This
is a remedy, take it, this is what you need to do [to use it]. This is remedy. That is a maleficium. That is a
maleficium. And that’s it.’ Then your drunkenness passes, and you leave the house, and ask yourself: ‘But where am
I?’ You’re outside, then you find the path in which you have come, you walk it, and then you find yourself at your
house. Then you recall: they showed me this herb, they showed me that herb... You go looking for it, find it, and
then you use it, but you cannot tell anyone; you can only use it. This is the principle for us, in our territory, who
knows how it works in the Uitoto territory? So, when you told me about the people you saw there [during my own
experience], I recalled of them. But those are the dead of Bogotá, who knows what happened to them, how they
died, why they arrived there... And the next time you go there, they will teach you things.”

Fisi’s explanation makes three important contributions to our discussion. First, it highlights that human
beings who have been killed and affinized by nonhumans can also play a positive role as mediators
between living people and nonhuman guardians of spells and remedies. Second, it reveals that living
humans can arrive voluntarily at the House of the Missing, particularly during initiation processes, such
as the one I experienced as an anthropologist studying the Andoque traditions. This contrasts with the
popular interpretation of the House of the Missing as a place to be avoided, because ritual specialists and
captains seek to enter this dangerous place during apprenticeship to gain knowledge, as they are
confident in their ability to leave it voluntarily after acquiring it. It is revealing that the person who
provided me with this interpretation, was Fisi, the person whose authority and possession of traditional
knowledge is the most widely acknowledged by other Andoque members. Fisi’s explanation shows that
apprenticeship and the acquisition of ritual knowledge and power depend on the ability to resist
affinization by nonhumans and to selectively incorporate nonhuman features. If we consider the House
of the Missing as a spatial model for the dynamics of human-nonhuman familiarization that have been
explored throughout this chapter, then Fisi’s explanation shows that a person’s capacity to master
nonhumans and exploit their powers is represented by their ability to actively go in and out of the House
of the Missing, rather than being passively caught there, which represents familiarization by nonhumans.
Finally, Fisi’s statement that a person capable of warding off harms by nonhuman beings becomes a
captain underscores the interconnection between this position and people’s protection from nonhumans.
This connection is also manifested in the other direction: a captain’s prestige and capacity of mobilizing

315

people depends on his demonstrated success in preventing predation by nonhumans, particularly through
the ultimate means of managing relations with them—i.e., ceremonial dances, as will be explored in
Chapter 11. Conversely, a captain’s failure to protect his personnel from the nonhuman world would
result in decline in his prestige and following.
In the next chapter, we will examine the secrecy commanded by the coca pounder in Raquel’s story and
the nonhuman teachers dwelling in the house in Fisi’s explanation, as part of a larger discussion of interhuman power dynamics and the ways in which they are affected by human-nonhuman dynamics.

316

Chapter 10. Power Dynamics Among Human Centers
Having explored the power dynamics among human and nonhuman centers in the previous chapter, this
chapter shifts our focus to relations among human ones, which are organized around notions and
practices of kinship more explicitly than human-nonhuman relations. Deviating from the Dravidian
model prevalent in most Amazonian societies, the Andoque’s cognatic kinship system considers all
relatives on both parental sides as consanguine kin, but also contains an inherent agnatic bias, where
members of one’s clan—whose membership typically follows the father—are considered “more kin.”
We shall recall that, in the past, besides war captives, “orphan” maloca residents who were the
maloquero’s matrilateral kin or otherwise relatives not pertaining to his patriclan, could be traded as
slaves. From the perspective of any given individual, the members of other clans, including consanguine
kin, and even more so those members of other ethnic groups, have a different origin and formation
(haǵtı̋ o) from their own. The Andoque cosmo-social relations can be described by a concentric model: an
agnatic core followed by cognatic consanguinity, then real affinity and, finally, the alterity of enmity and
potential affinity:

Figure 19. The concentric model of the Andoque’s cosmo-social relations

Two Andoque terms designate the unknown Other: yóʼo and saámḭ. Yóʼo means “enemy,” as well as any
Indigenous or non-Indigenous person who is not related to the speaker by blood or marriage, and who

317

represents potential danger. Children were once cautioned by their parents to avoid irritating visiting
strangers, who, as yóʼo, may bewitch them. On the other hand, saámḭ is the term employed by figures in
Andoque myths—animals in their former or parallel mode of existence as humans—to address unknown
or non-kin figures. When narrating these myths today, Andoque members translate saámḭ using the term
paisano, following the colloquial use of the word among Indigenous people in Colombia for other
Indigenous individuals. However, outside the mythical context, the term saámḭ most frequently means
“lover”—a person with whom one engages in sexual activity outside the social norms of accepted
marriage practices—and, more generally, can also designate non-kin with whom relations are not
regulated and are characterized by mocking. Bridging the gap between the mythical and current use of
the term is the notion of potential affinity that exists among human groups lying outside the scope of
consanguinity and real marital alliances, and which extends to nonhuman entities with whom marriage
per se cannot be contracted and thus matrimonial exchange takes other, a-social forms, such as
predation. Indeed, mythology frequently attests to slippage between the two practices among its
“humanized animal” figures. Hence, between yóʼo and saámḭ, the image of the Other ranges from an
enemy to a sexual partner, whose respective unpredictable dangers and seductive forces derive from
their existence outside one’s kinship network.
In this chapter, I address the two interrelated questions: What are the power dynamics between people
pertaining from different centers with distinct origins, and how do these dynamics influence, and are
influenced by, the previously examined relations with nonhumans? The following sections discuss
themes such as women exchange, anthropophagy, incest, sorcery, ritual competition, and secrecy.
Through these discussions, I explore how Andoque members attempt to achieve asymmetries in
appropriating bodies and agencies from other Andoque and non-Andoque clans in their vicinity or on
their ancestral land, and how they counteract similar efforts by rival centers. I argue that these dynamics
unfold against the backdrop of antagonistic relations with nonhuman beings. Rival human centers are
perceived as continuous with nonhuman ones or instrumentalized in managing relations with them. This
antagonism also impacts the tension between agnatic and cognatic principles, a topic underexplored
among the People of the Center, that helps understanding the significance of the clan and affinal
exchanges for these people. By highlighting the continuity between inter-human interactions and the
human-nonhuman asymmetries explored in the previous chapter, this chapter aims to reveal the
complexity of power dynamics among diverse agentive centers. Additionally, I highlight how these
dynamics play out within a historical context marked by demographic decline and recovery efforts, the
318

depletion of oral traditions, the rise of modern representative politics, and significant changes in
marriage practices. I thus try to capture several main contemporary dynamics and reconstruct previous
ones insofar as their underlying logic helps understanding today’s reality.
Lumping together Andoque and non-Andoque clan centers is not without problems. In recent history,
members of surviving Andoque clans lived in proximity and shared economic and ritual activities, and
most of today’s elders who are versed in different traditions were initiated by the same man—namely,
Yiñékɒ. This shared history causes the Andoque to sometimes view members of other clans as sharing a
center with them, while in other contexts, they see them as belonging to different centers. While Yiñékɒ
strove to establish one Andoque center headed by one captain in the aftermath of the rubber genocide
(Chapter 4), my interlocutors assert that he foresaw a moment in the future when population growth
would require multiple captains, each one leading his own clan, and prepared individuals from younger
generations to eventually lead their clans. Even Fisi, who typically upholds the previously mentioned
claim that the Andoque have always had only one sole cacique, acknowledged on different occasions,
like other members, the internal strife among Andoque clans. If not in quality, then in degree, other
Andoque centers emerge as distinct from non-Andoque ones—they are perceived as less dangerous.
Marital exchange is often preferred with them, and sharing knowledge with them is seen as less risky.
Power Dynamics in View of the Human-Nonhuman Continuum
Power dynamics among human actors cannot be understood separately from the adversarial interactions
between humans and nonhumans explored in the previous chapter. Travelers in the nineteenth century
remarked on warfare among ethnic groups in the Caquetá-Putumayo region, often involving the capture
of wives or individuals of both sexes for the slave trade or cannibalistic consumption (Marcoy 1869,
386; Crévaux 1883, 371, 375; von Spix and von Martius 1981 [1831], 235, 244–45). While the Andoque
sometimes married individuals of other ethnic groups, they preferred to obtain spouses from other
Andoque clans. Consequently, they were more alarmed by raids from other clans seeking women than
by slave raids led by the Murui-Muina and Carijona (Jara 1995, 157). My interlocutors often mentioned
rampant pre-genocide warfare among the Andoque clans, both through overt and covert means, the latter
including summoning epidemics to annihilate entire rival clans, such as the Tinamou and Bat Clans,
which were eradicated by measles before the Casa Arana period (see also Gómez López et al. 1998,
122–23). Venturing into another clan’s territory could have deadly repercussions, as evidenced by
stories passed down to my interlocutors from their ancestors. Even accidental run-ins between different

319

clans on forest paths could spiral into violence, leading to murder or rape. Regardless of whether these
conflicts resulted in the capture of slaves, wives, or human bodies for consumption, the primary goal of
this violence was to strengthen one’s clan by appropriating external persons and bodies, who could then
be offered to external agents, either non-Indigenous or nonhuman, as slaves or human sacrifice, in
exchange for material or spiritual support.
As was demonstrated in Chapter 4, the post-genocide recuperation process involved changes to
mythology that were aimed at downplaying aggressions and antagonism among Andoque clans and
instead emphasize these clans’ shared destiny, centered on economic activity and exchange with nonIndigenous agents. Landaburu illustrated this shift through the myth on the war of the Speaking Tree,
where the enemy fighting the center—the center being the Eagle Clan, as the narrator belonged to that
clan—transitioned from the Deer Clan to Egret of the River Mouth (1993, 148). Nevertheless,
antagonism and suspicion between clans persist to this day. When a man from the Sun Clan and his wife
relocated to the Atta Ant settlement after a family tragedy, onlookers from other clans opined that he
was making a big mistake, as these new neighbors would do anything, even steal his wife, because they
belonged to another clan and were endowed with a different thinking, a different principle (otro
principio).
The pervasive suspicion toward members of other clans and ethnic groups is deeply connected to the
predatory dynamics between human and nonhuman beings, as discussed in the previous chapter. People
often doubt others’ capacity to resist these predatory influences, suspecting they might be dominated by
nonhumans, or at least are more susceptible to such domination, rather than being in control themselves.
A common way to express this is by referring to others’ “lack of faith” (no tienen fe), which translates
the quality of not being a hnnna̰kńní, or “yessayer.” This shortcoming alludes to the weakness of the
tutelary spirit (yono̰píi) and a lack of adherence to their clan’s teachings. Often, after telling me about
the dangers caused by powerful nonhuman beings, my interlocutor would say: “but today, people no
longer believe in that; for them, everything is a lie (la gente ya no lo cree; para ellos, todo es mentira).”
Those “people” would typically be members of other families and clans, including elders, as well as
younger people from the speaker’s own family. Those “non-believers” are said to go hunting even in
ominous weather conditions, or feed their children game that should be avoided for the young. A lack of
faith is often cited as a reason why some individuals overhunt, overfish, or neglect to make necessary
offerings to owner-persons, explaining both the tragic retaliation exacted on these people by the latter, as
well as their frequent encounters with diablos and other malevolent beings. As was discussed in Chapter
320

9, the patient’s “faith” (hnnḛ́’ḭ́ ) in the Creator and the healer’s power is vital for the success of healing
procedures, as it signifies the patient’s adherence to humanity and rejection of consubstantiality with
nonhumans. Conversely, a person’s lack of faith in the teachings of the patriclan and the broader human
group—subsumed under “one’s origin”—along with their disregard for warnings, indicates the
weakness of their tutelary spirit and increased susceptibility to falling prey to nonhumans.
In Londoño’s analysis of how the Féénemɨna perceive nonhuman predation on humans, he notes that
people’s critiques of others for exhibiting “animal speech” and being dominated by animals aim at
correcting the immoral and asocial behavior of the criticized individual and ratifying common moral
standards (2012, 48–68). However, the accounts that I heard from Andoque members of the
susceptibility of other people to familiarization by nonhumans were expressed behind these people’s
backs and as such could not serve to correct their behavior. While such accounts might serve to reinforce
moral standards among listeners, they must also be considered within the broader context that involves
competition for power and prestige between clans and maloquero families. Within this context, a
narrator may attempt to question or deny the legitimacy of the criticized person to lead others or hold
ritual activities. To follow such a person or allow him to carry out ritual would entail not only social
problems, but may also result in illnesses, accidents, and death.
For example, after repeatedly hearing from the members of a certain maloca that a publication by
another anthropologist was “full of lies,” I bought a copy in Bogotá and read it in their maloca. That
anthropologist had primarily collected her data among the members of another clan, and my hosts were
eager to point out inconsistencies with their clan’s traditions, referring to them as “lies.” When I read
aloud that clan’s version of a myth, which diverged in some crucial respects from the version that they
had previously shared with me, my hosts concluded: “If they are telling this story in this way, it’s no
wonder the X [an animal, one of the beautiful and dangerous beings] always hangs around their
settlement!”
It should be emphasized here that the attribution of specific misfortunes to attacks or retaliation by
nonhuman entities, which was discussed in the previous chapter, is far from unanimous among Andoque
members, with the divergent interpretations of the same mishap reflecting claims about other members’
inferior competence to manage relationships with these entities. Rubio’s* insanity, mentioned in the
previous chapter, illustrates this well. Members of other clans view this sudden mental decline as part of
a series of retaliatory strikes by a powerful site-person against Rubio’s clan, following gold excavations

321

inland that had not been authorized by this site-person. Conversely, his own clan, particularly the
excavation leader, attributes his episodes to his past work on a gold mining raft, associating them with
heavy drinking during that time.
Similarly, some interlocutors attributed the health issues faced by two individuals, as well as a violent
confrontation between two brothers that took place shortly after a ceremonial dance, to another
maloquero’s failure to properly organize the dance and provide its owner-person with the appropriate
offerings. Conversely, members of the host maloca argued that these health problems started a long time
before the dance and the violent conflict had many causes, including sorcery done years earlier to one of
the brothers involved in it. In this manner, attributing misfortunes to attacks by nonhumans suggests a
non-differentiation between the victim (or their family members) and nonhuman entities, as the latter
cannot control exchange with these entities and are purportedly prone to being familiarized by them,
potentially putting others at risk. Conversely, attributing such mishaps to other factors denies this
continuity.
Non-Andoque Indigenous individuals can also be suspected of insufficient knowledge that exposes them
(and others) to harms from nonhumans. While interlocutors often express appreciation of their nonAndoque Indigenous relatives or friends who are well acquainted with their ancestral territories and their
site-persons and can thus safely lead these Andoque fellows through it, they also note that some
neighboring Indigenous communities are inauthentic and lack such fundamental knowledge. This is
because they no longer speak their respective native language but have adopted that of another group, or
they do not speak it correctly, which they believe impedes proper engagement in spiritual dialogues to
ensure well-being. Other communities are said to have lost this knowledge because of their early
exposure to non-Indigenous schooling, and yet other individuals and communities living outside their
ancestral lands—such as those living within the Andoque’s ancestral territory—are thought to lack the
essential knowledge needed to conduct appropriate ritual procedures specific to their current location.
As explored in Chapter 8, such claims are linked to land claims. However, they should also be
understood within the framework where nonhuman entities are an agentive side in territorial
contestations because one’s failure to conduct necessary ritual procedures within the territory reflects
one’s vulnerability to nonhuman aggressiveness.
Beyond merely suspecting that members of other clans and especially non-Andoque groups are potential
victims to nonhuman aggressiveness, my interlocutors mentioned ways to actively turn them into such

322

victims. In Chapter 7, we discussed the victimization of other people in the context of human-nonhuman
relations, whereby a dreamer transfers their ominous dream elsewhere to spare themselves and their kin
from predation and familiarization by nonhumans by exposing other people to them. This scheme of
action manifests in other contexts where a person may seek to assimilate other human centers to
nonhuman ones in order to divert such fate from themselves. For instance, if the theme of the
dangerously seductive dolphins arises during a mambeadero session in a manner that might summon
these beings to seek out and attack any of the attendees or their kin, participants may laugh about the
sexual promiscuity of a distant individual—often a woman—so that the eavesdropping dolphins pursue
this indication and affect their harms elsewhere, away from the present gathering. Another illustration of
this tactic is the reported past practice of dicing the meat of large pests, such as collared peccaries, that
ravaged people’s gardens and distributing it among others. This was done so that the animals would be
drawn to the gardens of those who received the meat, thereby sparing the gardens of the original victims.
My interlocutors also described this practice as one of the principles of an englobing Amazonian geocosmopolitics. As Nestor explained to me during a mambeadero conversation that took place a day after
a severe gun incident that cost a teen his life:
“Every Indigenous people—the Uitoto, the Miraña, the Yucuna, everyone—when its elders notice that something goes
wrong, that the weather (tiempo) becomes dangerous, they talk about it in the mambeadero. When they meet, they
mambeate (ellos mambean), they tell stories, they ask each other: ‘What do you think about the weather?’ [after
hearing the answer, they say:] ‘ahhh, this is so’ (así es). This way, they analyze the weather together, and they push
away the bad thing elsewhere (empujan la maldad a otra parte), so it will happen there, and not where they live. And
this way every group with its elders pushes the weather along the river. And because here [among the Andoque] the
elders do not convene and mambeate and analyze the weather [together], all these bad things befall the Andoque, who,
on top of that, live right in the middle between the Yucuna and the peoples of the Mirití and Apaporis [Rivers], and
the Uitoto and the Putumayo [River]. Each people turns to its own god in its own language, and this god does both
good and evil, one cannot tell him ‘Don’t do evil,’ one simply asks him to do it elsewhere.”119

Indigenous elders from all nations are believed to not only push away evils to protect themselves but
also to bring about misfortunes similar to those happening to themselves during times of grief. During
the same mambeadero conversation, the members of the household discussed a murder that had occurred

119

The beliefs underpinning this practice mirror another widespread Amazonian idea: that life, souls, and vital energy are
limited and scarce, and as such they merely circulate among beings, who, unable to create new ones, must appropriate them
from others (Santos Granero 2009b, 14; Taylor 1993b, 658).

323

in Araracuara about three weeks earlier, where a Murui-Muina man had killed a Yucuna. “This made
everything dangerous,” Nestor explained to me, “one must be cautious. We the Indigenous, when
something like that happens to us, it’s not from sorcery, but from sorrow that we say: ‘Why is it
happening to us? The one who makes fun of it (burlar)—let it happen to him! And we push that thing
elsewhere.” For this reason, my interlocutors emphasized, both on this and other occasions, that upon
receiving such grim news, it is important to express sympathy for the victim and their family. If one fails
to do so, yá’dosé—the mournful spirit of their powerful elder relatives that roams the vast stretches of
the region’s forest on nights of grief—might target and afflict the unsympathetic individual with a
similar misfortune. This demonstrates how the boundary between humanity and nonhumanity, which
people are reluctant to cross, renders kinship distinctions among humans (kin, affine, non-kin) more
flexible and relative, highlighting their performative nature. While the transfer of misfortunes elsewhere
is rooted in, and reinforces, the perception of those people as non-kin, who can thus be delivered to
malevolent nonhuman forces, expressing empathy towards those suffering, whether near or far, is a
strategic move, by which an individual identifies with the victim as kin to exclude him or herself from
the predatory rage of the mourners.
Transforming other human beings into prey for nonhuman entities, thereby pushing them outside the
realm of humanity, also has implications for the relationship between the agent facilitating this
transformation and the nonhuman predator. As discussed in the previous chapter, sorcery involves
offering human victims to nonhuman entities, in a way that contributes to establishing or maintaining an
asymmetrical familiarization between the sorcerer and the relevant nonhuman entity. The
anthropophagous dances antedating the rubber genocide are arguably another example of the use of
other human beings to nurture asymmetrical relations with nonhumans. Certainly, these dances,
common throughout the Caquetá-Putumayo, were rich in symbolism and, like other rituals, cannot be
reduced to one function or meaning. Similar to their neighbors, the Andoque are not eager to talk about
these dances nowadays and did not provide me with more than a few partial and contradictory accounts
passed down to them by their parents and grandparents. Like Pineda’s Murui-Muina sources (2005,
226), my interlocutors maintain that the victims in these dances could be both prisoners from other
groups and transgressive group members, with the corresponding objectives of terrorizing external
enemies and disciplining group members by making justice known, respectively. Contrary to what is
described in Marcoy’s testimony concerning the Miraña (1869, 387) and in Karadimas’ reconstruction
(2001), my interlocutors did not mention any practice where the prisoner was assigned the role of a son324

in-law. They also did not hint at any process of de-affinization or “de-enemization” of the prisoner,
where his powers might be extracted and assimilated or his body parts used for healing, as described in
relation to other groups (García 2018, 140–42, 298–312; Karadimas 2001, 86, 161; Lucas 2019, 123–27;
Pineda Camacho 2005, 232–24), although we cannot rule out that such beliefs and practices existed
among the Andoque as well.
Andoque members concur that these dances were organized by powerful shamans, who used them to
communicate with Sı̰ ́di, the cosmic cannibal principle and leader of jaguars—the Andoque counterpart
to the god Juziñamui, to whom human sacrifices were made in the Murui-Muina dances (Pineda
Camacho 2005). They also described the communication with Sı̰ ́di as crucial for gaining the ability to
heal extremely severe illnesses and deformities, such as hɵpɵ yayo’fía (“anaconda egret”), bei yayo’fía
(“fish egret”) and tiḭsu yo’fí (“animal transformation egret”), which are inflicted by the owner-persons of
anacondas, fish, and animals as retribution for harming their respective protégés. Here a comparison
with evidence concerning the Murui-Muina may also be revealing. In the cannibal chants of this group,
the singer (and flesh consumer) identifies as Father Buinaima and expresses the intention to eat the
victim, referred to as Buinaima, in the form of various fruits and fish. Buinaima occupies in the MuruiMuina mythology a somewhat equivalent position to the Andoque’s Egret (Yo’fí), in being the son of
Juziñmui (who is also referred to as the Creator) who establishes order and culture (García 2018, 122,
n.108, 159; Urbina Rangel 2010, 41),120 and thus stands for captaincy in the same way that Yo’fi does so
in Andoque discourse. According to García, these chants include a dual game of “de-enemization” and
“re-enemization” of the victim, where he is portrayed as a distinct captain, and, as such, a powerful
affine, before he is consumed as a fish or fruit—an entity with lesser retaliatory agency—by a captain
positioned vertically above him in a consanguineal relationship (Father Buinaima) (2018, 303–4). It is
possible that the Andoque participants in anthropophagous dances in the past acquired the capacity to
heal severe yo’fí illnesses and disfigurations by identifying the victim with the captain (yo’fí) of aquatic
and terrestrial animals. Consequently, by consuming the human victim, they could prey on these
powerful nonhuman entities and thus heal or reverse the harms inflicted by them. The symbolic
consumption of the owner-person, required to heal a human who has been severely disfigured or made
ill by that owner-person as recompense for harm to its nonhuman creatures, makes the cannibalistic
dances a clear representation of homosubstitutive logic. Interestingly, without these dances, the yo’fí

120

Several Murui individuals married to Andoque members also pointed this equivalence out to me.

afflictions are now considered incurable, hinting at the limits of compensation through heterosubstitutive
offerings.
The healing capacity granted through cannibalistic consumption does not only depend on
communication with Sı̰ ́di, but also on commensality with him. My interlocutors described how
participants used to emit growls resembling voracious jaguars during these dances and were required to
maintain a certain distance from each other to avoid contact with other dancers. Any physical contact or
stumbling, as well as faltering singing voices, were regarded as omens indicating that that individual
would be the next victim. In addition to the general significance of stumbles and faltering voices as
ominous signs during any dance (see Chapter 7), the distinctiveness of this ceremony lies in the
prohibition against touching other dancers. This sets it apart from other dances where physical contact
between dancers is common, such as male dancers holding hands or female companions placing their
hands on them. This practice, along with the growling sounds and the consumption of human flesh,
contributes to the transformation of the dancers-consumers from social human beings into jaguars,
which are solitary predators. The transformation into jaguars appears to have aligned the participants
with Sı̰ ́di, who consumed human flesh through their mediation, much like offerings to owner-persons in
ceremonial dances and other contexts are mediated through their consumption by the human
participants. This shows that one of the purposes of the literal predation of past Andoque people on other
human beings enabled to appropriate the forces of nonhuman entities such as Sı̰ ́di to establish
asymmetrical familiarizing relations with other nonhuman entities, which in turn acted to prevent
counter-predation on the consumers and their kin.
As per the information shared by Fisi with Jara (1995, 157), the victims chosen for anthropophagous
dances at times included prisoners who were captured in retaliatory raids following the abduction of
women. This connection underscores the link between cannibalism and marital exchange, as well as the
connection between negative reciprocity and symmetrical forms of alliance. It also highlights the
broader affinal nature of rival human centers, which will be discussed in the next section.
Predation and Influence Between Affinal Centers
Women could be given to the party that has lost kin to cannibal consumption, and marital exchange has
served, until recently, as compensation following fatal aggressions, in order to prevent future reprisals
and counter-reprisals. I learned of three such cases from oral historical accounts by my interlocutors,
spanning from the 1950s to the 1980s. These cases involved Murui or Féénemɨna individuals who asked

326

Andoque fathers to give them their daughters as wives, either for themselves or their sons. These
requests were based on past murders committed by the father’s relative against the non-Andoque’s
relative, whether involving cannibalistic consumption or not. This practice is compensatory in that the
woman of the transgressing party contributes to the reproduction of the aggrieved party. The negative
reciprocity becomes symmetrical, paving to way for a more extended alliance between families that
includes additional matrimonial exchange. This is evident in the case of the Atta Ant Clan and the
aggrieved Féénemɨna family. After an Atta Ant woman married a Féénemɨna man, the latter’s mixed
Féénemɨna-Murui female relative married the brother of the Atta Ant bride.
This practice reflects the ideal of homosubstitutive exchange among Indigenous human centers.
Whereas humans could be traded for goods with Whites during the slave trade, and nonhuman ownerpersons can accept vegetal offerings as compensation for their animals, among Indigenous clans, as my
interlocutors have noted on several occasions, “a life can only be paid through another life” (una vida
solo se paga con otra vida).121 To my knowledge, there was but one heterosubstitutive marital transaction
in the Andoque’s recent history: in the early 1950s, an Andoque man persuaded the Féénemɨna widow
of a Murui-Muina man to marry him, compensating her brother-in-law, who had intended to enact the
levirate, with a rifle.
The homosubstitutive logic also underlies marital exchange that occurs after the successful healing of
severe illnesses, where a relative of the recovered patient gives a wife to the healer or his son. I was told
of two such cases, the first dating to the 1960s, when Yiñékɒ offered his daughter Irene to a MuruiMuina man who saved the life of her brother Rodolfo, and another dating to the 1990s, involving a man
from the Atta Ant Clan who gave his daughter to the son of a healer responsible for saving his niece’s
life. Beyond sincere expression of gratitude, we can also discern in this practice an effort to avoid
expressing ingratitude towards a person who, as an accomplished healer, is often also suspected to
possess potent sorcery abilities. Such a healer may harbor resentment upon witnessing the female
relatives of those he has saved marrying into other families, while he or his sons remain unmarried.
Consequently, he may bewitch these women or their kin.
While marriage alliance can serve to prevent aggressions and predation, they are also imbued with
predatory logics, just as predatory dynamics with nonhumans reflect principles of affinal exchange. Real

Interestingly, the noun ḭnhḛ́sói applies to the two human objects of exchange, both slaves and wives (Andoque Andoque
and Landaburu, forthcoming).
121

327

affines are recognized as centers with a similar agency to ego’s, who refers to their co-parents-in-law as
oño̰e, or “persons.” Like site-persons (’i’bo ño̰e), affines represent the independent, dangerous agency
epitomized by the jaguar (ḭño̰). Similar to the jaguar and the site-persons, parents-in-law may “devour”
their children’s spouses. In previous chapters we encountered various myths in which the father-in-law
is the predatory Sun, intent on consuming his sons-in-law. These myths resemble Miraña mythical
narratives featuring jaguar fathers-in-law (Karadimas 2005b, 161) and are typical of the Amazonian
affinal asymmetry between father-in-law and son-in-law, and the expectation of reciprocity, where the
groom remains at risk of being consumed himself, e.g., through brideservice, as long as he does not
compensate his father-in-law with a counter-transfer of a woman to be consumed by one of his sons
(Viveiros de Castro 1993, 190–91). However, we also encountered myths in which the father-in-law is
Shadow Egg, who occupies a position of prey vis-à-vis his sons-in-law. Like site-persons, parents-in-law
are not only predatory agents, but also the owners of “game”—i.e., men and women whom other
individuals can seize and “consume,” both as spouses and workers at their malocas. A marriage alliance
thus involves a predatory struggle between a father-in-law and son-in-law over the reciprocity in the
transfers and counter-transfers of women, but also as to whether either side manages to impose its
project on the other and incorporate the other, or some of its constituents, to its group, thereby turning
them into its workers—or “orphans,” a notion to which we will return below.
Upon marriage, spouses refer to their fathers-in-law as se or suegro and to their mothers-in-law as sóɨ or
suegra, but they often address them using consanguineal terms, such as bɵbɵ or papá (“father”) and iyo
or mamá (“mother”). Similarly, the brothers of the parents-in-law can be addressed as “uncles” (yodɨ;
tio), and their sisters as “mothers.” The underlying logic of “upwards familiarization” behind this
divesting of affines of their affinity (Viveiros De Castro 2001, 24; see also Taylor 1983), becomes more
apparent with the use of the term ’baó to adress parents-in-law and their siblings, a term that is not used
today due to the dwindling use of the native language among young people. My elder interlocutors
explain that ’baó is also the term through which parents guided their children on how to address their
playmates to promote harmony and prevent quarrels (“this is your ’baó, don’t fight with him”). By
contrast, parents-in-law may use Spanish consanguineal terms to address the spouses of their children,
but not consanguineal terms or the term ’baó in the native language (SW is kn, while DH is ńkɒ).
The Andoque terms for sibings-in-law—opókn for brother-in-law and opómi for sister-in-law—display
more symmetry, and may be derived from the root pó, which signifies clarity and gaze, as seen in no
pó’kni: “I am looking.” This suggests that one’s sibling-in-law is the person with whom one exchanges
328

glances (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm., November 2022). The ideal relationship, as described by
Andoque members, between a man and his brother-in-law centers around mutual visits and collaboration
in maloca construction and garden clearing. However, the collaborative relationship between maloquero
brothers-in-law is infused with notions of rivalry and competition that are less central in relationships
between non-maloquero brothers-in-law.
Distinct from other People of the Center, where a ceremonial alliance can only be formed between two
maloqueros who are unrelated to each other by blood or marriage, or “potential affines” (Gasché 2009,
14), the Andoque consider the actual brother-in-law as the preferred partner for exchanging ceremonies,
a relationship that encompasses both collaboration and competition. These ceremonial partners are
expected to engage in dialogue (pɨsékái, literally: “tell stories”) to assess the weather and imminent
dangers jointly and to consult with one another regarding the rituals essential for the proper management
of the territory. A maloquero’s ceremonial partner is often his ḭtáu’fa, “the one who receives tobacco” to
attend dances organized by the former. As a guest at the dance, the ceremonial partner manifests a
ritualistically antagonistic demeanor (to be explored in Chapter 11) which the host will reciprocate when
it is his turn to serve as the ḭtáu’fa at a ceremonial dance hosted by his partner. This alternation of
ceremonial dances involves a competition that builds prestige for the partners if they successfully
navigate and even surpass the ritual challenges posed by each other, in dynamics that may have
exhibited a more “potlach”-like nature before the rubber upheaval (Gasché 2003). For this reason, a
maloquero’s ceremonial partner should ideally be someone at a similar stage in his ritual career, which
explains the preference for an individual from G+0. However, my interlocutors explained that a
maloquero’s partner cannot be someone who has collaborated with him or his father in dance
organization, presumably because they share similar knowledge and ritual practices that turn this
alliance akin to incest. Engaging in such a partnership is crucial for a maloquero’s progression. My
interlocutors noted that the end of several maloqueros’ ceremonial careers could be traced back to the
loss of their ceremonial partners, whether due to death or emigration.
Similar to how the role of a brother-in-law encompasses both assistance and rivalry, their clan
represents, from a given ego’s point of view, both the opportunity for social reproduction and the risk of
deviation from ego’s own clan principles and traditions. This tension is typical of “house societies,”
where cognatic kinship coexists with patrilineal descent, and societies worldwide, as well as other
People of the Center and the Tukanoan-Arawakan groups of Northwest Amazonia, differ in the relative
weight they give to each of these components (Carsten and Hugh-Jones 1995; Karadimas 2000b, 610–
329

11). This tension is often represented by the in-marrying woman, who embodies, in a patrilineal and
patrilocal society, the perilous agency of her patriclan of origin. “In this sense,” as S. Hugh-Jones
observes for the Tukanoan context, “such women are ‘gifts’—they embody their source” (2013, 370).
This notion has been discussed in Chapter 6 in relation to the concept of “a woman’s word” (tí’i nihɵɵ́i),
which refers both to tasks and substances associated with women and to any sentiment, thought or
advice that is perceived as going against the efforts of men to organize the group and promote what they
perceive to be in the group’s benefit. Egret of the River Mouth epitomizes the vulnerability to “a
woman’s word” because in the myth of “The War of the Speaking Tree” (M4), he fails to carry out his
original plans and cannot control his desire and anger after being distracted by his host’s wife (see
Chapter 1). Women are viewed by men as capable of diverting them from their endeavors to carry out
projects or acquire new skills and knowledge, hence, I was told, a man should only pay attention to or
turn his gaze on women after completing the mission that he has set forth for himself. The perception by
a given man of women as representing the dangerous affinal nature of their origin clans has also been
mentioned in Chapter 6 in relation to the attempts made by the (male) producers and consumers of coca
and tobacco to disentangle these substances from their mythical affinal and feminine associations and to
steer away from feminine influences during their preparation and production, in order to ensure that
these substances serve them as a tool to familiarize others, rather than being familiarized by them.
Various myths reflect the ideal that a woman shows greater allegiance to her husband (and by extension,
the clan to which she marries) than to her origin family and clan. In the myth recounting the origin of
peach palm, the hero obtains this fruit from his aquatic in-laws thanks to his fish wife, who hides one pit
in her vagina—the only place in a woman’s body where a brother should not search (Landaburu and
Pineda 1984, 190–201).122 In the myth of the pipe blower M7 (see Appendix 1), it is the lover himself
whom the woman hides in her vagina to protect him from her brothers. On the other hand, the portrayal
of brothers-in-law as the wives’ lovers in other myths, such as M22 (as well as in M7 according to one
narrator; see footnote 188 in Appendix 1), reflects husbands’ suspicion that their wives have not been
adequately familiarized and that they maintain a greater allegiance to their origin family. From a
feminine point of view, an elder woman told me that women are advised by their parents not to share
their clan’s origin stories or myth versions with their husbands. If a woman happens to hear a myth
version that contradicts the one she is familiar with, she may approach her parents and ask them about
Interestingly, this way of hiding is absent from the Miraña and Bora variants, where the hero hides the pit from his fish
brothers-in-law by swallowing it (Karadimas 2007, 111–12; Lucas 2019, 322.).
