its accuracy. In such cases, the father is likely to reassure her that their own clan’s version is indeed true.
She concluded: “The husband’s people [family] are nothing [son nada], they are different people [otra
gente].”
While intricately linked to a conflictive perception of affinal exchange, the concept of “a woman’s
word” also bears consequences for women’s involvement in contemporary political structures, like the
reserve. Despite some men arguing that this concept should not constrain women’s active engagement in
community assemblies and meetings within the reserve with external agency representatives, several
women emphasized to me that “a woman’s word” indeed conveys exactly that. The average female
attendance at the six internal reserve assemblies, which took place during my research and concerned its
economic management or preparation for meetings with non-Indigenous agents, was six women,
compared to 15 men. Female attendance was higher at two reserve meetings funded by or involving
non-Indigenous agents, which focused on the garden project and women’s association (12 women vs. 11
men at one meeting, 9 vs. 15 at another). Additionally, numerous other meetings funded by external
agents, which included the purchase of local produce from members and its consumption—and, as such,
were also seen as festive social gatherings—also saw higher female attendance. During both internal
assemblies and those with external participants, women tend to sit towards the rear of the maloca (“the
women’s side”) and participate in discussions significantly less than men. My female interlocutors
mentioned that even these rare interventions were absent a few years ago. They attributed this increase
in participation to the influence of Murui-Muina women from La Chorrera, where women are said to
have a more active role in representative organizations. Some of these women either married into the
Andoque community or left an impression of the female members of the reserve due to their active
engagement in regional assemblies that the latter attended. These experiences resonate with accounts of
women’s negotiation of their participation in modern political arenas in other societies in Northwest
Amazonia, as they navigate between new democratic structures and their marginal, even somewhat
external position in relation to their groups as enshrined in regional agnatic ideologies (Rosas Riaño
2021; Rossi Idárraga 2020a; 2020b).
The liberating influence of non-Andoque women on female reserve members is viewed as a threat by
Andoque men and could be interpreted as an embodiment of “a woman’s word” that poses a risk to them
due to its connection with another affinal center—one that is perceived as even more perilous than
competing Andoque clan centers. This dynamic is reflected in the failure of the Indigenous Women
Association of the Andoque People, where such influences seem to have played a role, among other
331

factors. This association emerged from a broader project aimed at ensuring food sovereignty and
preserving sustainable economic practices by revitalizing the women’s work in the gardens. This project
was funded by Parques, as part of this agency’s efforts to secure the consent of the Indigenous neighbors
of its Chiribiquete National Natural Park to the park’s expansion and to promote ecologically sustainable
land uses among the park’s neighbors (see Chapter 8). The project also aimed at empowering women
and upholding the transmission of their traditional knowledge. The first assembly for project
consolidation took place in 2015, where it was decided that the participants would explore Andoque
gardening traditions by clearing together and working in the family gardens of its participants, thereby
reviving the custom of collective garden work (minga), which would culminate with the cultivation of
the garden in the Deer Clan settlement and the subsequent celebration of a Fruit ceremonial dance at
Mario’s maloca. Since many of the adult female reserve members are not of Andoque origin and do not
speak this language, the project participants also sought to promote knowledge of Andoque botanical
nomenclature. This topic gained further weight over time, and at the community assembly that I
attended in May 2018 to bring the association, its objectives, and a scheme of co-funding developed
with Parques to the elders’ authorization, it was already presented as the “preservation of the Andoque
language.”
The focus on language and traditional Andoque knowledge was one of the aspects that deterred
Andoque men, primarily because the association was headed by Lina*, a woman of a neighboring group
married to an Andoque man. Certainly, the association garnered various critics. Some association
members and their spouses voiced concerns about lack of reciprocity in the cycle of family garden
clearings, as well as the perceived diversion of the project’s resources to Lina and her husband’s family.
Other members criticized her alleged tyrannic attitude and mistreatment of members, whom she
purportedly treated as her workers. The association members were particularly disappointed to learn that
instead of receiving work tools such as boots and machetes from Parques, Lina had requested the agency
electronic equipment, such as a computer and camera. By contrast, the male participants at the assembly
were primarily concerned about the association’s goals of exploring Andoque botanical knowledge,
engaging with the Andoque language, and preserving ceremonial dances connected to garden work.
Hernando, the reserve governor, stated that the topic of language preservation should be promoted in a
project involving the entire community and all its elders, not just its female members; the elder Rodolfo
hurled that the women try to “touch” something that is “too deep” and will consequently fail; and Mario
complained that the Fruit Dance at his maloca left him indebted to the spirits due to the insufficient
332

contribution of coca and vegetal salt, responsibilities that fell upon the women, and blamed Lina for not
ensuring the proper completion of the required ritual procedures. After these complaints were raised,
Lina addressed the elephant in the room when she said: “I know that some people say, ‘Oh, this X [her
Indigenous group], she came here to give us orders…’ So, if anyone objects to me being the coordinator,
I will resign.” She even offered Raquel, an elder of the Deer Clan, to co-lead the association with her.
None of the participants admitted that their objection was related to Lina’s non-Andoque origin, and one
elder from the Beetle Clan even stated: “Lina is already one of us, she is Andoque.” Lina’s nonAndoque mother-in-law, one of the few in-marrying women to master the Andoque language, asserted
that being born to a different Indigenous origin does not negate allegiance to the Andoque people. “I am
also Andoque already,” she stated, a declaration echoed by several other women of both non-Andoque
and mixed descent. Lina stepped down from leading the association, and Parques’ representative
decided to suspend the project in October, when they attended a meeting where the same disagreements
resurfaced and without any other woman volunteering to replace Lina.
In the weeks following the May assembly, I spoke with various reserve members who maintained that
Lina’s ethnic origin was not relevant to their objection to her leadership. It was only a few months later
that several men said that they could not accept her as the association coordinator due to her nonAndoque origin, as they believed that she attempted to impose her vision on the association and interfere
with Andoque traditions. One elder, in particular, conveyed to me that gardens created through
collective efforts such as those cleared in the project, should be dedicated to ceremonial dances and
other traditional practices encompassed by the term la cultura. The crops they yield should be suitable
not just for basic consumption, but also for contemplation and communication with nonhuman entities.
Therefore, it is crucial that the gardens are cleared, crops are planted, and they grow with the appropriate
mindset. However, according to this elder, this was not the case with the association and its nonAndoque coordinator, whose “thinking was not from here”—from the Andoque territory. This brings us
back to the efforts aimed at familiarizing cultivars so that they can effectively facilitate the subsequent
familiarization of both human and nonhuman entities and serve as a defense against becoming affinized
by these beings. It appears that in addition to usual criticisms of project coordination, like resource
misallocation, Andoque members perceived that the women’s association posed a threat because it was
led by “a woman’s word” that could readily be traced to a rival affinal center.
Therefore, notwithstanding the rivalry and suspicion among Andoque clans, Andoque members
associate other ethnic groups with more acute affinal dangers. However, non-Indigenous others are not
333

homogenous in this respect. Andoque members express more fear, suspicion, and criticism toward
certain neighboring communities than they do toward two small ethnic communities living downriver
from the Aduche Reserve. They explicitly trace this attitude to the critical decades of post-genocide
reconstruction, when the founder families of these communities lived alongside the Andoque or
exchanged women and dance invitations with them, something that was not achieved with the other and
significantly larger Indigenous populations surrounding them. In other words, these smaller
communities represent less hostile affinal centers because they have been familiarized by the Andoque
through past exchange and alliance.123 The existence of prior exchange and consequent familiarity with
certain centers would certainly hold true in respect to other Andoque clans from the point of view of any
Andoque member, accounting for why other Andoque individuals are feared less than non-Andoque
neighbors. For this reason, parents often express the desire that their children would find Andoque
spouses. This tendency stems from the concentric differentiation between consanguines, real affines, and
non-kin, and may represent a modern manifestation, expressed through the idiom of ethnicity, of the
more ingrained preference among the People of the Center to marry those who are genealogically closest
to ego among people considered non-consanguine (Gasché 1976; Karadimas 2000; Lucas 2019, 161).
This also manifests in people’s attitude toward ceremonial relationships modeled upon affinal ties,
where members of other Andoque clans are deemed more familiar and thus safer than non-Andoque
individuals. Fisi mentioned that Andoque maloqueros prefer inviting Andoque guests to their ceremonial
dances instead of non-Andoque ones, explaining: “We don’t have sufficient mambe and ambíl, and we
don’t want the others [guests from other groups] to be upset that we invite them if we don’t have
enough. If they sing here and I don’t give them enough mambe and ambíl they can bewitch me. But if I
invite Tañe, I know that he doesn’t have more ambíl than I have, so he won’t be upset with what I give
him.” The theme of sorcery plays a crucial role in the dynamics between affinal centers, and it is to this
theme that we now turn.
De-familiarization Through Incest and Sorcery
The predatory dimension of the Andoque’s perception of marriage is most marked in its association with
sorcery. When José* told me M3, he said that the suitors who preceded Egret of the River Source were
all devoured by the woman’s father after they addressed him as “father-in-law.” “This story teaches one
This information is substantiated by the disproportion observed in my kinship corpus regarding the marriage relations
formed between the Andoque and various ethnic groups, in comparison to the population size of these groups. However, I
have opted not to present this data here to avoid a clearer identification of the specific groups mentioned.

123

334

not to say ‘father-in-law’ to someone who can bewitch him,” he said. For this reason, his son told me,
when he went to La Chorrera to look for a wife and spent a long time with Murui-Muina and Bora
people whose might he feared, he used to call men older than himself as either “uncle” or “grandfather.”
Another elder told me that he used to fear the son-in-law of his classificatory cousin, a strong-bodied
Brazilian gold miner with an unknown past, until the latter started calling him “uncle,” similar to how
this cousin’s children address him. Addressing another man as an affine implies alterity and thus
unpredictibility that may elicit an aggressive stance, while addressing him as a consanguine implies a
more peaceful stance that may elicit from him a more protective approach. This section elucidates how
sorcery, and incest as well, function in the opposite direction, acting to dissociate consanguinity and
treat members of one’s own human center, or an affinally allied one, as non-kin, and engaging in a
predatory exchange with them.
The potential use of the term ño̰e for co-parents-in-law demarcates the extension of ego’s family and the
(ideally) benevolent exchange taking place in it. I will explain this by discussing the Andoque’s incest
prohibitions and previous efforts by anthropologists of neighboring peoples to uncover these societies’
marriage preferences. Similar to other People of the Center, the Andoque consider the marriage of both
real and classificatory cousins within three degrees as incest. For instance, in the figure below, a male
ego [1] cannot marry most of his G+0 relatives, to whom he refers as tii (“sister”) or ḭ́ ekó tii (“poor
sister,” meaning female cousin). The closest matrimony into which he could enter would be with [2],
who can be classified as his cousin, but does not belong to any of the four patriclans of his grandparents.

Figure 20. Marriageable relatives from a male spouse’s perspective (colors: clan membership)

335

The kinship systems of the Caquetá-Putumayo region do not include positive marriage rules as is typical
in Amazonian Dravidianate, although the kinship terminologies of the Andoque’s Miraña and Bora
neighbors contain what Karadimas termed “a Dravidian touch,” where a person employs the same term
to address both their parents-in-law and their parents’ siblings (Karadimas 2000, 611; Lucas 2019, 155;
see also García 2018, 167 n.16). In the Andoque language, this trait is slightly more hidden. The
reference term for father-in-law (WF and HF) is se (in contrast to sóɨ for mother-in-law, WM or HM),
and reference to an uncle (a sibling of either parent, as well as that sibling’s husband) is done through
yodɨ. Both the maternal and paternal aunts are referred to as píta, while the paternal aunt, as well as
one’s MBW, is sen, “the father-in-law’s wife.” Karadimas uses this Dravidian trait as further support in
his argument that the Miraña system may not contain positive marriage rules from the point of view of
an ego seeking marriage for themselves, but, if the point of departure is ego’s parents—who, in the past,
were the ones to seek spouses for their children—then a marriage preference does appear. The parent
would search a spouse for their child among the children of their own classificatory siblings (cousins)
who do not belong to any of the four clans of their child’s grandparents. These potential spouses are thus
classified as the nieces and nephews of the parent of the marrying ego, but would lack a kinship term
from ego’s point of view—therefore, they would not be viewed as kin (Karadimas 2000b, 607).
Thus, if we redraw the figure to consider the parental matchmaker as ego [1], none of the children of
their siblings (referred to as tii for a male ego’s sister, yohɵ for a female ego’s brother, or ɵɵ for any
ego’s same-sex sibling) can serve as spouses. However, the children of their classificatory siblings, who
are the matchmaker’s cousins and, as such, are referred to as “poor siblings” (ḭ́ ekó tii, ḭ́ ekó yohɵ or ḭ́ ekó
’ɵɵ), may be suitable candidates—for example, the children of [2].

336

Figure 21. Marriageable relatives from the perspective of a male spouse’s father (colors: clan membership)

We may suppose that these siblings are “poor” precisely because they may cease being siblings
altogether if their children do not belong to any of the four patriclans of the prospective match, and thus
become—again, from the point of view of the parental matchmaker—co-parents-in-law.124 Their
designation as ño̰e would detach them from the kinship network of the parental matchmaker (and that of
their children), marking them as independent agents counting as a separate human center.
One objection to incestuous relationships is attributed to the partners’ parents, who find it shameful to
call their siblings or real cousins “co-parents-in-law.” This objection is attributed to Pa̰’fó and Pedro,
two cousins from the generation that survived the genocide, whose respective children, Irene and Tañe,
expressed their desire to marry. My interlocutors explained that it was shameful for the parents to start
addressing their cousins as ño̰e because it shows a lack of respect for the cousin. The shameful aspect
appears to be the treatment of kinsperson as independent enough, such that one sees their children, and
ultimately, this kin, as a potential prey for one’s children. However, my interlocutors told me that Pedro
and Yiñékɒ, Pa̰’fó’s husband, agreed to simply ignore this marriage on the level of terminology, and
kept adressing each other as “brother-in-law,” while Pa̰’fó and Pedro remained “cousins.”
In Karadimas and Lucas’ analyses of the Miraña and Bora kinship systems, the “Dravidian touch” is
also connected to the maloqueros’ custom during the slave trade to select both potential spouses for their
children and “orphans” to be exchanged with outsiders for metal instruments and other goods from the

For Murui-Muina and Bora references to cousins as weakened or “external” versions of siblings, see Gasché 1976, 153
and Lucas 2019, 163.

124

337

category of “nephews” (furthermore, in the Miraña language, the term for “orphan” is very similar to
“nephew”; Karadimas 2001, 93; Lucas 2019, 207–09). A maloquero’s classificatory nephew born from a
union with one of the maloquero’s female relatives and thus belonging to another patriclan, could
become an orphan if he were to live in this maloquero’s house due to various reasons, instead of residing
in his own patriclan’s maloca. In this situation, being a relatively distant non-member of the
maloquero’s clan, he could potentially be sold into slavery. The Andoque term for co-parents-in-law
also illustrates how a classificatory nephew-turned-spouse can transition into a state of “orphanhood.”
Similar to how an orphan (’ihɵ́ɵ) lacks the predatory agency implied in the term ño̰, an individual can
become an orphan if, upon marriage, they lack parents or other patrilineal ancestors who can be
recognized as ño̰e by their parents-in-law. As among the Murui-Muina, marital alliance with them,
therefore, does not represent real exchange with their lineage (García 2016, 46). Not being valid subjects
of exchange, they used to run the risk, during the slavery period, of becoming its objects.
The presence of a “Dravidian touch” among the Andoque and other People of the Center brings to mind
two points of divergence from the Dravidianate of neighboring groups. Firstly, it creates longer periods
of asymmetry between clans, as a woman taken by a certain clan will only have her departure
compensated through a counter-transfer several generations later. This may explain the past preference
of men—which appears to have practically ceased (see Chapter 3)— for “eliminating” their debt by
naming a daughter after her mother’s clan. Second, unlike in a Dravidian model, Andoque incest rules
prevent spouses from sharing not only parents but also grandparents. This suggests that the latter’s role
in people’s lives may shed light on these incest rules. As noted in previous chapters, a person most
frequently addresses powerful ritual instruments and the nonhuman entities from whom they seek
protection or assistance as “grandfathers” (yo’tapɵ), followed by “grandmothers” (yota) or “uncles”
(yodɨ). Since they are typically considered more knowledgeable than a child’s parents, grandparents are
the primary ones to cure foodstuffs and perform other healing procedures for them. Andoque members
frequently comment that while parents may lack the patience to convey intricate knowledge to their
children—who, in turn, are said to often exhibit impertinence and disobedience towards their parents—
the more affable dynamics of relationship betwen grandchildren and grandparents position the latter as
favored teachers for learning myths and various ritual practices for their defense and well-being.
The protective role of a grandfather can assume an aggressive aspect towards a grandchild’s spouse in
cases of incest. This reaction highlights the predatory implications of sexual relations and the tension
between cognatic kinship and agnatic clan membership. In a sexual relationship that concluded shortly
338

before my fieldwork, Luisa*, a fifteen-years old girl, became pregnant by Jorge*, a twenty-six-years
man. Pregnancy in such an age is usually considered undesirable by the girl’s parents, although it is not
uncommon in the region. This particular situation might have been more readily accepted by Luisa’s
family if it were not for the fact that Jorge was her cousin (FZS):

Jorge

Luisa

Figure 22. The incestuous relationship between Jorge and Luisa

Luisa’s father sought out his nephew in order to kill him, and the parents denounced him for rape at
Puerto Santander’s corregimiento (the girl claimed that the relations were consensual, but, again, she
was a minor). The girl’s father also threatened to kill the future baby, and things only calmed once Jorge
left the region following an assembly of Andoque elders. Jorge thus spent a few months in Bogotá until
after the birth, and did not resume the relationship with Luisa upon his return. When the baby was a few
months old, I spent a month at the house of Luisa and her parents, which is located in the same
settlement as the house of the grandparent of the two cousins (Luisa’s FF and Jorge’s MF), and at some
distance from the house of Jorge’s mother. Onlookers from other families who witnessed Jorge’s
frequent abuse of alcohol and resulting loss of control, attributed it to the grandfather’s sorcery, which
supposedly aimed at causing his grandson to engage in bar fights and consequently die. The grandfather,
on the other hand, told me on more than one occasion that Jorge is dangerous because he practices
“black magic,” which he has supposedly learned from books one finds in Bogotá as well as in boarding
schools, and especially from his non-Andoque paternal uncle who, like his father, lives in La Chorrera
(and whom people claim to be the man’s real father).
When considering clan affiliation (as indicated by the colors in Figure 22), we observe that Luisa
belongs to her paternal grandfather’s clan, while Jorge is a member of his father’s Murui-Muina clan.
This context may suggest that the problem may stem from a lack of reciprocal exchange of women
between the clans. However, more women from Jorge’s clan have married into Luisa’s clan, with only
339

Jorge’s mother moving in the opposite direction. The sexual relationship and subsequent pregnancy
were seemingly perceived as acts of aggression by Jorge against Luisa. Whether any of the sorcery
allegations surrounding this case is real holds little significance for our current purpose. What stands out
is the response to this perceived sexual aggression: the grandfather defended the grandchild from his
own clan and accused the grandson from the other clan of sorcery, leading observers to believe he
intended to bewitch him. Given the perception of sexual and marital bonds as the wife’s capture by the
husband’s clan, such incestuous unions highlight the inherent tension between cognatic affiliation and
agnatic identity, potentially leading grandparents, who are ideally protective figures for all their
grandchildren, to adopt aggressive stances toward non-agnatic kin.
The sorcery allegations accompanying this incest case reveal a conjunction between sorcery and incest
that among the Qom of the Gran Chaco has been interpreted as two manifestations of relational excess
(Tola 2019). In the Andoque case, given the tension between patrilineal identity and cognatic affiliation,
and the tendency to view the world of non-kin as governed by a generalized predatory logic, these two
phenomena represent two modes of resisting consanguinity and adopting an aggressive position towards
kin. While incest involves flouting the rules of consanguinity, sorcery often involves real affines
resisting the familiarization implied in the actualization of marital exchange, and preserving, or even
exaggerating, the inimical stance of the yóʼo or the unrestrained sexual voracity of the saámḭ.
My data records 44 sorcery accusations from the last century (circa 1920s–present), and I will restrict
myself to the 40 accusations that specify the identity of both sorcerer and victim. I classified these cases
into three degrees of severity: category 1 includes interventions in the behaviour or appearance of the
victim in a way that does not represent direct health or fatal risks (for example, causing a boy to remain
short-statured, or the maleficium to cause the victim to age, mentioned in Chapter 9); category 2, with
cases involving the infliction of physical and mental ailments or other misfortunes that seriously disrupt
a person’s functioning and may turn fatal only in the long term, from barrenness to madness and
terminal illnesses; and category 3 which is limited to direct mortal assaults. I further classified the
kinship status of the victim from the sorcerer’s perspective, as consanguine (a person with whom
marriage would be considered incestuous), real affine, affine’s associate—representing victims who are
the lovers of a real affinal victim of the sorcerer or healers who treated affinal victims to save them from
the harms inflicted by the sorcerer—and “other,” a category encompassing individuals who are unrelated
to the sorcerer by blood or marriage.

It is striking that half of all accusations (numbering 20) are raised against real affines, as compared with
17.5% against consanguines and 25% against people found outside of the victim’s immediate kinship
network (7 and 10 cases, respectively). This number reaches 57.5% if we merge it with the three cases
of “affine’s associate.” If we restrict ourselves to the more severe witchcraft and examine only the 25
accusations of categories 2 and 3, attacks by real affines raise to 56% of the cases (14 accusations) or
64%, if “affine associates” are added (2 cases), while attacks by consanguines represent 20% (5 cases)
and those by other people represent only 16% of the cases (4 accusations).
If we indeed “view witchcraft as the antithesis of society, its dark side or alter ego” (Heckenberger 2004,
179), then it is not surprising that in a cognatic society whose members nonetheless put a stark emphasis
on agnatic descent, real affines are perceived as threats and accused of different misfortunes as a way to
express the tension between cognatic and agnatic membership. As in other societies worldwide, sorcery
accusations follow misfortunes, as people attempt to relate an unfortunate situation or event that has
affected themselves or someone else with a prior interaction between the victim and another person, who
is henceforth regarded as the sorcerer (Gluckman 2014, 374). In Evans-Pritchard’s words, misfortunes
are typically traced back to individuals with whom the sufferer “come[s] into closest contact, when this
contact is not softened by sentiments of kinship or is not buffered by distinctions of age, sex, and class”
(1976, 47–48). Andoque members justify the requirement of proximity to affect witchcraft in that a
sorcerer is not likely to risk themselves attacking a person whose gods or guardian spirits they do not
know lest the unknown forces possessed by these protective beings overwhelm them. Conversely,
knowing a person’s clan origin myth and other myths on which they rely ensures a more effective
assault.

341

The statistical correlation between sorcery and affinity resonates with Donald Pollock’s (2004) data
regarding the Kulina, where sorcery is articulated as the opposite of siblingship, and is projected on
villages where potential and sometimes real affines live in order to preserve social harmony and cool
down tensions between households within the village, whose members are conceived as siblings who
would never seek each other’s harm. While the Andoque sometimes accuse co-residents, they typically
project the sources of social tension outside the Andoque clan system, such that only eight cases concern
an Andoque sorcerer and an Andoque victim, five of which being in severity class 1 and merely three in
class 2. The correlation between sorcery and affinity is not surprising if we take into account the
perception of sorcery as a kind of predation and the association between predation and affinity, as well
as the discussions in Chapter 9 of the infliction of harms through sexual seduction. Londoño discusses a
more general Féénemɨna tendency to consider affines as immoral people who are capable of sorcery, and
who are also sometimes viewed as bewitching their in-laws (2012, 139). An analysis of the Andoque
data suggests a more specific interpretation of the association between affinity and sorcery.
Six sorcery attacks in severity classes 2 and 3 against affinal relatives and their associates out of 16
involve motives that are also present in accusations against individuals located outside of their victims’
kinship network, such as envy or revenge over insolence, or perceived harm to kin or property. Two
other assaults are more specific to affinal relations in that they involve killing the son born to the wife of
the sorcerer or his relative and the man for whom she has left the sorcerer or relative. Affecting these
harm reflects the sorcerer’s transition from a real affine of the victim to her enemy, or yóʼo.
The exaggeration of affinity implied in sorcery is more noted in the common logic of the eight other
severe assaults, as these are specifically related to the sorcerers’ position as real affines who, instead of
diminishing their affinal traits when engaging in actual matrimonial exchange, preserve their affinal
nature and insist on the unbounded predatory attitude it implies. Casio* serves as a good example to this
tendency. A non-Andoque man whose sons and daughters married in the 1950s and 1960s Andoque
individuals and who lived at the maloca of his Andoque co-parents-in-law, Casio was accused in no less
than five assaults in varying degrees against these individuals or their consanguine relatives, in addition
to a reported attack against Yiñékɒ because the latter attempted to shield his people from these attacks.
Two of these assaults were allegedly triggered by the refusal by Casio’s Andoque affinal relatives to
provide him with the fish he ordered them to catch for him when they went fishing or after they caught
an abundant yield. Similar to other Amazonian societies, a sorcerer is described as a person who cannot
control his desire and would thus attack those who do not gratify his misplaced requests (da Matta 1982,
342

152; Ewart 2000, 114–15). In Casio’s case, these disproportionate attacks—in one he set illnessinducing dolphins on the refuser and in the other he killed the refuser’s child—are the expressions, at the
culinary level, of his unsatiated voracity, which, at the sexual level, manifested in his reported coveting
of the female blood relatives of his sons and daughters-in-law, including the married mothers of the
latter. Casio is said to have bewitched women who refused his sexual advances or their relatives whom
he considered as obstacles to such gratification. While the matrimonial exchange in which he was
immersed and his orphan status as resident at the maloca of his co-parents-in-law were supposed to
reduce his predatory-affinal tendencies, Casio preserved the aggressiveness and unrestrained sexuality
characterizing potential affines. Casio’s case is also interesting from another perspective. Since he had
been previously rejected by another ethnic settlement due to similar suspicions, and considering that my
interlocutors mentioned his belonging to a powerful lineage, these accusations may also reflect the
atypical post-genocide situation. It seems that during this time, there was doubt about whether some
individuals, lacking surviving fellow clan members and unable to establish their own malocas, could
truly assume the subordinate orphan role within the malocas that took them in. More generally, this
situation attests to the potential power that orphans may hold, or are suspected to hold, despite being
defined as lacking agency.
More recently, another non-Andoque sorcerer is said to have attacked four persons in the past decade
because one of them—his sister-in-law—refused his sexual advances, the other victims being this
woman’s brother and two men whom the sorcerer suspected as her lovers. In this case, the sorcerer
sought sexual access to the woman although, as his brother’s wife, she was supposed to be off-limits to
him. In refusing the familiarizing efforts at play when affinity is actualized, sorcery by in-laws
represents a radicalization of their affinity and entrenchment in the potential affinal position of a yó’o, or
enemy, who cannot be pacified, or saámḭ, whose sexual voracity flouts the norms of accepted alliance.
Consanguineal witchcraft reflects the sorcerer’s similar attempts to distance themselves from kinship
ties with the victim. This is evident in four of the seven cases of sorcery against consanguines, where the
dissociation from consanguinity takes various forms (by contrast, the remaining three accusations can be
classified as pedagogic punishments as they involve an insolent young victim and an elder target of
disrespect). One case concerns the sisters of Lucía*, a non-Andoque woman married to an Andoque man
whose sister, who was married to their brother, left him for another man. The sisters then demanded
Lucía to leave her husband, and, after she refused doing so, they affected a maleficium to prevent her
from giving him any more children, resulting in her own death during childbirth. We may suppose that
343

Lucía’s refusal to comply with the demand of her origin family and what they saw as the family’s best
interest was allegedly perceived by her sisters as her own detachment from that family and preference of
her husband’s interests, for which reason they no longer considered her as their kin. Another case
concerns the Carijona/Yucuna man who was purportedly Agustín’s biological father, and who
bewitched and killed the latter because he preferred to live with his non-real father than with him. Here
again sorcery is practiced against a person who is perceived as already detaching himself from
consanguineal ties with the sorcerer. The third case concerns the non-Andoque wife of an Andoque
member, who was bewitched by her uncle after she refused to have sexual relations with him. The
uncle’s attempt at incestuous contact reflects his shift from regarding his niece as a consanguineal
relative deserving protection to considering her as a potential affine who can be preyed. Finally, Jorge’s
alcohol abuse is attributed to sorcery by his grandfather, reflecting the latter’s aggression towards a
consanguine who is not a clan member, and who had assumed an affinal and aggressive attitude towards
a granddaughter who is a clan member.
Another illuminating case, which I excluded from the table due to its involvement of several aggressors,
concerns Zacarias.* Zacarias, despite being born to a non-Andoque father and an Andoque mother,
strongly self-identifies as Andoque. He co-owned a maloca with his mother and organized ceremonial
dances. Just before my fieldwork began, Zacarias’ wife left him because of his alleged violent behaviour
toward her. His subsequent violent outburst toward his brother in 2018 led to both his brother and his
mother relocating to Leticia. This left Zacarias without a female partner to assist in raising his children
and maintaining the maloca. Discussing these events with me, Zacarias identified several Andoque
elders (among them three consanguineal relatives) as the culprits behind the witchcraft that he believed
caused his deviation from the appropriate path of a maloquero and his subsequent violent outbursts.
When I inquired about their motives, he responded that they disapproved of a man without patrilineal
Andoque descent overseeing an Andoque maloca. In essence, these elders allegedly bewitched Zacarias
to clarify that, when forced to decide between the two coexistent yet competing kinship logics of
agnation and cognation, his maternal connections to several of them make him more of a non-kin than
kin. Therefore, he is seen as belonging to a distinctly separate human center.
As was discussed in Chapter 9, the victims of sorcery are conceived as the food that the sorcerer
provides to the owner-persons of the witchcraft spell, with the latter thereby becoming his pets. In the
framework developed in this dissertation on the continuity between inter-human relations and the
relations between humans and nonhumans, it is thus important to note that the dissociation of human
344

kinship through sorcery is utilized to establish or maintain relations of familiarization (or meta-kinship)
with nonhuman entities. In the next section we delve into the Andoque’s ways to manage the tension
between rivalry and alliance in recent decades.
Agnatic Predation and Competitive Alliances
The coexistence of cognatic and agnatic principles in defining the boundaries of human centers is
interlinked to a tension in the Andoque’s attitudes towards marital exchange, between their aspiration
for mutual exchanges that foster ceremonial ties and deter conflicts between involved parties, and their
pronounced agnatic ideology, which, in some contexts, favors the clan’s benefit over symmetrical
exchange with others. This is reminiscent of tensions among other Northwest Amazonian peoples
between marriage ideals that represent a descent-based and an alliance-based conceptions of society (K.
Århem 1981, 153; Goldman 1963, 142–43). The agnatic ideology reflects, for instance, in the
Andoque’s levirate practice, which is represented by two present marriage unions, the recent of which
was formed shortly after I finished my fieldwork. My interlocutors attribute such marriages between a
man and the widowed wife of his real or classificatory brother to the desire to prevent the loss of the
children of a late clan member to the clan of the widow’s future potential husband and to spare them
“orphanhood,” as they might face maltreatment there.
In the context of a virilocal residence pattern, the agnatic ideology is also apparent in the preference for
sons over daughters. I was often told by both male and female interlocutors that sons are more
trustworthy than daughters because they are likely to stay by their parents and take care of them as they
grow old, whereas daughters marry outside the group and move to their husbands’ settlements. One man
related that for this reason, when he discovered that his wife planned to leave him, he took their two
sons into hiding and allowed her to take only the daughter. “Giving birth to girls is giving wives to your
enemy, but boys will continue your tradition,” his brother remarked. By contrast, sons marry women
who then ideally collaborate with their mothers-in-law. Individuals with only daughters are sometimes
seen as victims of sorcery. For female victims of such sorcery, the suspected sorcerer is often a
frustrated suitor or a relative of an ex-husband, determined to prevent any male progeny contributions to
the new husband’s clan by a woman who refused to benefit his own clan. Two interlocutors mentioned
female infanticide practices by a few women as recently as the 1950s, with one revealing she would
have been killed by her mother (who already had a daughter) if not for her father and maternal

345

grandmother’s intervention. I was also told that control of a prospective baby’s sex could be achieved by
consuming certain herbs or invoking animals associated with masculinity.
This preference for male descendants gained further impetus in the aftermath of the rubber genocide,
when the small group of Andoque survivors sought demographic increase. Yiñékɒ played a central role
in promoting gender disproportion. Several interlocutors reported that during the ceremonial dances he
organized over the years, he would give Andoque participants a manicuera impregnated with a potent
spell aimed at promoting the birth of more sons. These sons would bring their future wives to the group
and produce Andoque offspring, as opposed to daughters who would join other groups upon marriage
and contribute to their demographic growth. Whether this or the other measures to control unborn
babies’ sex were effective or not, the demographic gap between male and female children born from the
1930s onwards is striking:

According to his data, in 1971, 65% of Andoque members aged 0–35 were male, while only 35% were
female. In comparison, my corpus indicates a smaller yet still significant disparity for 1935-2019: 56.5%
male vs. 43.5% female. This difference becomes even more pronounced when considering only the
children born between 1935 and 1999, whose parents were alive in the 1960s and 1970s to receive
Yiñékɒ’s manicuera: 114 boys (59.68%), compared with 77 girls (40.31%).
Thus, the rehabilitation of predatory capacity, deemed crucial for the Andoque’s cultural and
demographic post-genocide recuperation process (see Chapter 4), was also intended to materialize in
actual asymmetrical matrimonial exchange with non-Andoque groups. However, although the Andoque
population has shown a remarkable demographic increase since its nadir in the 1930s, we can conclude
that the gender disproportion has not translated into an overall asymmetrical exchange of women, where
the Andoque receive significantly more women from other groups than they give, but has instead
resulted in a balance of in-marrying and out-marrying women. This is evident when considering the
marriages contracted by the members born between 1930 and 1999, while the gender disproportion was
still high (above 10%), and who had reached the age of marriageability, or married, or died without
having married, by the time I lived on their territory.

Guzmán’s observations from five decades ago led him to assert that “the main criterion for admitting a
person or a group of people into the community is their contribution to the group’s numerical growth
and augmentation of power. For this reason, what interests the Andoque and their captain most is the
integration of women” (1971, 73; my translation). To this, we can add the preference for orphans, who
do not pose the risk of a separate competitive center and would not require bride service from the

348

groom. In the second half of the 1950s, a Nonuya man named Julio married to a Féénemɨna woman
sought refuge in Andoque territory after fleeing conflicts in a Féénemɨna community. Julio had two sons
and three daughters, the eldest of whom he offered to Yiñékɒ as wife for his elder son Fisi from the
outset. Although Yiñékɒ accepted him to the group, he declined the matrimonial plan because of his
son’s relatively young age. The woman then married one of the sons of Joselito of the Eagle Clan, so
Julio moved into Joselito’s house. Over time, Julio became affiliated with To̰fi’s maloca. His eldest son
Elias married To̰fi’s daughter Raquel, and Julio relocated to that maloca, where his son became one of
his father-in-law’s workers. During this period, Julio’s youngest daughter formed a couple with To̰fi’s
son before she married an Andoque man of the Atta Ant Clan, and another brother of hers married an
Andoque woman from the Spix’s Guan Clan, who was the daughter of one of To̰fi’s workers.
Interestingly, although the initial marriage between Elias and Raquel dissolved after To̰fi’s death around
1970, the influences of To̰fi’s heritage and residence among the Andoque were strong enough for two of
the three children born of that union to continue self-identifying as Andoque and members of the Deer
Clan, with one of them, also called Elias, eventually constructing his own Andoque maloca with his
mother. After this marriage dissolved, Julio maintained an orphan-like position, moving to the house
where his youngest daughter lived with her husband from the Atta Ant Clan. Only his sons later
constructed malocas, after separating from the Andoque group and moving downriver.
In 1959, when incorporating the Murui group found during rubber gathering (see Chapter 4), the
interests of rubber boss Alberto Zumaeta in enhancing economic production aligned with Yiñékɒ’s aim
to boost the Andoque’s social reproductive capacity. Initially, the Murui group consisted of between
eight and ten women and only three men, with a notable rate of incestuous unions, which my
interlocutors believe the women were eager to end. While the Murui men stayed in the forest to gather
rubber for Zumaeta, Yiñékɒ brought the women back with him and introduced them to the Andoque
men. As a result, four Murui women became part of Andoque households, including those of To̰fi and
Yiñékɒ; however, only two of these unions persisted, and they were with other Andoque men. The
perceived inferiority of the Murui group members in the eyes of the Andoque intensified after the
former’s unsuccessful attempt to integrate into an upriver Murui community and their return to the
Andoque territory, an inferiority that reflected in reports of sexual aggressions against the group’s
women. From this group, only one Murui man married an Andoque woman—the same Raquel.
Tellingly, Raquel named their sole male child after her father To̰fi, and one of their daughters also selfidentifies as Andoque, and chose as an adult a name from her Andoque grandmother’s clan repository.
349

While the asymmetrical exchange of women was viewed as essential for increasing the Andoque
population, more balanced marital exchange strategies were established between the two Andoque
maloqueros, Yiñékɒ and To̰fi, and non-Andoque captains with whom they aimed to form alliances or
prevent hostilities. The Andoque’s “women exchange” does not necessarily imply a direct swap where
two women move from one family to another at a specific point in time, as is idealized by other groups
like the Macuna (K. Århem 1981, 156–57). A suitor might hint at the availability of a sister or cousin
who could potentially marry the prospective wife’s brothers when expressing his marriage intentions to
a potential father-in-law, with symmetry materializing several months or years after the initial marriage.
In the 1950s, To̰fi gave his eldest daughter—the first girl to be born after the return to the ancestral
territory—to a Féénemɨna man whose male relative had been killed years earlier by Yinñéfɵkn, To̰fi’s
collaborator in dances, and whose female relative was already married to To̰fi’s worker, Duñékɒ. This
betrothal was not merely to rectify the imbalance caused by two Féénemɨna individuals being taken
from their community due to Andoque actions. It was also part of a broader effort to foster dialogue
between the Andoque and the captain of that Féénemɨna group. This initiative eventually resulted in
further exchanges and reciprocal arrangements involving women from both groups. The Féénemɨna
groom undertook an extended period of bride service at To̰fi’s maloca and was only allowed to move to
his parental home with his wife after the birth and ceremonial naming of their two sons by To̰fi.
In the 1960s, Yiñékɒ consented to the betrothal of his daughter, Irene, to a Murui-Muina man named
Calixto against her will. Calixto, who was away from his family and engaged in rubber gathering
alongside the Andoque, had previously saved the life of Yiñékɒ’s younger son. While residing at
Yiñékɒ’s maloca, Calixto earned the captain’s respect with his diligence and dedication. During a visit
to Calixto’s family, Irene and Calixto brought his sister Edelmira back with them. Calixto proposed
Edelmira as a bride for Mario, To̰fi’s son, deepening the marital ties between the families. However,
after briefly living with Mario, Edelmira fell for one of Joselito’s sons and chose to marry him instead.
Following the death of Calixto’s father, his mother and another sister, Regina, relocated to Joselito’s
settlement. Calixto later arranged, in collaboration with Yiñékɒ and his son Rodolfo, for Rodolfo to
marry Regina, which eventually took place.
In these instances, the maloqueros consented to the marriages of their daughters as restitution to nonAndoque men. This strategy aimed at establishing balanced alliances with these men and their respective
groups. The goal was to avoid potential conflicts arising from past misdeeds by Andoque individuals or

350

as a form of gratitude for lives saved by these non-Andoque men. In such scenarios and others, the
daughters of both maloquero and non-maloquero men were critical resources in forming alliances or
circumventing hostilities. However, as K. Århem highlighted for the Macuna, the ideals of marital
exchange can mistakenly suggest that women are sweepingly coerced into these unions, but marital
arrangements that utterly overlook a woman’s desires or interests might lead to the breakdown of these
arrangements, potentially escalating tensions between groups (1981, 157–58). Despite their aim to
solidify ceremonial and marital ties with other communities and increase their ranks by bringing in nonAndoque sons-in-law, To̰fi and Yiñékɒ remained deeply concerned about their daughters’ well-being
post-marriage and respected their children’s decisions. After a few years, To̰fi separated his daughter
from her Féénemɨna husband upon discovering she was being mistreated. In a similar vein, Yiñékɒ’s
Murui-Muina son-in-law departed from his maloca after Irene eloped with Tañe of the Sun Clan. This
relationship was initially frowned upon by both Irene and Tañe’s parents due to its perceived incestuous
nature but was eventually accepted.
The capacity to mobilize children for marriage, especially daughters, was a crucial component of a
maloquero’s power. This recalls the “political economy of control” (in Viveiros de Castro’s [1996]
terms), which Rivière and Turner found in the uxorilocal societies of Guyana and Central Brazil (Rivière
1983; T. Turner 2003), where elder men’s control over marriages and resultant relocations granted them
power over the labor and reproductive capabilities of the younger population. Indeed, as noted earlier,
enforcing temporary uxorilocality enhances a maloquero’s labor force and prestige. However, within the
Andoque’s landscape of patrilineal ideology, virilocal residence, and the perception of a generalized
predation among human and nonhuman groups, this matrimonial authority should be viewed primarily
as enhancing the maloquero’s capacity to navigate the delicate exchanges with other human centers.
Thus, while orphans, as non-consanguine maloca members, were transacted in heterosubstitutive trade
for non-Indigenous goods, the maloquero’s closer kin, particularly his children, were transacted in such
homosubstitutive exchanges between clans. In the past, parents’ matrimonial authority depended on the
relative distance between clan settlements. Occasional maloca visits and, more importantly, ceremonial
dances became primary occasions for young men and women to interact, though typically under the
watchful eyes of their elder kin. However, this dynamic has undergone notable shifts since the 1970s
and 1980s due to a range of factors, such as the increasing spatial mobility in the region (and from it to
other parts of Colombia) and the establishment of the boarding school in Araracuara. At this school,
teenage boys and girls socialize with members of their age group and often engage in romantic and
351

sexual affairs with them, without the mediation of their elder relatives. However, parents retain subtle
means of influence that sidestep overt coercion. As one interlocutor explained, a father might evoke
Tatoañei, the mythical figure whose sons captivated Shadow Egg’s daughters, to kindle his son’s interest
in a particular woman. Thus, in a manner akin to the love perfumes described in the previous chapter,
the capabilities of nonhuman entities can be harnessed to navigate marital exchanges with other human
centers.
In the accounts of my interlocutors, parental marriage arrangements from the 1970s onwards seem
relatively loose and flexible. Parents can indicate to their son that the parents of a particular woman are
likely to approve of a potential marriage between their daughter and him. Raquel shared an anecdote
with me: after her eldest daughter, Miryan, was born in 1964, Yiñékɒ’s wife, Pa̰’fó, convinced her to, in
due course, betroth her daughter to Pa̰’fó’s youngest son, Ignacio. Raquel emphasizes that she never
proactively encouraged this union. However, Ignacio’s mother informed him that Raquel had already
consented, leading to a situation where Miryan later approached her mother to reveal that Ignacio was
courting her and she was keen to marry him. Raquel, naturally, gave her blessing.
In a separate instance from the 1990s, Rodolfo’s daughter from the Eagle Clan fell for Celestino, a
Murui-Muina man from La Chorrera working in the Araracuara sector. The two wed, and she relocated
to Celestino’s family. During a visit, Rodolfo mentioned to Celestino’s family the challenges his sons
faced in finding wives due to the prevalence of close family ties among the Andoque. The hosts, seeing
an opportunity, suggested intermarriages with women from their family. Subsequently, one of Rodolfo’s
sons journeyed to La Chorrera, returning soon after with Celestino’s niece. His cousin followed suit,
staying for around three months and bringing back the woman’s sister. Later, Rodolfo’s youngest son
also married in La Chorrera, taking Celestino’s cousin as a wife. The growing disparity in the exchange,
where three women joined Rodolfo’s family and only one joined Celestino’s, seemed to demand
extended bride service durations. This is evident as Rodolfo’s youngest son lived with his wife’s family
for over a year before bringing her home.
In these cases, the parental arrangement did not imply forcing the couple, and especially the women,
into marriage. Instead, it was more about addressing any concerns of overt or covert violence that might
deter a young man and his kin from seeking a wife elsewhere. Contrasting this strategy is bride capture
or “stealing” (fɨ). The three cases of bride capture in my data set, occurring between the late 1960s and
2021, did not involve the kidnapping of an unwilling woman. Rather, it was about the young couple

352

eloping without consulting the bride’s father. This elopement ideally lasts long enough to evidence an
emerging pregnancy, making opposition to the union from their families less likely. Interestingly, all
three instances involved two Andoque individuals. This might be due to the risk of overt or covert
violence from the bride’s family, which could be viewed as too significant when involving nonAndoque people. However, it might be deemed improbable or manageable when involving Andoque
members with whom the groom’s family has stronger ties. Thus, while suitors might aim for
matrimonial exchange based on past reciprocity or the promise of future ones when dealing with more
distant affinal centers, they might risk defying this norm when seeking union with a member of a closer
family, which might not be perceived as threatening to these particular suitors.
When discussing a period where parental marital arrangements are less frequent and systematic and
young individuals have greater freedom to seek spouses themselves without prioritizing their clan
interests, it is important to examine not only the power dynamics that marriage strategies aim to achieve
but also those that actual marriage unions produce. In the Andoque case, the two most notable
phenomena are the marginalization of the Eagle Clan, and especially the Harpy Eagle lineage, and the
competitive alliance between this lineage and the Sun Clan, that I will discuss in this order.
As observed in Chapter 4, Yiñékɒ’s leadership after the rubber genocide was intricately connected to his
marriage with Pa̰’fó, which transformed many individuals into his real affines and workers. Due to
Pa̰’fó’s central position in the kinship network among the small group of survivors and Yiñékɒ’s
(distant) blood ties with To̰fi, his descendants of the Harpy Eagle lineage found themselves in a
consanguineal centrality that precluded matrimony with numerous other Andoque individuals, as these
would be deemed incestuous. In the first generation born after their return to the territory, most of
Yiñékɒ’s efforts to seek outward marital alliances were thwarted, and four of his five children wedded
the few Andoque individuals to whom they were not related by blood, or with whom blood relations
could be suitably minimized. However, the pool of potential Andoque spouses for the children of these
unions, as well as for his sons’ unions with non-Andoque women, was notably limited. This pattern was
also evident in the broader Eagle Clan. Despite the clan’s significantly larger population over the
generations—105 members in 2018 compared to the next largest, the Atta Ant Clan, with 54 members
(Table 1, Chapter 3)—fewer men from the Eagle Clan than from the Sun Clan chose Andoque women as
their primary spouses. In contrast, the Eagle Clan predominantly provided women as spouses for other
Andoque clans.

The comparison with the Sun Clan is salient. This clan consists of the descendants of Pedro, a Miraña
man who was a marginal, orphan member of Yiñékɒ’s group. Their non-Andoque descent freed the
members of this clan from consanguineal ties to most Andoque members in the first generation born
after the return to the territory, resulting in their rise to a central position in the Andoque kinship
network and maintaining of this position ever since. Three of Pedro’s four sons married Andoque wives,
and this clan’s ability to continue marrying Andoque individuals persisted in the following generation,
as five of their children have had Andoque spouses. The members of the Deer, Beetle, and Atta Ant
Clans also had larger pools of potential Andoque spouses to choose from.

Table 8. Proportion of children born to two Andoque parents in the five main Andoque clans (1930–2019)129

As the table shows, the proportion of children from the Eagle Clan who also have Andoque mothers has
sharply declined over the years, accounting for only 24.39% among those born in the last examined
period (1990–2019). By contrast, during that same period, the Atta Ant and Sun Clans led in the
percentage of children born to Andoque mothers, registering 58.06% and 50%, respectively. Over the
broader timeframe (1930–2019), these two clans consistently demonstrated high rates of endogamous
parenthood—46.55% for the Atta Ant Clan and 62.5% for the Sun Clan.130
Regarding power dynamics, what are the benefits of endogamous unions? As discussed earlier,
endogamous unions are perceived as safer for the parties involved, given that the majority of individuals
accused of sorcery are non-Andoque, especially those who are real affines. As was also mentioned,
while marriage relations can create competition between brothers-in-law, they can also encourage

both Andoque and Murui—they are represented in this table as “Andoque mothers.” On the other hand, they are not
considered members of the Deer Clan. Therefore, while their own births are not recorded in the table, the births resulting
from their unions with Andoque men are included.
