mutual visits and cooperation between in-laws. An endogamous union typically implies closer
geographical proximity between a man and his in-laws, increasing the likelihood of mutual visits
between allied families and more frequent shared mambeadero sessions. During my fieldwork, I
observed that members of the Eagle Clan primarily visited the mambeaderos of their blood relatives and
mostly received visits from younger members of the Deer Clan. In contrast, members of the Sun Clan
engaged in more frequent visits both to and from mambeaderos of the Atta Ant and Beetle Clans.
However, endogamous unions and parenthood have further implications in today’s context, as members
of distinct Andoque-speaking clans own land collectively, receive resources, manage a community
school, and negotiate with state agencies, as well as other companies and organizations, as Andoque,
rather than as separate clans. The marital relations between the Sun, Atta Ant, and Beetle Clans—and
the more frequent visits their members exchange—correlate with their numerous instances of solidarity
in community assemblies concerning reserve leadership and management. During my fieldwork,
members of the three clans often formed a critical opposition to the reserve governor Hernando, Fisi’s
son from the Eagle Clan, who garnered support primarily from his own family and the Deer Clan.
Before my fieldwork, members of the Atta Ant Clan supported the candidacy of a member of the Sun
Clan for reserve governorship. After my fieldwork, they received backing from that clan for the
governorship candidacy of one of their own. In addition to the large number of children in the Atta Ant
Clan and the proximity in which families of that clan live, the alliance between the Atta Ant and the Sun
Clan underpinned their campaign to relocate the community school from Fisi’s settlement to the Atta
Ant settlement in 2002, citing allegations of the school’s mismanagement. In its current location, the
school predominantly serves the children of the Atta Ant Clan and provides income to members of this
clan who either work at the school or sell it food products.
Whereas marital exchange created collaborative affinal relations between the Sun Clan and the Atta Ant
and Beetle Clans, it created competitive dynamics between this clan and the Eagle Clan, following a
union that became pivotal for the Andoque people—namely, the matrimony between Tañe and Irene. In
the latter half of the 1960s, Irene left her Murui-Muina husband for Tañe, and shortly afterward gave
birth to Yiñékɒ’s first male grandson. However, Irene joined Tañe in the rubber camp, and when the
baby was a few months old, he died there. His death was first attributed to sorcery by the abandoned
husband and later to sorcery by another affinal relative, together with a lack of observation of dietary
rules by the parents, and Yiñékɒ became angry with Tañe for not protecting his grandson. Irene
describes the period following the baby’s death as a bleak period for Yiñékɒ when he did not have a
356

maloca and was full of negative, vengeful thoughts, which resulted in the insufficient spiritual protection
of four other Andoque babies who also died. Therefore, Yiñékɒ rejoiced when Irene gave birth to
another son in 1970, and this time preferred to monitor his son-in-law up close. He summoned Tañe for
a few intensive weeks of nocturnal mambeadero sessions, teaching him different healing procedures and
imparting essential knowledge for protecting his family. Tañe continued to frequent Yiñékɒ’s
mambeaderos over the years, listening to different myths and instructions from him. Irene remembers
how her father told her, when his grandson Wilson was three months old: “Now that I have a grandson,
I’ll build a maloca, I will give him a name, we will dance. I am thinking ‘good’ now (páa bɵ fg̋ ñḛkn
ḭtúañei).” Although Wilson was not Yiñékɒ’s only grandson by then—Irene’s younger brother had
become a father to a son shortly afterwards—he was the first one to be given a name by Yiñékɒ in a
ceremonial dance. Specifically, Yiñékɒ named Wilson (Hɵ́ñoi, “[the Moon’s Face is] Beautiful”) during
the red ritual specialization dance River Turtle-Carrier Band, associated with aggressiveness and
leadership (see the next chapter).
My interlocutors unanimously agree that Yiñékɒ destined Wilson to be a captain. Most of them, from all
clans, also assert that he saw Wilson as the future cacique, or captain above clan level, just like himself.
Wilson told me that he possesses superior capacity to engage in dialogues with the nonhuman entities of
the territory and provide them with more effective ḭtaséa (offerings) than any other Andoque member
today, because as a child, he managed to learn from Yiñékɒ for a few years before the latter’s death.
While several other interlocutors claimed that Wilson was too young back then to go through an
apprenticeship process, they concurred that Yiñékɒ “blessed” certain foodstuffs for his grandson, so that
the latter would carry Yiñékɒ’s knowledge within his stomach.
Tañe played an intermediary role in the transmission of knowledge between grandfather and grandson,
as he was instructed by Yiñékɒ to pass on the same teachings provided to him to his son as he grew up.
However, according to the account of the member of another family, Yiñékɒ had entrusted Tañe with
only the essentials required to care for his grandson, allowing the young boy to develop his own mature
thinking independently. Although Tañe did not belong to a maloquero family and had received a name
associated with the low-prestige Armadillo or Fern Dance during his childhood, which is linked with
white specialization, he grew to appreciate the prestige linked with the red specialization that Yiñékɒ
intended for his son. Tañe explained to me that when Yiñékɒ bestowed a name upon Wilson during a
“red” dance, he was also extending the red specialization to him. Tañe stated, “I wasn’t born to a red
career, but to Armadillo [Dance], whose origin is the fern (ti’ñḛdɨ, Pteridaceae sp.), and fern is also the
357

origin of the Tu’sí (the Multiplying Tree Dance) [of the red specialization]. With that origin, Yiñeko
switched my color from white to red.” Tañe was malleable, much like his father Pedro, who embraced
Andoque identity despite his Miraña upbringing. This set him apart from his brother-in-law, Yiñékɒ’s
younger son. Although this younger son fathered Yiñékɒ’s first surviving grandson, his own son was not
chosen for captaincy by the grandfather. This decision was attributed to his parents’ reputed bad temper,
particularly the father’s inclination to display defiance and contradict Yiñékɒ. Despite Yiñékɒ naming
the firstborn son of his elder son Fisi in the River Turtle-Carrier Band Dance in the following years,
none of my interlocutors attributed a similar process of knowledge and power transmission as involved
Wilson to that or any other grandson.
Irene recounted to me how, after she and Tañe moved to their current settlement, Yiñékɒ came “to fix
(hɵ́íkaí) the place where my daughter is going to live.” Tañe further described the collaborative effort
between his father and Yiñékɒ to drive away animals from the site that had been sent by a sorcerer to
harm his family. More generally, Tañe said that Yiñékɒ had explained to him that his clan, the Sun Clan,
is descended from the Piercers (Yɒ’nnkn), who lived along the Caquetá River. In contrast, Yiñékɒ’s
Eagle Clan and the other surviving clans trace their origins to the Shadows (Ká’hɵi síɵ́hɵ), who resided
further inland. As a result, according to Tañe, the majority of Andoque people now resides within the
ancestral territory of the Sun Clan, including the children of Yiñékɒ, who acknowledged not living
within his clan’s designated territory.
In 1986, three years after Yiñékɒ’s death, Tañe became the first member of his generation to construct a
maloca, a year ahead of his brother-in-law Fisi, Yiñékɒ’s son, who was Tañe’s main competitor for
leadership among Yiñékɒ’s mentees. Unlike his younger brother Rodolfo, who received his name in the
Fausíya “white” dance, Fisi did not have a ceremonial name bestowed upon him by his father. However,
according to Fisi, “I told my father, ‘I have a long tongue, I can tell many stories,’ and he listened to me
telling one story after another. He said: ‘You can [you have proved your capacities]!’ He changed my
name to Fi’siɒi (“Rock’s Edge”) when I was fourteen years old, almost fifteen. My mother said that
giving me such a name of a sorcerer [brujo, i.e., a powerful, wise man] was too heavy, that it was
dangerous, but he told her: ‘yes, he can [manage the powers contained in this name].’” Fisi received
teachings from his father on numerous occasions, especially during five years of intensive mambeadero
sessions following his separation from his first wife in the latter half of the 1960s. When Jon Landaburu
began working with the Andoque in 1969, Fisi became his assistant, collaborating to transcribe and
interpret myths narrated by Yiñékɒ and other elders. This experience, along with Fisi’s extensive
358

training under his father, positioned him in the eyes of most Andoque members as the ultimate authority
on mythology and other traditions. This also paved the way for a series of collaborations with
anthropologists and researchers, as well as invitations to participate in conferences worldwide.
While Fisi represented Andoque traditions in such instances, Tañe and other members of the Sun Clan
served as intermediaries between the Andoque and the non-Indigenous world. This trend began with
Margarita, Tañe’s maternal grandmother, who married a non-Indigenous Venezuelan man and raised her
family at the mouth of Macaw River, distanced from Yiñékɒ’s maloca. This location earned her family
the moniker “the River Mouth People” (ɵkɒ́ ño̰e), a designation linked with Whites. Before Margarita’s
daughter Ines married Pedro, she lived with both Miguel Zumaeta, from whom she bore Amazonas, and
another mestizo man, from whom she bore Alisia. While Amazonas solidified the blood connection
between the Sun Clan and the Zumaeta family, Alisia played a pivotal affinal role by marrying Alberto
Zumaeta, Amazonas’ half-brother (who is not biologically related to her). Delio and Tañe, Pedro’s sons,
became integral collaborators alongside their brother-in-law Alberto and their nephew Jairo in various
economic ventures that ensued after rubber extraction, such as animal pelt hunting and fishing. In one of
these ventures during the 1980s, Andoque members would submit raw materials at Tañe’s maloca and
collect their pay there. This pay arrived in the form of goods purchased in Bogotá, harking back to the
classic role of the maloca as the center of economic exchange with Whites and as a repository for goods
obtained through such exchanges. This legacy persisted until shortly before my fieldwork, when
Alberto’s son Carlos allied with Delio and Tañe’s sons, Orlando and Levy, to legalize gold mining in the
Andoque territory (Audren 2017). Interestingly, the Sun Clan’s business orientation, which implies a
more extractive and utilitarian attitude toward nonhuman entities, aligns with their descent from the
Piercers. As suggested in Chapter 8, the Piercers represent greater human determination vis-à-vis
nonhumans and domination over them.
Today, Fisi and the members of his household discredit Tañe’s first maloca on account of these business
relations, attributing its construction not to his commitment to the ceremonial tradition but as part of a
specific economic initiative that necessitated traditional settings. They also explain Fisi’s personal delay
in building a maloca after Yiñékɒ’s death by his intention to wait in the wings for his brother Rodolfo to
construct one. This choice allegedly reflects Fisi’s respect for Yiñékɒ’s action of conferring a
ceremonial name to Rodolfo rather than to himself. This is because when two brothers reside in the same
settlement, as was the case for Fisi and Rodolfo, they cannot each lead separate malocas, but are
expected to collaborate and support the one who undertakes such a project. Fisi finally constructed his
359

own maloca when he realized that Rodolfo would not initiate the process, spurred by the requests of
several Andoque women.
Tañe and Fisi became ceremonial allies and competitors, exchanging invitations to most of the dances
they organized, as expected of brothers-in-law. However, their mutual criticism, at times, appear to
undermine the vital competitive dynamics between maloqueros. They each hold different versions of
several myths and ritual traditions learned from Yiñékɒ, such as the myth of the origin of Multiplying
Tree (for Fisi’s version see M11 in Appendix 1, vs. Tañe’s versions in de la Hoz Melo 2005, 38–42) or
the story of Tofidei’s war against the anacondas of the River Mouth (Fisi’s version: M23 in Appendix 1;
Tañe’s version: de la Hoz Melo 2005, 38–42). In the case of the myth regarding the war between the
Sun and the Moon (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 45–52), which serves as the origin story of Tañe’s clan,
the two narrators allocate the actions of the protagonists differently. Fisi emphasizes the violent and
malicious nature of Sun, whereas Tañe underscores his role as the benefactor providing light and life to
humanity. As discussed in Chapter 4, they each also hold different versions in relation to the extent of
Mnkoena’s guidance and the corresponding significance of lineage membership in Yiñékɒ’s
apprenticeship process. Though both maloqueros claim to be true adherents of Yiñékɒ’s teachings, Tañe
and his family members point out Fisi’s invention of concepts and practices that Yiñékɒ never imparted.
On the other hand, Fisi and his household members raise questions about the adequacy of Tañe’s
knowledge in myth and ritual.
Fisi and his family members present Tañe as an inferior rival. They recount how Tañe invited Fisi to his
first Multiplying Tree Dance, but when it came to replicating the songs sung by Fisi during that dance at
Fisi’s reciprocated event where Tañe was the guest, Tañe stumbled. Despite continuing to invite Tañe as
a guest, Fisi downplayed his singing abilities and relied on Alfonso from the Atta Ant Clan for that role.
Of greater significance, Fisi invited Tañe for a Fausíya Dance in 1997, but the latter did not respond
with a reciprocal invitation for the same dance, because he never organized one. According to Fisi, this
has resulted in a debt owed by both maloqueros to the dance’s owner-person, a situation that puts them
at risk. Consequently, Fisi explained, he had stopped inviting Tañe to dances because the latter “ya no
pudo”—he proved that he could not keep up with his rival’s challenges. Fisi’s family members
emphasize that this has left Fisi without a ceremonial partner, leading to a decline in the dances he has
organized since. Although Fisi invited Alfonso to sing at several dances, he was aware that the latter,
lacking a maloca, could not extend reciprocal dance invitations to him. Although Fisi was invited

360

several times by Mario, he reciprocated by inviting Mario back only infrequently, as the latter had
previously collaborated with him and his father in dance organization.
While Fisi and his family members criticize Tañe for lacking the necessary competence in myth and
ritual, which is essential for a maloquero, Tañe counters by highlighting their deficiency in another
crucial aspect—organizing people for collaborative work efforts and efficiently allocating resources, a
skill for which many individuals commend him. Moreover, according to Tañe and his family, the
cessation of reciprocal invitations between them and Fisi stemmed from a different rationale. The
construction of their second maloca in 2000 was intended to groom Wilson for the role of maloquero.
Wilson embraced greater ceremonial responsibilities, arranging dances to which he invited his own
brother-in-law, Elias, who also had his own maloca by then and reciprocated the dance invitations. In
essence, what Fisi and his family perceive as a manifestation of Tañe’s inadequate ceremonial prowess,
Tañe interprets as adherence to Yiñékɒ’s intentions and the seamless transfer of ceremonial duties to the
next generation—a transfer that, in his view, is absent in Fisi’s household, signaling Fisi’s shortcomings
in preparing his sons for the role of maloquero.
In conclusion, the competitive alliance between Fisi and Tañe is the outcome of the unforeseen union
between Irene and Tañe, and of Yiñékɒ’s bending agnatic logic. In this exceptional scenario, the
maternal grandfather bestowed knowledge and power that he may not have shared with his
grandchildren from his own clan, upon a grandson who belongs to another clan—a clan that the
grandfather had nevertheless founded and shaped himself. Whether we adopt Fisi’s perspective on
Tañe’s insufficient competence or Tañe’s interpretation of his role as an intermediary link between
Yiñékɒ and the predestined captain, Wilson, we discern that the boundaries of this alliance were also
inscribed within the unique circumstances that brought it about. However, the transition of the vital
competitive alliance between brother-in-law maloqueros to the younger generation was short-lived. In
2012, Wilson moved with his family to Leticia following security issues that he encountered in the
Araracuara sector. Elias expressed sorrow at losing his ritual partner, and in 2018, he and his mother
departed from their maloca due to familial problems. In that same year, Tañe and his brother took the
uncommon initiative of collaborating with Fisi in a ceremonial dance that Fisi organized. This
occurrence had the potential to transform their relationship from one of rivalry to cooperation, guided by
a more hierarchical dynamic. However, this potential shift was hindered by the subsequent allegations
voiced by both parties following the dance, as well as Tañe’s construction of a new maloca in 2020. In

361

the upcoming section, we delve into the Andoque politics of knowledge, which will provide deeper
insight into this rivalry and others within the group.
Political Knowledge Among Centers
Knowledge is a crucial, scarce, and highly contested resource for shaping exchanges with competing
human and nonhuman centers, and it is subject to a complex politics of concealment and disclosure
among individuals and groups. Fisi and Tañe are not the only presumed heirs to Yiñékɒ’s knowledge
and captaincy skills. Three other elders, who were initiated to different traditions by Yiñékɒ, told me
that the knowledge that he granted them was accompanied by a bestowal of power, representing his
recognition in their worth and support for their actions—something not necessarily extended to others.
During a session in his maloca, one of the elders, having explained to me the symbols and logic of
dream interpretation that Yiñékɒ had taught him, remarked:
Interlocutor X: Yiñékɒ spoke to me. He told me all of that when we were alone in the maloca.
Eliran: Y was not there? Z was not there?
X: No one. Whenever someone arrived, he would tell me, “That’s enough, I am not going to talk anymore so that no
one can say ‘Yiñékɒ is teaching X, X used to accompany Yiñékɒ, he knows,’ and then they would accuse you, and
everyone would point and say, ‘You’re the one who knows, you’re the one who knows…’”
E: What would they accuse you of?
X: Because they saw him speaking to me a lot.
E: But why would they accuse you? Isn’t it a good thing that he spoke to you?
X: It’s good, but it’s also bad, isn’t it?
E: Why is it bad?
X: Because the one who knows can screw people (joder), he can overtake them in thinking (ganar en pensamiento), or
something of that sort.

According to my interlocutors, Yiñékɒ never explicitly designated a specific person as his successor or
as someone entrusted by him to lead dances, and some said that the Andoque do not do such things.131
However, when attempting to negate the power or advantage of certain individuals in terms of
leadership or dance organization, people often bring up an incident they either witnessed themselves or
heard about, where Yiñékɒ told the disciple, “You will not be capable” (no va a poder), following that
person’s disorderly drunken behavior or violent outburst. While the concealment of knowledge

This does not necessarily occur with other People of the Center. In October 2018 I attended a ceremonial dance at a
Féénemɨna maloca in the upriver Monochoa reserve that was especially designated for the transference of leadership from the
old maloquero to his son, and included a speech where the former entrusted the authority to continue ceremonial activity to
the latter.
131

362

acquisition and the dismissal of others’ knowledge, along with the power it holds, have specific aspects
unique to this succession struggle within its historical context, they also characterize the broader
Andoque politics of knowledge. Understanding these dynamics is crucial for comprehending the
interactions among human centers and the ways they operate within the context of relations with
nonhumans.
Yiñékɒ’s centrality in the post-genocide period and in the initiation processes of several of today’s
elders in the 1960s and 1970s is evident in the frequents references to Yiñékɒ by many members when
recounting myths or discussing Andoque traditions, more so than with other elders of the post-genocide
generation or—when these members are not Yiñékɒ’s children—their own parents. Anchoring the
interpretation or version of myths, ritual practices, or other customs in Yiñékɒ’s teachings—even his
pronunciation of specific Andoque words—serves to legitimize arguments and positions. This practice
inevitably implies a dismissal of competing interpretations, versions, or pronunciations.
Fisi embodies an extreme manifestation of this approach. During one of the first internal assemblies in
which I participated in September 2018, I proposed collaborating with the elders to document
ceremonial songs and create a booklet for schoolchildren. While many members liked the idea and
agreed to cooperate in private conversations, during the assembly the participants raised numerous
logistical concerns to reject the proposal. Fisi, however, voiced a different kind of concern: “I am the
only one who knows, so-so (medio-medio), the songs of the ten main Andoque dances, and I should
work in this project. Others don’t know and might provide incorrect versions. Moreover, many here
don’t pronounce the [Andoque] language well. Only a few of us—Raquel, Sabina, Henri, and I
[pronounce it well]. And also I, I could only sit in the mambeadero with my father for five years; after
that, I wanted to leave…” On another occasion, Fisi suggested to me collaborating to document myths
not included in Landaburu and Pineda’s anthology from 1984, as well as re-record some myths already
published there, once again for schoolchildren. Fisi explained that although these authors primarily
worked with his father, they also incorporated fragments from different myth versions recorded among
several elders of that generation while editing the final document. Consequently, their anthology
contains numerous errors—these errors being the divergences from Yiñékɒ’s versions. Evidently, the
context of these statements by Fisi is crucial. Both the internal assembly and our conversation about
compiling myths took place in the initial months of my stay. During this time, members were attempting
to assess the extent of my access to material resources and anticipated that research initiatives would be
associated with projects funded by an organization, including compensation for informants. This sheds
363

light on the economic factors underpinning Fisi’s portrayal of myth documentation as an urgent task and
his assertion as the sole dependable source for such tasks. Fisi’s approach echoes the strategies of other
Amazonians who seek material benefits from non-Indigenous agents, particularly researchers, in
exchange for sharing knowledge that is unevenly distributed. At the local level, the worth and content of
this knowledge are derived from an individual’s personal relationships with both human and nonhuman
agents. Yet, its value to outsiders relies on its consideration as collective immaterial heritage, which it
only becomes in the context of such communication with the outside (de Vienne and Allard 2005). In
the Andoque case, these instances speak to Fisi’s (publicly stated) claims of having a monopoly over
Yiñékɒ’s legacy, which—given that the latter served as a prime funnel for Andoque oral traditions
following the genocide—extends to the broader Andoque lore as well.
On the other hand, Andoque members—along with Fisi during certain mambeadero sessions and
internal assemblies—often acknowledge the validity of different versions of the same myths or ritual
practices. They explain that the survival of specific clans after the rubber genocide and the continuous
reproduction of their members serve as evidence for the veracity of these myth versions and traditions,
which have safeguarded them. During my initial stay at Mario’s maloca after months of visiting other
families, he, like many others, was curious about what I had learned in other mambeaderos. When I
mentioned that I would not divulge information from one place in another, he shared a story: “When I
was young, I used to move from one mambeadero to another, just like my sons do now. But later, after
having a wife and a son, I only attended Yiñékɒ’s mambeadero. Once, when he told me a story, I said: ‘I
was told this story differently elsewhere.’ Yiñékɒ told me, ‘It’s the same thing. What you heard is not an
invention, but that’s the way their clan recounts it.’ So this is what you are doing.” During our
conversations, various members invoked Yiñékɒ’s memory to criticize Fisi. They stated that, unlike his
son, Yiñékɒ always respected the teachings of others and the traditions of different clans. We may
rightfully suspect that the consensus surrounding Yiñékɒ’s figure in contemporary Andoque discourse
partially arises from his absence and a general nostalgia for his era; people also mentioned instances
where he discredited practices or interpretations by other elders. However, it seems that one of the
peacemaking responsibilities of an ideal cacique, or a leader above the clan level, is to recognize the
coexistence of diverse versions and traditions, and not to favor those of his own clan.
“There is an ‘Indigenous politics,’” Tañe explained as he recounted his initiation process with Yiñékɒ,
“For example, Cacique [Fisi] once asked me: ‘What site does your power come from?’ and I told him, ‘Parrot
Savanna.’ And he said that it’s a lie. I told him, ‘This is what your deceased father taught me.’ Yet, the deceased

364

[Yiñékɒ] had already said all this. He said, ‘People will try to correct you, but ignore them. You heard it from me, and
everything else is a lie.’ This is why I don’t tell others what I know. Otherwise, people will say ‘You’re talking lies.’
When somebody tells you you’re wrong and tries to explain to you, and you know that what you said is true, within
his words there’s a spirit that takes away your power of thought, and your thought fades away (se pierde). And
everyone is doing the same as I do. I don’t know, for example, what are Mario and Cacique’s thoughts.”

While Tañe’s anecdotes attest to the peculiarity of contemporary competition over knowledge between
elders of different clans who were trained by the same person due to the massive depletion of oral
traditions in the past century, they also reflect the centrality of the notion of secrecy in the Andoque’s
more general politics of knowledge.
Secrecy in Amazonia has been explored across various contexts, three of which are relevant for our
current purpose. First, anthropologists have noted that Amazonians feign ignorance about sorcery and
other shamanic skills or choose not to acquire them to avoid sorcery accusations or assaults by other
shamans who wish to compete with them or avenge harms that would be attributed to them (Buchillet
2004; Heckenberger 2004; High 2015). Second, among the Jivaro, the potency of an arutam vision,
centered on its owner’s encounter with a nonhuman entity, relies on its secrecy and abandons the owner
who translates it into symbols, which are then communicated with others (Harner 1984, 139; Rubenstein
2007; 2012). Finally, ethnographers of the Tukanoan-Arawakan complex in the Upper Rio NegroVaupés region pointed out the calculated economy between the possession of secret knowledge and its
publication as a sign to and key for political prerogatives and prestige (Andrello 2010; Figalli de Angelo
2020; S. Hugh-Jones 2010; 2019).
In the Andoque case, one tends to keep to oneself both the knowledge and shamanic skills one
possesses, and one’s knowledge of such capacities held by others. The notion that a person’s power,
well-being, and even their very life are contingent upon their mastery of specific stories, particularly
their clan’s origin myth, leads individuals to feign ignorance or disinterest in narratives known to others
and other forms of knowledge they possess. This precaution is taken to avert potential blame should any
misfortune befall others. Alongside the fear that engaging in serious thinking about other people,
especially those living at a great distance, exposes one’s tutelary spirit (yono̰píi) to unexpected spiritual
assaults (see Chapter 7), and unlike the doctrine of “the opacity of other minds” in the Pacific, which
concerns mainly guessing other people’s motives (e.g., Stasch 2008; Robbins and Rumsey 2008), the
underlying notion here is that knowing what other people think is not impossible, but dangerous.

365

In addition to discretion over what others may know, and although their downplaying of the knowledge
held by others may imply the speaker’s own superiority in that domain, Andoque members speak highly
of humility in relation to what one knows. One elder recounted an anecdote from his youth when he
restored old Yiñékɒ from a temporary state of madness. According to that interlocutor, when Yiñékɒ
regained his senses, he told him: “You know how to heal!” My interlocutor humbly replied: “No, I don’t
know anything. My father showed it to me, and I did it.” This modest response earned him the
appreciation of Yiñékɒ, who commented, “This is exactly what I like to hear! Other people boast that
they can cure everything, but in fact they don’t know a thing! And one has to say just like you did: ‘I
don’t know.’” My interlocutor added that Yiñékɒ himself used to say: “Everyone is afraid of Yiñékɒ,
but I don’t know anything.”
While the elders at whose settlements I stayed shared with me in their mambeaderos different myths and
traditions and mentioned some skills that they mastered, they emphasized that they would not flaunt this
knowledge in front of other members or Indigenous people of the region. Indeed, I observed their silence
whenever these skills or topics were broached in communal settings or gatherings outside their own
mambeaderos. This was particularly notable during the six-day workshop held in November-December
2018 to formulate the first parts of the cultural plan for territorial management mentioned in Chapter 8.
The workshop convened over twenty elders and younger men and women at the community school in
the settlement of the Atta Ant Clan to discuss the basic definitions of territorial components, traditional
management principles, and the ecological calendar. However, the elder participants were reluctant to
share their knowledge. The laconic information exchanged during the daytime sessions paled in
comparison with the detailed and more specific explanations offered by Fisi, his sons, and their two
Andoque guests to me and to each other in the mambeadero sessions throughout the workshop week.
Boasting about knowledge is risky as it may invite challenges from others who might use harmful
practices. Knowing (do, “to know, to see”) something depends on the relationship with the entity from
which it was learned, such as the instructor of a myth and, more significantly, its nonhuman ownerperson, whereas a skill, like sorcery or healing procedures, depends on effective mastery over its ownerperson. Therefore, competitors over skills and knowledge strive to demonstrate a closer relationship
with those owner-persons. This can result in the contestant’s monopoly over the relationship and the
cessation of communication between it and the braggart, and/or convincing that owner-person to inflict
harm—preferably related to what was bragged about—on the braggart. For example, an interlocutor
shared that he had been a skilled male midwife until he bragged about it, causing someone to take away
366

this capacity. Another interlocutor recalled how, in her youth, she and her husband had sought to gather
larvae from a tree near the house of a woman who eventually forbade them from taking “her larvae.”
Upon recounting this to Yiñékɒ, he said, “If that’s what she said, let’s see who’s the real owner of these
larvae.” Reportedly, Yiñékɒ then expelled the specific larva not only from the woman’s tree but the
entire area—and it has not returned to this day. More severe competitions over knowledge and power
are attributed to the period before the rubber genocide, when sorcerers allegedly wiped-out entire clans
through epidemics due to not being invited to dances organized by those clans, based on their perception
of the lack of invitation as a dismissal of their knowledge and status.
Similar to the Jivaro notion mentioned earlier, where the potency of an arutam vision relies on its
secrecy, Andoque members maintain that disclosing knowledge undermines its possession. I first
encountered this notion one month into fieldwork during a hunting expedition with Hector’s* son, as we
gathered a particular leaf from the forest and chewed it for protection against snake venom. When we
returned home, Hector instructed me that I should not share this information with anyone, as it would
cause it to lose its effectiveness for me. This is what happened to his wife’s brother in the past. The
brother could not cure Hector’s wife after she was bitten by a snake because he had previously revealed
this remedy. However, when Hector administered the remedy, it worked. Knowledge about healing
methods can only be shared after the successful treatment of two or more patients, which demonstrates
the assimilation of the remedy’s power into one’s own reservoir of capabilities, where it becomes
‘locked in’ and cannot dissipate. Even then, such sharing should be limited to one’s children and
siblings; in my case, they shared the secret due to my participation in the expedition. However, it is
typical for patients not to be informed about the components of the remedy or the accompanying
incantation, and healers might also request patients not to disclose who treated them.
Later during fieldwork, I encountered this belief and the prohibition on disclosing information from
other interlocutors. Within the context of healing practices, some of them emphasized its particular
relevance to procedures involving the recounting of myth segments (ǵ’a) or the invocation of the spirit
master connected to the procedure or plant in question, as opposed to simple herbal cures (ɵ’nó̰sé).
However, interlocutors asserted that this risk applies to any procedure or task governed by an ownerperson. Sharing such knowledge before fully mastering its owner-person or without obtaining
permission from it is referred to as sapiar, or “ratting,” on the owner-person, who would consequently
retract its support from the practitioner. (Interestingly, however, the procedure may work for the person
in whose ears the practitioner illegitimately explained it). “Cures are like people,” Hector’s nephew told
367

me, “When you cure someone, you give him [the person whom the cure embodies] an order, and just
like people get annoyed when too many people boss them around, and then stop working, so does the
cure. The cure is sacred, you cannot harass it.” This linkage of potent action to discretion echoes the
episode in M3, where Egret of the River Source halted his effort-free roofing of the maloca upon the
arrival of his father-in-law, leaving the laborious, time-consuming task of pui weaving to the latter, and
by extension, to humanity today. A similar incident is recounted in M6, where the axe ceased to work
autonomously upon the arrival of the father-in-law, suggesting a certain incongruence between one’s
knowledge and affines, to which we will return below.
This discretion is particularly important for myths underpinning one’s core capacities, like the myths
involving Egret of the Center for a captain or the myths centered around Shadow Egg for a healer. It is
also highly relevant for the myths affecting one’s well-being and very life, as is the clan origin myth of
any given individual. Ethnographers have documented the tendency among the People of the Center to
hide their clan origin myths from members of other clans (and ethnic group) or only provide them with
thin versions of these stories (García 2018, 415 n.21; Londoño Sulkin 2000, 330). Similar to their
neighbors, the Andoque perceive these origin myths as containing the keys to both heal and bewitch clan
members. Outsiders can latch onto specific malevolent episodes within these stories and distort them
against those individuals whose identities are embedded in them. For instance, the narrative of the war
between Sun and Moon (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 45–52) can be manipulated to sow discord
between brothers from the Sun Clan over a woman. Similarly, the tale of the cannibal Eagle can be
invoked to unleash the destructive fury of the Eagle Clan (see M9). For this reason, several interlocutors
refused to tell me their clan origin myth and only provided succinct outlines of other stories that hold
significance in shaping their personal identities. The secrecy shrouding clan origin myths is a clear
example of the boundary that agnatic ideology sets to the process of familiarization and the
consanguinizing dimensions of commensality, precluding the consideration of co-residents as complete
consanguines unless they are clan members.
Additionally, people refrain from recounting myths that encapsulate the essential vitality and potential
hazards of their territory and its beings in the presence of non-Andoque Indigenous individuals, due to
their concern that these outsiders would set the nonhuman entities of the territory against its Andoque
inhabitants or seek establishing a stronger link with them. In this context, the Nɨpóde teacher’s active
participation in the above-mentioned workshop to draft the cultural plan for territorial management had
a significant impact. It served as another reason why the Andoque participants exercised caution in
368

selecting the information they disclosed. They were wary that members of the teacher’s group might
exploit this shared information against them, either through shamanic modes of communication with
nonhuman entities or through modern means of communication with the state—i.e., by publishing
documents appropriating Andoque knowledge about the territory’s sites and their owners.
How should we understand these Andoque notions of secrecy? According to Georg Simmel’s classic
formula, the formal characteristics of the secret hold greater significance than its content. The secret
multiplies reality and creates a unique relationship between the concealers, which consequently shapes
their behavior towards the larger society, regardless of the specific content of the secret (1950, 330–31,
345). The secret’s value and the fascination it evokes depend, to a large extent, on the exclusion of
others from it (ibid, 332). It is important to note that Simmel’s argument assumes a distinction between
knowledge and practice, while the Andoque resemble other Indigenous peoples near and far (e.g.,
Londoño Sulkin 2012, 76; Norton-Smith 2010, 55–76), in viewing knowledge as inherently practical, its
value lying in its application in reality, achieving specific goals or fulfilling desires. Furthermore, in the
Andoque case, we encounter a form of secrecy that seems, at first glance, to revolve around the
individual rather than the group. It does not necessarily imply either the existence of a synchronic
“secret society,” or the diachronic reception of occult knowledge from another person, as it may also
concern knowledge acquired directly through personal experience with a plant or another substance. As
such, we might benefit from Gilbert Herdt’s (1990) perspective, which shifts our focus from viewing
secrets as a means of social differentiation between outsiders and insiders, to considering the secret as a
major ontological mechanism for the formation of the self.
Within this context, Fausto and Costa’s argument that the pet-master relations are crucial for
understanding the constitution of the “animist subject” (2019, 214–15) offers a good avenue for
exploring Andoque notions of secrecy. In Fausto’s comparative analysis of Amazonian secret flute cults
(2020, 73–121), he emphasizes the pet-master relationship established between the flute and its male
player, which involves the player feeding the flute and the flute’s dependence on the player. The human
breath fosters an identification between the player and the flute, as its flow marks the continuity between
the flute and the tubes within the human owner’s body. This melding of bodies signifies the alignment of
the flute’s agency and the spirit it embodies with that of its human owner, a relationship aiming to
enhance the reproductive capacities of the owner and, by extension, his group. The secrecy surrounding
these flutes establishes a three-term relational structure: the men who can hear and see the flutes, the
women who can only hear them, and the spirits of the flutes (ibid, 77). This framework, rooted in
369

Indigenous ontological understandings about the distribution of agency and intentionality among
nonhumans as well, counters Simmel’s assumption that the social realities that secrets create involve
only human subjects, and brings us closer to understanding the Andoque notions of secrecy.
In Simmel’s terms, the simplest structure of human sociality is a dyad, consisting of two human
elements (1950, 118–25), with the triad enriching this social reality, as each one of its three components
“operates as an intermediary between the other two, exhibiting the twofold function of such an organ,
which is to unite and to separate” (ibid, 135). By contrast, for an animist society like the Andoque’s, the
simplest inter-human social structure is not merely a dyad of two humans, but a triad that also includes a
nonhuman element, such as the coca or game they share, or the owner-person of the maloca where they
sit. By expanding Simmel’s model of the secret accordingly to encompass also nonhuman actors, we can
view an individual’s secret related to a shamanic skill, such as a healing procedure, as a social
relationship maintained by the individual with the owner-person of that skill and excluding other human
actors. The value of the secret—here, the efficacy of the remedy—is inversely proportional to the
number of individuals in the know, as the remedy would lose its potency if it became public knowledge,
“just like people get annoyed when too many people boss them around.” Such value grants the secretkeeper the power to either enforce asymmetry upon others through sorcery or to counteract such
attempts via healing.
Yet another essential asymmetry in the Andoque case, vital for a skill’s efficacy, lies between the human
practitioner and the nonhuman entity. This master-pet dynamic, as discussed in Chapter 9, aims to
minimize the likelihood of the entity resisting the practitioner’s wishes and its vulnerability to being
enlisted and mastered by another human—as might occur when someone deprives another of a
previously held skill. Hence, one can only pass on a healing method after having successfully
implemented it multiple times, or, as Fisi recounts Yiñékɒ saying, “You can only say that you know
how to cure foodstuffs for children once your youngest child gives you a grandchild,” the latter acting as
tangible evidence of the grandfather’s remedial expertise. It is also essential to remember that gaining
mastery over the nonhuman owner of a skill, for a practitioner, requires prior secrets with other
nonhuman elements, such as the owner-persons of coca and tobacco or the clan origin. This, in turn,
presupposes a continuous exchange with human clan members, ensuring the possession of a soul
(mo̰no̰i) that is in tune with the human body it inhabits. Thus, Andoque practical knowledge emerges as
a recursive framework where, on each level, human and nonhuman agencies strive to impose
asymmetries on one another or counteract them.
370

This brings us to the distinction that Andoque members make between advertising knowledge
indiscreetly and transmitting it within the clan or during an initiation process. Whereas “ratting” on an
owner-person of a skill results from the capricious, unauthorized expansion of the secret group of the
owner-person and the practitioner to include a third secret sharer, an initiation process (yitai) can be
interpreted as representing or effecting the expansion of the tutor’s body to include that third sharer. A
similar notion has been observed among the Min of Papua New Guinea, where the transmission of
important knowledge, referred to as awem and previously assumed by researchers to be limited to male
initiates, is conceptualized as “exchanging skin” (Crook 2007). Within households, individuals share
secrets with male and female members with whom they also share food and care. Such “exchanges
involving knowledge would be understood as the mutual support of persons who become encompassed
together as if they were one person” (ibid, 11).
Andoque members describe the ideal initiation process as one in which a parent or grandparent imparts
knowledge to their child or grandchild. These elder kin bestow knowledge on their younger kin out of
love—a sentiment expressed through the construct ḭ́ ’tú (“be in one’s heart”), which denotes care and
protection. Knowledge is encoded in myths, which the Andoque distinguish from other “stories” (pɨséi)
or “words, sayings” (hɵɵ́i). Myths are designated through the word ḭpoíkó, which links them with the
notion of patriclan: “that which becomes a father,” or “that which comes from the father” (Landaburu
and Pineda 1984, 80 n.46). Knowledge is, by definition, the project of a given clan center. It is created,
preserved, and shared among consanguine kins in a bid to ensure the survival of this center through the
survival and well-being of these kins. The clan survival at which knowledge aims is its survival in a
world populated by competing human and nonhuman affinal centers that attempt to hijack the members
of this clan into their respective realities. The mutual dependence between the clan and its members
recalls Herdt’s (1990) perspective on the importance of the secret for the formation and existence of the
self/person, and to his substitution of Simmel’s simple dichotomy between inside/outside with that
between multiple secret collectives and their respective ontologies. Hence, rather than simply engaging
in politics of knowledge, Andoque members envisage knowledge as inherently (cosmo)political.
This provides additional context for understanding the sexual and culinary instructions and prohibitions
surrounding apprenticeship to different specializations, such as healing, sorcery, or captaincy, that I
mentioned in Chapter 9: the success of this process in ensuring protection from this affinal world would
be thwarted if this process were accompanied by sharing foodstuffs and bodies with affines. On the
contrary, during apprenticeship, the apprentice provides the tutor with food and ritual substances in
371

exchange for teachings, such that if they are not kin yet, this nourishing enhances consubstantiality
between them. This way, an orphan residing at the maloca of another clan can access some of the
maloquero’s knowledge—work and the provision of alimentary substances compensate for the lack of
blood ties. The consubstantiality between tutor and apprentice makes the former responsible for the
latter in respect to the owner-persons of the transmitted knowledge. This is why Andoque members say
that if an apprentice disobeys his tutor by engaging in sexual activity during the initiation period, he runs
the risk of being bewitched by the tutor, who is also jeopardized by this breach.
The term for “secret” in Andoque is ̰osoi, which literally means “hidden thing,” and knowledge
concealment is often referred to through expressions such as “this is not to be told” (hɵ́má nie hɵɵ́ni).
However, there is a native concept that Andoque members consistently translate into Spanish as secretos
(“secrets”), and I argue that this concept is paradigmatic to the notion of secret knowledge crucial for the
clan’s survival and its members’ capacity to establish and maintain asymmetries with human and
nonhuman centers. This concept is ḭtasé.
While ḭtasé, as explained in the previous chapter, may refer to any offering, it is only in context of
ceremonial dances that it is translated as secretos. These special offerings of coca powder, tobacco paste,
vegetal salt, manicuera, and caguana are prepared in small amounts before the dance by male and female
consanguineous relatives of the maloquero or other workers with whom consubstantiality has been
established through prolonged exchange. Upon preparation, these offerings are kept out of reach of the
many people who typically frequent the maloca prior to a dance, until they are consumed by the
maloquero and several dance workers, and through them—by the Creator, or the owner-persons of the
dance and human group. Special attention is also paid to ensure that these offerings are not snatched
before consumption by the spirits safeguarding animals—a snatching inferred from any immoral or
aggressive behaviour by the workers during dance preparation, representing the “feeding” of malevolent
nonhumans. If this happens, the Creator would refuse the offerings, and their consumption by the
maloquero could be fatal, as reportedly occurred to one dance organizer in recent decades.
The consumption of these offerings is done on the eve of a dance—in the case of major dances, at the
opening part of the ritual of caguana distribution which precedes these dances (see next chapter). Since I
did not attend any Andoque dance, I was only informed by my interlocutors about the main happenings
of this secret moment. The maloquero and several other male workers gather at the mambeadero, and the
former summons the Creator, dedicating the offerings. He samples each of the substances and passes

372

them to the other men present. Two other men guard the maloca entrance, urging anyone outside to
enter; otherwise, the malevolent animal spirits might take them. The last man at the mambeadero to
receive caguana initiates the song (nni) of the distribution ritual, and the last to receive manicuera joins
in with reply verses. These men are joined in song by two women who “complete the words” (fohɵɵ́i) of
the song by echoing the last sounds of each verse. When the song concludes, the manguaré drums are
played. This marks the end of the secret moment, whose content—the words addressed at the Creator
and the song—is kept from anyone not present. It is especially concealed from the guest of the dance,
though he may attend the caguana distribution that follows the manguaré drumming. In sum, for the
Andoque, the essence of secrecy is this potent interaction with nonhuman entities to ensure the wellbeing of the human group, hidden from affinal relatives.
To conclude this chapter’s discussions on key power dynamics among human centers, I wish to connect
this discussion on the politics of knowledge to the concept of affinization through sorcery. Witchcraft,
beyond signifying the victim’s distancing from the sorcerer, may also draw the former closer to the
affinal world by separating them from their own consanguineously-transmitted thinking and knowledge.
One way to describe sorcery is through the verb yoíkói, which means “to deviate”—understood as a
deviation from one’s “thinking” as enshrined in clan origin myths, which serves as one’s protection
against familiarization attempts by nonhumans. A powerful curse that one can cast on another is páso’i,
giving them “a new word” to distract them from their protective words of origin. Such a curse can cause
effects ranging from relatively small nuisances like socially inappropriate behavior or bodily habits,
such as a disagreeable laughter or excessive consumption of coca, to a complete acceptance of foreign
modes of thinking and the subsequent abandonment of ritual and other practices, that typically shield
one from predation and familiarization by nonhumans. Origin myths and other stories on which a
person’s power and vitality are based must be kept hidden, lest another introduces “a new word” into
them. A similar risk exists upon the incorporation of an in-marrying wife into a household, as she may
impose, in different ways, her “woman’s word” on her husband and his clan—which, in turn, represents
the ongoing danger of familiarization by her relatives, with whom a man ideally engages in an ongoing
exchange of words, work, and substances. Therefore, all contact with non-consanguine kin involves the
risk of deviation from patrilineally-transmitted traditions, which would then leave one vulnerable to
affinization by nonhuman entities. This is one of the reasons why the familiarization of substances used
for ritual, such as coca, tobacco, and manicuera (see Chapter 6), is also crucial within the context of
communication and exchange with other human beings. This demonstrates how the Andoque’s notion of
373

power is deeply intertwined with a concentric conception of kinship, spanning from agnatic and cognatic
consanguinity to real and potential affinity or enmity, as well as a continuity between inter-human
relations and relations between humans and nonhumans. As this and the former chapter have
demonstrated, this continuity unfolds through a complex interplay of forces. The establishment of
beneficial asymmetries with other human centers and the prevention of such disadvantageous
asymmetries reinforce beneficial asymmetries with nonhumans and counteract harmful asymmetries
with them, and vice versa. In the next chapter, I will demonstrate how both the relational continuity and
the efforts to establish asymmetries manifest in the ritual context.

374

Chapter 11. Exchange and Subordination in Ceremonial Dances
In the previous chapter, while discussing rivalry and hostility between human centers and their potential
instrumentalization of each other for managing relationships with nonhuman centers, I explored the
significance of the competitive ceremonial alliance between maloquero brothers-in-law and the concept
of secrecy exemplified in the dialogues held for ceremonial purposes between one human group and
nonhumans, concealed from other human groups. In this chapter, I continue the discussion on the
Andoque’s power dynamics by examining ceremonial dances. I discuss how reciprocity and asymmetry
are managed in these pivotal moments where the relationships explored in earlier chapters between
human centers and their interactions with nonhuman entities converge.
Andoque members often describe ceremonial dances (nni) as the ultimate means of managing the
territory to ensure safe resource use by the human group and preventing predation by nonhuman entities
through illnesses, accidents, conflicts, and other misfortunes. Ceremonial dances are thus perceived as
key to enhancing reproduction—of the human group, its crops, and other flora and fauna on which its
sustenance relies—by engaging in a dialog with the territory (ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí ɵma hɵɵ́ñe). Regarding human
reproduction, this is also achieved by bringing individuals from different clans together in a festive
atmosphere, involving hours of enthusiastic dancing, which can lead to the formation of new love affairs
and eventually marriages. However, a poorly organized dance, as well as any missteps taken by
individual dancers, can have the opposite effect, resulting in epidemics and other instances of increased
predation of humans by the nonhuman entities of their territory. The stress, fatigue, and hunger during
dance preparation can lead to worker conflicts, perceived as harm caused by nonhumans, and we may
also assume that historically, dances bringing together groups from remote places may have served as
prime locations for the spread of epidemics originating from Whites that decimated entire Indigenous
populations. For these reasons, successful dance organization, reflected in the general well-being,
prosperity, and demographic increase of the group in the period following the dance, enhances a
maloquero’s prestige and capacity to mobilize people for future endeavors, ceremonial or otherwise.
This chapter delves into the interplay of dynamics that are central to the successful execution of a dance:
the hierarchy within a given human center—i.e., the non-coercive authority of a captain over his group;
the rivalry between human centers—namely, between the host and guest captains, and their respective
groups; and the hostility between human groups and the nonhuman owners of sites and species of the

375

territory. In the first section, I outline a general model that elucidates how ceremonial dances serve to
dramatize and mitigate tensions between captains and their workers, as well as conflicts between affinal
groups, as a way for addressing and alleviating antagonisms with the nonhuman entities of the territory.
In the second section, I explore the tension in Andoque dances between agnatic ideology and affinal
exchange, which corresponds to the varying degrees of symmetry or asymmetry in relations with
potential nonhuman affines that each dance seeks to achieve through familiarization.
The scarcity of contemporary Andoque dances posed limitations on my analysis. The only ceremonial
dance to have taken place during my fieldwork period was held during my stay in Bogotá due to health
issues. Therefore, my analysis relies on accounts provided by my interlocutors, recordings of songs from
various dances, narrations of origin myths, and discussions following my visits to dances at nonAndoque malocas, which allowed us to compare Andoque practices with those of neighboring groups
and delve into specific ritual elements and dynamics. During my visit in July-August 2021, I attended an
Opossum Dance organized as part of a project to revitalize the Andoque language, which included only
songs and dances, but not the more elaborate ritual dynamics discussed below. Due to these limitations,
the analysis presented here provides a general overview of ceremonial dynamics, and further
understanding of each dance and the overall system would benefit from participant observation and
micro-analyses of these dances.
Critiques and Offerings
The Andoque distinguish between “ordinary dances” (bailes ordinarios) that can be organized by any
maloquero and involve lesser prestige and fewer risks if performed incorrectly, and “proper dances”
(bailes propíos), which we may also be termed tutelary dances. Like other things which are “proper” to
one, the dances of the latter category incur more prestige to their organizers, imply a greater exercise of
power for managing exchanges with humans and nonhumans, but also involve heavier risks if performed
incorrectly. Most of them serve as venues for name giving for children (or name changing for adults),
and divide into two ritual specializations, as we will explore in the next section. The following table
indicates the contemporary Andoque dances:
