A few preliminary words are in order before turning to exchanges in ceremonial dances. As García
defined it for the Murui-Muina, a ceremonial dance is an assemblage of various ceremonies and ritual
actions (2016, 44). Therefore, the occasion in which an event is performed, or the performance or
omission of a certain ritual in it would qualify it as one dance and not another. For example, different
dances would be categorized as “Dance for Repairing Maloca” or “Dance for Destroying Maloca” if
they take place in proximity to these events and include certain songs and dances alluding to them. The
Opossum Dance has several variations. Some interlocutors describe it as identical to the Maloca
Sweeping Dance, with the distinction that the latter is only performed to inaugurate a new maloca after
roofing it. Additionally, The Fruit Dance includes Opossum songs, along with references to other
animals and, notably, riddles, that my interlocutors described as less complex in the Opossum Dance or
completely absent from it. While the Fruits Dance typically includes a ritually-invited guest, whose
group members pose the riddles, the Opossum Dance is often conducted without such a guest, as is the
case with the Garden Work Dance—a variation of the Opossum Dance that includes riddles and is
performed after clearing a new swidden. These variations shed light on the general dynamics in
Andoque dances.
The Opossum Dance and its variations are typically conducted at the beginning of a young captain’s
ritual career, which will gradually include more complex and prestigious dances over time, or a new
maloca’s ceremonial cycle. The Opossum Dance is celebrated by the group that constructs a maloca
after setting up the main poles and framework and thatching the roof. According to Fisi, it is based on
the story of an opossum (toé; Didelphis marsupialis) who built a house, in the form of a pile of sticks

132

According to de la Hoz Melo, Fʉ’ii means “interlocking the arms” (2005, 27).

377

and leaves, in a forest plot where other people were felling trees and later burning them to create a new
swidden. After the fire had extinguished, they saw that Opossum’s house remained intact; neither he nor
his children were harmed because he extended his tail outside of it and waved it to divert the flames.
Opossum stated: “The man who knows my spell will be able to save his house and family, just as I did.
His maloca would never burn, and his children would remain safe and healthy.” In its variation of
maloca inauguration and sweeping, the participants evoke the dens and nests of the opossum and other
birds and animals in an attempt to draw upon the protective properties and stability of these structures,
as well as the well-being of those residing in them. They may sing, for instance:
Opossum is sweeping it, so he says, he is sweeping it.
For his children Opossum is sweeping, is sweeping.
“I am doing this to live with my children,”
So he says, so says Opossum.

The dancers’ heavy stomping across the maloca’s inner space for long hours to flatten and even it,
making it safe and convenient for people to move around it and for children to play inside. Much like the
central functions of similar dances among the Murui-Muina and Féénemɨna (García 2018, 486–89;
Londoño Sulkin 2000, 387–88), this action resembles the “sweeping” (bɵ́’) of the space, clearing it of
pests and erasing the traces and odors left by dangerous animals that once frequented it when it was still
a forested area.
Pineda records another interpretation of the opossum figure, representing orphans who live in shacks
until they are incorporated into a captain’s maloca; the properties of the opossum’s tail, known for its
prehensile ability to grab leaves and sticks, here symbolize the dedication to work expected of orphans
(2014, 92). Indeed, some narrators include the toé opossum sub-specie among the orphans who were
spared from the flood by climbing the to’nnkn tree (M10; Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 83 n.130) and
associate the fire used for swidden clearing with the fiery water that once flooded the earth. This
interpretation explains why Opossum Dances, in their simpler variations, do not necessarily involve
guests from outside the maloca. Instead, they are dedicated to the maloca’s personnel and workers,
ensuring their protection both by and from their captain. During these dances, participants can gauge the
benevolent attitude of the captain towards them by singing:
He ate (ma̰’a) it, he ate it,
Did he really eat it?
Bush Dog (pʉdoɵ) ate it,

378

He ate the avocado.
The pet of fellow countryman’s daughter (saámḭ yaɵ́tɵ niéna̰) ate it.

The ceremonial songs of the People of the Center often involve critiques of the maloquero and his wife,
and to a lesser extent, other members of the organizing household (Griffiths 1998, 176; Londoño Sulkin
2000, 400–401; Lucas 2019, 313). In Andoque, such critique is referred to through the harsh verb kɒ,
which carries the aggressive connotation of an allegation, or the euphemistic verb nnhḛ, meaning “to
sing [about] someone.” According to Pineda, critiques in Andoque dances aim at raising problems
within the community in order to address and solve them (1979, 39). Londoño, whose studies among the
Féénemɨna underscore the moral aspect of their practices, suggests that dance participants use these
events as opportunities to criticize the maloquero and his household members, with the hope of
encouraging them to change their behavior (2000, 400–401; 2012, 89). My discussion of this and other
instances of Andoque criticism songs aims to provide greater specificity as it examines the function of
these songs within the context of power dynamics, where the captain attempts to organize an event that
would help him navigate both the competition with his ceremonial partner and the predatory hostility of
nonhuman entities.
In the case of this song, to dispel suspicion and address critique, the maloquero provides tobacco liquid
(yʉbʉdíe) to the singer. Through this act of commensality, the maloquero also reaffirms his own status
as a human being: his daughter, and by extension, himself, do not provide food to animals but to fellow
human household members—specifically, the singer (see also Pineda Camacho 1982, 17). Additionally,
such reactions towards human dance participants serve to redirect potential dangers and aggressions by
nonhuman entities, which are not considered legitimate commensals within that maloca. These entities
may include the bush dog, as referenced in this song, or the jaguar from the river mouth, symbolizing
the dangers associated with commerce with Whites, as illustrated in the following Opossum song:
The Son of Jaguar of Goods of the River Mouth (Okɒ́ ɵdoha ḭño̰ yaɵ́tɵ)
Is crying: “Mother, father, I want to drink.”
Above fellow countryman’s (saámḭ) harbor,
He is crying (mniɵ):
“Mother, father, I want to drink.”

Here, the maloquero rejects any potential association with a predatory force and instead adopts a
consanguineous attitude toward his personnel. These exchanges of songs and foodstuffs, aimed at
ensuring peaceful conviviality within the maloca, clarify why, unlike other dances, the presence of

379

individuals unaffiliated with that maloca, such as affinal relatives, is not imperative. In several Opossum
Dances reported by Andoque members in recent decades, there were no official guests. Instead, the
maloquero spread the word about the upcoming dance informally to those who had participated in
maloca construction, as well as to other Andoque families.
The Garden Work variation of the Opossum Dance (Bʉ́őkn Nni), held at the conclusion of a collective
swidden clearing and planting (fokaa), can also be conducted without a formally invited external guest.
In the past, when Andoque malocas were more populous and clans were larger, a maloquero could
collaborate with an internal guest—such as an elder man among his personnel who would lead the rest
of the workers, engaging in a dialogue that includes the necessary offerings to the owner-persons of the
different phases of the work. The critique songs in the dance, involving allusions to fruits and other
foodstuffs, represent the workers’ complaints against the captain and his household members—despite
their hard work, the dance does not provide enough food. In such critiques, we may perceive an
expression of a “society against the state” (Clastres 1989) where group members check the captain’s
power and clarify the limits they would accept regarding any accumulation or misuse of it. The
provision of tobacco paste and manicuera to the singers represents the captain’s response, demonstrating
to the workers that the products of their labor are available and that he did not exploit them or abused his
authority. This familiarizing commensality contrasts with the undesirable expression of anger by the
captain and other dance organizers in response to such critiques, a reaction that would reflect a predatory
attitude toward the singers and the personnel in general.
The harvest of a garden created through such collective efforts is directed at collective ends—which will
also contribute to the captain’s accumulation of prestige—as it is used to hold future ceremonial dances
at the maloca. In this way, Opossum Dances, which may include only the maloca or clan personnel
without necessarily involving a formally invited guest, presuppose and prepare the ground for the
eventual organization of dances with external guests, and the captain’s ceremonial alliance with another
maloquero, who is ideally his brother-in-law. The Fruit Dance, which is celebrated after the creation of a
new garden, typically involves such external participation.
A central component of this dance is riddle songs concerning offerings of fruits and propagules for
planting in the new garden, or small game associated with it, by the participants. Carrying the offering
hidden on his shoulder and protecting it from the dance organizers, the participant sings a song alluding
to a specific origin story of their offering, referencing one of its properties or an animal or plant

380

associated with it. He only releases the offering once the host solves the riddle. This component
introduces a competitive dimension to the dance, which is either absent or less pronounced in internal
Opossum Dances that do not involve formally invited guests. As noted by ethnographers of neighboring
peoples with a similar dance, these riddle songs may be enjoyable for most of the participants who dance
and rejoice, but the host and his men struggle to solve them (Griffiths 1998, 166; Londoño Sulkin 2000,
393–96; Lucas 2019, 328–29). This song, for example, is a riddle referring to chili:
We are going to call grandmother.
To mother, to grandmother,
From today to tomorrow (níɒ̰pɵ unńka) she will give fruits (oinabɨi).

By demonstrating his knowledge of the origin of the different cultivars and solving the riddles, the host
decontaminates them from the potential harms they may contain, ensuring safe, life-giving nutrition for
his personnel. As among the Murui-Muina, successfully responding to all these riddles demonstrates the
host’s legitimacy as captain—the successor of Egret of the River Source who created the first maloca
and garden (García 2018, 708). By contrast, failing to solve a riddle is humiliating for the host, who
could not keep up with the challenges posed by his guests, and it exposes him to malevolent nonhuman
entities who take note of his vulnerability concerning certain flora and fauna.
Both the host and guest rely on their prior participation in such dances, where they paid careful attention
to the songs. They gather with their respective groups to narrate and learn relevant origin stories during
the mambeadero sessions preceding the dance. If the host and his group encounter difficulties in solving
the riddle, the singer may include hint verses in his song to assist them. Thus, the competitive dimension
is complemented by an element of alliance and collaboration. This collaborative aspect is further evident
in the fact, recurring in other dances, that the rivalry with the guest (and his group) affords the host (and
his group) an opportunity to assert control and exercise domination over potentially harmful nonhuman
entities, thereby safeguarding the well-being of his personnel. When inviting the guest, the host can
specify the category of plants they wish to receive and learn to control, beginning with domesticated
cultivars and progressing to wilder plants. Similar to other instances where hosts can, to some extent,
coordinate songs and offerings with their guests, this demonstrates the idea that rivalry between
maloqueros helps them effectively manage interactions with nonhuman entities. Finally, the act of
planting seeds and propagules in the garden the following day symbolizes the fertilization of the host
group by the guest’s group and the commensality between them. This symmetrical exchange between

381

human affines (ideally, real ones) thus serves to achieve an asymmetrical exchange between them and
nonhuman potential affines.
Similar to other ritual contexts worldwide (e.g., Eade 1992; Sallnow 1981), the tension between
collaboration and rivalry in ceremonial alliances is an essential dimension in Andoque dances. In the
Andoque case, this tension is vital for enhancing the maloqueros’ ability to manage their interactions
with nonhumans. Although my Andoque interlocutors do not put it in these terms, I suggest that this
duality is also constitutive of the guest’s status, who, from the host’s point of view, is located midway
between the latter’s consanguine kin and nonhuman entities, on a spectrum of alterity. This duality
begins at the invitation ritual, which occurs approximately one week after the host maloquero and his
wife have gathered their personnel, shared coca powder, tobacco paste, and manicuera with them to
align their agencies to their own and achieve unanimity among the workers, and made satisfactory
progress with some of the preparation tasks. During these days, the host sends a messenger to informally
notify the guest of the dance and of his forthcoming visit to extend a formal invitation. Subsequently, the
guest dispatches his own men to go for an initial hunting expedition. The formal invitation ritual is
marked by the joint consumption of tobacco paste brought by the host,133 which the guest also shares
with his personnel. On this occasion, the host provides the guest with a substantial quantity of coca
powder and a “salt cake” to distribute among his men, and places a hot casabe on the guest’s shoulders
to remove his anger. If the guest and his personnel have already obtained game, he exchanges it with the
host for the tobacco paste and salt, thereby making this animal one of the focal points of the ceremony’s
songs.
From this moment on, the guest and his personnel are referred to as the ḭtáu’fa, “the one(s) who
receive(s) tobacco.” This term signifies their reception of tobacco paste, both at the time of the invitation
and while they dance in the ceremony. This term is also used to describe the dances that occur at the
beginning of the ceremony in the afternoon and during its final hours before sunrise, which involve the
guest group, thereby emphasizing the central role of the guest in the dance. These phases are considered
more serious, in the sense of being more significant for the intended negotiation with nonhuman entities
during the dance, and they pose greater challenges and risks for a singer-dancer who falters, compared to
the intermediate phase, which is seen as mere diversion. The latter part is called nnhḛ nni, or “singing
ball,” primarily celebrated by participants who have not received formal invitations to the dance but
133

For a similar practice among neighboring peoples, see García 2018, 604; Londoño Sulkin 2012, 98.

382

attend because they enjoy singing and dancing (nnhḛ). Dancers from the guest group typically refrain
from participating in this phase to conserve their energy and prepare for their early morning
performance. During the regional dances I attended, it was common for a maloquero who had not
received a formal invitation to the dance to refrain from attending, as being included among the common
participants was considered demeaning (his wife and children might still attend). While the dance
organizers provide food for the guest group, they are not responsible for uninvited participants, who
bring their own supplies or may purchase snacks from participant sellers or even the non-Indigenous
peddlers coming for business from Puerto Santander. A clear division is thus maintained between the
formal guest and his group of dancers and the rest of the non-organizing participants.
After the invitation ritual concludes, the guest must coordinate the training of his men for the songs and
dances they will perform during the ceremony, prepare any necessary costumes or accessories for this
particular ceremony, and procure additional game to repay the tobacco paste and salt provided to them.
As with other People of the Center (Gasché 2009, 26), the tobacco paste and, especially, the salt cake
given by the host to the guest are intended to enhance hunting by their consumers, so that the nonhuman
owners of animals and sites of the territory would release for them their “orphans.” Any animal hunted
by the members of the guest’s group, as well as individuals affiliated with them, during the preparation
days must be brought to the host’s maloca. In the interpretation I propose in this section, from this
invitation ritual on, the guest and his personnel serve as a mediating channel between the host and the
nonhuman entities of the territory. While the members of the guest’s group, as affinal human relatives
(and ideally, real ones), are closer to the nonhuman realm of potential affines than the host’s
consanguine kin, the consumption of the ritual substances provided by the host establishes
consubstantiality whereby the host has familiarized them and influenced their actions. However, the
process of familiarization does not go in the other direction, as the host must not receive contributions of
raw cultivars or prepared ritual substances for the dance from members of the guest’s group, even if he
encounters a shortage of such cultivars or substances before the event.
The guest group becomes dependent on the thoughts and behavior of the dance organizers, a term
encompassing here both the maloquero and his personnel. Any intention or expression of violence,
anger, or sexuality among the organizers during the preparation period can put them at risk of illnesses,
snake bites, and accidents during their own preparatory tasks, including hunting expeditions and travel
to the event. The organizers must observe these behavioral “diet” rules (dieta) the violation of which

383

jeopardizes themselves as well. I heard several accounts about dance organizers and workers who
fainted, referred to through the root yi, like “illness,” after conflicts with their co-workers. As García
observed for the Murui-Muina (2018, 489–90), the Andoque believe that during dance preparation,
malevolent nonhuman entities, aware that the dance seeks to enhance human reproduction at their
expense, are determined to sabotage it by provoking such inappropriate behavior and sentiments among
the members of the organizing group. Another restriction on which my interlocutors commented sheds
light not only on the reason why violence, anger, and sexuality are particularly problematic, but also on
why they endanger the guest group as well. This restriction concerns looking at a mirror, with one
interlocutor stating that when a dance worker sees their face in the mirror, the animals become alert (se
levantan) and provoke various forms of aggression. As he vaguely explained, “something there flips
over” (algo ahí se voltea). The gaze is associated with sorcery and predation (Pineda Camacho 1979,
40), and turning it toward oneself represents the cannibal tendency to direct it also toward one’s kin. To
achieve the dance’s general aim of safeguarding the human group by familiarizing harmful nonhuman
potential affines, the dance organizers and workers must ensure that their relationships are not
influenced by predatory affinizing tendencies, such as aggressiveness or sexuality, which is also
conceived as a form of predation. Such tendencies would represent the converse, undesired situation of
their own familiarization by the animals. Given that the guest group has become a consanguineous
extension of the organizers through the commensality of the invitation ritual, any affinization of the
latter by nonhuman entities can also transfer to the guests, causing misfortunes that would be interpreted
as predation by nonhumans.
The only material transaction in the opposite direction, from guests to organizers, is game, which is
subject to a multistep compensation procedure with significant implications for the dance’s objective of
“territorial management.” This game is referred to by the general term ḭsía (“that which is one’s own”)
or nḭhḛ́fɒta, specific to ceremonial dances. The verb ḭhḛ́, meaning “to finish [food],” alludes to the
consumption of the meat during the event. Game can be brought to the host’s maloca either as food for
the workers before the dance or for the opening of the dance itself. As the hunter approaches the maloca,
he sings a yó’sói song alluding to the animal and the site where it was hunted. Upon receiving the game,
the host and his wife must provide tobacco paste and manicuera. Similar to the Murui-Muina (García
2018, 677–78), the Andoque perceive the hunters as carriers of the heat and odors of the forest and its
numerous hostile agencies. Providing tobacco and manicuera calms down (sḭ́ ) these intermediaries
between the maloca and the forest, between consanguinity and affinal alterity. A hunter who delivers
384

game at the beginning of the event enters the maloca dancing and playing a flute, and a woman from the
host group accompanies him, symbolizing an additional form of compensation for his contribution,
which helps to calm him. These measures prevent the hunters from transmitting the dangerous properties
of nonhuman entities to the dance organizers, as such transmission can have harmful consequences. For
instance, a temporary state of madness experienced by Yiñékɒ before one dance, which he oversaw, is
attributed to the young maloquera’s failure to offer manicuera to the hunters.
At the beginning of the dance, after all the hunters have delivered their game to the organizers, the
organizers repay them (ɵpáha) for their game and any costumes they may have prepared for that specific
dance. Compensation is provided in the form of various domestic products, including casabe, chili broth,
tobacco paste, and peanuts. To ensure that each hunter receives compensation commensurate with their
contribution, as well as women and uninvited participants who brought lesser categories of game
(including gathered larvae or purchased products from Puerto Santander), the organizers raise each
contribution, shouting: “Whose is it?” While among neighboring people, such as the Féénemɨna whose
dance I attended and the Nɨpóde as described by Griffiths (1998, 167), the hunters respond by shouting
“Yours!” (suyo, in the second person singular), indicating the host as the game’s new owner, the
Andoque reply “Mine!” (oɵsi kḛ). This can be seen as the Andoque’s attempt to delay the transfer of
ownership until actual remuneration, accompanied by the host’s declaration, such as ódo kḛ knsia osaa:
“this is my [value in] casabe [for] your game” (Jon Landaburu 2007, 26). This exchange represents the
taming of dangerous external faunal products through the use of domestic maloca products.
The guest’s personnel are provided with ritual substances as a group, facilitated by their leader and his
wife, who are offered dry tobacco paste (yʉbʉ yɵkɒkn), a salt cake, and manicuera by the host and his
wife before they enter the maloca to distribute among their personnel. These substances remove their
anger and ensure their consubstantiality with the organizers. However, as noted above, this
commensality can pose risks if these substances have not been properly prepared. The vegetal salt,
prepared for a dance, involves stricter and more numerous rules regarding sexuality, speech, movement,
and the presence of women (see Chapter 6). It serves as a “litmus test” to assess the organizers’
adherence to the dance preparation etiquette. If a guest receives an imperfect salt cake, such as one with
a dark color or full of holes, its appearance can reveal which rules the workers have violated. This
jeopardizes both the host and guest groups, potentially rendering the dance ineffective or even
dangerous, especially if malevolent spirits have already seized the ritual offerings. The guest can also

385

discern issues with the dance organization from adverse weather conditions, such as rainfall on the way
to the event, which may soak his men’s costumes and accessories, making it challenging to dance
effectively, because an adept host would prevent such adverse weather through spells, communication
with spirits, and restriction of his own contact with liquids.
If members of the guest group have such complaints against the organizers, or if they have encountered
accidents or illnesses in the preceding days, they can harshly criticize them in their songs, and in more
extreme cases, resort to more aggressive measures. I was told about a dance organized in La Savana by a
Féénemɨna captain in the 1950s with Yiñékɒ as a guest. On their way there, several members of the
Andoque group, including two of Yiñékɒ’s children, fell ill and experienced accidents. Since these
incidents were perceived as the result of the dance organizers’ lack of adherence to the proper behavioral
“diet” and the suspected incompetence of their captain in conducting dances, upon approaching the host
maloca, the Andoque delegation damaged the gardens through which they passed, felling fruit trees and
singing the songs of the ko’yaiɵ monkey (Cebus albifrons), known for his rude behavior. Upon reaching
the maloca, they used an improvised thatch fork to damage the maloca’s roof, to the horrified cries of
women and children inside.
This recalls the rivalrous dynamics between the two groups, an initial distrust and antagonism that the
sharing of foodstuffs must alleviate and replace with more benevolent tendencies. Similar to other
Amazonian welcoming ceremonies (Costa 2017, 160–61; Surrallés 2003), far from minimizing the
tension and competition between affinal groups, the parties, and especially the guest group, exaggerate
them through identification with dangerous or unruly nonhuman entities. The thatch fork attack is a case
in point, as this tool is typically used during a special ceremony to disassemble the maloca of a retiring
captain. During this ceremony of costume enactment (i’kɒisétai, “head toy”), which opens the dance in
which it takes place, two dancers from the guest group tear down the roof from outside the maloca in
their impersonation of the powerful winds from the river source and river mouth. Meanwhile, dancers in
animal costumes sow chaos inside the maloca: woodpeckers banging the main poles with sticks,
dragonflies sullying the ground with red caguana, and monkeys ravaging the space and harassing the
participants. The dancers only calm down after they are provided sufficient tobacco paste and manicuera
by the host’s personnel.
The songs of the ḭtáu’fa phases likewise attest to the rivalrous and competitive dynamics between the
host and guest, the overcoming of which, like in the Fruit Dance, is a condition for managing

386

relationships and achieving asymmetries with nonhuman entities. Since these songs are perceived as
more powerful and dangerous than the “singing ball” songs, it was more difficult for me to record them.
However, I gathered from people’s explanations that these songs address core themes of the dance and
its associated myths, as well as the origin of the game animals brought to the dance and the sites where
they were hunted. These songs maintain the tone of critique and dissatisfaction with the host and the
organizers’ actions, eliciting from them the provision of tobacco liquid (yʉbʉdíe) and manicuera that
would prove the opposite. For example, a song from the Multiplying Tree Dance goes:
The cold of Rainbow Anaconda (dónn̵̋ɵ hɵpɵ yano̰síkői)
With it the tree was formed (tiɵ)
And with this you are playing (i’kɒniɵ)?
Was it formed together with you?
With this tree you are playing.
Before everything else (ḭpɵikóañé),
When the Speaking Tree was formed
This tree was formed,
And you are playing with it.

The singer suggests that the host of the Multiplying Tree Dance is not treating the tu’sí beam, around
which the dance is centered, with the seriousness it deserves. By providing him with ritual substances,
the host assures the singer that he knows and respects the relevant origin myths, thereby strengthening
his hold over the nonhuman entities whose agencies he wishes to appropriate. In this way, the challenges
posed by the singers grant the host an opportunity to increase his control over the nonhuman world.
Another song from the same dance expresses suspicion that the maloca’s beam does not embody its
proper owner-persons, which enhance social reproduction, but rather violent forces from the river mouth
that are detrimental to the Andoque:
Where is it, where is the seat of goods (dohai ɵkupa)
To which we have come?
Seat of Goods of the River Mouth (ɵkɒ́ dú’dɨ yakupa) Came here.
Thunder of Goods (dohai dú’dɨ) came here.
Thunder of the River Mouth (ɵkɒ́ dú’dɨ) is here.
Jaguar of the Axe (pɵɵḭño̰) is at your place.

By offering the singer ritual substances, the host wards off these dangerous forces and establishes the
benevolence of his multiplying beam. In the Head Dance, which is based on M18 that narrates the
387

transformation of a group of dance guests into peccaries, the provision of substances to the singer who
reminds the participants of that misfortune prevents its reoccurrence:
At this time of the day
All of them
Went from one garden to another.
Are they not ashamed (ñó̰kn)?
We transformed (yokatiani) them, we transformed them,
[They are] yours no more.
We transformed them, we transformed them.
Your orphans (íhɵ́ɵá)
We transformed your animals.

This way, offering tobacco paste and manicuera to the singers who evoke potent nonhuman entities
rejects the harms that some of them seek to inflict on the group celebrating the dance, while embracing
the capabilities with which others can endow it.
In various dances, notwithstanding the rewards that the host gives the guest, the final song with which
the guest dancers leave the maloca attests to their bitter feeling of not being sufficiently compensated.
For instance, this is how they express their farewell in the River Turtle-Carrier Band Dance:
These are, these are
The youth of Rainbow Anaconda (Dónn̵̋ɵ Hɵpɵ yayɨḛn),
Who stayed the night at your place,
Without licking [tobacco].
They have already left,
without drinking [manicuera]
They have already left.

Although my interlocutors assured me that this song carries a humorous tone, from the reports that I
have gathered on Andoque dances and from my observations at ceremonies of neighboring
communities, I did not receive the impression that, by the end of the dance, the host and guest groups
form a single, undifferentiated group, as S. Hugh-Jones reports for the Tukanoans of the Vaupés River
(2001, 266–67).
The songs addressing the game animals brought to the dance, the sites where they were obtained and
their site-persons are crucial for the successful achievement of territorial management. Unlike their
Murui-Muina neighbors, the Andoque do not perceive the animals hunted before dances as the
388

troublemakers among their respective groups, whom their owner-persons would happily discard (García
2018, 493–95). Neither have I received from them clues to the existence of a similar belief to the MuruiMuina’s perception that hunting animals in itself is a victory over the diseases and moral dangers that
they embody (Echeverri 2022, 148–61; but see my discussion in Chapter 9 that concerns specific
shamanic acts). For these reasons, the animals’ owner-persons are angry and vengeful toward the dance
participants, and overcoming the diseases and dangers carried by their “children” is achieved by
providing offerings to these spirits. By evoking these nonhuman entities, the singer draws their attention
to that maloca, where they are provided offerings of tobacco paste and manicuera by the host group
through their provision to the singer, who, as part of the guest group, serves as an intermediary channel
between the organizers and the faunal world. Although a dance can be organized to compensate and
appease the owner-persons after a period of excessive faunal harvest, additional hunting for the event
itself is key for demonstrating to these entities who their specific “children” are, for which the human
participants want to compensate them, ensuring that the offerings would have an effect. Therefore, the
more categories of game brought to a dance, the more diverse the nonhuman owner-persons provided
offerings, and the more comprehensive the territorial management aimed at preventing potential harms
by these entities.
By invoking the animals’ owner-persons in his song, the hunter absolves himself from any “debt” he
may have incurred to these entities through hunting their personnel. Instead, this debt is transferred to
the host, who, along with his group members, will face the consequences of retaliation by the nonhuman
entities if he fails to provide them with sufficient ritual substances through the mediation of the guest
group. Any illnesses and misfortunes that occur in the period following a ceremonial dance are often
interpreted as inadequate compensation for songs related to game and other songs that evoke nonhuman
entities. Insufficient offerings for game or the songs sung about it may necessitate the organization of
another dance, for which more game must be brought, along with more generous compensation.
The host maloquero thus faces a dilemma. On the one hand, bringing more game to his dance allows
him to negotiate and appease a larger number of nonhuman entities, providing broader protection against
potential harm to his people. This can also enhance his prestige, as he becomes known as a captain who
can manage significant amounts of game, protect the territory, and secure the necessary labor for such
endeavors. On the other hand, Andoque maloqueros frequently complain about their challenges in
securing a dedicated and capable workforce for dances, as well as contributions of tobacco and manioc

389

from fellow members who are not part of the guest group. If they fail to reciprocate game and songs
with a sufficient amount of ritual substances derived from these cultivars, the consequences can be
catastrophic.
In making his case for the relevance of the gift paradigm to Amazonia, S. Hugh-Jones argued that in
Northwest Amazonian ceremonial dances, foodstuff exchanged between guests and hosts represent
detached parts of their donors, thereby embodying them (2001, 271–72). More specifically, guests who
give fish or meat incarnate the spirits of fish and animals, such that, “in an inversion of predatory
cannibalism, the guests detach parts of themselves, metaphorically their children or kin, and offer these
up as sacrificial substitutes for consumption by their hosts” (idem 2013, 371–72). In other words, gift
replaces predation, and consuming game replaces the consumption of the guest. While the foodstuff
exchanged before and during Andoque dances certainly carry the gift characteristic of representing their
donors and their actions, my impressions concerning the Andoque’s (and other People of the Center’s)
ritual practices does not lead me to conclude that game substitutes for the guests. Nonetheless, the guests
do represent nonhumans as they mediate the exchange with them. However, the transacted items have
functions beyond (hetero)substitution, as I have shown. Akin to the wider meanings of ḭtasé offerings,
they also have manipulative and thought-shaping functions, intended to tame, calm, and ultimately
dominate nonhuman beings. As we shall now see, one such function is to demonstrate the host’s
superior relationship with nonhuman entities in comparison with the guest, who is here a human rival of
the host, rather than a representative of nonhumans or mediator in exchange with them.
To ensure that the guest does not bring game in classes and quantities that are beyond the host’s ability
to compensate, the latter often resorts to a common Andoque solution: hiding game animals from the
guest. While giving him a salt cake upon the invitation for success in hunting, the host limits this success
by burying another salt cake at his own maloca, under the spot in the mambeadero where yarumo ashes
are burned. Additionally, the salt given to the guest may also be manipulated, guiding him toward
encountering only the types of game desired by the host. However, while the host may try to minimize
his debt to the spirits, the guest works to maximize it, in a way that emphasizes the competition between
the two. The hunters of that group attempt to bring as much game as they can, which attest to both their
hunting skills—an important sign of masculine prowess—and to their greater command over the ownerpersons, who revealed their animals despite the host’s maneuvers. The occurrence of most tutelary
Andoque dances—the ones with the largest attendance and where the importance of the dialog with

390

spirits is magnified—in July-August makes the host’s control over a maximum amount of obtained
game more difficult. While this period is marked by the abundance of the mauritia fruits used to concoct
the special caguana for the distribution ritual on the eve of these dances, as the height of the rainy season
where water levels are at their peak, it is also the time when coveted land animals are concentrated in the
ever-smaller stretches of non-inundated forest and are thus easier to spot. The timing of those dances
also complicates the host’s task of rain prevention. All these factors combine to heighten the challenge
that the guest presents to the host, raising the stakes of their competition for prestige and their usual
rivalry as maloquero in-laws by summoning nonhuman entities to whom the parties could become
indebted. The outcome of this challenge may be, for the host, either predation by these entities or a more
effective familiarization and domination over them, which will typically lead him to pose a greater
challenge to his ceremonial partner when it is the latter’s turn to host a dance.
The “singing ball” songs, typically sang by participants who do not belong to the invited maloquero’s
group, also heighten the challenge. These songs criticize the host and his household members for their
stinginess, laziness, diversion from ancestral teachings, and other vices that contribute to the lack of
sufficient ritual substances at the dance. In the River Turtle-Bamboo Dance, for example, they may sing:
At the central pole of the maloca,
Here was prepared the caguana that we came in order to drink.
You did not offer us a drink.
“My daughter, serve me
The abundant caguana of your father,
Which I have come in order to drink,”
I am asking her.
Without bathing, she prepared it.
I do not want to receive it from you,
I do not want to receive it from you,
At the place to which we arrived.

Although these songs do not require the host to provide the singers with ritual substances whose absence
may prove dangerous, they should be viewed as contributing to the general pressure that he is under.
Sung by non-maloquero individuals, including non-members of the host’s household who are
nonetheless affiliated to his maloca, and considered inappropriate for a captain, they represent the
tendency of “ordinary members”—as already noted in relation to the Opossum songs—to check and
restrain their captain’s power, reminding him of his dependence on their work and contributions, and of

391

their expectations for reward and recognition in exchange. This brings us back to the relevance of the
relationship between captain and ordinary men to understand ritual dynamics. In order to successfully
respond to his guest’s challenges and secure the desired domination over nonhumans, the host depends
on workers to maintain the maloca in good shape and produce large amounts of food and ritual
substances. The larger the workforce, the more ritual substances can be provided to meet the guest’s
challenges.
Summing up, the horizontal exchange of foodstuffs and words for ceremonial substances with the
(ideally, real) affinal ceremonial partner, which is necessary to turn the dangerously symmetrical
relationship with nonhuman potential affines into an asymmetrical exchange of agencies and (animal)
bodies that is beneficial for the human group, assumes the existence of a vertical exchange of agencies
and substances between the maloquero and his personnel. The presentation of gift-like items, which
serve as extensions of their donors, before and during ceremonies, derives its significance from a
broader context of generalized predation, whose potential adversarial consequences they are intended to
mitigate. As we have noted in passing throughout Part III, the captain’s prestige and related capacity to
mobilize people for work or establish and maintain ceremonial alliances with others depends on his
demonstrated success in negotiating with nonhuman entities, particularly through ceremonial dances.
Therefore, we may conclude that these three classes of relationships (captain/ordinary people; two
maloqueros; human-nonhuman) contain tensions, the manifestation and alleviation of each is crucial for
the alleviation of the tensions inherent in the other classes of relationships, and, thus, for the
advantageous management of these relationships.
Agnatic and Human Asymmetries in Ceremonial Dances
So far, I have analyzed the general dynamics of antagonism and exchange within Andoque dances. The
emphasis on exchange between humans and nonhumans in these dances should not be misconstrued as
striving for equilibrium and harmony. Instead, it primarily seeks to establish asymmetry between the two
parties with the goal of ensuring the well-being, prosperity, and social reproduction of members of the
human group, to benefit from the bodies and agencies of nonhuman entities while preventing any
reciprocal transfers in the opposite direction. In this section, I further explore the asymmetrical power
relations that the Andoque strive to establish with nonhuman beings by focusing on the tutelary dances
and Andoque members’ perspectives on the importance and dangerousness of these dances, as well as
their respective centrality or marginality in contemporary ritual practice. This asymmetry involves a

392

degradation in the agencies of some of the nonhuman entities of the territory, and is intricately linked
with agnatic ideology, as the dances that are more esteemed and conducted more frequently emphasize
patrilineal descent, at the expense of affinal exchange.
The Andoque categorize their tutelary dances into two ritual specializations, to which they refer as
“careers” (carrera), alluding to a maloquero’s gradual inclusion of more complex and prestigious dances
into his repertoire: “Red” (Peɒɵsí; literally: “essentially red”) and “White” (Pó’fiɵ). The Multiplying
Tree and River Turtle-Carrier Band Dances fall into the red category, while the Head, River TurtleBamboo, Armadillo, and Fausíya are classified as white.134 The following table will serve for reference
in our discussion on the two ritual specializations:

Table 10. The dances of the two ritual specializations

People become associated with either specialization if they are given a name in a red or white dance,
give their children names in such a dance, or otherwise organize them. Therefore, not all Andoque
members are associated with this or that specialization. Besides the distribution of several dances
between the two specializations, those affiliated with either specialization sing different songs from the
ones sung by members of the other specialization, and they also dance differently from them, often using
distinct ritual instruments, in the dances they organize.
Each of the two colors is associated with other colors. Red (peɒi), symbolizing blood, is associated with
black (huɒi), which represents war. Conversely, white (pó’te̋) is thought to encompass the colors yellow

Although the Peach Palm Dance is generally considered a non-tutelary ceremony that does not fit into either category, my
interlocutors made vague, decontextualized references to its red characteristics. On the one hand, the association between the
hero of its origin myth and Sun, a “red” figure (Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 53 n.3, 190), can partly account for a possible
red characterization of this dance. On the other hand, unlike the other tutelary dances, the Peach Palm Dance is held at the
peak of the dry season (January-February) when peach palms are ripe, rather than at the peak of the wet season, and does not
include the distribution of a caguana made of mauritia, whose fruits abound in the that season. I attribute the defiance of the
red-white classification by the Peach Palm Dance to its recent introduction into the Andoque repertoire, as it appears to have
been imported by Yiñékɒ or other individuals in the generations preceding him from downstream regions. Its main songs (of
the mask part) are in another Indigenous language, which some interlocutors identify as Tanimuka and others as Letuama and
Macuna, and refer to mythical events that occurred further downstream from Drawing River (Hḭ’ḭse), located at the
downriver limit of the Andoque ancestral territory (ibid, 190–201), toward the territories of the Miraña, Yucuna, and
eventually Tanimuka, Letuama, and Macuna (see also Pineda Camacho 1976, IV; for similar views among the Miraña, see
Karadimas 2007, 108). Therefore, I will not treat this dance here as a red one.
134

(dóői), green (payɒi), and blue (pa̰ ̰así),135 which overall represent life and prosperity (although one
interlocutor commented on yellow’s association with disease). Since naming a person in a certain way is
thought to shape their personality, I learned during my first weeks among the Andoque that they
perceive those named in a red dance as people of war, prone to outbursts of anger, and those named in
white dances as calm, peaceful, and polite.
However, from an early stage, I also discovered the disdain and distrust that many members harbor
toward the white specialization, even among individuals who are themselves affiliated with it, in
contrast to the red specialization, which is almost unanimously held in high esteem. As we will see,
white dances are celebrated today less than red ones, with fewer children given names in them and fewer
malocas dedicated to them. At first glance, this tendency seems surprising when compared with accounts
of the general shift among the People of the Center from a bellicose, predatory pre-genocide discourse
referred to as the “Basket of Darkness,” upon which people draw only on rare occasions and in limited
contexts, to the “Basket of Life,” representing public discourse suited for inter-clan and inter-ethnic
cooperation (Echeverri 2010). As we have seen in Chapter 4, the red Multiplying Tree, which involves
bellicose songs and exhibits a predatory discourse, became crucial for the Andoque’s post-genocide
recuperation, complicating the simple dichotomy between bellicosity and peace or life. On the other
hand, the Bora’s way to conceptualize their recent history may prove more useful to understand the
Andoque’s preference for one ritual specialization over another. As Lucas shows, the Bora divide their
history between a pre-genocide “Time of Animals,” marked with communication with nonhuman
entities for sorcery, healing, and other ends, and the contemporary “Time of Abundance,” in which
people act and protect themselves through direct communication with tobacco, to which humans, in
contrast with animals, have privileged access (2019, 115–40). This resonates with the Andoque’s
distinction between Animal Stories and Captaincy Stories, as discussed in Part I. Therefore, the peaceful
or aggressive dispositions associated with the white and red specializations are to be sought primarily in
the ways in which each attempts to manage relations with and contain dangers posed by nonhuman
potential affines and the human agents mediating communication with them in dances—i.e., real affines.
The main traits of the Andoque tutelary dances are found in several of the myths narrated in previous
chapters, and I will provide here additional information on each dance that is relevant to this section’s
purpose. The red Multiplying Tree Dance, as explored in Chapter 4 and demonstrated by M11 (in
135

People often conflate the two latter colors.

394

Appendix 1), revolves around a phallic dancing beam embodying a red anaconda and enhancing the
reproduction of group members and their crops. This beam is perceived as aggressive and predatory, and
the dance is considered the seat (kupa) of all other dances, anchoring the exchange occurring in them
within a firm patrilineal identity. As we have seen, the ceremonial songs likewise include allusions to
the seat. It is described as the first dance in Andoque mythology, but the last one that a maloquero
organizes, following lesser, more recent dances. The multiplying beam is related with the river source—
the direction of fertility and ancestry—through its association with Purple Tapir (Bu Ḭtɵ), who, after the
flood, went to the river source and appeared in that direction as the auspicious morning rainbow,
foretelling the abundance of crops (see also de la Hoz Melo 2005, 42). This is why, in dances, the
multiplying beam is painted with the colors of the rainbow. The preparation of a new beam takes place
in the forest, where the maloquero and his men choose and fell a suitable itauba (Mezilaurus itabua) or
balata (Manilkara sp.) tree, according to Tañe (ibid, 74), or itauba or makapádɨ (comino real;
unidentified), according to Fisi. Women must not be present during the preparation process. When a new
beam is introduced into the maloca, workers and participants who are neither the beam carriers or the
organizing couple must not look at it—particularly women. As my interlocutors explained to me, this
reflects the dangerousness of this anaconda, which ceases to jeopardize the celebrating group only after
its carriers have received coca paste and manicuera from the hosts. Participants can leave their hiding
spots or open their eyes only once they hear the carriers produce sounds with the beam inside the
maloca. This custom represents another example of the center’s efforts to familiarize elements
associated with the river sources in order to harness their forces. The specific prohibition against
women’s presence in the elaboration process highlights the phallic beam’s association with agnatic
ideology and the dangers that marital exchange, vital for reproduction, poses to patrilineal continuity.
During the dance, the guest—ideally, the maloquero’s brother-in-law—and his group only enter the
maloca after the host and his personnel have performed several songs to safeguard the beam (de la Hoz
Melo 2005, 77–79). These practices are rooted in M11, where the multiplying beam is threatened by
(and protected from) Green Tapir, a figure representing the dangers of affinal exchange (M22). During
the dance, the guests violently shake the multiplying beam with their feet, as if they were trying to break
it; the sound that the beam makes represents its ability to resist these aggressions.

395

Figure 23. Tañe offering tobacco to the guests who stomp on his multiplying beam
during a dance at his maloca. Photo taken from a video recorded by Levy Andoke Andoke

The Multiplying Tree Dance can serve as an occasion to give names to several adult members.
Emphasizing the multiplicity of name recipients appears essential to distinguish these relatively lowerstatus name givings from the higher prestige ones performed for newborn children, where individual
name givings are customary (the term “adults” also includes children past the age of individual naming).
While my interlocutors did not explicitly mention such a rule, my data reveals that the only newborn
children who receive names in this dance are the firstborn daughters of maloquero families or the
daughters of men trained to be maloqueros.
By contrast, firstborn sons of maloqueros or of men trained for this position are given a name in the
other red dance, River Turtle-Carrier Band (Bɨsokń Pádɨ; hereafter: Carrier Dance), with their sister or
cousin also likely to join them and be named in the dance. Like the Multiplying Tree, the Carrier Dance
also centers around a phallic element: Tofidei’s transformation of his anaconda enemies from downriver
into trees, islands, and rocks, by exposing them to his red-painted penis (M23, in Appendix 1). The
transformation of enemies to immobile beings, as discussed in Chapter 9, earned this ceremony the
name Transformation Dance (Tii Nni). This dance is associated with captaincy, among other things,
because the reddish mauritia-mixed caguana drank at it is perceived to be the transformed personnel of
Tofidei—whose own name means “Pounding Mauritia Juice”—that gave that captain more power to
defeat his enemies. The “singing ball” part is common to this and the other River Turtle dance—namely,
Bamboo—and addresses the prevention of dangers originating from the river mouth, and, to some
extent, related to commerce with Whites. For example,

396

[Like] Cacambra, Cacambra, Lady Cacambra (kaókamikn)
She is looking at her husband’s trail of goods (nikɒ yadohaio̰bɨ),
It is here, to her, that we came.

By providing tobacco liquid and manicuera to the singer, the host couple assures him that the maloquera
is not like the myth’s treacherous Lady Cacambra, thereby warding off potential harms from the river
mouth, similar to the ones that threatened Tofidei.
The guests prepare rods for this dance, painting them in different colors and adorning them with stripes
made from the bark of the bɨsokń tree (Castaño sp.), that give the dance its name. Unlike in other
dances, these rods are personal, and the dancers cannot exchange them with each other. One interlocutor
drew a direct connection between the dancing rods and Tofidei’s penis, an aspect also noted by
Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 107 n.39). This is also illustrated in the song with which the guest dancers
enter the dance, where they refer to the preparation of their rods by Toi (another name for Tofidei):
Are we the ones to have created this tree
That Toi painted,
The tree that you are asking us (ḭnntoni)?
We came here to your place.
He struck it, struck it for you.
Beautiful (hɵ́tuíkőkn), he struck it next to you.
The land [will make the sound] “nndo, nndo,”
The land [will make the sound] “tiya, tiya.”

In other songs, the guest dancers identify themselves as the “youth” (or workers) of Dónn̋ɵ Hɵpɵ, the
beneficial early morning rainbow-anaconda from the river source that bestowed the rods with their
colors. It thus appears that the guest group represents the phallic power that the host wishes to acquire,
and while I could not record a sufficient number of songs from the guest ḭtáu’fa parts, it seems his
dancers test the host’s readiness to possess this power. Finally, at the end of their last song in the early
morning, when they leave the maloca, the dancers hand their rods to the host. The host keeps these
objects, which symbolize the might from upriver and enhance his power to overcome disease and other
problems originating from downriver, until his guest reciprocates with another Carrier Dance.

397

Figure 24. A Carrier Dance rod outside Fisi’s maloca (Photo by the author)

Fisi and Nestor explained to me that Tofidei’s deed gave rise to a dangerous war ritual called the Spear
Dance (Fɨ’ɵfá Nni) after the weapon held by this hero. Therefore, to conduct a life-giving dance and
ensure the protection of the children, the organizer relies on another myth, M25, which is detailed in
Appendix 1. This myth recounts how Woodpecker managed to save the dangerous Stingray and carry
him on his back to Blazing Lake without the latter devouring him, by using a strong carrier crafted from
the bark of the bɨsokń tree. This earned this tree Stingray’s blessing for longevity and rejuvenation. For
this reason, naming a child in a dance associated with the bɨsokń tree is believed to ensure their health
and longevity. Babies were once carried in carriers elaborated from the bark of this tree, and I was told
that they are still carried in it for name-giving ceremonies in the Carrier Dance as well as other dances.
Decorating Tofidei’s “spears” with stripes crafted from bɨsokń bark shifts this dance from a context of
war to one of life and rejuvenation.

398

Figure 25. A Murui-Muina carrier band.
Source: Musée du quai Branly, Inventory no. 71.1975.26.65.

As noted earlier, the Carrier Dance shares the middle “singing ball” part with River Turtle-Bamboo
Dance (Hɨka Pádɨ), hereafter referred to as “Bamboo.” This white dance is based on the origin story of
dolphins (M22, Appendix 1; see also Chapter 9). The identity of the hero of this story, Green Tapir, also
hints at the commonality between this dance and Carrier Dance, since the latter is portrayed as Tofidei’s
brother. Like his brother, Green Tapir confronts aggressive aquatic beings from downriver. In the longer
version of the myth, as narrated by Fisi, after Green Tapir transforms his wife and her brother into
dolphins and sends them to Egret of the River Mouth, his three sons join their mother downriver, while
Green Tapir marries another woman. When his sons learn that he organizes a dance with her, they
become upset, saying, “Our father never held a dance when he lived with our mother!” and go upriver to
avenge their mother’s expulsion, equipped with a club. However, when they arrive at their father’s
maloca, the latter appeases them, together with his new wife, by providing them with coca powder,
tobacco paste, manicuera, peanuts, and mocambo (Theobroma bicolor) seeds. He manages to take away
their club, and they return to the river mouth without having caused any damage.
The Bamboo Dance is specifically seen as a defense against problems, illnesses, accidents, and conflicts
that originate from Whites, who are associated with dolphins, as well as their goods, instruments, and
weapons. However, in contrast with the aggressive approach employed by Tofidei and reenacted in the
Carrier Dance, the Bamboo Dance reenacts Green Tapir’s strategy to neutralize the dangers from that

399

direction by sharing substances with it. In other words, this dance seeks to impose reciprocal exchange
on the incestuous entities of the river mouth. Reciprocity is thus key to this dance, with the guest being
obligated to organize another such dance to invite his former host. Control over restraining anger and
managing sexuality among dance organizers is essential to steer clear of the same self-predatory
tendencies that characterize the river mouth. Conversely, a failure to observe these behavioral rules
would lead to envy among group members regarding externally manufactured goods, conflicts involving
firearms, accidents involving machines and metal tools, and seduction by dolphins in human guise who
frequent this dance.
The difference between the aggressiveness of the red specialization and the more diplomatic attitude of
the white one can be illustrated by examining the dance instruments employed in the two River Turtle
Dances. In these dances, individuals affiliated with the red specialization dance with balso [kóo;
Ochroma pyramidale?] rods, while white dancers use bamboo (hɨka) canes. But why is bamboo used in
this context? In an episode from M22, shared with me by Fisi and Nestor on another occasion, Green
Tapir’s former wife and her brother return after their expulsion to seek revenge on Green Tapir’s people.
They appear well-groomed with face and body paint and attempt to cause harm by seducing human
beings into having sexual intercourse with them. The sister tries to attract men’s attention through her
painted gourd vessel (clearly an allusion to her genitals), but all the men she encounters resist her
advances. On the other hand, the brother manages to seduce one woman, who falls in love with his
charms and the beautifully painted bamboo cane with which he strikes the ground as he walks. After
sleeping with him, the woman becomes ill with a high fever, but her father manages to heal her. As
Nestor and Fisi explained to me, by dancing with the bamboo cane in the dance and striking it on the
ground, the dancers essentially name the wrongdoers from downriver, putting them to shame and
making it clear that they are not welcome at that maloca, where the origin stories and cures against their
harms are known. In other words, while the rods of the red dancers symbolize Tofidei’s penis and spear,
with which he petrified his enemies, the white dancers exhibit a more intricate strategy. To some extent,
they identify with their enemies by using the instrument through which harm was inflicted on
humankind, but they use it to ward off harm. This complexity is also tied to the moral ambiguity of

400

Green Tapir, to whom Fisi attributed, on other occasions, the seduction of women and the subsequent
infliction of fatal internal bleeding through a bamboo cane.136
Another dance that belongs to white specialization is the Head Dance (Ḭtai), which involves a dialogue
with guardian spirits of forest animals to prevent a transformation of humans into nonhumans, similar to
the one narrated in M18 (Appendix 1, see Chapter 9). The preferred game for this dance is white-lipped
peccaries that have been caught in a collective expedition using net casting, much like in that myth. It is
also essential to adequately compensate the hunters, and through them, the owner-persons of peccaries,
to prevent similar damages to the maloca and gardens as were inflicted by the peccary herd in the story.
As demonstrated in the Head song above, providing offerings to the singers helps prevent the
transformation of members of the human group into animals through disease and other misfortunes.
The Head Dance is also closely related to the manguaré monoxylic drums (ku’dɨ), whose origin is
narrated in a M26, a myth recorded by Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 84–90) and summarized in
Appendix 1. This myth describes events following the flood caused by the eagle’s damming of the river
with its outspread wings. After the floodwaters receded, the people who remained on the parched earth
kept playing the síiru flute made from the eagle bone. These people, who should now be understood as
animals due to their retreat below the earth once they were subjected to a predatory gaze, were led by
Pineapple (Tomirepa; or “Pineapple Anaconda,” Tomḭ Hɵpɵ), whose son had the flute as his toy. The
ocelots of the stars descended to earth and stole the flute. When Pineapple failed to retrieve it by
shooting arrows to the stars, the sick Péífirú volunteered to ascend and recover the instrument. After
negotiating with Nénéfi, the captain of the stars, Péífirú received the manguaré and healing herbs to aid
his group’s recovery from a devastating flood. Unfortunately, the manguaré shattered as it fell to Earth,
transforming into various animals and a small, nocturnal version of itself. To rectify this, Nénéfi
dispatched his men with the correct manguaré to Earth. Its arrival and installation in Pineapple’s maloca
were marked by a Head Dance.

136

Within this context, it is also tempting to engage in “thinking through tubes,” as suggested by S. Hugh-Jones (2019c).
Unlike the solid rods used by the red dancers, the bamboo cane is a hollow tube (it can also be used as a flute, referred to as
hɨka). Being a tube, it represents a more complex form than the univocal rod, masculine from the outside and feminine from
the inside. When used as a weapon, in the form of a blowpipe, a tube demands calmness, patience, and self-control—the
virtues associated with the white specialization—instead of the explosive violence associated with killing using a spear (idem
2019a, 109).

401

The manguaré is thus the instrument of game animals granted to them by predatory entities—the star
ocelots, led by the eagle god Nénéfi—to increase in numbers, as it bestows aggressive capacities upon
them as well. This aggressive capacity is the one demonstrated by Ka’ákɵpidɨ, who took the hunters
eyes out in M18—a predatory episode that serves as the starting point of the negotiation and exchange
with nonhuman entities in the Head Dance. Indeed, the two main nonhuman owner-persons of this
dance, to whom offerings are provided, are Ka’ákɵpidɨ (or, in his other name, Dó’ákɵidɨ, meaning “Eye
Extractor”) and Péífirú (or Pineapple—see the footnotes accompanying M26 in Appendix 1), whose
vulnerable men, the game animals, gained the predatory capacity that has led humans to want to engage
in negotiations with them.
The Fausíya Dance (an Andoque word, related to the tyrannidae species faukuya) is the one about which
I possess the least information. Although it is widely associated with the white specialization, Fisi
claims that it is “less white” than the Head or Bamboo Dances. He classifies it as “sort of yellow,”
falling midway between the two specializations because it is rooted in a dance during which the birds
received their current colors from the full range of color palette. Similar to the Peach Palm Dance, I
attribute the defiance of the red-white classification by the Fausíya to its apparent relatively recent
introduction into the Andoque ritual repertoire. In the Fausíya case, it seems to be an elaboration by
Yiñékɒ to restore a sense of peace to the territory after the genocide (Landaburu 1993, 156), with a large
dependence on the mythology of the Head Dance and a specific indication to be celebrated only at
generational intervals. The origin myth of the Fausíya (M27), as recorded by Landaburu and Pineda
(1984, 84–85) and narrated here with additional details provided by my interlocutors, reflects a
transformation of the manguaré myth (M26), which explains its classification as a white dance. After the
War of the Speaking Tree, Nénéfi proposed his brother Pineapple to conduct the Fausíya Dance, which
he had learned from their father, Training Anaconda (Yitai Hɵpɵ), in order to rectify everything and
establish order (hɵ́ikai). However, Pineapple refused the offer. Subsequently, Nénéfi climbed to the sky
with his sister, Lady Dance Rattle (Paidikn), whom he transformed into manguaré drums by hanging her
upside down, so that her breasts become the two drums. Playing these drums, he ordered his sister to
summon her brothers, the faukuya birds, to sing and dance. When Pineapple, who had remained on
Earth, heard these sounds from above, he regretted rejecting this dance, and set off for Nénéfi’s abode,
to obtain the manguaré—this time, an instrument whose main function is to promote peaceful existence.
In the Fausiya dance, both children and adults can be given names or have their names changed. The
dance participants don the feathers of the faukuya bird as ornaments. The reader may recall that in M18,
402

the origin of the Head Dance, the peccary band ascends to Faukuyadefɵ, the forest of these birds. This
detail represents another association between the two dances and the affinal connotations of both, as
peccaries and birds for feather ornaments are two classes of animals to which brothers-in-law can
transform in Amerindian mythology, representing, according to Lévi-Strauss, either “nature” or
“culture,” respectively (1964, 100–102). I will return to the connection between this dance and the Head
Dance below.
Lastly, the Armadillo Dance (Féíkɵ), categorized as white as well, is performed to name and protect
children. It is also known as Fern Dance (Ti’ñḛdɨ Nni) after a herb of the Pteridaceae family used during
this ceremony for the child’s defense, alongside other protective measures, such as a(n unidentified)
plant referred to as ant cotton (poso̰), genipa body paint, the black bakʉdʉ́kn paint for teeth protection,
and a special carrier elaborated from a higuerón tree (Estrada Añokazi 2017, 256). According to Estrada,
the guests bring only small game animals to this dance that do not pose risks to children, unlike large
game (ibid, ibid).
The dance draws on a version of M20 (see Appendix 1), which, as shared with me by Fisi (M28,
2/1/19), concerns only one seduced woman without including her sister, but refers also to her giving
birth, specifying that the eventual healing and protection primarily applies to her child. In this version,
Tatoañei’s jaguar son seduces Shadow Egg’s daughter, Hummingbird, drawing her to the site where he
burns plants for salt production in a bid to burn her as well. After his mother instructs the woman to flee
from her voracious son, the woman first finds shelter in Acouchi’s hole in a tree trunk and then under
Anaconda’s chest. While Anaconda was hiding the woman, he impregnated her, and when the jaguar
came looking for her, threatening to eat her accomplice, Anaconda laughed at him, suggesting that he
can devour the jaguar instead. After the woman finally finds shelter under Kingfisher’s wing and goes
underwater with him as he dives, she gives birth to a certain pintadillo fish along with the fern, which is
the defense with which Anaconda has equipped his son. Hummingbird safeguards her son with the fern
and ant cotton, and, thus, she is the owner-person of the Armadillo Dance.137
The Armadillo Dance safeguards both the boy or girl named in it and all the other children brought to it,
imbuing them with the cool principle, stemming from the anaconda, which is essential for warding off
the forest’s hot diseases that are so dangerous for children in their early years. While this defense is
This story does not explain why this ceremony is associated with the armadillo. I was succinctly told that this name owes
to the physical resemblance between this animal and the ornaments on the rods employed for dancing at this ceremony.

crucial, the children named in this dance do not belong to a maloquero family and are generally not

with a ritual specialization and does not involve the preliminary ritual of caguana distribution. Andoque
members explain that a new father who wishes to name his child in this dance must approach a

and labor, and ideally inviting his brother-in-law as a guest.
Many of the songs of this dance, as they were shared with me, express criticism of the female host, who
is the mother of the named child. For instance:
Her husband ate with her.
It’s [The game animal] gone, [its] old age (yodá), go wash it away!
She was not dirty (fḭḭ́ kó),
She became old because of her husband.
[Previously, her beauty] could make one cry (mnḛḭ).

Providing tobacco and manicuera to the singers reassures them of the mother’s humanity and correct
behavior, thereby deterring any attempts by nonhuman entities to prey on her and, particularly, her
newborn child.
As noted earlier, while the red ritual specialization is held in high esteem by almost all my Andoque
interlocutors, the white one is more ambiguous. Certain interlocutors told me that both specializations
are necessary, acknowledging that sometimes an aggressive position is needed, and at other times—a
reconciliatory one. Fisi says that the white specialization is equally important as the red one but
perceives the white dances as “sad” due to the episode from M26 (in Appendix 1), where Pineapple’s
personnel abandon him, his maloca, his manguaré drums, and the Head rituals he was celebrating, once
the orphans craft their own “red” drums and multiplying beam. In one conversation, Fisi even distanced

404

Yiñéko, who organized white dances, from this specialization, saying in a scornful tone, “My father
never got into this pó’fiɵ business (mi papá nunca se metió en ese pó’fiɵ).” Tañe is the most radical
speaker against the white specialization, claiming that he wants nothing to do with it. Once, when I
asked him why he, who had been given a name in the white Armadillo Dance, later named his three sons
in red dances, he said: “I’m afraid of the origin stories of animals (nacimiento de animales), I’m human
(soy gente), not an animal. In the dances of Head and River Turtle[-Bamboo] you [the maloquero]
receive ambíl from the animals, and it makes me sick (me da asco).”
As in Tañe’s statement, the contempt, suspicion, and fear that Andoque members express toward the
white specialization are primarily focused on the Head and Bamboo Dances. Fisi’s sister Irene, who was
given a name in the white Fausíya Dance claimed that she is appalled by the Head Dance, as did several
other interlocutors. Even several people who were named in this dance or have organized it nevertheless
distance themselves from it, assuring that the version in which they have been involved is the safer,
more benign one, as it appears that there exist several categories of the Head Dance. However, since my
interlocutors were unwilling to delve into this dangerous conversation topic, I possess no information on
the differences between the Head categories, besides a comment by Raquel, who was named in this
dance, and which explains some of people’s contemporary disdain toward it, that the anthropophagous
ritual was also among these categories.
People’s ambivalence toward the white specialization also translates to a decline in the frequency of
white dances, and, most notably, a decline in the number of white name givings, in comparison with red
