White name givings have decreased since the 1960s, while red name givings reached their peak in the
1970s and maintained a relative stability in smaller numbers since the 1980s, consistently surpassing

405

white ones almost continuously since that decade. This contrast is even more evident if we exclude
name givings in the Armadillo Dance and the 19 individuals who were given a name as adults in one
Fausíya Dance in the 1950s, as these name givings carry little prestige and these individuals are not
trained to become maloqueros or organize the main Andoque dances. By counting as “white” the
children given a name in Head or Fausíya Dances, we witness the near disappearance of white namings
since the 1960s, with only one girl given a name in the Head ritual in the past twenty years. Even as the
Andoque conduct fewer ceremonial dances in recent decades, they prefer the organization of red dances
and naming children in them over white dances.
Another indicator highlighting the predominance of the red specialization is the number of maloqueros
subscribing to each specialization since the 1930s, who have continued beyond their initial maloca. Six
maloqueros have predominantly engaged in red dances, with five of them building more than one
maloca throughout their lifetime. By contrast, among the four maloqueros engaging in white dances,
only one continued beyond his first maloca. The only maloquero to have completed a white ritual cycle
that included name giving to his two elder daughters, demonstrated a strong inclination towards red
rituals in the final years of his maloca and even expressed a desire to name his firstborn male son in a
red dance. There were two white malocas and three red ones when I arrived in the Andoque territory in
2018, and as of September 2023, there are two red malocas and one white maloca. However, the latter
maloca is relatively inactive, remote, and considered marginal by most members, bearing only a loose
association with the white specialization, as its owner was named in the mass name-giving ceremony of
the Fausíya Dance in the 1950s, rather than in an exclusive manner in this dance or Head.
To understand the rise of the red specialization and the decline of the white one, we need to delve deeper
into the different ways of engaging with human and nonhuman entities reflected by each tutelary dance.
To achieve this, we must uncover the underlying correspondence between the two ceremonial
specializations and birth order. This, in turn, requires a comparative analysis with similar systems of
ritual prerogatives among other People of the Center. Certainly, the themes and instruments of the
Andoque dances exhibit notable similarities with dances celebrated by other People of the Center
(Gasché 2009; Echeverri 2022, 285–305). Concerning tutelary dances, however, Echeverri argues for
Andoque singularity due to the presence of two ritual specializations among them, in contrast with three

406

or four such specializations among neighboring peoples (2022, 305).138 However, I propose viewing the
Andoque specializations as a variation of the underlying logic found in the Murui-Muina and Miraña
systems, where ritual prerogatives are linked to birth order.
The Murui-Muina and Miraña models, as documented by ethnographers such as Gasché, García, and
Karadimas, describe the ideal situation, whose limited materialization in practice in present times has
undoubtedly been influenced by the demographic upheaval of the rubber genocide. Among the MuruiMuina, a maloquero’s firstborn son holds the privilege to create a dancing beam and conduct the Yadiko
ceremony to communicate with the Creator Father. The second or third son, depending on whose model
(Gasché or García), can perform the Zɨkɨi Dance for managing relations with forest animals or the
Menizaɨ River Turtle Dance, involving negotiation with aquatic beings. The fourth son celebrates the
Yuakɨ Fruit Dance (García 2018, 133–34; Gasché 2009, 15–18). The hierarchical logic also reflects the
notion of privilege accumulation, where a maloquero can perform not only the dance associated with his
birth order but also those of his younger brothers. Therefore, the Fruit Dance can be performed by any
maloquero, similar to the Andoque’s perception of this and other variants of the Opossum Dance as the
basis of any ceremonial career. In Gasché’s account, the second son (and, therefore, also the firstborn)
can create a pair of manguaré drums associated with the Zɨkɨi Dance (2009, 15–16). The Murui-Muina
model also corresponds, to some extent, to the Miraña ritual system. In this system, a maloquero’s
firstborn son holds the privilege to inaugurate a maloca with the dance beam ceremony; the second son
celebrates the Tšákómɨ nomination dance, and the third son and his younger brothers can perform the
carrying band ceremony (Pítšópa) to name a newborn child and celebrate the harvest of seasonal fruits
(Karadimas 2005, 38–40).
Five of the Andoque red and white dances mentioned above mirror these Murui-Muina and Miraña
ritual prerogatives. Similar to the firstborn ceremonies in both groups, the Multiplying Tree Dance
centers around a dance beam associated with ancestry and promoting demographic growth, which holds
a higher rank than the manguaré drums associated with the Head Dance. The latter dance is also linked
to forest animals, akin to the Murui-Muina Zɨkɨi, while the two River Turtle Dances (Bamboo and
Carrier) parallel the Menizaɨ in their association with aquatic beings. Lastly, the Armadillo Dance is
dedicated to name giving for babies in a special carrying band, resembling the Miraña’s Pítšópa.

It should be noted that Echeverri’s comparison largely draws on Estrada Añokazi’s (2018) research among the Andoque,
whose data diverges, in several cases, from the analysis put forward in this chapter.

Furthermore, an analysis of Andoque naming ceremonies since the 1930s demonstrates a certain
correspondence between the tutelary dances where names have been given and the birth order of the
named individual. In the Andoque case, the parent’s maloquero or non-maloquero status is also relevant,
because also non-maloquero children can be given a name in the Armadillo Dance. Based on my data,
firstborn daughters of maloqueros or individuals trained to be maloqueros are typically given names in
the Multiplying Tree Dance, while firstborn sons of such individuals receive names in the red Carrier
Dance which is closely connected with Multiplying Tree, and which grants these individuals the
authority to create the multiplying beam. The fact that the Andoque associate primogeniture, and not the
laterborn son, with a river dance, differs from the Murui-Muina model, and I will return to it below,
alongside the notable exception found in the sole tutelary dance where naming is not permitted. This
dance, Bamboo, is also connected with aquatic life, akin to the Murui-Muina’s Menizaɨ. Individuals
named in other white dances are eligible to hold Bamboo as well. Second-born sons of maloqueros
receive names in the Head or Fausíya Dances, with the latter, which has no equivalent among
neighboring peoples, seeming to be a derivative of the Head Dance and its associated traditions. Finally,
firstborn sons of non-maloquero men, who are considered the younger brothers of their respective clan
captains, can receive a name in an Armadillo Dance and are likewise classified as white.
Against this backdrop, I propose the following hypothesis: in the past, the Andoque also operated within
a quadripolar system, characterized by an ideal correlation between ritual prerogatives and the birth
order of a maloquero’s four sons. In this system, the firstborn son held the right to celebrate the
Multiplying Tree Dance and construct the corresponding beam; the second son could craft a manguaré
and organize the Head Dance; the third son had the privilege of celebrating a River Turtle Dance, which
included name-giving a name-giving ceremony; and the fourth son was responsible for the Armadillo
Dance, a ritual focused solely on protecting children. As seen in Table 12. this reconstructed system
resembled those of neighboring peoples:

However, I suggest that these four specializations gradually gravitated into a dual division, consolidating
into two career paths—the red career, consisting of ceremonies centered on patrilineal continuity and led
by the firstborn son, and the white career, encompassing the specializations of the three other brothers
and primarily focused on managing relations with both real and potential affinal relatives. I will
substantiate and elaborate on my argument through the five following points.
First, Andoque members’ practice of referring to their clan captain as “elder brother” highlights the
connection between primogeniture and patrilineal identity, where the elder brother maintains a
privileged connection with the father and the clan’s origin and core, which he mediates for his younger
brothers and subordinates. The link between the red specialization and primogeniture is also suggested
by the former’s name, peɒɵsí, which shares the concept of “essence” (ɵsí) with the term for “elder
brother,” ḭhaǵɵsí, while the younger sibling is perceived as the “final” person (ḭɒi), what remains after
their elder. This idea finds illustration in the story of the war between Sun and Moon. These two
brothers, who are associated with the red and white specializations emerged from the same dove egg
(Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 45). Sun, the elder brother, emerged from the neatly defined yolk, while
the younger Moon represents the egg white—the disorganized, amorphic matter surrounding the yolk.
As the guardian of his group’s essence, the elder brother holds the privilege of crafting the material
representation of its phallus, fertilizing the group, and boosting its population through the Multiplying
Tree Dance. Similarly to equivalent dances among neighboring peoples, this dance symbolizes the
firstborn’s identification with the father, maintaining the connection with the ancestors (Gasché 2009,
15; Urbina Rangel 2010, 39). While it is understandable that following the rubber genocide, as part of
the Andoque’s desire to recover demographically, they would hold in greater esteem this dance and
related practices aimed at consolidating the essence of their identity and ensuring its continuity, what
remains to be explained is their contempt and suspicion toward the dances that are classified as white.

409

Second, an important step in the bipolarization of the Andoque ceremonial system appears to be the
absorption of the name giving component of the river-related dance into the elder brother’s ritual
specialization. The identity between the “singing ball” parts of both Carrier and Bamboo Dances points
to their common origin, as one River Turtle Dance for managing relations with aquatic entities and other
agents associated with the river and the river mouth, such as Whites.139 However, I suggest that as
exchange with the latter became more central to the Andoque’s lives and economy, the more powerful
and prestigious maloqueros of the Multiplying Tree career appropriated the river ceremony. They did
this by duplicating the River Turtle dance and adding the spear-rod dances, reflecting a more aggressive
attitude toward riverine agents. Furthermore, they inserted the “carrier band” component to name their
own sons, destined for leadership, instead of naming them in the Multiplying Tree Dance, and at the
expense of the children of their younger brothers, who retained an impoverished version of the River
Turtle Dance. Evidence of this impoverishment of the younger brother’s dance is expressed through the
mythical register in M8 (see Appendix 1), where a captain loses his son after receiving jaguar fangs as
game in a Bamboo Dance (see also Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 122–23).140 For this reason, the
Bamboo Dance is today considered infelicitous for children and suitable only for old, childless
maloqueros.
In the Bamboo Dance, the “river turtle” component is also associated with the failure of that maloquero
and his genealogical discontinuity. When I asked Fisi upon his narration the Bamboo Dance’s origin
myth why this dance alludes to this animal, he explained to me that when the jaguar was burned in that
mythic dance, one bone turned into a bamboo stick, another became another type of flute, and his eye
popped out, transforming into a beetle which, during that period, was called pádɨ—the same word used
today to refer to river turtles (an episode resembling M16). By contrast, the way the “river turtle”
component was integrated into the traditions of the Carrier Dance reflects an association with the red
specialization and its emphasis on patrilineal continuity. Fisi explained to me that in Blazing Lake,
where Woodpecker carried Stingray in M25, the river turtles saw dragonflies dancing the Multiplying
Tree up high on the trees, using the root of the açai palm as their beam. The river turtles called the
dragonflies to descend and dance a River Turtle-Carrier Band with them, which the dragonflies did, and

they all danced with rods decorated with the bark of the bɨsokń tree, whose benefits for child protection
are here explained through its resemblance to the açai, as it does not heat up or die. The river turtle is
thus an important owner-person of this dance because this species was the first to dance it with
ornamented rods, as people do today, instead of using Tofidei’s simple spears, thereby turning it into a
life-giving ritual. By associating the bɨsokń tree with the Multiplying Tree Dance and the açai, which
served as the proto-multiplying beam, this episode establishes the link between the River Turtle Dance
and the red specialization, essential for justifying the appropriation of the former’s name giving
component by the latter.
Third, it is important to address another distinction between the Andoque’s dual specializations and the
Murui-Muina model: the existence of the Fausíya Dance, which does not have any equivalent
throughout the region. As previously mentioned, this ceremony appears to be a derivative of the Head
Dance. I suggest that Yiñékɒ foregrounded this dance as an alternative to Head’s conception of dynamic
and relatively symmetrical exchange between different categories of predator and prey. In this
alternative, the exchange is unidirectional, with the agency of game animals enhanced through the
capacities bestowed upon them by celestial predators, and its practice is restricted— once a generation,
as I was informed. It is possible that the infrequency of this dance is intended to ensure a particular
allegorical interpretation by its participants, one that M27 invites listeners to consider through the
allusion to the flood. In this interpretation, game animals do not represent themselves, and the powerful
rhythm bestowed upon them by the stars does not pose a threat to humans. Instead, these vulnerable
animals symbolize post-diluvian humanity—or, in the case of the Andoque, the survivors of genocide—
and the musical instrument they receive signifies the empowerment of human victims.
The only children who received a name in a prestigious manner in a Fausíya Dance—in contrast to mass
name-givings or changes for other children and adults on another occasion—were Yiñékɒ’s second male
son Rodolfo and his elder sister Irene, with Rodolfo being the primary name recipient. I propose that,
unable to name this son in the red Carrier Dance (as he was not his firstborn)141 and unwilling to name
him in a Head Dance for a similar aversion toward the white specialization as the one discussed below,
Yiñékɒ used the Fausíya as a “white” alternative to Head for naming second-born children.

My interlocutors, including Fisi, were unable to explain why Yiñékɒ had not named his eldest son, Fisi, in the Carrier
Dance or any other dance. Although I do not have the exact year when Yiñékɒ built his first maloca, I presume that he did not
name Fisi in a dance either because he did not possess a maloca at that period, or because he did not yet feel confident in his
ability to perform complicated dances like Carrier.

141

411

Fourth, while the red specialization focuses on maintaining patrilineal continuity, the central white
dances—namely, Head and Bamboo—revolve around affinal exchange and the familiarization of such
non-kin to counter hostilities by them. In these two ceremonies, the guests, who are ideally the host’s
real affines, serve as intermediaries with nonhuman potential affines, and providing them with
familiarizing foodstuffs and ritual substances functions to appease and familiarize the masters of forest
animals and of the river and aquatic beings. The etiological myths of both dances (M18 and M22)
narrate the failed attempt to celebrate a dance which is the blueprint of the one whose origin the myth
recounts, a failure connected to the inappropriate behavior of the host’s brothers-in-law. In M18, the
group of overhunting affines arrive at the maloca as peccaries and sows disorder, while in M22, Pretty
expresses his refusal to participate in reciprocal exchange with his brother-in-law by sleeping with his
own sister and Green Tapir’s wife. To repair these damaged relations with affinal relatives and prevent
further harms by them, both dances involve commensality with sylvan and aquatic nonhuman affines.142
Tellingly, although Andoque members often translate the term for the white specialization, pó’fiɵ, as
“peace” (paz), a more exact translation would hint at notions of clarity or gaze indicated by the root pó’.
This root is also shared with the kinship term “brother-in-law” (pókn), which suggests a possible
association between the two terms (Jon Landaburu, pers. comm., November 2023). This possible
association may revolve around the notion of symmetry—the symmetrical exchange in the Head and
Bamboo Dances, and the symmetry underlying relations between brothers-in-law, in contrast with the
asymmetrical relations between father and son and between father-in-law and son-in-law.
The tension that the Andoque acknowledge between affinal exchange and agnatic ideology is best
illustrated in M11, where Green Tapir—who, in the context of the Bamboo Dance, embodies the failure
of the exchange with his wife’s family—tries to break the multiplying beam. This episode captures the
risk that exogamy poses to patrilineal continuity. By contrast, the Multiplying Tree Dance is associated
with the dance inaugurated by Green Tapir’s brother, Tofidei—one narrator even referred to him as
Green Tapir’s elder brother—who reflects an endogamous ideal by marrying his own sister after a
similar matrimonial failure.
Finally, in contrast with the two central and powerful white dances, the less prestigious Armadillo
Dance is primarily concerned with defending human group members from engaging in commensality

fails to reciprocate the game provided to him (see Appendix 1).

142

412

(and coupling) with potential nonhuman affines, rather than appeasing them through such commensality.
While this dance bears certain resemblances to the Miraña’s name giving ceremony linked with
ultimogeniture, it appears that if it was indeed associated with a specific birth order, it dissociated from
this model and became identified with a non-maloquero status. Unlike the relational orientation of
affinal exchange characterizing the Head and Bamboo Dances, in its non-maloquero position, the
Armadillo Dance reflects the submission of ordinary members’ to the maloquero. They should approach
the maloquero to name their child in this dance, symbolizing allegiance to the patrilineal authority he
represents, and their desire to benefit from the protection that his patrilineally-transmitted traditions can
provide to their newborn child. In the terms of M28, they seek the maloquero’s enhanced paternity to
shield their child from the affinal world—similar to how the anaconda saved the child by imposing its
paternity over the jaguar’s.143
The distinct relational orientations of the red dances, on the one hand, and of the two central white
dances, Head and Bamboo, on the other, represent a variation of the Amazonian division between two
ideal types of shamanism, termed vertical and horizontal shamanism by S. Hugh-Jones (1994). In HughJones’ definition, vertical shamanism relies on esoteric knowledge transmitted within a small elite,
whereas horizontal shamanism is accessible to individuals outside the political elites and involves
personalized and corporal experiences of trance and possession. In the Northwest Amazonian context
that Hugh-Jones focused on, where Tukanoan and Arawakan-speaking clans, or sibs, emphasize agnatic
descent and hierarchy while also striving for symmetrical marital exchange, this duality is observed in
the distinction between the ~kubu and payé. The ~kubu relies on patrilineally-transmitted knowledge,
gains further authority with age, and is responsible for communication with the ancestor. His position
often converges with leadership, and he practices his powers within the maloca for the benefit of the
wider community, with rituals associated with forest fruits and gathering. By contrast, the payé relies on
personal experience and physical transmission of knowledge. He represents youth and holds a lower
status, communicating with animals, affines, and enemies outside the house for the benefit of the
specific individuals seeking his services. His rituals are associated with venatic activities and warfare,
aspiring for reciprocal exchange with spirits.

Among the Miraña, the fern, whose use in the name-giving dance parallels its employment in the Andoque’s Armadillo
Dance, is associated with the clan’s past generations, thereby symbolizing patrilineal continuity (Karadimas 2005b, 335–36).
This may account for Yiñékɒ’s use of the fern component of the Armadillo Dance, in which Tañe was named, to shift the
latter’s ritual specialization from the white to the red one, associated with a strong patrilineal identity (see Chapter 10).
143

413

The Andoque division between the red and white specializations mirrors some dimensions of the duality
between vertical and horizontal shamanism. Akin to vertical shamanism, the red specialization is
associated with leadership and seniority, and centers around patrilineal continuity. Furthermore, the
creation and recreation of forest trees as a defensive measure in M23 and Carrier Dance resonates with
the Tukanoan-Arawakan link between this type of shamanism and the forest’s growth. On the contrary,
the two main dances of the white specialization bear resemblance to the horizontal shamanism ideal,
marked by lower status and association with juniority. They prioritize reciprocal exchange with affines
and aim to navigate relations with sylvan and aquatic animals. I also put forth the hypothesis that the
white specialization represents an attempt to institutionalize horizontal shamanic powers in order to
contain them within the socially acceptable borders of the maloca. This hypothesis is based on several
similarities between this specialization and the more individualistic roles of healer and sorcerer, which
are the most representative of the horizontal type. It is thus possible that the moral ambiguity
characterizing these roles contributes to the ambivalence surrounding the white specialization.
The aversion expressed by Andoque members toward the white specialization, particularly the Head and
Bamboo dances, bears a resemblance to their disinclination toward sorcerers and even healers, who are
morally ambiguous, drawing on Animal Stories and maintaining a close relationship with nonhuman
entities that they may also exploit to inflict harm on others. Here we should also recall the apparent
continuum mentioned above, which existed before the genocide, between cannibal dances— now
regarded as diabólicos and a clear expression of commensality with nonhuman predators at the expense
of human sociality for acquiring sorcery and healing skills—and the Head Dance. Yinñéfɵkn from the
survivors’ generation, who was reportedly a healer and a sorcerer, also belonged to the white
specialization. More specifically, he was associated with the Bamboo Dance, which he allegedly
organized as part of his ongoing dialogue and exchange with dolphins and other malevolent entities.
César from that generation is also depicted today as a healer and a practitioner of the Head and other
white dances. Joselito from that generation represents an interesting case, because he was a healer and is
also described today by many members as a sorcerer, who chose to change his own name and name
several of his sons in the mass naming of the white Fausíya Dance organized by “his elder brother”
Yiñékɒ before the event that created the schism between these two Eagle lineages—namely, Joselito’s
son death. However, when Joselito constructed his own maloca years after that event, he chose to
inaugurate it with the red River Turtle-Carrier Band Dance associated with primogeniture, thus signaling
his breaking away with Yiñékɒ’s authority. Today, the elder who is the most associated with the white
414

specialization is also considered a healer, with people expressing suspicions about sorcery actions he
may have undertaken.
However, my interlocutors also distinguish between sorcerers and healers on the one hand, and the white
specialization on the other. While healers and especially sorcerers are depicted as asocial individuals
who stereotypically live alone, without a wife and children, practicing their lore in their remote forest
cabin, the practitioners of the white specialization, like any other captain, can and should construct
malocas, organize people for work and hold dances for the benefit of the wider group.
In this context, it is interesting to note the correlation between sorcery and healing, younger birth order,
and negative social evaluation among the Bora, where, unlike the Murui-Muina and Miraña, a system of
correspondences between ritual prerogatives and birth order has not been observed. Among the Bora, a
maloquero’s firstborn son and daughter inherit “beautiful” names, with the son also inheriting the
father’s ritual specialization and the expectation to construct a maloca and serve as captain. By contrast,
the maloquero’s second-born son and daughter inherit “ugly” names. This son also typically assumes a
trickster position, both protecting and insulting his elder brother, and tends to practice healing and
sorcery, both of which assumes contact with animals (Lucas 2019, 172; on beautiful and ugly names
among the Miraña, see Karadimas 2005, 38–39). This negative evaluation of younger siblings and their
inclination for horizontal shamanic practices is reminiscent of the Andoque’s lower regard for the white
specialization. However, in the Andoque case, the negative evaluation of the ritual specialization that is
continuous with sorcery/healing is not as formalized as among the Bora. The Andoque’s informal
negative evaluation of the white specialization seems to rest on people’s inferences about the risks
surrounding white dances. Similar to the exchange with powerful nonhuman entities in sorcery and
healing, white maloqueros may be unable to control the dangerous exchange with nonhumans,
potentially leading to their familiarization by these entities instead of them familiarizing the latter.
By contrast, the more aggressive stance of the red specialization correlates with a stronger emphasis on
patrilineal descent and identity, a higher tendency for asymmetry in exchange with nonhuman entities,
and a degradation of their agency—like Tofidei’s petrification of his enemies in M23—which renders
the inversion potential inherent in the logic of familiarizing predation less likely. Foregrounding the
kinship and inter-species dimensions of the Andoque’s notions of power, the domination over
nonhumans is linked with agnatic ideology and a dwindling emphasis on reciprocity between affines. To
complete the picture, we must reintroduce the distinction between homosubstitution and

415

heterosubstitution into the discussion. In S. Hugh-Jones’ model of dual shamanism, the Tukanoan
spiritual negotiation of game in exchange for an equivalent number of human souls is classified under
the horizontal pole (1994, 41). This means that horizontal shamanism, along with the white
specialization as its variation, aligns more closely with homosubstitutive exchanges with nonhumans.
Conversely, as I have argued in previous chapters, the role of captaincy, associated with the red
specialization, enables the engagement of inferior items in heterosubstitutive exchange. We thus receive
the following set of correspondences:

Table 13. Two ritual specializations in their broad context

The rise of the red specialization and the decline of the white one can thus be seen as another
Amazonian instance of the persistence of vertical shamanism and decline of horizontal shamanism (S.
Hugh-Jones 1994)—or “dejaguarization” in Fausto’s (2007) terms, given the reliance of horizontal
shamans on the power of the jaguar—which has owed to different reasons in each geographical,
historical, and cultural context. Within a small group like the Andoque’s, historical trends can
undoubtedly be explained, in part, by recourse to chance occurrences and specific circumstances. In this
case, a key circumstance was the unparalleled prominence of Yiñékɒ, who belonged to the red
specialization. While today’s elders recount specific teachings that they received in their youth from
Yinñéfɵkn and Joselito, these teachings mainly encompass healing and singing skills, rather than
captaincy or dance organization. Yiñékɒ trained many of young Andoque men in the 1960s and 1970s,
even ones affiliated with the white specialization, like his son Rodolfo. As we have seen in the previous
chapter, the unplanned union between his daughter and Tañe led him to train the latter, whom he had
originally named in the Armadillo Dance, for the red specialization. Yiñékɒ also trained the children of
his ceremonial ally, To̰fi—a unique situation that certainly owed to Yiñékɒ’s central role in the cultural
revitalization efforts, as well as to To̰fi’s premature death before he could properly instruct his children.
However, in addition to these specific circumstances, I propose that three underlying factors have also
contributed to the current dominance of the red career and the decline of the white one. The first factor

416

has already been discussed in Chapter 4—the Andoque’s goal to reproduce and recover their agency
after the rubber genocide, for which the red Multiplying Tree, with its predatory connotations and
emphasis on agnatic descent at the expense of symmetrical exchange with human and nonhuman beings,
was instrumental. Conversely, the Fausíya Dance, which is also associated with the “flood” and tasked
with ensuring peaceful existence in the territory post-event, did not foster self-identification as pó’fiɵ
among those who received their names during its mass name-giving ceremony in the 1950s. Nor did it
lead these individuals to name their children in this dance or the Armadillo or the other white dances.
Furthermore, Fisi’s Fausíya Dance in 1997 did not include a naming ceremony, neither on an individual
nor on a collective basis.
The second factor was the specific measures taken by Yiñékɒ to facilitate the future consolidation of
distinct clan centers. During the 1960s and 1970s, among the various training processes in which Yiñékɒ
was involved, he prepared his son Fisi and two other men of that generation—the firstborn sons of his
ceremonial ally To̰fi and his brother-in-law César—for clan leadership, specifically through the training
into the red specialization. In the case of César’s son, this training contradicted his father’s affiliation
with the white specialization; in the case of Mario, To̰fi’s son, the youngest of the three, this training
also included naming in the Carrier Dance, closely associated with leadership. In the following
generation, Yiñékɒ took an important step in consolidating the future distinct identities of Andoque
clans by naming the firstborn sons of two of his children (Irene and Fisi) and two other men from his
children’s generation in the Carrier Dance. These name givings made the named individuals and their
fathers more committed to the red specialization. It is possible that in the future, once Andoque members
feel that their clan identities are sufficiently consolidated, they will celebrate and express a higher
evaluation of white dances. However, the following factor makes it, in my view, less likely.
This last factor is the growing perception of human beings as superior to nonhumans and the inclination
to engage in asymmetrical exchange with them. These tendencies have been discussed in relation to the
Andoque’s notion of “the Creator” and their general perception of human-nonhuman power dynamics
within their ancestral territory. It is possible that these tendencies are also related to the increasing direct
and indirect contact with Christianity and general Modern assumptions of human domination over
nonhuman entities and the right that human beings supposedly hold to use the latter as they please. More
concretely, the Andoque’s participation in the extractive economy, starting from their return to rubber
work after the genocide, has led to various measures for restricting the agency of the nonhuman entities

417

that they have extracted and traded to prevent eventual damages and retaliation by these entities or the
spirits safeguarding them. These measures, as will be explored in Chapter 13, resonate with the red
ceremonial specialization, especially with its strive to establish the superiority of the human group and
its more stable domination over nonhuman entities. Similar to the Bora’s generalized treatment of
animals as orphans with whom humans, in their generalized status as chiefs, maintain an asymmetrical
relation of protection and domination (Lucas 2021, 21–22), the Andoque’s increasing perception of
nonhuman entities as inferior to humans and the possibility to degrade their agencies obviate the more
reciprocal exchange with them, as promoted by the main white dances. Therefore, while the relatively
general disdain for the white specialization contradicts the regional shift toward a discourse of peace, it
aligns with a growing conception of ontological asymmetry between humans and nonhumans.
In the context of Part III’s discussion of power dynamics among centers, we can conclude that the rise of
the red specialization and the widespread disdain toward the white one are linked with power dynamics
both among human centers and between human and nonhuman ones. The emphasis in red dances on
patrilineal identity and continuity has been vital for the competition between human centers, securing
the independence of one human center from another, and preserving the distinctions between them.
Concomitantly, the empowerment of agnatic agency in these dances envisages the disempowerment of
real and potential human and nonhuman affinal centers. Consequently, this encourages the engagement
in a more aggressive or non-reciprocal exchange with them. Therefore, whereas the interweaving of
inter-human and human-nonhuman relations manifest in the complex general dynamics of conflict
dramatization and mitigation in ceremonial dances, the rise of the red specialization reflects the
interconnection between agnatic ideology in the realm of inter-human relations and human superiority in
the realm of human-nonhuman relations. This reiterates the continuity between asymmetrical exchanges
in inter-human relations and in human-nonhuman relations, as explored in the previous chapters.
As I have shown, several of the dances are specifically associated with the river mouth, representing
non-Indigenous people. The next part of this dissertation will explore this dimension of Andoque dances
within a broader discussion tackling the theme of power dynamics in interactions and exchange with
Whites—a theme which is undoubtedly essential for a fuller understanding of power dynamics among
human centers and between them and nonhuman ones.

418

Part IV
Power Relations with the River Mouth

419

420

Introduction
In the preceding chapters, the presence of non-Indigenous agents and their impact on the Andoque’s
power relations—assessed through the capacity to establish beneficially asymmetrical exchanges of
goods, bodies, vital principles, and agencies among human individuals and groups, as well as between
them and nonhumans—have been mentioned but not directly explored. In this part of the dissertation, I
complete the analysis of power dynamics within Andoque society by tackling key aspects of nonIndigenous presence and impact, addressing the question: How do the Andoque perceive and influence
power dynamics in their interaction with Whites, and how do these interactions affect the Andoque’s
power relations with nonhuman entities? This chapter does not discuss how exchanges with nonIndigenous people have altered power relations among the Andoque themselves. Such impacts have
been examined in previous chapters, specifically focusing on two crucial dimensions: the increased
influence of captains as slave traders and goods distributors, and the role that alliances with nonIndigenous agents have played in the rivalry between the Sun and Eagle Clans.
Ethnographers of the Andoque and other People of the Center have commented on the existence of
longstanding exchange, dating back as early as the seventeenth century, between them and nonIndigenous merchants and slave traders, as well as their Indigenous intermediaries, mainly from areas
downriver controlled by the Portuguese and later Brazilians. They studied the integration of metal axes
and other goods and instruments originating from commerce with non-Indigenous agents into the
Indigenous economy, and the perception of the higher yields and productivity they allow as beneficial
for social reproduction, the nurturing of social relations, the establishment of an exchange network, and
defense from hostile nonhuman beings (Echeverri 2022, 96–103; Griffiths 1998, 232, 246–48; Pineda
Camacho 1975). These accounts correspond to what Sahlins termed the “indigenization of modernity,” a
process by which Indigenous people globally utilize resources acquired from colonial powers to advance
their own development projects and other endeavors inscribed within their respective cosmologies
(Sahlins 1994; 2000). In the Amazonian context, Fausto showed how this approach draws from a
structuralist legacy, particularly on its focus on the assimilation of the Other for fostering social
reproduction (Fausto 2007b). In this respect, it is continuous with notions of appropriating affinal
powers through processes of familiarization explored in this dissertation.
However, as Sahlins (1994) stresses, resource appropriation is certainly not one-sided; non-Indigenous
agents also utilize Indigenous resources for their own goals, which may align more readily with

421

hegemonic endeavors and can ultimately turn against the Indigenous party. In the Andoque case, for
example, Fisi and other members recount that Yiñékɒ managed to impose the Andoque agricultural and
ritual calendar on Miguel Zumaeta during the post-genocide rubber-tapping period, effectively asserting
in which seasons work would be ceased for garden creation and dance celebrations. However, Guzman’s
(1971) observations of the Andoque’s participation in this economy in the 1970s led him to the
somewhat opposite conclusion that their traditional subsistence economic practices were a necessary
condition for the functioning of rubber-tapping activities by allowing the labor force to sustain itself
with minimal investment by the rubber boss, whose profits thus increased. Furthermore, economic
engagements between Indigenous Amazonians and non-Indigenous parties have resulted in dependence
on the external goods and their providers “in the classic sense that on their own, they [can] no longer
produce all the necessary preconditions for the reproduction of their social relations” (Fisher 2000, 13),
thereby subjecting themselves and their territories to exploitative and destructive economic activities.
Andoque members often portray themselves as poor and vulnerable vis-à-vis Whites, citing their
necesidades (needs), a term referring to objects manufactured outside the region. This term translates
two Andoque expressions with distinct meanings and possible associations with two myths narrated in
earlier chapters and discussed below: kahɵ́ɵi, or “our missing [things],” and kama ɵhɵ́ñői, or “that which
we find pretty.” While the latter expression carries a tone of seduction by pretty yet dangerous things
similar to the dolphins figuring in M22, the former brings to mind M5 and a nostalgia for the items
initially engendered at the center to be appropriated by the river mouth (“these [things] are that which
we were missing [kahɵ́ɵi]”, says the son of Egret of the Center to his father), and also, we may presume,
a nostalgia for greater economic independence. Hence, while not referring strictly to items that are
necessary for human existence as opposed to luxury items, as the Spanish term suggests, necesidades
reflects a deeper notion of dependence on the outside.144
Similar to other Indigenous Amazonians (e.g., Buitron and Deshoullière 2023; Kelly 2011), the
Andoque do not oppose the market economy or capitalist logic per se but are primarily concerned about
their persistently disadvantageous position in asymmetric exchanges with non-Indigenous people,
seeking to balance this asymmetry and even utilize resources obtained from non-Indigenous agents for
their own projects and social reproduction. The following chapters, broadly categorized into themes of
consumption, extraction and production, and preservation, demonstrate how the Andoque contemplate
144

For the Amazonian lack of distinction necessities and luxuries see Fisher 2000, 2; S. Hugh-Jones 1992.

422

these asymmetries through the lenses of the predatory relational schema, the kinship notion of
familiarizing affines, and the ontological manipulation of value. In this context, as Chapter 12 shows,
the White is yet another potential affine who must be familiarized if his predatory intentions are to be
thwarted, and his products are to be appropriated and used felicitously. However, the transactions
between Andoque and Whites do not involve only the human transactors, but also nonhuman objects of
transaction—those harvested, detached from their territory and social groups, and traded between
parties. The extractive economy triggers its own predatory reactions by the nonhuman owner-persons of
the harvested entities and destabilizes or complicates relationships of mastery and familiarization with
them that are necessary for achieving specific goals and, more broadly, for territorial management and
social reproduction. This aspect of exchange with non-Indigenous agents, less explored in research, is
the focus of Chapter 13. The final chapter tackles the interactions between the Andoque and Whites in
the relatively new context of environmental action, contemplating the meaning and power dimensions
that the relational triangle between these two parties and nonhumans assumes when non-Indigenous
agents try to mobilize Indigenous people for the protection, rather than harvest, of nonhuman entities.

423

424

Chapter 12. Predation by and Familiarization of the River Mouth
Similar to neighboring People of the Center (Echeverri 2022, 106–8), the Andoque language contains
two terms for non-Indigenous people: “Burners” (duiɵ́hɵ) and “Traders” (dohaɵ́hɵ). In the Andoque
case, this duality alludes to the two manifestations of the White Man in Andoque mythology, either as
an enemy or as an affine, and, as such, an exchange partner. In this chapter, I discuss the different
images of Whites as enemies and affines in Andoque myth, ritual, and other discursive contexts, and
explore the dangers of predation and seduction by the river mouth and the various mechanisms through
which the Andoque attempt to cope with these dangers and impose reciprocal exchange on Whites.
These dangers and the mechanisms for counteracting them are expressed and operate through the
categories of space, kinship, and humanity examined throughout this dissertation: the positions of river
source, center, and mouth; affinal exchange and the familiarization of non-kin; and human beings vs.
nonhuman beings.
The Axe Jaguar and Other Predators
The inimical, dangerous nature of non-Indigenous agents is encoded in the aggressions undertaken by
Egret of the River Mouth in the myth about the “War of the Speaking Tree,” briefly discussed in
Chapter 1. However, the reason for the rage that this hero nurtures toward Egret of the Center—namely,
the desire for the latter’s wife that leads to his humiliation and almost costs him his life—hints at his
nature as a potential affine. This potential materializes in M5, where Egret of the River Mouth takes the
daughter of Egret of the Center and the goods to which she has given birth, appropriating the
reproductive capacity of these goods, and eventually trading some of them with his brother-in-law from
the center—a trade that can also be understood as the counter-transfer of women. It is noteworthy that
“Trader” does not refer only to Whites, but also to Andoque and other Indigenous individuals trading
with them. In other words, it signifies a relation, not a defined collective.
The affinal nature with which the Andoque invest the non-Indigenous hero, and the moral obligation to
which marital exchange with him gives rise, are not to be taken for granted. Myths narrated by
neighboring Peoples of the Center on the origin of non-Indigenous people, their goods, or commerce
with them allude to only one of these components but not both. The Bora, for example, tell about trade
in goods without marital exchange (Lucas 2019, 372–73), while the Miraña tell about sexual seduction
without an eventual union and reproduction, even describing something we may call “co-parenting”
without a sexual union (Karadimas 2005, 171–75, 360–67). The Nɨpóde, on the other hand, locate the
425

discrepancy in reproductive capacity of manufactured goods between Indigenous and non-Indigenous
people within the consanguineal relation between a White and Indigenous sister (Griffiths 1998, 247),
rather than in the moments preceding and following the union with the White hero, as in M5. The
comparison with the Andoque’s farther neighbors, the Tukanoan groups of the Vaupes River, is the most
salient. For these groups, whose strong emphasis on agnatic descent is complemented by a strive for
balanced matrimonial exchange between language groups, the mythical hero representing Whites is cast
out of the system of ritual and exogamic exchange. After the Indigenous ancestors chose the bow and
ritual ornaments offered to them by the creator god, the White was left with the gun, symbolizing his
transformation from affine to enemy and explaining why war is the equivalent of ritual for nonIndigenous people (S. Hugh-Jones 1988, 144–45).
The act of locating Whites within the Amazonian complex of enmity and affinity, along with the
accompanying desire to transition them from behaving like the former to adopting the latter role, is also
documented among other groups in the region (e.g., Grenand and Grenand 2000). However, in the case
of the Andoque, these inclinations are conveyed through the language of spatial concepts. The
distinction between “Burners” and “Traders” is inherent to M5, where it is conveyed through the spatial
categories of river source and river mouth: Egret of the River Mouth is the trader brother-in-law, while
Egret of the River Source is the frustrated, violent burner. In my interlocutors’ interpretation, this
spatialization reflects both the historical fact of the arrival of the first non-Indigenous merchants and
their Indigenous middlemen, and later the agents of the Casa Arana, from downriver, on the one hand,
and a prophecy concerning the descent of Colombian dissident armed groups from the cordillera, and
hence, the river source, on the other. However, within the perspectivist framework for understanding
spatial categories employed throughout this dissertation, we may put it in the following terms: placing
Whites toward the river source implies that the Andoque are relegated to the position of their prey, while
placing them toward the river mouth preserves the position of predator for the Andoque. Exchange of
goods is thus possible, desired, or beneficial for one insofar as one is found in the position of predator,
but impossible, undesired, or detrimental insofar as one is found in a position of prey. A central
Andoque ambition is to ensure that the non-Indigenous agents they encounter act like traders from the
river mouth and not like burners from the river source, or, put differently, to employ an upstream
position in relation to them. This is another instance in which the cannibalistic fluvial system underlies
the captaincy fluvial system, as explored in Part I.

426

In ceremonial songs, the predatory nature of Whites is expressed through terms such as “Jaguar of the
River Mouth” (ɵkɒ́ ḭño̰), “Axe Jaguar of the River Mouth” (pɵɵ ɵkɒ́ ḭño̰), “Jaguar of Goods” (dohai ḭño̰),
or “Goods Thunder of the River Mouth” (dohai dú’dɨ ḭño̰), as well as other combinations of these and
other components (Pineda Camacho 1979, 43). Equally frequent is the reference to Whites in these
songs as enemies, yó’o. The predatory nature of non-Indigenous people, their nonhuman status, and their
interconnected immoral behavior have become common themes in descriptions of Indigenous
Amazonian understandings (Buchillet 2000; Bonilla 2005; Overing 1996; Severi 1988; van Velthem
2000). The use of such predatory metaphors when referring to Whites may allude to various dimensions
and effects of interactions with them. Firstly, as Griffiths documents for the Nɨpóde, these metaphors
may record the memory of the “devouring” of Indigenous individuals who were captured or purchased
by slave traders from downstream, never to return to their families (1998, 247, n.33). Secondly, given
that death from various misfortunes is typically interpreted as predation by the agent responsible for the
misfortune and assimilation into their place of origin, these predatory metaphors may also refer to the
massive death caused by epidemics. The Andoque associate these epidemics with the river mouth,
explaining that they shadowed the highly coveted metal tools and other goods obtained from Whites.
The association of non-Indigenous people with epidemics and misfortunes linked to the river mouth is
prominent in dreams, which serve as a medium for learning about impending events. Following the
metonymical interpretation mode of dreams discussed in Appendix 5, several interlocutors explained to
me that dreaming about a church, priests, or nuns represents an epidemic associated with fish,
originating from downriver, of which these non-Indigenous religious figures are considered the ownerpersons. Dreams featuring certain objects symbolizing the might of Whites, particularly airplanes and
the city, foretell death or a complete departure from ancestral traditions and beliefs, potentially leaving
the person vulnerable to fatal misfortunes. The concentration of such epidemics around the Caquetá
River, which served as a prime course of transport, is encoded in the figure of Bone Egret (Yo’fítanń), a
powerful captain who lived on the south bank of the river, roughly around Parrot/Pet Savanna. He would
seduce people to follow him when he played his flute,145 taking them with him and “enchanting them”
(los encantó), thereby transforming them into nonhuman entities.
Considering the discussion on ritual dynamics in the previous chapter, it becomes evident that invoking
the aggressions and damages caused by Whites during ceremonial dances, along with other forms of

145

427

direct and indirect predation by them, serves as an opportunity for the dance organizers to ward off these
dangers. They achieve this by offering ritual substances to the visible dance participants, and through
them, to the invisible forces associated with the river mouth. However, in this context, I would also like
to propose a more specific hypothesis related to obiikoi, the ritual of caguana distribution that precedes
five of the tutelary dances—Multiplying Tree, Head, Fausíya, and the two River Turtle Dances.
While all ceremonial dances involve risks for the hosts and guests—for instance, if the former fail to
provide adequate compensation for games and songs, or if the latter falter in their song-dances— these
five dances are deemed particularly perilous. This is because performing them inadequately can trigger
large-scale catastrophes, such as warfare and, especially, epidemics. My interlocutors explained to me
that the caguana distribution ceremony, conducted on the eve of these dances, serves as a safeguard
against such occurrences. But what is it about these dances that necessitates extra protection, and what is
it about the caguana beverage that provides this protection? We might assume that the more complex
relationships and broader alliances sought to be established and activated by these dances, along with the
elevated prestige associated with them—particularly if we accept the model presented in the previous
chapter concerning birth order and the corresponding rights to partake in specific ceremonies—
historically attracted larger attendances compared to other, less prestigious dances. During the postcontact centuries characterized by waves of epidemics that decimated Indigenous populations, this
higher attendance may have turned these central dances into potential vectors for contagion. People
could subsequently link the extinction of entire clans and other populations to these preceding events.
Paradoxically, this zenith of the captain’s prestige and his ability to negotiate with nonhuman entities
and “manage the territory” also represented a significant vulnerability, as it exposed entire groups to
predation by malevolent pathogenic agents associated with the river mouth.
In a similar vein to how individuals manipulate nonhuman entities in conflicts with other human beings,
this connection between tutelary dances and epidemic outbreaks is remembered today in anecdotes
recounting how powerful elders who were not invited to these dances employed sorcery to summon the
agents responsible for such plagues and directed them to attack the groups of the captains who neglected
to invite them. According to Fisi, the powerful sorcerer Fisidú’dɨ (“Stone Thunder”), was responsible for
the disappearance of the Tinamou and Tufted Capuchin Clans due to measles.146 Furthermore, in Fisi’s
story of Bone Egret, this enigmatic figure roamed from one clan territory to another, leaving death and
146

Fisi also alluded to these incidents in an interview found in Gómez López et al. 1998, 122–23.

428

chaos in his wake. One sorcerer, whose house Bone Egret visited, recognized the visitor and chose not to
resist but to welcome and treat him well. This sorcerer then succeeded in forming an alliance with Bone
Egret and gained the ability to harness his epidemics for his own purposes. This adds a further
dimension to our discussion in Part III of the continuity between power asymmetries in inter-human and
human-nonhuman relations. While the nonhumans concerned in those cases are beings inhabiting the
Andoque territory, here we observe the manipulation of nonhuman entities associated with Whites.
I suggest that over the long period of such epidemic cycles, the Andoque—and possibly other People of
the Center, who also practice this ceremony (Gasché 2009, 28–29; Echeverri 2022, 36)—incorporated
the ritual of caguana distribution on the eve of major dances as a safeguard for participants against such
predation. This ceremony is conducted by and for the dance workers, i.e., the organizing clan, with a
man and a woman offering vessels of caguana to the participants, while singing songs that typically
include critique of the captain and fellow clan members (de la Hoz Melo 2005, 67–74). As de la Hoz
showed, many caguana songs allude to relations with Whites (ibid, 70), and some songs make explicit
references to the slave trade:
You treated me like I am worthless (hɵ́’tá; also: “empty”).
You did not talk to me well,
You wanted to send (pa̰; also “to command”) me away with your merchant (hadoha),
But after I am gone, who else can accompany (ɵʼɵhɵ; also: “to help”) you with your calabash vessel (ha’podi)?147

I was explained that before the caguana ceremony begins, the host iterates a prayer to Egret (Yo’fí)—
who, in this context, represents Whites, and is also referred to as yó’o (enemy)—beseeching him to avert
his gaze and not to observe the celebrants, thereby avoiding harm to them. The interlocutor who
provided me this explanation did not agree to share the prayer with me, as it is considered particularly
dangerous, while others refrained from recording the opening verse of the first song of caguana
distribution for the same reason. Nonetheless, one interlocutor described the general message of this
song, which consists of the singer’s appeal to the participants as the children of Egret, imploring them
not to heed “ugly things” (see also de la Hoz Melo 2005, 69). Another interlocutor recorded the verses
with which a singer belonging to the white ritual specialization can reply to the opening verses:
This is the calabash vessel of tnknñe149
That we are drinking.
With his generation he drank this tnknñe calabash vessel.

The narrative T4 on the adventures of the Piercers told by Raquel (see Appendix 2) attests to the link
between Egret, epidemics, and the defense provided by drinking caguana. The caguana distribution
songs emerge as critical means to build immunity from Bone Egret’s epidemics and to ensure the
survival of human beings, an outcome the Piercers could have achieved had they performed them
correctly. The examples that Raquel gives for the Piercers’ incorrect use of the Andoque language—
namely, the replacement of the male form with the female one—may relate to their inability to benefit
from the protection that the caguana distribution could have provided them, for the same reason that
they could not properly give themselves names: they could not tap into a strong origin, which, as it
passes down the patriline, depends on men self-identifying as such and as the successors of elder male
relatives and ancestors.150 It thus seems that the caguana distribution ceremony aims to safeguard dance

Pineda (1979, 46) decisively states that the caguana distribution ceremony is also called Egret Dance without justifying
this statement. My Andoque interlocutors largely refrained from telling me about the Egret Dance, since it is no longer held
today (while the caguana distribution ceremony is still celebrated). From the few hints that I have gathered on this ritual, it
seems to have been a violent event with certain similarities to anthropophagous dances, before which the captive was forcibly
fed. Prior to an Egret Dance, a live egret would be captured and fed with fish obtained from a massive harvest (possibly by
asphyxiating plants) within a small stream. One interlocutor told me that during the ceremony, people would dance with the
egret, with the dancer in whose hands it dies being put to death. This practice mirrors the exaggerated “omens” of cannibal
dances, where any social gesture costed an individual’s life. This arbitrariness, as opposed to the captain’s decision as to
which of his men dies or traded, could mark the Egret Dance as an “anti-captaincy” dance. It is possible that the captive egret
represented slave traffickers operating along the river. Based on my hypothesis above, the caguana distribution ceremony

organizers and workers by creating a strong agnatic identification before the exogamic exchanges with
real and potential, human and nonhuman affines taking place during the actual dance, as a buffer against
epidemics representing massive predation by the affinal powers associated with the river mouth.
The goal of preventing predation from the river mouth sheds light on another aspect of the caguana
distribution ceremony: the naming of the maloquero’s daughters during this specific ceremony, unlike
their brothers who receive their names within the tutelary dances that follow, or their girlfriends who do
not belong to a maloca family, and whose naming in the Armadillo Dance takes place during the dance
itself. Given that past maloqueros, when short of war captives and in need of non-Indigenous goods,
preferred to trade distant kin connected through female relatives over clan members, naming daughters
in a ceremony associated with agnatic protection seems intended to ensure that future captains—namely,
their brothers—consider the daughters’ descendants as true kin rather than as disposable orphans. This is
supported by my interlocutors’ statements that the protection afforded by naming extends to the named
person’s siblings and offspring. By naming his daughter in this ceremony, a maloquero infuses his clan
identity into her, ensuring that her children—likely bearing her husband’s clan identity—are treated as
genuine kin.
The fact that non-Indigenous goods were often accompanied by epidemics signifies that exchange with
Whites is not an automatic guarantee from being aggressed and preyed upon by them. Even as a trader,
the White can commission yoóka, or “deviating things.”151 In some contexts, this term refers to useless
things, such as certain objects obtained from Whites whose use and benefit to people their Indigenous
recipients could not understand, as opposed to bɨ’iá, or “working tools,” whose benefit was clear to the
recipients from the outsets. However, my interlocutors explain that yoóka also designates any externally
manufactured goods insofar as their use eventually appears to have resulted in aches, diseases, accidents,
envy, and conflicts among its users—i.e., in different forms whereby the latter diverge from their
original intentions and end up in undesired mental, physical, and social states. In this meaning, it is also
opposed to bɨ’iá, a term which extends to encompassing any goods that eventually serve to pursue the
user’s projects and contribute to the well-being, prosperity, and reproduction of themselves and their
family.

would thus not be identical to the Egret Dance, but rather may have been perceived as an antidote against the predatory harms
wrought by “egrets”—both non-Indigenous merchants and the Indigenous captains trading with them.

The narration of M5 plays a crucial role in ensuring that the goods arriving at the Andoque would serve
as “working tools” rather than “deviating things.” Upon revisiting this story, we can observe that Trader
Egret of the River Mouth initially offers his brother-in-law from the center perfume and red cloth,
symbolizing the flu and anger, which the latter wisely refuses, choosing to bring back only work
instruments.152 Andoque members explain that when engaging in exchange with Whites, M5 is
recounted during mambeadero sessions to reject any deviations or risks that may result from the
reception of non-Indigenous goods, in a bid to transform these objects of exchange into life-giving
artifacts. Symbolic manipulation is employed to render them harmless to the Andoque, allowing them to
utilize metal tools for their own social reproduction projects instead of being harmed by them in
accidents or conflicts where these tools might be used as weapons, thus jeopardizing their existence as
true human beings. For example, rifles are transformed into productive hunting tools rather than
dangerous instruments for interpersonal attacks by naming them ḭkn—a term referring to any rod,
including those used in dances to manage the territory—instead of duidi, or “burner tube,” an object
operating on its own “hot” inclination. Similarly, regarding alcohol, Fisi explained to me that a
mambeador can benefit from the ambivalence of the term poɵdíe, which signifies both “sleep-water”
and “axe-water,” to direct its use for harmless sleep instead of the potentially dangerous axe-related
activities. One interlocutor provided a version of the story where, upon receiving the bottle of alcohol
from Egret of the River Mouth with his left hand, Egret of the Center tricked his rival by passing it
behind his back, placing it in his right hand and thus avoiding from consuming a drink whose deleterious
effects he intuited. This element of the story can be told to steer away from alcohol consumption. More
generally, the depiction of the metal axe and the other items stolen by Egret of the River Mouth as
originally engendered by the daughter of Egret of the Center places them as essentially consanguineal
kin of the Andoque. Once conceived as such, these items should not bring them harm but rather offer
them support.
Additionally, in the context of exchange with Whites, the narration of this myth is typically
accompanied by the offering of ritual substances, namely, tobacco paste, coca powder, and manicuera,
to the Mother of Merchandise or Lady Counting. In M5, these substances allow the word of Egret of the
Center to gain prominence over that of Egret of the River Mouth. We may here recall that M3 traces
these ritual substances back to the river source, while other myths associate coca and tobacco, or their

correct preparation, with other directions and altitudes (M1; M14; M15).153 Although this interpretation
was not suggested by my Andoque interlocutors, I propose that M3 was crafted and narrated to
constitute these cultivars, along with the maloca, as a counterweight to resist the influence and
aggression of the river mouth. This represents a specific manifestation for the role that Amerindian
myths, according to Lévi-Strauss, have played in absorbing the shocks of history and helping the people
who conceive them come to terms with history (Lévi-Strauss 1981, 607; see also Gow 2001, 10–11).
This manifestation was shaped and became effective through the Andoque’s spatial logic, serving not
solely to reconcile them with historical processes but also as a key symbolic instrument in power
dynamics involving central agents of these processes—namely, Whites. Within the spatial logic of the
egret river universe, these familiarizing substances enable the upstream retrieval of some of the objects
begotten in the center by Lady Counting, which were appropriated by the river mouth. More generally,
the blanket association of cultivars as well as the maloca with that direction may be part of a strategic
portrayal of the river source as an arsenal against the river mouth, aiding the center in overcoming it.
The vivid and horrific “Tale on the Boat of Goods” (T5) recounts a specific case of massive predation
by agents from the river mouth and is widely shared by Andoque members. According to these
interlocutors, the narrated event dates to a time before the late nineteenth-century rubber boom. During
that period, merchants from downriver sailed on the Caquetá, trading goods with the Andoque clans
inhabiting the river margin, especially the Cacambra Clan (kaó; Daptridus ater), in exchange for the
salted fish that the latter caught in excessive quantities. Once, when a trade boat approached their
settlement, the Cacambra rushed onboard to admire the goods brought by the merchants. They tried on
hats, admired their appearance in the mirrors, and sprayed themselves with perfume. In Miraña, the
language of the Indigenous people residing downstream from the Andoque, one merchant said to
another, “Today we go.” When they suddenly left port, the people became trapped, and the goods turned
malevolent: the hats caused headaches, and the perfumes caused the flu. Those looking at the mirrors
went mad. Downriver from the mouth of the Macaw River, at Swelling Falls (Po̰fisia), the boat sank,
and all the Cacambra, except for their captain who had refused to embark on the boat, disappeared with
the merchants. Despite the language they spoke, these merchants were not Miraña; they were kakńño̰e
(“People of Below”), or, more precisely, dolphins: an embodiment of the river masters. They were
