The Seductive Dolphin
The image of the dolphin encodes for the Andoque the danger of disadvantageous exchange with nonIndigenous agents, where the latter repay transfers of goods or persons from Indigenous people with no
compensation or with “deviating things” which lead to illnesses, accidents, conflicts, and death. As
explored in Chapter 9, the Andoque share with many other Indigenous and fishermen societies in the
Caquetá-Putumayo and Amazonia the association between dolphins and Whites, as well as the emphasis
on sexual and erotic seduction as a prime means through which both dolphins and Whites lure
individuals into their habitats, cities, and this way incorporate them into a nonhuman or non-Indigenous
existence (Arregui 2019; Echeverri and Pereira 2005, 133; Karadimas 2005, 360–68; Maués 2006;
Reichel 1989; Slater 1994). Andoque interlocutors emphasize that dolphins are human (son gente) with
a frequency and intensity that go beyond the typical belief that all animals were once human and
maintain a human-like existence in the realm of mythology. Although the Andoque’s taxonomy does not
classify the dolphin as an aquatic mammal, they recognize that, while it inhabits the aquatic sphere
where humans cannot survive, it differs from fish in its mode of breathing, sexual organs resembling
those of humans,154 and intelligence, by which fishermen sometimes find themselves outsmarted when
competing with dolphins for fish. Therefore, the dolphin mirrors human beings, similar to how Whites
mirror Indigenous people. It is a being homologous to humans in a different realm, of which it is often
considered the owner-person. As discussed in Chapter 9, dolphins appear as charming, beautiful men
and women dressed in white clothes and decorated with fancy accessories, like hats, watches, ties, and
more, resembling non-Indigenous foreigners and even city-dwellers. However, sexual contact with
them, mostly in dreams triggered by one’s gesture of approval or interest during one’s waking hours can
154

For similar views among the Yucuna-Matapí, see Reichel 1989, 114.

434

prove fatal. As Echeverri and Pereira (2005) cogently argued, the word through which the Andoque, like
other Peoples of the Center, designate dolphins—ama̰na̰—was borrowed from Tupi. This borrowing
likely took place in the nineteenth century, as these hinterland peoples approached the main rivers for
trade with Whites, increasingly discovering both the seductive forces of their goods and these new
aquatic beings.
M22, the origin story of dolphins, traces their dangerousness to a deceptive transaction. Within the
idiom of kinship, this deception is conceived as incest: the sexual union between Lady Peccary and her
brother Pretty, which indicates the former’s preference for her family of origin over a sincere
incorporation into her husband’s projects, and her brother’s withholding of the person whom he has
allegedly given to Green Tapir. The aggressiveness displayed by these siblings, now transformed into
dolphins, and Lady Peccary’s sons, stems from this incestuous union. As Lévi-Strauss (1969) argued,
such a union symbolizes the incestuous person’s reluctance to establish a kinship alliance and suspend
enmity with others—in essence, to collectively build culture and society. The association between
Whites, their aggressiveness, and incest also appears in Tukanoan mythology. In this case, this
association is tied to their non-participation in the regional system of linguistic exogamy and ritual
exchange, which is aimed at maintaining a balance between agnatic descent and marital alliances, and is
deeply rooted in the settlement patterns along the river (S. Hugh-Jones 1988, 145). For the Andoque,
who do not participate in such a marital exchange system, the theme of incest can be understood within
the cosmo-spatial framework which distributes differential predatory agencies across the river course
and its corresponding elevations. Reciprocal and beneficial exchange with a person from downriver,
who, by virtue of their position, should possess a lesser predatory agency than ego, is more probable
than with a person from upstream, endowed with a greater such agency and capable of appropriating
things and persons through more aggressive means. Therefore, while the danger emanating from the
river source is overt predation, that of the river mouth is associated with deceptive exchanges.155

The theme of incest is subtly suggested in M5. In a version of the myth relayed to me by Raquel, Lady Counting becomes
pregnant after inhaling the smoke of tobacco paste prepared by her brother, who had previously cautioned her against
approaching it. While it is the vegetal salt added to tobacco paste after its preparation that is linked to semen (Chapter 6), the
warning against accessing her brother’s property and her subsequent disregard for it hint at an incestuous encounter, which
might have been more explicit in the story’s earlier versions. If my assumption holds true, and considering the association
between sexual relations and predation, it could be inferred that the introduction of non-Indigenous agents resulted from
internal, possibly domestic, conflicts, thereby aligning with other Amerindian myths regarding contact with Whites (Mason
1990 in Overing 1996, 59). Goods that are (nowadays) manufactured externally could be seen as inherently risky because
they were initially engendered too internally during mythic times.

155

435

The River Turtle-Bamboo Dance confronts the dangers from the river mouth, including overt violence,
epidemics, and harmful goods, by calming down the anger (mntúi) of entities from that direction, which
is perceived as animating these dangers, through ritual offerings. Here, both the imported goods and the
offered substances possess the gift dimension of serving as extensions of their producers, embodying
their intentions. The fact that these intentions revolve around predation or resisting it illustrates the
encompassment of gift-like transactions by predatory dynamics. To reduce the anger animating imported
goods, many of the songs of this dance evoke weapons, with the expectation that providing ritual
substances to the singer-dancers will familiarize these entities. Since this anger and aggressiveness are
linked with the non-reciprocity of incest, the Bamboo Dance is perceived as a dance of exogamous
exchange (Pineda Camacho 1979, 48), which puts a stronger emphasis on reciprocity between host and
guest than other ceremonies—reciprocity which, in the case of the equivalent dance among the Bora,
even concerns the species of game animals that the host of the first dance must bring as a guest to the
second dance (Lucas 2019, 330–31). Although Andoque members agree on the importance of this
dance, they report that the last time it was held was in 2002, as part of the efforts to shield the group
from violence committed by and against the armed dissident groups that controlled the region during
that time.
As we have seen in the previous chapter, the other River Turtle Dance—namely, Carrier Dance—
overcomes the dangers stemming from the river mouth by adhering to agnatic identity. This alternative
strategy, which, in line with the general rise to prominence of the red ritual specialization, presently
gains further ground, also underlies the general perception of dolphin assaults as resulting from
promiscuous behavior or exaggerate sexual desire. As explored in Chapter 9, such behavior and
inclinations indicate one’s dispositions to consubstantiality with affines, which the dolphin (and other
dangerous beings) would take as interest in sexual intercourse. By contrast, a person’s stronger focus on
their patriclan identity and traditions would protect them from drifting toward this world of human and
nonhuman, Indigenous and non-Indigenous affinity. Furthermore, within a patrilocal society such as the
Andoque’s, women, who anticipate leaving their origin clan upon marriage, are relatively marginal
members of the clan and, as such, are more likely to be attracted by such potential affines with whom
matrimony is undesired. For this reason, women are considered more vulnerable to become ill by the
rain accompanying the afternoon rainbow, which appears downstream. Some interlocutors associate this
rainbow with Lady Peccary, who, in their version of M22, illuminated the earth once her brother Pretty
set out to seduce women at the center, thus assisting his misdeeds. On the other hand, others describe
436

this rainbow as an embodiment of Green Tapir, who himself became a miscreant figure in this myth,
operating like his brother-in-law after pacifying his vengeful sons. Either way, Andoque members are
unanimous as to women’s higher vulnerability to illnesses transmitted through sexual seduction and
associated with this rainbow.
Similar to how death caused by misfortunes attributed to nonhuman entities is perceived as an
incorporation into their societies, we can consider the process of incorporation into the non-Indigenous
society as continuous with predation by the river mouth and its agents. “Becoming White” is referred to
in the Andoque language as duíhɵ tii, or “becoming burners.” While seduction by dolphins primarily
communicates the risk to the seduced individual, “becoming burners” communicates the risk that the
transformed person poses to their Indigenous (ex-)kin. This is illustrated in the following River TurtleBamboo song:
Where did your father go?
To the end of another land (kusíka ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí)
The peccaries (ḭń) have taken the otter.
Is it the land where we were formed (katini)?
In the forest where your father was born (yapɵ otidefɵ),
The peccaries took the otter (fɨɵ) down there.
Unaware that it was him,
And although it was his father, he wanted to burn him (yaya dú’ini).

Some interlocutors view this song as a criticism of the maloquero, who, much like the otter, has
allegedly been hijacked by the Whites (the peccaries, like Lady Peccary who swam to the river mouth
and her sons) and turned against his own kin and origin, symbolized by his father, wishing to exercise on
them a form of violence associated with Whites—i.e., burning. On a more quotidian register, various
interlocutors, both youth and elders, express concerns about Andoque individuals who have relocated to
the city or acquired non-Indigenous education. They worry that these individuals may take actions
detrimental to their relatives who continue to live in the ancestral territory, potentially favoring their new
non-Indigenous allies. Given this context, we can view the persistence of reciprocal exchange between
the Andoque living in the territory and their relatives in the cities as an attempt to uphold commensality,
consubstantiality, and consequently, consanguinity. Within this exchange, the inhabitants of the
ancestral territory send fish, game, and manioc products to their city-dwelling relatives, who, in turn,
reciprocate with bread, pastries, clothing, and other non-Indigenous items that their relatives may

437

require. In recent years, Andoque territory and city dwellers have also ventured into business
collaborations, where city dwellers sell products such as coca powder, and to a lesser extent, vegetal salt
and tobacco paste, all produced by their relatives in the reserves. This collaborative effort not only helps
those in the reserves earn income but also allows those in the cities to collect a sales commission,
maintaining their connection to the nourishing resources of the ancestral territory.
This connection is important because, as we have seen in previous chapters, one is regarded as truly
human when living within their ancestral territory, nourishing themselves with its plants and animals,
and being part of a group that communicates with the nonhuman inhabitants of the territory for the
safety and well-being of its members. On several occasions, doubts about the human status of
Indigenous individuals who have relocated from the reserves and lost contact with their relatives living
there have been raised, primarily by elders. Just as Whites are associated with predatory and immoral
beings that are not considered as truly human, the process of becoming White may result in such a loss
of one’s full human status. In this context, it is critical to note that, from the Andoque’s point of view, as
observed by Kelly (2011) among the Yanomami, becoming White and being Indigenous are not
mutually exclusive options. While I would not assert the existence of a “duiɵ́hɵ transformational axis”
among the Andoque, as Kelly observed among the Yanomami, where individuals assume the role of a
non-Indigenous person when interacting with people located upstream and that of an Indigenous person
when interacting with those residing downstream, statements made by Andoque members reflect the
notion that, to some extent, they have all become White. This holds implications for power dynamics
with nonhuman entities.
The Andoque occasionally describe themselves as “civilized” (civilizados), positioning themselves on a
spectrum that spans between the categories of Indians (índios) and Whites (blancos). Initial impressions
garnered from statements by interlocutors suggest that one’s place along this spectrum is determined by
their degree of engagement with and dependence on non-Indigenous commodities and cultivars.
Consequently, uncontacted Indigenous groups said to inhabit their vicinity and Indigenous communities
dwelling along the Apaporis and Vaupés Rivers, who are reported not to possess items such as shoes and
clothing, are frequently cited as exemplars of true “Indians,” and people may say “I am very Indian”
when explaining their dislike of some non-Indigenous foodstuffs. Conversely, urban residents represent
the White category, with the city often referred to as “the Whites’ Land” in the native language (duiɵ́hɵ
ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí). Hence, some interlocutors do not classify settlers, who share relatively similar economic

438

circumstances with the Andoque, as White but view them as constituting a distinct category within this
spectrum. However, less conspicuous factors that contribute to determining one’s “Whiteness” or
“Indianness” encompass cognitive and spiritual dimensions, such as possessing skills and aptitudes
associated with formal education, including literacy and numeracy, on one hand, and the ability to
engage with one’s clan heritage or mythology on the other. Elders who uphold these cultural principles
are praised as índios. The notion of being “civilized” refers to incorporating elements from both ends of
this spectrum.156
As demonstrated in the descriptions of the consequences of consuming non-Indigenous foodstuffs in
Chapter 9, the economic and cognitive-spiritual parameters are interconnected, as this consumption
makes one unamenable to sorcery and healing procedures and hinders the communication with spirits
required to perform these practices. As discussed in that section, the strong flavors of some of these
foodstuffs impede the consubstantiality with spirits necessary for acting as either the agent or the patient
of these procedures. On the other hand, consuming such foodstuffs and other non-Indigenous items
makes consubstantiality with certain entities more likely, as the following example shows. During one of
my stays at Fisi’s maloca, members of the family spotted jaguar footprints on the long path connecting
the house to a harbor on the Caquetá River. Over the following week, they expressed their concerns
about going there, especially alone, for fear of a jaguar attack. When I mentioned that I was planning to
go there to make a phone call and enjoy the better reception by the Caquetá, one of Fisi’s sons cautioned
me about the jaguar. However, Fisi reassured me, stating that I had nothing to fear because jaguars
dislike the smells of soap and perfume, which are characteristic of non-Indigenous people, including
myself. He added that these scents, on the other hand, attract dolphins. Based on this anecdote, we can
surmise that dolphins are drawn to the Andoque and assault them not only because they wish to
incorporate them into their society but also because they already discern something “White,” and as
such, dolphin-like, in the Andoque, a predilection for non-Indigenous commodities and comfort. After
all, the dolphin often seduces people near the main rivers, to which the Andoque have ventured due to
their desire for trade with Whites. Therefore, “becoming white” is associated with a certain vulnerability
to nonhuman attacks, and a reduced capacity to master relations with them.
As this dissertation aims to unravel the construction and operation of power dynamics at the crossroads
of human-nonhuman relations and Indigenous-non-Indigenous interactions, it is imperative to delve

156

For a similar perception of White/Indigenous duality, see Vilaça 2007.

439

deeper into the precise nature of the association between dolphins and non-Indigenous actors. Much of
the anthropological literature surrounding this Amazonian association, including the previously cited
works, adheres to a representative framework, where dolphins are viewed as symbolic representations of
Whites, and the potential risks associated with engaging with dolphins are considered as metaphors
illustrating the perils posed by non-Indigenous agents or the process of assimilation into their society
(e.g., de Magalhães Lima 2014; Reichel 1989; Slater 1994). By contrast, my perspective on this matter
is inspired by Viveiros de Castro’s (2004) critique of the division between the literal and metaphorical
and anthropologists’ corresponding tendency to go beyond their interlocutors’ literal messages on the
nonhuman world, discussing them as encoded messages restricted to the social domain concerning interhuman relations. Metaphor involves the presumption of a discontinuity between target and source, and at
a broader semiotic level, it implies a hierarchy between sign and referent, language and world. In
anthropology, it often manifests in the method of “cultural translation,” which compares the symbolic
interpretations that a given object, postulated by the anthropologist, receives across societies. On the
other hand, the Deleuzian framework employed by Viveiros de Castro emphasizes the notion of
immanence, favoring semiotic processes that assume less or no hierarchy between language and reality
and the existence of continuities between domains of signification, such as metonymy, indexicality, and
literality (idem 2014, 102–6). In anthropology, Viveiros de Castro calls for the application of this
framework through a “perspectival translation,” examining the transductive function that the same sign
can assume in different ontologies (2004, 20).
My data reveals that, in the Andoque case, the connection between the dolphin and Whites is not the
vertical one of metaphor, but the horizontal one of continuity between the domain of human-nonhuman
interactions and that of inter-human relations. As we saw in Chapter 9, the dolphin is not the sole
nonhuman entity preying on humans through confusion and seduction. Other beings, such as the
earthworm, deer, tapir, and fi’du beings, which do not exhibit any apparent connection to Whites, share
similar modes of action. Likewise, the consequences of consubstantiality with dolphins are not unique
but rather continuous with the Andoque’s discourse on illnesses as predation and familiarization by
nonhumans, which the Andoque perceive as real dangers and as continuous with unfavorable
interactions with human beings. Therefore, instead of being a simple metaphor from the nonhuman
realm for an external object—i.e., assimilation into the non-Indigenous society—interaction with
dolphins serve as transducers, converting the ontology of inter-human relations into that of humannonhuman relations, and vice versa. Consequently, we should consider becoming White and
440

incorporation into the non-Indigenous society and economy as one pathway through which individuals
risk falling prey to nonhumans and losing the human body that distinguishes them from the world of
nonhuman potential affines. This is indeed the message conveyed by T5 on the boat of goods:
assimilation into the non-Indigenous economy and enchantment by their commodities would result in
familiarizing predation by nonhumans.
The notion of continuity between interactions with non-Indigenous agents and the relations with
nonhuman entities also appears to underlie a common critique directed towards maloqueros. This
critique centers around the funding of their malocas or specific ceremonial dances, either by the
Colombian government or through projects involving state or other non-Indigenous agencies. As
explored in previous chapters, this critique may imply that the maloquero in question lacks the necessary
knowledge to manage a maloca or conduct dances, or that they cannot secure the required manpower for
maloca construction and operation without monetary incentives. However, such external funding not
only reflects inadequate ritual or leadership skills but may also lead to adverse consequences. Upon
witnessing the proliferation of illnesses and violent incidents following a certain dance, several
interlocutors attributed these misfortunes to the fact that the initiative and resources for organizing the
dance came from outside the territory. Allegedly, they were linked to the project in which that
maloquero and their family members participated, rather than arising from their own commitment to
tradition. While the dance organizers consistently claimed the opposite, it seems that the underlying
critique suggests that deviation by non-kin others in the form of the resources they grant the maloquero
and his group members can leave them vulnerable to predation by nonhuman potential affines,
manifested in such misfortunes.
Despite the existence of various strategies of diverse means to manage and control exchange with
Whites to counteract predation by agents associated with the river mouth, it would be erroneous to infer
that the Andoque are satisfied with this exchange. Andoque members frequently point to numerous
accidents, violent conflicts, and internal disorder as indicators that this exchange is not effectively
managed. As mentioned earlier, there has been a decline in the practice of the River Turtle-Bamboo
Dance in recent decades, and in general, dances—including the River Turtle-Carrier Band and the
caguana distribution rituals preceding the major dances—are held less frequently than many believe they
should be. According to Fisi, the strategic narration of M5 and the spiritual dialogue and ritual offerings
to Lady Counting are no longer performed today as they were in Yiñékɒ’s days, because exchange with
Whites ceased being collective and managed by the captains or cacique. Similar to the other myths,
441

narrating it in inappropriate settings or without adequate offerings amounts to a careless invocation of
powerful nonhuman entities who will consequently seek out the narrator and their kins. However, Fisi’s
statement cannot be separated from his general idealization of captaincy during his father’s period and
his lamentation of contemporary political fragmentation among the Andoque. Other elders and clan
captains, who know this story as well and often hint to it, did not share similar statements with me. The
widespread perception of this myth as a framework to understanding exchanges with Whites suggests
that Andoque individuals draw, or may draw, on its elements to navigate such exchanges on smaller
scales. On various occasions, my interlocutors used the precedent of exchange of ritual substances set in
the story to legitimize today’s consumption of alcohol and cigarettes by the Andoque, on the one hand,
and the sale of coca powder and tobacco paste to Whites, on the other. It may thus also be the case that
the advantage that the elements from the river source give to the figures from the center over the river
mouth in this myth empowers them in their personal dealings with non-Indigenous merchants, settlers,
and entrepreneurs.
Nonetheless, in line with Fisi’s argument concerning the contextual boundaries for the effective
narration of M5, I propose that another transformation from Yiñékɒ’s period to today, which may limit
the effectiveness of M5, is the increased monetization of the Andoque’s trade with Whites. While many
interlocutors emphasize Yiñékɒ’s pivotal role in negotiating the exchange of rubber for manufactured
goods with the rubber bosses Miguel and later Alberto Zumaeta, a closer examination of accounts
provided by Andoque elders reveals that the exchange operated on an individual basis. Yiñékɒ’s role
was primarily to supervise the distribution of goods, which occurred mainly in his maloca, and to ensure
through spiritual and ritual means that the received goods benefit his personnel. Male Andoque members
had personal accounts with the Zumaeta bosses, with as much as 2/3 of the value of rubber they
collected during a fábrico covering the goods—particularly food and clothes—advanced to them during
the same fábrico (Guzmán Gonzalez 1971, 106–07). Money primarily served as a unit of account,
translating the value of imported goods into that of exported rubber (C-M-C), with the bosses charging
their workers higher prices for the goods they imported and purchasing rubber from them for
significantly lower prices than the ones they would get in the city. Upon settling their debts, the workers
could decide if they preferred to receive the remaining difference—if there was any—in cash or kind.
The payment was given to adult male workers on an individual basis, even though the work often
involved the collaboration of their family members, such as spouses and relatively grown children.
While a substantial portion of the debt represented goods advanced for the benefit of the entire family,
442

male workers often chose to spend their cash income within a few days on drinking in Puerto Santander
(ibid, 106). This way, as Guzmán observed, money functioned “as a hidden wheel within the social
organization” (ibid, ibid; my translation). The monetization of Indigenous economic activities in the
Araracuara sector progressed slowly until as late as the mid-1990s, when it was explored by Griffiths,
who documented how the Zumaeta family, the leading fish merchants whose payments represented a
major income source in the region, kept advancing credit in kind to their fishermen (1998, 225–26) (they
still do so today, but mostly in relation to fishing equipment).
Andoque members frequently compare money to vegetal salt, because, as the currency and medium of
communication in the Whites’ world, it mirrors the role that vegetal salt—which is paradigmatic of other
ritual substances—plays in their ancestral territory among humans and nonhumans. (Some note that
while salt once held this role exclusively, it is no longer considered an acceptable form of payment in
most transactions among people today—money has taken its place). However, this analogy does not
seem to be rooted in mythology, and, as far as I know, money does not appear at all in Andoque myths.
The term for money in Andoque is ḭ́ ̰ɒ́ nnkóba, which literally means “the round, disc-shaped thing of a
necklace.” Andoque elders recount that their mothers and grandmothers used to carry necklaces with
money coins that they would pierce and use as charms and pendants. “When the Whites started bringing
bills here, the old ladies got rid of their coins,” Fisi told me. “I picked up the coins that my mother
threw, fixed them, and bought myself candy in the village. When they first got the coins, they didn’t
know what money served for. And we still don’t know,” he chuckled. “If we knew, you wouldn’t see us
drinking in the village like that.” By that comment, Fisi referred to the frequent spending habits of
Andoque men of all ages, and to a lesser extent, women, who often use their earnings from the sale of
game, local products, or work for NGOs, state agencies, or settlers to engage in binge drinking sessions
with their family and friends. I will not explore this phenomenon further here,157 except to note that
while such practices may reflect the Andoque’s tendency to share surplus wealth with kin, reinforcing
social bonds, Andoque members, including the drinkers themselves when sober, criticize the behavior.

157
This phenomenon, documented among other Indigenous peoples in Amazonia and elsewhere (Langdon 2005), can be
attributed to a variety of factors into which I cannot delve exhaustively here. Besides the tendency to share surplus wealth,
these reasons encompass the irregularity of cash income and the difficulty of saving money in the absence of a regional
banking system. In the Araracuara sector, the proximity of the settler village and integration into its economy on one hand,
coupled with the historical trauma of the rubber genocide on the other, may also play key roles in shaping patterns of alcohol
consumption.

443

They recognize its link to domestic and general violence, as well as a waning commitment to ceremonial
life. Notably, “to be drunk” is expressed with the verb yi, which also means to die or become ill.
Examining this matter within the framework of myth and ritual as explained above, it becomes apparent
that money exists outside the system where the captain and elders transform “deviating things” into
“working tools.” The absence of money in M5, where it is not presented as another object created by
Lady Counting and appropriated by Egret of the River Mouth, might explain why Andoque members
find it challenging to manage money, as they themselves often state. We can conceptualize money as the
economic equivalent of the fi’du entities, who are more dangerous than other nonhuman entities
precisely because they resist symbolization. Just as coins limit the agency of money by lending it
visibility (Graeber 2001, 91–115), incorporating it into mythology could potentially tame it, allowing for
strategies of symbolic manipulation akin to those used with work tools or alcoholic drinks. This might
lead to people having a better capacity for handling money in ways they find satisfactory. In essence,
while Egret of the Center’s provision of three ritual substances to his rival in M5, compared to the
latter’s provision of only two, granted him a surplus and advantage of agency, the absence of money
from this myth reflects a surplus of “the Real,” in Lacan’s terms, which, in actual economic transactions,
is often readily converted into alcohol.158 Reflecting on the analogy drawn by Andoque members
between money and vegetal salt, we note that in contrast with the latter substance—whose agency is
tamed in M13 by the hero who recognizes a plant where other figures perceive a person, and whose
preparation includes elaborate etiquette aimed at transforming it into a semen-like element allowing its
producer to familiarize human and nonhuman beings—money remains a perilous agent from the affinal
outside.159
In summary, in this chapter I have examined the Andoque’s perceptions of non-Indigenous agents as
predatory and inimical, as well as their strategic, though not always enacted, responses to mitigate
associated dangers and to foster more reciprocal, marital-like exchange. In short, to assume an upriver

position towards them, rather than a downriver one. I have also demonstrated how engaging with nonIndigenous societies and their goods could undermine the Andoque’s status in power dynamics with

with Whites that derive from what the Indigenous party surrenders in this trade—specifically, persons or
