445

446

Chapter 13. Trading the Persons of the Land
Similar to other People of the Center (Cure 2020, 176; Lucas 2019, 32), the Andoque view their recent
history as a sequence of periods, or tiempos, each named after the main resource that they extracted and
traded with Whites during that time. The periods, in chronological order, are: the era of slavery (ending
in the nineteenth century, possibly starting as early as the seventeenth [Pineda Camacho and Llanos
1982; Pineda Camacho 1985]); rubber extraction (la cauchería), including labor for Casa Arana from the
early twentieth century to the 1930s (also referred to as el tiempo de Perú/de los Peruanos) and
subsequently with the independent Zumaetas until the 1970s; trading ocelot and other animal pelts in the
1970s (la tigrillada), mainly by one family; cocaine production in the 1980s (sometimes called el tiempo
de la mafia); and gold mining in the 2000s (la minería). Additionally, several economic activities have
not been limited to specific periods and continue today or have not been predominant enough to
delineate their own tiempos—these include commercial fishing that began in the 1970s, environmental
and cultural preservation projects starting in the 1990s, and coca powder sales from the mid-2010s
onward.
How does the Andoque’s participation in these economic activities affect their relations with the
nonhuman entities they involve? As Brightman argued in relation to plants, the trade in nonhuman
entities in Amazonia should be examined against the backdrop of local perceptions of such entities as
persons (2008, 153–54). In the Andoque case, for instance, economic engagement with Whites and their
intermediaries began precisely with the active trade of human persons, sold to merchants from
downriver as slaves by captains who were either their captors, their former protectors, or even nonagnatic kin. My analysis in this chapter is guided by Gow’s insight that for Indigenous Amazonians
history is kinship—the time in which kinship ties are formed and dissolved and what gives them
meaning (Gow 1991, 3). Therefore, in line with this dissertation’s interest in the Andoque’s power
relations with both human and nonhuman beings, I focus in this chapter on the ways in which kinship
processes of familiarization and affinization with nonhuman persons have unfolded in the different
extractive periods and were affected by the different economic activities. Considering the example of the
slave trade, the rise of this activity and the concurrent decline of anthropophagic rituals meant that
yielding orphans and captives to enslavement also implied the loss of support of powerful nonhuman
entities, whose wisdom and capacities were accessed through the cannibalistic consumption of such
individuals. This may be the first instance in the Andoque’s history where exchange with Whites came
at the expense of exchange with, and familiarization of, nonhuman entities.
447

Ethnographers of animist Indigenous peoples in Asia have found a decline in animist dispositions in
certain economic conditions, like altered access to means of production among Vietnam’s Katuic (N.
Århem 2014), or departure from immediacy in the production-consumption nexus among India’s
Nayaka (Naveh and Bird-David 2014). As we will see, the accounts collected among the Andoque
reveal not a reduction in animist sentiments but an increased sense of threat from the animated
nonhuman entities sharing their territory, with whom their ability to negotiate is diminishing. In
Amazonia, anthropologists have offered only limited analyses of how Indigenous people perceive their
own involvement in extractive activities and the methods for safely engaging in them, as opposed to
Indigenous views on unrestrained extractive practices by outsiders (e.g., Tilkin Gallois 1987; 1990).
Researchers’ neglect of Indigenous perceptions of how certain economic activities affect their
relationships with the nonhuman entities involved in these activities is starkly evident in the case of the
commodification of medicinal and psychotropic plants, such as ayahuasca. These plants are typically
regarded as animated or under the ownership of powerful spirits, engaging in dialogue with whom is
deemed essential for achieving various objectives. Nevertheless, ethnographers have largely overlooked
how such economic activities affect these crucial dialogues (e.g., Homan 2017; Meneses 2020;
Slaghenauffi 2020).
In this chapter, I delve into several extractive activities engaged in by the Andoque, not necessarily
following the chronological order of their occurrence. My discussion centers on how these activities
have influenced the Andoque’s dynamics of power with the nonhuman entities within their territory.
Firstly, I explore activities that have provoked retaliatory predation by the owner-persons of the
resources extracted, placing this predation within a triangular framework of predatory actions involving
the Andoque, non-Indigenous peoples, and nonhuman entities. Secondly, I address activities that have
threatened people’s mastery over the traded entities, often with wider consequences for managing power
relationships with other nonhuman beings and both Indigenous and non-Indigenous people. Focusing on
coca powder commerce, I deploy the etic distinction between gifts and commodities, as well as the emic
differences between pets and orphans regarding their degree of agency and alienability, to elucidate the
Andoque’s ambivalent position in this complex web of power relations.

448

The Predatory Triangle of Extractivism
I will commence my discussion with the extractive activity associated with the most significant and
devastating catastrophe to have ever impacted the Andoque people—namely, rubber tapping, certain
dimensions of which I discussed in Chapter 4. Prior to the emergence of the rubber economy in the
Caquetá-Putumayo region, the Andoque utilized the elastic latex from various plants to cover the sticks
used to beat the manguaré drums or attach tree barks or feathers to their bodies as ornaments (Pineda
Camacho 1982, 48). Nevertheless, the extensive exploitation of rubber trees (Hevea guianensis and
Hevea benthamiana) under the directives of the Casa Arana posed significant risks. In her thesis on
Andoque gold mining, Audren cites Levy, who advocated for the legalization of mining and the
inclusion of ritual activities during excavations (see below). Levy referred to the rubber genocide,
stating “It wasn’t rubber tapping [la cauchería] that ate the Andoque, but the territory” (2017, 107). In
conversations about the Casa Arana era, other interlocutors echoed similar sentiments, suggesting that
the excessive exploitation of rubber trees by the Andoque triggered a retaliatory response from the
owner-persons of the territory, resulting in the Casa Arana’s brutal violence. Indeed, during that period,
rubber was collected by making numerous deep incisions into the tree trunk with a machete (Robuchon
2010, 118), leading to the tree’s deterioration after multiple harvests and the subsequent depletion of its
latex. In my conversation with Fisi and his son Nestor about that time (C1 in the Appendix 2), they
attributed the violent behavior of the company agents both to their late arrival in the Andoque territory,
allegedly after suffering losses inflicted by other Indigenous groups who wrongfully blamed the
Andoque, and to the captains’ lack of familiarity with M5 on the origin of trade. On another occasion,
they explained to me that, by contrast, Yiñékɒ possessed the knowledge to manage interactions with the
Whites. He enforced the Andoque’s ritual calendar on Miguel Zumaeta, ensuring that his men could
cultivate gardens and partake in dances appropriately. More importantly, Yiñékɒ symbolically
manipulated the wild trees from which latex was to be extracted because he was familiar with (and it is
possible that he even elaborated) the final episode of M5 (for the full myth, see Appendix 1):
Trader Egret of the River Mouth returned to his home and then came back to the center, bringing a harpy eagle with
him. He pulled out rubber (tekámn) from the eagle’s nostrils and stretched it. “With this you need to pay (ɵpáhai)
me,” he said. Egret of the Center thought about how he could obtain that material, when his younger son said: “I saw
something similar in the manioc garden, which also stretches like that.” He took them to the garden, broke a manioc
stick and showed them the sap. “This is rubber,” Egret of the Center named this material. “This is how we are going to

449

work from now on,” said Trader Egret of the River Mouth, “this is how you are going to pay (ɵpáhai) me”. This is
how the exchange with the Whites started.

Nestor and Fisi explained that one significant measure undertaken by Yiñékɒ to safeguard the Andoque
during the post-genocide rubber-tapping period, involved the transformation of wild rubber trees (teka)
into manioc plants (pánn) during ritual and mambeadero sessions. This transformation was based on the
physical resemblance between the latex of rubber trees and the sap of manioc plants.160 The association
between rubber and manioc also appears in Andoque dream interpretation. Whereas dreaming of rubber
foretells the shedding of human blood—possibly due to the suffering and extermination caused by the
Casa Arana—an Andoque rubber gatherer’s dream of manioc plants served as a guide to locating rubber
trees for exploitation. Based on these dreams, gatherers could then lead their colleagues to these
valuable resources. The symbolic transformation of rubber into manioc can be seen as an act of
familiarization, where a wild resource from the forest’s affinal domain is converted into a domestic
plant, in relation to which humans play certain parental roles—caretakers, protectors, and guarantors of
reproduction—and hold the important position of legitimate consumers. Similar to a human gardener
acting as the captain of his cultivars and being able to dispose of them as “orphans,” naming rubber trees
after the manioc plant made it safer, in Andoque eyes, to exploit and exchange their latex, because it
eliminated any potential claims to ownership and objections from the owner-persons of the territory.
Depending on demand, the Zumaeta bosses sought to produce latex not only from Hevea trees but also
from balata (Castilla ulei) and juansoco (Couma macrocarpa) trees. Interestingly, while the Andoque’s
spiritual management of rubber tapping made it safer than during the Casa Arana period, as it was now
considered their legitimate “property” rather than that of the forest’s owner-persons, the later period was
also marked by greater ecological sustainability. This sustainability was achieved through the use of
scrapers that allowed for shallow grating of the tree bark, enabling the trunk to regenerate within several
days. Each worker maintained several “trails” connecting to “his” rubber trees, with a rotation system
where each day the worker would visit the trees along one trail, leaving to rest those along the other
trails. While my interlocutors did not explicitly suggest this interpretation, we can draw an analogy
between these work technique and routine—which were probably imposed by the rubber boss—and

As observed by S. Hugh-Jones (pers. comm., January 2024), rubber and manioc indeed share common qualities, being
euphorbias with edible fruit or tubers requiring the removal of poison prior to consumption.

160

450

women’s replanting of manioc sticks as propagules after uprooting tubers attached to them, allowing for
the plant’s regeneration and future yield. In a sense, the rubber trail became the worker’s “garden.”
The transactions in M5 and the exploitation of natural resources on which they rely serve as blueprint
for later trade and extractivism. After Fisi finished the narration of this myth as it is presented above, he
continued with this short monolog in Andoque:
They paid (ɵpáhai) the axe with rubber. Ever since, we were to negotiate (dohai) everything, even cassava [laughing].
It was said that we were to negotiate trees. We were to negotiate animals, [paying their owner-persons] ambíl for the
value (ɵpáhakn móna̰) of the animal. Everything we negotiate, we must present ambíl, coca, and manicuera as
offerings (ɵtasé), provide the value (ɵpáha) of the animal. This is the offering (ḭtaséa), this way you can seize it
[game]. This is how we can seize gold here, with offerings (taséa). It is not complicated for us, no one can do us any
harm for doing it. This is what we do not know [how to actually do it today?], this is why the owner [of gold] gives us
anger.

Trade involving nonhuman entities with outsiders thus depends on ɵpáha offerings to placate the
entities’ owner-persons. These offerings aim to replace the harvested entity with vegetal substances of
similar value, and ḭtasé offerings are made to convince these powerful guardians to agree to this
heterosubstitutive exchange, instead of taking revenge through homosubstitutive predation. This
acquiescence to exchange can be interpreted, to some extent, as the enlistment of the owner-persons as
“pets” or “companions” of the offeror. However, as Nestor and Fisi explained to me on another
occasion, not all resources are equal in how easily their owner-persons can be appeased. Rubber
gathering could be managed effectively, and the territory’s owner-persons could be appeased for its
extraction, because rubber is a vegetal material, and as such—even as a wild tree—was made for human
use. By contrast, the large-scale harvesting of fish and animals, which possess greater agency, for
commercial purposes could not be easily compensated in the eyes of their owner-persons. Such actions
would only be tolerated if they were committed in the context of a ceremonial dance.
In the previous chapter, I alluded to the first economic activity reported by my interlocutors, where
faunal beings were harvested for trade with Whites—namely, the massive fishing in the Caquetá River
by the Cacambra and Spix’s Guan Clans as narrated in T5. Whether this activity unfolded exactly as the
Andoque describe it is of limited importance to our current discussion, as it serves as a cautionary tale
among contemporary Andoque, underscoring the fatal consequences of the excessive exploitation of
nonhuman entities. The image of the dolphin as an attractive sexual predator and the seductive
techniques employed by the sailor-dolphins to lure the members of these two clans onto the ill-fated boat
451

convey the idea that extensive harvesting of nonhuman potential affines leads to the mass affinization of
human beings, integrating them into the nonhuman domain.
Besides this ancient and historically questionable fishing bonanza, the Andoque have been involved in
fishing and hunting for commercial purposes at varying intensities since the establishment of the
Araracuara Penal Colony in 1938, which purchased game from neighboring Indigenous communities. In
the 1960s, Joselito of the Eagle Clan and his sons, following the unfortunate passing of his son Agustín
during rubber tapping (as described in Chapter 4), became pioneers in dedicating themselves to fishing
for sale. They resorted to salting their catch due to the absence of a cold storage facility. In the 1970s,
such a facility was introduced by Lisardo Zumaeta, who thus inaugurated the commercial fishing, a
venture in which many Andoque have participated ever since. In the 1980s, Alberto Zumaeta followed
suit, launching his own fishing initiative in the Caquetá (which he later closed down), and other
merchants joined Lisardo, along with his son and grandson who inherited his business in subsequent
years. Today, the core group of fishermen who derive their livelihood from harvesting fish in Araracuara
rapids and selling them to merchants, who then export them to Bogotá, consists primarily of nonAndoque residents of Puerto Santander and Araracuara. However, many Andoque men also sell fish to
these merchants with a frequency varying according to seasonal availability and economic needs.
Additionally, many individuals occasionally sell fish and certain types of game, such as tapirs, peccaries,
and paca, to settlers, soldiers, and Indigenous residents of Araracuara and Puerto Santander. However,
these occasional sales do not constitute a full-time pursuit.
In light of the discussion in Chapter 9 regarding the vengeful responses by animals and their ownerpersons to overhunting and overfishing, it should come as no surprise that the practice of harvesting
animals for commercial purposes is viewed as perilous. Andoque members explain that such activities
would only be tolerated by the owner-persons of fish and game if conducted in moderation to provide
sustenance and meet the immediate needs of the hunter and their family. The members of various
families, except for Joselito’s descendants, attribute the untimely deaths of many of his sons and some of
his grandsons to their involvement in commercial fishing. Many members also express concerns about
potential retaliation from the site-person of Araracuara rapids and other owner-persons of fish due to
excessive fishing, but, in the same breath, they acknowledge the need to meet their families’ necessities.

452

In this respect, the predation by Whites discussed in the previous chapter, reflected, inter alia, in the
asymmetrical exchange that the Andoque maintain with them, leads to the Andoque’s excessive
predation on nonhuman beings in the form of hunting, fishing, and exploitation of other resources,
which leads, in turn, to the predation of Andoque members by nonhumans as revenge. These dynamics
are illustrated by the following figure:

Figure 26. The triangle of Indigenous, non-Indigenous, and nonhuman predation in the Andoque territory

Yet, people’s financial mismanagement and their allocation of earnings to reckless spending, such as
drinking binges, also play a role in this context. An elderly woman with whom I stayed expressed worry
of her son’s tendency to spend his earning from sales of game on alcohol, that leads him to hunt more in
the hope of providing for his children. Once, when he was out searching white-lipped peccaries several
days after selling a large amount of meat and drinking with the money he had earned, she told his son in
my presence, alluding to the risk of animal transformation in M18 (Appendix 1): “This is why one keeps
the money, not to kill [animals] every day; don’t you see that the father of peccaries confused them?”
While the surest way to avoid such retaliation is to refrain from engaging in overexploitation in the first
place, my interlocutors mentioned the organization of the Peach Palm Dance as a means to mitigate
potential reprisals. The narrators of T5 made note of the captain of the Cacambra Clan, who, sensing

453

danger, chose to climb a tree by the harbor instead of embarking with his men. From this vantage point,
he witnessed the boat leaving the port and eventually sinking. Subsequently, he retraced the course of
the Macaw River in the opposite direction, running upriver to warn other clans about the catastrophe he
had just witnessed. Upon hearing his report, the captain of the Pɵ’pɵdɨ Frog Clan organized the Peach
Palm Dance (No̰ḛpa Nni), whose songs, particularly those belonging to the part of mask performances
(Pɨdapódi, or “Tar Face”), the Pɵ’pɵdɨ captain had learned from peoples living downriver, in the Lower
Caquetá and the tributaries of the Apaporis River, such as the Letuama, Tanimuka, and Macuna.
Nonetheless, according to my interlocutors, these peoples, in turn, learned the myth commemorated in
this dance from the Andoque.
This myth, whose reenactment in the dance serves to mitigate affinization by the owner-persons of fish,
tells the story of Capybara (Sɒ̰’ḛ ́ ), who stole the peach palm fruit from his aquatic brothers-in-law during
a visit to his in-laws downriver (M29; Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 190–201). Capybara’s theft was
made possible with the help of his fish-wife, who concealed one pit in her vagina, bringing it back with
them to the center for planting. They managed to plant the pit only after spilling the dough of already
grated peach palm fruits into the river, tempting Capybara’s in-laws to swim upstream, where he killed
them by asphyxiation. In the dance—a Yucuna version of which I attended with several Andoque
companions—masked dancers impersonate various harmful aquatic and non-aquatic animals, including
dolphins. They mock-assault female dance attendants, directing oversized wooden phalluses toward
their vaginas—the place where the primordial fish-woman kept the coveted pit. The dancers only cease
their actions once the women compel them to consume large quantities of (non-alcoholic) peach palm
beer, a man-made derivative that allows humans to maintain control over the raw material from which it
is prepared. Following this “Tar Face” (P¦d́ apódi) part, other song-dances commemorate additional
aspects and episodes from the story, particularly the fish’s asphyxiation (see also Pineda Camacho
1976). Singing and providing peach palm beer to these beings ensure their departure from the maloca
without retaliating against the human participants. One interlocutor also explained that by disguising
themselves as fish and other nonhuman beings, the dance participants mislead the malevolent entities
downstream into believing that they resemble them and should not be attacked.
In one mambeadero session, Fisi and his son Nestor explained to me that the defensive effects of the
Peach Palm Dance held by the Pɵ’pɵdɨ Clan captain linger today, protecting the Andoque from
retaliation by the owner-persons of fish, but this defense is not everlasting and will eventually expire.

454

They said that Yiñékɒ tried to organize this dance twice to learn and teach the younger generation how
to hold it appropriately, and Fisi later organized two such dances in collaboration with a Yucuna man.
Despite this effort, they lamented that while some of today’s elders have learned the Andoque songs of
the dance, none of the members knows the song-dances of the Tar Face part, making it unlikely for a
complete future dance of this category to be organized.
While the harvest and trade of fauna present a more uncertain endeavor than those of flora, which can, in
principle, be managed to allay its owner-persons, Andoque members hold contrasting views regarding
the possibility of reconciling with the guardian spirits of the territory in the context of a relatively recent
extractive activity in which many of them were involved between 2000 and 2017, namely, gold mining.
This requires a short description of the Andoque’s involvement in this economic bonanza, which can be
divided into four periods: the first gold rush (2000–2003), the Andoque’s fluvial mining (2005–2009),
the second gold rush (2009–2013), and the Andoque’s legalization efforts (2013–2017). This economic
activity involved several women from the community who worked as raft cooks, and the majority of
men whose ages ranged from 20 to 50 years old when I arrived in 2018. The participation in gold
mining, much like rubber tapping for their parents and grandparents, was a significant and defining
experience for an entire generation in the Araracuara sector.
Initially, gold mining was conducted in rivers and operated from rafts. The first gold rush (2000–2003)
coincided with the increased influence that the Colombian Revolutionary Armed Forces-People’s Army
(FARC-EP) exerted on the area from its seat in the Demilitarized Zone of San Vicente del Caguán. The
rafts operating during that period were predominantly owned and managed by Brazilian miners who
employed relatively few Andoque men. They also paid taxes to the dissident group and to the
Indigenous communities in whose reserves they operated. This mining boom, like the one of 2009–
2013, attracted workers, merchants, and prostitutes to the region, and resulted in rising prices for food,
gasoline, and other goods (Romero Mendoza 2016, 62). When it began, this mining activity was
informal but not strictly illegal. It was eventually categorized as such as part of stricter regulation on
extractive activities, which led to the creation of the Mining Code of 2001 (Audren 2017, 41).
When the Colombian army regained control of the region in 2003, the rafts were abandoned, and many
Brazilian miners returned to their home country or were expelled. However, two years later, two
Brazilian miners returned to the Andoque territory. They became bosses for some Andoque members

455

and business partners for others, sharing their knowledge and experience. Several Andoque individuals
took hold of abandoned rafts that remained hidden in the region, equipped them, and ran their own
fluvial mining operations. During this second period, mining occurred without pressure from the FARCEP and with the consent of the military stationed in Araracuara. When one of the Brazilian miners
passed away in 2006, a member of the Zumaeta family, who resided in Bogotá, partnered with an
Andoque raft owner and invested in his raft. This marked yet another extractive activity carried out by
the Andoque and involving the Zumaeta family.
During that period, and to a somewhat lesser extent during the mining booms before and after it, gold
mining was regulated by the Andoque community, although my interlocutors had differing views on the
effectiveness of this regulation. In order to distribute work and benefits among as many members and
families as possible, shifts on the rafts had specific durations and rotations. However, some interlocutors
complained that they or their relatives received fewer shifts than others. The taxes collected by the
cabildo had various purposes, including supporting the community school, conducting internal
assemblies, assisting members during medical treatments in the city, and acquiring resources for the
cabildo, such as boats. At times, these funds were simply distributed among the families. Nonetheless,
my interlocutors mentioned that tax collection was not always rigorous, and the funds were occasionally
diverted from their intended purposes by cabildo members, who allegedly used them for drinking
parties. More generally, my interlocutors unanimously highlighted the issue of excessive alcohol
consumption and the resulting violence during that period. Many of those who worked on rafts or owned
them reported that, despite earning relatively high profits from this activity, they often spent most of
their earnings on alcohol. While some used their profits to purchase outboard motors, electric
appliances, build houses, or send their children to study in the city, alcohol remained a significant
temptation. To address this issue, the elders and cabildo attempted to impose sanctions on
troublemakers, primarily through work suspensions, but with limited success.
In 2009, the Andoque’s social and work regulations and tax collection were disrupted by another gold
rush. Large numbers of Brazilian and Colombian miners and raft owners flocked to the Middle Caquetá,
with many of them concentrating their efforts near Araracuara. This second boom came to an end
following a military operation in 2013, but some Andoque members continued mining both within and
outside their territory until shortly before my arrival. In these later years of fluvial gold mining, several
Andoque raft owners and workers faced arrests and incarceration. During my initial months of

456

fieldwork, a raft was positioned in front of one of the clan settlements, and several members of that clan
expressed their intention to resume work on it. However, they did not proceed with this plan during my
stay, and the raft eventually sank.
In 2013, several Andoque individuals embarked on an endeavor to legalize gold mining, but this time on
land. This initiative was led by Levy and his father Tañe of the Sun Clan, who held the position of
governor at that time. It consisted of three interrelated efforts: 1) obtaining the title of “Indigenous
Mining Zone” for up to 98% of the Indigenous Reserve Andoque de Aduche on the north bank of the
Caquetá; 2) securing two individual mining concessions; 3) and obtaining permanent mining permits for
Duxon, a Colombian company headed by Orlando Andoque of the Sun Clan and his cousin Carlos
Zumaeta (son of Alberto), with financial backing from a Canadian investor (Audren 2017, 22). Starting
in 2014, Duxon hired Andoque workers to carry out excavation work within a specified area in
Araracuara, under a temporary mining permit. The purpose of this endeavor was to confirm the presence
of gold deposits in the region and demonstrate the company’s profitability. As the family affiliations
mentioned earlier suggest, members of the Sun Clan, particularly Levy, played a central role and were
the primary advocates of this initiative. In contrast, most other Andoque members remained (and still
are) largely undecided (ibid, 47). Throughout a series of community assemblies, meetings with the
National Mining Agency, and consultations with non-governmental environmental organizations,
Andoque members vacillated between supporting the legalization initiative and opposing it. Eventually,
they suspended the titling request a few days before my arrival in April 2018. Even Levy, who spoke
enthusiastically to me about gold mining in May of that year, redirected his efforts toward carbon offsets
only a few months later—an economic activity precluding large-scale mining operations.
We can now return from this historical digression to our discussion on the risks that extractive activities
pose to the Andoque’s power relations with nonhumans. Despite widespread Andoque involvement in
gold mining, many individuals, including former miners, describe this activity as highly hazardous.
They point to numerous accidents and illnesses that befell those engaged in it, as well as the overall
violence and disorder during that period, viewing these hardships as the retribution from the ownerpersons of gold and the territory for the harm caused by this activity. Despite Fisi’s earlier quote that the
owner-persons can potentially be appeased for gold mining, on other occasions he explained that this
only applies to the extraction of small quantities and for limited durations to meet specific needs,
because mythology, particularly M5, does not contain any direct hints for the possibility of mining gold,

457

as it does for tapping rubber. As his son Nestor explained, the earth was intended for humans to cultivate
crops, bury the dead, and excavate stone axes and clay to craft various utensils. These activities were
only permitted after specific and intricate offerings were made. Gold, on the other hand, was not created
for human use. Some people mention that the elders initially disapproved of mining due to these
concerns. However, the disapproval waned due to fear of the foreign, unknown miners and the guerilla
which backed the activity at different moments, and once the elders too began to enjoy some of the
profits, either in the form of taxes or the wages earned by their children. Fisi and his sons likewise said
that when the fluvial mining began, community members initially envisioned working only during the
dry season when the river water level is low, rather than during the wet season. This seasonal
arrangement was seen as a way to appease the owner-persons of gold and the territory.161 However, the
influx of non-Indigenous miners and the enthusiasm of Indigenous workers led to year-round mining
operations.
However, for other Andoque members, gold mining is not entirely foreign to their mythology and
tradition, and they believe in the possibility of engaging in a spiritual dialog to safely extract it. For
example, Tañe and other members of the Sun Clan, the protagonists of the legalization and inland
mining project, do not view gold mining as a novelty that is opposed to “legitimate” extracted resources,
such as stone axes and clay. Instead, they consider these latter resources as precursors, whose excavation
in earlier periods predicted and justifies contemporary gold mining. Audren cites Levy as saying that the
Sun Clan holds the privilege to mine gold in Araracuara because it is the site where mythical Sun was
born (2017, 115). In one of our conversations, Levy claimed that gold mining is attested in mythology
through an episode from the story of the war between Sun and Moon. This episode, that I had never
encountered in the version published by Landaburu and Pineda (1984, 45–55) or in any of the five
versions of the myth narrated to me by Andoque elders, involves Sun’s purchasing the wife of his
brother Moon in exchange for gold, which, according to Levy, must have been previously dug.
Another approach is exemplified by Rodolfo, Yiñékɒ’s son and a reputed healer who was given a name
in the “white” Fausiya Dance. In general, Rodolfo perceives non-renewable natural resources as
analogous to the blood and vital elements constituting the bodies of their respective owner-persons, who
would thus punish those who extract them without obtaining their permission. He attributes the death of

161

A similar arrangement was reported among the Waiãpi, see Tilkin Gallois 1990, 53.

458

an eighteen-year-old Andoque miner in 2010 to such a punishment, stating that the owner-person of gold
fomented anger among two more experienced miners, causing them to miss the calls of their young
colleague whose leg got trapped in the raft’s powerful suction machine while diving, until he finally
died (cf. Fisi’s comment above, “This [the offering to the gold’s owner-person] is what we do not know,
this is why the owner [of gold] gives us anger”). However, during the elaboration of the legalization
project, Rodolfo volunteered to negotiate with the owner-person of gold to ensure the safety of miners
and their kin and, during Duxon’s excavations, he oversaw work at the mining site and would halt
operations upon sensing the disapproval of these nonhuman entities to prevent harm to the miners.
Rodolfo once shared with me, while we were picking coca during my early months of fieldwork, that
during the initial project discussions, he remained silent until he communicated with the owner-person
of gold. The spirit revealed its consent to mining, stating that they could dig the earth, remove “stems”
(tallos) of gold, and plant them in Bogotá, thus selling them to Whites in COP$20,000 a stem (roughly
€4.5). However, under no circumstances should the excavated gold remain in the Andoque territory.
When I sought clarification, Rodolfo explained that gold occupies a role for its owner-person similar to
the one manioc holds for humans. Just as manioc plants grow from a stem taken from another plant, so
can gold be removed from Andoque soil and planted in Bogotá, where it would be taken care of by
Whites. Rodolfo emphasized that the gold should not remain in their territory, as he explained, “because
what can an Indian do with gold? We’ve never had gold; we had the axe.” Leaving excavated gold in
their territory would result in punishment from the owner-person causing various illnesses. In contrast,
the presence of gold would not harm the non-Indigenous inhabitants of Bogotá. On another occasion
while we were picking coca, Rodolfo slyly asked me: “Would you like to know the name of the owner
of gold?” Naturally, I wanted to. “Dui,” he responded and translated it as “Burner” (quemador). Rodolfo
said that they had formed a close bond (nos hicimos amigos), and now Dui would only communicate
with him, not with any other human being. Rodolfo added that the Andoque are the only Indigenous
people in the Caquetá-Putumayo region who can safely extract gold or any other non-renewable
resource because they are the only ones to have mined stone axes in the past, trading these axes for
various goods.
The parallel drawn by Rodolfo between gold and manioc echoes his father’s transformation of wild
rubber latex into the tame manioc sap in order to render its extraction safer for his men. However, rubber
was used by the Andoque before and independently of trade with non-Indigenous people, while Dui’s

459

sine qua non for mining gold was to export it from the territory. How can we understand this condition,
as well as the idea that, while endangering the Andoque, gold does not represent any risk for Whites?
In the Andoque language, gold is referred to as dónsɒ̰n, meaning “yellow sand,” and dú’sɒ̰n, “burned
sand.” Based on the latter and more current term, Orlando named the company he founded with Carlos
Zumaeta “Duxon,” infusing it with an Anglo-Saxon flavor that conveys an international business
orientation. Gold carries associations with fire: firstly, through the name of its owner-person Dui—an
element which is also shared with Whites, duiɵ́hɵ (“Burners”); and secondly, in one theory linking its
origin to the ashes of trees burned during the flood of fiery water, which remained underground. Gold is
also linked to the sun. In one myth, Sun’s son is captured by si’deknkn ants and taken into a tree trunk.
Sun burns the trunk, and its ashes become gunpowder. Subsequently, Sun encounters Fi’du, who
possesses a gun. Sun confiscates Fi’du’s gun and loads it with gunpowder. When this weapon reaches
humans, it becomes duidi—the gun of the river source. The river source, we may recall, indicates the
direction of the Andean cordillera, where Bogotá is located, and is associated with the “burner” type of
Whites. A detail from another myth, this time M6, adds further insight into the relationship between
gold, the sun, and Whites. This detail was shared with me by Orlando, who had learned it, in turn, from
Rodolfo during discussions about negotiations with the owner-person of gold. According to Orlando, the
fruits of the “stone tree,” which Sun kept in his garden to deceive and kill his daughter’s suitors, turned
into gold powder upon hitting the ground. I recall the reader that, in this myth, the suitor who overcame
Sun and safely felled the stone tree was Egret of the River Mouth, also known as Axe Egret because he
used his metal axe. This detail suggests that Whites—in their capacity as traders—are the legitimate
owners of the stone tree and the gold it produced, having overcome the first owner, Sun. Thus, gold,
which is owned by Whites in mythology but now found underground in the Andoque’s territory, may
occupy a diametrically opposed position compared to metal axes, which were initially owned by the
Andoque in mythology until they were usurped by Whites, who possess them in contemporary times.
Therefore, this detail from M6 may justify exporting gold to the river source in exchanges with Whites
who “use their metal axes” and occupy the role of traders from the river mouth, just as narrating M5
legitimizes the importation of metal axes (and other goods) into the center, and their safe use there.
Therefore, while gold can provoke the anger and violence associated with heat and fire among the
Andoque, it would not harm the Whites, who can “cultivate” it much like the Andoque cultivate manioc.

460

Whether my hypothesis is correct or not, the broader discussion of the Andoque’s engagement in gold
mining highlights the diverse perspectives that can emerge regarding the risk of predation by nonhuman
entities due to specific extractive activities, and the capacity that different individuals hold, or consider
possible, to draw upon mythology and past experiences as strategies for mitigating these risks. In the
forthcoming chapter, we will delve into additional facets of the Andoque’s gold mining endeavors,
revealing the extent to which these negotiations with nonhuman entities intersect with their interactions
with non-Indigenous entities, primarily the state. However, prior to exploring these aspects, we will shift
our focus in the next section to other extractive activities in which the Andoque have faced challenges
that are not related to predation by resource owner-persons, but rather concern their ability to familiarize
and thus enjoy the assistance of these resources.
Commodification: Between Losing Pets and Trading Orphans
The growing global appreciation of Indigenous cultures in recent decades, the recognition of the
environmental benefits of their ancestral knowledge in an era of ecological destruction, and the interest
in the substances produced by such peoples perceived as “authentic,” have led to the export of items
from the Andoque territory that differ from those discussed in the previous section. These items are not
raw materials but products crafted and prepared by the Andoque. I am primarily referring to Indigenous
knowledge and coca powder, the trade or sharing of which with to non-Indigenous agents are perceived
by the Andoque as posing a risk to their own capacity to benefit from these items.
Evidently, as a researcher who has traveled great distances and made specific career choices to study an
Indigenous people, the Andoque’s perspective on sharing their knowledge with outsiders held personal
significance for me. Some of the challenges associated with sharing certain types of data with
researchers can be deduced from the discussions in previous chapters regarding the Andoque’s concerns
about losing control over specific spells by teaching them to others, exposing themselves to external
threats by disclosing their origins, or invoking powerful nonhuman owner-persons without appropriate
offerings. For instance, my interlocutors mentioned that certain medicinal plants were no longer as
effective for several elders. They attributed this decline to their involvement a few years ago in a project
led by an Italian educational foundation dedicated to preserving traditional medicinal knowledge, in
which they provided information about various such plants. However, the participants in such research
typically hold a different perspective. Several participants in the ethnobotanical project assured me on

461

different occasions that they had only shared information with the researchers regarding plants for which
knowledge had already been widely distributed among the Indigenous population, and whose
effectiveness was no longer dependent on secrecy.
Participating in research projects organized by governmental and non-governmental agencies, as well as
collaborating with individual researchers, sometimes includes compensation. This leads some
Indigenous onlookers to assume that their fellows indiscriminately “sell” their knowledge when they
take part in research. Researchers, for their part, are often perceived as exploiting and profiting from the
information provided by their informants. The accumulation of knowledge by research institutions and
other agencies raises concerns that it could eventually be used against the Indigenous population. This
concern underpinned Fisi’s statement during the “cultural workshop for environmental management,”
where he expressed worry that the State might force him to carry out a ceremonial dance in a particular
season, based on the published Andoque ecological calendar (Chapter 8). Several interlocutors have
criticized the prevalent practice of not crediting specific individuals for the versions of myths and other
knowledge they contribute to publications. This results in researchers being viewed as the primary
source of knowledge, leading interested students to seek them out rather than the Indigenous elders who
originally shared this knowledge. Since traditional training includes the reciprocal exchange of food and
ritual substances from the apprentice to the teacher, the informant who cannot compete with the
published researcher is left impoverished and neglected. In essence, the researcher is accused of
expropriating the informant’s knowledge and detaching it from the social relations in which it is
embedded—similar to the perception of ethnographic research among other Amazonian peoples (e.g.,
Gongora 2016; de Vienne and Allard 2005).
For the Andoque, this expropriation is encoded in the image of the Head-Choppers, or cortacabezas.
This figure, widespread in Leticia and the Colombian Amazon, is a variation on the Andean figure of the
pishtaco, along with other monsters whose modes of action and aggressiveness serve as embodied
representations and parodies of colonial and capitalist injustices experienced by Indigenous peoples
(Ansión 1989; Burman 2018; Cure 2010; Gow 2001, 258–72; Magazine 2018; Santos Granero 1998,
137–38). My interlocutors asserted that the Head-Choppers had never arrived at their ancestral territory,
but shared with me testimonies that they had heard directly or indirectly from individuals from upriver,
in the Monochoa Indigenous Reserve, or from other Amazonians they had encountered. The HeadChoppers operate in several modes. They typically ambush solitary fishermen under the cover of night,

462

casting an intense, disorienting light from their aircraft—often likened to small flying saucers—leaving
their victims bewildered and vulnerable. They proceed to decapitate their victim, eviscerate their
abdomen, and extract the liver and heart, which they then replace with stacks of money. Such attacks
can also happen in gardens during the daytime and sometimes follow research conducted by
anthropologists or other scientists documenting people’s fishing practices or mapping garden locations.
The Head-Choppers are said to be gringos, whose exact nationality is unclear. “They come from where
you do: Americans, Japanese, Israelis,” one man told me. Several of their laboratories have been found
and their operations stopped thanks to guerilla intervention—while the Colombian army was allegedly
complicit in giving them a free hand in the areas it controlled.
People’s accounts of the Head-Choppers were almost always tinged with a mixture of concern,
uncertainty, and humor. Unlike with other mythical or historical accounts they shared, it was clear that
my interlocutors were ambivalent about the existence or real threat of these figures. They seemed to be
gauging my reaction to their stories, sometimes teasingly asking, “You’re not one of them, are you?”
When queried about the motives behind the Head-Choppers’ actions, my interlocutors suggested that
these beings sought to harvest Indigenous knowledge from their victims; one added that it might be part
of a grander scheme to create intelligent robots. Cure (2010) interprets the Head-Chopper rumors in
Leticia as emblematic of the perils posed by non-Indigenous foreigners in general and the ills of global
capitalism. However, the motives ascribed to the Head-Choppers and the targeted references to
anthropologists and other scientists suggest that for the Andoque—and potentially for the wider Middle
Caquetá region as well—this figure symbolizes the theft of Indigenous knowledge by outsiders, akin to
the Bolivian kharisiri (Burman 2018). This notion was echoed in a rumor an interlocutor recounted
about an Andoque elder with a “gringo son.” This elder, valued by Colombian and foreign researchers
for his mythological knowledge, was invited to a conference in New York, where he was allegedly
seduced by an American academic into sleeping with her and impregnating her. As the rumor has it, the
academic’s aim was to perform experiments on her child to extract the elder’s knowledge directly from
the child’s brain. While this rumor does not directly involve Head-Choppers, it is driven by the same
logic—that knowledge is physically stored and can be usurped from Indigenous individuals by outsiders
with a voracious appetite for this information.
The idea that knowledge can be thus usurped is at odds with the English expression “sharing
knowledge,” as used above. Teaching things to outsiders is not considered as sharing knowledge that is

463

consequently held by both parties, but as a total transfer of that knowledge from the Indigenous party to
the non-Indigenous one. This perspective became clear to me during my stay at one of the malocas,
when I read aloud from an ethnographic book about a dance held years earlier at another Andoque
maloca, in which my hosts had shown interest. As I read a section where the anthropologist mentioned
being taught by the maloquera how to make the manicuera beverage for dancers (but not for ritual
offerings), my hosts reacted strongly. They recalled an incident several years after the reported dance
where the same maloquera made a diluted manicuera that led to rain during a dance in their own maloca.
They concluded that by imparting the knowledge on manicuera preparation to the researcher, the
maloquera handed over (entregar) that “word” (palabra) to her, and consequently, lost the power (poder)
to produce a potent version of the drink herself. They further clarified that that loss of power is because
the nonhuman owner-persons, who are expected to partake in the offerings, trust only those they
recognize as skilled makers, a recognition dependent on the maker’s unique scent. However, when such
knowledge is given away, the individual loses this distinctive scent, leading the owner-persons to reject
their offerings. Meanwhile, they asserted that as a non-Indigenous woman, the aforementioned
anthropologist is unlikely to construct her own maloca, host a dance, and serve manicuera to her guests.
Knowledge is essentially practical and thus useless when solely published in books and not enacted in
specific contexts. Hence, knowledge ceded to outsiders is effectively extracted and absent from
Andoque territory.
As Fisi explained regarding the risks of sharing information with external researchers, “One is left only
with the story, while the spirit goes away.” To escape this risk, members may choose to disclose only
the superficial aspects of mythology (por encima) to researchers they work with. An informant might
also protect themselves from a loss of power, or accusations of such, by the manner in which they
characterize the knowledge-sharing process. For instance, to safeguard against potential claims from
onlookers who observed our extended discussions, Fisi once said to me after completing the narration of
a myth:
“You cannot later say, ‘Fisi handed over this word to me,’ but rather, ‘I heard Fisi [pronouncing it].’ Because this
word is not mine, neither my father’s; who knows how long it has been with us? And you cannot say, ‘Fisi told it to
me,’ because I do not tell it to you, because I don’t build a maloca and sit down to tell you, but rather, you listen while
I am narrating [usted escucha mientras yo cuento].”

464

These perspectives depict participation in research as yet another form of extraction that depletes the
Andoque territory. Since knowledge is seen as arising from the ongoing communication with specific
owner-persons, removing it threatens people’s ability to effectively engage in this communication and
achieve the practical ends depending on it. As these practical ends often involve establishing and
maintaining beneficial asymmetrical relationships with various human and nonhuman entities—and
mitigating adverse relationships—the extraction of knowledge endangers their well-being, prosperity,
and reproduction.
Another product whose export from the Andoque territory in recent years affects people’s
communication and power relations with human and nonhuman beings is coca powder, a central
substance explored in Chapter 6, and to which I will refer throughout the rest of this chapter as “mambe”
to distinguish it from the coca plant. Unlike the economic activities discussed in the previous section,
which mostly took place before my arrival in the Andoque territory and were learned about through
retrospective accounts from my interlocutors, I was able to directly observe the production of mambe for
sale during my fieldwork. The varying perspectives held by Andoque members regarding this trade, the
disparities between their discourse on it and their actual practice, and the connections they draw between
it and other economic and ritual activities, position mambe sale as an exceptional case study for delving
into their perceptions of power dynamics within the realm of market involvement.
While occasional mambe sale to fishermen and miners in the Araracuara sector was reported as early as
the 1990s (Londoño Sulkin 2012, 121), Andoque members date the beginning of mambe shipments to
Bogotá (and sometimes other cities) to 2015. During my fieldwork, many Andoque men and several
women (usually their wives) used to send mambe to their relatives and other acquaintances living in the
cities upon the latter’s demand. These brokers pay the mambe producers between COP$80,000 and
140,000 per kilo (around €18–32), selling it informally through restricted distribution chains and
charging a commission of around COP$40,000 per kilo (approximately €9). The clients include
academics and workers of governmental and non-governmental agencies working in Amazonia or with
Indigenous groups, who have developed a liking for mambe consumption during their research or
environmental and state interventions in Indigenous territories. Additionally, students, particularly those
studying at the university campus in Leticia, are among the clients. In the absence of demand from their
city brokers, Andoque producers may sell lower-quality mambe, which requires less preparation time, to
merchants and residents of Puerto Santander and Araracuara at lower prices. The preparation of mambe

465

for sale may undergo instrumentalization that would be inconceivable when preparing it for any other
end. Producers may hire younger individuals to gather coca leaves for them, divide the preparation
process into distinct stages performed on separate days to enhance efficiency for larger quantities, store
powdered coca leaves in anticipation of future demand, or use a manual meat grinder for pulverizing the
leaves instead of the traditional pestle and mortar method.
Two months into my fieldwork, during a mambeadero session at Fisi’s maloca and a week after assisting
in the preparation of mambe for sale in San José, the Sun Clan settlement, I engaged in a conversation
with Fisi and his sons regarding the Andoque’s involvement in the gold rush. When they mentioned that
some members had been involved in selling coca leaves for cocaine production in the 1980s, I inquired
if this activity posed similar risks to its participants as gold mining did. Fisi elaborated, stating that
selling coca in any form, even as mambe powder, compromises the plant’s human owner. He explained,
“The person who prepares the coca, he has a certain intention in mind, a thought on how to use it, let’s say to organize
a dance. But who knows what the person consuming it in Bogotá will do. Even if he is Indigenous; what will he think
about? The [human] owner loses control over his coca, and the plant [from which the coca powder was made] gets
angry with him, dries up and dies. But the coca that you grow for your own use will become big and pretty.”

The idea that the thoughts and actions of the mambe consumers affect the relationship between the
producer and the coca plant points to mambe’s inalienability. We have already encountered this notion
of coca’s inalienability in Chapter 6’s discussion concerning how coca constitutes its producerconsumers as true human beings, on the one hand, and the belief that the stories narrated by the
producer-consumer when consuming the powder shape their future coca produce, on the other.
In the following months, other Andoque members also reported this risk of mambe commerce. While
Fisi mentioned damage to the specific plants used in mambe production for sale, a reputed healer
asserted that such commerce could potentially lead to a complete withdrawal of support from the spirit
in the seller’s actions, which is critical in his case, as he relies on it for healing procedures. People often
explained these risks by drawing comparisons with previous economic activities, into which I do not
delve here due to their marginality or legal sensitivity. For instance, the healer claimed that mambe
commerce poses greater risks to people’s relationship with the coca spirit compared to the sale of leaves
to cocaine producers in the 1980s. This heightened risk is attributed to the more intimate nature of the
relationship required for the former activity than the latter. By contrast, Nestor, Fisi’s son, corroborated

466

his father’s assertion that the commerce involving coca in any form is problematic. He recounted that
during the 1980s, the then-elders condemned the supply of leaves for cocaine production, likening it to
the previous activity where jaguars, anacondas and caimans had been hunted for their pelts and skins,
and claiming that involvement in such hunting could not be compensated through ritual actions vis-à-vis
the nonhuman owner-persons. He explained that, similar to these animals, the coca spirit is a powerful
owner-person invoked for healing, who would refuse helping people once the plant it oversees has been
used for malevolent purposes and “making people go crazy,” as cocaine does.162 In essence, extracting
and trading such entities would render their help, as pets or companions, significantly less certain.
Interestingly, although the elaboration of tobacco paste and vegetal salt requires much stricter adherence
to dietary rules and etiquette than mambe production, my interlocutors expressed far less concern about
the occasional trade in these substances. It appears that the Andoque’s greater daily reliance on coca
than tobacco for various purposes, including less specialized healing procedures, makes mambe
commerce a more problematic activity.
