While the condemnations of mambe commerce that I heard during my first months of fieldwork in
April-June 2018 primarily targeted people from other families and clans, as time progressed, I witnessed
some of those who had expressed such condemnations, or their close relatives, engage themselves in that
commerce. My male interlocutors, particularly those involved in this trade, seemed genuinely
ambivalent about the risks of this activity. For instance, Nestor, a staunch opponent of mambe
commerce during my initial stay at his father’s maloca, turned out to be an industrious producer of this
powder for sale when I returned there in October of that year. When I reminded him of his previous
stance while we were picking coca for sale, he responded, “It’s true, selling coca endangers us, and so
we need to manage it. You need to mambeate the first spoon from the first round of filtering while
thinking about the territory, so that that coca would help you think properly. Whatever comes out
afterwards [in the next rounds of filtering] are the leftovers (sobras), the husk (bagazo), and that is what
we sell.” Later that day, during the nocturnal mambeadero session, when he talked about the spirits’
potential retaliation against the Andoque due to their excessive fishing and past involvement in gold
mining, he juxtaposed these activities with mambe trade: “The coca that we send, we send it with good
intentions (buen pensamiento), so that people will use it for their studies, so that the paisanos (fellow
Indigenous) in Bogotá will hold dances and do cures.” This perspective on mambe commerce as not
inherently negative contradicts a statement he would make two months later during discussions in the
workshop aimed at formulating a “cultural plan for territorial management,” suggesting that this activity
conflicts with fundamental Andoque principles. During these discussions, some aspects of which were
explored in Chapter 8, participants frequently referenced the “law of origin,” which refers to the codes
of proper conduct between the territory’s human and nonhuman co-dwellers laid down for the Andoque
“since the beginning” (katakádɨñḛ́ nḭe ɵ́ḛ́kńḭ́ sofa). In response to the repeated calls by both young and
old participants to adhere to their law of origin, Nestor interrupted, stating, “But we don’t obey our law
of origin if we catch tons of simi [the Callophysus macropterus fish] and send mambe to Bogotá. Then
maybe it’s not our law of origin after all…”
Like Nestor, other interlocutors mentioned measures to mitigate the risks of mambe commerce. The
ideal solution appears to involve the creation of separate gardens or plots within a garden for plants
intended for commercial ends, on the one hand, and for ceremonial ends and self-use—for thinking,
healing, and sharing in mambeadero sessions—on the other. All my interlocutors asserted that coca
harvested from gardens previously used for commerce would be entirely ineffective for ceremonial
dances. However, on several occasions, when I joined different men in the preparation of mambe for
468

personal consumption from gardens and plots where we had previously harvested mambe for sale, I
reminded them of their earlier statements advocating for such separation. One elder, who occasionally
sells coca, chuckled at my question, “Anyone telling you he’s separating gardens for [personal]
mambeating and for selling is lying; it’s simply double work!”.163
Delio, an elder uninvolved in mambe commerce, expressed a similar flexibility, linking it to coca’s
inherent flexibility. He asserted that while mambe from plants intended for sale could under no
circumstances serve as offerings to spirits in dances and other ritual settings, it could still be used for
thinking and to perform relatively simple healing procedures. “Anyway,” he said, “one transforms
(volver) the coca into what one wants it to be. When one wants to earn money, one turns the coca into a
devil (diablo);164 when one wants to bewitch, one turns it into an eagle, a jaguar, a devil. And so, one can
also turn it into something good, to think and cure with it.” The intention with which coca is planted or
prepared is thus decisive in determining its potency for meditation and healing.
For Delio’s brother, Tañe, who often sells mambe, garden separation assumes a temporal rather than a
spatial nature. According to him, the first harvest of any garden must be reserved for personal
consumption or a dance, with only subsequent harvests used for commerce. “Coca that is suitable for
mambeating is coca that, during planting, you think of the territory, you think with the territory,” he
explained, echoing Nestor’s view of mambe for sale as the leftovers of mambe intended for personal and
territory-centered consumption. This implies that coca planted with thoughts of money or things from
other lands is not suitable for meditation. According to Iai, Delio and Tañe’s brother who also frequently
sells mambe, consuming coca that was intended for sale does not directly endanger the producerconsumer. However, his explanation is crucial for understanding the broader risks associated with this
activity:
“Nothing happens if you mambeate coca that you’ve planned on selling, but it hasn’t been made for thinking. For
example, if I want to think how to cure my son, the thought [on how to perform the cure properly] will not come to me
[while consuming such coca]. It’s like a cure, for example, a cure for blindness that I openly talk about [publicar]
would no longer work for me.”

163
For a similar inconsistency among the Nɨpóde regarding garden or plot separation into those used for personal or family
consumption and those used for sale or exchange, see Griffiths 1998, 245.
164
I am not sure whether Delio was referring here to the fi’du entities referred to as diablos in Spanish or to the Christian
devil, who is sometimes mentioned as the master of money—a belief likely influenced by Colombian settlers and largely
detached from local practice or discourse (see Taussig 1980).

469

The comparison that Iai draws between coca commerce and the indiscreet publication of healing
procedures brings us back to the interrelated notions of mastery and familiarization. In our discussion of
the Andoque’s politics of knowledge and the assistance received from nonhuman entities in Chapter 10,
I mentioned the belief that indiscreetly sharing knowledge before achieving sufficient mastery over its
owner-person—often referred to as “ratting”—causes that owner-person to relinquish its “pet” position
in relation to the person who shared the information. Similarly, coca intended for sale is coca that has
already been “ratted on,” and its spiritual powers are no longer accessible to the seller. We may recall
that, while it is an inalienable item for the person producing and consuming it, coca also remains
essentially “alien.” Albeit described in M2 as a consanguine—namely, a transformed father imparting
knowledge on its children—in M1, coca also appears as an affinal figure—a transformed earthworm
suitor governed by a female hero. Much like other faunal and floral elements in the Andoque’s
environment, one must familiarize coca in order to harness its beneficial potential—to draw on the
forces of the earthworm suitor and steal the plant from its female owner to finally recognize its
connection to one’s own paternal lineage. Only thus coca will “accompany,” or assist, the producerconsumer, and not the other way around. However, as Fausto and Costa argue, familiarization is “always
an unfinished business: one hardly ever completely extinguishes the alterity of the other” (2013, 159).
Coca thus remains essentially alien to the person growing and preparing it, from whom it is, nonetheless,
inalienable.
This unfinished familiarization explains why selling mambe to others is risky. The thoughts and actions
by urban mambe consumers may represent principles that differ or go against those posited by the
producer’s traditions. This may result in the familiarization of mambe in the “wrong direction”—by its
new consumers—hindering the producer’s mastery over the coca spirit. With its agency no longer
aligned to the producer’s, the unmastered coca spirit would beget only few, feeble “children,” in the
form of the desiccated, small plants feared by Fisi and others, and may cease to heed commands from
people during its use in healing, rituals, ceremonial dances, and other spiritual interactions with
nonhuman entities. The centrality and daily use of mambe in such spiritual contexts for ensuring
people’s well-being and managing their relationships with a multitude of nonhuman entities,
underscores the critical nature of maintaining mastery over it.
This problem becomes even more pronounced if we accept two hypotheses proposed in this dissertation
(see my discussions in Chapters 6 and 12): first, concerning the Andoque’s perception of coca as an

470

important shield against affinization by human and nonhuman beings, and second, regarding the role of
elements associated with the river source—including coca—in counterbalancing the influence of things
and persons originating from the river mouth. More specifically, we may recall that in M5, Egret of the
Center gains an advantage over Egret of the River Mouth because while the latter offers the former two
substances—cigarettes and liquor—the former provides three—tobacco paste, manicuera, and coca
powder. As narrated to me by Fisi, the myth draws parallels between manicuera and Egret of the River
Mouth’s liquor, referred to as “axe-manicuera” (pɵɵkó’koa), and between cigarettes and tobacco paste,
with Egret of the Center’s words being “it is tobacco, just like yours.” Given these parallels, we are left
with the impression that the “surplus” substance giving Egret of the Center an advantage over his
opponent was mambe, for which the latter had no equivalent counterpart.
The risk of mambe commerce is, therefore, losing control in relationships with nonhuman entities which
may result in engaging in disadvantageous interactions with other human beings. But how are we to
understand the ideal solution proposed (although not necessarily adhered) by various interlocutors—
separating gardens (or periods) for coca for commercial and personal/ceremonial purposes? S. HughJones (1992, 47) described a similar Barasana practice of garden segregation during the cocaine boom as
an attempt to isolate gift from commodity. Given the gift characteristics of coca sharing discussed in
Chapter 6 and other chapters, this heuristic distinction proves useful for the Andoque case as well.
In Gregory’s (2015 [1982]) framework, commodity economy involves the exchange of alienable items
between transactors and the establishment of a relation of equality—i.e., value—between heterogenous
objects, aimed at maximizing profit. By contrast, gift economy involves the exchange of inalienable,
personified items between transactors and the establishment of a relation of rank between the transacting
subjects, in a bid to maximize debtors (ibid, 6, 46). While the price tag put on mambe in the context of
economic transactions certainly represents its “commodification,” its personified aspect and
inalienability from its producer demonstrates that it retains critical gift dimensions. The coexistence of
both gift-like and commodity-like characteristics in an item, such as mambe, does not necessarily imply
that we should abandon the gift/commodity distinction and collapse commodity and exchange, as
proposed by Arjun Appadurai, for whom exchangeability is the defining characteristic in the
“commodity situation” of an item (1986). As Laurent Fontaine (2003) argues in relation to the Yucuna,
and as we have seen throughout the dissertation, one defining characteristic of mambe is its
exchangeability, which plays out also in contexts that cannot count as “commodity situations,” such as

471

when mambe is given in exchange to myth narration or training in healing. Instead, I align with Valeri’s
(1994) approach, exemplified in his study of Huaulu marriage exchange, which employs the
gift/commodity categories in a relative and temporalized manner. This approach allows us to understand
the intricate, dialectical structure of certain economic processes, where gift-like and commodity-like
elements and phases mutually constitute each other, rather than treating these categories in an absolute
manner that reduces the entire process to one pole or the other.
In his critique of Appadurai’s approach, Michael Goddard (2000) convincingly suggests that
in/alienability serves as the distinguishing factor for differentiating gifts from commodities. It thus
appears that the widely cited strategy of segregating gardens does not only aim at isolating gift from
commodity, but at furthering the commodity status of the plants intended for commodification by
increasing their alienability from the producer. By thus achieving its idealized alienation, the
consumption of this mambe by urban consumers does not contaminate and potentially affinize the rest of
the producer’s coca, which remains inalienable. This preservation of inalienability for some of the plants
allows the producer to familiarize and master the spirit of the plant and other nonhuman entities. Hence,
it is the operation of a gift logic—which, far from equating gift exchange with benevolence, also
recognizes the dangers involved in transacting inalienable items (Parry 1989)—that dialectically
contributes to the Andoque’s conceptual enhancement of mambe commodification.
The same logic explains the two other cited strategies—thinking on the territory when consuming the
first spoon and defining the rest as “leftovers,” and using a garden’s first harvest for a ceremonial dance,
while following harvests can serve for whatever purpose. In both, mambe as a gift—consumed while
thinking or acting in line with one’s origin to ensure one’s well-being and that of one’s group—is
segregated from mambe as a commodity: an alienable substance whose uses would not further affinize
the other coca plants and frustrate the plans of its producer.
Returning from the gift/commodity distinction to Andoque concepts, we may say that, while the
producer intends to keep certain coca plants as his “pets” (ḭéna̰)—who may withhold support from their
master or retaliate if neglected—he treats others as his “orphans,” who possess less agency and can be
traded relatively safely by their captain. Given the Andoque’s association between orphans and
cultivars, I have already suggested in the previous section that the notion of orphanhood underpinned the
ontological manipulation and commodification of rubber trees in the Yiñékɒ’s period. While not

472

proposed explicitly by my interlocutors, these examples of treating different nonhuman entities as
orphans resonate with Lucas’ interpretation of the neighboring Bora’s post-genocide generalization of
the orphan position to animals, coupled with the generalization of the captaincy position for all humans
(2021, 21). However, as explained by Lucas, the Bora’s attribution of the orphan status to animals could
derive from the acceptance of Christian teachings and is rooted in the moral perception of orphans as not
“real humans.” By contrast, for the Andoque, orphanhood primarily revolves around lack of predatory
agency, and their statements reflect the more important role of economic dynamics in their active
manipulation of agency of some entities, to evade adversary consequences upon utilizing them during
specific extractive endeavors. Orphanhood may thus be viewed as the Andoque’s native conceptual
equivalent of commodification, yet the analogy has its boundaries. While a commodity is an object open
to manipulation, an orphan retains agency as a subject capable of influencing its captain. The slave trade
provides a clear example for this residual agency. In the historical accounts recounted by Andoque
members, the merchants from downriver who bought fish from the Cacambra and Spix’s Guan Clans—
transactions that proved fatal for these clans—were Andoque slaves, now serving their non-Indigenous
masters as intermediaries, who could communicate with Andoque fishermen precisely because they
shared the same language. Therefore, orphans traded by their captains can later return and contribute to
their downfall. As we will see in the following chapter as well, ontological manipulations can reduce,
but not completely obliterate, the agency of the Other.
To be sure, Andoque mambe sellers also justify this activity by referring to M5, which prophesies the
consumption of coca by non-Indigenous people. In this regard, the Andoque do not perceive mambe
commerce as a complete novelty because of its continuity with coca’s mythic potentiality to tame
Whites and replace their predatory dispositions with a trade orientation. This resonates with Marcelo
Fiorini and Christopher Ball’s (2006) argument against labeling the Xinguano Wauja’s performance of
their Atujuwá ritual in France upon request as mere commodification, because the ritual’s central theme,
predating that performance, revolves around contact with non-Indigenous agents and involves
familiarizing monstruous beings representing non-Indigenous people and the calamitous events of
contact with them. However, in the Andoque case, to achieve the taming and familiarization implied in
M5, mambe cannot be fully commodified; instead, it must be treated as a gift—an inalienable item that
requires a certain degree of personalization for exchange. Nevertheless, mambe commerce tends to be
impersonal, and it is this aspect that represents a novelty.

473

Various members proudly mention that government officials responsible for Indigenous issues and
workers from environmental organizations prefer Andoque mambe over that of other Indigenous groups.
They claim that through this preference, Andoque producers can influence the policies and initiatives
promoted by these non-Indigenous individuals. However, when directly questioned about it, my
interlocutors acknowledge that such familiarization demands a more personal exchange. Nestor, for
example, explained that to guide the thoughts and actions of an urban consumer, he needs to know who
that person is, a detail on which he does not insist when communicating with his sister, who resides in
Bogotá and acts as the broker in the transactions. Levy, who often sells the mambe prepared by his
family members from the Sun Clan in Bogotá, offered another perspective on the need for
personalization when influencing coca consumers. He explained that coca can only have an impact on
people’s minds when it is accompanied by explicit discourse and spoken words, which the powder then
helps to entrench more permanently within the listener’s body. While in a privileged position to share
both mambe and words due to his frequent participation in face-to-face meetings with non-Indigenous
people, Levy acknowledges that to influence people in this manner, he would need to personally prepare
the mambe and infuse it with his intentions, which is not something he typically does.
These considerations provide insight into the intricate nature of mambe commerce and the consequences
of coca’s dual status as both a gift and a commodity—or the vacillation between treating it as a pet and
treating it as an orphan—for the power dynamics between the Andoque and non-Indigenous and
nonhuman agents. On the one hand, by treating coca as a pet and transacting mambe as a gift, Andoque
producers can dominate urban consumers by familiarizing them, but take the risk that the thoughts and
actions of these urban consumers upon consumption would affinize the product, undermining the
producer’s ability to dominate the coca spirit and other nonhuman entities. On the other, commodifying
mambe and transacting it as an orphan shields the producer from such affinization but precludes the
domination of the consumer. However, the disconnect between people’s discourse and practice, evident
in their lack of personalization of coca commerce and failure to implement the idealized solution of
garden segregation, demonstrates that they do not to exhaust either the gift or commodity potentialities
of transactions involving a plant which is central to their identity and relations with both non-Indigenous
people and nonhumans.
In conclusion, if we consider the Andoque’s statements on mambe commerce as genuinely reflective of
their perspective, their challenges in adhering to the proposed strategies to mitigate related risks and

474

seizing opportunities to shape consumer attitudes underscore a general indecision as to how to navigate
power relations with the nonhuman and non-Indigenous entities involved. Viewed against their reported
divergence, as explored in this and the previous chapter, from rituals intended to counteract predatory
dispositions and actions by both Whites—the interactions with whom they seek turning into a reciprocal
exchange—and nonhuman owner-persons—on whose personnel they seek to prey without retaliation—
this indecision seems to extend to their capacity to optimally navigate these intricate power relations at
present. The question remains open: Are they resolute and cohesive—as individuals, distinct clans, or a
people—and prepared to enforce the measures necessary to navigate these power relations? As an
observer, it is not my place to provide an answer, but rather to express hope for their self-determined
success.
In the next chapter, we encounter a context in which Andoque attitudes and tactics point to one possible
avenue for navigating the complex power relations involving nonhuman and non-Indigenous agents—
namely, negotiations with environmental agencies. This preservationist context will also aid in our
contemplation of the extractive dynamics we have examined thus far.

475

476

Chapter 14. Environmental Action and the Encompassment of Worlds
This dissertation began with a tense meeting between the Andoque and a representative from the
Colombian National Natural Parks Agency (hereafter, Parques), setting the stage for my inquiry into the
notion of power and the power dynamics involving the human and nonhuman agents who either
participated in the meeting directly or influenced the positions undertaken by the participants indirectly.
Throughout, I have examined various aspects of this extensive topic, exploring the Andoque’s concept
of power rooted in a “center” and linked to a “river source.” I have analyzed the shifting power
dynamics among human and nonhuman centers, and delved into the Andoque’s perceptions and
strategies for influencing power relations with the non-Indigenous “river mouth.” Previous chapters
touched on environmental initiatives in relation to discussed themes. Now, I turn directly to the
Andoque’s perspectives on and expectations of environmental agencies. In this chapter, I address these
two interrelated questions: How do the Andoque perceive the impact of these agencies on their power
relations with nonhuman as well as with other non-Indigenous agents, and how do they seek to use
preservation-oriented initiatives to secure their position within these broader relations?
Akin to other Indigenous peoples in Amazonia and elsewhere, the Andoque and their neighbors in the
Middle Caquetá have been approached since the 1980s by various governmental and non-governmental
organizations aiming for environmental conservation and viewing them as potential allies because of
their long history of sustainable land and resource use. These entities, including Parques, SINCHI, Gaia
Amazonas, Tropenbos, and Amazon Conservation Team, have introduced projects that include
strengthening Indigenous territoriality and ancestral knowledge, conducting preservation-focused
research, and encouraging traditional and sometimes new ecologically sustainable economic practices.
Studies of such relationships worldwide benefitted from the political ecology framework to effectively
reveal continuities between environmental interventions and wider colonial (Eichler and Baumeister
2018; Nelson 2003) and capitalist (Brockington and Duffy 2011; Sodikoff 2012) forms of dispossession
and marginalization of Indigenous peoples and local communities. In Amazonia, these interactions were
contextualized within the advancement of perennial frontiers, each one exploiting and commodifying
different resources (Little 2001)—this resource being, in the environmental case, the very idea of nature
(Rubenstein 2004, 152–53). The interactions between Indigenous Amazonians and Western
environmentalists were described as occurring in a fragile “middle ground” of misunderstandings and

477

only partly overlapping interests, reached by two unequal parties in terms of access to economic and
symbolic power: conservation-minded Westerners, on the one hand, and Indigenous people seeking to
secure land claims and livelihoods, on the other (Conklin and Graham 1995).
The Ontological Turn brought attention to Indigenous perceptions of environmental struggles that
challenge the “naturalist” assumptions underlying research that explores power relations as occurring
solely among human beings and downplaying the nonhuman agencies central to Indigenous thinking.
Scholars associated with this approach have called to extend politics to “cosmopolitics” that
acknowledges the political agency of nonhuman entities and seeks nonrepresentational methods of
engagement with these entities to include their voices and agency in politics, drawing upon Indigenous
and other non-modern scientific understandings (de la Cadena 2010). Underscoring the fragility of the
“middle ground” between Indigenous people and environmentalists, these anthropologists tend to
describe a radical alterity between “naturalist” environmentalists and Indigenous people, reflected in the
distinct realities that each side seeks to conserve: either an objectified Nature or interpersonal
relationships with nonhuman beings (See, for Amazonia, Blaser 2009; Hirtzel 2007; and for other
regions, Bird-David and Naveh 2008; Novellino 2004). A prominent example of this perspective is
Mario Blaser (2009), who suggests that the Paraguayan Yshiro and conservation biologists aim to
preserve two disparate realities—while the former seek the preservation of the matrix of humannonhuman exchange referred to as Yrmo, the latter seek the preservation of the naturalist
“environment.” Blaser advocates for an inter-ontological dialogue between two ostensibly ahistorical
ontologies within a framework he terms “political ontology,” which, distinct from political economy and
political ecology, does not examine power and conflict as unevenly distributed within one universal
reality but across multiple realities.
Certainly, the ontological approach proves useful for understanding the Andoque’s interactions with
environmentalists. We have already observed in previous chapters the critical role that agentive
nonhuman beings, endowed with both beneficial and calamitous potentialities for humans, occupy in the
Andoque’s socio-cosmos, as well as the Andoque’s understanding of the territory as being owned by
countless powerful nonhuman entities. These perceptions form a significant backdrop to their dealings
with environmentalists and non-Indigenous agents in general. However, I strongly side with critics of
the Ontological Turn who focus on the claim to an Indigenous radical alterity in relation to nonIndigenous people. As these scholars have demonstrated, this approach tends to flatten ethnographic

478

complexities, relies on authoritative perspectives to define ontologies, and results in political
ineffectiveness due to over-emphasis of cosmopolitical futures and downplaying of present political
problems (Bessire and Bond 2014; Graeber 2015). Rather, day-to-day experience and ethnographic
evidence suggest that many entities are ontologically indeterminate for both Indigenous and nonIndigenous actors, who perceive them as subjects in some contexts and objects in others (Nadasdy
2021).
Contrary to Blaser’s assertions of incommensurability between realities, the Andoque’s version of
perspectivism and multiplicity of worlds, as explored in Chapter 8, emphasizes overlaps that signify
one’s ability to adhere to multiple connectivity logics and allow for asymmetrical encompassment
between worlds and their respective logics. In addition, as the opening anecdote illustrates, far from
reflecting radical alterity, Andoque members project it on their Apaporis neighbors, whom
environmentalists allegedly want the Andoque to emulate and who live “naked, barefoot, but happy, but
we have needs!” These needs are commensurate with those of non-Indigenous people and require
commensurate rewards to theirs (“like Parques, an Andoque only works for money”). Furthermore, the
Andoque’s strategies for manipulating and diminishing nonhuman agency, as explored in the previous
chapter, also form a crucial ontological factor that approximates—without merging with—modern
scientific and economic views of an agential gap between humans and nonhumans, with the latter
readily serving as resources for the former. This nuanced proximity is key to grasping the Andoque’s
stance towards environmentalists and their projects.
Therefore, this chapter revolves around the Andoque’s dual approach to nonhumans in the context of
environmental initiatives and public policy, treating them as both subordinate entities that can be utilized
and as largely hostile independent agents. I suggest that the Andoque’s primary goal in interactions with
environmentalists and the State is to assert their asymmetrical exchanges with nonhumans, often deemphasizing nonhuman agency, to mitigate imbalanced exchanges with non-Indigenous people. Yet,
since nonhuman agency cannot be extinguished, they remain potential adversaries, and environmental
initiatives are leveraged to repair or redefine relations with them, which economic engagement with
Whites has weakened, ensuring the preservation of the Indigenous ability to dictate asymmetrical
exchanges with nonhumans—a key condition for human well-being and reproduction.
Finally, based on the broad scope of the Andoque’s engagements with environmentalists, I consider
these interactions as a privileged arena in the unfolding of the complex relational triangle among the

479

Andoque, non-Indigenous people, and nonhuman entities. Unlike transactions with individual
merchants, miners, and settlers, dealings with environmentalists involve the entire Andoque people, span
whole reserves or ancestral lands, and affect a multitude of nonhuman entities. Additionally,
environmentalists often represent larger collectives, such as nation-states or the international bodies
funding their work. Therefore, in line with this dissertation’s definition of territory/world as connectivity
and the Andoque notion of encompassing worlds, I suggest that the Andoque’s negotiations with
environmentalists reflect a desire to reverse the encompassment of their ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí by the Whites world
under the current model of extractive economy.
Nobles and Miners
A central Andoque motivation in their interactions with environmental agencies is to safeguard
territorial rights and pursue resource sovereignty, with the latter cause often treated with suspicion by
environmentalists. As the vignette opening this dissertation demonstrated, the Andoque often contest the
environmentalists’ expectations that they adhere to the image of “the Ecologically Noble Savage”—a
“green” offshoot of the Enlightenment’s “Noble Savage” trope, who supposedly leads a harmonious
existence with nature through an unchanging economy with a minimal ecological footprint. Widely
refuted as empirical reality (Hames 2007), this image remains a powerful construct among global
audiences. Authors have shown that the portrayal of Indigenous people as achieved or failed “ecological
nobles” according to Euro-American standards of environmentalism is a powerful discursive mechanism
for governmental and non-governmental organizations to tell friend from foe, allocate resources, and
discipline communities (Harkin and Lewis 2007; Redford 1991). In response, the Andoque categorize
organizations into those attempting to preserve or restore an alleged “authentic” Indigenous lifestyle and
those acknowledging their self-determination and recognizing their current circumstances, necessities,
and desires.
Notably, the criterion of governmental affiliation or the lack thereof is less important for the Andoque.
While the NGO Gaia Amazonas epitomizes, for them, the desire of non-Indigenous people to maintain
Indigenous peoples in a state of technological dearth and inferiority, the Cahuinarí National Natural
Park’s monitoring program of arrau river turtles (Podocnemis expansa) conducted with their Miraña
neighbors serves as a critical warning of the loss of economic autonomy due to imposition of hunting
quotas by environmentalists. They view the State as primarily conservationist when it comes to

480

Indigenous people, while NGOs do not necessarily embody a defense from State abuse as they may do
in other contexts (e.g., Conklin and Graham 1995). Andoque members rightfully detect the frequent
collaboration between State organs and NGOs. They note the concessions that State entities make to
NGOs, particularly in managing projects and funds from international donors, and track the career paths
of individuals who specialize in environmental and Indigenous matters as they move between these two
types of organizations in the precarious Colombian labor market.
The Andoque’s pursuit of resource sovereignty was highlighted in their appeal to State tutelage against
the State-run REDD+ program (Reducing Emissions from Deforestation and Forest Degradation, and
the Role of Conservation, Sustainable Management of Forests, and Enhancement of Forest Carbon
Stocks in Developing Countries) Visión Amazonía in 2017–19. As I discussed in collaboration with
Levy, who initiated this legal action in October 2017, and other co-authors in Andoke et al. (2023), the
Andoque protested the State’s failure to seek their Free, Prior, and Informed Consent for including their
territory and carbon stock in this emission reduction payment scheme that allocated disproportionately
low share of the benefits to Indigenous landholders. While more than a half of the program’s budget
derived from carbon stored in Indigenous reserves covering roughly 56% of the Colombian Amazonian
biomass, only 22% of the benefits were allotted to Indigenous communities, with this participation being
contingent upon adherence to pre-set, unconsented project guidelines.
The appeal was discussed in the Administrative Court of Cundinamarca (the department of Bogotá),
which rejected its demands in March 2018, and the Constitutional Court, which revisited the case in
February 2019. Although not included in the original appeal, the Andoque—and primarily Levy, the
reserve member most involved in the legal process—added claims over property rights during the
second stage, as part of their response to the Constitutional Court’s decision to revisit the case (STC063/2019, 2019). They argued that Visión Amazonía’s prohibition against double counting recorded
emission reductions, a general principle of the REDD+ framework, impacted their rights. Specifically,
by using their forest resources from 2013–17 without prior consent, the program prevented them from
independently negotiating with other parties over alternative carbon offset schemes referring to these
years. Still in February 2019, the Constitutional Court partially overturned the lower court’s ruling,
ordering the State to consult the Andoque and seek their Free, Prior, and Informed Consent on the
Indigenous component of the program, to ensure that any project they submitted would not be
constrained by a document to which they had not contributed.

481

As regards resource sovereignty, it is notable that the interrelated issues of carbon rights and unequal
benefit distribution were not addressed by either of the two courts. Throughout the proceedings, the nonIndigenous actors (the two court judges and appellees from governmental agencies) and the Indigenous
ones (besides the Andoque, these were the members of CRIMA and participants in the Indigenous pillar
workshops) employed distinct discourses. The former based its assessment of infringement on the
Andoque’s rights on changes to their current situation, while the latter asserted that their rights were
violated due to their inability to exercise self-determination and collective property rights over their
resources, including historically conserved carbon stocks. The underlying premise of the non-Indigenous
discourse and legal reasoning appeared to be the notion of the “ahistorical Indian,” whose life conditions
are presumed to remain unchanged unless affected by external influences. Conversely, the Indigenous
rightsholders articulated their legitimate economic entitlements to equitable participation in the
formulation, implementation, and benefits of a program funded by forest carbon, a significant portion of
which they own.
The consultation eventually took place in the Andoque reserve in July 2019, after my departure from
their territory. During this consultation, the Andoque did not make changes to the guidelines document.
Instead, they used the urgency of implementing the Court’s ruling to secure substantial funding for
projects that have been largely elaborated earlier and aligned with the original document. I return to the
outcome of this legal case further below.
In the Andoque’s struggle for resource sovereignty, the prevention of resource expropriation by
outsiders is complemented by efforts to obtain State recognition of their own legitimacy in managing
these entities. This is exemplified by the Andoque’s campaign to legalize gold mining, an activity that
has contributed to their negative image among environmental entities, as the opening anecdote
demonstrated. Environmentalists often overlooked labor on, or even ownership of, mining rafts by other
Indigenous peoples in the region, attributing it to coercion by dissident groups or a submission to the
temporary lure of high profits in a precarious economic periphery. However, they could not overlook the
Andoque’s 2013 request to declare their northern reserve as an Indigenous Mining Zone. This request

482

led to consequences such as the withdrawal of support from Parques for the Andoque’s efforts to expand
that same reserve.165
From the Andoque’s perspective, their legalization request was in line with the reserve’s expansion plan,
as both initiatives concerned control over space. While the expansion request was about accessing an
area stretching northward on the horizontal plane, the mining title concerned access to space lying
vertically below them, in the subsoil layer, which Colombian law defines as state property. Some
Andoque members explained that they supported the legalization request to protect their territory by
preventing actual mining projects there. This motive should be understood in light of the uncontrolled
influx of illegal foreign miners into their territory a few years earlier. It might also reflect the discourse
of state agents, particularly the National Mining Agency, which encouraged Indigenous populations to
open their reserves for mining on the grounds that state regulation would help them protect specific
“sacred sites” from extraction (Audren 2017, 53). Indeed, Audren notes that the 2001 Mining Code was
intended to allow the state to regulate informal mining in Indigenous reserves and to grant Indigenous
communities a means for economic development, thereby enabling the state to also profit from the
riches underneath hitherto unmined reserves. Hence, while the National Mining Agency courted the
Andoque to convince them to open their territory for mining, another State organ, Parques, withdrew its
support for the same reason.
In the internal debate over gold mining, with members vacillating between supporting and opposing its
legalization, resource sovereignty appears to have been a more important factor than the environmental
impacts of this activity, some of which may be coded in the broader notion of retaliation by powerful
owner-persons. This notion is captured in the title of Audren’s thesis on the legalization initiative, “The
Masters of Gold” (Les maîtres de l’or): Who are the masters of gold? The nonhuman spirits, the
Andoque people, the State seeking profits from its underground property, or the Andoque protagonists
of this initiative and the enterprises they collaborate with? We must return to the fact that negotiations
with the nonhuman owner of gold only commenced when the Andoque began pursuing the legalization
of inland excavations, rather than during earlier river extractions. One hypothesis for this is that ownerpersons are more likely to retaliate, or do so more severely, for inland rather than fluvial mining—an

Parques had previously committed to provide this support in 2012, during prior consultation assemblies held with
Indigenous reserves within the “influence zone” of the National Natural Park Serranía de Chiribiquete, as a condition for the
Andoque’s consent to the park’s expansion (PNN 2018, 16).
165

483

idea that my interlocutors have never confirmed. Another possibility is that such negotiations, while
considered essential, were not held due to a lack of interest from the miners. Rodolfo explained that he
could not engage in dialog with Dui during the period of fluvial mining to ensure the miners’ safety,
including his own sons, because they had not requested it, mentioning that the safe and effective practice
of such a risky spiritual endeavor requires the engagement of those for whom it is performed. It is
possible that the idea to conduct spiritual negotiations as part of the legalization project was a tactical
move by the project initiators, who might have wanted to demonstrate to the state their compliance with
a “traditional” protocol and to build consensus among Andoque members, thereby improving their
chances of securing the mining title. For his part, Orlando, the partner-owner of Duxon, claimed that the
elders first insisted on such dialog when the idea of legalization emerged. Regardless, the crucial point is
that negotiations with the owner-person of gold were only pursued when success in negotiations with the
State were at stake. As Audren concluded, the Andoque turned to nonhuman owner-persons as strategic
allies, and their negotiations with them were part of a broader endeavor to secure the recognition of
external agents, such as the State and non-Indigenous entrepreneurs, of their resource control (2017,
140). My data likewise emphasize the continuity, in Andoque eyes, between the legitimacy granted for
mining by nonhuman entities of the territory and the legitimacy they sought from the State. During my
excursion with Tañe in May 2019 to Axe (Pɵɵ), where stone axes had been extracted, we sat beside one
of the excavation holes. Gazing at it, he remarked, “This is a mine, isn’t it? This story [of the Piercers’
discovery of the axe repository] already indicated that the Andoque territory has everything, and that in
the future, we can extract more things to satisfy our needs. This is why I sometimes wonder, ‘Why must
we also seek approval from the Ministry of Mining?’” Andoque protagonists strove to compel the State
to acknowledge their mastery over the owner-persons of their territory and the latter’s consent for the
Andoque to safely utilize their “personnel.” In this case, the notion of resource sovereignty renders, in
legal terms, the Andoque’s aspiration that the State recognize their asymmetrical relationship with the
nonhuman entities of the territory or that it would not otherwise interfere with their relationships with
these entities.
The State’s capacity to prohibit gold mining has made it a rallying point for sovereignty among many
Andoque members, including those who originally objected to or hesitated about this activity due to
concerns over nonhuman retaliation. An example of this was evident during the workshop to formulate
the “cultural plan for territorial management” in November-December 2018, when the Andoque
participants discussed the components of their ancestral territory and eventually reached the topic of
484

“subsoil.” As they brainstormed various concepts from their language and mythology for what lies
beneath the earth’s surface, Nestor—who, on other occasions, expressed opposition to inland mining—
cautioned that they should not discuss this matter hastily, saying, “This is where they blindside us [nos
dan en la nuca].” Consequently, the final document detailed several subsoil layers, associating them with
Andoque mythology, starting from the uppermost containing the roots and tubers of garden cultivars, to
that where the dead are buried, down to petrol deposits embodying the fat of Nocturnal Curassow from
M10, and finally the tetee fire stone located at the earth’s core, which is also mentioned in that myth.
This brings us back to our discussion in Chapter 8, on how the workshop for drafting the “territorial
plan” served as an opportunity to assert human-nonhuman asymmetry. There, I examined how the
Andoque participants defined the territory to prevent interventions by non-Indigenous agents for
environmental conservation and explored the asymmetrical version of animism underlying this
definition. For the participants, protecting their territory and livelihood from such interference was on
par with protecting themselves from aggressions by nonhumans threatening their human status. During
the discussions on the categories of humanity and animality, and when reaching the topic of the
Piercers—the proto-human beings who stripped potent animals of their primordial powers to make the
territory habitable for present-day humans—a Murui woman, married to an Andoque man, suggested
that the territorial plan would serve a similar purpose, as a means for their descendants to ward off
different dangers and live peacefully. Many participants agreed with her statement. We should
remember that the Piercers embody a more aggressive and intrusive stance toward nonhuman beings, a
position we might even label as “extractive,” as illustrated in the tradition according to which they
excavated the stone axes. By contrast, for Parques, which funded the workshop, the activity’s goal was
preservationist. During our meeting in Bogotá before the workshop to hand me stationery the Andoque
needed, the senior representative of Parques in charge of communication with them intimated to me that
he hoped that the territorial plan would restore awareness among these people, whom Parques
considered to be slipping into a campesino (peasant) existence, of traditional ecological principles.
A short digression is in order to note that Andoque members are concerned about restrictions on
accessing their territory’s resources or their expropriation not only by the State in its role as a
preservationist entity but also by other non-Indigenous actors, as well as fellow members who ally with
them. This concern harks back to the period of mining legalization efforts. Several interlocutors told me
that while they were interested in pursuing illegal fluvial mining, they opposed the legalization initiative.

485

They feared that it would privilege non-Indigenous entrepreneurs because they would be the only ones
with sufficient capital to conduct costly inland excavations, suspecting that such individuals would gain
access to the reserve through Levy. Their worries centered not so much on pollution, which river
excavations also cause, but rather on dispossession of their resources by outsiders collaborating with an
Andoque member who, having graduated from a private university and residing in Bogotá, is affiliated
with politicians and businessmen and is suspected of possessing non-Indigenous thinking. Throughout
her thesis, Audren skillfully describes Levy’s dual position as both Andoque and White, mentioning
suspicions among Andoque members about his greater allegiance to his non-Indigenous allies than to his
own kin, as evidenced by a woman’s question during a community assembly, asking Levy if rumors of
him selling Andoque territory to outsiders were true (2017, 135). The Andoque continue to ponder
Levy’s loyalties. In a conversation with an Andoque elder, he recounted a dream another elder had told
him about some two years earlier (around 2017). In the dream, Levy arrived at his clan settlement of San
José in a new motorboat from Bogotá. Members of his clan joined him, but they traveled only a short
distance before drowning and losing both the boat and motor. While this dream narrative vividly echoes
T5, the two elders saw the drowning of the motorboat as the most important detail, concluding that it
symbolized Levy shedding his previous non-Indigenous mindset. My interlocutor cited Levy’s
abandonment of the mining project shortly afterwards as proof for the dream’s message. The private
market carbon offset project, which Levy campaigned for in 2019 while informing the Andoque about
the Visión Amazonía case’s outcome, elicited similar concerns among individuals from all clans. These
concerns were communicated to me during that period and again in my 2021 visit. By 2022, however,
the Andoque had ultimately given their consent to the project. Assessing the project’s impact and the
resulting cosmo-social transformations will require additional fieldwork.
My Enemy’s Friend
Although an asymmetry is sought between humans and nonhumans, the Andoque recognize that
nonhuman entities, guarded by potent owner-persons, maintain their capacity for danger and are not
reduced to mere objects. Therefore, Andoque members view environmental measures that protect these
entities as meddling with the established power dynamics within their territory. A complementary aspect
of this protection is the tendency of environmental agencies to overlook the economic hardships faced
by the people themselves—which are largely the product of the historical conquest, abuse, and
asymmetrical exchange with non-Indigenous agents. The critique of protecting flora and fauna while

486

neglecting (Indigenous) humans was echoed in the claim cited in the opening vignette: “The Whites
only give rights to trees, not to people.” This critique was also raised by Andoque members during an
assembly with a delegate of the Ministry of Environment and Sustainable Development (hereafter, the
Ministry) and a representative of Parques, which took place in the Andoque reserve in October 2018.
The objective of this encounter was to secure confirmation from the Ministry that the reserve fulfills its
ecological function, a prerequisite for the Andoque to pursue the desired expansion of the reserve’s
territory. During the assembly, the delegate and community members scrutinized the reserve’s recent
ecological history, analyzed current contamination sources, and finally brainstormed for future damage
reduction measures. Initially, active participation was impeded because the delegate employed scientific
jargon that was incomprehensible to the participants. When asked to explain the term “fauna,” he said:
“Fauna are animals; what’s an animal?”. Delio, an elder from the Sun Clan, was quick to provide a
provocative answer: “Animals are our enemies.” Baffled, the delegate ignored this definition. When he
asked: “what is Nature?” Alfonso, an elder form the Atta Ant Clan replied: “Nature is everything,
animals, trees, diablos, patasola [One Leg]…”, thereby adding nonhuman entities harmful to humans to
the list. It appears that by stating these definitions, the participants sought to make the delegate
understand that the nonhuman beings he was protecting were not innocent entities. On the other hand,
they were defensive when he suggested there could be potential environmental damage resulting from
their activities. When he mentioned the risk of species depletion due to overhunting, the participants
acknowledged that the danger existed but countered that they would not resort to hunting for
commercial purposes if they had economic alternatives. In response to his advice about controlling fires
in traditional slash-and-burn practices to prevent air pollution, the people argued that their contribution
to air pollution pales in comparison to that of cities like Bogotá. Fisi, who had traveled for conferences
globally, contributed an observation: “I’ve been to London and seen smoke from petrol refinery
chimneys rising some eighty meters into the air reaching who knows where—it might even get here, and
nobody does anything. Yet, when we burn a chagrita [diminutive for chagra, or garden], the smoke
doesn’t even rise fifty meters.” This remark, adding to the overall sentiment, underscored the Andoque’s
perception of environmental preservation efforts as an affront to their way of life. The delegate finally
returned to the thorny issue of animal depletion: “How can we regulate hunting?”. “We can’t,” one
participant said. “As long as they don’t have other income sources, people will kill the fauna.”

487

The delegate was ready to terminate the meeting, since he felt that his didactic goal of raising the
community’s ecological awareness had been accomplished, but the participants insisted on economic
solutions. In the end he referred them to other institutional bodies, saying that it was not in his power to
provide redress. His suggestion to seek out governmental sustainable development projects led some to
protest that the budgets earmarked for these projects for Indigenous people were nothing in comparison
to those allotted to settlers. “The money goes to those who fell trees, not to those who take care of the
forest,” said one participant. The Parques representative explained the logic beyond the larger
investment in projects incentivizing people to abandon non-sustainable land uses, such as agrobusiness.
“It seems wrong,” he said apologetically, “but it was devised for settlers, whose economic system
damages the environment. People believe that such investment isn’t needed for Indigenous people, since
they don’t have a deforestation problem.” “Well then,” said one participant in his forties, summarizing
the general dissatisfaction, “we will clear the forest for livestock so that the government will pay
attention to us as well!”.
In their claims, Andoque participants portrayed themselves simultaneously as forest protectors and
potential destructors. Their threats reflect a perception of policymakers as only taking seriously those
individuals and collectives who treat their environment as a resource depository for irresponsible
extraction, rather than those employing more ecologically sustainable practices.166 Therefore, State
recognition is here sought based on a similarity between the Andoque and non-Indigenous settlers, as
well as State agents, in treating nonhumans as resources with less agency than humans. However, the
Andoque and non-Indigenous perspectives of nonhuman agency do not fully merge, because, for the
Andoque, nonhumans remain inimical, potentially dangerous agents. As Delio replied to the Ministry’s
delegate, animals are their enemies—entities whom human ancestors overcame in the transition from
mythical times to present ones in order to become fully human, and whom actual humans have to
overcome to maintain their full human status, stay healthy and alive, and bequeath this status to their
children. As Alfonso pointed out in his short list of the components of nature, this concept contains
beings such as the fi’du entities and One Leg, who are particularly dangerous in their capacity to

The grievance over prioritizing deforestation over forest conservation was intended to be addressed by the REDD+
framework, which devised economic transfers to landowners in developing countries possessing large carbon stocks,
incentivizing them to enhance or refrain from harming these stocks. However, the benefit-sharing mechanism of the REDD+
program Visión Amazonía mirrored similar budgetary priorities. This mechanism, as discussed by Andoke et al. (2023),
allocated larger budgetary shares to actors responsible for deforestation to create for them alternative economic activities,
whilst Indigenous forest guardians received a smaller share of overall budgets.

166
