transform humans into nonhumans precisely because of their defiance of clear definitions, epitomized by
their capacity to transform themselves.
During a mambeadero session at Fisi’s maloca in one of the nights of the “territorial plan” workshop
week, I discussed my research and aspiration to advocate for Indigenous people through its publication
with the maloca residents, Elias, and Nelson—two ex-maloqueros staying there that week. Elias
highlighted the hardships for Indigenous peoples created by the State, complaining that it simply prefers
them to stay as they are—this is why it gives monetary incentives to conserve the forest to the settlers
and not to them. I resorted to the explanation provided by Parques’ representative, to which Elias
reiterated the idea to deforest until the State pays attention to them. When the topic switched to cultural
preservation, he said: “We need to teach the children our language, but how can I do that when I need to
buy food, clothes, all those necessities?” Nelson intervened, saying: “So we will use our territory if they
don’t help us. We will damage the forest so that they pay us to stop.” Nestor agreed, but his father Fisi
calmed them down, saying: “But we don’t want to finish like the Cacambra, there’s always danger from
that side too.” Therefore, while the Andoque can mobilize asymmetries between humans and
nonhumans to enhance their status within national society, these asymmetries are not fixed; the threat of
retribution from owner-persons looms, as evidenced by the aftermath of the Cacambra Clan’s fishing
activity.
While my interlocutors have never said it explicitly, I suggest that the Andoque’s perception of
nonhuman enmity and hostility underlies not only their relations with nonhumans, but also with
environmentalists. According to Karadimas, the Miraña express suspicion over the assumption of
responsibility for the life and reproduction of the animals within the Cahuinarí National Natural Park,
which partly overlaps with their reserve, because such responsibility is normally assumed by the
guardian spirits of animals (2013, 195). Similarly, from the Andoque’s point of view, the protection of
flora and fauna by environmental organizations as guarantors of their “rights”—i.e., their capacity to
exist and reproduce—is analogous to these masters’ actions, with whom, we should remember, Andoque
members maintain a complex relationship of hostility, seduction, and familiarization. We can even
daringly apply the non-Indigenous concept of “agency” to reflect how, much like owner-persons (ño̰e)
representing the personhood and agency (ño̰) of the nonhuman entities they safeguard, these
organizations are “environmental agencies” also in the sense of embodying the capacity of flora and
fauna to act. However, I would not go as far as arguing, as Vincent Hirtzel (2007, 76–77) did for the

489

Bolivian Yuracaré, that the Andoque perceive environmental entities as a reconfiguration of these
owner-persons. According to Hirtzel, while these guardian spirits would release game animals to the
Yuracaré upon a shaman’s request, the park manager, either unable or unwilling to give them game, can
instead offer work tools and other objects when appealed to for his generosity. These items, in relation
to the park manager, occupy a position analogous to that which game animals hold in relation to their
guardian spirits. The Andoque, on the other hand, are well aware that environmentalists are distinct from
owner-persons, and, as shown above, they base their interactions with the former on their asymmetrical
relations with the latter. Thus, the sense of resource sovereignty precludes such appeals to generosity,
thereby making interactions with environmentalists more transactional. Environmental entities assuming
the role of safeguarding nonhumans are expected to compensate the Andoque for restricting access to
these resources, which they illegitimately usurped. Furthermore, the notion of the Animal World being
encompassed by the Andoque’s ño̰ ́ ḭ́ fɵsí (Chapter 8) views outside attempts at stewardship over
nonhumans as an infringement on the principles of their world and origins, making interactions with
environmentalists more confrontational. As the saying goes, my enemy’s friend—or protector—is also
my enemy.
Respecting Knowledge, Respecting Boundaries
Given the central role of knowledge in power relations with human and nonhuman centers, as explored
in Chapters 9 and 10, the attitude of environmental agencies towards Indigenous knowledge is also a
crucial aspect of the Andoque’s stance towards these entities. The concerns related to Indigenous
knowledge were a central issue of another meeting between the Andoque and Parques in March 2019.
This meeting also included their Murui-Muina and Féénemɨna neighbors from the upriver Monochoa
Reserve, as well as a representative from the NGO Fundación Puerto Rastrojo. This organization had
been contracted by Parques to inventory the flora and fauna within the expanded area of Chiribiquete
National Natural Park, aiming to establish the conservation principles for this area. The World Bank, as
the funding entity, required the sharing of this information with the Park’s Indigenous neighbors and
consultation with them on the matter. Consequently, Parques organized a meeting at Fisi’s maloca with
the Andoque and representatives from Monochoa, who had stayed at the maloca the previous night
following a different meeting.

490

During the mambeadero session on the evening before the meeting with Parques, members from both
reserves expressed their concerns about the expanded Park’s increased influence, which might
eventually result in restrictions on hunting and other land use practices. The governor of Monochoa
warned that if Parques identified species of special global interest for preservation, Indigenous access to
the expanded area could be restricted, violating previous consultation accords; others even expressed
fears over potential hunting restrictions within the reserves. Many participants voiced demands for
reconocimiento (recognition) of Indigenous knowledge in a double sense—both acknowledging its
scientific value and providing remuneration for it. They criticized environmental organizations for hiring
outsiders to conduct research in their forest, relegating local elders with vast knowledge to merely
adorning their reports with Indigenous folklore. This practice, they argued, diminished the value of their
knowledge and ignored the wisdom encapsulated in myths or even in the names of plants and animals. A
point raised by a Nɨpóde member of the Andoque reserve garnered broad agreement: it was Indigenous
knowledge that had preserved the forest thus far; if the Whites seek preservation, they should pay for
that knowledge.
The meeting the following morning began with an explanation from Parques’ representative about the
rationale for the expedition, mentioning also the meeting’s secondary objective: hiring locals to assist
researchers as trailblazers, hunters and fishermen, and general manual laborers for the month-long
activity. The representative drew parallels between the conservation principles that the expedition aimed
to elaborate and the territorial plans formulated by the Indigenous reserves. He stated that the scientific
findings from the expedition would eventually be shared with the park’s Indigenous neighbors, enabling
them to use the relevant results for their own territorial plans. Additionally, he mentioned a future phase,
termed “management of knowledges” (gestión de conocimientos), involving dialogue between Western
and traditional knowledge. The Indigenous participants sought clarification on the date and agenda of
this future phase, but the representative evaded a direct response, admitting that it had not been planned
yet. Elias and other Indigenous participants, suspecting that a collaborative moment might never occur
or lack reciprocity, insisted on the immediate inclusion of Indigenous experts (conocedores) and
scientists (científicos)— terms referring to elders knowledgeable in their traditions—in the expedition,
alongside Western scientists. Contrary to the prior consultation accords between the two reserves and
Parques regarding the park’s expansion, which stated that research in the expanded area must recognize,
respect, and protect the traditional and ancestral knowledge of the Indigenous peoples, Parques’

491

representative maintained that the study could proceed as planned, as it was confined to the Park’s
boundaries.
The representative from Puerto Rastrojo then took the floor and outlined the tasks for the laborers, as
well as the composition of the scientific group. He noted that the group would include specialists for
every class of flora and fauna, such as ornithologists, entomologists, etc., to study species within their
expertise. In response, the governor of Monochoa argued that, for this very reason, an Indigenous expert
should be included to provide the Indigenous perspective on species found in both the park’s expanded
area and the Indigenous territories —specifically, “the notion of this species as it is held by the
Indigenous (el concepto propio de este especie como lo está pensando el indígena).” The representatives
from both organizations acknowledged the importance of this recommendation but stated that its
implementation would have to wait for future projects.
Puerto Rastrojo’s representative then read aloud the environmental safeguards for the project, which
included a comprehensive list of routine environmental protection measures that the laborers were
expected to follow. Discussing these regulations at length in front of a large group, most of whom would
not be directly involved in the work, seemed to serve only as a means of indoctrinating the audience in
“correct” environmental practices. Subsequently, Parques’ representative read aloud the social
safeguards required by the World Bank. One primary measure was the consultation of Indigenous
communities bordering the park and the incorporation of their knowledge throughout the project’s
phases (cf. World Bank 2016). When local participants tentatively pointed out that they had been
excluded from the project’s planning, hence the measure had not been honored, Puerto Rastrojo’s
representative claimed that these were general safeguards that applied differently in each project. He
argued that since the expedition was a scientific endeavor, it did not necessitate the inclusion of
traditional knowledge. Parques’ representative even suggested that safeguards should not be interpreted
too rigidly (“al pie de la letra”). Interestingly, while, to my knowledge, no Indigenous experts were
ultimately employed in the expedition, the publication on Parques’ website suggests otherwise (See
PNN 2019).
Beyond merely expecting economic benefits for local experts, the Indigenous pursuit for the inclusion of
their knowledge should be understood within the context of concerns about possible restrictive actions
by Parques, a perceived alliance between environmentalists and nonhuman entities, and the strategic role

492

of knowledge within the Indigenous cosmos. As we have seen in previous chapters, knowing the names
and origin stories of beings in one’s environment enables communication with these beings, the
countering of their predatory attempts and other harmful effects, and the enlistment of these beings for
one’s benefit. Thus, Indigenous knowledge of nonhumans enables the knower to safeguard themselves
and their kin from nonhuman aggressions and guarantee their own reproduction. Conversely, studying
nonhuman beings primarily for their own protection and reproduction, without the involvement of
Indigenous experts, can lead to the development of a knowledge base that endangers and restricts the
Indigenous people who coexist with these nonhumans.
In addition to lack of respect for their knowledge, Andoque members (and their neighbors) are also
concerned about the imposition of foreign categories of knowledge on their territories. At a CRIMA
conference in Araracuara in May 2019, the organization’s vice president shared information on the
Ministry’s new Indigenous Environmental Management System (SIMA) that would subsume the PredioPutumayo reserve within a larger management zone called the Caquetá Axis. Levy, who was also
present at the conference, contextualized this initiative as part of the emerging trend of macro-territorial
management among environmental agencies, of which Gaia Amazonas’s Triple A project (AndesAmazon-Atlantic) was an alarming forerunner:
Some anthropologists now claim there’s one Indigenous way of thinking from the Andes to the Amazon delta.167
They say that the Yuruparí gods [of Indigenous peoples of the Vaupes-Apaporis Rivers] go as far as Araracuara. The
struggle over the subsoil is already lost, so we must be wary of another defeat. There are Indigenous peoples that
encourage anthropologists to grant trees, the forest, and the land the same rights that humans have—peoples who
talk about the Pachamama, about Mother Earth… We must be wary of that, it’s dangerous for us. Tree felling is
already criminalized, we don’t want to lose this battle too.

The participants of all ethnicities agreed. A Féénemɨna elder noted that Indigenous perspectives on
territorial management are completely opposed to the Ministry’s top-down vision:
We already have our own SIMA, but ours is not based on imaginary lines like the Whites’ SIMA: here it is the
Caquetá Department, and there it’s the Amazonas [Department], and they only destroy everything. For us, each
territory has its own laws, its own thinking, and when a maloquero from here joins his thinking to a maloquero from

In local discourse, antropólogos means both anthropologists and other specialists advocating for Indigenous peoples
and/or counseling governmental and non-governmental agencies on them.
167

493

downriver, and that one joins his to that of a maloquero from Brazil [farther downriver], they create the ‘famous’
‘Caquetá Axis’ that the Whites talk about.

Based on the same principle that enables a sorcerer to harm another person by thinking and manipulating
the latter’s origin story and the stories of different elements in their surroundings, a powerful shaman
can also turn the owner-persons of a given territory against its inhabitants by focusing on that territory
and its origin myths. Additionally, as Rodolfo’s claim to exclusivity of his relationship with the ownerperson of gold, knowledge can grant a monopoly over safe land and resource use.168 These conceptions
highlight why the Andoque (and their neighbors) are apprehensive that imposing foreign categories of
knowledge on their territory could threaten their livelihoods and well-being, and may even be viewed as
a violation of their territorial integrity.
In his study of the efforts to integrate Indigenous knowledge and Western science in processes of
resource management and environmental impact assessment in the North American Arctic and
Subarctic, Nadasdy (1999) emphasized the one-sided nature of this integration. This unidirectionality is
evident in how Indigenous knowledge is compartmentalized and distilled to fit into Western science,
without challenging the latter’s methodology and underlying epistemology. According to Nadasdy, this
approach perpetuates the power imbalance between the two parties and marginalizes Indigenous
knowledge, subordinating it to the non-Indigenous center of calculation and conceptual production.
Blaser sees such dynamics as indicative of “ontological conflicts,” where Western scientists tend to
diminish Indigenous knowledge, considering their ontologies as mere cultural interpretations of a
universal Nature, the ultimate understanding of which is reserved for the Western scientists disposed to
the naturalist ontology (Blaser 2013). Interestingly, the conflict in the Middle Caquetá goes beyond a
simple clash between Indigenous and non-Indigenous ontologies, as the centers of conceptual
production, as cited by Levy, extend beyond Europe, North America, or the Global North; they also
exist in the Vaupés and the Andes. The foreign categories that Levy warned the conference attendees
about include concepts from other Indigenous peoples that align more easily with non-Indigenous
preservation objectives and are thus adopted by environmental organizations. Levy’s reference to the
Vaupés in particular is significant. The fear of conceptual projection from there echoes the Andoque’s
ascription of “ecological nobility” to the Tukanoan-Arawakan Indigenous population of that region,

For a similar notion of control over resources through relations with nonhuman beings outside Amazonia, among the
Siberian Evenki, see Anderson 1998, 75.

168

494

which makes them favorite partners for several environmental agencies, as well as the Andoque’s more
general disdain for these groups for their ideal of reciprocal exchange with nonhumans. In essence, from
the Andoque’s perspective, the imposition of both Indigenous and non-Indigenous categories on their
territory is intrusive and poses threats to territorial integrity and safe interactions with nonhuman
entities.
Therefore, Andoque members emphasize the need to structure environmental projects around local
“thinking” (pensamiento) rather than a foreign one. At an internal assembly in May 2019, Nestor briefed
the participants on a regional meeting with Parques he had attended the previous week. During this
meeting, Parques proposed including the Andoque reserve in their project for the monitoring and
preservation of the arrau river turtle (charapa), which they conduct within the neighboring Miraña
reserve. Nestor relayed that the organization had provided a grim report on the conditions in the remote
parts of their reserve downstream, along the border with the Miraña—an area seldom visited by the
Andoque—describing how charapa hunters from downriver were exploiting the absence of monitoring
on the Andoque stretch of the river. The participants at the internal assembly were both surprised by the
news and angered by these invasions into their territory and the consequent depletion of the river turtle
population. Despite their general indignation towards Parques, they expressed a desire to participate in
the program. However, Adán from the Atta Ant Clan tempered this enthusiasm by saying:
“When an organization begins by looking after the charapas, before you know it, they’re claiming the whole territory
for themselves (se adueñan de todo el territorio). So, we’ve got to think about the risks that come with this program.
Bit by bit, we could end up losing grip on our land. First, they’re on the riverbanks with the charapas, and next thing
you know, Parques will say they’re breeding in the lakes too and start poking around there as well.”

Other participants mentioned that they already have all the knowledge about charapas that they need
from their own traditions, and do not see the point in studying their life cycle or breeding grounds the
way Parques does. Orlando said they should make it clear to Parques that they will handle the charapa
protection with their own thinking, and from their own mambeaderos and malocas; all they would need
from Parques is the resources to do so, like boats, gas, and money. Anchoring a project in local
knowledge is crucial to prevent externally funded projects from undermining territorial integrity and
Indigenous ways of life, ensuring that territorial coexistence with nonhumans is conducted on terms that
are appropriate for humans. In the following section, I will explore additional goals the Andoque have
for collaborating with environmentalists.

495

Converting Money into Salt
What do the Andoque attempt to achieve by their eventual participation in most of the environmental
initiatives proposed to them? In Echeverri’s discussion of the negotiations between their Miraña
neighbors and Parques, with whose Cahuinarí Park their reserve overlaps, he observed the different
goals that the Indigenous and institutional parties attach to the concept of “territorial management.”
While Indigenous management strives to reproduce human life by forming relations with nonhumans
within their territory, preservation policies demarcate human-exclusive areas for wildlife reproduction
(Echeverri 2005, 241). Based on the Miraña’s understanding of “territory” as body, appetite, or desire,
the difference in objectives between the two parties can also be examined through the lens of specific
exchanges between them. According to Echeverri, while Parques emphasized the importance of
intercultural dialogue for exchanging concepts and principles for proper management, the Indigenous
party primarily sought the exchange of food and other objects, as well as access to job vacancies in the
park. Echeverri draws a perspectivist conclusion from this disjunction: for the Miraña, the issue was
“not a question of constructing ‘souls’ (as the conceptual principles of a management programme would
have) but the construction of bodies” (2005, 244), for which relationships with others are essential. This
insight also illuminates the Andoque’s tendency to inflate project budgets for logistics, as described in
the opening anecdote and observed in most other interactions with environmentalists during my
fieldwork. In this final section, I will make a similar claim, but on a broader scope, by shifting the focus
from bodies to territories/worlds as potentially encompassing/encompassed logics of connectivity.
Additionally, in line with this dissertation’s focus, I will stress a/symmetries in exchange—in this case,
with non-Indigenous and nonhuman agents.
When proposing projects to environmental organizations, most Andoque members manifest a
“traditionalist bias” toward projects strengthening la cultura: native language, gardening, maloca
construction, ceremonial life, and traditional craftwork. Although they often complain of economic
distress, most men and women, young and old—except for Levy—show little interest in development
projects that can benefit from external funding to create sustainable income sources, like cacao or
cashew cultivation.
At first glance, the traditionalist bias can be seen as an instrument for obtaining resources for community
members, given that environmental organizations typically prefer funding Indigenous practices and
institutions that are perceived as traditional and, as such, translate to a minimal ecological footprint.
496

While this remains a possibility, Andoque members also show this bias when they have a freer hand in
project elaboration. This was evident in the outcome of the prior consultation process concerning the
REDD+ program Visión Amazonía in July 2019. Despite being practically given free rein by court
ruling to create and implement any ecologically sustainable project with substantial funding, the
Andoque’s proposed projects reflected their traditionalist bias. These included a language revitalization
project, one to strengthen women’s horticultural practices, and another for maloca construction across
all ethnic communities under CRIMA’s jurisdiction.
The traditionalist bias is closely linked with the expectation of monetizing certain activities. This is
evident in the case of the language project. It was first discussed at an internal assembly a month before
the Court ruling. On more than one occasion, and particularly at that assembly, community members
voiced their fear of language loss. As among the Florida Seminole (Cattelino 2008, 71–72), the Andoque
perceive their native language as essential both for ethnic distinctiveness, which is important to benefit
from affirmative action policies, and for exchanges with the land’s nonhuman co-dwellers. As
mentioned in previous chapters, people are largely undecided whether individual dialogue with the
spirits for safety during hunting and fishing is as effective in Spanish as it is in Andoque, but all agree
that ceremonial dances can only be performed in the latter. At the assembly, people agreed that the
elders should urgently teach the language to the younger generation, and that they should immediately
start speaking it more with them. However, this did not translate into any observable increase in intergenerational native language use because community members were waiting for the project to
materialize. However, apart from bringing in a linguist to help them devise a study program, the
project’s core budgetary components were coca purchase for mambeaderos in which the language would
be taught, travel expenses to attend them, and remuneration for elders teaching their relatives. Although
a well-structured study program could facilitate this process, it seemed that the bottleneck that made the
Andoque await a project addressing a pressing problem was the remuneration for elders and logistical
issues that they could have resolved another way. I will revisit this project further ahead.
As seen in Elias’s speech in Fisi’s mambeadero, “necessities” were sometimes cited as an obstacle to
speaking and teaching the language within the nuclear family. During a discussion at an assembly with
SINCHI in April 2019 on promoting native language skills within the family, an Andoque schoolteacher
questioned who would compensate the parents for this task. To be sure, while the Andoque’s views on
the legitimate boundaries of monetizing social transactions may differ in some respects from those in

497

non-Indigenous societies with more disembedded economies, they certainly do not seek payment from
their children for the items or services they provide them. What is interesting in these statements is that
the money that is presumably needed for these intra-family transactions is expected to come from
outside, non-Indigenous sources.
To explain the Andoque’s traditionalist bias and the associated expectation for external funding of
certain local transactions, we need to zoom out to the Andoque’s overall involvement in the market
economy. The previous chapter discussed the dangers faced by the Andoque from nonhuman entities
due to increased pressure on territorial resources. This pressure arises from their participation in
extractive economic activities, which is driven by a need to satisfy their necesidades—that is, to acquire
externally manufactured goods. In the dynamics I described, the more imbalanced the Andoque’s
exchanges with Whites are, the more intense the natural exploitation becomes, leading to an escalation
in retaliatory actions by nonhumans.
In this context, it is important to note that externally manufactured goods have become “necessities” also
because they offer protection against faunal harm. Western medicine is valued for its ability to treat
certain local diseases thought to stem from animals; boots shield people from diseases and pains that are
believed to be contracted through animal footprints, and flashlights and shotguns serve as potent
defenses against animals and indispensable utilities for hunting, taking the place of Indigenous tools that
many no longer know how to make or use. Although technological solutions may partly obviate
cosmological ones (Ingold 2000, 216), Andoque members say that they engage in fewer humannonhuman ceremonial negotiations because they are absorbed by “necessities.” Aside from the time and
energy spent to sustain themselves in unfavorable economic conditions, they say that under the current
conditions, “the people’s mind is elsewhere” (la gente está pensando otra cosa) and specifically
concerned with earning money. As Griffiths (1998, 246) noted for the Nipóde, the Andoque conceive of
the dual economy—in which economic activities directly linking production with consumption coexist
with market-mediated activities—not so much in terms of different activities (e.g., hunting or coca
cultivation can be deployed for both), but in terms of the specific thinking (pensamiento) they apply to
each activity. This means invoking the origin myths that apply to the materials, procedures, and
objectives of each activity and the owner-persons ensuring success and safety in them, including those
concerning trade with Whites. Accordingly, rather than merely diverting attention from subsistence and
ritual life, economic and monetary needs orient people’s thoughts around another cosmological axis,

498

creating different dispositions. Consequently, my interlocutors described a dynamic where the more they
are oppressed economically, the less they engage in and prepare their youth for the ritual activity that
has traditionally protected them from nonhumans. On several occasions, while discussing his different
initiatives, Levy told me that “I will see people dancing” once their income is assured, reflecting a
prioritization pattern found among other Amerindians (e.g., Cattelino 2008, 63). However, we should
critically examine such a needs-based perspective of the economy. The term necesidades refers not only
to the mythic expropriation of specific items, which, along with their derivatives, are now sought
(kahɵ́ɵi, “our missing things”), but also to “that which we find pretty” (kama hɵ́ñői)—a concept that
recognizes the dynamism of desire and the potential for the creation of new needs. As Gordon observed
among the Xikrin, the range of necessities tends to expand in direct relation to the influx of external
resources (Gordon 2006).
The critical role of thinking in distinguishing the two economic models points to an ontology of the dual
economy in which world/territory, or ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí—as defined through the concepts of “connectivity” and
“encompassment” in Chapter 8—is the main category. Similar to how notions such as “The Creator”
indicate (or create) the encompassment of the Animals World by the Andoque World, the dual economy
in the Middle Caquetá represents the encompassment of the connectivity of the Andoque World by the
connectivity of the Whites World. This is evidenced in the fact that many Andoque members frequently
engage in various paid economic activities to acquire access to externally manufactured goods, in a
chain of extraction or production, exchange and consumption activities that link them to non-Indigenous
merchants, consumers, and producers, at the cost of their jeopardized relationships with countless
nonhuman entities in their territory. Within this logic, the use of the term “necessities” also points to the
inconvenient and vulnerable position of the individual caught between two worlds, or two kinds of
connectivity, with the Andoque’s critiques of environmental interventions expressing concerns over the
precariousness of their position in these two worlds.
In the relational framework developed here, I propose that Andoque members strive to preserve and
promote certain Indigenous cultural practices through externally financed projects so that their
engagement in these practices will not result in an even greater economic marginalization. In doing so,
they can nourish their relationships with the human and nonhuman beings of their ñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí without
worsening their position in relationships governed by the logic of the Whites World, and which heavily
rely on monetary access, and perhaps even improve their chances to navigate them. This explains, for

499

example, the enthusiasm of the participants at the territorial management workshop in December 2018,
which surprised me given the many objections these same people had previously expressed at meetings
with Parques—such as the one in the opening vignette—and which could communicate disinterest. They
were interested in it but getting paid for discussing their territorial management allowed them to manage
their position in the Whites World as well, if only to a limited extent.
Furthermore, similar to other Indigenous groups (Nahum-Claudel 2018; Whyte 2017, 157), common
affirmations at Andoque internal assemblies suggest that environmental initiatives are viewed as
opportunities to use funding from non-Indigenous agents to reestablish dialogs with nonhuman entities
and redefine the relationships with them that have been disrupted by unbalanced exchanges with nonIndigenous agents. During the internal assembly in May 2019 where the arrau turtle preservation project
was discussed, participants also considered potential projects to propose to Visión Amazonía following
the prior consultation. Orlando suggested a comprehensive project for territorial management in the
same remote downstream frontier affected by arrau poachers and loggers, focusing on the broader floral
and faunal populations. In this project, he said, community members could inventory the names of the
trees and animals, and the elders would recount the origin myths that prompt their reproduction. Hence,
external funding was deemed necessary for tasks that concern dialogs with nonhuman owner-persons,
which we might categorize as spiritual or ritual.
We can now return to the language project. During my visit in July-August 2021 I followed up on the
progress of this project, which had started a year earlier. Most of the almost COP$600,000,000
(approximately €136,000) that it had received from the government was dedicated to “carnivals”
(carnavales), where members of all age groups and clans participated, and children, younger generations
and in-marrying women of other ethnicities demonstrated the language skills taught to them by elders.
The carnivals included communal meals with local foodstuffs bought from the participants themselves,
and most ended with a non-ritualized version of the Opossum Dance to teach the children traditional
songs. This did not seem to me to be particularly effective in improving spoken language skills, and the
students did not seem to have made significant progress as compared to the general level I had observed
two years earlier. But the project’s importance for its participants seemed to lie elsewhere. My
impression was that it was used for the dual aim of distributing benefits among as many families as

500

possible and enhancing the specific language skills required for negotiations with nonhuman entities in
the ceremonial songs, which is crucial, in turn, for social reproduction.169
Thus, Andoque preferences suggest that environmental initiatives might counterbalance the unequal
exchanges with Whites, at least partially. These initiatives represent a limited reversal of the extractive
logic, which appropriates resources from the Andoque World, undermining its relational network and
the Andoque’s position in it. By contrast, under the preferred model, resources extracted from the
Whites World are fed into the web of relationships constituting the Andoque territory, potentially
enhancing Andoque lives and enabling them to set the tone in interactions with nonhumans. Drawing on
the frequent Andoque comparison of money to vegetal salt, we can interpret this approach as converting
money into salt: transforming the means of communication, exchange, and power and domination in the
Whites World, into a means of communication, exchange, familiarization, and counter-predation in the
Andoque’s ancestral territory. This hypothesis thus illustrates the relatively new form that the
competition over asymmetrical exchanges involving humans and nonhumans, as explored in this
dissertation, takes within the context of the contradicting non-Indigenous dispositions for large-scale
extraction and preservation.
In some respects, this reflects a “conversion between transactional orders,” as defined by Bloch and
Parry (1989), where gains from short-term transactions involving competing individuals are used to
reproduce the long-term social or cosmic order. However, unlike the individual-focused short-term
transactions described by Bloch and Parry, these environmental projects are collective, impacting the
entire reserve rather than just individual members. More generally, this conversion echoes other
Indigenous Amazonian strategies to counterbalance disadvantageous asymmetrical exchanges with
Whites by harnessing their resources for Indigenous advantage (Buitron and Deshoullière 2023; Kelly
2011), an approach that can be termed, in this context, “Indigenizing environmentalism.”
However, I would like to stress here the ontological dimension of this conversion. The metaphoric
conversion of money into salt serves as an example for how, akin to the principle of capital conversion
(Bourdieu 1986), power can be translated from one ontology—or the world where it is stabilized,
understood as connectivity—into another. This concept lays the groundwork for a political ontological
The Andoque are not the only Amazonian society where intra-community reciprocity and sharing is associated with
peaceful coexistence with nonhumans (Blaser 2009; Nahum-Claudel 2018), an association whose ontological meaning has
yet to be explored and theorized.

169

501

approach that, unlike Blaser’s (2009; 2013) focus on the competition among radically incommensurate
ontologies vying for marginalization, replacement, or annihilation of each other, delves into more subtle
processes of continuity between political actions and power dynamics occurring in different, yet
partially overlapping, regimes of connectivity. In the present case, the overlap concerns the Andoque’s
perception of human-nonhuman asymmetry and the strategies they employ to minimize nonhuman
agencies.
The Andoque’s “hierarchical animism” and ontological manipulations underpin their claim to resource
sovereignty. While not reducing their territory’s nonhuman components to mere objects, they indicate in
interactions with environmentalists their recognition of possessing valuable assets in the Whites World,
and insist that the latter acknowledge this value similarly. Based on this recognition, the Andoque wish
to receive funds for projects, which they would then employ to improve connectivity with and exert
greater control over these nonhuman entities, to avert the dangerous potential of their agencies, and this
way participate more safely also in economic exchanges with Whites. The conversion of money to salt,
or the movement across worlds of connectivity, becomes feasible through these strategic shifts in
agency, which has served Andoque captains and ordinary members, as well as clans, in navigating both
predatory and trade exchanges with nonhuman and non-Indigenous actors in the diverse past and present
contexts explored throughout this dissertation.

502

Conclusion: Agnatic Identity and Hierarchical Animism in Amazonia
Throughout this dissertation, I have explored the Andoque’s notions of power and the dynamics of
power within various relational contexts: among group members, between them and nonhuman entities,
and between them and non-Indigenous agents. My discussion addressed three blind spots and underexamined areas in research: first, the anthropocentric bias in the general debate on power within social
sciences and political thinking, which, based on naturalist assumptions, excludes nonhuman entities
from the range of agentive players in power dynamics; second, the tendency in the ethnography of
animist societies, especially Amazonian ones, that acknowledges Indigenous conceptions of nonhuman
agency, to overlook power dynamics, especially ontological asymmetries and socio-political forms of
domination; and lastly, the gap between ontological and political-economic approaches that obstructs
symmetrical analyses of Indigenous peoples’ simultaneous embeddedness in interactions with
nonhuman entities and with non-Indigenous agents, including macro-institutions such as the State and
the Market. In confronting these identified shortcomings in the research, I defined power as the ability to
transition from symmetrical exchanges—of bodies, vital principles, actions, agency, and goods—to
asymmetrical ones that increase one’s capacity to produce persons and counteract harmful asymmetries
or those that do not serve one’s goal of person production. This definition enabled me to trace the
continuities between inter-human power relations and those involving humans and nonhumans. It also
allowed me to simultaneously encompass the Andoque’s strong ethos of trade, the gift dimensions of the
circulating items, and the predatory logic that pervades their cosmology and everyday understandings.
The concept of exchange, which assumes a minimum of three participants—two transacting and one
transacted—paved the way for considering persons not only as subjects of exchange but also as the
transactees, as seen with human orphans traded for axes and nonhuman orphans for vegetal offerings. In
such varied contexts, using the distinction between homosubstitution and heterosubstitution, I illustrated
how power is both founded on and facilitates ontological manipulations and the degradation of agency
among human and nonhuman beings to engage in heterosubstitutive trade with Whites and avoid the
damages of homosubstitutive retaliations by nonhumans.
Drawing on the Andoque’s cosmo-spatial conceptions, I demonstrated how the power of a given river
center relies on the alterity and forces associated with the river source to establish itself, navigate
relationships with other centers, both human and nonhuman, and with the river mouth, which is
associated with Whites. Power in its social form is embodied in the tne’túi force of predation, associated

503

with the river source but pervading all cosmic relations—akin to the pervasive nature of power in
Foucault’s theory. However, mastery and familiarization, two processes anchored in the Andoque’s
strong agnatic ideology and the identity of patriclan centers, are essential for channeling this force and
recasting symmetrical relations of predation and other exchanges with Others into asymmetrical terms.
Yet, the power equilibrium that ensues cannot be captured by such substantive notions as “property,”
which imply possession by an individual or a group (and that, under specific conditions, could become a
“capital”), as it is contingent upon the ongoing success in harnessing the agencies of others in the myriad
relationships involved. It is a form of magnification (Costa and Fausto 2019, 214), that, in the Andoque
case, is best conceptualized as emanation from a given center, from one’s seat (kupa), itself linked with
the clan’s origin. Space and kinship thus emerge as potent idioms for articulating, generating, and
challenging asymmetries.
The shift from “articulation” to “generation,” or from representation to action, captures a key theme of
this dissertation. My analysis of Andoque mythology and its practical implications, along with people’s
sense of being dumbfounded when confronted with fi’du beings—or money, as I have suggested—
reveals that symbolization in Andoque ontology transcends the mere depiction of objects (or likely
subjects) in reality. It functions as an instrument of power, serving to contain this object (or subject),
revealing its potentials and vulnerabilities, with the aim, optimistically, of mastery. Within this context,
the notion of agnatic descent is pivotal. The term for myth, ḭpoíkó, which means “that which becomes a
father” or “that which originates from the father,” casts the patriclan as the protagonist in the endeavor
of symbolizing the world and making it manageable, much like Nietzsche’s concept of “will to power.”
However, my research has also demonstrated that knowledge is a scarce and contested resource in a
symbolic political economy—or cosmopolitical economy, as it centers around powerful nonhuman
entities whose assistance is far from assured.
Evidently, viewing nonhumans as agents within power relations—guided by the animist ontological
assumptions of my interlocutors—marks a significant departure from conventional social sciences and
political theory. In these fields, agency is often reserved for humans, who are considered the sole social,
moral, and political actors, while nonhumans are relegated to the status of objects for exploitation,
manipulation, or at best “actants” that influence outcomes (Latour 2005). However, my dissertation has
repeatedly emphasized a model of sociality where the interaction between two individuals invariably
includes an additional, non-physically human actor, such as shared food or coca powder, or the maloca

504

in which they sit. This broadening of the social realm introduces a level of instability to power
asymmetries within specific relationships, as these asymmetries are contingent upon prior established
imbalances between human and nonhuman actors, which may shift due to events within this or other
inter-human relations involving the same human participant. However, as both my research and prior
studies have demonstrated (Descola 2005, 31–32, 488–490), animism is an inherently creative and
dynamic ontology, characterized by the capacity for manipulation of actors and their agency: a sorcerer
taking the form of a jaguar and turning his victim into game, a grandfather changing meat given to his
grandchild to a fruit, or an Andoque captain transforming rubber trees into manioc plant. Therefore, the
potential to manipulate or reduce the agency of nonhuman entities exists as a viable action, yet this
diminishment is unlikely to be permanent or to reduce the nonhuman entirely to an object.
A key finding of this dissertation is the correlation between agnatic ideology and the reduction of
agency, or the near objectification, of affinal Others. Beyond the previously discussed concept of clanbased symbolization, I have traced the growing aspirations for patrilineal continuity and asymmetry in
affinal exchange to the Andoque’s desire for demographic growth following the rubber genocide and
their participation in the region’s extractive economy. Lastly, I delineated the complex power relations
formed through predatory and trade exchanges between the Andoque, non-Indigenous agents, and
nonhuman entities, where the agency of the latter is simultaneously manipulated or minimized, feared,
and required to assist the Andoque in achieving various goals and coexisting peacefully alongside these
and other nonhumans within their territory.
At this juncture, it is essential to return to the analogy drawn in the introduction between violence and
power/domination, on the one hand, and predation/alliance and familiarization and mastery, on the
other. Similar to violence, predation/alliance has the potential for symmetry and operates with
mechanisms inherent in the “given” plane of reality, which, in Andoque ontology, is affinity.
Conversely, familiarization and mastery resemble power/domination in producing asymmetry through
the “constructed” dimension of reality, which, as per the Andoque, is consanguinity. In their advocacy
for mastery as an idiom to unravel and comprehend Amazonian asymmetrical relations, Costa and
Fausto specify their preference for “dominion” over “domination,” as the latter denotes greater hierarchy
and relates to non-Amazonian practices like hospitality and domestication (2019, 217). Nonetheless, I
argue that the Andoque’s exercise or power through the “agnatic” version of familiarization and
mastery, which sometimes leads to a greater reduction of agency and subordination of the “pets”

505

conceptualized as orphans, indeed verges on domination. This suggests positioning the Andoque’s
animism closer to the hierarchical end of a spectrum that spans from egalitarian to hierarchical animism.
I will elaborate on this point by positioning my findings within the context of the ethnography of the
Caquetá-Putumayo and, subsequently, of broader Northwest Amazonia.
My study offered additional insights into the recent history of the People of the Center, which
anthropologists have previously interpreted through the transition from the “Basket of Darkness” to the
“Basket of Life,” and from the “Time of Animals” to the “Time of Abundance”—transformations
actively enacted by these peoples in the wake of the Casa Arana genocide (Echeverri 2010; Lucas 2019,
115–40). Among the Murui-Muina, Féénemɨna, and Bora, this shift is characterized by the dichotomy
between war, predation, and aggressive clan identities on the one hand, and peace, production,
reproduction, and ethnic inclusion, on the other. While the latter is celebrated and prioritized in public
discourse, the former is concealed and limited to the private realms of sorcery and healing. Similarly, for
the Andoque, post-genocide recovery also entailed the cessation of inter-clan warfare. Landaburu
(1993) described this period’s shift not only as one from war to peace but also from war to trade,
symbolized by the replacement of the old god Ñé’ñéfi, the central figure in myths, by the more
contemporary Egret of the Center, marking a transition from the cannibal eagle to the trading egret.
Following Landaburu’s analysis, I have examined these two mythic layers as representative of two
distinct cosmological and politico-economic systems of exchange: the cannibalistic-homosubstitutive
system and the captaincy-heterosubstitutive one. While the former aligns with the regional “Basket of
Darkness,” my exploration of the latter reveals essential elements of hierarchy and graded agency that,
while acknowledged in the People of the Center’s ethnography, are not directly associated with the
discourse of the “Basket of Life.” The baskets paradigm is closely linked to the scholarly interest in the
regional moral discourse, as the Basket of Life is “instrumental in constructing the ideology of a united
moral community” (Echeverri 2022, 78–79, my translation). Accordingly, anthropologists of the People
of the Center have emphasized morality as the key factor explaining a perceived ontological gap and
inherent asymmetries between humanity and nonhumanity (Echeverri 2001; Griffiths 1998; Londoño
Sulkin 2012). By contrast, due to the ambiguity of moral discourse among the Andoque, I was able to
uncover the predatory logic underlying it and demonstrate how this gap is actively produced and is
continuous with asymmetries among human agents.

506

Significantly, I have shown that the heterosubstitutive aspects of the captaincy system are compatible
not only with recent peaceful activities but also with the pre-genocide slave trade and the region-wide
practice of substitutive vegetal offerings to owner-persons, which likely predates the rubber boom by a
considerable margin, and which reflects the predatory logic of non-reciprocity. Thus, rather than framing
this as a diachronic rupture, and while acknowledging the recent consolidation of the egret mythical
layer, I highlight the synchronic coexistence of the two exchange systems both before and after the
genocide. My findings challenge the notion of a conclusive shift away from war and predation,
underlining the importance of the belligerent Multiplying Tree Dance and other literary and ritual
practices that have facilitated the Andoque’s resurgence in predatory prowess and their pursuit of
asymmetrical marital exchanges in the years following their regrouping. Lastly, my inquiry into ritual
transformations complicates the binary of war and peace. The prevalent appreciation for the red,
bellicose specialization and the devaluation of the white, “calm” specialization directs me to reframe this
shift as increasing emphasis on agnatic descent over affinal reciprocity. Adding to Lucas’ (2019, 138)
observation on the “verticalization,” in S. Hugh-Jones’ terms (1994), of Bora shamanism in the
transition from the Time of Animals to the Time of Abundance, my conclusion suggests that the recent
history of the People of the Center also involved a tectonic movement between the two competing
kinship conceptions underlying these two ideal types.
This conclusion also advances the argument recently presented by Lucas, in which she shifts the
discussion of ontological asymmetry between humans and nonhumans in the Caquetá-Putumayo region
from morality to politics. She posits that this asymmetry is modeled on the captain-orphan relationship.
By conceptualizing the captain-orphan hierarchy in terms of agency and investigating the connection
between the patriclan, its origins, and traditions with its members’ agency, my analysis leads to a
Hegelian-like conclusion: the captain-orphan hierarchy is a particular manifestation of the perpetual
ambition of individuals to utilize affines and members of other clans to achieve the objectives set forth
by their origin—whether as workers, or, as mythology suggests, as yarumo plants for coca preparation—
when this ambition encounters no substantial agency to oppose it. Consequently, the agency of the
affinal other may be diminished but never wholly extinguished. Thus, the increasing ontological
asymmetry between humans and nonhumans should be considered in the context of the evolving tension
between clan identity and affinal reciprocity.

507

This prompts us to expand the geographical scope of our discussion to the Tukanoan-Arawakan peoples
of Northwest Amazonia. The Tukanoans and Arawakans residing among them, such as the Yucuna and
Cabiyari (unlike those of the Upper Río Negro), are typically noted in regional anthropology for their
reciprocal exchanges with nonhumans that are analogous to their reciprocal affinal exchanges among
distinct language groups (Descola 1998; 2013, 345–52). This stands in stark contrast to the People of the
Center’s efforts to deny reciprocity with animals, whom they regard with aversion, and their disdainful
reference to these neighbors as “People of Yuruparí” or “People of Animals” (Karadimas 2005b, 30).
Thus, Echeverri (2001) has specifically delineated the ontological human-nonhuman asymmetry of the
People of the Center in contrast to the Tukanoans. Considering the significant role of Tukanoan
ethnography in shaping the concept of “perspectivism” (K. Århem 1993; Viveiros de Castro 1998, 471),
Londoño’s (2017) argument that the People of the Center possess a substantive version of perspectivism
can also be seen as a counterpoint to their “Tukanoization.”
Nonetheless, these groups share many similarities with the Andoque and other Peoples of the Center not
found among most other Amazonians. These similarities include notions of hierarchy, the political
economy of knowledge, consumption of coca powder, patrilocal residence, and most importantly, an
ideology of agnatic descent, as well as the concept of competition and rivalry among affinal groups.
However, a crucial distinction between the Andoque and these groups, potentially explaining their
differing attitudes towards nonhumans, lies in the fact that among the Tukanoans and Arawakans,
agnatic ideology and inter-clan competition are closely complemented by an alliance-based ideology and
an egalitarian ethos that fosters reciprocity between affines, alongside ritual and spatial mechanisms
facilitating the inclusion of matrilateral consanguines (K. Århem 1981; Cayón 2011; Estorniolo 2020,
18; Hill 1984; S. Hugh-Jones 1993). Such mechanisms are either absent or not as pronounced among the
Andoque. The white specialization, which seems to serve this role, is currently in decline, as is the
practice of naming daughters after their mothers’ clans. As a counter-image of the Tukanoans, the
Andoque’s less pronounced focus on inter-clan reciprocity parallels their perception of nonhumans as
enemies, with whom relations follow a logic of mutual predation. In this aspect, they resemble the
Arawak groups of the Upper Río Negro (Kurripaco, Wakuenai, and Baniwa), who are also patrilineal,
patrilocal, hierarchical, linguistically endogamous, and, like the People of the Center but unlike the
Tukanoans, practiced cannibalism in the past. However, similar to the Tukanoans, these Arawakans
maintain a Dravidian preference for cross-cousin marriage, reflecting a more immediate reciprocity
between affinal groups than observed among the Andoque.
508

In other words, in Northwest Amazonia, there exists a spectrum of ideologies: some exclusively
prioritize patriclan identity and hierarchy, while others complement them with affinal reciprocity, each
corresponding to differing perspectives on nonhumans and their agency. A pronounced emphasis on
affinal exchange with both humans and nonhumans, as seen with the Tukanoan peoples, tends to
correlate with a more ontological symmetry. Conversely, a strong emphasis on patrilineal continuity,
with fewer mechanisms in place to ensure affinal reciprocity, may lead to ontological asymmetries. In
the case of the Andoque, this is manifested by a tendency to diminish the agency of nonhumans, to
regard them more as resources than as social entities, and to view their worlds and origins as subordinate
to their own. This contrast may also be articulated through a moral discourse, which appears to play a
more significant role among neighboring Peoples of the Center than it does with the Andoque. Thus, I
propose that further investigation into the tension between patrilineality and affinity among other
Peoples of the Center, particularly examining how each pole relates to agency and interactions with
nonhumans, could illuminate the intricate links between morality, ontology, and power dynamics in
post- and possibly also pre-genocide periods.
Here it is noteworthy that the Tukanoan universe is not devoid of ontological asymmetry either.
Substantive perspectivism with a notion of “Real Humanity” reserved only for human-bodied persons
also features in Tukanoan mythology, particularly in layers related to “vertical shamanism” linked with
sacred paraphernalia transmitted within patrilines and embedded within social hierarchy (S. Hugh-Jones
2009). As I have shown in Chapter 9, the ɵpáha substitutive offering modality, which is based on the
perception of vegetal substances as hierarchically inferior to human souls, is only attested in Northwest
Amazonia, among these groups as well. While earlier analyses of human-nonhuman affinal reciprocity
within the Vaupés social complex highlighted human-nonhuman symmetry, particularly through
Reichel-Dolmatoff’s thermodynamic model (Reichel 1989; Reichel-Dolmatoff 1971; 1976; van der
Hammen 1992; von Hildebrand 1983) later studies on the Tukanoan Macuna emphasized the asymmetry
that reflects the privileged role of humans, especially shamans, in fertilizing nonhuman species and
maintaining cosmic order (K. Århem 2001; Cayón 2011; 2017). This asymmetry has clear agnatic
connotations, as is evident in the role of the yuruparí rituals transmitted within the patriclan—with their
secret flutes cult, male initiation, and strong association with agnatic ancestors—in ordering the cosmos,
fertilizing it and making it safe for humans (K. Århem 1981; Cayón 2010; Hill 1984; Cayón 2011; S.
Hugh-Jones 1979). Although the Andoque and other People of the Center often refer to these groups as
“the People of Yuruparí,” this ritual may not serve as the best hallmark for capturing the differences
509

between the two cultural complexes. Ethnographers of People of the Center have pointed out rituals that
show similarities to the yuruparí cult (Guyot 1972, 167; Londoño Sulkin 2000, 386; Lucas 2019, 342–
43), and Karadimas (2008) has impressively revealed continuities between this cult and the ceremonies
and myths of the Peoples of the Center, rooted in the model of the parasitic wasp and its reproductive
mode—recalling that Sḭ́ di, a central deity for the Andoque associated with ancestry and fertility, is a
wasp. As I have demonstrated, the symbol that captures the difference between the Tukanoan complex
and the People of the Center may well be their distinct forms of tobacco consumption—smoking or
sniffing versus using it as a paste, respectively. While tobacco is associated with affinal relatives
throughout Northwestern Amazonian mythology, the People of the Center’s practice of mixing it with
vegetal salt—linked with semen—serves to make it safe for the patriclan, and, among some of them, as
the patriclan’s very essence. This powerful substance’s role in dominating nonhumans is contingent
upon the prior domination of human affines.
Returning to the yuruparí ritual, the presence and strength of mechanisms that counterbalance such
agnatically-linked cults and the varying degrees of human-nonhuman asymmetry they entail are
significant. These differences may have implications for the strategies employed by each cultural
complex in engaging with extractivism and the contemporary “green economy.” As mentioned in
Chapter 14, the Andoque project their environmental intervention-related frustrations and fears onto the
Indigenous peoples of the Tukanoan complex, specifically because of the latter’s increased reciprocity
with nonhumans.170 A comparative study could investigate the similarities and differences in how each
complex interacts with environmental agencies, considering the possible correlation with perceptions of
nonhumans as enemies, allies, or “orphans.”
The presence of hierarchical animism among the Peoples of the Center, as well as the Tukanoans and
Arawakans, is evidenced by their practice of substituting animal and human souls with vegetal offerings
(K. Århem 1996, 192; van der Hammen 1992, 317; von Hildebrand 1983, 57), suggesting that hierarchy
can coexist with animism, as observed in Southeast Asia (K. Århem 2015b; Sprenger 2015). Fausto’s
work also supports the existence of agentive hierarchy in Amazonia, indexed by the food chain (Fausto
2007a, 503). Contrary to Descola’s (2001, 113) argument, my study demonstrates that heterosubstitutive
exchanges—a characteristic of hierarchical animism—occur in Lowland South America with indigenous
Echeverri: “Perhaps, the People of Animals would better suit the environmental notion of the ‘ecologically noble savage’”
(2022, 273, n.91; my translation).

170

510

items, not just those introduced by non-Indigenous agents. The heterosubstitutive logic of the Andoque’s
offerings cannot be attributed solely to the influence of the slave trade. This is clear from the
heterosubstitutive offerings of the Tukanoans and Arawakans, who only traded their Makú servants for
non-Indigenous goods on rare occasions (Santos Granero 2009b, 70). According to Descola,
heterosubstitution requires instrumental and subordinating dispositions towards nonhumans, as are
evident in animal domestication, which is absent in Amazonia. He suggests that Amazonian societies
only display heterosubstitutive homologies between natural kinds and artifacts, on one hand, and
persons, on the other, in societies with secret flute cults, where these elements are nonetheless
considered inalienable possessions (Descola 2001, 111–13). For K. Århem, animal husbandry is a key
condition for the development of hierarchical animism—which entails heterosubstitutive sacrifices—
alongside village-centered domestication, where the forest is cleared for human habitation (2015a).
Building on this, I argue that plant domestication and cultivation can also underpin hierarchical animism
and the heterosubstitution it facilitates, particularly when linked with agnatic descent notions.
In Andoque mythology, an agnatic emphasis reshapes the typical Amazonian narrative, which often
attributes the origin of various cultural items and practices to exchanges with affinal relatives, either
through gifting or theft (Lévi-Strauss 1964). Andoque myths portray the acquisition of the three main
cultivars—manioc, tobacco, and coca—as assertions of agnatic agency, simultaneously diminishing or
contesting the agency of the affinal relatives from whom these vital plants were claimed (M1; M3; M14;
M12). As I have argued, the sexual ethic surrounding the production of coca and tobacco among this and
other People of the Center, as well as some of their myths (García 2018, 412–22; Karadimas 2005b,
129–42), reflect a similar notion. It is in this light that we should consider Echeverri’s (2001) argument,
which posits horticulture and the “decontamination” involved in processing foodstuffs, rather than
hunting, as central to the ethos and cosmology of these peoples. Such “agnatization” represents a more
dominant relationship with plants and eventually allows for greater freedom in trading their derivatives
than common Amazonian appropriative acts of familiarization. While the Andoque may not engage in
an ancestor cult, hold elaborate funerary rites, or possess a robust conception of “the good death,” the
pronounced agnatic ideology they share with other Northwest Amazonians reflects a notion of ancestry,
which, in its more developed form, distinguishes hierarchic animism from egalitarian animism, as the
comparison between Southeast Asia and Amazonia shows (K. Århem 2015a, 289–92). Therefore, we
may see the Andoque’s animism as positioned halfway between these two models.

511

As Descola suggests in his comparison between Melanesia and Amazonia, “it seems reasonable to
assume that what may account for the greater institutional complexity of Melanesia is the multiplicity of
options opened up by the various combinations between what we may call ‘homosubstitution’ and
‘heterosubstitution’” (2001, 110). Similarly, in Andoque animism, power dynamics involve alternating
between these two types of exchange in a bidirectional movement: from the “trading egret” and the
captaincy system to the “cannibal eagle” and the cannibalistic cosmo-economic system reminiscent of a
Clastrian “society against the State,” with its foregrounding of violence over domination, the mercurial
nature of power, and the looming threat to eat the captain’s son, thus denying him continuity (see M9).
Power allows those attuned to Sḭ́ di and his transformed form, Egret of the River Source, to successfully
navigate relationships with humans and nonhumans, appropriating more bodies, agencies, vital
principles, and goods, than they relinquish. Despite the waning of the captaincy institution—as
evidenced by the diminished economic role of captains, decreased assistance in dance organization and
maloca construction, and the emergence of alternative leadership roles among the younger members—
the heterosubstitutive rationale that underpins it remains pervasive within the Andoque cosmos and
society. Owner-persons and ordinary members are still seen as captains who manage exchangeable
orphan/crops.
However, through my conversations with Andoque men and women of various ages and clans, including
their non-Andoque spouses, I learned that the potential for hierarchy and asymmetry in their ontology
does not necessarily mean that Andoque members are comfortable or feel secure in their current position
within power dynamics involving non-Indigenous agents, nonhuman entities, and even among
themselves. They express genuine concern over non-reciprocal exchanges with Whites, illnesses and
misfortunes resulting from owner-persons retaliating against those who exploit their personnel,
insufficient ritual actions to appease these entities, the allure of drug use among the youth, the prevailing
distrust between captains, cabildo leaders, and other members, the diminished authority of captains in
the eyes of younger or non-maloquero individuals, and the lack of vital competition among them. Given
the historical backdrop of the Andoque’s genocidal exploitation, near demographic extinction and
unfathomable loss of oral traditions, increasing assimilation into Colombian society, and ongoing
precarious position in the regional economy, it is pertinent to note that this research has examined power
within a society enduring a persistent crisis of power.

512

Key factors in this crisis include the constructs of “community” and its territorial counterpart, “reserve.”
Due to the broad scope of this dissertation, these have not been analyzed here as actors in power
dynamics, particularly those among the Andoque as members of distinct clans. However, the interrelated
concepts of clan identity and the rivalry and suspicion among clans provide much of the necessary
background to understand the challenges faced by a “community” composed of different clans. The
collaboration among clans within a shared framework is often compromised by ongoing disputes.
Similar to other People of the Center grappling with the concept of an “Indigenous community”
(Echeverri 2009), the Andoque seem to struggle with reconciling clan with community membership.
Yiñékɒ’s remarkable feat of uniting individuals of diverse “origins” and aligning them with a common
project—if it indeed functioned as seamlessly as members recall—did not survive him. In retrospect,
this unity appears to have hinged on the unique conditions of that period, such as the immediate trauma
of the genocide and his personal charisma. Accepting Landaburu’s (1993) persuasive argument that
Yiñékɒ anchored his group’s overarching, supra-clan identity in the name “People of the Axe,” with its
connotations of trade, labor, and productivity, it becomes clear that the Andoque’s involvement in a
collective economic endeavor, namely rubber tapping, was pivotal in uniting diverse clans. It is to be
hoped that the communal framework for participating in contemporary environmental initiatives,
particularly those generating income flux like carbon trading, may likewise be a significant factor in
fostering effective cooperation among members of different clans in other areas.
Things are far from ideal on a clan basis, either. Precisely one year prior to penning this conclusion, on
December 24, 2022, I awoke to a text message from an Andoque woman residing in Bogotá. She
conveyed the harrowing news that my dear friend Lisimaco, Fisi’s son, had been murdered the day
before. The perpetrator, whom I knew well and with whom I had stayed during my fieldwork as well,
was his patrilateral cousin. The murder, carried out under the influence of alcohol acquired with profits
from an environmental project, was also, as witnesses have informed me, a deliberate act, culminating a
series of violent exchanges between the families of Fisi and his brother under similar circumstances. I
was immediately reminded of the cannibal eagle tale—the Eagle Clan’s downfall, as I had been told, is
its unrestrained anger. This myth, along with the concepts of familiarization and resisting affinization,
which until then had been merely academic to me, took on a chillingly tangible form, becoming a matter
of life and death. Again, Nénéfi failed to rein in his voracious “pet,” or tutelary spirit, nourished by his

513

wife until it chose to prey on its owner’s kin and personnel.171 Could this tragic misidentification of kin
be the result of “affinization” by money that had not been properly converted into salt, having not been
tempered through the symbolization of myth and ritual to subjugate it to one’s project of well-being and
prosperity, leading men to regard their cousins as enemies instead? Salt itself was capricious, as
Lisimaco once pointed out when I stumbled on a slick forest path under the burden of the plants we had
collected to prepare salt, and when he shouldered my load on our journey back, ensuring that when
cooked, not a speck of this vital substance would be lost, so crucial is it for managing the world. But
perhaps these are simply the follies of Lady Salt’s elder sons, who allowed themselves to be beguiled by
strangers along their path.172 It may be that the youngest son will soon see the salt plant for what it truly
is, hold it tight, and dominate it.

M1. Coca of the Animals (Nestor and Fisi, 20/10/18)173
Lady Sun (Ḭɒ̰pakamikn), the daughter of Shadow Egg (Ká’hoi hádi), planted an earthworm that had
sucked blood from her sister’s leg while she was planting peanuts, thus creating the first coca.174 She
took charge of it, and the animals, who were the men of that time, came to her place to consume coca.
She commanded them, teaching them how to prepare coca and instructing them on what to do: picking
the leaves correctly, toasting them, sifting the coca powder... She tested them to see who would learn her
teachings, such as not cutting off the buds while picking the leaves and weeding around the plants. She
sent people to find taafi, yarumo leaves for ashes [to mix with the toasted leaves’ powder]. The first
worker encountered a man in the forest. “Where are you going?” the man asked him. “I am looking for
yarumo,” the worker replied. “Well, so go look for it!” said the man, who was the yarumo tree himself,
sending him away. The worker returned to Lady Sun, saying, “I couldn’t find any.” “Good, so you go
now,” she said to another, but the same thing happened to him, and so on, until she sent Egret (Yo’fí).
Egret said, “I for one will find it!” He left, and when he encountered a man who asked him, “Where are
you going?”, Egret immediately replied: “I came looking for you!” Embracing him, he carried him back
home under his armpit [similar to how men carry yarumo leaves today]. That is why egrets have a small
plumage under their wings—it is the yarumo that Egret once held there. When he returned, Lady Sun
said: “You indeed paid attention [to what I have taught you]! This one is learning alright!” When it was
time to sift the coca powder, she ordered different people to do it. Parrot sifted too hard and ended up
covered with powder, which is why this parrot is green today. She ordered Owl to sift, but he kept
touching his face and hair, and so became wrinkled and grey-haired. To this day, whenever someone
touches his face or hair while sifting or consuming coca, the touched area becomes wrinkled, and the
touched hair turns grey. Only Egret remained white and clean without powder on him of all the sifters
because he sat peacefully. That is why whatever one does the first time one consumes coca, sticks with
them. When it was time to finish sifting, most animals had only a small amount of coca powder, except
for Egret, whose calabash vessel was full. The sifters served coca to each other. Almost everyone
immediately swallowed the powder they were served, but Egret kept his dry inside his beak to add it
later to his calabash vessel, adding it to the coca he was sifting. Tapir consumed some coca, laid down
Nestor was the main narrator, with Fisi correcting and commenting on his version.
In other versions, where she does not create the coca out of an earthworm, she is called Mánóḛḭkamikn—Lady Protector,
which also indicates her filiation with Mánóḛḭdɨ (Protector) who appears in M2 (see Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 162).
