and started farting. He remained in that state the next day and ever since. Those who consumed coca,
fell asleep, and remained asleep the next day, became nocturnal animals, while those who woke up early
after consuming coca remained that way, becoming the animals that are already awake at 5 am. Bodido
[Momotus momota?], who was once very beautiful, consumed coca, returned home, slept with his wife,
and his beautiful colors faded away at once. He became grey and old, and remained grey to this day.
And so, a young man who consumes coca and sleeps with a woman immediately turns old. [The story
provides other examples of animals who consumed coca and remained ever since with the same
appearances or behavior they exhibited at that first formative coca consumption]. That people will
remain as they behaved when they first consumed coca—that was the curse that Lady Sun cast on
humanity. The people became upset, saying: “How can a woman control us like that?” Parrot, realizing
that Egret was about to win Lady Sun’s contest, took a bá’si [a red, guayaba-like unidentified fruit] and
smeared a red spot on her seat. When the spot was brought to her attention, she felt ashamed, thinking
that she was menstruating. She went to her hammock in the rear of the maloca and relinquished her
place to Parrot. Upon realizing that she had been tricked, she cast a curse on us men: “Well, now that
you have done this to me, the coca will stay for you. But we’ll see if you can handle it. If you cannot
control yourselves, maintain the necessary diet, abstain from anger, laziness, and thought about women,
you will end up even worse than as you are today.” But if everything had continued as it was, she would
have simply passed the control over coca to one of them—to Egret—making it much easier for us today
to manage coca.
M2. Coca of the Orphans175
He was called Protector (Mánóḛḭdɨ); he ruled well, and he was good. The people liked going to his
place. He used to organize great assemblies with food for the people in the center. He is Egret of the
Center (Dʉiyo’fí); he is also called Source of Abundance (Tó̰’ḛ ́ ḭdɨ). He is the one who felled the
Speaking Tree [M4]. His wife was named Yellow Leaf (Dópukn), or else Lady Manioc for Manicuera
(Pa̰ḛ ́ pakn). She became angry with him for not doing anything; he used to pass the time seated, thinking.
Once, when he asked her for casabe to eat, she reproached him, so he said: “I am not going to eat
anymore. I need to think from what else my sons will live off after I disappear from this place.” And he
left; he went under the earth. The sons reproached their mother for his absence. “You reproached our
father for your casabe, and now no one is going to eat it! You will eat it by yourself!” Then, for that
175

Source: Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 73–74.

550

reason, she also disappeared, becoming manioc for manicuera (pa̰ḛ́pa). After her disappearance they
became orphans, alone at home. The younger brother sustained himself by licking a pot in which the
manicuera (kó’ko) had been prepared. The elder brother did not feel hunger. He remained seated,
thinking: “What will we do now that we have neither mother nor father? How will we live? Why did our
parents abandon us?” While he was thinking that, underneath them, underneath the earth, the one who
had been buried, the father, made a sound: tan! And then he did it again. The following night he made a
louder sound: hum! The younger brother heard it. He went and sat down next to his elder brother. The
elder brother asked him: “What was that sound?” “You should now! As my elder, you should know!”
The following night, it was heard even louder. The elder brother said: “This is what I am talking about.
What is it?” “You should know, you who are elder than I.” “But what can it be?”. “This is our father
coming,” said the younger brother. The following night, it already sounded closer to the house. The
elder said: “This is what I have been talking about. What is it?” “I don’t know, go and have a look. It
makes a sound over there, under the peach palm.” The elder brother then went to search. The younger
remained seated in the house, at the place where yarumo leaves are burnt for coca preparation. They saw
a leaf budding like a needle, like a thorn. The elder brother said: “This is the thing that makes a sound.
But what is it?” “What can it be! This is called hí’pı̋ e (coca)”, the younger brother named it and said:
“This is coca. Do not touch it!” The elder asked: “And what are we going to do?” “What do you mean,
‘what are we going to do?’” It is going to explain what we are going to do. Our father turned into that to
explain to us. He is going to teach us. He will tell us what we should do. Whoever wants to know in the
future, must do just as we do.” The younger brother sent the elder brother to where the coca was. The
younger brother asked the father, and the father said: “Son! Do it like this. Behave like that. I have
disappeared in order to teach you.” He showed them where to make the mambeadero. The father
continued, saying: “I am going to live above. Listen to me and you will see that you are learning.” The
younger brother listened, and the father made the sound: taa kan huuuuu [a thunder]. The other brother
asked: “What is it?” “It’s our father. It is Sḭ́ di, it is Carnivorous Thunder (Sḭ́ di Dú’di).” “And what does
he say?” “He says that this land will be flooded. He says that the water of fire is coming from the east
and will burn the entire earth. This is what Sḭ́ di is telling us […].”

M3. Origin of the Maloca and Cultivars (Fisi, 19/7/19)
Egret of the River Source came down from the river source to the center to live with the youngest daughter
of Shadow Egg (Ká’hoihádi).176 Shadow Egg did not have a proper maloca, he lived under a pile of leaves
and thorns.177 His daughter had had many previous suitors, but the father used to confuse them (yoóka
iboñe nyatii, literally: “he made them useless”), hiding the trees so that they could not perceive them and
build a maloca.178 Egret of the River Source thought: “I am capable of doing it!.” He arrived one afternoon
at Shadow Egg’s house. “Have you arrived?” asked Shadow Egg. “I have arrived,” replied Egret of the
River Source. “Good,” said the father-in-law, “here is my hammock, take a rest there; it’s right next to my
daughter’s, look at her! But eat first!” He ordered his daughter to serve him food so he could confuse him,
as he had done to the previous suitors, but Egret of the River Source refused to eat or drink, nor did he
sleep. He remained seated silently, looking all around him. He went for a walk around the house. When
he returned, the father-in-law asked him, “Son-in-law, where have you gone?” “No, I just went for a walk,”
replied Egret of the River Source. “What are you thinking of?” asked the father-in-law. “No, just thinking
that I want to build myself a shack,” replied Egret of the River Source. “But I couldn’t find anything here;
there are no trees around.” When he passed by the daughter’s hammock, she told him: “My father hid all
the trees; he has them hidden on the other side of the stream. Go there, and the trees will talk to you as if
they were humans, but you must say: ‘It is you I am coming for!’” She also told him to catch a tinamou
(Crypturellus undulatus), smoke it on top of some vegetal salt, and say a certain spell to be able to find
the pui palms (Lepidocaryum tenue) required for the rooftop. Egret of the River Source did as she told
him, found anacondas that he turned into posts and beams and found the pui for the roof. He erected the
posts and tied the beams, then climbed to the top beam and spread the pui leaves, that immediately became
the thatched four main sides of the maloca. Shadow Egg then arrived, and Egret of the River Source told
him: “Why did you come before I am finished? It’s your fault I haven’t finished the roof, now help me to
thatch the remaining four corners.” Before Shadow Egg wove the remaining pui, Egret of the River Source
invited him to consume the coca he had brought with him from the river source and lick the ambíl that he
had brought. If Shadow Egg did not intrude upon Egret of the River Source, today we would also be able
to make the roof that way, instead of working so laboriously in thatching it. Next, Egret of the River

Source made the coca mortar, the mambeadero, the macana club. Then he invited his father-in-law to
consume coca and lick ambíl with him and told him that he was going. “Stay here with your wife; she
wants to live with you,” said Shadow Egg. “No,” said Egret of the River Source, “I am going to the house
of my father and my mother, and she should stay with her father and her mother.” He gave Shadow Egg
a torch and told him: “when you hear a thunder from the river source, use it to burn my garden that I made
down the path, where you see a coco leaf.” And he went upriver. When Shadow Egg heard the thunder,
he went to where his son-in-law had told him to go, but could not see any garden; it seemed to him like a
usual forest plot. He lit it with the torch, and everything burned at once, becoming a vast garden. The
smoke that rose to the sky fell back on the earth as rain. With it, all the fruits and cultivars that “our
mother” (katí), whose name is Lady Beetle of Life (Pḭɵfikn), Egret of the River Source’s mother,179 had
taken with her to the sky when the flood had begun, in the past, came down to the garden and became
planted there. These were all the classes of proper fruits and cultivars, for humans, that we eat today—
pineapple, bitter manioc, sweet manioc, everything. Previously, there had only been wild fruits for
animals. By naming each one of them, Egret of the River Source made us these fruits so we can live like
human beings. Egret of the River Source returned to Shadow Egg, who was surprised that the garden was
full of planted cultivars, and told him, his wife, his son, and his daughter how to collect and prepare coca,
pineapple, tobacco, and manioc for manicuera, respectively. Egret of the River Source’s mother descended
as well and prepared caguana and manicuera beverages. When these were ready, she gave them to her
daughter-in-law, who drank the caguana first and the manicuera second, and Egret of the River Source
did the same, to have first a boy and then a girl. When the daughter-in-law peeled the manioc for
manicuera—that species was Egret of the River Source’s grandmother, who had transformed into the
plant—the tuber made a sound: “Po!”. That sound augured that her son will be a captain, po’soɵ. Egret of
the River Source invited his father-in-law to consume coca from the freshly harvested coca and invited
him and his mother-in-law to lick from the freshly harvested tobacco. Egret of the River Source then
organized a dance, to protect the maloca and guarantee there would be plenty of crops in the future. After
the first song, when Egret of the River Source sat down on his seat (kupa) at the mambeadero, his name
changed to Egret of the Center. He then said:180 “I am Egret of the Center. We are going to consume coca,
we are going to lick tobacco. Yes. This is my name. I am from the Center of the Earth. Come. Here I am

M5. Origin of Trade with Whites (Fisi 15/12/2018)
Egret of the Center’s daughter, Lady Counting (Otiaikn),181 became pregnant without ever having been
with a man. When she gave birth, a sound was heard. “Sister, what did you have?” Asked the brother.
“A dog (ḭño̰, the same word for “jaguar”) to serve as your companion (ɵ́ɵhɵ),” answered the sister. He
then heard another sound. “Sister, what did you have?”— “Axe-Liana (pɵtano̰, i.e., leash) to tie the dog,
so that it would not bite people.”182 Then, another sound. “Sister, what did you have?”—“[Metal] axe
(pɵɵ), a tool (bɨi’á) for you to work with.” [This sequence follows with the machete, knife, metal pot,
plate, cloth, needle, hook, and perfume]. Finally, she emitted some blood that coagulated on the ground
[the placenta], and she put it on the rooftop beam. People started talking: “Egret of the Center’s daughter
gave birth to the axe; I don’t know what an axe is, let’s go have a look!”183 Trader Egret of the River
Mouth (Okɒ́yo’fí Dohaɵ́hɵ) also came.184 He told the brother that he desired his sister and took her and
most of the goods that she had engendered to the river mouth; a smaller part of the goods remained at
the maloca. The axes that Egret of the River Mouth took were of metal, whereas those that remained at
the center, in Axe Hill (Pɵɵ Tuɒ́i) were of stone. The blood that the sister hid on the rooftop became the
[unidentified] small red jaguar bɵ’ɵdeisu, that followed his mother to the river mouth, where it still
terrorizes people. Next, Burner Egret of the River Source (Obaiyo’fí Duiɵ́hɵ) also arrived in search for
the daughter. When he was told that she had already gone with Trader Egret of the River Mouth, he got
mad of his horse and beat him, accusing him of losing her because the latter did not run fast enough.
After he left, the brother told his father: “I am going to my sister’s house to look for merchandise
(dohai).” He took his coca and tobacco paste and left. “Brother-in-law, what have you come for?” asked
him Trader Egret of the River Mouth.—“I have come looking for the axe.”—“well, here it is. What else
do you want?”—“I am looking for a needle, to sew my cloth for coca filtering; I am looking for a thread

two. “Good,” said Trader Egret of the River Mouth, “you have paid me (ɵpáhai, literally: “you have
realized my value”). Egret of the Center has made the offering (ɵyaɵtaséai) and paid him (oyapáhai).
Trader Egret of the River Mouth returned to his home and then came back to the center, bringing a harpy
eagle with him. He pulled out rubber (tekámn) from the eagle’s nostrils and stretched it. “With this you
need to pay (ɵpáhai) me,” he said. Egret of the Center thought about how he could obtain that material,
when his younger son said: “I saw something similar in the manioc garden, which also stretches like
that.” He took them to the garden, broke a manioc stick and showed them the sap. “This is rubber,”
Egret of the Center named this material. “This is how we are going to work from now on,” said Trader
Egret of the River Mouth, “this is how you are going to pay (ɵpáhai) me”. This is how the exchange
with the Whites started.
M6. Origin of the Swidden185
The first person to have had a garden was Sun (Ḭɒ̰). However, since he did not possess a metal axe, he
used fire and a stone axe to fell trees, leaving many thick trees standing in his garden. Sun would
command his daughter’s numerous suitors to cut down those trees using fire. As the suitors toiled with
their stone axes, the falling fruits would crush them, and Sun would devour them. Egret of the River
Mouth (Okɒ́yo’fí), also named Axe Egret (Pɵɵyo’fí) and Work Egret (Báőiyo’fí), also sought to marry
185

Source: Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 176–79.

555

Sun’s daughter. He came with his metal axe that operated by itself, but when Sun looked at the axe, it
ceased functioning. Hence, nowadays, we must attach a handle to the axe and hold it in our hands. After
Egret of the River Mouth built the house and thatched the roof, he was instructed by Sun to cut down
one of the remaining trees in the garden. Since Egret of the River Mouth did not sleep with Sun’s
daughter, she revealed her father’s trick to him and advised him to protect himself while working with a
light covering. Egret of the River Mouth followed her advice, and his life was spared when the fruits fell
on the covering and did not land on him. However, the trunk remained upright. Egret of the River Mouth
then commanded Marmoset (Cebuella pygmaea; ḭɒ̰dǵñḛ, “protection from Sun”) to climb and sever the
vine connecting the trunk to different points at the river mouth, river source, and other directions. He
then sent the horseflies to bite whoever held the vine at these points, forcing them to release it. The tree
then fell. There was a termite nest on the tree, and when Egret of the River Mouth went to bathe after his
success, Sun stumbled upon the nest and consumed it, mistakenly believing it to be his deceased son-inlaw. Upon returning to the tree, Egret of the River Mouth caught Sun in the act, “What are you doing?”
“Nothing,” replied Sun, “just looking around.”
M7. The Orphan Pipe Blower (José* 24/8/18)186
After their father Pa̰tonʉpa’s died, his five orphaned children lived with their mother, who kept
fertilizing a peach palm, in the hollow stump of which her lover (saámḭ), Earthworm, resided. The
children would hunt in the forest, where they befriended an iguana that became their pet. Upon their
afternoon return, they handed the game to their mother, who cooked it and prepared casabe. Despite
eating heartily, they remained thin. Puzzled by this, they asked Iguana to stay home and observe their
mother, which he did. He witnessed the mother reclining in her hammock, her earthworm lover
ascending it to copulate with her, and a palm petiole on the ground beneath the hammock collecting the
secreted fluids. After their lovemaking, the mother mixed these fluids with the dough for most of the
casabe cakes she baked but kept one cake untainted. She stacked the soiled casabe atop the clean one
and awaited her children’s return. They handed her the game and went to bathe, where Iguana recounted
what he had seen. At dinner, they told her, “Today, Pa̰tonʉpa’s sons want to eat from below!” and chose
the bottom cake, leaving the tainted ones for her. After eating they told her, “Tomorrow we will burn the
peach palm in the patio!” The mother protested, “Don’t burn it; this palm reminds me of your father.”
They defied her and burned the tree and the lover within. The mother took her pot of pí’na̰ [rotten
186

This myth is also found in Landaburu and Pineda 1984, 133–36.

556

manioc leaves] broth into the forest, spilling it around, thereby creating tamarin monkeys (sima̰de;
Saguinus fuscicollis). She scolded them, “You damage your father’s tree instead of hunting these
tamarins!” They pursued the tamarins with blowpipes (uipeɨkń), but each hit caused the tamarins to
multiply and elude them further into the forest, until they heard the yopakoɵ tinamou sing in the
afternoon, “For Pa̰tonʉpa’s sons the world has turned upside down” (Pa̰tonʉpa ɵɵ́tɵ síɵ́hɵ ma páa bɵ
nñó̰ḭ́ fɵsí yo̰pá’anni, literally: “For Pa̰tonʉpa’s sons, the world is in the new/unknown”).
Struggling to find their way, they wandered until they noticed a bright spot, like a clearing. They
cautioned each other, “Here there must be someone; an enemy.” Arriving, they discovered a large
maloca of a yo’fí [captain], with a tidy patio. They deliberated, “What should we do? They might eat
us!” “We’ll enter singing ‘We’re venom, we’re venom (yiknkn bɵ kḛn, yiknkn bɵ kḛn),” proposed one.
Though they entered singing and using their blowpipes as dance rods, the maloquero’s sons captured
and devoured four of them, while their sister concealed the fifth, the fairest one she desired, within her
vagina. Afterward, her brothers, counting the blowpipes, questioned, “There were five, yet we killed
only four; where is the fifth?” They searched everywhere and interrogated their sister, who deceived
them, “There were four men; one had two blowpipes!” They inspected her thoroughly, avoiding only the
one place on a sister’s body a brother would not look. As her brothers gave up, she escaped to the
garden, released the hunter, and coupled with him. In time, her belly swelled. Her brothers inquired,
“Sister, how are you pregnant without a husband?” “I impregnated myself,” she claimed. They persisted,
“Are you concealing your husband? Fear not, we won’t harm him; he’s our brother-in-law now. We just
want to meet him.” She introduced him then. These brothers were human by day but nocturnal monkeys
(hoósa; Aotus sp.) by night, dwelling in a hole in a tree trunk. Once, passing this tree, the hunter
mentioned his intent to shoot the monkeys. His wife, knowing these were her brothers, discouraged him,
but in vain. The next day, he climbed the tree and approached the monkeys, but as he reached for one, it
retreated into the trunk. He thrust his hand into the hole, and then his entire arm; he sensed the monkey
was near but could not catch it, so he stuck his head inside to get a better look at the prey, but then the
monkeys decapitated him. They perforated his skull, crafting from it a musical instrument that emitted a
deep “hoo… hoo…” sound—the sound this monkey makes. The wife, upon finding his body, replaced
his head with a yam tuber, attached another yam tuber to his body as a foot, and inserted a sugar cane
flower into his hindquarters as a tail, telling him, “Now go to the river source!” He did so, transforming
into a giant anteater (seiɵkn; Myrmecophaga tridactyla). She then gave birth to a boy, whom she bathed
and encouraged to sip water from every stream they encountered. At Speaking River, she had him sip
557

water to initiate speaking; at Sitting River, to begin sitting; at Crawling River, to start crawling; at
Standing River, to stand; at Walking River, to walk; and at Running River, to run. She continued this
process, visiting each stream named for a stage of a man’s development, until they reached Dancing Rod
River, where she had him sip water so he could dance in ceremonies. Only after this did she return home
with her son.
The boy used to join his mother in the garden, where he would make toy blowpipes from whatever he
found and shoot at insects. He asked his mother, “How come everyone has a father except for me?
Didn’t I have a father?” “Yes, you had a father,” she replied. “So what happened to him?” he continued.
“A jaguar ate him,” said the mother. The boy left to look for a jaguar in the woods and, upon finding
one, he approached it, but the jaguar did not eat him. He returned to his mother and said, “You lied; I
found a jaguar, but it did not eat me! What really happened to my father?” “He fell from a tree,” she
replied. The boy climbed a tall tree and jumped, but he did not die, so he returned to his mother with the
same question. She then told him his father had died from a snakebite. As this also proved harmless to
the boy, he ceased to believe his mother.
One day, the boy saw a fly approaching his grandfather, who was searching his testicles for sand fleas
(tʉ́’e; Tunga Sp.). The boy shot at the fly but missed, hitting his grandfather instead, who immediately
shouted, “You are just like your father!” The boy thus learned he indeed had a father, although he did
not know what had happened to him. Feeling sad, he sat on the patio and, seeing a bat fly by, hit it with
a cane, saying, “Don’t you dare mock me!” The bat responded, “Why do you hit me instead of pursuing
those who killed your father? If you heal me, I will tell you what happened to him.” The boy healed him
by attaching a tobacco leaf in place of the broken wing, and the bat revealed, “Your mother’s brothers
killed your father. They decapitated him and used his head to make the ‘hoo… hoo…’ sound. They hid
your father’s blowpipe in the roof ridge, the darts on one post, and the cotton for the darts in your
mother’s bosom. With these, you can kill them. There’s a buekn [unidentified] tree where your uncles go
to eat fruits; I eat there too. At night, when I see them, I will make the sound ‘chichichichichi…
chichichichichi…’ so you’ll know when to shoot; just be careful not to hit me.” The next day, the boy,
disregarding his mother’s warnings, climbed the roof ridge and found his father’s blowpipe; he found

558

the darts on a post and took the cotton and poison (yiknkn) from his mother’s bosom while pretending to
breastfeed;187 he was now armed with a real blowpipe and darts.
He went to the forest, located the buekn tree, and positioned himself on a branch of another tree, ready to
shoot at the right moment. Beforehand, he made an agreement with an ocelot, telling it, “I’ll be shooting
monkeys from up here; whatever falls to the ground is yours to eat.” The ocelot, eager for the feast,
agreed. As night fell, he waited for the bat’s signal. When he heard the “chichichichichi,” he aimed into
the darkness and shot, hitting his target, which fell to the ground. He continued this until dawn. Below
him, the ocelot was feasting on the bodies. Returning home and finding his uncles absent, he inquired of
his mother, who replied, “They went to the forest looking for salt [plants to make salt] to prepare your
earrings (hakóa).” He then offered to remove the sand fleas from his grandfather’s testicles, applying
achiote to the treated areas. That evening, he resumed his vigil in the forest, instructing the ocelot,
“Tonight, don’t eat the fallen body right away; let me inspect it first, then it’s yours.” Heeding the bat’s
call, he shot and, descending from his perch, discovered a monkey’s corpse with red-painted testicles
beneath the tree. Recognizing his grandfather, he resolved, “Now I have avenged my father.”188 With
that, he joined the ocelot, accompanying it to its dwelling among the stars.189
M8. False Egret and the Manguaré (Nestor and Fisi, 26/10/18; Fisi, 11/1/19)

his next resting spot, the blood drops gave birth to the si’pɨ ant. At the following resting spot, the tu’ko
ant arose from the blood drops. At the final resting spot, the kapada ant was formed in the same manner,

M10. The Orphans’ Flood (Fisi, 1/12/18; 12/7/21)
Tatoañei’s son, an earthworm, had sexual relations with Shadow Egg’s daughter. After she planted
peanuts in her garden, she discovered Hummingbird Egg (Pá̰di hádɨ) there and brought it home to
nurture and warm it. Hummingbird Egg made sounds that it was about to hatch, but the girl impatiently
pierced the egg with a thorn to see the bird inside. This is why Hummingbird Egg was born with one
blind eye. Nocturnal Curassow (Sábúdui; Nothocrax urumutum) used to taunt Hummingbird Egg by
singing, “Hummingbird Egg is one-eyed!” Hummingbird Egg was determined to find out who was
making fun of him, so he set traps for birds, forcing each one caught to sing its song. After a long search
[for the narration of which, the narrator imitates one after the other the songs of the different birds that
were trapped], one bird, Nocturnal Curassow, sang “Hummingbird Egg is one-eyed,” revealing that it
was he who had sung it all along. Hummingbird Egg broke his neck on the spot, Sı̰ ́di cooked him, and
the inhabitants of the Site of Tears ate him. Sı̰ ́di then ordered the two orphaned children (i’hɵ́ɵá síɵ́hɵ)
living at the Site of Tears to throw Nocturnal Curassow’s bone to the river and not to bite it.192 “But
there must be some more meat here,” said the younger brother to his elder, who initially refused to bite
the bone, but he eventually joined his stubborn brother in chewing on Nocturnal Curassow’s marrow.
However, even after the brothers passed the bone back and forth several times, they could not finish the
entire liquid. Eventually, they stuck the bone into the ground, and the marrow seeped into the earth,
becoming petrol. As it was boiling, the liquid burned the ground. Darkness fell. It was at this point that
the eagle dammed the river with its wings, and the inhabitants of the Site of Tears covered their maloca
with mud. Left outside when the water level rose, the two orphans found a seed of the tree to’nnkń

As orphans, they are the servants of the inhabitants of the Site of Tears, which was then still an above-ground maloca.

(Parkia multijuga), which was washed downriver from Egret Lake (Yo’finsí) near Hummingbird Hill
(Pá̰di Tuɒ́i, the hills of Angusturas canyon). One of them planted the seed between his toes, and it

From their vantage point, they saw Hummingbird Egg and Paternity Canoe going downriver in a canoe

extinguished theirs. Upon their arrival there, Hummingbird Egg approached Egret of the River Mouth’s
fireplace. When Egret of the River Mouth’s daughter saw him, she told her father: “What a beautiful
Hummingbird fledgling, I want to take care of him!” “No,” said her father, “he is not a fledgling, he’s
old.” The daughter insisted, putting Hummingbird Egg near the fire, to warm up, but the father knew
Hummingbird Egg’s real intention and closed the maloca’s door with a net. Once he was next to the fire,
Hummingbird Egg examined each ember to determine which one would not burn out, until he found the
right one and ran away, burning the net which covered the maloca’s door with that ember and breaking
free. When he returned to Site of Tears, Crestless Curassow (i’hayo; Mitu tomentosum) swallowed the
ember, leaving the inhabitants of the Site without fire again. But when Crestless Curassow defecated, the
excrement came out as the tetee stone for igniting fire.
Meanwhile, the orphans heard a sudden “to!” from the tree they were on, and a fruit fell toward the river
mouth, becoming the guan of dawn (pó’kn sói, literally, “guan of sight”; pipile pipile). Another “turu!”
sounded, and another fruit fell, this time toward the river source, becoming the bird kń’fɒ of dawn
(scientific name unidentified; regional Spanish: pava colorada). Then another fruit opened, its seeds fell
to the river, becoming the sardine toya of dawn; the fruit’s peel fell and hit the to’nnkń tree, becoming
the to’nnkńteákn bat. The tree was called to’nnkń because of “to,” the sound of the falling fruit to burst,
and nńkn, “day,” because these animals prefigured the dawn. The orphans saw the sun shining from the
east and realized that they would soon become human (hɵ́ihɵ́) again. Suddenly, their mother, who had
ascended to the sky when the flood began and taken the cultivars with her, dropped chili pepper on them

from above.194 “Our mother is feeding us,” said one orphan to the other, and they ate the food their

M11. The Multiplying Tree (Fisi, 2/1/19)
Pe’pai, a red anaconda and one of the Creator’s sons, entrenched himself underneath the Site of Tears
during the flood when it was still a maloca, traversing the maloca in the same way as the multiplying
beam traverses the maloca today. After the flood and the destruction of humanity, the orphans said to
each other: “Let’s multiply humanity again, let’s find Multiplying Anaconda (Tu’sí Hɵpɵ).” As the
waters receded, Cricket (kɵdɒ) sang to bring forth the reemergence of all that existed before the flood:
people, and all kinds of trees. As a result, the comino real tree (ma̰kapádɨ; unidentified), that had
previously also been an anaconda, grew anew, and Toucan (padase’hɵ) sat on top of it, guiding the
people, who were ants at that time, to the designated tree to fell. Cricket blessed the tree from below,
and the people felled it, carried it back home and crafted a multiplying beam from it. Upon the beam,
Green Tapir (Pa’si Ḭtɵ) and Green Earthworm (Pa’si Ḭtá) came to dance in an attempt to break it, but
Crestless Curassow (i’hayo) swallowed Green Earthworm, and so Green Tapir was unable to dance on
the beam and break it. To safeguard the beam, Crestless Curassow and Toucan danced upon it while
singing the first song of the Multiplying Tree Dance:
This is our cooled down seat (kau’ɵikupa)
Good seat (hóñóɒ kupa)
We have come here happy (hóño).

The people said: “We will multiply once again on this beam (natuɵ), we’ll multiply everything: people,
trees, food, water…” My father used to hold his Multiplying Tree dances with this story.

Iguana (kadɨ) used to wander all around and, because he shot the blowpipe, he was also called Pipe
Blower (U’ḭknñemn). In his wanderings during the dry season, Pipe Blower saw two women called ípɨ196
who were following the course of a drying water stream, catching small fish, crabs, and shrimps with a
sieve. He cast his blowpipe aside and entered the stream at a spot ahead of them, lying down under a big
leaf. When they reached that spot, the women caught an iguana in their sieve and bit its neck to check if
he was alive; despite the pain, Pipe Blower managed to play dead. The women took him and returned
home, elated to have found a larger catch than expected. As they approached the house where they lived
alone, Pipe Blower made them hear voices and the sound of pots boiling from inside. Fearing they
would have to share their catch, they hid the iguana nearby and went inside, planning to wait for the
supposed guests to leave. However, upon entering and finding the house empty, then returning to
discover their catch also gone, they realized it was Pipe Blower, who had transformed back into an
iguana and produced the sounds to escape. Determined to catch him, the next day they went searching
him and, recognizing him by the wound on his neck, confronted him. He pleaded, “Don’t eat me, I’m
human just like you,” and offered to fish for them. After catching many fish, he joined them at home for
the meal. To his surprise, he observed them defecating from their mouths, as they lacked anuses.197 He
then proposed creating anuses for them, an offer they eagerly accepted. Removing the dart from his
blowpipe, he instructed them to turn around and then pierced their behinds, thereby creating anuses and
simultaneously transforming them into collared peccaries.
In one house he arrived at, Pipe Blower found the three children of the bʉsé beetle, who were left alone
while their parents went hunting. Before leaving, the parents had instructed their children not to play
with fire and to beware of Pipe Blower, telling them to say, if he asked, that their parents were nearby
and about to return. “Where are your parents?” asked Pipe Blower. “They are working nearby,” one
child answered. “And what did they tell you before leaving?” he inquired. “Not to play with fire,” said
the youngest child. “Can you fart like me?” asked Pipe Blower and then farted. “No, our father does not
allow us to do that,” they replied. “Why?” Pipe Blower wondered. “Because farts would burn down the
house,” the youngest answered. “He was lying; look at me, I’m farting and nothing happens!” Pipe

their pots upriver but could not get any pí’na̰ on their meat. Suspecting Pipe Blower, they checked his

ran away with his blowpipe in hand. To enclose the area, the people planted “devil pineapple” (fi’dudi),

tinamou to carry him on its back and fly over it. The tinamou explained it could not fly long distances,
but Pipe Blower said he would invigorate it by spitting in its mouth. The tinamou then allowed Pipe
Blower to ride on its back, flying short distances before landing and continuing only after receiving Pipe

Pipe Blower is the one who fell down the manioc tree (máa̋dɵidɨtakn). In that era, manioc grew on that
tree as fruits, not as tubers, and it was the animals’ food. Lady Agouti (tɒɒkamikn; Dasyprocta sp.),
Lady Paca (ɵ́’ɵkamikn; Cuniculus paca), Lady Acouchi (si’ɵhɨkamikn; Myoprocta pratti), and Lady
Collared Peccary (sɵ’mékamikn; Dicotyles tajacu) used to pick the fruits and extract their starch that
could be used for the preparation of casabe cakes and caguana beverage on the same day. Pipe Blower
saw these women preparing manioc and accepted their offer to taste the casabe, but he immediately
became poisoned (yeḭyií). The manioc poison induced visions of future times when people would
receive manioc from the sky, growing as tubers underground, and would not be able to consume the
starch on the same day it was extracted, but only three days later. He also dreamed that manioc
preparation would become laborious, with men clearing forest plots for gardens and women toiling to
pull tubers and extract starch. In his vision, he saw all the instruments currently used for manioc work
[those not obtained from Whites or using their technology, like grating machines]. He then led the
people to cut down the manioc tree. The top of this enormous tree landed towards the river source, while
its roots pointed towards the river mouth, and its branches on the right and left fell in the directions of
the north and south banks of the Caquetá River, respectively. Different mushrooms formed on the trunk
of the fallen tree, which now provide starch for forest animals.
M14. Origin of Tobacco for Captaincy201
Paternity Canoe (O̰poipúkn; today it is the Heliornis fulica sungrebe; koé) was sent fishing with his wife
by his father-in-law, Shadow Egg. At night, while by the river, Paternity Canoe heard sighs: “Uh! ah!
ah!” coming from his father’s mambeadero, from where his father used to smoke fish. The following
morning, he found a small plant there and said, “So this is my father’s heritage! I’m going to live like
my father. I am going to have personnel like him!” Paternity Canoe blew on the plant. The People of the
Stars (fɵɵ’ko síɵ́hɵ) blew on the plant, blessing it for him, through the dew, so that it will not dry out in
the sun. The to̰’ḛdi nocturnal butterflies blew on it with their wings and fed on its flowers. Hummingbird
did the same. Paternity Canoe prepared ambíl and shared it with people. The latter said: “The captain of

M15. Origin of Tobacco for Healing (Fisi, 19/7/19)202
Paternity Canoe, whose late father used to smoke fish, lived with Sun’s daughter. One night he took her
fishing in his canoe. “What have you caught?”, she asked him upon catching the first fish. “Finger fish,”
he replied and threw it into the canoe, where she, sitting behind his back, ate it. Then he caught another.
“What have you caught?” she asked. “Arm fish,” he replied, and she ate it as well. She went on asking,
he went on naming body parts—foot, leg, stomach, head—and she went on eating the fish. In the
morning he turned back to look at her, but there remained only blood, as the fish anaconda had eaten her
members one by one during the night. He informed his father-in-law, who told him: “you must find my
daughter, otherwise I will eat you up! [hası̰ ́ di ɵnotii, literally: ‘I do Sı̰ ́di with you’].”203 Paternity Canoe
was thinking what to do when he heard a yell at the same place where his father used to smoke fish. He
thought, “that is my father’s shadow yelling.” He went there and found a tobacco plant budding, with
four leaves. “This is Shadow Tobacco (ká’hoi tá’u),” he said. He started fishing, until a kingfisher bird
passed by, saying “Che-che-che-che-che,” thus signaling where Cashew Apple-Anaconda (Kɒ̰́n̋nkn
Hɵpɵ) was found. He managed to catch the anaconda and dragged it to the riverbank. He cut the
anaconda’s belly open and took out his wife’s bones. By blowing tobacco smoke, he put the bones back
together, recreated the veins, the flash, the blood, gave her breath again, opened her eyes, made her
stand up, and gave her back to her father, alive.

ascended once more. When Egret of the Center, the trap’s owner, came to check his trap, he found the
fish missing and decided to conceal himself to ambush the thief. Upon the two ocelots’ return for new
prey, they removed their clothes [outward appearance; séa], placed them on the riverbank, and dived to

bees all said: “We will fly, our name shall be Flying Heap, we will build a home from our father’s
remnants; beside the peach palm lies our mother’s rotten leaf.” They amassed leaves and assorted debris
into a mound over the charred skull and took residence there, foraging for fruits and flowers to nourish
their offspring. They proliferated until their father’s spirit addressed them as humans do. Sı̰ ́di, another
bumblebee from above, spotted the bees and ascended to report. Consequently, Machichi, the jaguar
spirit who had sent the fish thieves, descended to earth. Wherever jaguar fangs are found, wherever
jaguar bones lie, Machichi’s song echoes, seeking vengeance for the deeds against his father.
M17. Sun and Pretty (Fisi 4/10/18)
Sun’s daughter had many suitors whom her father tested in different ways. He took his son-in-law Pretty
(Sɵ’oi) to look for plants to prepare vegetal salt. At night, after each one gathered salt plants, they lit
separate fires to burn them. While Sun was burning his plants, he saw that Pretty was lying down on the
ground to rest. “Go on, burn your salt!” shouted the father-in-law. “Fine,” replied the latter, but
remained on the ground. At midnight, Sun called him again, “Burn your salt!” “Yes, I am doing it right
away,” replied the son-in-law, and then piled the salt plants and laid next to them. The next time that
Sun called his son-in-law, the latter did not answer as he had fallen asleep, and at dawn when he would
still not reply, Sun approached him and saw that the atta ants had eaten his flesh, leaving only his bones
and head. “What happened, son-in-law?” asked Sun, and Pretty said: “Nothing, I will get up right away
and burn the salt.” When Sun returned to his maloca, he told his men—his daughter’s other suitors—that
his son-in-law would arrive in the afternoon, which he did; his head, which was all that remained of him,
bounced all the way back home. “Have you made salt?” asked him the father-in-law, and Pretty said that

567

he had, so the former went back to the forest and indeed found salt, that he could now mix with tobacco
paste. Sun informed his men: “Tomorrow we’re going to build a house together.” “But how will the
head carry the posts?” they wondered. The next day the head managed to carry them by inserting them
into the holes for earrings he had in his lobes and bouncing all the way back from the forest, doing
several such rounds. The other men goaded him to work faster; they ordered him to dig holes to plant the
posts in the ground, then scolded him by saying that the hole he dug was not deep enough. After he
jumped into that hole to deepen it, he realized what they were in fact plotting, so he started digging
horizontally, and when the other men threw sand in the hole to bury him alive, he was able to escape
through the horizontal tunnel he had created. While the others were sure that they had killed him, he
continued with his tunnel until he arrived at a water stream in which Sun’s daughter was catching small
fish and shrimps. Holding the girl’s feet, the head was swallowed by a fish, and after the latter was
caught by the girl, the head emerged from its stomach and settled on her shoulder. Whenever she tried to
eat, the head snatched her food and ate it, so she became thinner and thinner. As he was especially fond
of larvae, Sun’s men invited him to join them to a garden and dig out larvae from a palm tree. The more
larvae he ate, the more pain the girl felt all over her body, and at some point, while he was eating the
larvae that people were serving him, she managed to take the parasitic head off her shoulder, leave it
aside, and run away. The people were then able to carry out their plan of burning the garden with the
head trapped there. “Mother, come take me!” he cried while he was burning. Only his nasal bone did not
burn down, and transformed into an ocelot.
M18. The Peccary Head (Fisi, 1/11/18; 1/12/18)
Around Blazing Lake (Yadoinsí) a man organized a dance and invited his brothers-in-law. On a hunting
expedition the guests caught an entire white-lipped peccary herd with a big net and killed them to bring
the meat to the dance. Camping in the forest for the night, they disemboweled the peccaries, smoked the
large amount of meat on a wooden grill, and left aside a cut-off peccary head.206 One of the men
preferred to eat an undulated tinamou (foí; Crypturellus undulatus) instead of peccary and left at dusk to
look for one. At some distance from the camp, he saw an old man called Ka’ákɵpidɨ taking out his own
eyes and using them, instead of strips of fiber, to weave a basket.207 Back at the camp, his fellow hunters

M20. The Seductive Deer (Raquel, 6/7/19)
Shadow Egg’s daughter, Hummingbird (Pá̰di), ignored her father’s warnings and recklessly left the
skins of manioc tubers overnight in her basket instead of disposing of them properly. One day, a
beautiful young man with painted face and body appeared in her garden. This man, called Yellow
Achiote Deer (Doékositoɵ),211 promised to take her and her younger sister to collect larvae from a
mauritia palm the next day. Excited, the girl skipped supper that evening and hid the casabe she made in
the pile of manioc skins in her basket so she could take it with her on the excursion. The next day,
despite her younger sister’s suspicions, she convinced her to join the excursion. At the palm, the man
felled the tree with an axe and served them the larvae he dug out to eat with their casabe, while he
himself refrained from eating. He left his axe on top of a hole in the ground leading to his underground
home to rest and noted the younger sister’s distrust of him. When the latter expressed her desire to eat
mauritia fruits from another tree he encouraged her to climb the tree herself since he could not do so. As
she found a position allowing her to cut off the mauritia bunch, he seized the elder sister and took her to
his home under the earth, whereupon the palm on which the other sister was sitting rose to the sky.
When he arrived home, he sealed the girl in a clay pot which he named “fire pot, illness [transformation]
pot” (ɵɵpadɵ, tidɵ), and left to search for firewood. His mother, who smelled a human being, found the
girl giggling inside the pot, and advised her to flee, saying that her son was not a human being but a
fi’du. The girl ran away while the mother put manioc dough in the pot to deceive her son. When the
man-deer returned, he cooked the pot and discovered his mother’s trick. He went looking for the girl,
who found shelter in Acouchi’s (si’ɵhɨ; Myoprocta pratti) hole in a tree trunk, under Anaconda’s (hɵpɵ)
“protected chest” (mánó̰ḛḭ-tutann), and under Kingfisher’s (sede; Chloroceryle amazona) “protected
wing” (mánó̰ḛḭ-púsékɵ) while he was diving in the water. The deer visited all of them one after the other
looking for his game (yasía), until the girl finally returned to her father. Meanwhile, the younger sister
was weak, hungry, and sick on top of the palm, and Red-Rumped Cacique (pʉdokɒ’ti; the Cacicus

M21. The Pineapple-Loving Tapir (Fisi, 8/12/18)
Dance Rod Painting used to damage his daughter-in-law’s garden by stomping her pineapple plants and
half-eating them, along with other fruits. The woman was sure that the intruder was a tapir, and
whenever she ate the bitten fruits she found in the garden, she suffered from different aches. The woman
asked her husband to catch the tapir, and his father recommended that he make a trap in the form of a
hole covered with leaves212 and leave a caguana from the heart of a wood, casabe, mambe, and tobacco
paste for the tapir in the mambeadero before going to sleep, which the husband did. To prepare the
particular caguana, the man poured a manioc caguana into a hole in a tree and waited for bees to enter
that hole and make honey, which he then gathered. When everyone was asleep, the father-in-law
consumed the caguana, casabe, mambe, and tobacco paste, went to the garden and fell into the trap. The
next morning, the husband checked the trap and found his father trapped inside. While on all fours, his
father ordered his son to fetch his mambe pouch, loincloth, and headdress from his hammock. When the
father put the coca pouch to his mouth, it became the tapir’s snout; when he put on the headdress, it
became the tapir’s shoulder humps, and the loincloth became the tapir’s inflated testicles when he wore
it. The husband then killed the tapir and left the game to his brothers-in-law from the river source.
M22. The Origin of Dolphins213
Green Tapir (Pa’si Ḭtɵ), who lived at the maloca of his father-in-law along the Green River (Pa’sise),
was preparing a ceremonial dance, when his sister, White Frog (Pɒyɒyɒ) told him that his wife, Lady
Peccary (Ḭńkn), sleeps with her own brother, Pretty (Sɵ’oi). Leaving his people to continue with the
dance preparation, Green Tapir set off to see his brother Tofidei,214 asking him for achiote for the dance.
After warning him that applying achiote is not a game, the brother gave him what he wanted. On his
way back home, Green Tapir prepared a spear by cutting a tree. Upon his return to his father-in-law’s

M23. Tofidei’s War (Nestor and Fisi, 14/8/18)215
Tofidei’s wife, Lady Cacambra (Kaókamikn; Daptridus ater), had a lover from the river mouth, a
dolphin-anaconda (ama̰na hɵpɵ) called Clearing flower (Pó’knñetaikn).216 Every day, after digging up
manioc tubers and peeling them in her garden, she used to go sit by the riverbank to wash them, where
she tapped on her gourd vessel to call the lover. The latter would then wrap himself around her leg,
climb upwards to have sex with her, and then return downriver. Consumed by desire for her lover, she
neglected her husband and no longer fed her pet (éna̰) parrot (kɒ́’i) with purple yam (Dioscorea alata).
When Tofidei was cooking the red kodi paint, the parrot approached the fireplace, cried of hunger, and
by stepping the firewood, he caused the paint to spill from the pot. Annoyed with the pet, Tofidei hit
him, and the latter told him: “You are angry at me, but you don’t know what your wife is doing! She no
longer cares for you because of her lover! Instead of me, you should hit him!” Tofidei then roasted a
yam for the parrot, who told him how his wife goes to the riverbank every day and calls her lover by
tapping on her gourd vessel. Tofidei then asked his brother-in-law Kingfisher (kokn sede; Chloroceryle
amazona) to help him catch the lover. The following day, after the woman went to the garden, Tofidei
went to the riverbank and tapped on the gourd like the parrot had instructed him. When the two dolphinanacondas, Tree Anaconda (Kń’ńdɨ Hɵpɵ) and Green/Blue Anaconda (Paseta Hɵpɵ),217 emerged from
Nestor was the main narrator, with his father Fisi occasionally commenting or correcting him.
Pó’kn: “dawn,” “clearing,” alluding to the clear view one enjoys by the river, contrary to the blocked sight within the
forest. As we will see below, these are two dolphins-anacondas.

war, and they all started upriver to take revenge of Tofidei. The anacondas, stingrays, caimans, and all
other aggressive fish advanced by water, coming in big boats; by land came the trees, that were still
anaconda people, and by air came the cranes káfɵ (Jabiru mycteria). Tofidei’s people, who were fewer
in numbers, were afraid of the enemies, asking their captain to flee: “They are about to finish us!”

between the legs!”219 Tofidei prepared a spear (fɨ’ɵfá), painted it with black poison for hunting and kodi
paint, and went to the maloca’s patio, telling his men not to look when he raised it. When he erected his
spear and shouted “Hʉhʉhʉ”, the approaching enemies became trees and stones, and the boats became
the islands along the Caquetá River. Only the cranes were not transformed. Some of his own men
watching him in this operation were also petrified and can still be seen as stones in Parrot Savanna. This
is how Tofidei managed to defend against his enemies.
M24. Toucan and Lady Sloth (Mario, 9/4/19)
Toucan (Padase’hɵ; the bird Ramphastos tucanus is called se’hɵ) was handsome and the two women,
Lady Rat (Po̰’ḭ́ kamikn; it is the nocturnal rat: po̰’ḭ́ [Holochilus sciureus?]) and Lady Sloth
(Keñeknkamikn; it is hoffman’s two-toed sloth: keñekn [Choloepus hoffmanni]), who was then called
Lady Arrogance (Okɵikamikn), fell for him and became his wives. Toucan used to lounge in his
hammock, serene with his eyes closed, next to the fireplace. Lady Rat would fan the fire to stoke it, each

stage she is given the name Lady Cacambra.

time spreading more ashes towards him. Over time, he became completely covered in ashes, turning
entirely grey. Eventually, he became infested with lice. While Lady Rat continued to love her husband
and prepared food for him, Lady Arrogance lost her desire for this now lazy, aged, and unattractive man.
Yet, she remained living with him, paying him little mind.
When everyone except Toucan was invited to a ceremonial dance at another maloca, Lady Arrogance
prepared herself to attend. “And your husband?” the people asked. “Why should I care about this
infested old man?” she responded. “But he’ll be upset with you!” they cautioned. Undeterred, she said,
“Tomorrow, we’re going to dance!” Lying down in his hammock, Toucan overheard her.
The next day, as the people prepared to depart, Lady Arrogance adorned herself with genipa, donned a
wreath, packed her hammock, and joined them. Watching her leave from his hammock, Toucan thought:
“Let her go! She does not know who I am!” Lady Rat inquired: “Should we join them?” “We’ll head
there shortly. No need to rush. I’ll gather some larvae to bring to the dance, prepare genipa for painting,
take my flute, and we’ll be off,” He replied. “But by then the sun will rise [ending the dance],” she
observed. “Let it rise,” he replied nonchalantly, leisurely preparing for the dance. He even decorated his
flute with chambira leaves and red paint. While Toucan was preparing to leave, his fellow Lizard arrived
and proposed they go together. “Alright,” said Toucan, “but first, paint me with this yellow clay.” Lizard
painted his own nose and Toucan’s, which is why the beak of today’s toucan has a yellow section on
top. “Now we can go!” said Toucan, who suddenly looked young, pretty, and lively. Lady Rat thought:
“How did he rejuvenate like that? He’s no ordinary man! He might do something to me [bewitch me], I
should stay by his side!”
They headed to the dance, and as they neared the maloca, Toucan suggested they announce their arrival
by playing the cricket’s song on their flutes. The attendees wondered aloud, “Who’s approaching?
Everyone’s already here. It must be the Toucan.” They then saw the two handsome young men with
their spouses arriving at the patio. The participants murmured, “Who’s that young man? It can’t be
Toucan!” From her spot near a maloca post, Lady Arrogance was taken aback. She was captivated by
this beautiful young man and told them: “This cannot be my husband. My husband is old and grey, full
of lice, how can this be him?” As Toucan sang and danced in the patio, Lady Arrogance could not take
her eyes off him. “But this is your husband!” The women told her, but she insisted he was someone else.
When Toucan and Lizard entered the maloca, singing and dancing, the maloquera joined them, gave
them manicuera and took their game [the larvae].

574

Lady Arrogance, from her spot near a maloca post, watched these dancers, and when the maloquera left
them, she got up to join the young man she was now in love with. Toucan hopped and leaped while
dancing, and she hopped and leaped with him, circling the maloca many times. When that dance ended
and the young dancers exited the maloca, Lady Arrogance waited at the entrance for the dancer’s return.
The other women whispered to each other, “This woman is silly, falling in love [nḭmá yahɵ́ñoi] with her
husband!” “I am going with this youth,” she told the others, “I am going to live with him!” “But that’s
your husband,” they reminded her, but she insisted: “How can it be my husband!” After he returned, she
spent the night dancing and talking with him. She slipped a piece of vegetal salt that she had previously
received from the organizers into his flute. He told himself: “This will happen to the man whose wife
dislikes him: she will eventually fall in love with him, mistaking him for another. And the wife who
likes him will never suffer.” “I want to live with you, do not forsake me, I don’t want to live with my
husband, I only want to live with you!” she told him. He thought to himself, “How can she think I’m
another man? I’m her husband—the one she despises.” As the dance was ending, Toucan asked his
brother-in-law, cricket sḭ’sḭ, to tangle the ropes of Lady Arrogance’s hammock to delay her after the
dance. The cricket obliged.
After the dance, Toucan bid farewell and left. Lady Arrogance hurried to untangle her hammock and
follow, but the knots delayed her. By the time she got home, Toucan was already lounging in his
hammock, old-looking and ugly as before. When she saw him, she went back to ignoring him. “How
was the dance?” he asked. “It was good,” she answered shortly. “But go on, tell me something… What
did they give you? Usually one does not return empty ended from a dance; they must have given you
something!” “No, I wasn’t given anything,” she answered. “Not even tobacco or salt? Well, then it
wasn’t a dance you went to! And why do you look so sad?” he asked, but she did not reply. “But I was
there,” he suddenly said to her, “Don’t you remember seeing me? Don’t you remember dancing with
me? Don’t you remember telling you wanted to live with me? Don’t you remember giving me this piece
of salt?” He showed her the piece she had given him. Silenced, she wondered how he had shed his old
looks and ugliness to appear as a handsome young man.
Toucan began to ignore Lady Arrogance, but the latter was again in love with him again. She watched
sorrowfully as he spoke and slept only with Lady Rat. Toucan wanted to get back at Lady Arrogance:
“She called me old and ugly, now I am going to turn her all grey-haired and wrinkled!” He went looking
for the chambira póñḛ́ḭ, whose leaves resemble long hairs. On returning to the maloca, he suggested to

575

Lady Arrogance that they bathe together, an offer she happily accepted. When they reached the small
water stream, he encouraged her to bathe first, and she agreed. She dived into the water, and while she
was submerged, he turned to a nearby short tree trunk, transforming it into her body by naming it as
such, and then attaching the chambira leaves to the top of the trunk. Uttering a spell to name the
chambira leaves after his wife’s hair, he proclaimed: “Just as white as these leaves, so too will her hair
turn white!” When Lady Arrogance resurfaced, her hair turned stark white, making her appear old. “You
were so arrogant, and now no one will desire you!” He declared. She remained this way—grey-haired,
ugly, and old. Though she still loved her husband, he no longer cared for her, and shared his hammock
only with her co-wife. Ashamed, she climbed the maloca’s posts, settling on the upper beams. With her
hands and legs tightly gripping them, she slowly made her way to the other side. Once there, she used
the ropes to descend towards her husband’s hammock. But as she reached him, Toucan grabbed her and
cast her out of the house. She landed on all fours and slowly walked away, fully transformed into a sloth.
Upset with her husband’s actions, she declared that from then on, only young men who have not yet
known a woman would be able to see her.
M25. Origin of the Carrier Band (Nestor and Fisi, 14/8/18)220
When summer arrived, Stingray (ñḛbánńéi hɵpɵ; Potamotrygonidae sp.) found itself trapped in a drying
puddle, crying for help. Woodpecker (ko’ói), felling trees nearby to clear a garden, heard the cries and
approached. While he initially feared that Stingray might eat him, the latter asked for his assistance,
requesting him to prepare a carrier band from a tree bark and carry him to its home in Blazing Lake
(Yadoinsí). Stingray promised not to eat Woodpecker as long as the latter ties the former to his back,
ensuring that Stingray’s mouth was not facing Woodpecker. After carefully weighing the risks,
Woodpecker fashioned a carrier from the bark of the bɵɵ (unidentified) tree but could only carry
Stingray a short distance before the carrier tore, causing Stingray to fall. In response, Stingray cursed
this tree, so that it would not live long. For this reason, this tree now dies shortly after bearing fruits.
Woodpecker then elaborated a carrier from the sénnkń (unidentified) tree,221 but it also tore after a short
distance, and was likewise cursed by Stingray. Subsequently, Woodpecker crafted a carrier from the
bark of the bɨsokń tree, with which he successfully transported Stingray all the way to Blazing Lake. As

Nestor was the main narrator, with Fisi correcting and commenting on his version. See also Landaburu and Pineda 1984,
184–88.

a result, Stingray blessed this tree: “This tree will never perish, whenever its bark is cut or peeled, it will
heal and regrow.”
M26. Origin of the Manguaré Drum222
The ocelots of the stars heard Pineapple’s (Tomirepa) son playing his flute and coveted it. When the son
went for a bath and asked his mother to keep his toy, the star ocelots descended to earth, disguising
themselves as the son and tricking the mother into giving them the flute. When the real son returned
from his bath and asked the flute from his mother, they realized it had been stolen. Pineapple paid close
attention to where its tunes now emanated from until he heard it from the sky above. Pineapple and his
men tried to shoot arrows to the stars but could not hit them. The sick Péífirú offered his help, which
everyone initially refused, because of his poor physical condition.223 However, using special spells,
Péífirú managed to have one arrow stick to Nénéfi’s maloca in the sky, and then created a bridge with a
stick reaching up to that maloca, and climbed there224 along with his two brothers-in-law, Sardine Ant
and Perfume Ant (toyaséa and tɵrɵko, respectively). Péífirú instructed them to search the maloca for the
flute while he engaged in conversation with Nénéfi, biting him when they found it. When he met with
Nénéfi, Péífirú said, “I have come to search my son’s toy.” Nénéfi initially denied having the flute. After
Péífirú’s brothers-in-law found it, they indicated its location to him using their agreed sign, and Péífirú
demonstrated to his host that he knew where it was. Nénéfi was impressed by his guest’s wisdom.
Admitting he indeed possessed the flute, he told Péífirú that his own son cherishes it dearly. Instead of
giving it back, Nénéfi offered Péífirú his son’s toy, which would help Péífirú’s group recover and
increase in numbers after the eagle had almost exterminated it. Péífirú agreed, and Nénéfi gave him the
manguaré, along with achiote and the herb popáisako to ensure that, upon playing the manguaré, his
men would transform into human beings. Péífirú’s brothers-in-law tried to descend the manguaré
through the stick bridge, but it fell and broke upon Earth. Its pieces transformed into the tinamou pǵtotó,

manguaré that emits sounds at night (hɵ́pɵɵ́ ku’dɨ). Nénéfi then provided Péífirú with another manguaré,
this time sending his own men as carriers—the birds tɒ́kɒ́ and boetadi and the butterflies dɨdʉpa, which

Appendix 2. Conversations and Tales
C1. Conversation on the rubber genocide and on Dóñékɒi (Fisi, Nestor, and Eliran 19/1/19)
Fisi: In the Time of Peru, Pei invited Dóñékɒi to a dance in the Savanna. Pei was a Muinane captain of
the Chambira Clan. He organized a dance in the Cahuinarí, in the Savanna, and invited Dóñékɒi. During
the dance, people said, he wanted to kill him. He and several other captains wanted to fight him. Usenai
from the Bora’s Tree Clan—Usenai means “Cold Leaf”—and a few others… The Tanager Clan, the
Beetle Clan, the Agouti Clan, and some Eagles [groups of the Eagle Clan], these were Dóñékɒi’s
people, they went with him to the dance. They wanted to kill them as well. But the Muinane of the
Worm and Agouti Clans, and the Umukutui, they were on Dóñékɒi’s side. When Dóñékɒi’s people
arrived, they took their weapons and put them in a big stack there, on the side [of the maloca]. Before,
when they were on their way, some people [from that maloca] went toward him and warned him, they
said what Pei was planning, that they would kill them all… Dóñékɒi arrived only with his revolver. At
that time, he also had a rifle and a carbine [carabina rifle], but he only went with that revolver, and with
Tofidei’s colors, he was painted with achiote like Tofidei [see M23], he said: “I am going there [and I
won’t back down]. I am going to dance with my rod.” Oh, and he also brought his thunder stone, yó’őnn.
He raised it when he arrived, right at the center [of the maloca’s patio?], he extended his arm like this
[Fisi imitates the gesture] and raised his yó’őnn, and it started raining in heavy drops. Usenai told his
sons: “Wait, do not to do anything.” They were sitting inside the maloca when Dóñékɒi entered it. He
entered singing, first he sang with his rod at the entrance, then he entered. He sang: “That the people of
Egret of the Center move to one side, get closer to the maloca.”
Eliran: What is this song?
Fisi: It’s a is a formula (oración) from the story of the Speaking Tree, when Egret of the Center stood in
the middle and his allies gathered around him. This is what Dóñékɒi did. He entered and took away their
power (les quitó el poder). Usenai told him, “There, we were going to kill you. But we couldn’t.”
[Instead] they consumed mambe, they spoke. At midnight he went to the center of the maloca, stood
there, and called all the captains to collect their weapon. At something like five in the morning Dóñékɒi
shot at a peach palm in the patio, the tree split in two, and people went to gather fruits, and they went
home. Dóñékɒi’s people fired shots into the air and left, while Pei stayed by himself, eager to fight.
Nestor: And how did everyone come to have weapons?

579

Fisi: [They received them] from the Peruvians. They gave weapons to all the groups, and to the captains
they gave a revolver, a rifle, and a carbine. That was during the time when Dóñékɒi still used to fight,
afterwards he set aside his weapon to become a cacique and organize dances. And Dóñékɒi’s father gave
Yobidi Kadanni, Yinñéfɵkn’s father, the power to fight when they [Dóñékɒi and Yinñéfɵkn] were still
children.
[…]
Fisi: The problem [that caused the genocide] was that in that period [of the Casa Arana] no captain knew
the origin (principio) of exchange with Whites, of the axe. Any sorcerer [who lived] around, I don’t
know [who], Whites arrived [to his maloca], and [if] he didn’t like them, there could happen whatever,
there could be a fight. So the Whites were angry.
Nestor: The Peruvians were angry, but it was other peoples’ fault. We were the last ones they got to.
Fisi: The Andoque was the last group that the Peruvians got to, they never arrived at the center.
Everything started when they sent some priests and nuns from La Chorrera to evangelize the Andoque,
and on their way here people killed them and raped one of the nuns, who managed to run back to La
Chorrera and tell what had happened. But those priests never arrived here. Maybe it was the People of
Ara or Toad or Opossum [Andoque clans] who killed them, who knows? The Peruvians were angry,
many people came looking for the killers, and everyone told them, ‘The Andoque, the Andoque [killed
them], [they live] there!” So they got here angry. They took the clan captains, made a pillory, put
Dóñékɒi, Foki-Foki [Yinñéfɵkn], in the pillory… When he [Dóñékɒi] was there they raped his wife,
Paifokn, they passed a stake through her vagina and this way they killed here. Then they killed his
father, Padamnta, they burned him. Foki-Foki saw everything. They burned many people, they chopped
them. They took many people, like [the number of people that can fill the distance] from here [the
maloca] to the Caquetá, people said, in two rows… to Matanzas. And they sent people to work, to bring
rubber.
Eliran: Why did they keep Dóñékɒi and Yinñéfɵkn in the pillory instead of killing them like they did to
the others?
Fisi: They put the captains in the pillory, and Dóñékɒi was a captain, he learned from his father about
the War of the Speaking Tree, [about] everything…
Nestor: And Jimmy Fuke [Yinñéfɵkn, who was not a captain]?

580

Fisi: He was young… They put many people in the pillory, and many people died. Dóñékɒi didn’t die.
He told Yinñéfɵkn, “You need to be a man, don’t cry! Nothing will happen to us, we will be fed from
the sky.” Then, I don’t know how, Popa, a woman gave them some water, she managed to secretly pour
them some water in the mouths, she managed to slip in their mouths a little bit of coca, a little bit of
ambíl…
Nestor: There was a family that they [the Peruvians] took as servants, and that woman passed by there
and gave them coca and ambíl, it gave him [Dóñékɒi] force to ask help from the Creator. And with that
coca they survived at the pillory. Many elders died there of hunger, but he sustained himself for a long
time, for months, with that casabe that fell on them from the sky, that we told you about the other day
[“The Orphans’ Flood”, M10 in Appendix 1]...
Fisi: [The casabe] of the Orphans!
Nestor: And they sent people to make a big garden, somewhere around here… to plant manioc, corn,
rice, sugar cane. And they would make alcohol from the sugar cane, and that Normand used to get
drunk, and that made the disorder all the bigger. In that big garden he forced women to work, and those
who wouldn’t work, he sent them to cut firewood, there was a large of pile of firewood… And those
who wouldn’t work, he roasted them on the fire and gave them to his dog as food, he had a dog that
loved to eat roasted people. And the women who worked in the garden, who had a child, because the
mother did not have time to feed the child, he cried, so they took and pum! [makes the sign of thrashing
the child against something].
Fisi: They held it by its feet, cut off its head, and threw it to the fire.
Nestor: And the dog ate it.
Fisi: If the mother cried, they would also throw her into the fire.
Nestor: That was at the garden. And they drank and killed the paisanos (Indigenous people). But then
arrived the investigation, to check if it was true that they killed them. They pricked my father’s
grandfather’s [Dóñékɒi] hand and drew blood, and saw that, “No, this man did not kill anyone.” So they
released him from the pillory, him and Yinñéfɵkn.
Eliran: What do you mean, how could they check that?
Fisi: We don’t know, but people said that they pricked people’s fingers and then squeezed the finger and
it bled on a piece of something like a mirror, people said, and then they said [to one man], “You killed,”
581

[and said to another] “You didn’t kill,” [they said to a third man] “You killed,” [and to a fourth] “You
didn’t kill.”
Eliran: And they found the ones who had killed the priests?
Nestor: Yes, and they killed them on the spot.
Fisi: These were the people that they burned. This is when people fled to the forest. And they sent
people to search them, to kill them and to bring only their fingers, of the right hand.
Nestor: And the captains that they released, they sent them to work rubber with their clans. Each clan
needed to work with its captain. It was then that the goods (mercancía) entered. It first entered through
the Muinane’s territory, to the Pineapple Clan, and after the captain of the Pineapple Clan, it entered the
Andoque [territory].
Fisi: The goods entered where the Andoque [lived] twice, people said, and I don’t know how many
times they went to leave rubber at La Chorrera, by land, and there they would also be killed.
Nestor: When people went to look for goods at the Muinane’s territory, Opossum Clan, Ara Clan, Toad
Clan, and Yarumo Clan are the ones who went.
Fisi: Only at the end, they arrived at Yobidi Káda̋nni [Yinñéfɵkn’s father, at his maloca].
Nestor: And the more the goods entered the Andoque territory, the more the goods were distributed
among the captains. So they made the captains commit to collect rubber to pay for the goods, axe,
machete, clothes, all the things. And because there were some Indigenous that received the goods but
did not work, as it always happens, then the captain remained indebted, because they accepted the goods
and ran away. Then it came to pass that they forced the captains to work to pay the debts. So by then it
was the people’s fault that the captains were punished, they needed to look for their own people, to make
them work.
Fisi: It was then that they gave them carbines.
Nestor: They gave them carbines to make the people work. And the more [rubber] they gathered, the
more they [the Casa Arana agents] wanted. And people say that initially they got a lot [of rubber], but
then as they cut the trees with machete more and more—because they used machete, not scraper
(rasqueta) like today [in more recent rubber work periods]—so the trees didn’t yield any more rubber,
they yielded just a little bit. And they [the company agents] wanted more, but the trees didn’t yield

582

anything, so people ran away. And they sent the Indigenous like soldiers, to catch those who had ran
away.
Eliran: And it never happened that people refused the goods?
Nestor: No, because of people’s needs (necesidades) no one refused it. And then people became
indebted, and this made them kill more Indigenous, because I think that the Arana, they were also
indebted to their bosses. But there was no longer any rubber. Throughout the territory, around La
Chorrera… the trees didn’t yield, didn’t yield, or very little. So they killed them, they even forced the
captains themselves to search them and kill them. And Arana contracted many people who would look
for others. He contracted the Andoque to search the Uitoto, and the Uitoto to search the Andoque. And
this way he instigated war among the paisanos themselves. And they gave them rifles, and everyone
were armed. After a long time… Oh and another way for them to torture people, that was for girls, they

killed them. This way we were exterminated. Until Miguel Zumaeta arrived. He was the one who pulled
out…
Fisi: He pulled out Normand.
Nestor: And people said that Normand had spoken Andoque perfectly.
Fisi: He spoke, he sang… Zumaeta arrived during an Andoque dance, and Normand was hiding among

[Zumaeta] arrested him.
Eliran: But why did Zumaeta arrest Normand?
Nestor: Because there was a commission that investigated and discovered that Normand was killing the
Indigenous, and it was already during the war with Peru, so the army arrived to pull him out.
Fisi: And Miguel Zumaeta was a soldier.
Nestor: He was a soldier, he was the commander of a unit that came to arrest Normand. From all around,
many [Peruvian] soldiers entered Colombia.
Eliran: So Zumaeta did not come here first for rubber; he came here as a soldier?

T4. The Adventures of the Piercers (Yɒ’nnkn; Raquel, 9/7/19)
The Piercers lived in Ádukoe (“Abode [?] of Red Macaw”), which is today the hill of Araracuara. But it
was already known by then that we, the real human beings, would be formed and replace the Piercers as
humanity. The Piercers spoke our language, but not very well. Instead of saying “him” (yika), they said
“her” (nḭka). When one said “I,” he would say ñemḭno̰ [using the feminine form instead of the masculine
one]. Their captain, Ádukoe, held a Carrier Band Dance to check if they could save themselves and
continue living like humans. “You have to sing,” he told them. The Piercers were stubborn and crazy,
they did everything wrong. During the caguana distribution ceremony, he ordered each to sing. The first
sang, but in Miraña and not in Andoque, “The tapir and agouti finished my manioc.” The second also
sang in Miraña, “In the mouth of this river, there is a pintadillo fish; we are going to shoot it with an
arrow.” But Ádukoe said, “No, this does not hold any sense of salvation. You try now,” he turned to his
brother-in-law. The latter raised and sang, “The manioc of our mother is our manioc of multiplying
people,” and Ádukoe’s cultivars cheered to express their joy—this is why he was spared. When the sun
rose, Ádukoe told the Piercers: “Today, [in the Carrier Dance], we must sing well.” He instructed them
to make dancing rods with stripes of the bɨsokn tree bark, but they could not use it properly—when they
approached the maloca, hitting the ground with their rods, they hit them on the pointed side [instead of
the flat one]. They sang in Andoque but added Miraña words, and Ádukoe expressed disapproval of
their songs. He told them, “Let’s give names, you need to give yourselves names, but do it well! After
all of you, I will also give myself a name.” One of them raised and declared, “As part of my clan, my
name is ‘She roasted an iguana with her sister-in-law.’” They said such nonsense, that Ádukoe said,
“No, not like that! Name yourselves well!” Another raised and declared, “As part of my clan, my name
is ‘My loincloth covers my loin.’” Ádukoe likewise disapproved of this naming, ordering a third Piercer
to raise and give himself a name, but the latter said, “According to my origin, I will call myself ‘Fallen
Shit.’” They were all crazy, didn’t I tell you? [Raquel is laughing]. Ádukoe said, “No, there is no
salvation here. Now will sing Egret Bone [Yo’fitann], but you must not go outside and look at him while
he sings; those looking will turn into animals. Only the ones who do not look will remain here with me.”

588

Egret Bone sang outside the maloca, in a song that sounded like a long whistle that reached to the sky.
Most of the Piercers could not resist the temptation to leave the maloca and behold the singer, thus
transformed into peccaries, tapirs, and other animals. Apart from Ádukoe, his brother-in-law, and his
wife Kasétañékn (“A Custom [Typical Event] of Our River [Caquetá]”), who were “enchanted” (se
encantaron) and keep living in an invisible mode in Araracuara, only three other Piercers survived—two
brothers and their sister.
These three survivors escaped by entering into the earth and then flying in the air until they reached La
Pedrera. But there they also heard Bone Egret singing, so they returned upriver, reaching the mouth of
the Hḭ’ḭse (Drawing River), where they killed an anaconda which was well painted—this is why they
named the river this way. They gave names to all the streams between the Hḭ’ḭse and the Áduse. At the
mouth of the Áduse, they saw a bird on top of a tall tree. “What is it?” asked one of them. “It is a red
macaw (ádu),” replied another, and so they named the stream Macaw River (Áduse). They followed
Macaw River till Tar Waterfall, where they made offerings, consumed them, and fought anacondas,
stingrays, and all other dangerous creatures that can endanger human beings. They continued to the
waterfall called Basketful of Entrails (Ḭñéfɵ́’piɵ), where the sister menstruated, but full of shame, she
kept preparing food for them, instead of abstaining from it due to her state. After the two brothers ate her
food, they dived into the water in a bid to fight monsters, but her menstruation had already cut down
their sorcery powers, and they lost the fight against the “scissor fish” (pǵ’ǵdɨ; unidentified) further
upstream. The scissor fish cut them by half, and so their lungs and entrails were carried downstream to
Scissor Fish, Lungs, and Basketful of Entrails Waterfalls (P¦́’¦́dɨfisia, Pe’sɒfisia, and Ḭñéfɵ́’piɵ,
respectively). This is how the Piercers ended, although others say that they continue living in other
forms, within the water; but I know that they ended like this, this is how Yinñéfɵkn told it to me.
